Maybe the leaders of the CCP [Chinese Communist Party] ask AI what a good political system would look like, and it gives them some better ideas.

Jerusalem Demsas: It tells them liberal democracy.

Matthew Yglesias: And they’re like, “Oh, you know, you’re making a lot of sense.” And we —

Jerusalem Demsas: I think in that case, that’s how we get to stop AI, is the CCP decides it’s a threat to their political control.

Matthew Yglesias: So, I used DeepSeek.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And I, so I dual AI’d it. And so, I had Claude do translations into and out of Chinese for me. And I — so I wrote Chinese characters into DeepSeek, and I asked it about the case sort of for and against democracy and some examples of different political systems. And so, it did pros and cons on democracy that came down pretty clearly in favor of democracy.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And then it told me that the United States and most of the countries of Western Europe — and it had some, like, weird phrasing to describe Taiwan — were all democracies.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And then it said that Cuba, Vietnam, and Laos are examples of one-party communist dictatorships. But then in China, they have eight parties that have a consultative process. So, something’s cooking in the Chinese AI.

Jerusalem Demsas: I mean, they figured out alignment, how to align to the CCP.

Matthew Yglesias: No, but it’s the fact that it’s lying to me, like, it has a guilty conscience, right? And I think, I think could lead them to a, to a better place ultimately, because…

By the way, that is not true. There’s no eight parties in China. I don’t, I don’t totally know what that’s even a reference to.

Jerusalem Demsas: Matt looked direct to camera for those who are just listening.

Matthew Yglesias: Yeah, I want to, you know, I do not want to spread misinformation here. China is a single-party state.

Jerusalem Demsas: So, fact-checked by DeepSeek: wrong.

Matthew Yglesias: I hope that that all works out. You know, and we can we can steer away. I mean, Trump is so idiosyncratic. Like, as of Saturday…

Jerusalem Demsas: “Let data rain.”

Matthew Yglesias: As of Saturday, I thought, look, Elon Musk is tweeting that we should be pacing the frontier. He’s Trump’s biggest donor.

Jerusalem Demsas: Mm-hmm.

Matthew Yglesias: AI is unpopular. Trump doesn’t have a principled commitment to free markets or whatever. So, why would Trump take a position that is unpopular with the public, that his No. 1 donor disagrees with, and that has fuck all to do with anything he cares about? And yet he did. Seemingly because David Sacks and Mark Zuckerberg talked him into it against the advice of his pollsters and everybody.

And that’s very upsetting to me because I went on an optimism to pessimism arc. Most of the people I know, most of the AI heads I agree are very pessimistic about diplomacy with China.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: I don’t want to say I’m super optimistic about it, but I don’t get what their basis of their pessimism is exactly.

Jerusalem Demsas: I think it’s because I actually think that often people who work on frontier technologies are extremely both removed from and pessimistic about political cooperation because, A, often the barriers that they’re facing all the time are often regulatory. And the entire ethos of places like the Bay Area are like, let’s operate outside the system and just try to do our product before the government catches up to us. And in many ways it can be very positive for humanity. In many ways it can be a problem as witnessing right now.

And I think it’s just, like, if you don’t work in politics, your dominant consumption of politics is dysfunction. And it happens all the time when I’m like, I mean, I’m sure it happens to you too when you travel outside D.C. and people are like, “Oh yeah, D.C., even very smart people, nothing gets done there, nothing happens, it’s completely fake and nothing good has ever occurred.” And I’m like, “Oh yeah, I mean, I agree things are not going well from my perspective, but I think there’s some bipartisan wins on some stuff that matters.”

And not in a, you know, calm down way, but in more of, like, a, I think that there’s often not awareness of the fact that the system can work and how you would make it work better is often doing more of that. So, for instance, like the CHIPS Act or the ROAD to Housing Act, these are bipartisan bills that were incredibly important for the respective industries that they were, you know, regulating.

And I think that what you see in the AI doom space, and I think what’s changing now, is that most of the people who have been working on it are not anywhere near political levers of power. I think that’s changing a lot. Like, you know, there are lots of people in D.C. all the time now who are working on AI safety.

Matthew Yglesias: They’re in our office.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah, in our office building. Yeah, I’m optimistic about it.

Matthew Yglesias: OK, so we reached consensus?

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah, me and Matt have aligned.

Matthew Yglesias: We’re cooperating.

Jerusalem Demsas: To do this podcast. All right, we’re gonna take a break and then we’re gonna do peer review.

Matthew Yglesias: All right, this is peer review, a section of the podcast where we talk about a piece of new or sometimes not so new research that’s relevant to our interests. Jerusalem, this week I’ve got a paper with a great title. It’s a banger. It’s just called “Meetings.” Meetings.

It’s by David Deming at Harvard, Katrine Vellesen Løken — maybe we’ll have to get our Danish colleague to tell me if I’m pronouncing that correctly — Alexander Willén, and Yaling Xu. The last three all from the Norwegian School of Economics. This paper features one of my personal favorite things for research, that is Nordic administrative data. And it is using administrative data from Norway to assess the question of why are there so many annoying meetings at work?

And they find that there are a lot of meetings, that they’re quite time-consuming, they’re costly, as they say, about 14% of firms’ wage bills are accounted for by the time that their workers spend in meetings. But tragically, from the standpoint of almost everybody who finds this annoying and really wants the answer to be that this is a huge waste and we’re all virtue signaling or something, it’s really useful. “Workers in meeting-intensive firms report greater on-the-job learning, and interactions with more senior colleagues are associated with stronger wage growth, suggesting that knowledge transmission within firms is an important mechanism.”

“Meetings are the broccoli of work — widely disliked, but probably good for us anyway.” And so, it’s like really, they go through it, but basically the things that you might think are the virtues of meetings are really there. People are learning, it’s useful. We’re gonna hold some more meetings.

Jerusalem Demsas: I’m a big fan of this finding in part because I am very — I’ve been very meeting skeptical in terms of, you don’t want meetings to eat up a bunch of your own time obviously because you feel like I want to get down and do my quote-unquote “real work” and I want to write and I want to edit and I don’t want to spend a bunch of time having to coordinate different things in different meetings. And I’ve been pretty harsh about deleting meetings off my calendar and being like, “This is a recurring meeting we have, we’re going to get rid of it.” And then we end up having to create another meeting in order to facilitate that thing.

And I think that, I don’t know, I think 60% of managers should never read this paper because they are not insufficiently efficient. They’re not sufficiently efficient about the meeting time that they’re putting on everyone else’s calendar. And then 40% of managers should definitely read this paper to relieve themselves of the anxiety of the fact that they’re in meetings a lot and that that’s to be treated as real work. And so, I’m worried that this is going to go and — convince a bunch of people that their shitty inefficient meetings are actually good, but not all meetings are good.

Matthew Yglesias: I will say, I mean, this paper does not speak to the question of the value of the marginal meeting.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yes.

Matthew Yglesias: What they show, I guess the way you would put it, is that the average meeting is very beneficial.

Jerusalem Demsas: And it’s beneficial for everyone. They find that for workers, it leads to higher wage growth and there’s more knowledge transmission. This feels very analogous to a lot of the papers that we’ve seen about remote work, too. I have, like — obviously The Argument is an in-person work environment, so is Slow Boring. And we like to work together. We also find it, like, very valuable to be in an office with people.

And I think also, knowledge transfer in particular I think is just really difficult to do digitally. I think when people are sharing information over Slack or in emails, hey, sometimes people don’t read the full email. Sometimes people are not as good at writing as they are at talking, and you need to, like, successive questions to get it. Sometimes the threads get excessively long so people can’t follow it, and then people need to have something reinforced in the room.

So, you know, you might want to send around a missive to everyone and say, like, “Hey, like, just a reminder that, you know, we need to, you know, clean up after ourselves in the kitchen” or whatever. And then, you know, no one reads that because it’s in the Slack channel that says reminders from HR and no one cares. But if you have your boss in a meeting say, like, “Hey, like, this is really important and this is, like, a company value” or whatever, I do think that that actually ends up changing people’s behavior more.

So, I think part of what’s going on here is not that it is literally impossible to transmit information through email. It’s that human beings are social creatures that require interaction in order to really let information sink in.

Matthew Yglesias: Yeah. I mean, that seems to be true. I mean, but I also think, I mean, there’s the information question, right? But there’s this aligning of stakeholders function of meetings also that I think is, you know, even more where the in-person helps, right? I mean, for better or worse, I think we see this in the way organizations turned dysfunctional —

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: During COVID or the way people behave on X, formerly known as Twitter, that something about the standoff communication style pushes people apart from each other. And a lot of what you do at a meeting is get everyone on board for the plan.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Right? Obviously, the nature of making decisions is that what is agreed upon is not exactly what everybody in the room would have wanted to do.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: But you come out of a good meeting with a positive vibe about the direction. Whereas I think discussions over remote text tend to push people further apart. Right? And so, they get your — you’re fighting, and you’re finding new things to fight about. Fight about and finding threads. The annoyingness of meetings is potentially helpful in this regard. People usually want the meeting to end, and the only way for the meeting to end is to resolve the topic of the meeting, right? Like, you have to reach a —

Jerusalem Demsas: OK, sometimes I found that people complain about meetings, but they actually do, like, like, at an observational level, clearly do like meetings because it’s like almost like you get to, like, not work.

Matthew Yglesias: Yeah.

Jerusalem Demsas: You know, I find a lot of fake kvetching about, like, “Oh, meetings, they suck,” but I’m gonna put, like, 15 extras on my calendar. And I’m like, “OK, do you hate meetings really? Or — “

Matthew Yglesias: Well, I don’t know about that. I mean, there’s a sort of, like — there’s a yin and a yang to that. I also do think that we work in a little bit of an unusual field where I don’t totally know how to generalize it. I mean, ’cause I have — there are meetings with people you know, we do a meeting about the podcast, and we are exchanging information, we’re making a plan. Most of my meetings are meetings with external people in which we’re shooting the shit.

Jerusalem Demsas: Interviews, yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And I do enjoy that, in part because I select who I meet with. But I do sometimes feel like it’s crowding out productive time. Writing and editing, but even just annoying, like, interoffice, you know, meeting type stuff. Also, when journalists hold meetings, a lot of time what we’re doing is editorial planning, which I think most people who like journalism enjoy.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Talking about their stories and pitching their ideas. And, you know, I mean, you, you can have a pitch that goes badly or something like that, but it’s in some ways more fun to talk about your idea than to —

Jerusalem Demsas: Do it?

Matthew Yglesias: Like, do it where you’re like, “Ugh, do I have evidence for this thesis?” You know, like, that can be a drag. And I don’t know how, you know, reflective that is.

I mean, David Deming was one of the authors on this paper. You know, he indicated to me that he was hoping that the result would come out the other way. He’s a scholar, but he’s also an administrator at Harvard, and I think, like many professors, acknowledges that you have to — the administrative work of the university department clearly has to be done, but that’s not why they got into that field.

Jerusalem Demsas: You already said the thing about the marginal meeting, it doesn’t really speak to that, but I think it also just — there are other stories one could tell for how you get to these results without the meetings themselves being valuable. For instance, maybe wage growth accrues to people who are in meetings because someone who’s on the promotion track gets invited to meetings. You know what I mean? Or companies that are successful just might need more coordination. So, it may not — if you are a poorly performing company or you have a bad product or a bad service that you’re offering that’s just getting — it’s not going to work, adding some meetings may do nothing to change the stakes for you.

Matthew Yglesias: My mom gave me the advice before I went to college that in any class I was in, I should make sure to go to the professor’s office hours.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Like, sometimes.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And I believe that I learned things talking to my professors in their office hours, but that’s not the point my mom was making to me.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: It was just that you will probably get a better grade if you seem like a curious person who is interested in this stuff, subject, and the way you will indicate that to the professor is by showing up at office hours. Now, of course, it’s a little bit both/and because if you show up at office hours and seem like a real shithead, that’s not gonna be helpful.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: The, the best way to appear to be a curious and engaged student is to actually be engaged with the material, you know? But still, the point my mom was making was that there’s benefits to —

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: to showing up and kissing ass and the meeting may be a forum in which that can take place. The other thing about the margin, which is a little disturbing to contemplate, but at the optimal organization, the marginal value of the meeting might be zero.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yes. Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Right? So, you could accurately perceive that it seems like you’re in these pointless meetings, and that’s actually a well-run organization, right? That if all the meetings are bangers, that’s you’re not having enough meetings, right? I think.

Jerusalem Demsas: Like, “Wow, we got, like, so much done in this meeting.” Like, yeah, we have a lot more to get done.

Matthew Yglesias: Right, right, right. That there’s plenty to do. And, you know, so I mean, everything about work like that is a little bit frustrating. It’s like the marginal Slow Boring article doesn’t perform well. Right. And I don’t know if that’s true. No, I mean, ’cause that’s, that’s sort of how it goes, you know? It’s like you’re not, you’re not doing enough.

Jerusalem Demsas: I just don’t want to say yes to that at, like, an absolute level. It felt, it felt rude.

Matthew Yglesias: Sure. No, no, no. But I mean, it’s just, it’s, it’s sort of the nature of, of life, right? Like, you’re leaving a lot on the table unless you eventually get into the really frustrating parts of the meeting curve or the how much written output do you do, even just how many hours do you put in at work, and we have trade-offs on time. So, you know, in some ways, maybe the best-run company, everybody’s working 65 hours a week, but then you wouldn’t want to work there.

Jerusalem Demsas: Well, one day we’ll have our AIs go to the meeting so we can continue doing our productive work and they can make decisions without us.

Matthew Yglesias: The AI gave me a briefing on the podcast meeting that we were gonna have. It was Jerusalem Demsas, editor-in-chief of —

Jerusalem Demsas: It gave you that information?

Matthew Yglesias: Yeah, it told me that.

Jerusalem Demsas: Wow!

Matthew Yglesias: It told me something about —

Jerusalem Demsas: What other secret information did it tell you?

Matthew Yglesias: Something about Justin’s background. Thank you for your efforts.

Jerusalem Demsas: To our video producer.

Matthew Yglesias: But it was — yeah, I did not find that to be super useful because you were all people who I knew. But superintelligence presumably could distinguish between a meeting between people who I actually know and total strangers or weirdos who show up, because it does also have that sometimes you find yourself on a Zoom with external stakeholders and you don’t really understand who some of the people on the call are.

Jerusalem Demsas: Many such cases.

Matthew Yglesias: They’re just colleagues and maybe too many people are in the meeting.

Jerusalem Demsas: Oh, this actually — OK, I get to do a movie reference now. This is going to be like The Devil Wears Prada where Emily and Andy are Miranda Priestly’s assistants and they’re perfectly calibrated to tell her who everyone is. It’s going to be a super, super intelligent…

Matthew Yglesias: Sure.

Jerusalem Demsas: I just never get to do movie references because you always do them, so I needed to throw one in.

Matthew Yglesias: Fair enough. That is a good movie. And it is, you know, I mean, I mean, to be optimistic about AI, I mean, I really do think that that is —

Jerusalem Demsas: Like, it would be great if I didn’t have to go to any meetings, but all the decisions that I would have made or are made as good, if not better, by, like, a Jerusalem agent, that would be fantastic. Like, “Oh, I don’t need to make decisions about, you know, the events or whatever. I can just write and and stuff.”

Matthew Yglesias: You think about this though, right? I mean, this is always sort of the question is, you know, if this assistant is so competent, like, why is she in that job, right? And the story of The Devil Wears Prada is that it — no, I mean, it’s a very junior role, right? And so, the idea is that you’re gonna do it. It’s very, very competitive. It’s like really top people get this kind of lowly role where Miranda Priestly treats you like crap. Like shit, but by excelling, you, you move up to the next kind of thing in your career.

So, you get these kind of ambitious, power-seeking people in the role, but they don’t seek power over, what’s it called, Runway, right? They’re going externally kind of out into the world. Those systems, and, you know, classic magazine journalism in its heyday, did sort of work like that.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: But it, but it’s hard to sustain, right, that kind of tempo of thing with the AIs who presumably are not angling for their next job.

Jerusalem Demsas: I was confused how you were getting this to be a positive story because I was like, this sounds like it’s going to be about AIs trying to get to their next job. But I guess you were saying that’s not going to happen.

Matthew Yglesias: I mean, if it works, they’re just happy to do it forever, right? And just be your loyal factotum that they work really, really hard at. They’re really competent, but they don’t have any further motives.

Jerusalem Demsas: Ulterior motives. Well, on that note, if you enjoyed this podcast, like, subscribe, tell your friends. We are still growing. Four eras of San Francisco tech culture

An anthropological reflection.

Noah Smith
Sep 25
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

The other day I went on the Monitoring the Situation livestream, and we talked about the history of San Francisco tech culture:

I’ve never actually worked in the tech industry, but I’ve lived on and off in the Bay Area for a quarter of a century now — including the last 10 years in San Francisco itself — and I’ve spent a lot of that time hanging out with people who work in or around the tech industry. Throughout much of that time, I was also reading some the same source materials that inspired lots of tech people — science fiction, futurist websites and books, nerdy forums and blogs, and so on.

Over that time, I’ve watched more and more people start to care about all this. Back in the early 2000s, as far as I could tell, pretty much nobody in the world cared about what some dorky hoodie-wearing computer programmers were up to on a Saturday night in SF. Fast forward 25 years, and the President of the United States is gathering opposition research on SF techie subcultures:

President Trump's allies are targeting Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei as the face of AI "doomerism" and a founding father of the effective altruism movement that's come under increasing political fire…Trump surrogates see Amodei as an easy foil because of his politics and focus on AI safety, sources told Axios…

A memo began circulating within the White House this week that seeks to paint effective altruism as a fringe, cultish collective out of touch with mainstream America. The memo, obtained by Axios, places Amodei at the foundation of the movement…Effective altruism “built the AI-doom pipeline,” states the memo, which was penned by a Trump political adviser…Critics of the movement, which has ties to the AI research community, have called out its obsession with AI safety, animal welfare (including musings on shrimp consciousness) and other values they deem far from the U.S. mainstream…

The document lists a veritable parade of horribles for the average conservative mind: abortion, veganism, devaluing human life by overvaluing animals or granting "digital minds" civil rights-like protections.

If you could go back in time and tell the 2001 version of me that the President’s allies are talking on national news about shrimp consciousness, I would have laughed out loud. (Until you told me who the President was, of course.) Not only that, but you have the New York Post talking about Effective Altruists’ sex lives, and op-eds debating EA philosophy in top blogs and the Washington Post.

Ladies and gentlemen, it really happened. The nerds took over the world. We have arrived.

I’ve never been an Effective Altruist,¹ of course, and I’ve only hung out a little bit in those circles. But in fact, EA is only one corner of the tech culture, and its influence on the AI safety discussion is probably a lot less than people think. In fact, the people talking about EA in the White House and in the news aren’t even really identifying the right group of people — the AI safety obsessives that the White House is taking aim at are the Rationalists, who are descended from a group of 1990s futurists called the Extropians. EA is a largely separate philosophical movement that appeals to some of the Rationalists, has some overlapping social circles, and jumped into the AI safety discussion later on after the basic ideas were all in place.

But anyway, that whole intellectual history is a story for another day (or you can just go ask AI). Today what I wanted to do is to give a brief anthropological history of the tech culture in San Francisco since the turn of the century, from my own quasi-outsider’s perspective. There have been four distinct eras over that time period:

  1. The Rebel Era (2001-2012)

  2. The Corporate Era (2012-2019)

  3. The Interregnum (2020-2022)

  4. The AI Era (2022-present)

But let’s start with some background.

The 20th century: SF tech pre-history

SF tech culture is the modern descendant of a very long lineage. It’s a branch off of the tree of computer science culture, which is closely intermingled with electrical engineering culture, and which are both branches off of the great broad trunk of science and technology culture more generally. But it’s important to realize that what became SF tech culture didn’t start in San Francisco — it started down on the peninsula to the south.

The modern tech industry began in the suburban towns around Stanford University — Menlo Park, Palo Alto, Cupertino, Sunnyvale, and so on. This had been a hub of the old electric equipment industry from World War 2 onward, and so William Shockley chose Mountain View to start the first semiconductor company in 1955. Fairchild broke off from Shockley, and Intel broke off from Fairchild. The whole area became a hub of semiconductor manufacturing in the 60s and 70s, then computer companies (Apple was founded in 1976 in Cupertino), then software companies like Oracle and Adobe. For a long time, Sand Hill Road in Palo Alto was the locus of the venture capital industry.

Today we use “Silicon Valley” to refer to the IT industry in general, but originally it meant the area around Menlo Park and Palo Alto. I wasn’t there to see this era, but a few good resources to learn about both the economics and the culture are:

  1. The book Regional Advantage, by Annalee Saxenian, which documents how and why Silicon Valley became America’s top tech cluster

  2. The documentary General Magic, which chronicles a failed but highly influential smartphone startup in the 90s

  3. The movie Office Space and the book Microserfs, which both satirize the stultifying experience of working for a big tech company in the 90s

  4. The book From Counterculture to Cyberculture, which chronicles the techno-hippie movement that grew up around the emerging computer industry

San Francisco began as a marginal bit player in the whole tech ecosystem. It was a place that some tech people would come up to party and network, especially during the dotcom era when a lot of money (at least, for those days) was splashing around.

But it did have a media industry, and in the 1990s, some people who worked in publishing, advertising, and other media started trying to get in on the internet gold rush. A few engineers and entrepreneurs who didn’t want to live in the boring suburban environment of Silicon Valley moved to SF to make tech media and web startups. Tony Hsieh’s autobiography, Delivering Happiness, tells the story of how he founded LinkExchange in San Francisco, while getting involved in the rave scene. At the same time, SF became a locus of tech media — Wired was founded there in 1993.

That, I think, was really the start of modern San Francisco tech culture as we know it. It bled directly into the first era of tech culture that I witnessed first-hand — the Rebel Era of the 2000s.

The Rebel Era (2001-2012)

In 2003, when people said “Silicon Valley”, they still meant the Peninsula. Google began there, Apple made its big comeback there, and when Facebook moved out west in 2004, this is where it went. Sand Hill Road was still the epicenter of tech — throughout the 2000s, people would still use “walk down Sand Hill Road” as a synonym for trying to get VC funding. If you wanted to make money in tech in the 2000s — and everyone knew there was still a lot of money to be made, despite the dotcom bust — you went to the Peninsula.

This was the land of office parks, cute but sterile shopping villages, overpriced single-family homes, big tracts of open space, Patagonia vests, and bland restaurants serving pancake brunch. It was where you went to tutor kids for $50 an hour² if you were a Stanford student who needed cash. It was also the land of starched button-down shirts, cubicles, and pointy-haired bosses who didn’t quite know what their engineers were up to. It was not a place to meet girls, go to parties, do drugs, wear grungy clothes, or dream big dreams about freeing society from the clutches of authority and tradition.

If you went up to SF to start a company in the 2000s instead of going down to the Peninsula like everyone else, it usually meant you were something of a rebel. A whole alternative tech culture grew up in the city — more laid-back, more politically liberal, less obviously focused on money and “success” and more focused on building fun products. Twitter was the most famous product of this time period — Evan Williams’s life project was to give a voice to the voiceless, and Jack Dorsey was a scruffy hippie kid who went to raves.

This is the time period when Burning Man — which had pretty much just been a punk art festival in the 90s — became a techie thing. Fire tornadoes and slapping LEDs on everything still felt like art. Everyone went to the Oakland warehouses to party, and for a brief shining moment, techies and artists got along. Psychedelic drugs were almost a matter of course — after all, Steve Jobs had done them, and Jobs was the great tech hero of that decade. Tech became more communal — instead of hacking together the next big thing in your parents’ garage or in a cubicle, you might go hang out and do it at Noisebridge in the Mission, surrounded by other techno-hippie hacker types like yourself.³

There was an ideological side to all this, too. There was a real belief — carried over from the 90s, but still strong — that the internet was going to liberate humanity. The tech rebels of the 2000s believed that social hierarchies were based on information control, and that if they simply broke that control, the hierarchies would be overturned. The information wanted to be free!

The most important touchstone of SF tech culture during this time wasn’t rationalism or the LessWrong forums — it was the Electronic Frontier Foundation, an organization dedicated to freedom of information on the internet. All the cool kids — the badass self-taught engineers and the brilliant cryptographers and the bohemian founders — were part of the EFF, or at least friendly with its goals.⁴ The anarchist tech prophet Cory Doctorow was an icon of the age, writing sci-fi about Burning Man colonizing the moon, tech founders taking down Disney, and so on. Everyone read BoingBoing and Gizmodo.

The Rebel Era gave tech a more liberal slant. Traditionally, engineers had been a little staid and conservative, and the big tech companies on the Peninsula were studiously apolitical. But Marc Benioff and other 2000s SF tech types waded (cautiously) into the political waters on the liberal side. This is also when education polarization in America really started to bite, meaning that most engineers were now libs in general. But there was a particular techno-liberalism, based around the idea of the internet flattening social and political hierarchies, that suffused the grungy SF tech scene in the 2000s.

In retrospect, the Rebel Era couldn’t last. Its bohemian, socially flattened culture was always predicated on a lack of money, and when money came in, SF tech was transformed.

The Corporate Era (2012-2019)

Five things put an end to the Rebel Era of SF tech culture and ushered in the Corporate Era. The first was the great financial crisis of 2008, and the Dodd-Frank legislation of 2010 that tamed the finance industry. In 2008, if you were a young ambitious Harvard graduate who wanted to make two million dollars a year, you moved to New York and went into finance; in 2016, you moved to San Francisco and went into the tech industry. The crisis had a lot to do with that.

The second change was Facebook. The company’s IPO in 2012 valued the company at $104 billion, more than any new U.S. public company had ever been valued. Ten billionaires and thousands of millionaires were minted overnight. Tech was big money, and America had its answer to the question of what comes next after finance. The post-dotcom era was over; the internet was back.

The third change was the institutionalization of venture capital. In the 00s and the 90s and earlier, VC was a very speculative, early-stage sort of investment — it managed a small amount of money, and wrote smallish checks to early-stage startups. Nine out of ten would fail, the tenth would more than make up for the failures, and the VCs would go skiing in Vail.

The 2010s changed that model. After investors saw that finance wasn’t going to make them big bucks anymore, and after they saw how much money Facebook had just made, they started handing giant piles of cash to venture capitalists out in California. VC’s assets under management tripled over the decade:

Deploying that much money requires a new model — one that invests at later stages, invests in more companies, and requires lower risk. As a result, VC started to become more of a corporate machine. Y Combinator and other “accelerators” became machines that would take in promising young startups and guide them to a fast launch. Big VC firms like Andreessen Horowitz invested later and later, dishing out more dollars and taking a more hands-on approach in terms of helping their portfolio companies succeed. Entrepreneurship became standardized in a way it hadn’t been before, with comparables, milestones, standardized investment terms, and so on.

This fundamentally changed the nature of tech entrepreneurship. Here we must invoke the economist Frank Knight, who distinguished between risk and uncertainty. Risk is when you know the odds and roll the dice; uncertainty is when you roll the dice without knowing how many sides they have. Knight believed that entrepreneurs tend to make outsized money not because they take on lots of risk, but because they take on lots of uncertainty.

When Bill Gates dropped out of college to start a software company or Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak decided to build personal computers in a garage, they had no idea how likely they were to succeed; no one had ever done anything like that before. They were pure explorers, bushwhacking their way into virgin, trackless wilderness. This, Knight would say, is why they were able to become so rich.

The tech entrepreneurship of the 2010s replaced a lot of uncertainty with risk. You didn’t totally know your odds of success, of course, but you had a lot more guidance, a lot better comparables, and even standardized techniques for building and scaling a tech startup. This opened up entrepreneurship to a whole class of people who would never venture into the unknown, but who were fine taking a calculated gamble (often because they had rich families or good outside career options), and directed gobs of money toward their companies.

The 2010s founder culture became almost a parody of the 2000s rebel ethos. Corporate execs started awkwardly wearing hoodies like a uniform. Everyone in tech went to Burning Man, but now it became glamping, and lost its punk edge; the turning point probably came in 2014 when a prominent Republican activist became the festival’s biggest fan.

And what kind of companies did they build? Mostly social and mobile startups. The iPhone came out in 2007, Facebook got popular in the late 2000s, and the combination of these platforms seemed to promise another giant internet bonanza. In 2015, Benedict Evans wrote “The Smartphone is the New Sun”, the blog post that defined the age. There was a standardized set of resources that went into creating a social-mobile startup — cloud computing, engineers of the typical type, a Google-imitation office with a snack bar and a nap room.

When uncertainty is replaced by risk — when entrepreneurship goes from exploration to a standardized procedure — returns go down. The most valuable social-mobile startup of the 2010s is Uber, whose market cap is currently $141 billion; adjusted for inflation, that’s less than Facebook’s valuation was when it IPO’d in 2012, and it’s about 7% of Meta’s valuation right now. A lot of people did make money on the social-mobile boom of the 2010s, but compared to what came before it was largely a bust. The smartphone was a wan, anemic sun indeed; U.S. productivity growth slowed to a crawl, and not because we somehow failed to capture the value of free internet services.

The internet did make big money in the 2010s, though — it just went to the big platforms. This was the fourth reason for the end of the Rebel Era — Big Tech became really big business. Google, Facebook, and the rest started hoovering up top talent, paying engineers half a million a year and mid-level managers two million. Big Tech became a brain trust that startups found it very hard to match. Tech yuppies could compare their salaries and their positions on the corporate ladder on specialized websites. Almost every conceivable internet function was absorbed by the big platforms, and they came to dominate not just the tech world, but the whole U.S. stock market.

The final, crucial change was that all of this was increasingly happening in San Francisco, rather than on the peninsula. In the 90s and 00s, boring corporate tech lived in the suburbs to the south, while rebels and hippies lived in their group houses in the city to the north. But in the 2010s, that changed.

One reason was software itself — Uber, DoorDash, and other gig economy apps made living in the city much more convenient, Facebook Events made it simple to find parties and other social gatherings, and online dating made it much easier to find large numbers of single folks. Many of these services were made artificially cheap by the VC boom, as investors created the famous “Millennial lifestyle subsidy” in the hopes of winning a monopoly. Nowhere was this subsidy more lavish than in San Francisco; in 2016 I could Uber anywhere in the city for $4.

There were other reasons tech moved north in the 2010s. Cloud computing removed the need for big server racks. SF Mayor Ed Lee courted tech businesses and built a bunch of new offices downtown. SF had become safer from the great crime decline, and so on.

The upshot of all this was that a city that had been the haunt of hippies and scruffy rebels and outsiders was suddenly flooded with untold numbers of corporate ladder-climbers, low-risk corporate engineers, by-the-books me-too founders, Patagonia-wearing VCs, and yuppies of every conceivable shape and size.

Just for fun, I asked GPT to draw a picture of what tech’s move up the peninsula looked like, and here’s what it drew me:

The city’s housing market, of course, couldn’t handle this, having NIMBY’d itself into total stagnation many decades earlier. Rents soared. Bohemian artists and middle-class young people alike couldn’t afford to live in the city, and there was an exodus. The YIMBY movement was born in SF, but failed to build housing fast enough to make any difference. “SF” started to become a one-industry town.

The town’s traditional first-wave gentrifiers — old hippies, “queerdos”, artists, and so on — began to hate techies with a (mostly unjustified) passion. Valiant attempts to preserve the old comity between techies and artists — such as Monument, a group house that tried to fill its rooms with equal numbers of each — failed, and everyone outside tech forgot that fire tornadoes and LEDs had ever been edgy and punk.

SF tech slowly started to drift toward political conservatism. The city’s new business-bro types viewed street people as health hazards rather than charming symbols of bohemian life. The Wokeness Wars of the 2010s fell hard on tech, with cancellations a-plenty, and loud activists demanding every conceivable concession to identity and progressive politics from their giant platform corporations.

This was the Corporate Era of SF tech — yuppies, Facebook events, Tinder, office cafeterias, email jobs, Big Tech salary bloat, Twitter drama, cheap Ubers, Burning Man camps, VC money everywhere, everyone pitching you on their startup.

And then one day in 2020, it all came to an end.

The Interregnum (2020-2022)

The Corporate Era of SF tech would have probably died of natural causes on its own. By the late 2010s it was becoming apparent that most of the big gains from the internet itself had already been harvested. The world was already wired up and connected. People were already spending all their time online, so the “attention economy” had become a zero-sum game. E-commerce and website subscriptions had established themselves as the only online revenue models that really worked. The most valuable new internet companies were slightly better ways of delivering taxicabs and hotels.

But we didn’t have the chance to find out, because the Corporate Era was murdered. The Covid pandemic swept in and drove everyone out of the downtown SF offices that Ed Lee had worked so hard to fill — and tech was an early adopter of remote work, creating a double whammy. With location suddenly irrelevant due to social distancing and work-from-home, lots of people avoided SF’s overpriced rents and dirty, disorderly streets by temporarily relocating to Miami, Austin, or elsewhere. There was much guff online about how those relocations were permanent, and SF was going to lose its crown to some other city, but I never gave it much credence. Clustering effects are strong.

But during the pandemic years, SF became a ghost town. The throngs of Millennial tech-yuppies who had moved in to eat at the corporate cafeteria and send emails while they browsed their Tinder matches⁵ realized that getting married and settling down in the ‘burbs with a couple of kids is actually not such a bad lifestyle after all; many of these went to Oakland or the Peninsula or Marin and just never came back. The cycle of life came for the Millennial generation in the end.

That ghost town was haunted. The specters that haunted it were the crypto people.

They say every tech boom ends in financialization. I don’t actually know if that’s true, but the internet boom did. The financialization of the internet was crypto — an online asset class that gained tremendous value simply because it told a good-sounding story and reinvigorated libertarian ideas that had been somewhat homeless since tech went progressive. Technologically speaking, there was never much use for crypto beyond evading the law, but socially speaking, it was very useful for Ponzi schemes, fraud, and government corruption.

It also bound together much of the tech industry into a political interest group — tech people had bought crypto because it was a Tech Thing, so the tech world now had a natural financial interest in fighting against restrictive regulation of crypto. That helped push tech back toward the political right.

For those strange three years of the pandemic, crypto ruled the increasingly bizarre, fragmented, and nearly-deserted SF tech scene. Ultra-low interest rates, meant to keep the economy going, pumped up crypto prices to the stratosphere, and suddenly some of the weirdest people you had ever met were throwing some of the tackiest parties you had ever attended. During those years it seemed like every tech event had its complement of strange, dolled-up Russian women who were all “in crypto” but whose role in that industry was highly uncertain.

These were not the bushwhacking explorers of yesteryear, rising from their garages and group houses to overturn the tech world once again. These were straight-up pirates — entrepreneurial in the sense that Edward Teach and Christopher Columbus were entrepreneurial. There were some serious engineers and some very fun nerds in the industry, but no corner of the crypto-world was free from the frisson of danger. I admit it was kind of fun, but I’m also glad it didn’t last.

A bunch of old rich internet guys, of course, cashed out and became even richer; such is the financialization at the end of a tech boom, I suppose.

Nor was crypto the only weird thing about SF tech during the interregnum. The pandemic drove everyone a little crazy, as pandemics tend to do. There were crazy parties, too many drugs, mental breakdowns, the dissolution of group houses, and lots of other silly stuff like that.

Three things brought this strange, unsettled Interregnum to an end. The first was the tech bust of 2022 — a now-almost-forgotten event, even within much of the industry. Interest rates rose to fight the post-pandemic inflation, startup valuations reset, internet stocks plunged. Google and Facebook and the rest suddenly discovered that they had not just over-hired by an enormous amount, but had allowed lots of their employees to coast at work. The easy attitude of job security, entitlement, and lack of responsibility that had made 2010s SF tech such a yuppie paradise vanished almost overnight, and the internet became just another mature industry.

The second thing was the big crypto bust of 2022. It turned out — gasp! — that one of the biggest crypto exchanges had been doing a bunch of fraud, and crypto high-flier Sam Bankman-Fried went to jail. A bunch of other crypto things failed, Silicon Valley Bank and some crypto-focused banks failed, and a lot of crypto guys moved out of the country to Southeast Asia or elsewhere — you know, just in case. Crypto itself became a much more staid and established industry, with its “killer app” being money market funds called “stablecoins”. Much of the energy and excitement went out of the space, though Donald Trump was still able to use “memecoins” to grab large amounts of cash from his followers.

The third thing that ended the Interregnum, of course, was AI.

The AI Era (2022-present)

The idea of AI had always been an important undercurrent in the tech world. The cyberneticists and extropians and futurists and sci-fi writers had long believed that AI would be tech’s crowning, ultimate invention — the creation of a machine that could do all our work and all our innovation for us, so that we could lay down our burdens. Or possibly so that we could be murdered by Earth’s new dominant species; opinions on that have always differed. But either way, people always knew that AI was the Big One, and that it was coming.

Discussions of the AI age had always been some of the liveliest — and, occasionally, the most bitter — in the tech culture writ large. Vernor Vinge, my favorite sci-fi author and one of the chief prophets of the coming of AI, correctly predicted the timing of the AI takeoff in 1993 but mostly refused to speculate on what would come afterwards, since he regarded this as inherently unknowable. In 2000, Eliezer Yudkowsky was yelling at people about AI risk on extropian mailing lists. In fact, it’s hard to think of any technology in history that has been as theorized, anticipated, agonized over, and predicted in advance as artificial intelligence.

Fun fact: The Singularity Institute, which birthed the Rationalist movement that the Trump administration is now confusing with the Effective Altruist movement, and which has been the main proponent of “AI doomerism”, was funded in the mid-2000s by none other than Trump ally Peter Thiel.

In 2012, it finally became apparent how AI would come about. It did not evolve spontaneously from the internet (as Vinge thought it might), nor was it grown in a simulated environment in a lab, nor was it made in the image of human brains. Instead, we built AI from the internet. One particular approach to AI — basically, creating a giant regression to learn from unimaginably huge amounts of data — turned out to work really well, and it started advancing really fast. But it wasn’t until 2022, with the release of ChatGPT — or even until 2025, with the release of Claude Code — that people realized just how fast things were moving and just how disruptive the change was likely to be.

During the 2010s, before that realization, AI had existed as a sort of parallel tech culture in SF. There were rationalists arguing endlessly online about AI, and how to make it not kill us. There were group houses where AI was all anyone could ever talk about. One of these, called the Archive, ended up producing many of the most accomplished and important AI engineers (as well as a number of other colorful and interesting figures, some of whom are my good friends to this day).

In the 2010s, some AI people got paid good money, but overall they weren’t very rich — they were a group of weird math nerds, more like professors than techbros. Everyone kind of acknowledged that AI was the next big thing, but the money existed on the fringe of the glamorous, exciting world of the social-mobile internet, in organizations like OpenAI.

The top tech guys all knew AI was going to be big, and took OpenAI very seriously, and aspiring engineers often got into AI because it was cool. But during the 2010s, it received less attention than it should have from the general public. There was even a hot second in 2021 or so when the AI people were sort of looking at the crypto guys and asking themselves how they had been eclipsed.

But AI would not be eclipsed for long, and certainly not by something as immaterial as crypto. When Anthropic IPOs later this year, its value will be almost equal to all of the cryptocurrencies in the world, combined. AI is shaping up to be bigger than the railroads.

Thanks to AI, SF is back. The weirdos I hung out and went to hot pot with in 2018 are now centimillionaires or billionaires — except for those whose startups have yet to hit the inflection point, of course. This is shaping up to be the greatest wealth creation event in human history — when Anthropic IPOs at $2 trillion later this year, it will be more than 4 times as valuable as all other San Francisco tech IPOs in history, combined. The company’s early employees are all going to be worth more than the founders of successful social-mobile companies were in the 2010s. VCs are throwing cash around like there’s no tomorrow, but even they are being surprised by how quickly that money is seeing eye-popping returns.

And yet SF’s AI boom, so far, is a strangely jobless one. Even as the labor market holds up well nationwide, and software engineers are getting hired en masse, San Francisco itself — and California in general — continues to bleed tech employment:

The excesses of the 2010s and the innocent days of the 1990s and 2000s are both gone. Despite all the money, the tone in SF feels grim. All of those years of discussing whether AI will kill us all, or just take all our jobs, are suddenly hitting with the force of reality; now is the moment we’ll get to find out.

Everyone is working as hard as they can, desperately trying to get their hands on as much capital as they can before the labor share goes to zero. One VC sighed to me that although he was getting rich, he wondered if human money would even mean anything in ten years. One veteran of the dotcom boom — I can’t find the quote now — said that if the birth of the internet was like a walk in a sunny park, the AI boom is like being strapped onto a rocket and fired into the sun.

This is the new era of SF tech — unimaginable riches, combined with universal anxiety. Everyone is working hard, and only a few stubborn optimists still look to the future with confidence. The researchers at the big labs almost all fear their own creations — they work hard every day not because they need to make even more millions, but because of fear that someone else will make it first and make it worse. The nerds have won everything, but the victory feels strangely hollow.

Personally, I think it’s likely AI won’t end up killing us, and I doubt this is the end for SF tech. This strange, dizzying era will end eventually, and we’ll be on to building the next thing — as crazy as the idea of “the next thing” sounds in the face of AI. Whatever that next thing is, it’s probably not getting a lot of attention in the news.

You’ll notice that some of the questions in today’s Mailbag don’t have links.

Those are from people who contributed to last November’s GiveDirectly fundraiser at a tier that entitles them to ask a must-answer Mailbag question. I’ve been a little bit remiss in getting to fulfilling my end of the bargain on that, but those answers should be rolling out over the next few weeks. If you’re feeling jealous, Slow Boring will be doing the fundraiser again this November, so look out for that!

M_McQ: If you were in charge, and weren’t worried about short term political consequences, what would you do about the Iran situation? The 2026 attack was clearly a mistake, but Iran does not want to return to the previous status quo. Is there a “least bad” deal we should be aiming for?

This is a case where I think it’s very important that Donald Trump try to actually fix the mess that he made because if the war somehow lingers for two more years and it becomes President Gavin Newsom’s problem, it’s going to be very challenging to resolve.

To see why, you need to go back to 2015 when the Obama administration was close to finalizing the negotiations on the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action and Tom Cotton tried to scuttle the deal by writing a letter cosigned by most Senate Republicans warning that the G.O.P. was not going to consider itself bound by anything Barack Obama agreed to, so a deal would be pointless from an Iranian point of view. The White House convinced the Iranians that this was wrong, and if Hillary Clinton had won in 2016, it might have been wrong. Indeed, even after Donald Trump won in 2016, there was some thought that he might find it pragmatic to abide by the terms of the deal after all. There were people inside his administration, in fact, who warned him against tearing it up. But he did tear it up, and the Iranians ended up in exactly the position Cotton had tried to warn them about. The Iranians stayed fairly chill about this, opting to try to wait Trump out and see what happened next.

What happened next was Joe Biden became president and his team essentially proposed going back to the Obama-era deal.

The Iranians, understandably, said there was no point in doing a deal that was just going to be broken if the next administration was Republican. They demanded front-loaded concessions from the Biden administration because they no longer felt that American diplomatic agreements were credible. The Biden administration, also understandably, did not want to make a bunch of politically toxic upfront concessions to a regime that is justifiably held in low regard by the American people. So they back-burnered the whole thing, tried to work on Saudi-Israel normalization, and hoped for the best. This diplomatic situation probably provided some of the impetus for the 10/7 attack, which, whatever else it did, does seem to have scuttled efforts to build a regional anti-Iranian coalition.

Then Trump came back and of course we know what happened there.

The point of all this is that not only do the Iranians not particularly want to return to the pre-war status quo, but I also think they really don’t want to negotiate with Democrats at all. They are aware that a Democratic administration is unlikely to bomb them — Biden did not and his team acted to restrain Israel in this regard as well — but they’re also aware that a Democratic administration can’t conclude agreements that will stick. So the basic shape of Biden-era diplomacy, where it’s objectively hard to reach a deal, will obtain in 2029. Offsetting that is the fact that the war is genuinely very bad for Iran — if you think Americans are mad about expensive diesel, things are much worse over there — so there is an incentive to try to resolve this. But it’s just challenging for Democrats to try to make the kind of commitments that the Iranians would want.

It’s, of course, also hard for Trump to resolve this.

But the Republicans are the ones who can make the commitments the Iranians care most about. And while any deal a Democrat makes would end up getting savaged by Republicans (and the rump of AIPAC-aligned Democrats in Congress), the worst that’s going to happen to Trump if he makes a weak deal is maybe a mean editorial in the Free Press. So in the spirit of “only Nixon could go to China,” Trump’s prospects for diplomacy are a lot more promising than someone else’s prospects after we muddle through for years.

In terms of what a deal should look like, I believe in the “Getting to Yes” view that you want to talk about principles rather than positions.

America’s core interests are:

  • We want Iran to verifiably commit to nuclear non-proliferation.

  • We want to uphold the principle of freedom of the seas, which has been a core value of American foreign policy since the Jefferson administration and the First Barbary War.

  • We want some kind of apology for the hostage-taking and other actions taken during the Iranian Revolution that sent the U.S.-Iran relationship into a tailspin.

If we can achieve credible commitments on those scores, we should be prepared to treat Iran like a normal country where we disapprove of the regime and its conduct and its human rights record but accept its legal legitimacy and are not subjecting it to military or economic coercion. This means accepting that Israel, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and the United Arab Emirates have a bunch of other major beefs with Iran about missiles and Hezbollah and Yemen and saying clearly that this is not our problem. If these countries want to collaborate with each other to form a rich, populous, and technologically advanced bloc of countries that check Iranian regional ambitions, that seems like a reasonable thing for them to do. But they need to work that out among themselves and reach among themselves some kind of resolution of the Palestinian situation that they find acceptable. They can’t be endlessly relying on the United States of America — a country on the other side of the world that does not even really import Middle Eastern oil — to do this for them.

But again, while I think Democrats can make progress toward this vision of being less involved in the Middle East, I think it is dramatically easier for a Republican administration to achieve this since they are the ones who’ve been insisting that America needs to serve as the pointy end of an Israeli or Saudi spear.

Marc Robbins: What is your greatest hope and fear for the world your son will be living in when he’s at your present age?

I’m going to choose to take this literally as “hopes for the world of 2060 when my son will be 45,” not specifically hopes about things that will impact him. So on the hope side, what I want to see is that two big trends that were present in an earlier part of my life but that have stalled out more recently will re-assert themselves.

  • One is rapid economic progress for the world’s poorest people. This was happening for a long time, driven primarily by China and India, but seems to have ended now that those countries are less poor rather than spreading to the still-poor countries of Africa and elsewhere.

  • The other is democracy and political liberalization. In the relatively recent past — even after Tiananmen and Vladimir Putin’s rise to power — there was a ton of optimism about the Arab Spring and democratization in the Middle East, but very little came of it.

In both cases, at one point we had what seemed like strong positive trends that it was widely believed would continue, and now I think the conventional wisdom has just flipped. I am a big believer in contingency, though, and don’t think we should give up on the possibility of a return to positive trends.

On fear, it’s all about the robot apocalypse.

Share

Mark Zuckerman: I grew up in Arlington County, VA, which remains my home. As you are probably aware, Arlington has (in my lifetime at least) always been reliably blue. In the last 30 years or so, Arlington County has basically only elected Democrats to the County Board (John Vihstadt being the notable exception, which took a variety of unique circumstances that are unlikely to be repeated anytime soon). Even as blue as it is, somewhere in the range of 15%-30% of Arlington voters vote Republican, and their voices basically never make it onto the County Board. I don’t love this, both because I’m more conservative than the average Arlington County Board member, but also because I think Arlington County hasn’t been well served by having basically no ideological disagreement on the Board. So I think that a fairer representation of the electorate would be better for Democrats (as it would blunt some of the echo chamber problem), but also would be good for local Republicans, as they would have an incentive to be more serious when they actually have a chance to hold power. I know that Arlington is experimenting with ranked choice voting, but given that board seats are up on a staggered basis, it doesn’t seem like this will make any difference. Do you see a fairer solution? Do you even view this as a problem? Is it possible that “fair” representation would just end up with Republicans electing a MAGA bomb thrower who will only make things worse?

This has a pretty straightforward solution.

Right now, Arlington elects a five-person board and each of the five members of the board is elected at-large for staggered terms. Because the terms are four years long, that means that three years out of four there is a single county-wide board race and then on the fourth year there are two races. That’s a little bizarre, and I think common sense is that if you’re going to use this system, the terms should be five years.

But also it’s a bad system. Because this is a 70-30 blue county, the Democratic Party nominee always wins. But then because the median Democratic Party primary voter is to the left of the median Arlington resident, this means all five members of the board will be to the left of the median voter in the county.

One potential mitigation would be to drop the at-large elections and have five geographically distinct districts. I don’t think that would create a “Republican seat,” but you would at least introduce some variety into the mix.

A better idea, though, would be to elect all five seats simultaneously using a single transferable vote system. This is, in effect, a form of proportional representation, except without relying on party lists. A whole bunch of candidates would run, and they could identify as Democrats or Republicans or whatever they want. Official party organizations could endorse a specific five-candidate slate. And then each voter would rank the candidates in whatever order they prefer. Then you count up everyone’s first choice votes. Anyone who gets more than 20 percent of the vote wins a seat. You then redistribute excess votes from the winners to the voters’ second choices and see if that gets anyone else over the threshold. If it doesn’t, you start eliminating the candidates who got the fewest votes and going to their supporters’ second choice. Here’s an explainer video if you need the details.

The upshot is that in a place like Arlington, you’d expect to elect one Republican and four Democrats (rather than 5-0), and of those Democrats either one or two would be moderates and either one or zero would be D.S.A. leftist types. Which is just to say the governance of the county would be in line with the views of its voters rather than the current situation where a fairly progressive electorate always gets a board that is even more progressive.

Auros Harman: I am running for local office -- a City Council seat in the Bay Area suburb of San Bruno. I wonder how you think the “Common Sense Democrat” platform should be expressed in local politics, when the old maxim that “all politics is local” has seemingly inverted, at least for the voters who have any kind of partisan identity? For some slice of the electorate, now, the only politics they’re paying attention to is national. […]

The big thing I’m trying to do differently this year is just to get started earlier, raise a bit more money than I did last time, and get translated mailers for the ~8% of the district that requests ballot materials in Spanish. I did very little foreign language outreach last time — a friend who’s a native speaker of Spanish was able to do one round of phonebanking, but that was it. But I’m also going back and forth on how much to lean into Common Sense Dem rhetoric that could perhaps reach the conservative segment of the electorate, versus trying to get some partisan messaging out, targeting households that I can identify as likely anti-Trump, on the fact that Marty’s not a Dem and doesn’t seem like somebody who’d be ready to, e.g., ask our local police, if ICE agents come to the Bay Area and act the way they did in Minnesota, to at minimum refuse to cooperate with anything beyond targeting criminals, and potentially even be ready to investigate criminal violations of rights -- if, G*d forbid, an Alex Pretti case were to happen, I’d want our locals to grab evidence, before Kash Patel’s goons can swoop in and obfuscate things.

I don’t want to give too much advice about running in a place I’ve never been to and don’t know anything about.

But I think the general points from my article “How the Center-Left Can Come Back in 2028” apply. What I’m saying here is that there are some stances that cost Democrats with swing voters but that Democratic Party primary voters really strongly believe in. There are certain kinds of places where I think it’s smart for Democrats to moderate on those issues even though primary voters don’t like it and simply plead political pragmatism. But in a presidential race, electability only takes you so far, and you do have to win the primary. So what a presidential candidate really needs is a list of moderations that do well with swing voters but also with Democratic Party primary voters.

Share

Of course, a local race in San Bruno is not a presidential primary. The dynamic applies, though, because you’re looking to find some opportunities to hit the NIMBY incumbent from the right without sacrificing appeals to partisanship in a town where Democrats outnumber Republicans. From the piece, citing work by David Broockman and Josh Kalla, the two moderations that are relevant to local government and popular with Democratic primary voters are:

  • Punishing people who commit property crimes like shoplifting

  • Merit pay for public school teachers

I don’t know to what extent shoplifting is a practical problem in San Bruno. I can tell you that over the past couple of weeks, the CVS near my house has started leaving most of the secure shelving they installed a couple of years ago unlocked (at least during daytime hours, maybe it’s locked up during the graveyard shift), and it’s a huge quality-of-life upgrade. I would really recommend taking this issue on to anyone who’s in a community where people can’t just grab soap off the shelf.

The merit pay thing, meanwhile, just happens to be the education issue that they polled. I suspect you would see similar results for a range of other “normie” education policy stances, like “kids who misbehave should be disciplined” and “the smart kids should take an advanced math class.” On a rank-and-file level it’s really Democrats, much more than Republicans, who are idealistic about education and really believe in its importance and have sort of normal ideas about what a good school should look like. It’s a strange narrow elite inside graduate schools of education and weird leftist blocs inside teachers’ unions who’ve imposed a lot of weird pedagogical fads that have very little support.

Again, depending on the town this may not apply at all. But those are the two areas where I think there’s likely to be the most juice in a “common sense” approach even in a progressive area.

lwdlyndale: Do you think the Dems should call for a national system of limits for online gambling? If so what should the policy be?

I want to draw a distinction here. My view is that ubiquitous legal gambling is bad for America and that there was no actual problem with the gambling status quo as it existed in, say, 1996. We were not living through some kind of costly “war on gambling” that was diverting resources from more critical law-enforcement tasks, and the prisons weren’t full of people who’d been busted running underground poker games. Enforcement was pretty low-key, people who wanted to bet on sports casually made bets with friends, there was a small black market, and Las Vegas and Atlantic City had lucrative casino industries because legal gambling was rare. On the merits, I would favor doing a ton to roll back legal gambling.

But should “the Dems” come out for this?

I think that depends what you mean. I don’t think this is a top five or top 10 or necessarily even top 20 significant issue in American life. It’s something that I think about a lot because I watch a lot of sports with my son and feel like I need to remind him three times a week not to get sucked into online sports gambling. But I want to hold myself on issues that I am interested in to the same standard I hold progressives to. If Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries hold a joint press conference tomorrow saying that Democrats want to crack down on online gambling, does that help Josh Turek and Mary Peltola and Bobby Pulido and my other favorite frontline candidates? I’d be open to persuasion on this point, but I’m pretty skeptical. I don’t think this addresses winnable voters’ doubts about the Democratic Party, and I think it might alienate some winnable voters and mobilize even more industry money against the Dems.

Which isn’t to say all Democrats should be gambling enthusiasts either. Say some of these people win. They’re going to have to actually do something in Congress. And a great thing for a frontline member to do is to get involved in some bipartisan bills. I think legal gambling has gone way too far, and I know a non-zero number of conservatives agree with me, so there is probably room for some bipartisan gambling bills. I’d love to see smart legislators get involved in that kind of thing. Then, depending on what the proposal looks like, I’ll be thrilled to consider it on the merits and also to see what the polling looks like.

Long story short, I think the bar for “party leadership takes up a new cause” should be pretty high. I’m serious when I say that Democrats need fewer big ideas not more. The party’s problem right now is that it’s struggling to set priorities and to construct a large enough tent. I’m very skeptical about putting new stuff on the agenda. Artificial intelligence is popping so much this fall that I don’t think it can possibly be evaded, but gambling doesn’t strike me as rising to that tier.

Taylor: After reading Hayek’s Road to Serfdom, do you think FDR’s legacy needs to be re-evaluated for his impact on the Great Depression?

Growing up, my history teachers always talked about him as if he got us out the Great Depression and “saved capitalism” from itself.

I think it’s well-documented that Hoover and the Federal Reserve made significant mistakes to contribute to the severity of the depression, but it seems like FDR’s own failures are often reframed as successes. The depression was far longer than previous ones, and, even from a Keynesian perspective, he didn’t engage in the kind of stimulus needed until WWII.

F.D.R.’s handling of the Depression was pretty flawed, but it was also a lot better than Herbert Hoover’s or than what we saw from Weimar Germany or Third Republic France, so I think his legacy is secure. But we should be clear that this is grading on a curve.

“Muddling through in an okay-but-not-great way” is in fact a lot better than failing catastrophically. And then, of course, F.D.R. followed it up with winning World War II. So I think he deserves his place in the Great Presidents Pantheon. But we shouldn’t understand that to mean “F.D.R.’s economic policies were amazingly good.” They were good compared with most of the other leading ideas on the table at the time, but we could have done a lot better.
