Our tradition is worth celebrating — but also genuinely upholding

Matthew Yglesias
Oct 13
 
READ IN APP
 

A couple of weekends ago, I went with friends to the Power to the People music festival in suburban Maryland. I was there primarily to see bands play, but part of the goal of the show was to raise money for a range of political causes, and I also got to hear brief political pitches from various artists.

The Dropkick Murphys shouted out organized labor in the building trades and brought the president of the painters’ union out on stage. I briefly got my hopes up that he would give people a pitch for taking the labor side of the labor-versus-green feud on data centers and permitting reform, but no such luck.

The show was fantastic. In addition to the Dropkick Murphys, it featured the Foo Fighters and Public Enemy along with legends like Joan Baez and Bruce Springsteen but also a surprisingly compelling performance by Jenny from “Gossip Girl,” who sang Soundgarden songs while Tom Morello played guitar.

At the climax, everyone came up on stage and the Boss led this whole crowd of musicians in a rousing rendition of Woody Guthrie’s classic leftist folk song “This Land Is Your Land.” Morello made a big deal about how they were going to sing the full version of the song, including the verses suppressed in many schools for their unduly leftist lyrics. (I was raised by weird leftists and taught this song at a very left-wing Ethical Culture day camp, so I had no idea there was any other version!)

Morello, at any rate, interrupted the song at one point to argue that Guthrie knew “that every inch of this land was stolen from the Indigenous people, so this land is actually their land.”

I don’t think this is factually correct about Guthrie’s politics. He and this song have long been a target of Native activists and intellectuals precisely because the rhetorical power of the song comes from denying the stolen land accusation. The point is that the American people (“you and me”) have a collective claim on American prosperity.

I was going to let this all go (it’s only a concert), but then I saw Marco Rubio fly to a foreign country and stage himself in front of the Acropolis specifically in order to lay claim to a transnational concept of “the West” but then proclaim himself strongly in favor of nationalism.

Department of State
@StateDept
The United States has made its choice. We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power.
9:32 PM · Oct 7, 2026 · 154K Views
255 Replies · 1.37K Reposts · 8.67K Likes

It’s a reminder that while Donald Trump and Rubio have substantively fumbled when it comes to defending the West and Western values or upholding American traditions, they do deserve credit for understanding the importance of symbolism to political life.

Especially in a country like ours that, contrary to the blood and soil trends in the MAGA movement, really is a credal nation, these choices of symbol matter. Guthrie’s song articulates a powerful message that is genuinely at odds with the political culture of land acknowledgments. And it’s worth defending America and the West and critical Western ideas from people like Trump, who are in fact tearing them down for a quick buck. But you have to be tough-minded about it and sing the songs correctly.

Progressive politics requires solidarity

Guthrie’s song, especially in its most controversially leftist verses, expresses outrage about the persistence of poverty in a land of plenty and skepticism about private property. This is meant to trouble us because if “this land was made for you and me,” then the idea is that “from California to the New York island” we all have a collective claim on American wealth.

This is just not compatible with the notion that the American national community is illegitimate.

Now what’s true is that Guthrie and other midcentury leftists, to their eternal credit, pushed for a more inclusive vision of the American national community.

The modern progressive coalition was forged by Black leaders like Martin Luther King demanding that Black Americans be accepted as fully equal members of the national community and by white liberals working with them to make it happen.

That’s why there’s a lot of patriotism associated with the high water mark of the civil rights movement — there were deliberate efforts to claim the Declaration of Independence and the iconography of Abraham Lincoln and the text of the Constitution as key validators. This same impulse toward racial equality also naturally and rightly leads progressives to care about what Native Americans think and to want to treat them better. And certainly on Guthrie’s terms, there’s plenty here to complain about. Native Americans have much lower household incomes and life expectancies than the American average, with worse educational and labor market opportunities. This is a failure of our national community, and it’s a failure worth trying to rectify.

But improving the conditions facing Native people is a hard problem that involves making tradeoffs and spending money. It’s a lot easier to throw a land acknowledgment into your program than to actually do something.

And I think it’s more toxic than generally realized to make symbolic concessions that undermine the legitimacy of the national community. One of the many questions facing Americans as we look at the rise of artificial intelligence is who should benefit from this boom. Should the rewards all go to the founders and shareholders of a handful of companies who’ll live out their remaining days among great wealth while consigning humanity to serving as a mere “biological bootloader” for their creations? Or should all the inhabitants of this land benefit from the upside and have a say in averting human extinction?

Elon Musk
@elonmusk
Propagating super intelligence to the stars is a great success condition for a biological bootloader
ALX (x/acc) 🎃🇺🇸 @alx
Elon was calling it SI in 2014
12:37 AM · Oct 5, 2026 · 5.55M Views
2.61K Replies · 2.46K Reposts · 20.4K Likes

The idea that we have obligations to each other — some of which are grounded in the general moral dignity of human life but some that are grounded in mutual membership in a legitimate political community — is at the core of progressive politics.

You can’t make sense of Social Security or Medicare or Medicaid or any of the other cornerstones of the progressive agenda without the idea that Americans owe something to each other simply because they’re all Americans.

The question of what exactly we do owe to Native Americans in light of their specific historical relationship to the political community is deep and hard. But while certainly the land was appropriated from people who were already living there, so was all the other land on Earth — including the lands appropriated by Native American groups from the different nations that were living there before they arrived.

What we can do, though, is remind ourselves that our country — unusually among the countries of the world — is founded on egalitarian ideas and imbued with concepts of universal human rights and that while we should take pride in that, it also imposes on us certain obligations.

MAGA against the West

Which brings us around to Rubio.

When I was in college, Samuel Huntington’s “The Clash of Civilizations” was a hot topic of discussion. He posited that with the Cold War over, the future of geopolitics would be “civilizational” conflict, in particular around the margins of the Muslim world and with the United States anchoring a Western civilization that needed to acknowledge that our ideas about things like democracy were not necessarily universal. Given how central Classical Greece is in the concept of “the West,” I always thought it was a little funny that Huntington defined modern Greece as outside the scope of Western civilization.

That’s because he (correctly) saw that relations between Russia and the West would not go well, which he interpreted as reflecting a civilizational divide between Orthodox Christianity and a Catholic/Protestant West. Consistency then required him to define Greece as non-Western. He also posited that Ukraine was part of the Russian-led Orthodox bloc. Huntington got the object-level question about Russia right, but he misdiagnosed the problem.

He also insisted that while Spain was part of the West, Spanish-speaking Catholics from Latin America were not and therefore Hispanic immigration posed a profound challenge to American identity. Rubio, like me, is a descendant of pre-Castro economic emigrants from Cuba who moved to the United States at a time when the borders between our country and the rest of the Western Hemisphere were nearly open.

I find Huntington’s effort to define a narrow West not only silly at times — Spain clearly has more in common culturally with Chile than with Latvia — but a fundamental misapprehension of what’s valuable about the Western tradition.

It has positive universalistic aspects such that a country like Ukraine can want to get in on them. Vladimir Putin has a very specific nationalist vision that makes it impossible for him to conceive of an independent Ukraine or of a Russia that would itself seek integration into the Western world. But if you know Russian intellectual history, you know that this debate between Westernizers and Slavophiles has been going on forever. And while Rubio is happy to fly to Athens and talk about American greatness and the importance of Western values, it’s clear that this administration is relentlessly hostile to helping the frontlines of the signature war for the defense of the West.

The official doctrine of the MAGA right is that this is because the real threat to Europe is from immigrants rather than from Russia.

There are serious problems with immigration in Europe. But as someone who cares about Western values, the biggest thing I worry about is that European liberals’ blundering on this issue is going to pass power over to parties like Alternative for Germany that are also hostile to European re-armament, to the defense of Ukraine, and to the fundamentals of democracy.

If Europeans want to elect immigration restrictionist parties like Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy, so be it. And I think it’s smart that Danish Social Democrats have moved to the center on this. But fundamentally, I don’t actually live in Europe. These are democratic countries, and they’re entitled to vote for whoever they want to.

As an American, I care primarily about the foreign policy choices of foreign democracies, and I want Europeans to elect pro-Ukraine Atlanticist parties that will try to cooperate with the United States on important issues. The idea of the American government deliberately promoting pro-Russian parties because it agrees with them about immigration is insane.

And yet, here we are.

A tradition worth defending

The other thing that I’ve had my eye on lately is that President Trump directed the federal government to start using taxpayer money to run election season ads boosting him. This became controversial — because it’s outrageous and obviously illegal — so he said he would reimburse the government for the costs. Then he flipped around and said he wouldn’t after all. Then a new tranche of ads started running. The latest thing I read is that he’s now again saying he will pay for the ads after all.

Is this the single worst thing anyone has ever done? No. Is it the worst thing Trump has done? Also no. Is it the worst thing that’s happened this fall? Almost certainly not.

But it’s so egregious in such obvious ways — don’t take my word for it, read Noah Rothman at National Review — that it’s just really hard to stomach being preached at about Pericles and the sacred nature of our traditions by a member of this administration.

The contemporary United States really is the heir to a long political tradition that predates current ideas about racial equality or democracy and that traces back before our Constitution to the English Civil War and ideas about the rule of law and the misappropriation of public funds. And Trump just clearly does not give a shit about any of it. The interest in American patriotism and the idea of the West does not extend beyond lending an air of grandiosity to the petty cruelty of deporting harmless Cubans to the Central African Republic.

There is zero real appreciation for any of our best traditions or ideas or what they mean; they’re just perpetrating a smash-and-grab operation on the country’s wealth.

I am mad as hell.

Yet to return to Power to the People, I don’t think you can defend American democracy or the rule of law or the basic humane interest in not seeing Medicaid and SNAP slashed while the administration cuts taxes for the rich and loots the Treasury for propaganda ads if you also accept the premise that the whole country is an illegitimate enterprise founded on theft.

It doesn’t make sense logically. It doesn’t work politically. It on some level fuels a kind of cynicism that just enables Trump and his gang of crooks.

We seem to be torn between a group of people who want to tear down the substance of all of our ideals and a group who want to tear down the notion that these ideals are worth having.

The latter camp is, I think, in practice quite small. At the end of the day, the festival ended with singing the song, even though Tom Morello gently threw it under the bus. But I think it’s actually worth everyone’s time to exert a little more tough-mindedness and to go with the rhetoric and ideas that make sense and can really win. MAGA is not going to save this country by tearing down everything that’s valuable in its traditions, and the resistance is not going to save it without displaying some real affection for it, either.

The Argument
You have to love America to save it
The philosopher Jean Baudrillard characterized the United States as “neither dream nor reality”; instead, he argued, it is “a hyperreality … a utopia which has behaved from the very beginning as though it were already achieved. Everything here is real and pragmatic, and yet it is all the stuff of dreams…

Elon Musk Shows Us Why Oligarchy is a Danger

Mega-billionaires are more dangerous to democracy than the merely rich

Paul Krugman
Oct 13
 
READ IN APP
 

Just a quick note of congratulations to Bob Hall and Mike Woodford for their richly deserved Nobel. I’ll write more another day. Also, for everyone saying that this isn’t a real Nobel: Indeed, the economics prize is just an award handed out by some Swedes. This is in contrast to the real Nobels, which are … just awards handed out by some Swedes.

In other words, don’t be that guy.

Today a relatively short note about how some political news bears on a controversy that has been brewing among some economists. Basically, some analysts are saying that we talk too much about mega-billionaires, and not enough about the merely very rich. Thus a new book by Owen Zidar and Eric Zwick, “The Everywhere Millionaire” — their Substack is here — points out that there are about 5 million Americans whose wealth exceeds $5 million. Of these, 3 million are what they call Main Street Millionaires, wealthy small business owners. And as they say, “Collectively, Main Street Millionaires have more than thirteen times the wealth of the Forbes 400.”

And they’re right that focusing only on the extremely (obscenely) rich misses the role played by wealthy small business owners.

Yet dismissing mega-billionaires — hey, they only own 4 percent or so of America — is deeply misleading, for these ultra-rich are at the heart of the rising power of big money in U.S. politics.

First, an economic observation: While the ultra-rich still don’t own as much of America’s wealthy as some may imagine, they have played a dominant role in the rising concentration of wealth.

Using data from realtimeinequality.org, the share of the top 1 percent — roughly corresponding to Zidar and Zwick’s definition of the wealthy — in U.S. wealth rose from 23.2 percent of total wealth in 1979 to 38.3 percent today. So one might think that the great rise in concentrated wealth was a “1 percent” phenomenon. But if we look at the changes in wealth share within the 1 percent, we find that very little of it involved the bottom 90 percent of that group, and most of it came from the top 0.01 percent — the one percent of the one percent:

The big rise in wealth concentration has come from the soaring wealth of a very small group, not the everyday millionaires.

And when it comes to political influence, billionaires wield power that vastly exceeds even their share of wealth. The Forbes 400 may only own 4 percent of U.S. wealth; but the New York Times found that 300 billionaires accounted for 19 percent of all reported federal campaign contributions in the 2024 election. And these are only reported, cash donations. Include other forms of influence — exemplified by Elon Musk’s purchase of Twitter and his conversion of the former public square into a site that elevates extreme right-wing propaganda — and it’s obvious that the malign political influence of a handful of the ultra-rich is much bigger than even those stunningly large donations suggest.

Now the Times reports that Musk is giving even more money in an attempt to help Republicans stave off midterm disaster than he gave in 2024:

Oh, and you won’t be surprised to learn that Musk repeatedly pushed a quickly refuted smear against James Talarico, the Democratic Senate nominee in Texas, and used his ownership of X, formerly Twitter, to amplify the smear.

Massive spending by Musk and other oligarchs probably won’t save Donald Trump’s party from a severe defeat — this time. And the vile smear against Talarico appears to be blowing up in Musk’s face (although how many voters heard the smear but never heard about its falsity?) But if Trump weren’t such a disaster as president, all that money might indeed have been effective.

And the only sustainable way to keep mega-billionaires from having so much power, so much ability to degrade democracy, is for them not to be so wealthy. Basically, a society that contains a class of ultra-wealthy oligarchs is well on its way to becoming a full-blown oligarchy.

So by all means let’s acknowledge that Musk, Bezos, Zuckerberg et al don’t own everything, that there are a lot of rich people who get less attention. But the oligarchs, not the Main Street Millionaires, are the clear and present danger to democracy.

Nerobefehl Nation

My fears for the next two years

Paul Krugman
Oct 14
 
READ IN APP
 

By the middle of March 1945 even Adolf Hitler knew that the war was lost. Soviet forces were within 45 miles of Berlin. American forces had crossed the Rhine and were well on their way to encircling the remaining German defenders. But Hitler didn’t believe that he had failed. He believed that he had been failed by the German people.

So on March 19 he issued the “Decree concerning demolitions in the Reich territory,” which has come to be known as the Nerobefehl or Nero decree. It ordered the destruction of Germany’s own infrastructure — supposedly to deny that infrastructure to the Allies, but the obvious purpose was to punish his own country.

Fortunately, Albert Speer and other Nazi officials didn’t carry out the order, although they apparently didn’t tell Hitler what was (not) happening.

Why am I recounting this history? Obviously because I’m thinking about what will happen after the midterms.

All indications are that Republicans are headed for massive defeat in elections that Trump has deliberately made a referendum on himself: “MAGA, pretend that I am on the ballot.” So what will he do when Americans show what they really think of him?

He will, of course, claim that the election was rigged and try to overturn the results. Assuming that he fails, however, then what?

Loss of Congress will limit Trump’s power, but by no means eliminate it. Above all, he will retain immense capacity to inflict destruction on America, not to mention America’s allies.

Over the past few days, according to President Zelenskyy, Ukraine has received no warning from the West about impending Russian missile strikes. This could reflect technical problems. But anyone dismissing the possibility that Trump is trying to punish Ukraine for daring to deny victory to his friend Vladimir Putin must have slept through the past two years.

At home, Trump officials suddenly cut down hundreds of trees at a public golf course in Washington. Trump has long wanted to remake that golf course to his own taste, but that’s unlikely to happen given the political winds, and in any case there was no need to rush the destruction. This was almost surely an act of spite, of deliberate act vandalism, undertaken precisely because Trump knows he won’t get his way.

And while a few hundred trees are not in themselves that big a deal, they represent the shape of things to come.

Think of the Kennedy Center, a national icon that Trump is destroying because he can’t put his own name on it, as the model for what is all too likely to happen to America over the next two years.

Can Democrats stop the coming reign of destruction? Unfortunately, a corrupt, partisan majority on the Supreme Court, invoking the “unitary executive” theory, has given Trump a huge amount of untrammeled power, especially because he is surrounded by minions — many approved by supine Republicans in Congress — who are willing, even eager to break the law. And he is also backed by oligarchs with vast resources who will continue to enable his attack on democracy even if their billions in political spending aren’t enough to buy this election.

But one thing Democrats can do is make it clear that everyone who aids and abets Trump in his Neroism can and will be held accountable to the full extent of the law. At this point anyone who says something like “We should look forward, not back” is making it significantly less likely that we will have anything to look forward to.

The right-wing obsession with “The Indian Question”

It’s not good!

Matthew Yglesias
Oct 14
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

Doing the podcast rounds to promote “One Billion Americans,” I was pleasantly surprised by how frequently I was able to get to yes with conservative hosts about immigration.

I would tell them that I broadly agreed with the view that illegal immigration should be taken seriously and that there are reasonable questions about the fiscal impact of low-earning immigrants.

But my counter was that there are hundreds of millions of people — 900 million in the latest Gallup survey — who say they’d like to leave the country they are currently living in. So it should be easy for a country like the United States to substantially increase the number of permanent residency slots we hand out while making all of the increase selective in the sense of bringing over people with above-average earnings.

I’m not going to tell you that every conservative I talked to loved this idea, but it was generally received warmly as a welcome alternative to progressive anti-patriotism or hostility to merit. I always did wonder, though, if they understood that in practice, this would mean a lot of people immigrating from South Asia.

I’ve been thinking about that a lot since Bo French, the G.O.P. nominee for railroad commissioner¹ in Texas, tweeted that “the problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined,” where “the problem” seemed to be students of South Asian ancestry attending a football game at the University of Texas. This remark generated quite a bit of backlash, and by happenstance, Democrats have a strong nominee opposing French in the form of Jon Rosenthal, a moderate veteran of the oil and gas industry who is not a gutter racist and who I hope Texans will elect in a few weeks.

Right-wingers who agree with French have, since that tweet, seemed to feel the need to come up with reasons why South Asian immigrants are bad. Hence the slightly bizarre spectacle of conservative pundits Jonathan Keeperman and Christopher Rufo doing a podcast on what they term “The Indian Question,” which Keeperman promoted by complaining that progressives have been able to “pathologize the desire for homogeneity and subdue any explicit political effort to maintain a white majority in the country.”

A lot of liberals are wondering what’s going on here. The Indian-American population, after all, is tiny. And this right-wing obsession with a small and successful group of people is exactly why my meeting of the minds with these conservative hosts felt so unstable — I think they were implicitly believing that an orderly and selective immigration system would only let white people in.

Conservatives raise a lot of specific objections to various subsets of immigrants — these people came illegally, those refugees are negatively selected, this family unification visa is a fiscal burden — but Indian-Americans overwhelmingly arrive through selective immigration pathways and are an elite group in the United States. According to Pew, Indian-Americans’ median household income is more than $150,000 and 77 percent of those 25 and older have a college degree. This is a great American success story, a clear benefit to the economy and the budget, and something you can’t raise a reasonable objection to other than — as Keeperman says — just objecting to ethnic change as such.

That’s an ugly sentiment that if indulged is going to lead to bad consequences for the country.

A Christian nation no more?

I think Keeperman slightly sold his own side of the argument short by referring to a desire for a “white majority.” What I think is even more true is that America’s identity as a Christian country is deeply important to a lot of conservatives.

Like most American Jews, I appreciate that conservatives tend to be polite about this and use the phrase “Judeo-Christian.” But we can’t help but notice that the mail doesn’t get delivered on Sunday and that schools are all closed on Christmas. The fact that it’s a Christian mass culture and not actually a “Judeo-Christian” one does not particularly bother me, but it’s a notable and real aspect of American life.

I also, as a person who is not Christian, don’t particularly believe in the importance of keeping it that way.

But I understand that others are going to disagree with that. I think that one important reason that Jewish presence in the United States has become uncontroversial with conservatives is that in the wake of the Holocaust and the foundation of Israel, the theoretical maximum Jewish population share in the United States is capped at a relatively low level. It’s not just that Jews are a small minority — we’re a minority that will always be small.

Back in the heyday of Ellis Island this was not the case. The Jewish share of the aggregate global population was much higher a century ago than it is today, and even though Zionism existed as a project and an ideology, on a practical level Jewish people had an overwhelming preference for moving to the United States rather than Palestine. Under those circumstances, Jewish immigration alarmed a lot of American restrictionists, and preventing Jews from coming here was one of the goals of the 1920s immigration clampdown.

Indian-Americans are a tiny number of people, but Indians in India are extremely numerous. I also don’t think the Bo Frenches of the world are very rigorously distinguishing between Indians, Pakistanis, and Bangladeshis, and the population of that whole region is absolutely enormous. Those countries are also poor enough that their residents are highly motivated to leave in a way that Italians or Germans aren’t.

So in a practical sense, even with a rigorously selective immigration system, there are lots of South Asians who’d qualify, and they will grow over time as a share of the population unless the United States either bluntly excludes them or else sharply curtails skilled immigration.

Raising “The Indian Question” is indelicate, but to serious nativists, it’s important because merely talking about illegal immigration or about immigrants who commit crimes or earn low wages or use welfare isn’t going to keep Indians out. Indian-American families are earning good livings, and their kids are doing well in school and attending flagship state universities and going to football games.

You either need to be willing to bite the bullet and say you’re eager to keep good people out or else you need to redefine good behavior as bad.

The turn against hard work

For a segment of the online right, the latter has become the preferred tactic. They argue that Americans are naturally repelled by hard work, that for example, it’s objectionable when Indian-Americans study for spelling bees.

@xwanyex
“You don’t study for the spelling bee” is a deep and important aspect of American culture. I was at a baseball game discussing some young players with a buddy one time and he said to me offhandedly, “hard work is fine, but nothing beats talent.” Americans have this sort of…
2:44 PM · Oct 5, 2026 · 1.76M Views
605 Replies · 331 Reposts · 6.48K Likes

This struck me as a particularly strange example because while natural talent is definitely real, I’m quite sure that studying hard is the only possible way to excel at a spelling bee. Most linguistic communities, as I understand it, don’t have contests of this kind because basically anyone literate in Italian or Finnish is going to know how to spell all the words. English spelling makes for an interesting game because there’s tons of stuff that has to be learned by brute force.

Keeperman on the podcast argued that “what actually makes America so dynamic — it’s not the kid who studies all night for the spelling-bee test. It’s the kid who is the fullback on the high-school football team, who puts his head down and is willing to run through a freaking wall on behalf of his teammates and then spends the night drinking beers at the kegger and wakes up in the morning and gets a 1500 on his SATs, okay?”

I’m a bit at a loss as to who we’re even talking about here.

It’s of course cooler to be smart and athletic rather than just smart. But everyone who’s good at anything works pretty hard at it. When I was in college, I got up unusually early, in part because I’m naturally kind of an early riser but in part because I wanted to spend a few hours blogging each day on top of my classes and the school paper. And the only other people I’d regularly see up that early were jocks. Ryan Fitzpatrick and Angie Ruggiero were way above the American population average in both athletic and academic achievements, and they worked extremely hard. And it’s not like only the very elite behave this way — my son wakes up at 4 a.m. to get to his 5 a.m. swim practices, and in the afternoons when he gets home from school he does extra math.

Far from being a country that places unusually little value on hard work, the United States is a global outlier in the number of people who say yes to the question of whether it’s important to work hard to get ahead in life.

I do want to be clear, though, because some people get a little turned around on this: My point here is not to valorize crazy aspects of grind culture or suggest that everybody needs to be spelling bee-maxxing all the time. I think a lot of immigrant parents are infamously excessively tough on their kids because they personally uprooted themselves to achieve a better life for their family and can be a little neurotic about ensuring their kids take every possible advantage of the situation. It’s definitely true that part of the multi-generational assimilation process is chilling out a little bit.

But in the grand scheme of things, having smart and hard-working people in the country is better than not having them.

A positive-sum world

On some level, this comes down to a positive-sum versus zero-sum mindset.

If you think of America as a fixed status hierarchy, then it’s true that smart South Asian kids can be a threat to your kids’ prospects. There’s only nine Supreme Court seats, and sooner or later, one of them is going to go to a person of South Asian ancestry. If Vivek Ramaswamy wasn’t the G.O.P. nominee for governor of Ohio, some white person probably would have gotten the gig. Indian immigration to Texas presumably does, in fact, make it harder for white kids to get into the flagship U.T. campus.

But it’s a serious error to see these zero-sum aspects of life as typical.

It is better to live in a country with more skilled surgeons, with more well-run businesses, with more smart engineers, and with more diligent middle managers. High-income people pay taxes and make Social Security and Medicare more sustainable. They are customers for other people’s work and businesses. I think most parents put too much weight on peer effects when thinking about their kids’ education, but all else being equal, you’d surely rather have studious classmates than unruly ones. And you’d rather have a school in your neighborhood than see it shut down and have to travel far away.

I’m not going to say you’re not “allowed” to just have a preference for homogeneity that trumps practical considerations.

I, personally, have a preference for diversity. The one summer I spent in Kerrville, Texas, one of the things I missed was having an Indian restaurant in town. But just as I have my preference, people can have a preference in the other direction.

What’s not okay is for them to wildly misportray the economic stakes. If someone is coming here from a foreign country and committing crimes, that’s bad. If they’re crowding out social assistance spending that could otherwise go to a native-born American, I get the complaint. But if not, their presence and economic activities are win-win. If they’re earning income in the top half of the distribution, they’re even making the structure of the labor market more egalitarian.

It’s not like America would instantly collapse without Arvind Krishna and Satya Nadella and Sundar Pichai and Vimal Kapur and Kal Penn and Mindy Kaling and Fareed Zakaria and Ajit Pai and Usha Vance and the other millions of successful Indian-Americans. But in the aggregate, being a place where talented and hard-working people move to is a boon to the United States, and the fact that we have a culture that is flexible enough to change over time is part of our success as a country.

The Trump administration’s ongoing effort to move beyond border security and interior enforcement to crack down on legal migration of skilled workers has been a really under-covered story with bad implications for American prosperity. And as much as it’s fair to get into the weeds of the exact details of program design, this “Indian Question” discourse really gives away the game here.

AI vs. the railroads

Are we in 1872?

Noah Smith
Oct 15
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

A little over a year ago, a bunch of people were worried that the AI data center boom would result in an epic bust, much like the railroad bust in 1873. I wrote about the possibility at the time:

Will data centers crash the economy?

Noah Smith
·
August 3, 2025
Read full story

The basic idea is that even if AI is an incredibly useful technology and creates enormous economic growth in the future, the people building the infrastructure (data centers) might borrow so much money that they can’t pay it back in time. Last summer, the AI industry’s revenue was growing, but not nearly as fast as the amount of money being spent. But the “hyperscalers” building the data centers were mostly spending their own cash instead of borrowing money, so the danger wasn’t imminent. The worry was mostly about the future — if spending continued to increase and revenue didn’t accelerate, there could be an 1873-style bust.

Well, now it’s the future, and two things happened. Spending did accelerate, and hyperscalers started having to borrow money to keep increasing their spending. But revenue accelerated even more. The release of Claude Code, Codex, and other agentic coding tools proved to be the “killer app” of AI, and suddenly Anthropic and (to a lesser extent) OpenAI were rolling in cash:

So like in summer 2025, we aren’t obviously heading for a big AI bust in the near future. But the stakes are higher now — because companies are borrowing a lot more money now, any slowdown in the torrid pace of AI revenue growth could cause a blowup.

The amounts of money being thrown around here are just staggering. A year and a half ago, the AI boom was still significantly smaller than the railroad boom of the late 1800s, as a percent of GDP. Now, there’s an active argument as to which one is bigger.

Which is bigger, AI or the railroads? (a pointless but fun debate)

This debate doesn’t really matter, because the basic message is just “Wow, it’s a lot of money.” But it’s fun to look at the numbers people are throwing around. Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh gives figures of 3.63% of GDP for AI and 2.24% of GDP for railroads:

But those percentages are over different amounts of time — the railroad boom lasted a very long time. According to some data sources, railroad spending peaked at around 5.4% of GDP:

And 19th century data are notoriously patchy and incomplete. Some sources claim much higher numbers for the railroad buildout:

Paul Graham
@paulg
There's never been an investment like the investment in railroads. (This graph has a log scale!)
12:40 PM · Apr 17, 2026 · 789K Views
227 Replies · 898 Reposts · 8.29K Likes

Nor do people agree on the size of the AI investment binge. Some sources yield numbers that are much lower than Van Nieuwerburgh’s:

Azeem Azhar
@azeem
Still baffled by AI capex? You should be. I still can't work out how van Nieuwerbergh's US estimate is 50% higher than others' global estimates, and what it would imply for chip sales in 2026. Not all exactly like for like below, but there is several hundred billion dollars
7:19 PM · Oct 13, 2026 · 8.05K Views
3 Replies · 8 Reposts · 42 Likes

As far as I can tell, the main difference here is assumptions about costs. The banks and ratings agencies are using announced dollar spending; Van Nieuwerburgh is using announced physical construction projects and then making assumptions about how much those projects will cost. The biggest reason he gets a higher number is that he assumes data centers are going to cost a lot more than the hyperscalers think.

Meanwhile, Dylan Patel claims over 6% for the AI boom already, once you include all types of AI-related infrastructure — fab equipment, chips, energy, and so on.¹

But whatever the correct numbers are, the basic point remains the same: AI is now one of the two biggest infrastructure booms in American history, by a large margin.

So it’s understandable that people are worried that the two booms could follow similar paths. For the railroads, that path included a big crash in 1873, which caused a huge decade-long depression in the U.S. economy. A lot of people are watching for something similar to happen with data centers, and the chorus of skeptical voices is beginning to swell again.

Hyperscalers are starting to borrow…a lot

OK anyway, on to the real point of this post. The flood of revenue that accompanied the rise of coding agents quieted the talk of an AI bubble for a while, but now it’s back. The first reason is the rise of AI-related debt. In the early years, the hyperscalers — data center builders like Amazon, Google, Meta, and Oracle — mostly paid in cash for the data centers. These companies get tons of cash from their software and cloud businesses, and they ended up spending most of it on AI infrastructure. But now the buildout has gotten so big that they’re having to borrow a bunch of money to keep ramping up spending:

For all of the hyperscalers except Microsoft, free cash flow either went negative in recent months or is expected to go negative late this year. This has been a giant boon for semiconductor companies — Nvidia, TSMC, and the rest:

All this debt creates a financial danger that didn’t exist before now. When they paid in cash, hyperscalers were safe — if AI revenue disappointed, their stock prices would go down, but their businesses would just keep going and they’d eventually recover their profitability. But the more hyperscalers borrow, the more revenue they’ll need just to stay solvent; if the revenue doesn’t arrive, they might have to default on their debt.

And that creates dangers for the U.S. economy as a whole. Corporate defaults by Oracle, Meta, or other big tech companies would rock the financial system, just as railroad defaults rocked it in 1873. Banks and other financial institutions would pull back lending, and a nasty recession would be likely. This is what Ben Bernanke’s most famous research was about, and there’s pretty good empirical evidence that the more debt is involved in a financial crash, the worse the economic pain that results.

The future of America’s big tech companies — and the short-term future of the economy itself — thus depends on whether the AI industry can generate absolutely enormous revenues for the hyperscalers.

Everyone is worried about AI revenue

How much revenue? Van Nieuwerburgh estimates that hyperscalers would need to earn $3.725 trillion of AI-related annual revenue by 2032. Assuming 4% nominal GDP growth, that comes out to about 9% of GDP. Hanno Lustig has a good blog post breaking down these numbers:

The Two Cents
Nine Percent of GDP.
When a new general purpose technology arrives (think railroads, electricity, the internet, etc), this is typically accompanied by a huge boom in infrastructure investment, as private investors start building the infrastructure that is needed to deploy this new technology. We are currently experiencing on of these GPT-fueled investment boom in the U.S…
Read more
18 days ago · 86 likes · 13 comments · Hanno Lustig

Here’s his chart, using Van Nieuwerburgh’s data:

Lustig argues that this is probably an underestimate of the size of the required revenue. It assumes that the chips in the data centers last 6 years, while in fact they often last only 3 years or less. Lustig shows how changing this assumption dramatically increases the fraction of GDP that hyperscalers will have to capture:

One factor Lustig and Van Nieuwerburgh both seem to miss, however, is that the 4% assumption for the NGDP growth rate is probably too low. In fact, NGDP is currently growing around 5%, and has been growing at least that fast for a while now:

If the AI boom accelerates real GDP growth by just 1 percentage point, and inflation stays at around 3% (which seems likely given high government deficits and red-hot demand from the data center boom itself), then 6% seems more reasonable than 4%. So that will push down the percentage of GDP that hyperscalers need to capture.

Also, hyperscalers don’t actually need to get a 10% rate of return on their investments in order to pay back their debt. That 10% number is a guess at a required rate of return — the return needed to (theoretically) justify the companies’ current stock prices. The actual interest rate that the companies are borrowing at is more like 4.5% to 7.5%. That will also push down the hyperscalers’ required revenue.

So Van Nieuwerburgh’s estimates are probably a little bit high, and Lustig’s are very high. Jared Bernstein and Ryan Cummings do their own calculation and find that hyperscalers’ required revenue peaks at only about 2/3 of Van Nieuwerburgh’s number:

5 to 6 percent of GDP is still big, but a lot less daunting than 9 to 14 percent!

That’s the good news. Now here’s the bad news: Whether hyperscalers need to capture 5-6% or 9-14% of GDP, that’s less than the total amount of GDP that the AI industry as a whole needs to capture in order to pay all that debt back. Remember that hyperscalers like Amazon and Google sell compute to modeling companies like Anthropic and OpenAI, who then sell AI services to customers. Unless they skate by on the knife-edge of unprofitability, Anthropic and OpenAI are going to take their cut before they pay the hyperscalers.

So the total amount that customers have to pay for American AI in order for hyperscalers to pay back their debt is actually more than the amount that hyperscalers have to earn. Greg Ip points out that 9% of GDP is a lot more than we spend on energy, or construction, or the computer industry as a whole. Well, if 9% is how much hyperscalers need, then AI as a whole needs even more.

Whether that’s plausible or not is a difficult question. But you can see why everyone is worried about AI revenue numbers, and why they’re anxiously watching the latest data for signs that the great AI spending binge of 2026 is winding down.

Is AI revenue sputtering?

We may now be seeing the first such signs. Ramp, an AI finance company, estimates that AI spending by the businesses it tracks hit a ceiling a couple of months ago:

As you can see from that chart, it’s not that businesses are using AI less — in fact, they’re using it more and more. But they’re beginning to bargain-hunt. For one thing, instead of shelling out big bucks for the latest and greatest version of Claude Code or ChatGPT, they’re trying out cheaper models:

They’re also switching between models more often, a clear sign of bargain-hunting:

Basically, it looks like there are a few companies spending huge amounts of money on AI, and it’s these companies that are suddenly hunting for bargains:

22 Replies · 27 Reposts · 209 Likes

These companies are the ones now bargain-hunting. Not only does this mean switching to cheaper models, but it’s also creating a price war between Anthropic, OpenAI, and a bunch of other companies like Google and SpaceX trying to catch them (and Chinese models, of course), as they all jockey for market share.

And these early heavy adopters might not be replaced by other “tokenmaxxers”. AI adoption looks like it might be plateauing, at least at the big labs:

The simplest explanation here is that it just takes a lot of time for companies to figure out how to use new tools. It took businesses decades to learn how to use electricity, railroads, computers, and the internet. AI is arguably even weirder and more disruptive than those previous revolutionary technologies; it’s likely that almost no one can even imagine what an AI-native business model looks like yet. So businesses are trying to shoehorn these incredibly powerful tools into their existing workflows, and the ROI from that sort of activity is OK but not spectacular.

That’s a hypothesis, of course. But it seems to have a lot of people on edge. When OpenAI reported that its annual run rate revenue is only $50 billion instead of the $68 billion that some had expected, a bunch of tech stocks fell, including Nvidia and some hyperscalers. Some sources, meanwhile, are reporting that Anthropic’s revenue growth has slowed:

That’s a third-party estimate, so take it with a grain of salt. But Anthropic’s own quarterly reports show annualized revenue increasing by less than 50% from Q2 to Q3, after more than doubling from Q1 to Q2. That’s still impressive growth, but also a big deceleration. Some analysts are claiming that Anthropic’s run rate revenue will surge again to $110 billion by the end of the year, but that remains to be seen, and others are very skeptical.

OpenAI and Anthropic’s revenue matters because if they don’t get paid, then the hyperscalers don’t get paid either. In the short term, the hyperscalers have some protection, as the labs have signed agreements to pay for compute whether or not it ends up being used. But in the longer term, hyperscalers can’t survive and pay back their debts if their main customers aren’t thriving.

That brings us to the final big question: Will AI labs have more of a moat than the railroads did?

Which has more of a moat, AI or the railroads?

A company’s “moat” is just a term for its ability to sustain profitability. This could be a network effect, a strong brand, hoarding of key talent, regulatory protection, intellectual property, etc.

The lack of a moat turned out to be a big problem for the railroads. Theoretically, owning a transportation network lets you make money with a network effect — smaller rail networks can’t compete because they don’t serve as many locations. For utilities, this network effect is so powerful that we usually don’t allow them to operate in a fully competitive environment.

But for railroads, network effects proved difficult to exploit. When you transport cargo, you don’t have to stay within one company’s rail network — it might cost a bit of money, but you can move the cargo from one railroad to another, or even to a different mode of transit like a boat. That fact encouraged a lot of competition between railroads. A bunch of different companies built parallel lines between major hubs in the boom of the 1870s, which drove down prices. Meanwhile, a series of state and federal laws in the 1880s required railroads to allow competitors to physically connect to their networks, which reduced their ability to exclude competitors.

As a result of both oversupply and competition, the price of railroad transportation plummeted in the 1860s and 1870s, and never recovered:

Although some railroad tycoons like Cornelius Vanderbilt did get rich, most of the value created by rail was captured by the companies who used rail to move their freight from one city to another.

For the AI labs, and the hyperscalers who depend on their business, the fundamental problem is similar — competition threatens to allow businesses to use AI cheaply. That means AI would still create a ton of economic value, but as in the days of the railroads, most of that value would flow to the users instead of the techies and infrastructure-builders. In fact, some people think this will happen — a research group called New Constructs just released a scathing report casting doubt on Anthropic’s ability to increase profit margins, and arguing that the top AI lab is worth much less than its IPO valuation of $2 trillion.

What moat can the AI labs use to prevent profits from collapsing? They don’t really have a network effect — whether I use Claude Code or Codex doesn’t really depend on who else is using it. They have brand value, but the rise in model-shopping shows that brand value has limits. Simple first-mover advantage conveys some profits — there are some adversarial applications like cybersecurity and quant trading, in which having the very best model is a necessity. But for most use cases, consumers are going to shop around for the cheapest good-enough provider — just like they did for railroads.

My suspicion is that the people inside the AI labs believe that their models themselves are the moat. This deserves a much longer post, but I suspect that the people who run Anthropic believe that Claude will soon be so smart that it will be able to simply take over any business it wants — Claude insurance, Claude factories, Claude entertainment, Claude real estate, and so on. Competing companies will have AI too, of course, but they won’t have the smartest, latest Claude — that Claude will be reserved for Anthropic’s exclusive use.

So perhaps if Anthropic stays ahead of the competition, the true frontier Claude can simply outsmart every other business (and government) in existence, and generate enough cash to keep funding the best research and keep Claude ahead of all rivals. The folks at OpenAI, meanwhile, probably believe that if they can seize the lead back from Anthropic, then GPT will confer them a similar supremacy.

It’s hard to say whether that will work or not. But even if it eventually does, Anthropic and OpenAI may not be able to spin up all those business lines before the data center boom becomes unsustainable. Already, there are some worrying signs. CoreWeave, a “neocloud” company — basically a mini-hyperscaler — is suddenly in big trouble:

CoreWeave shares plunged as much as 17% on Wednesday, the biggest drop since February. Its debt due in 2032, which investors bought at par four months ago, traded at less than 78 cents on the dollar…Credit-default swaps on the company are pricing in a more than 50% chance of default within the next five years…

CoreWeave has drawn outsized attention for being an early entrant in the business that has been heavily reliant on the high-yield debt markets to finance its buildout. Worries have seeped into the bonds backing data centers tied to CoreWeave, with at least seven such securities trading lower this week…

As the largest public company among so-called neoclouds, the company’s growth has served as a barometer for AI demand and as a proxy for concerns of a slowdown.

This probably isn’t the equivalent of the failure of Northern Pacific Railroad in 1873, which touched off the great railroad bust. But it could be the harbinger of more dramatic disruptions to come.

An AI bust wouldn’t spell the end of AI, of course, any more than the bust of 1873 spelled the end for the railroads or for the industrial age as a whole. In fact, the railroad boom of the early 1870s was only the first of several, with two later booms being even bigger:

Even if there’s a bust, AI will still keep getting better, and the infrastructure for the technology will keep getting built. This technology is for real — it’s the most powerful and important thing invented in our lifetimes, and it will end up utterly transforming our world in ways we can barely begin to imagine. This is just the beginning.

But before that all happens, we might have a little bit of financial and economic chaos.

Financial disclosure: I own shares in a number of AI-related startups. It’s not clear which of these would suffer in a general AI bust, but probably a lot of them would.

Subscribed

Share

1

In fact, Dylan’s estimate may involve some double-counting, because it measures total spending instead of value added. If a company pays Anthropic $1000 to use Claude, and Anthropic pays $800 of that to Amazon for compute, and Amazon pays $600 of that to Nvidia for chips, and Nvidia pays TSMC $400 to actually make the chips, total investment is $1000, not $2800. You can get that by looking at the spend on the final product, or adding up each company’s revenue and subtracting its costs to find its value added. But if you add up all categories of “AI-related spending” in this chain, it’s $2800. I also suspect that similar double-counting is behind Paul Graham’s extremely high estimate of railroad spending, but I can’t locate the source of his numbers.

The perils of organizing chum

Why anti-Israel protestors are targeting New York’s anti-Zionist mayor

The perils of organizing chum

Matthew Yglesias
Oct 15
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

After you’ve read today’s post, I hope you’ll check out the latest episode of “The Argument” podcast, where Jerusalem and I debate which historical figures deserve to be canceled — and which deserve a comeback. Paid subscribers can watch or listen ad free and read the transcript and show notes here. Free subscribers can watch the episode on YouTube here or listen wherever you get your podcasts.

Subscribe: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts

Zohran Mamdani, as mayor of New York City, is not really a key actor in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.

Conversely, handling the Israeli-Palestinian conflict is not very high up on the list of things within his area of responsibility. But he is central to the symbolic politics of Israel within the United States of America because he’s both a vocal and uncompromising anti-Zionist and mayor of the city that has long been the center of Jewish-American political, economic, and cultural power.

So I’m not particularly surprised that Mamdani found himself heckled by anti-Israel protestors who shouted “We charge you with genocide” when he attended an October 7 vigil. This happened in part because the global Palestinian activist movement is full of people with extreme views. But the specific thing they’re asking for here — a new police commissioner and a disbanding of the N.Y.P.D. unit that does crowd control at protests — is not per se extreme. It just seems tangential to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.

These activists are picking a nasty fight with a guy who seems to be mostly on their side about something that seems low stakes because of a larger structural theory of organizing and political power, one that is widespread in left activist circles but I think is consistently misunderstood and under-explained in journalistic circles, even by those with deep left-wing sympathies. Mehdi Hasan, for example, whose views on the substance of the conflict are much closer to the protestors’ than they are to mine, is baffled by this.

Mehdi Hasan
@mehdirhasan
If you’re protesting and blaming *checks notes* Zohran Mamdani for the Gaza genocide you may, you just may, need to check yourself into a mental health facility.
Chris Sommerfeldt @C_Sommerfeldt
Pro-Palestinian protesters gather outside City Hall to call out Mayor Zohran Mamdani for what they see as his betrayal of the movement. "Mayor Mamdani, you can't hide we charge you with genocide" was a chant that just rang out.
3:11 AM · Oct 8, 2026 · 962K Views
1.03K Replies · 2.82K Reposts · 36.5K Likes

Mamdani, after all, is very plainly not personally responsible for Israeli military action in Gaza, so why would you pretend that he is? He’s also not even remotely the pivotal actor in American foreign policy. Why would you protest the mayor of New York City when he agrees with you rather than the foreign policy officials who don’t? One possible explanation is that the protestors are dumb and don’t understand that their theory of blame attribution doesn’t make sense.

Mehdi Hasan
@mehdirhasan
The dumbest people in the world
Peter Sterne @petersterne
Mamdani is stone-faced as the protesters call him a traitor and sellout.
4:22 PM · Oct 8, 2026 · 622K Views
1.2K Replies · 832 Reposts · 15.9K Likes

I agree with Hasan that this approach of targeting Mamdani is not a good way to do politics. But dismissing it as “dumb” is a mistake.

The activists are deploying a playbook that left-wing activists use across different issue areas in a way that connects pretty deeply to their overall view about how politics works. They’re aware that there is no short-term pathway to transform American policy toward Israel, but they don’t want to just tell everyone to go home for two years and worry about it then. So they’re picking some short-term political fights over the way the N.Y.P.D. handles protests and the identity of the police commissioner, demanding that Mamdani fire Jessica Tisch and replace her with some unknown alternative.

The fact that Mamdani is so well-regarded by so many progressives that many outside of activist circles are inclined to see this move as irrational is, I think, a teachable moment and worth a conversation about whether the broader arc of left-wing activist strategy makes sense.

Activists pick fights to drive more organizing

The underlying ideas in play here have nothing to do with the particulars of Palestine, New York City, or Mamdani and instead relate to a broader theory of political organizing.

If you read Saul Alinsky’s “Rules for Radicals,” for example, the whole idea is that you need to build political power outside the arena of electoral politics and the way to do this is through picking specific fights that may only relate tangentially to your ultimate policy goals.

On his list of rules are items like number two, “never go outside the experience of your people,” number eight, “keep the pressure on,” and number 13, “pick the target, freeze it, personalize it, and polarize it.”

Back in Barack Obama’s second term, when people were arguing about the Keystone XL pipeline, I was deeply confused as to why so much of the climate movement had pivoted away from talking about things that could have a major impact on the world’s long-term emissions trajectory and toward fighting about a pipeline whose actual climate implications were minuscule.

David Roberts at the time explained this to me and others as a gap between wonk logic and activist logic.

The wonks saw Keystone as a distraction from more important things and found it perverse to be picking fights with Obama (who broadly favored climate action) rather than with Republicans (who did not). But activist logic, as Roberts writes, does not see activist campaigns as expenditures of political capital; it sees them as opportunities to build strength.

“There are benefits to an activated, impassioned constituency and the social and political machinery that brings them together in large numbers,” he wrote, and “intensity is built through conflict, through the drawing of political and moral lines.”

To me, that line-drawing exercise always felt unfair. You had the most visible faces of the climate movement painting Obama as this awful bad guy on climate because he was reluctant to expend political capital on an anti-pipeline campaign that was marginal to climate change. Similarly, the proximate thing that activists are demanding Mamdani do is fire New York’s well-regarded police commissioner — a move that has a fair amount of downside political risk and no real upside for him.

It would be one thing to ask him to run a big risk for the sake of dramatically transforming the situation in Palestine, but obviously, changing the leadership at the N.Y.P.D. isn’t going to accomplish that. The cost of personalizing and polarizing a fight is that you end up misstating the stakes in a way that has never sat well with me.

That said, the core inspiration for a lot of left-wing work in the United States is the civil rights movement. And you can certainly imagine someone sitting around in 1955, wondering whether the question of seating arrangements on the bus in Montgomery, Ala., is really the main question about racial justice in the United States. And moderates within the civil rights camp absolutely did raise objections to the whole idea of a 1963 March on Washington, specifically on the grounds that it didn’t make sense to make life more difficult for the Kennedy administration, which was broadly on their side.

The general theory of the bus boycott, though, was that picking a concrete winnable fight was not going to be a “distraction” from the larger cause but an opportunity to get lots of people involved and build more power. I think that anchoring on the civil rights movement is a mistake — that the movement is such a striking example precisely because the dynamics around it are historically unusual — but it’s not crazy or stupid to take inspiration from it. That’s a deep and profound idea worth taking seriously.

Why the left picks fights with friends over small beer

In a world with a lot of partisan polarization (unlike the 1950s and 1960s), one thing that makes these activist campaigns so contentious is that they tend to involve activists protesting their friends rather than their enemies. That feels a little perverse. But the basic organizing logic is that to have a compelling fight:

  1. You always need to be asking for something from someone.

  2. The someone has to be someone whose reputation you can wreck.

  3. The something has to be something the someone can give you.

The case against picking a fight with Mamdani about the police commissioner is that (a) Mamdani is an ally of the movement and (b) the identity of the police commissioner has basically nothing to do with conditions on the ground in Palestine. But the case for it is that Mamdani clearly has the power to do this and Mamdani has built a lot of his political identity around the idea that he is an ally of the Palestinian cause. If you can make a lot of people think that his management of the N.Y.P.D. constitutes a betrayal of Palestine, that has a meaningful impact on his political standing. Marco Rubio and Donald Trump and JD Vance don’t claim to be allies of Palestine, so pro-Palestinian activists saying things about them doesn’t hurt them.

If you want to flex short-term muscle, you need to target someone you can hurt, and that means a friend rather than an enemy. And if you target a friend, you need to pick something under his control, which in this case means blowing the stakes out of proportion.

Subscribed

We saw that with Obama and Keystone. We also saw it during the 2020 presidential campaign when pressure was (successfully) brought to bear on Democratic candidates to come out in favor of a “deportation moratorium.”

The idea was that you shouldn’t let Democrats off the hook by allowing them to just say they were in favor of a path to citizenship for millions of long-term unauthorized residents, because whether this happened was subject to dynamics in Congress. You had to ask them for something objectively less important that they could unilaterally deliver because that’s a proper organizing target.

Similarly, there was a lot of focus during the early years of Joe Biden’s administration on executive action to unilaterally cancel student debt. From a wonk viewpoint, it was a distraction from systemic reform of higher education finance. But from an activist viewpoint, it was important to have a concrete fight with the Biden administration and not get bogged down in the vagaries of legislation.

I think it’s important to understand this logic not because I agree with it but because it’s worth appreciating just how widespread it is.

And while activism as a genre of activity can be very helpful in specific situations, it’s actually not a good idea to take the civil rights movement as a model for political change. The activist viewpoint on these specific controversies isn’t exactly wrong; it’s more that Do More Activism is wrong as a general approach to politics.

Rules for meliorists

I think this whole episode is really interesting. As someone who doesn’t really agree with Mamdani’s takes on Israel but who also acknowledges that pro-Israel politics is fading fast in the United States, it feels obvious to me that one of the best things that could possibly happen for AIPAC would be for Mamdani to screw up some totally unrelated aspect of New York City governance.

Fundamentally, his success or failure as a mayor is not going to hinge on anything he says or does about Israel, but when winners win, that generates a positive halo for everything they’re associated with.

By the same token, successful campaigns to push Obama and Hillary Clinton to take political risks on climate and immigration ultimately helped elect Trump in 2016.

Conversely, I think that if Mary Peltola and James Talarico can win elections in Alaska and Texas on platforms that emphasize their support for American oil and gas production but that also acknowledge the existence of climate change as a real problem that deserves solutions, that will be a huge win for climate as a substantive policy issue.

I know some people in climate world who believe that the drift of activist energy away from climate and toward Palestine has been bad for climate as a cause. I actually think it’s potentially quite good for climate as a cause because it’s created space for politicians like Martin Heinrich and Sheldon Whitehouse to engage in pragmatic deal-making. The smart thing to do politically is normally to identify your champions — Mamdani on Palestine, Whitehouse on climate, etc. — and then let them cook. I think YIMBYs keep putting legislative wins on the board by trying to have a good attitude about incremental change rather than coming up with new demands to put on Scott Wiener.

I do want to acknowledge, though, that these are not just tactical disagreements.

The rise of interest in pro-Palestinian activism has unquestionably been bad for climate activism. I think it’s been neutral-to-positive for progress on climate change because I don’t think activism is as helpful as its proponents believe. But activists, of course, do believe in activism, so telling them “just do nothing and let Zohran handle the police department however he wants” is not very compelling. And while I think the civil rights movement is more the exception that proves the rule than a model for others to emulate, I do understand why people want to align themselves with the spirit of the single most high-profile and morally urgent campaign for progressive change in American history.

Accusing Mamdani of complicity in genocide is a kind of reductio ad absurdum of this whole approach to politics, but it really does follow from the broader logic.

On Inflation, Trump Snatched Defeat from the Jaws of Victory

There’s no way to shift the blame this time

Paul Krugman
Oct 15
 
READ IN APP
 

One of the great ironies of American politics is that Donald Trump won the 2024 election basically because a significant number of credulous voters believed his promises to bring prices down beginning on “day one.”

What actually happened was that America, along with the rest of the world, experienced a temporary surge in inflation in 2021-22, mainly because of the lingering effects of Covid disruptions. And voters still blamed Joe Biden for that surge.

But by 2024 the war against inflation had been largely won, at startlingly low cost — the recession many analysts claimed would be necessary to get inflation down never happened, but inflation came way down anyway.

And then Trump snatched defeat from the jaws of victory.

There is still some controversy among economists about how much responsibility Biden administration policies bear for the 2021-22 inflation surge. My view is, very little. But there is no question who is responsible for the resurgence in inflation: this is all on Trump, first the tariffs and then then the Iran war.

And there’s a big risk that the succession of inflation shocks will do what the post-Covid shock didn’t: get entrenched in expectations, so that we will need a recession to get inflation back down.

I’m in Oxford, giving the James Martin Memorial Lecture this afternoon. So that’s all for today.

The Bad News on Inflation Just Keeps Coming

And it’s all about Trump

Paul Krugman
Oct 16
 
READ IN APP
 

War is peace. Freedom is slavery. Ignorance is strength. Inflation is down. Or at least that’s what Donald Trump says.

I wrote yesterday, following the release of the latest Consumer Price Index, that Trump had snatched inflation defeat from the jaws of victory. Now the Bureau of Labor Statistics has released its other inflation measure, the Producer Price Index, which measures wholesale prices, and it was even worse, running substantially hotter than forecasters expected:

My basic point — that Trump inherited a relatively benign inflation picture and threw that inheritance away with his tariffs and war — is even clearer from the PPI than the CPI. And the PPI is often a leading indicator of future consumer prices, so there’s no relief visible in the near future.

There’s no mystery about what’s going on: it’s mostly about the prices of petroleum products, especially diesel. Diesel prices have risen more than twice as much as gasoline prices over the past year — and the rising price of diesel cascades through the economy, raising business costs and driving inflation across a wide range of products.

But didn’t Trump just make a deal to buy Russian diesel? Yes, and it was shameful. It was also ineffective: Even if Putin can deliver the fuel, which is doubtful — the Ukrainians have resumed their strikes on Russian refineries — the quantity was much too small to make much difference. Indeed, wholesale diesel prices remain significantly higher than they were at the height of the shooting war with Iran, let alone before Trump started that war:

In any case, Trump’s response to the dismal inflation news — even worse for him politically because of the extravagant promises he made in the past — is denial: He keeps insisting that inflation is way down. Is he deliberately lying, or does he truly not know what’s going on? We shouldn’t rule out the latter possibility. Bear in mind that Trump doesn’t read, and he certainly doesn’t read BLS data releases. And while he presumably has aides who do know what the numbers say, are they willing to tell him things he doesn’t want to hear? Probably not.

Then again, I may be making a category error. As far as I can tell, Trump doesn’t believe that there is such a thing as objective truth, there’s only what he wants to be true. Hence my Orwell reference at the top of this piece. Trump doesn’t have the full powers of a totalitarian ruler, but often behaves as if he did (and is enabled in that behavior by almost the entire GOP.) And Orwell wrote about the mutability of history under totalitarian regimes:

If the Leader says of such and such an event, ‘It never happened’ – well, it never happened.

In this case what never happened was surging inflation.

But while Trump is surrounded by lackeys willing to deny reality, according to the latest Fox News poll, 55 percent of voters say that inflation is “not at all” under control — and that includes 30 percent of Republicans.

Inflation won’t be the only issue in the midterms. That same Fox News poll shows voters even more concerned about “corruption in government.” But that is also not exactly a source of Republican strength.

If these numbers don’t generate a blue wave, nothing will.

I have another day of playing academic statesman at Oxford, so that’s it for today.
