Our culture is way too eager to embrace deception

We desperately need to rebuild an ethic of probity and integrity.

Matthew Yglesias
Oct 20
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

This post discusses “You Can See Everything” in some detail. If you have somehow avoided spoilers to this point but are also interested in seeing a highly touted three-hour documentary, I would strongly suggest you go see the movie first before reading the article. The upside is that if you haven’t seen the movie and don’t want to or don’t care about spoilers, I think you should understand the article and its argument just fine. Consider yourself spoiler-warned!

At one point in the brilliant new documentary “You Can See Everything,” Nathan Fielder is pressing Elizabeth Holmes on her honesty, and she preposterously proclaims not only that she was honest about everything that happened with Theranos but that she’s never lied, ever, about anything.

In this moment more than any other we can see that she must be a truly sociopathic liar, because nobody would say something that obviously false. And Fielder really presses her: You never told a white lie? You never said you couldn’t make it to a party because you were feeling sick when actually you just didn’t want to go?

She kind of relents at that point, suggesting she didn’t really mean that kind of lie.

Which is striking because her insistence on her own honesty deprives her of the best possible defense of her conduct, namely the clear reality that lots of successful entrepreneurs lie.

Whatever line divides Elizabeth Holmes, a criminal, from any number of successful and celebrated tech C.E.O.s, it cannot actually be that she said things about her product and her company that aren’t true. Just as we’ve all told white lies to get out of awkward social situations, basically everyone in Silicon Valley is telling some whoppers.

In other words, while almost everyone agrees that lying is bad and you shouldn’t do it, it’s also the case that everybody lies. That’s true to the point that the most obviously dishonest thing a person could do, genuinely, is claim to never lie. And yet, despite the universality of this behavior, I think we’ve come to a point where we’re too tolerant of dishonesty — and, even more so, willfully misleading behavior.

Tech entrepreneurs say lots of stuff that isn’t true

I’m wildly more literal-minded and less creative than Fielder or Lance Oppenheim, so if I were to produce something about Holmes, it would be about my obsession with the fact that she was operating in an industry where people are constantly saying things that aren’t true.

I don’t know anything specific about the Alex Gibney documentary on Elon Musk, but it’s by all accounts a very negative portrait of Musk, and I don’t see how any negative portrait of Musk could avoid the fact that he says a lot of things that aren’t true. Musk’s aspirations for self-driving cars, for example, are a notorious cesspool of overpromising and underdelivering:

And yet, it is also true that in 2026, the Tesla self-driving features are extremely impressive. Tesla provides the best vehicle autonomy available in a consumer car product, and it’s second best behind Waymo in terms of developing an autonomous taxi service. It’s not clear to me that Musk is right that his approach to developing this technology will beat the Google/Waymo approach, but it’s also not clear to me that he’s wrong.

Similarly, SpaceX has been consistently behind Musk’s promised timelines. But if somehow Musk had never spoken in public about SpaceX and just released the products, then I think everyone would agree that the rockets work and Starlink works and it’s all very impressive.

As Musk has become an increasingly political figure, his habit of lying has shifted into increasingly political terrain, which makes him seem increasingly villainous.

But Steve Jobs was also a notorious overpromiser who nonetheless really did deliver impressive technology. As a journalist who is aware of the tech industry but doesn’t really cover it professionally, it’s clear that this kind of whopper is an endemic business strategy. I don’t think you’d reasonably say that Apple or SpaceX are fraudulent business enterprises. But it’s also the case that part of how business gets done in the tech field is you need to paint these glorious visions of the triumphant future, and it doesn’t always work out.

This is not to say that Musk’s behavior was identical to Holmes’s — this was actually litigated and a court ruled that a certain amount of “corporate puffery” is an acceptable, non-fraudulent business practice. Musk’s cars and rockets work; Theranos’s product didn’t. But I do think this culture of hype and overstatement is important context for Holmes’s behavior, along with the evident desire not just in the media but among investors to get behind a heroic female founder.

It also made me think about a more recent fraudster, Sam Bankman-Fried, who pulled a con that was if anything more egregiously illegal.

In contrast to Holmes insisting to Fielder that she would never lie about anything, part of how Bankman-Fried tricked people (certainly including me) is that he was pretty open about the fact that he was a bit shady. His infamous explanation to Matt Levine of “yield farming” made smart people (or at least me) trust him more rather than less because it seemed like he wasn’t insulting our intelligence.

Even in retrospect, I find the whole episode extremely vexing because looking back, the Apollo Program for Biodefense that he was trying to get Congress to enact was a really good idea and FTX’s investment in Anthropic would have paid off enormously had Bankman-Fried gotten away with his scam. FTX’s valuation peaked at $32 billion in 2022 and the Anthropic shares it owned would be worth $75 billion today if they hadn’t been sold in a bankruptcy auction.

That’s not to defend Holmes or Bankman-Fried (whose fraud was, if anything, more egregious) but just to emphasize that there’s a wide range of “fake it ’til you make it” practices out there in the business world, some of which are more legal than others and some of which do pay off.

The era of “reality”

The film does not explore any of this wider context. Instead, it dives deeper into questions about the nature of truth.

In the second half of the film, Fielder collaborates with Amanda Seyfried, who portrayed Holmes in a Hulu dramatization of the Theranos story. The film includes both Fielder’s (supposedly) real interactions with the real Seyfried and Seyfried re-enacting conversations that Fielder had with Holmes but could not film because she was in prison at the time. Fielder also confronts Seyfried with the fact that the events portrayed in “The Dropout” are not 100 percent accurate, which makes her a little defensive, but she says it’s just television. This, I think, raises the question of whether the re-enactments that Seyfried and Fielder stage are, in fact, accurate depictions of the conversations they purport to be documenting.

We seem to have a consensus in society that what Holmes did (lying for personal gain) is not okay but that introducing fictional elements into a “based on a true story” miniseries for personal gain is totally fine.

I personally am not so sure about this.

I watched and enjoyed “The Social Network” when it came out, but I think the power of the film is considerably compromised by the fact that in the real world, Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan have been dating since before TheFacebook launched. It doesn’t change the fact that it’s a well-made movie on a lot of levels, but to me ranking it the 10th best movie of the 21st century (like the New York Times did) or even the best movie of the century (like “The Big Picture” did) is a little bit crazy. “Citizen Kane” is inspired by the life of William Randolph Hearst, but it does not present itself as a documentary about William Randolph Hearst. It’s about Charles Foster Kane, a fictional character.

I think it’s cheating to add weight and significance to your character study by saying it’s about a real person but then add depth to your character study by making up critical facts.

Part of the strangeness of the documentary is that while co-director Lance Oppenheim is a documentary filmmaker, Fielder just isn’t. “Nathan for You” and “The Rehearsal” are unscripted and feature real people rather than actors, but they’re not news shows or documentaries. They’re closer to the spirit of what we’ve come to know as reality television, which is fake — it just doesn’t involve professional actors or screenwriters.

The current president of the United States, of course, was a very successful reality TV personality before he was a politician. And I’m sort of obsessed with the fact that a guy who is transparently a huge liar is often praised by his supporters for authenticity.

On the left, too, people who want to underplay the importance of issue-positioning often talk about the value of authenticity. Clearly the thing that people call “authenticity” is in fact a relevant political skill. But Donald Trump is a critical illustration of the fact that the actual skill here is not being authentic; it’s acting. Seyfried-as-Holmes seems much more authentic — which is to say relaxed, un-mannered, and natural — than Holmes as herself. That’s because Seyfried has been acting professionally for her whole adult life and she’s very good at it. A normal person’s authentic reaction to being asked questions on camera is to be nervous and weird.

Accurate information is important

Probably my worst take ever was that back in 2010 I defended advocates making overstated ridership estimates for high-speed rail projects on the grounds that investing in high-speed rail was a good idea and that the advocates on the other side were also being dishonest so it didn’t really make sense to insist on unilateral disarmament.

The vast majority of people, I think, manage to avoid ever stating “lying is fine” as baldly as I did.

But I also think it’s pretty clear that the vast majority of the people involved in funding political advocacy organizations — on most sides of most issues — have decided that the stakes of politics are so high and their enemies so low and unprincipled that the only way to succeed is primarily by funding propaganda efforts.

Very little priority is given to trying to support truth-seeking inquiry. You can see this in the generally low quality of the work coming out of political advocacy shops. But you can also see it in the overall shape of the staffing. The teams are too big and too heavily weighted toward relatively cheap people with relatively little experience or technical credentials. And these kinds of attitudes spread. Just as the line between “corporate puffery” or a Jobsian “reality distortion field” (his ability to convince people that the impossible was possible) and an outright fraud can be murkier than we might like to think. Movements that start out doing a little light propaganda, deliberate oversimplification, or aggressive spin eventually start putting out commentary that is completely nonsensical.

The MAGA movement reasoning that cutting imports will increase G.D.P. is a particularly egregious big-picture example. And it’s notable that nothing has done more damage to the MAGA political project than the analytical errors behind the war in Iran and Trump’s trade policy. The basic normative core of Trumpism would be in much better shape if the actual policy analysis had been better.

The ongoing fiasco of California high-speed rail is trivial in contrast to the invasion of Iran, but it’s salient to me because that was the specific thing I embarrassed myself defending propaganda about.

The truth is, a high-speed rail network linking San Francisco, San Jose, and Sacramento to Los Angeles with onward connections going to San Diego, Phoenix, and Las Vegas is a perfectly reasonable idea. If such a train existed, lots of people would ride it and there would be ancillary benefits for the smaller markets on the way like Fresno and Modesto. But building trains turns out to be a somewhat complicated engineering project that involves a lot of tradeoffs. A train like this would be useful but not infinitely useful (people fly and it’s fine), so whether it’s worth it actually depends on the technical implementation details. Pushing ahead with furious political momentum and no real plan turned out to be a recipe for a train to nowhere. Not an administration-killing fiasco like the war in Iran, but certainly a huge waste of money that torched the credibility of rail advocacy and left the whole project further from its goal than it was before.

What these things have in common is that public policy questions are genuinely hard.

The bigger and more important the issue you’re working on, the harder they get. You can’t transform the global energy system or rework all of American health care with a lot of propaganda and nonsense. A logic of superficial sloganeering is how you get reasoning like “if exclusionary zoning is bad, then inclusionary zoning must be good” when, if you actually model it properly, inclusionary zoning makes housing shortages worse.

A culture of probity

If Steve Jobs says Apple is never going to make a stylus and then years later they roll out the Apple Pencil, it’s not the biggest deal. Jobs was notorious to Apple-watchers for pulling this kind of thing.

When the first iPhone launched, it had inferior data speeds and there was no App Store. Instead of saying something reasonable like, “this is an incredibly impressive product in a lot of ways that also has some obvious shortcomings that we will iterate on in coming years,” he made a big deal of insisting that actually the data speed was fine and web apps were way better than native applications anyway.

Then lo and behold, he introduces an iPhone with 3G speeds and it’s way more popular.

I think it’s interesting that successful tech companies have managed to create the kind of corporate culture where they bullshit about complicated technical issues (literal rocket science in Musk’s case) while retaining a reasonable degree of internal discipline around the fact that the products have to actually work. Obviously this does generate the occasional Holmes whose products don’t work or investor enthusiasm for something absurd like WeWork. But products that do work keep emerging from this milieu.

With Jobs, the bullshit was at least cabined to a defined sphere of consumer products. Musk, though, is deeply involved in real-world politics while constantly saying untrue things about public affairs in a way that I find deeply disturbing. Sam Altman is not perpetrating a fraud on the public — OpenAI’s products are incredibly impressive — but he also has a terrible record on honesty that I find very disturbing. Anthropic’s claims to be more ethical strike me as credible, but that is possibly the Bankman-Fried version of ethical rather than the “I’m telling you true things” version of ethical.

Holmes herself probably meant well in some sense. She wasn’t running a smash and grab. She didn’t sell her shares and abscond to Malaysia. Had her machine worked, that would’ve been great for humanity. But it didn’t work. She needed more time and money to keep working on it, and the way to do that was to lie — fake it ’til you make it.

Trump’s supporters think that he is basically right about the need to crush the woke left and that the ends fundamentally justify the means on this score. The climate movement thinks their issue is so critically important that they need to tell everyone that a crash decarbonization program can be executed with zero tradeoffs.

As Dan Williams writes, the idea of “speaking truth to power” becomes an excuse for all kinds of intellectuals to skip the part where you just speak the truth — your allies are the noble underdogs, after all.

In the realm of public affairs, I think these attitudes are toxic. They make it extremely hard to actually govern because you create a group of confused people who don’t understand the levers of power they’re trying to operate. You’re propagating a set of norms in which clear, accurate communication is disparaged and it’s hard to adapt to new questions swiftly. You’re also creating a landscape that is friendly to frauds and grifters. As bad as Trump is, there’s something almost more disturbing about the way that JD Vance and Marco Rubio both explained the mechanics of the Trump con perfectly before deciding to become the two leading succession options.

As a work of art, the nesting doll of Nathan Fielder interrogating Amanda Seyfried in character as Elizabeth Holmes about the nature of truth is fascinating. But the extent to which the very top layers of politics and business now operate on this level of mind-bending dishonesty is disturbing.

And the answer, to be clear, is not to say that the bad guys are so vicious and opportunistic that we need to beat them by any means necessary! It’s to try to rebuild an ethic of basic probity, honesty, and factual accuracy from the ground up.

“You Can See Everything” and the nature of liars

A movie review, plus some thoughts on dishonesty, belief, and human communication.

Noah Smith
Oct 21
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

WARNING: This post contains spoilers for the movie You Can See Everything.

A few days ago, I had the great pleasure of seeing Nathan Fielder’s new film, You Can See Everything. I’ve been a fan of Fielder’s work for a long time, so I basically knew what to expect, but it was still incredible — every bit as good as you’ve heard. Go see it if you haven’t.

The film is a documentary about the notorious fraudster Elizabeth Holmes (of Theranos fame) and her partner Billy Evans. But it’s also sort of a horror movie about liars. That was interesting enough that it made me want to write a post about the movie — about the nature of lying, and of belief, and of human communication in general.

If you read even a little bit about the history of Theranos, there is absolutely no question that Elizabeth Holmes is a deliberate fraudster and a prolific, aggressive liar. Holmes presented potential investors with fake financial results in 2015. She personally added fake logos of pharmaceutical companies to Theranos’ own reports. She flatly stated that Theranos didn’t dilute blood samples, then admitted in court that she intentionally concealed the fact that they did dilute blood samples. Theranos employees detailed the whole deliberate fraud in anonymous online posts years before the story broke.

But You Can See Everything doesn’t cover much of this actual history. Fielder doesn’t bother to indict Holmes and prove that she committed fraud — the court case already did that. Instead, he offers a window into the psychology of someone who could commit such an epic fraud. Holmes and Evans allow Fielder into their home with the goal of proving that they’re just regular, good people trying to improve the world. Instead, Fielder depicts the couple — quite accurately — as monsters of deception and manipulation.

It’s doubtful that any other filmmaker could have done nearly as good a job of this. The blurry line between what’s real and what’s fake has always been a major theme of Nathan Fielder’s work — he loves hiring actors to simulate past and future interactions, constructing facsimiles of whole buildings, and so on. And of course he’s very skilled with the tricks of the visual storyteller’s trade, using deliberate cuts, camera angles, and creative edits to make the audience think and feel what he wants them to.

Whereas many filmmakers would have regarded Holmes as a subject to be studied, Fielder seems to see her as an opponent to be challenged and beaten. If he can shoot what Holmes wants him to shoot, but ultimately seize control of the narrative, then he’s the more powerful storyteller. This, I think, is why he doesn’t bring in outside evidence to show what a well-documented liar Holmes is. That would be cheating. Instead, he has to venture into the monster’s lair alone, and defeat her in single combat. He has to film the movie that she asks him to film, and let her show him only what she wants him to see, and still have audiences walk away having seen the story that he wants to tell.

And of course he succeeds, because he’s very good, but also because he gets to edit the film, and editing is more powerful than acting. Score one for the good guys.

(Major spoilers begin here.)

How does Fielder win the contest? Over the course of You Can See Everything, he captures Elizabeth Holmes saying a number of strange and extraordinary things:

  1. Near the beginning, Holmes tells Fielder that she’s never lied in her life. After he presses her, she half-admits that she may have told small white lies out of convenience. But the audience gets to watch her repeatedly assert something obviously, fantastically false, always with the same sincere, relaxed, wide-eyed expression on her face.

  2. Later on, Fielder shows Holmes the famous “Who’s on first?” comedy routine, which she claims never to have seen. After watching it, Holmes claims not to have realized that the baseball player’s name is “Who” — thus missing the entire point of the sketch.

  3. Fielder recruits Amanda Seyfried, who played Holmes in the miniseries The Dropout, to help him figure out what’s going on with Holmes and her partner. At one point, Holmes is calling on the phone from prison. Seyfried asks Holmes if she knew Seyfried would be on the call, and Holmes says “I’m not sure if I knew.”

It’s moments like these, more than any simple lie, that reveal Holmes’ true character. In fact, Fielder seems like he passes up several chances to catch Holmes in a straight-up lie on camera. After all, what would one lie, or even three lies, really prove? Everyone lies sometimes, and capturing a couple of those instances during weeks of living with Holmes wouldn’t be hard. It would be a cheap trick, and it wouldn’t really prove that Holmes is a liar in general.

Instead, the moments Fielder captures demonstrate something deeper and far more unnerving about Holmes’ relationship to the truth. Holmes is a very special and powerful kind of liar — someone for whom deception and manipulation are as automatic and as continuous as breathing.

Type 1 liars and Type 2 liars

“Maybe it’s something inside/ Maybe it’s something I can’t explain” — Henry Rollins

Suppose you want to tell a lie. Suppose you made a blood test device that didn’t work, and you want investors to believe it did work, so that they’ll give you money, and your parents and your boyfriend and the national press will give you fame and respect. Here are two ways you could tell that lie:

Method 1: Deception

First, assess the truth of the matter. Realize that the device doesn’t work. Then think about which facts you have to falsify or conceal in order to convince investors that the device does work. Concoct a fake story with those specific fake facts, and tell that story to the investors.

Method 2: Fantasy

Ignore the real world completely, and simply imagine the world in which the device does work. Start describing that world to the investors. Watch which details of your description grab the investors’ interest or seem to convince them, and repeat those over and over (adding additional detail and embellishments if necessary).

Ultimately, these two types of lying achieve the same goal — they convince your victims of things that aren’t true, so that you can take advantage of them. But the first method has some distinct disadvantages. It’s very costly in terms of memory — you have to remember not only the fake story you told, but also what’s actually real. You’re carrying around two realities in your head — the truth, and your lies — and you have to keep them separate and consistent.

That’s hard! It’s the reason for the old Latin proverb “Mendacem memorem esse oportet” — “A liar must be good at remembering”.

But what if you didn’t have to be good at remembering? Method 2 lets you dispense with the truth entirely. You don’t have to think about what’s real — you only remember the fantasy world you’ve created. The more you tell your fantasy stories, the better you remember them — the memory of saying the things begins to feel as real, or almost as real, as a memory of the things actually happening would have felt.¹

The downside of Method 2 is that it’s much bigger and more grandiose. You’re not just falsifying a few details; you’re spinning an entire fantasy world. That takes a lot of effort — a lot of narrations and spiels and pronouncements and conversations. The lie has to become your life. You have to actually move into the fantasy world you created, and live there 24/7.

To use Method 2 really well also requires a very unusual type of personality. Most people instinctively go around constructing a model of the truth — they’re constantly thinking “What’s really going on in the world around me?”. This interferes with Type 2 lying — if you have them create a fictitious autobiography for themselves, they won’t actually believe in it, because it conflicts with the model of the real world that they’re always automatically generating.

For the really good Type 2 liars, “What’s really going on in the world around me?” often just isn’t a very interesting or important question. Instead, they’re thinking “How can I get things from this person I’m talking to?”. They’re like a hill-climbing algorithm — a large language model that bullshits people, observes the results, and then learns to bullshit in the direction that achieves more money, more fame, more whatever. These are the pathological liars you’ve heard about.²

Billy Evans, Elizabeth Holmes’ partner, is a Type 1 liar. In the middle part of You Can See Everything, Fielder easily catches Evans in a number of falsehoods. Evans is always clumsily trying to keep Fielder from the truth or conceal information in order to defend Holmes’ reputation. He knows, more or less, what the truth is; all of his lies are defined in opposition to that truth, and so they’re easy to catch, because they don’t hang together in a coherent whole.

But Holmes is the real deal — an incredibly powerful and proficient Type 2 liar. I went to see You Can See Everything with a big group of people, and much of the discussion after the movie revolved around whether or not Holmes actually believes the things she tells people. I argued that “belief” was simply the wrong way to think about it.

Think about this question for a moment: What does it actually mean to “believe” something? For economists, it means that you’re willing to bet on something being true.³ We believe the dining room table exists because we walk around the table when we go through the dining room, instead of trying to walk right through it. For economists, a “belief” is part of someone’s model of reality.

But in a lot of cases, “belief” actually means something else — it means a type of emotion. Go ask a devout Christian or Muslim if they believe that God is omnipotent. They’ll say “Yes.” But as everyone who has taken a freshman philosophy class knows, true omnipotence is a logically incoherent concept. Can God create a rock too heavy for Him to lift? And so on. When people say “I believe God is omnipotent”, what they mean is that when they utter the sentence “God is omnipotent”, they get a warm feeling of rightness — the feeling that they’ve just said something true. They might die for that belief, without ever having a clear grasp of what it meant.

My guess — which is supported by a fair amount of psychological research, though it’s not a consensus — is that Type 2 liars “believe” their fantasies in the second sense, but often not the first. If you forced them to bet on their fantasies being correct in some measurable sense — a medical device producing reliable test results, or Amanda Seyfried being present in a room — they might or might not make that bet. But they feel a warm, good feeling when they utter their fantasies, because those fantasies will presumably get them what they want. To a Type 2 liar, the questions “Do I believe this?” and “Is it to my advantage to say this?” are not different questions.

Human beings talk to each other for many reasons. We want companionship and entertainment. We want people to understand us. We need to gather and convey information about the world. And yes, we need to get each other to do things for us. A Type 2 liar is someone for whom the last of these imperatives dominates the others.

Here’s what I’m guessing is happening with Elizabeth Holmes in the weird moments I described above. When she tells Nathan Fielder she’s never lied, she does so because telling him she had lied seems like it would be contrary to her purposes — it would presumably make the tone of his documentary more negative and accusatory. So she says “I’ve never lied.” And when she speaks those words, she gets a warm feeling of having said something right and good.

When she claims not to understand the “Who’s on first?” sketch, it’s because seeming not to understand it serves her purpose — it paints her as someone on the autism spectrum, implying that she just thinks different, and that the people who sent her to prison for fraud just don’t understand the strange way she thinks. And of course, the sense that she’s successfully promulgating that useful image gives her the warm feeling that religious people get when they say “God is omnipotent.”

The most telling moment, though, is during the phone call from prison, when Amanda Seyfried asks if Holmes knew she was in the room, and Holmes says “I’m not sure if I knew.” This statement seems nonsensical — how could you not know whether you knew something like that? — until you think about it from the perspective of a Type 2 liar. Holmes is actually saying: “I’m not sure whether it’s to my advantage to say I knew or that I didn’t know.”

To the Type 2 liar, uncertainty about your own best interest feels like epistemic uncertainty.

This is what I think is going on, anyway. My guess is that Nathan Fielder saw the nature of Holmes’ personality pretty quickly, or even surmised it in advance, and simply made sure to include scenes that illustrate it to the audience. At one point, he wonders whether she’s “the most manipulative person who has ever lived.”⁴ This is why I see You Can See Everything as a sort of monster movie — a character sketch of a kind of alien that walks unseen among us, insensate to the truth, forever babbling at us in an effort to make us do its bidding.

And Nathan defeats the monster. He beards Elizabeth Holmes in her den, confronts her on ground of her own choosing, lets her do the talking, and still manages to expose her for what she is. And having exposed her, he is magnanimous in victory. In the film’s closing montage, he paints Holmes as a defanged predator — a criminal behind bars, a sociopath who enjoys being a mom, a woman who honestly loves her clumsy liar boyfriend in whatever strange way they both know how.

It’s a very good movie.

In fact, this is an important way that false memories arise.

2

Actually, the overlap isn’t complete. What I’m calling “Type 2 liars” are actually a subset of what psychologists call “pathological liars”; a different subset are people who lie compulsively with no thought for personal gain. Also, the term “pathological liar” is contentious and disputed, and means different things to different people. Welcome to psychology!

3

Actually, not quite. Several other things affect people’s willingness to bet on outcomes. One of these is idiosyncratic risk — if Trump winning the election would really hurt my business, I may bet a lot of money on him winning even if I don’t think it’s likely, just as a hedge. Another factor is risk aversion, which is different for different people. And a third complicating factor is someone’s portfolio of other bets — I might bet on Trump winning the election just to hedge another bet I made on Trump losing the election. So you can’t actually tell what people believe from how they bet.

4

That’s an exaggeration, obviously — Elizabeth Holmes is in prison, while plenty of master manipulators are still walking free. There might even be one living in the White House right now.

Trump is Destroying Americans’ Healthcare

Twelve million have lost coverage — and it’s getting worse

Paul Krugman
Oct 21
 
READ IN APP
 

On the eve of the midterm election, American families are feeling financially stressed As the chart above shows, the percentage of families who say that their financial situation is good has plunged. For the first time since the post-Covid inflation of 2022, it has fallen below the percentage who say that their financial situation is bad.

Rising prices are the obvious explanation for this stress. And while presidents usually have much less influence on the economy than is generally recognized, the current outbreak of high inflation is all on Donald Trump. He began this with two wars of choice: one, a trade war with his destructive tariffs, and then an unwinnable military war in the most important energy transit point in the world.

There is, however, a third factor behind Americans’ anger, and it isn’t getting nearly as much attention as it should. There has been a catastrophic decline in health insurance coverage combined with sharply rising premiums for many of those who have managed to hang on to their coverage. And this, too, is all on Trump.

Here’s what happened: Trump and his congressional minions refused to renew the expanded subsidies that had made health insurance affordable for millions of Americans during the Biden years. At the same time the One Big Beautiful Bill imposed punitive work requirements that made it far more difficult for families to obtain Medicaid coverage.

And we haven’t felt the full effect of these changes yet — Republicans tried to backload the effects of the OBBB so that much of the pain will come after the midterms. But the consequences of this attack on healthcare have already been dire.

By June 2026 enrollment in Medicaid and the Childrens’ Health Insurance Program had declined by more than 6 million since January 2025; 2.5 million of those losing coverage were children. KFF estimates that enrollment in individual plans, mainly via the Affordable Care Act, was down almost 5 million by June. The redoubtable Charles Gaba, putting these numbers together with other information, estimates that around 12 million Americans have lost health insurance under Trump 2.0.

That’s a lot of lost coverage, even in a nation as big as ours. And because many of the savage cuts Trump and his allies have imposed on healthcare have yet to kick in, the situation will get much worse in the years ahead. It’s worth noting thatkicking children off healthcare coverage is especially personally and socially destructive because it compromises their health and earnings potential for their entire lifetimes.

By the way, Trump, after all these years, is once again promising that he’ll come up with a “truly great” healthcare plan any day now. He’s now saying that he’ll send money directly to Americans, stopping payments to insurance companies — thereby demonstrating that he still has no idea how insurance works.

In any case, we’re now in the midst of an enormous healthcare disaster — a disaster that is receiving surprisingly little media coverage with, as far as I can tell, no recent articles on massive coverage losses in any of the major newspapers. I know that there’s a lot going on, but this seems odd.

Voters, however, have noticed. KFF’s tracking poll finds that the cost of healthcare is near the top of voters’ economic worries:

As an overall issue, health care ranks second only to the overall cost of living — and above the Iran war:

This ongoing healthcare disaster is all on Trump and his party. And again, voters appear to have noticed, giving Democrats a large and growing edge on the issue:

So if there is a blue wave 13 days from now, it won’t just be the result of inflation and Trump’s vainglorious wars. It will also in part be the result of a quiet but massive healthcare disaster.

And ultimately, of course, the political implications are a secondary concern. What really matters is that Trump and his party have done all they can to deny healthcare to millions of Americans. They have done this partly to save money — not to reduce the budget deficit, but to make room for tax cuts for the wealthy. They have also done it out of sheer cruelty.

There are many terrible things happening in America right now, from the debacle in Iran to the depredations of ICE. But the healthcare disaster, which will ruin many people financially and in some cases kill Americans who can no longer afford essential care, deserves much more attention than it is getting.

I’m way more online than I should be, and you probably are too.

Americans need to get out of the house

I’m way more online than I should be, and you probably are too.

Matthew Yglesias
Oct 21
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

Let me tell you a little about my weekend.

For various reasons, we didn’t have our normal editorial meeting at work last week, so I spent a fair amount of time on Saturday logged on to X, scrolling around seeking inspiration for stories. Dominating my feed were images of the riots in France and, even more so, annoying takes on the riots in France.

I wasn’t even so much seeing people tweeting dumb takes about the riots as seeing sensible people executing good dunks on dumb takes about the riots. But I still had to see both the underlying dumb takes and also the under-underlying riot images. There was also plenty of discourse (some of which I ended up contributing to) in the broad space of “people who agree that Abdul El-Sayed winning is preferable to Mike Rogers winning but are fighting about El-Sayed.”

The France stuff I kind of find entrancing in a doomscrolling kind of way, but El-Sayed discourse is real catnip for me in terms of getting into it with other people. In both cases, though, X engineers are evidently pretty smart and good at their jobs and were successfully executing on their mission of keeping me engaged.

Did it make me feel happy and satisfied with my life? No. Did it help me execute on my actual goal in logging on to X? Also no. But it’s not their job to make my life better. Their job is to keep me scrolling — and mission accomplished.

It’s good to do things

Some other things that happened over the weekend:

I met up with two friends to see the new “Street Fighter” movie. It was incredibly dumb, but I have to admit that it contained individual scenes — from video game nostalgia to hearing White Zombie’s “More Human Than Human” for the first time in years — that brought my lizard brain joy.

It was also good to see my friends, albeit briefly. I like those guys! Later I drove to a middle-school debate tournament where I was supposed to pick up my kid and one of his friends. It turned out that it was running late, so I went in to sit with my son and watch the handing out of awards. In the auditorium, I ran into a writer whose book I like but who I’d only met once before, and we chatted briefly. She introduced me to another dad who I’ve seen around the neighborhood but never met. I said “hi” to some kids who I know slightly, and one of them said something funny. Then I drove up to my kid’s friend’s house to drop him off while he and my son bickered in the back seat like an old married couple. Driving back to our house, my son and I listened to Stan Van Gundy on “The Zach Lowe Show,” and they were saying Boston is going to be good this year, so my son and I talked about how The Ringer spent the whole summer melting down about the Jaylen Brown trade but is now coming around to our view that the Celtics are in good shape for next season and the trade set them up with better flexibility for the future.

Soon after we got home, two adult friends of ours stopped by. They had plans, but one of them has two kids, and we’d agreed with them that the kids could hang out at our house while the adults went out. Our friends’ adult plans turned out to be a bust, so they came home early. All of us adults wound up hanging out while two of the kids played Minecraft and the third read a book. Eventually everyone went home, probably slightly late relative to everyone’s statutory bedtimes. But a good time was had by all.

What really struck me about all of this was that none of it was particularly perfect, or even planned.

The movie was terrible. I was in the auditorium because the debate was off schedule. The drive home from the other kid’s house ended up taking a weirdly long time due to unexpected traffic. The kids coming over was us doing a favor, not a fun plan we deliberately devised. Our friends’ plans ended up being bad. But in the end it was all for the best!

The limits of revealed preferences

Unlike X, of which I am an unhealthily obsessive user, I almost never log on to Instagram. But I did on Saturday after our friends left because someone sent me a link to a post.

Since I rarely use Instagram, its algorithm is terribly tuned and has no idea what to show me. That meant I got an Instagram reel of a young female influencer, Ryan Weitz, talking about why “dating in D.C. is so bad.”

Some of what she says seems normal, like she’s frequently traveling for work on the weekend, which makes it hard to meet people. She also feels that the guys she does meet are often immature. But then she says that while she tells herself she’s going to go out on the weekends when she is in town, more often than not she ends up staying in because she realizes “Oh, I want to like chill and rest.”

I did not find this content particularly engaging in a classic social-media sense — I wasn’t inspired to comment or keep scrolling — but it did give me what I’d been seeking (and failing to find) on X: something to write about!

Weitz is illustrating the difference between stated and revealed preferences but also, I think, the limits of revealed preferences as a framework. Weitz, like most people, says she would like to be in a relationship (stated preference), but she also says that in practice she values her downtime on weekends and dates are often annoying (revealed preferences). While I know men who enjoyed the process of dating — the thrill of the chase or what have you — that was definitely not me and, to the best of my recollection, it wasn’t most people I know. Talking to strangers and having them mostly reject you is not my idea of a fun time. I’d much rather watch dumb movies with my friends or sit home alone trading bon mots on Twitter.

But this is one of those things where you have to engage in a modicum of long-term thinking. I don’t enjoy flossing, but I do it anyway. I am overdue for a tooth cleaning at the dentist, and I believe that statistically speaking I have reached colonoscopy age, and now that I find myself typing this sentence I’m going to go do the grownup thing and book those appointments. A happy life is not an unbroken sequence of joyous occasions. Sometimes, to get ahead, you need to put eyedroppers full of heavy cream in a senior editor’s coffee.

And I think a growing problem in our society is people leaning too hard into the revealed preference for frictionless existence and plenty of alone time.

Not much is going on

A great Data for Progress survey shows how Americans’ social lives have changed since the mid-1990s, and the big shift is toward doing less of almost everything.

I mentioned my disquiet over the rise of remote work online the other day and heard a lot from remote workers who love it about the obvious advantages in terms of reduced commute time and greater flexibility about where to live. It definitely sounds great. And I heard from one friend who lives in the suburbs with three school-aged kids and a wife with a high-powered career of her own, and skipping the commute really does seem great for them.

But clearly, people on average are not having more kids. And they’re also not taking advantage of their increased freedom and flexibility to spend more time entertaining or visiting with friends. And they’re not doing less home-based entertaining because they’re out at restaurants and bars more or joining clubs. There’s been a modest rise in the frequency with which people go see live music or attend exercise classes. But these are still uncommon pursuits compared to the frequency with which people used to go to club meetings.

The big thing is that people are online more and they play more video games.

That’s where, in the aggregate, the extra time has gone. Instead of dealing with the hassles of interacting with flawed humans in the real world, people are spending more time at home alone using the internet. And they do not seem to be better off for it.

A struggling nation

A recent report from Gallup and The Rippel Foundation on whether people are “thriving” or “struggling” in America revealed a well-being ratio that has dipped slightly below the levels associated with the peak of the Great Recession.

I recognize that the energy price spike associated with Trump’s war in Iran is bad, but it’s hard to square this survey with the objective economic data. Both diesel and gasoline are cheaper in real terms today than they were in 2008, for example, and the unemployment rate is strikingly lower.

The well-being decline is also notably stratified by age. Back in 2008, when I was young, people my age mostly said we were “thriving.” Now that we’re middle-aged, we’re doing worse than we used to be. And the new crop of young people that’s come up behind us is doing much worse. The thing preventing total collapse is that senior citizens are doing better.

Some of this is economic in nature. The housing market is rigged against young people, and government benefits for the retired have gotten more generous. But young people were definitely struggling economically in 2010. We were just also young and having fun.

As Halina wrote the other day about “Girls,” you can have a lot of fun as a broke 20-something hanging out with your friends. Going online mostly makes people miserable. You find out that France is on fire and all your political enemies are evil and everyone else is secretly richer and better-looking than you’ll ever be. Every interaction is a minefield of potential problems. And that’s the business model! If you feel inspired to go do something, that’s bad for engagement.

This is bad for everyone.

Derek Thompson has been pushing the difference between “loneliness” (a subjective desire to spend more time with others) and “aloneness” (just being alone because that’s what you want). But I think this is kind of like how a lot of us, if left to our own inclinations, are prone to overeating and not exercising enough. There’s a revealed preference to be fat and lazy, and it doesn’t make us happy or align with what we really want out of life.

I wonder if there isn’t something deep in the evolved history of our brains that just assumes we’ll never have enough personal space or alone time, and we just don’t know how to deal with the possibility of endless streaming video and food delivery.

I just know that for me, getting thrown chaotically into the happenstance of real life tends to generate happy accidents, while the deliberate pursuit of algorithmic pleasures tends — at best — to leave me staying up an hour later than I intended to and feeling a little worse for the wear the next day.

France and the limits of liberalism

Immigration, the welfare state, and Keynesian economics are all showing signs of strain.

Noah Smith
Oct 22
 
READ IN APP
 

I’m writing about this a little bit late, but France has been having some pretty bad riots:

After widespread rioting at the weekend – estimated to have cost several hundred million dollars in property damage and theft – France faces a toxic mix of urban rebellion, political drift and economic crisis…There was rampant looting in Paris, Marseille, Bordeaux and other cities, while the city hall in Limoges, which survived two world wars, was badly damaged by fire and its clock spire collapsed.

The violence at the weekend, which led to some 2,400 arrests, followed weeks of protests by French students angry about crumbling schools, a lack of teachers and dismal job prospects.

If there’s a reason I’m writing about this a bit late, it’s because “rioting in France” is a little like “rain in Seattle” — it’s not exactly an unusual occurrence. In 2023, France had a week of nationwide riots over a police killing. From 2018 to 2020, France was rocked by over a year and a half of near-continuous “Yellow Vest” protests and riots over economic issues. I remember two decades ago, reading about weeks of rioting in the French suburbs, accompanied by endless photos of burning cars. And so on.

French people like to riot. But this time, things are a little bit different, for a couple of reasons. First of all, this wave of unrest is accompanied by serious economic troubles. France’s long-term interest rates, like rates throughout the world, are surging:

But unlike some countries whose rates have also risen, investors have serious doubts that France’s government will take the necessary steps to pay back what it owes. The price that investors have to pay to insure against a French sovereign default has shot up even more abruptly than interest rates:

Basically, investors are starting to think that France won’t pay back its debt — that instead of raising taxes or cutting spending, the country will simply pay the cost of rising interest rates by borrowing even more money. Instead, investors are starting to worry that France will simply default on its bonds.

In a widely read post a couple of weeks ago, Paul Krugman argued that the problem lies with France’s old-age pensions, which are eating an increasingly enormous amount of the country’s GDP and seem politically immune to any cuts:

The rise in interest rates on French government bonds is largely driven by heightened perceptions of the risk that France could default on its national debt…France is on a fiscally unsustainable path. Debt is already very high as a percentage of GDP, and the French government is adding to that debt by running large budget deficits even though there is no emergency like a war, a severe recession, or a pandemic to justify such deficits. Furthermore, France has an aging population, which means that pension costs will, other things equal, grow much faster than revenue…

France does stand out, even among fiscally troubled nations, in one main way: its persistent inability to get realistic about retirement…The official French retirement age…was only 62 in 2023…The average actual age of retirement…was lower in France than anywhere else in Western Europe…Macron’s center-right government was on track to gradually raise the retirement age to 64, still low by the standards of other advanced nations. But due to opposition by the extreme right and the extreme left parties in France, this rise has been frozen until after next year’s election.

In other words, France needs austerity, but it can’t get it, because the French people demand ever-increasing spending. France’s government already takes up a larger share of GDP than almost any other rich country — significantly more than Sweden or Denmark:

And indeed, a very hefty chunk of that social spending goes to either old-age pensions or to health (which is heavily weighted toward the old):

Of course, there’s another way to do austerity besides cutting spending — France could raise taxes. But this will also be tough. France’s taxes are already higher as a share of its GDP than any other rich country, including the famously high-tax Scandinavian countries:

Could taxes go up even more? It’ll be difficult. In 2019, I wrote about the underwhelming results of France’s previous experiments:

The wealth tax might have generated social solidarity, but as a practical matter it was a disappointment. The revenue it raised was rather paltry; only a few billion euros at its peak, or about 1% of France’s total revenue from all taxes. At least 10,000 wealthy people left the country to avoid paying the tax; most moved to neighboring Belgium, which has a large French-speaking population. When these individuals left, France lost not only their wealth tax revenue but their income taxes and other taxes as well. French economist Eric Pichet estimates that this ended up costing the French government almost twice as much revenue as the total yielded by the wealth tax…

Another French experiment was the so-called supertax, a 75% levy on incomes of more than 1 million euros. Introduced by socialist President François Hollande in 2012, the supertax added to the exodus of wealthy individuals, most notably actor Gerard Depardieu and Bernard Arnault, chairman of LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton. Star soccer players threatened to go on strike, and there was fear that France would become a wasteland for entrepreneurs. Meanwhile, the supertax raised much less money than even the wealth tax had -- only 160 million euros in 2014. The unpopular tax was repealed two years after its adoption.

France is in a difficult position here. Its membership in the EU, and its location near to other French-speaking countries like Belgium, Switzerland, and Luxembourg, make it trivially easy for rich French people to pick up and move to other countries if they see their fortunes under threat of confiscation.

France could, of course, try taxing the middle class to pay for expanded social spending, perhaps by an increase in the VAT. But this burden would fall on many of the same people who are now protesting and rioting in the streets, so it’s probably a political nonstarter as well.

In fact, the current riots are making the strains in France’s bond market worse, by making the politics of austerity seem more intractable. Various groups of protesters and rioters are demanding enormous amounts of additional government largesse — billions of euros of increased spending on schools, increases in pensions, increases in social benefits, and even subsidies for consumer goods like fuel. That demonstrates that there’s still enormous grassroots political pressure for higher government spending; even if France’s leadership doesn’t cave in to this pressure, leaders will probably be averse to making the deep cuts to spending required to put France on a sustainable fiscal path.

And that, in turn, is probably making it harder to enact any of the spending that the protesters are demanding. When protesters demand increased spending, bond markets respond by charging higher rates on French government borrowing. That increases interest costs for the government, which makes it harder to raise social spending — the exact opposite of what the protesters wanted.

Fundamentally, the French riots show the limits of the European left-liberal welfarism that has been the region’s default approach to governance for the last half-century — and which American progressives want to emulate. The French populace — or at least a powerful chunk of it — simply doesn’t seem to be able to recognize the difference between a sustainable welfare state and an unsustainable one. Instead, social benefits seem to be a one-way ratchet — higher benefits raise expectations for even higher benefits, until even the most milquetoast and inadequate of austerity measures end up causing cities to burn.

That one-way ratchet also calls into question the viability of Keynesian fiscal stimulus — the main tool that left-liberals (including me) prefer to combat deep recessions. Few serious macroeconomists now question that stimulus is effective in raising aggregate demand in a severe downturn. But Keynesian policy requires that fiscal largesse during a bust be matched by fiscal austerity during a boom, so that deficits don’t grow unsustainably. The problem is that while “austerity during the boom” is easy to say, it’s politically very hard to enact.

Hanno Lustig, reading Krugman’s post about the unsustainability of France’s borrowing, recalls the years of the Euro crisis, in which Krugman urged France to spend, spend, spend to fight the recession:

Hanno Lustig
@HannoLustig
May come as a bit of a surprise to those of us who were following Paul's writings in the 2010s when he was railing against Eurozone "austerity craziness". With interest rates at the zero lower bound, he argued that fiscal consolidation in a depressed economy was self-defeating:…
Bloomberg @business
Nobel Prize-winning economist Paul Krugman warned that France’s deteriorating public finances are on an “unsustainble path” and at risk of unleashing a debt crisis across the euro area https://t.co/M4BodYe5k6
3:43 PM · Oct 10, 2026 · 101K Views
35 Replies · 135 Reposts · 685 Likes

Lustig is being a little unfair to Krugman here. In fact, here’s what Krugman actually wrote in 2011, in the first post that Lustig cites:

[W]e won’t always be in a liquidity trap. Someday private demand will be high enough that the Fed will have good reason to raise interest rates above zero, to limit inflation. And when that happens, deficits — and the perceived willingness of the government to raise enough revenue to cover its spending — will matter…At a future date, when we’re out of the liquidity trap, public finances will matter…[T]he biggest source of our long-run deficit isn’t the overhang of debt, it’s the prospective current cost of paying for retirement, health care, and defense. So such a crisis — again, it’s very much hypothetical — could spiral into something very nasty, with very high inflation and, yes, hyperinflation.

Krugman was actually talking about the U.S., but he might as well have been talking about France. Keynesians don’t just say “more government spending is good” — they recognize that there are limits, so they urge governments to cut spending during good economic times.

But Lustig has a point, nonetheless. The Keynesian prescription — deficits during the bust, austerity during the boom — requires that whoever is in power during the boom take the political hit for doing the austerity. In practice, you can sometimes find politicians willing to spend their political capital on taking that hit, but it’s tough. Even Macron caved in the end.

When we look at actual French borrowing and spending during the Euro crisis of the early 2010s, it’s clear that neither the austerity Krugman feared nor the stimulus he desired was actually happening. Look at the charts above, and you’ll see that government spending didn’t rise or dip during the 2010s — it just sailed on, unperturbed, as if the recession didn’t even exist. The same was true of French government debt:

Germany actually did do austerity during the bust. France did not. In fact, they didn’t do anything — they just kept borrowing and spending.

That points to a political-economic problem for Keynesian liberalism. It suggests — as James Buchanan foresaw — that spending is often less likely to be determined by the wise judgement of technocrats, and more likely to be determined by angry ignorant people burning down government buildings.

Finally, France’s riots show the limits of one more pillar of modern left-liberalism — tolerance toward mass immigration.

It’s not obvious that African or Middle Eastern immigrants are disproportionately behind these riots. Viral videos of rioters and looters — including the famous video of the French video game store owner trying to defend his shop against young hoodlums — show a racially mixed crowd of rioters with plenty of white representation. Some past waves of riots have been driven by immigrants and their children — for example, the anti-police riots of 2023. But others, like the much longer-running Yellow Vest riots of the late 2010s, were mostly white.

Still, France’s public appears more and more inclined to blame “migrants” for the chaos in their streets. When the disorder began, the political fortunes of the anti-immigration right-wing candidate Marine Le Pen soared:

In contrast, the chances of the only major left-wing candidate, Jean-Luc Melenchon, didn’t budge. Melenchon is promising lavish increases in social spending, but the public is disinterested; instead, as in Germany with AfD, and indeed all over Europe, the people are gravitating toward whoever promises to stop immigration.

America is not France, of course. Our immigrant mix is very different, and our ability to assimilate large numbers of immigrants is much greater. Our attitudes toward immigration have turned positive again, at least partly as a reaction against Trump’s brutality. But France shows that the left-liberal approach to immigration simply doesn’t work equally well for all countries.

So France’s riots aren’t just one more case of French people going wild in the streets. They demonstrate the limits of European-style left-liberalism — the lavish welfare state, the tolerant attitude toward mass immigration, and the trust in Keynesian demand management. Left-liberalism built some very beautiful and kindly societies, but its powers are not infinite.

It’s Time to Take Starlink Away from Elon Musk

Americans did not give him the right to make national security policy

Paul Krugman
Oct 22
 
READ IN APP
 

Did Elon Musk decide by personal fiat to cut off Ukraine’s access to vital communications? Although Musk claims that the decision was made by Trump, according to the Wall Street Journal, some U.S. officials state that Musk did indeed take it upon himself to pull the plug on Ukraine. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is quoted as saying that the administration was blind-sided: “There was no foreknowledge.”

Now, perhaps Donald Trump told him to do it, sotto voce, Mafia-style: (“This Zelenskyy guy is a problem. Someone should do something about it.”) And Trump could demand, but hasn’t, that Musk restore Ukraine’s access.

However, given that there is now finger-pointing going on and there are credible statements that Musk himself was the instigator, we now need to seriously consider the implications. No private individual should, or indeed even have the capability to, make national security policy. Slowing down Starlink was, in effect, a U.S. intervention in a foreign conflict. It helped Russia, our long-time adversary, and hobbled Ukraine, during a very critical time in this war. It also helped Russia at a time when Putin is increasingly emboldened to menace Europe through acts of sabotage, intimidation and support of the extreme right such as the AfD in Germany. (Recall that Musk has openly supported the AfD.)

While Trump and Musk are now openly supporting Vladimir Putin, their actions are unpopular with the American public. Very few Americans agree that the U.S. should be supporting, not opposing, a brutal dictator’s attempt to conquer a democracy:

Let’s be clear about the current state of the war between Russia and Ukraine. On the military battlefield, Ukraine has been gaining the upper hand. Hence Putin has turned to attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, electricity in particular. If Musk doesn’t restore that access quickly, the result will be the deaths of thousands of innocent Ukrainians. Moreover, he will embolden Putin to further menace and attack our Nato allies, as well as supporting neo-Nazis like the AfD.

Some may object as follows: Musk owns Starlink. Doesn’t he have the right to do what he wants with a business he owns?

No.

Yes, America has a market economy. And to make this economy work, we need to respect property rights. But we are, first and foremost, a democracy. And in a democracy, the rights of private property don’t and never have included the right to act against the nation’s interest — where democratically elected representatives of the people, not business owners, should decide what is in the nation’s interest. Capitalism is not an excuse for treason.

Let’s look at a hypothetical case. Taiwan’s air force flies F16s made by Lockheed Martin. Imagine that for some reason — perhaps as part of a business deal with China — Lockheed Martin suddenly moved to degrade Taiwan’s military capability by cutting off access to spare parts, upgrades, munitions, computer networks and more. Would anyone consider such action acceptable, a legitimate exercise of property rights? Surely not. There would be immediate demands that Lockheed Martin reverse its actions — and if it refused, the federal government would step in to temporarily take control of the company.

This has actually happened in the past.

U.S. mobilization during World War II relied overwhelmingly on private contractors. But these contractors weren’t free to do as they pleased. Among other things, the federal government was anxious to avoid labor conflict that might impede the war effort. So the National War Labor Board negotiated mandatory settlements between management and workers.

Some businessmen didn’t want to go along. In particular, Sewell Avery, the chairman of Montgomery Ward, simply refused to comply with the terms of collective bargaining agreements that had been hammered out with the United Retail, Wholesale and Department Store Union.

At the time, Montgomery Ward was both a major retailer and a major manufacturer, whose production of tractors, auto parts and more were important parts of the war effort. But Avery placed a higher priority on resisting unionization than on defeating the Nazis.

So in April 1944 FDR ordered the Army National Guard to seize Montgomery Ward’s main plant in Chicago. National Guard troops literally had to carry Avery out of his office:

Later that year the federal government also seized a number of other Montgomery Ward facilities.

It’s important to realize that none of these actions were attempts to impose long-term government control of the economy. There was never an intent to permanently nationalize Montgomery Ward. But the principle was clear: private individuals do not have the right to undermine national security. And if temporary nationalization is the only way to stop them from doing so, so be it.

So, back to Elon Musk: In modern warfare, where communication and real-time information are as important as rockets and artillery, Starlink is as central to national security as Lockheed Martin. Decisions about which countries have full access to Starlink’s capacity are as much a matter of foreign policy and national security as decisions about which countries will be allowed to buy and operate U.S. high-tech weapons.

Such decisions cannot, must not, be left up to private individuals. This would be true even if these individuals were patriots who supported democracy and American values. They definitely shouldn’t be left in the hands of this guy.

Musk will surely, and rightly, be the focus of many investigations if Democrats win the midterms. But don’t expect this to chasten him: His response to the prospect has been to make menacing threats:

Which reinforces the point that control of Starlink must, one way or another, be taken away from Elon Musk. It’s a matter of national security: we cannot let private individuals make foreign and defense policy, and it would be totally irresponsible to leave a crucial military asset in the hands of a racist, authoritarian conspiracy theorist.
