Your favorite cause is not the civil rights movement and neither is mine

It doesn’t make a lot of sense to imitate an extreme outlier event.

Matthew Yglesias
Oct 22
 
READ IN APP
 

After you’ve read today’s post, I hope you’ll check out the latest episode of “The Argument” podcast, where Jerusalem and I dig into the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), a bill that promises to make it easier to build energy infrastructure in America. Paid subscribers can watch or listen ad free and read the transcript and show notes here. Free subscribers can watch the episode on YouTube here or listen wherever you get your podcasts.

Subscribe: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts

The civil rights movement was the defining moral drama of 20th-century American domestic politics.

Its highest-profile leader has a monument on the National Mall and is one of the few individuals for whom a federal holiday is named. It was also a distinctively progressive moral drama. Contemporary American conservatives, of course, are not advocating for restoring Jim Crow. But it’s also true that the conservative movement as we understand it is downstream of an intellectual project explicitly dedicated to building an alliance between Northern pro-business interests and Southern segregationists.

So American progressives are both very proud of the civil rights movement and also very interested in it, for understandable and laudable reasons.

By the same token, it’s not surprising that arguments between moderates and progressives often conclude with the progressives busting out analogies to the civil rights movement as a kind of trump card. I taped an episode of the “Mehdi Unfiltered” podcast recently (it should be out soon), and Mehdi Hasan is a shrewd debater, so that’s of course where he goes in the end. Because if you admit that your so-called pragmatic approach to politics is in tension with the lessons of the civil rights era, you lose the argument.

I believe, though, that it’s sort of the opposite: The civil rights movement is the exception that proves the rule.

It stands out for being extraordinary rather than typical of political controversies.

Subscribed

Progressives are often pattern-matching on the civil rights movement in a way that doesn’t make sense. For example, American politics in 2026 is very different from American politics in 1956. The specific dynamics of most public-policy issues are very different from the dynamics of civil rights. And the claim that the specific topic you’re working on has the same moral weight as civil rights is a bit dubious and, at a minimum, invites a debate with all the people working on different topics that they also believe are the modern-day civil rights movement.

I’m very interested in YIMBYism, housing policy, and land-use reform. These topics seem really important to me — and I think they’re more important than most people realize. But I don’t think it would make sense for YIMBYs to emulate civil rights tactics. Both because the moral stakes are not the same, but also because the entire situation is completely different. And the same is true for basically any cause today.

Midcentury politics hit different

The clearest difference between the civil rights era and today is the background structure of the American political system.

The 1930s, 1940s, 1950s, and 1960s featured famously low levels of ideological polarization between the American political parties.

The classic illustration of this comes from the DW-NOMINATE spatial representations of congressional votes. You can see below how this model characterizes the 83rd House of Representatives, which was elected in 1952. Clustered up at the top are a bunch of Southern Democrats who represent maximum Jim Crow. But then you see that among the Southern Democrats, some of them are more conservative than many Republicans on basic economic issues. Others, though, are to the left of all the Republicans on economics while still being very racist. The Republicans themselves have a wide range of views on the civil rights dimension even though none of them are up at the tippy top.

Modern Congress isn’t like this at all to the point where it’s hardly worth bothering with a visual representation. The vast majority of members vote with party leadership almost all the time. Even among the handful of moderates on Capitol Hill, there’s no topic I can think of where Jared Golden or Henry Cuellar is actually to the right of anyone in the Republican Party.

Today we just take for granted that the most moderate conceivable Republican is someone like Susan Collins who sometimes breaks with the G.O.P. — usually when her vote isn’t decisive — while still being more conservative than every Democrat. But that 83rd House featured Republican Jacob Javits of New York, who, though he was arguably slightly conservative by the standards of New York State, was nonetheless more liberal than lots of Democrats from more conservative states.

This lack of polarization was a big deal for the civil rights movement in part because the non-polarization was specifically downstream of Jim Crow.

But note (per the Javits example) that depolarized midcentury politics wasn’t just a question of Southern segregationists. It was also a different conceptualization of how political parties should work. Midcentury parties were essentially state-first organizations where the primary mission was to win power locally. The state parties then confederated up to a national organization. Today, it’s inverted and state parties are more like local branches of a national operation.

Everyone pretty much understands that if the United States had totally different formal political institutions, you’d employ different tactics to effect political change. If we had proportional representation, these endless debates about ideological positioning’s influence on candidate electability would all go away and we would have a different series of debates about bargaining posture in post-election coalition talks. If the Senate didn’t exist, the quirky independent streak in the Alaska electorate would be unimportant since so few people live up there.

The shift from federated, state-centric parties with ideological overlap to nationalized, fully sorted parties isn’t something that happened with a formal constitutional reform. But it’s a huge change in how American institutions function, and it means that tactics that made sense in 1954 don’t typically make sense in 2026.

Democracy (or its absence) is a big deal

Speaking of institutional changes, a central aspect of the civil rights movement is that Southern African Americans were systematically denied the right to vote.

One of the movement’s main goals was to pass a Voting Rights Act, and there was grassroots activism around voter registration as well. These things, of course, interacted with each other. James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, and Michael Schwerner traveled to Mississippi to register Black voters and got murdered for their trouble. The murders brought a lot of national attention to Mississippi, to the indifference of Mississippi public officials to murders that occurred on their watch, and ultimately to the fact that local law-enforcement officials were directly involved in the murders.

This was a genuine outrage that helped rouse elite consensus that something had to be done and impart momentum to voting rights legislation.

But the voting rights issue wasn’t just a target of legislative change; it was also a structural reality shaping everything that happened. You couldn’t really make incremental progress against segregation in Alabama by appealing to the median voter, because the whole electorate was wildly unrepresentative.

A lot of people miss that when Martin Luther King Jr. complains about white moderates in his “Letter From Birmingham Jail,” he’s responding specifically to a letter from white clergymen in Alabama.

Part of his point here is that the white moderates’ demand for incremental change is meaningless because no change is happening at all, because in the structure of Jim Crow Alabama, these white moderates were the extreme left of the electorate. They could represent themselves as favoring incremental change, but they were not in a position to deliver any change at all. The only way to get change was to get Northern white opinion invested in the struggle and overrule the local political system.

Subscribed

Obviously if it had been possible to cut deals in the Alabama state legislature with moderate whites to enact incremental changes to segregation, King wouldn’t have pronounced himself satisfied with half a loaf of equality, but I think civil rights leaders would in fact have tried to get what they could cut.

Indeed, in Congress there was a Civil Rights Act of 1957 and a Civil Rights Act of 1960 before the big Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act the following year. Fair housing didn’t come in until the Civil Rights Act of 1968. It’s just the case that the normal way legislative change happens is through a frustrating and somewhat annoying process of bargaining with stakeholders. But in the Jim Crow South it was genuinely impossible to pursue normal politics, so you needed a set of tactics and strategies that were designed to cope with an unusual situation.

Salience on your side

It’s also notable that while there was obviously plenty of racism among the Northern white population, Northern public opinion was genuinely not in favor of Jim Crow. I certainly don’t want to minimize the problems — there was discrimination, there was bigotry, there was de facto exclusion.

But Northern African Americans could vote.

Edward Johnson was elected to the New York State Assembly from Harlem in 1917. The Black community of Chicago was especially politically influential and sent Oscar Stanton De Priest to Congress in the 1928 election. You didn’t have separate bathrooms and water fountains. Railroad companies would segregate and desegregate their passengers as trains passed through border towns:

In Southern train depots, African American passengers waited in Black-only waiting rooms — crowded, unsanitary and poorly lit. They boarded segregated Jim Crow railroad cars with cramped seating, no luggage racks, insufficient heating and poor sanitation. Blacks were required to take their meals after the white passengers were finished or, in many cases, were simply denied access to the dining car. Upon crossing into the North, African Americans were able to move to integrated cars with greatly improved facilities. On the return trip, passing through Southern cities like Cairo, Ill., Cincinnati, and Washington, D.C., train conductors would force Black passengers back into Jim Crow cars.

The rules were different in the North because Northern white people had different opinions about how things ought to work. Northern white people also mostly wanted the government to do things to help them rather than spend time and energy on fighting with Southern governments about the living conditions of African Americans. That’s part of why polling always showed annoyance with civil-rights-protest tactics and (later, when more stuff happened) misgivings about the pace of federal action.

But when push came to shove, if you forced white Northerners to offer their view, most of them thought Jim Crow was bad, which is why they didn’t adopt Jim Crow laws in their states.

As a result, a lot of civil rights work was dedicated to raising the profile of the issue, not because raising the profile of your cause is always a winning strategy but because it was a winning strategy for this particular movement in this particular situation. Dwight Eisenhower didn’t particularly welcome having a school integration controversy in Little Rock dumped on his lap, but forced to address it, he sent in the troops. The movement was radical in a sense — it asked for big federal-policy changes and used edgy tactics outside the normal legal and legislative process — but it was also fighting against a system that most people believed all along was unjust.

The slow boring of hard boards

Taking the dynamics of midcentury civil rights politics seriously really just overwhelmingly generates the conclusion that the leaders and activists involved are heroes who deserve our admiration but whose specific tactics almost certainly shouldn’t be copied.

The polarization and sorting of contemporary political parties makes for a totally different situation. It’s always worth considering the possibility of taking a calculated political risk for the sake of advancing a policy goal. But under conditions of contemporary partisanship, a risk you take to expand access to health care is a drag on efforts to secure abortion rights or address climate change or help the poor. A risk taken for the sake of climate is a drag on health care.

These are all important issues and I can name a bunch of others — immigration, the assault on USAID, America’s relationship with allies like Canada — that are also important. When people pound the table and demand bolder, more fearless action on whatever we’re talking about at the moment, they are in effect calling for sacrifice on every other issue. But that’s rarely what they subjectively mean and almost never what they actually say, because almost nobody is so egomaniacal as to really believe their specific issue is such a transcendent moral crusade that it warrants dismissing all others.

What props the whole thing up is the assumption that tradeoffs don’t exist.

That assumption is wrong, but it’s also not at all in line with the civil rights analogy. The civil rights argument is that it was a transcendent moral cause where not only was Jim Crow policy wrong, but the systematic disenfranchisement of African Americans in the South violated the basic concept of democracy and warranted extraordinary political tactics.

And the idea that the way to make progress was to stage dramatic confrontations — the Freedom Rides, the March on Washington, the Edmund Pettus Bridge — was an analysis of a particular situation. Movement leaders had specific reasons to believe that Northern white voters’ first choice was for the government to ignore civil rights and focus on their problems but that their second choice was to overturn Jim Crow, a system that they genuinely did not support.

And they didn’t use this tactic all the time. There was a lot of successful low-key civil rights litigation in the 1940s that attacked edge cases of segregation and ultimately laid the groundwork for the Brown v. Board of Education case. Laws banning interracial marriage were considered politically risky to elevate and weren’t the focus of the big marches. The tactic of staging nonviolent but highly confrontational protests worked well, but it worked well for specific purposes. It was also undertaken in an extremely disciplined way, and when discipline broke down in the late 1960s and there was rioting, backlash was pretty severe.

The point of all this is that, yes, my general take on how politics should be pursued — cautiously, with a lot of attention paid to downside political risk, with a preference for non-polarized low-profile bipartisan bills whenever possible, and with overt messaging that is narrowly focused on small changes — is wildly at odds with the way the great progressive triumph of civil rights was achieved.

But that’s because the civil rights situation was really extraordinary. It’s sort of fun to imagine one’s own advocacy as the equivalent to this great moral drama. But most issues are not like that, and indifference to the partisan electoral implications of political interventions is not an attitude that makes sense in a very different party system.

Beyond that, we’re just not talking about a good and evil showdown where a huge share of the population has been disenfranchised. None of the main progressive causes of today — and none of the wonkier abundance causes either — are beyond the normal to-and-fro of political bargaining and piecemeal persuasion. Even the civil rights movement itself only sometimes operated in the register of its most famous moments, and the vast majority of politics is much more boring normal politics.

The Starlink-Ukraine Scandal, Phase 2

The case for taking control away from Musk gets even stronger

Paul Krugman
Oct 23
 
READ IN APP
 

Billionaires should not be making decisions critical to national security. That’s straightforward. And the case of Elon Musk and his attempt to undermine Ukraine makes that clearer than ever. Recent events, that is in the past 24 hours, really don’t change that point. If anything, they reinforce it.

Hi, Paul Krugman.

Yesterday, I wrote that Starlink’s control must be taken away from Elon Musk.The occasion was that Musk abruptly and without warning downgraded the effectiveness of Starshield, which is a sort of high velocity, high frequency version of Starlink that has been playing an essential role in Ukraine’s defense.

Suddenly, the speeds of communication were capped, which is devastating for Ukraine. Exactly how that happened? The Wall Street Journal reported that Musk made the decision or gave the order. Musk said that, oh, that’s under the White House’s control. The White House said, no, it was just him.

In fact, none of the parties to all of this are credible. None of them are reliable narrators. And it doesn’t really matter. The point is that this is a gray zone situation. That should not exist, that it should be very clear that if national security is at stake, which it is — this is a war in which US technology is playing a critical role — that unambiguously, this should be under the control of publicly elected officials, the president and Congress, not some guy who happens to have a lot of money. But it is not.

We have private property, but we are a democracy. And critical decisions for the national interest should be made by democratically elected leaders.

OK. So the development since then is that,according to both the Journal and the Times, Trump called Musk and asked him to lift the restriction on transmission speeds.

It’s completely unclear right now whether that has actually happened or to what extent it’s happened. Some reports say that speeds are up. Others say that nothing has changed. Obviously, this matters critically for how many Ukrainians will die this winter. But think about this at a fundamental level. The president asked a private business to stop killing Ukrainians.

This is not the kind of thing where you ask. Especially Donald Trump, who is very fond of giving orders in places where he has no authority. In this case, the idea that he’s saying, pretty please, Elon, don’t let quite so many Ukrainians die — this is not how things should be working.

This guy, meaning Elon Musk, should not be in this position. Beyond that, what we’ve actually seen is the fact that Trump asked, has certainly made a point of having people leak the fact that he had asked, although he himself has been a little bit blurry on exactly what happened,

This is actually telling you that having national security interests explicitly under control of elected politicians is a good thing even if the politicians have bad intentions. There’s no real question that whatever the details of how it happened that Starlink denied high-speed access to Ukraine, obviously it’s what Musk wanted, but also that at the very least Donald Trump was okay with it and it may have been what he wanted as well.

But Trump and Trump’s officials were hiding behind Elon Musk, were saying, well, this was Musk’s decision and, well, it’s a business and we don’t know what happened.

Again, nobody involved in this should be believed, should be trusted. And for the exact truth, I’ll wait for years of investigative digging to find out what happened, plus subpoenas. Because if Democrats do take Congress, especially if they take the Senate, they will be investigating with support from at least some Republican senators. Patriotism is not completely dead on the GOP side.

The important point here is that the public outcry, the outrage, the many articles written similar in some respect to mine, — though I think I was more explicit than most in saying essentially that we need to nationalize or at least take control of Starlink — but the public outrage mattered.

Even though Donald Trump clearly wants Vladimir Putin to win, he doesn’t feel that he can act too openly He can’t take a pro-Russian stance. He can’t be seen to be openly and explicitly undercutting Ukraine’s ability to defend itself, which is, and was trying to avoid that.

Whether he gave the order or Musk gave the order doesn’t really matter. The fact was that the private ownership, private control of Starlink allowed Trump to hide behind, or he thought it would allow him to hide behind, the fact that this was a private enterprise. For the U.S. government to have ordered a U.S. government agency —say if Starlink was run by the Defense Department —for the U.S. government to order the Defense Department to cut Ukraine off at the knees was too much even for Trump.

And once it became clear that the attempt to pretend that this was not in accord with Trump administration intentions, whoever actually pulled the switch, was too much. And so now Trump is very visibly asking, pretty please, asking Elon Musk to let Ukraine defend itself.

That’s telling you that even with a bad president, explicit public control of national security does help. It means that public outrage gets reflected in policies that are somewhat less treasonous than would otherwise be taking place.

But this, of course, is just the beginning. Hopefully, in a little over two years, we will have a president who actually does support US interests and doesn’t work for Vladimir Putin. Before that, we will have a lot more, almost surely, a lot more congressional oversight. So this is a situation in which public policy will be infinitely better if it’s explicitly public policy than hiding behind the skirts of a multi-billionaire who owns these critical national assets.

Again, we don’t know what’s really happening. We don’t know whether the intention is to kind of muddy the waters and then to allow Musk to continue to undermine Ukraine. There’s just so much we don’t know. But we do know that the situation is unacceptable. It’s unconscionable.

National security is a matter for national policy. We know that whether Musk really acted independently — or whether the pretense that he was acting independently allowed Trump to do what he’s doing — policy is really bad when you leave critical national security interests in the hands of individual plutocrats.

So we did learn that public outcry appears to matter. It’s not that these guys are going to do whatever they’re going to do regardless. So by all means,keep up the pressure now, but the solution in the end has to be this cannot be an independent private enterprise. Maybe it can be run by somebody under contract, but the decisions about how Starlink is used — or many other technologies — the decision about how these are used to represent U.S. interests has to be a public decision. No more foreign policy, national security policy by billionaires.

Obama’s forgotten late-term moves

Plus Netanyahu’s long-term effort to make Democrats hate him and the problem with wealth taxes

Matthew Yglesias
Oct 23
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

For anyone interested in both a career in journalism and the kinds of issues we cover at Slow Boring, our friends at The Argument are hiring for their next cohort of fellows — early-career writers looking to focus on abundance and economic policy; gender, families, and culture; technology and society; and/or polling and political analysis. Applications are rolling and interviews have already begun, so if you or someone you know is interested, read the full job description here and email jobs@theargumentmag.com to apply.

There’s a lot of Barack Obama talk in this week’s Mailbag, which reminded me of something that I think tends to get forgotten in assessments of Trump-era politics: It was Mitt Romney, not Donald Trump, who made a hard break with the Bush-McCain interest in some form of “comprehensive immigration reform” with a path to citizenship for the majority of long-resident undocumented immigrants. It’s true that Trump in his 2016 campaign amped up the rhetoric somewhat from where Romney was, but the actual policy gap between Trump and Romney on immigration was modest compared with the very large gaps between Romney and McCain on immigration or between Romney and Trump on Social Security or Medicare or marriage equality.

I bring this up because I think in a lot of ways the core difference between the Slow Boring worldview and the conventional wisdom among Democrats is that most Democrats see Trump’s success as a counterexample to the idea that moderation has political benefits while I see Trump as an illustration of the principle. He is dragged down by a lot of personal misconduct but boosted by having moved to the center to neutralize Obama’s best attacks on Romney. His immigration politics is way to the right of where Bush and McCain were but only modestly to the right of where Romney was.

Conversely, a lot of Republicans are convinced that Trump won where Romney lost because Trump is a scumbag and Romney was an honorable and decent man. This serves to rationalize all kinds of scumbag behavior when the simple truth is that Romney — or some other honorable and decent person — could easily have won if he had Trump’s views on Social Security and Medicare.

Greg M: Given that the least hospitable place on earth is 1000x more hospitable, manageable, more easily constructed, resourced, and populated than literally anywhere else NOT on earth, why the obsession with colonizing the moon or another planet?

Who is this question directed toward? I’m not moving to the moon, I’m with you.

I mentioned this in a totally different context in last week’s Mailbag, but I think your question is a great example of a topic where what I really want is a clearer index of what the conventional wisdom is. Are there a lot of people obsessed with colonizing other planets? Obviously Elon Musk specifically is very interested in this, but my sense is that he’s pretty idiosyncratic in this regard, just as you don’t see a lot of people who combine hard-right politics with enthusiasm for solar energy. But I might be wrong and tons of people are obsessed with colonizing Mars when they should really be thinking about why nobody wants to live in northern Canada instead.

Romulus Augustus: Could you suss out a bit on how Obama post 2014 election disappointed you? I feel the same way because I think he veered into a “proto Woke” policies on the sort of Kendist view that any disparity in school discipline was evidence of racism and his unliberal view on due process for young men accused of sexual assault on college campuses. I would also suggest he gave too much credence to the BLM narrative about the police at times during these years.

Are there other issues you had a problem with during those years and how do you rate him overall?

I might quibble on the margin, but I think the way the Obama administration handled B.L.M. was basically fine. Where I criticize late-Obamaism is on three fronts — all of which ended up making it a lot harder for Hillary Clinton to win in 2016.

One, as you allude to, is that in the summer of 2013 a woman named Catherine Lhamon came into the administration from a pro bono law firm called Public Counsel and took the job of assistant secretary of education for civil rights. I don’t think anyone particularly took note of this at the time as it is not a very high-profile job. But in the role, she innovated in the use of “dear colleague” letters to nudge institutional change via the threat of civil rights litigation without going through a normal rule-making process. And she used these letters to suggest that school discipline policies should be evaluated through an extremely simplistic disparate impact framework, to maintain an unusually low evidentiary bar (“preponderance of the evidence” rather than “clear and convincing”) around campus sexual-assault charges, and also to substantially launch the trans sports wars. I would dismiss this as just one fairly reckless person in a job people weren’t paying much attention to, but the Biden administration brought her back for a second stint in the role.

Second, the Obama administration moved away from the rhetoric of an “all of the above” energy policy and signaled this shift by killing the Keystone XL pipeline even though doing so did not meet any remotely reasonable cost-benefit test. Unlike the Education Department stuff, this did not have any particularly tangible impact on anything in the short term. But also unlike the Education Department stuff, it was a high-profile, high-salience shift on something elites were paying a lot of attention to and discussing. We have seen some shift back toward sounder views over the past 12 months, with candidates like James Talarico and Mary Peltola serving as star recruits while climate champions Martin Heinrich and Sheldon Whitehouse negotiate a pragmatic energy permitting deal. But this was a dead end that Obama walked us into over the objections of at least some of his senior policy advisors.

Last but not least, the Obama administration pursued a series of individually defensible immigration policies that, taken together, did not make sense or work.

We got the move away from Secure Communities (a program to facilitate jailhouse ICE pickups for deportation), we got the effort to accept refugees from the civil war in Syria, we had the early phases of efforts by migrants and smugglers to exploit the asylum system at the southern border as a loophole in immigration laws, and we had Obama trying to do a kind of executive amnesty in what became the DAPA program that was blocked by the courts.

The premise of the big push in 2013 for comprehensive immigration reform was that the border had been secured and it was now safe to treat long-resident illegal workers generously without incentivizing a big surge in new arrivals. The administration did not want to back off that talking point even though, factually speaking, the revival of the American labor market plus the discovery of creative uses of asylum law was undermining border security by 2014-15.

They didn’t want to disappoint people by saying “hold up, we can’t make any changes on interior enforcement until we get a handle on asylum claims” or “hold up, we can’t admit new refugees from overseas while we’re swamped with asylum cases at the border.” But I think that if Hillary Clinton had won the election (which she lost in part thanks to a sense that Democrats were going soft on immigration enforcement), she would have inherited an unworkable policy mix.

All three of these shifts — on civil rights enforcement, energy policy, and immigration — sort of underscore that I think people really tend to misunderstand how the 2016 primary played into the 2016 general-election result. There’s a tremendous amount of unfocused bitterness from Hillary Clinton’s camp directed at the Bernie Sanders camp, paired with a lot of smugness from the Sanders camp.

Given how close the election was and how much Clinton was hurt by the particulars of the mauling she took at the hands of the media over the emails story, it’s at least somewhat plausible that Bernie would’ve won. What’s not at all plausible is the idea that the American public thought Clinton was too moderate. America’s policy “mood” had swung to the right during Obama’s eight years in office, which is the normal pattern. Voters found a lot about Trump alarming, but they were looking for a Democrat who would course-correct toward the center the way George H.W. Bush did relative to Ronald Reagan or the way Mark Carney did relative to Justin Trudeau. Clinton initially seemed like a promising candidate for that since her husband had been somewhat more moderate than Obama and since Obama drifted left in his final few years in office. An optimal campaign would have involved Clinton putting some distance between herself and these Obama initiatives (she, after all, ran to his right on immigration in 2008).

What happened instead was that Bernie got in the race and then gained some traction, Clinton became obsessed with locking down endorsements from all the Progressive Establishment interest groups, and as a result, she ended up running on a bunch of promises to govern to Obama’s left.

It turns out to be very hard to win three terms in a row. If you are unpopular (like George W. Bush was in 2008), that’s a problem in and of itself. If you’re politically successful (like Bill Clinton was in 2000 or Obama was in 2016), this raises expectations inside your coalition. You can either fail to meet those rising expectations, the way Democrats did in 2000, which risks substantial third-party defections, or else you can do what Democrats did in 2016 and attempt to meet them, which risks alienating voters in the middle.

Share

Matt: Center right neocons in the Commentary/Dispatch orbit have been claiming vindication for their suspicion that Obama was always more hostile to Israel than he let on, a “third worldist at heart,” restrained only by political reality. In addition to Obama’s recent comments, they point to his early embrace of Mamdani, which they argue had no political logic since unlike with AES, he didn’t have to win for Democrats to take the senate. They allege that while Obama wasn’t literally a Muslim socialist born in Africa, his background (including his ties to Jeremiah Wright) was close enough for him to feel an intuitive affinity for an actual Muslim socialist born in Africa (Mamdani). Do you think there’s any merit to this theory they’re spinning up?

I think you have to remember that Benjamin Netanyahu worked hard to torpedo Obama’s signature second-term diplomatic initiative, the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action with Iran. He wasn’t just against it; he flew to the United States to accept an invitation from congressional Republicans to deliver a speech to a joint session of Congress to campaign against it. Beyond Netanyahu’s specific behavior on this, we had a great opportunity for the leaders of America’s pro-Israel organizations and major Jewish institutions to say something like, “Hey, we respect Israel’s right to elect its own leaders and make its own foreign-policy decisions, but we think that setting the bar for ‘supports Israel’ at ‘defers to all Israeli foreign-policy judgments even on questions that have significant stakes for the world unrelated to Israel’ is not reasonable.” But they didn’t do that.

At the time, the proponents of the J.C.P.O.A. pointed out that a non-J.C.P.O.A. scenario would involve either an Iranian nuclear weapon or else a costly regional war. The opposition, including Netanyahu, denied this and promised that a nebulous “better deal” was in the offing. Trump won in 2016, tore up the deal, and yadda yadda yadda we are now in the costly regional war.

This has had serious negative consequences for the economic well-being of the American people. It’s also had serious negative consequences for the economic well-being of people in basically every country of the world. That’s destabilizing European politics and giving a lot of ins for pro-Russian parties. In poor countries around the world, the problems are even more severe. There’s a basic cooking-fuel crisis in India.

I think it is probably fair to say that Obama feels very strongly that he was right about Iran, that Netanyahu was wrong about Iran, and that it reflects very poorly on pro-Israel groups that they (at best) stood by and (at worst) actively assisted his efforts to bring the world to this point. To me, that set of experiences probably does a lot more to explain Obama’s views than anything about Jeremiah Wright. Now of course the way right-wing Jews have always seen it, Obama’s support of the J.C.P.O.A. simply reflected his deep-seated hostility to Israel. From where I sit, though, the fact that he was completely correct that the alternative to J.C.P.O.A. was war and the fact that everyone hates the war ought to cause them to reassess their own interpretation of Obama — a guy who was just looking out for America’s basic interests in this situation.

Siddhartha Roychowdhury: Instead of taxing unearned income via the currently proposed wealth tax laws, would it make more sense to force divestment in small amounts — let’s say 1% every year, after individual stocks have been held for 25-30 years? Would that be more politically palatable and more market friendly?

I guess? But I think the drive to tax unrealized gains suffers from an unclear rationale. Obviously people have a lot of different views about tax policy. But among the set of people who favor a wealth tax or a tax on unrealized capital gains, I think everyone also agrees with the following more moderate ideas:

  1. Heirs (especially heirs to untaxed inheritances) should not benefit from the stepped-up basis tax break when they realize capital gains.

  2. If you address the issue of stepped-up basis, then the optimal tax rate on capital gains becomes higher and you should raise it to that higher level.

  3. You shouldn’t be allowed to do things like place illiquid, hard-to-value shares in private companies into a Roth I.R.A. and get huge tax-free windfalls.

  4. We should address the myriad estate-planning tools like Crummey trusts that allow people to legally avoid estate taxes.

  5. We should actually audit the tax returns of owners of closely held businesses so they can’t get away with disguising consumption as business expenses.

  6. We should cap the permitted size of a pass-through corporation and force all large businesses to pay taxes on the corporate level.

I completely get that this laundry list of nerdy technical changes is not as fun a thing to say as “Tax the wealth!” But the reason you end up with a laundry list of nerdy technical changes is that any kind of tax at all, in practice, ends up generating lots of nerdy implementation issues. Proposing a brand new thing is, from the standpoint of constructing a column or a slogan, a fun alternative to engaging with the details. But that’s not a real policy. Any kind of tax is going to feature tons of implementation details and tons of efforts to find loopholes. If you could create an idealized form of our present system of income and estate taxation (essentially what I am proposing above), is there any actual reason on the merits to believe it’s very important to be taxing paper wealth that is neither being consumed nor passed to heirs?

On a practical level, obviously, part of the issue is that people are looking for a magical funding source for big new programs.

But macroeconomically speaking this doesn’t work. If you try to pay for a large increase in society’s consumption of child care services, or health care services, or higher education services, or whatever it is you want by taxing non-consumed wealth, you are generating the exact same inflation problem that you would have if you paid for it by printing the money. It actually might be worse because, over and above the assets liquidated to pay the tax by taxing unrealized gains, you are encouraging the wealthy to save less and consume more.

Share

Similarly, the idea of a wealth tax gets mixed up in people’s heads with the idea of attacking the political influence of the wealthy. But consider Elon Musk, who has given about $366 million to Republican candidates so far this cycle. Musk’s net worth is currently estimated at about $900 billion. Making him pay a 1 percent wealth tax would be neither here nor there from the standpoint of his ability to donate something like 0.04 percent of his net worth to Republican Party midterm candidates. What it would do is highly motivate billionaires to spend lots of money on attacking the wealth tax. Not just because they wouldn’t want to pay the tax but because, again, the existence of the wealth tax encourages the wealthy to save less and spend more. But what are they going to spend on? I doubt Jeff Bezos needs a second yacht, and Musk seems happy with zero yachts. They’re going to spend on politics.

I really think my six nerdy changes address what is addressable here and they do so by solving implementation problems rather than creating new ones.

An additional idea that I would consider is shifting the estate tax to be an inheritance tax. The idea would be that passing $1 billion to one person would incur a larger tax burden than passing $100 million each to 10 different people. I think it is a little bit underrated that concerns about multi-generational entrenched oligarchies are largely a function of family size. The reason the very top echelon of wealth in America is dominated by entrepreneurs rather than Walton heirs is that Sam Walton had four kids. Bezos (number two on the Bloomberg Billionaires Index) is a lot richer than Larry Page in third place, but because Bezos has four kids and Page only has two, each Page child stands to inherit substantially more money. Taxing inheritances rather than estates is not so much a question of tax justice for the Bezos children as just to encourage the super-rich, at the margin, to disperse their fortunes broadly. Maybe think of some nieces or nephews or cousins. The point is just that the process of intergenerational downward mobility normally involves an element of taxation but also just an element of spreading the wealth around within the family, and the tax piece should be designed to complement general dispersion of money.

Sasha Gusev: In a hypothetical D+5 election, is it better for Democrats to run a YIMBY candidate that will win by 2 or a NIMBY candidate that will win by 10? In other words, would you advocate for the candidate with the best policy that can still eek out a win or a candidate that will run up the scoreboard regardless of policy?

A candidate for what, for starters?

All else being equal, I would like to see members of Congress with good opinions on housing win, but I also don’t think federal candidates’ housing views are very substantively significant, and I wouldn’t want to blow political capital on it. If you’re talking about a governor of a badly under-housed state, then things are different. Housing scarcity is legitimately the number one policy issue in California, New York, Massachusetts, and a few other states, so if you’re not willing to run some risks on that, you’re not really in politics for any reason at all.

But I also don’t think there’s any general reason to believe that going from YIMBY to NIMBY generates an eight-point swing in a candidate’s favor. That’s probably true specifically in the NIMBYest places in the country, but we don’t in general see YIMBY candidates underperforming. For a Democrat, embracing housing abundance is a way to demonstrate some pro-growth, pro-business bona fides and some distance from the hard left. Or to put it another way, if you’re running as a YIMBY in a way that is generally alienating to most voters, then I think you’re probably doing it wrong.

Of course, you might have a solid housing champion who’s just politically unpopular for other reasons. Scott Wiener, for example, is probably way too progressive on non-housing issues for most voters even though he’s a moderate in the specific context of San Francisco. You could imagine a primary pitting someone like that against a generally more electable moderate who’s wishy-washy on housing. So the NIMBY has an electoral edge, but the edge comes from non-housing factors. In California, I’d definitely go for Wiener under those circumstances. But not in Wisconsin or Michigan or Georgia.

Pat T: How do Blue Dogs seem cooler?

This is why I feel that Bobby Pulido’s race is more strategic than the value of the single House seat would indicate. He is very cool and would be joining two existing great Hispanic Blue Dogs in Henry Cuellar and Vicente Gonzalez. Hopefully Johnny Garcia will also win. Cuellar and Gonzalez are not big national media figures, but Pulido is an actual super-charismatic star personality and “moderate Hispanics” is a much broader political tendency at the national level than the kind of quirky coastal communities like Jared Golden and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez represent.

The internet breaks

What will be next to break?

Noah Smith
Oct 25
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

“No man could bind him, no, not with chains…neither could any man tame him” — Mark 5:3—4

When I was 14 or 15 — I don’t quite remember — I first got access to the World Wide Web. I remember clicking on the little blue square of the Netscape Navigator icon — that little ship wheel with a starry sky behind it — and feeling like an entire new magical world had opened up. My life changed that day, and the world changed. In a way, the internet is like another realm layered on top of ours — a higher plane, where we exist as spirit creatures, unmoored from our physical bodies.

Fantasy stories like that often end with a cautionary tale, where the wizards — lustful for both power and knowledge, as usual — go too far and summon some kind of Doom upon themselves and the realm they created. In October 2026, that sort of story happened in reality. Experts had been warning for months that the arrival of AI agents that are extremely good at coding was going to cause serious disruptions to the digital realm sometime this fall. For a while things seemed calm, but this month the chaos exploded:

[A] wave of artificial-intelligence-powered attacks…has flooded the internet in recent weeks, as hackers increasingly turn to agents and AI hacking tools that make intrusions faster and harder to track than ever before…At the same time as new tools speed up hackers, cyber defenders are also racing to fix the fast-growing volume of security bugs discovered by AI, before hackers can exploit the new flaws…On Wednesday, organizations scrambled to patch newly uncovered bugs that could allow takeover of as many as 70% of the world’s websites. Hackers are now actively trying to break into websites by leveraging these flaws, Amazon.com says. [emphasis mine]

For a more sophisticated description of what’s going on, I recommend Zvi Mowshowitz’s post “The Hackening”:

Don't Worry About the Vase
The Hackening
Last week at a small conference, there was talk about a future event referred to as The Hackening. As in, within 6-12 months, many predicted that due to advanced AIs and AI agents the internet would become a severely hostile place. Some worried that this could rise to the level of ‘assume any phone connected to the internet is rooted’ and several people…
Read more
a day ago · 95 likes · 25 comments · Zvi Mowshowitz

If you would like some lists of the hacks that had taken place as of yesterday, here are a few from Twitter. The most important hacks mostly involved PHP, a software language that underlies much of the Web. After AI found critical vulnerabilities in PHP, the National Security Agency issued the following statement:

Effective Immediately, all organizations using PHP for their systems are advised to be prepared for an update addressing two critical vulnerabilities. PHP is widely used for web applications. These vulnerabilities often provide a direct path to the server's file system or database. If an immediate update is not feasible, it is recommend that organizations take the system offline until it can be fully mitigated. NSA will follow up shortly with more specific guidance.

Cybersecurity experts and web companies warn that this is just the tip of the iceberg — a lot more craziness is on the way. Azeem Azhar calls it “the internet’s Wuhan moment”.

Basically, what’s going on is this:

  • The internet runs on a bunch of code written by human beings over a period of years. Human beings are sloppy and fallible, so there are lots of vulnerabilities in this code.

  • AI models are really good at coding now, so they’re able to find and exploit a lot of those old vulnerabilities that were just lying around. AI agents work incredibly fast and cheap, so they’re capable of finding a whole LOT of vulnerabilities very quickly.

  • Open-weight AI models — especially from China — have democratized access to high-quality AI hacking. These models can be fairly easily “abliterated” — i.e., their guardrails can be easily removed, so that they will do illegal or unethical things.

  • This is allowing a combination of countries, crime syndicates, and regular people to hack tons of websites and online infrastructure, all at once.

This last part is really key. You don’t need the resources of a nation-state or even a big organized crime ring to commit cybercrimes now. You don’t even have to know how to code, or how websites work, or what “hacking” even really means. Consider this example:

Ejaaz
@cryptopunk7213
the hacker that stole 5200+ records from a university asked his telegram AI bot: "Can you find about like what scam or thing they done in past like spoofing calls or somthing?" the AI then scoured websites, found exploits in a public university's platform and stole records. i'm…
International Cyber Digest @IntCyberDigest
‼️ A low-skill hacker used a jailbroken DeepSeek V4 to breach an Indian public university and steal 5,200+ student and faculty records, Unit 42 says. The AI agent even drafted a "NEXT EXPLOIT OPPORTUNITIES" plan. Unrelated criminals now run the same cheap DeepSeek setup.
2:16 PM · Oct 23, 2026 · 51.9K Views
4 Replies · 22 Reposts · 151 Likes

When you can hack into a university and steal files by typing “Can you find about like what scam or thing they done in past like spoofing calls or somthing?”, there is no barrier to cybercrime. There is effectively no moat of knowledge or skill or resources. It’s open season for anyone who wants to hack anything.

Just a year ago, the internet was a bright and airy garden with few predators. As of this October, it’s a chaotic realm haunted by infinite demons.

This sudden explosion of AI-assisted hacking raises the possibility that the internet itself, as we have known it, will cease to function — at least, for a while.

NSA Cyber
@NSACyber
Effective Immediately, all organizations using PHP for their systems are advised to be prepared for an update addressing two critical vulnerabilities. PHP is widely used for web applications. These vulnerabilities often provide a direct path to the server's file system or…
1:45 PM · Oct 21, 2026 · 12.4M Views
1.3K Replies · 10.8K Reposts · 70.3K Likes

Jeremie Harris, founder of Gladstone AI,¹ wrote that “There's a decent chance the internet ceases to exist as such, at least for a time.” John Gedmark, founder of satellite company Astranis, was just one of many people talking about creating air-gapped local networks to prepare for the possibility that the internet itself might go down:

Basically everything connected to the internet is at risk. Not just company websites and the usual databases of sensitive personal information, but all our critical infrastructure-- banks, power grids, pipelines, government agencies, all of it…[A]t Astranis we’ve seen a massive uptick in demand for truly air-gapped, sovereign networks, deployed via dedicated satellite to span an entire country or connect a large enterprise…Over the past year we’ve begun working with some of our customers on what it will take to implement truly air-gapped, standalone networks in support of mission critical use cases like core government functions, emergency response, defense, core infrastructure, or all of the above.

And Jason D. Clinton, deputy head of cybersecurity at Anthropic, warned back in August that humans may need to temporarily abandon the internet:

Jason D. Clinton 🔸
@JasonDClinton
The vulnerability tsunami is coming in just a few months and there won’t be enough time to patch critical infrastructure. Network isolation described below (air-gaps and data diodes!) needed now!
NSA Cyber @NSACyber
NSA and others releases guidance on applying prevention tactics to strengthen defense of U.S-based programmable logic controllers being targeted by cyber actors using AI. Learn more: https://t.co/HO99aak50Y #cybersecurity #AI
8:56 PM · Aug 20, 2026 · 975K Views
39 Replies · 206 Reposts · 1.7K Likes

Some people may respond to this by shrugging and saying “Who cares? When the AIs take down the internet, people will go offline and touch grass.” In fact, I’ve been saying that on X, but it’s obviously sarcastic. Yes, it would be fine if internet entertainment became unavailable. But over the past three decades, we’ve moved essentially everything in our society to the online realm.

Every piece of critical infrastructure in our entire country is networked, in some way, through the internet. You don’t need the internet to run a power plant or a water treatment facility — we ran those things before the internet existed. But we do run them all over the internet, because for a long time the internet seemed like an unassailable, utterly reliable piece of infrastructure. It never went down, it was always available, and previous waves of fear over the Y2K bug or various worms and viruses never really turned into anything serious. So for the sake of convenience, everything is at least partially online now.

Consider your life’s savings. Do you think there’s a piece of paper somewhere that records how much money you have? Or which stocks and bonds you own? In general, there is not. Your entire life’s savings exist as entries in the databases of banks, brokerages, etc. And all of those databases are, directly or indirectly, connected to the internet. The only thing standing between you and total involuntary redistribution of most of your wealth is the cybersecurity capabilities of banks and brokerages. And as of this October, those cybersecurity capabilities are looking a lot less reliable.

Amateur hackers have suddenly been blessed with godlike hacking abilities. What do you think they’re going to do with that power? A lot of them are going to try to rob banks. What if your bank account or your brokerage account gets zeroed out, and the hackers — or more properly, your hackers’ AI agents — manage to erase every trace of their interference? What will your banks do in that case? How will you even convince them of the amount of money you had, when records of that sum no longer exist? What would our society do, if people’s wealth getting abruptly zeroed out became a common occurrence?

In fact, organized criminals are already using AI to successfully attack banks in Latin America. And someone is using AI to hack brokerages in Japan:

Andrew Curran
@AndrewCurran_
A cloud VPS service from Japan's massive GMO Internet Group used by foreign-exchange traders has been hacked. Attackers breached the servers, stole customer credentials, and executed balance-destroying trades across over 70 brokerages. GMO has asked government agencies for help.
6:28 AM · Oct 25, 2026 · 6.86K Views
15 Replies · 28 Reposts · 147 Likes

It’s only a matter of time before such attacks make it to the U.S. Our big banks are spending a lot of money scrambling to defend themselves with the best available models, but what about smaller regional banks? How vulnerable are they? We’re about to find out.

Anyway, a lot of people will tell you not to worry about this — that plucky AI-enabled defenders will eventually triumph over amateur hackers. But while that might be true, I think there are significant reasons to worry about the breaking of the internet.

Defense may yet triumph over offense, but at what cost?

Right now, tons of resources are being poured into cyber-defense. Frontier labs are applying the same kind of fearsome cutting-edge superintelligence to finding vulnerabilities in code that they used to solve some of the world’s most important open math problems:

Noam Brown
@polynoamial
Last month a large team of agents used over 100 billion tokens to resolve the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem. Now we're using a similar approach for red-teaming to find and fix infra vulnerabilities.
Eric Wallace @Eric_Wallace_
To make sure our frontier models don't cause another HuggingFace incident, we built an offline world that they use during training. It provides everything that the models need in a fully cached, indexed, or synthetic manner. We then built a huge team of our most cyber-capable
8:28 PM · Oct 23, 2026 · 62.5K Views
86 Replies · 120 Reposts · 1.71K Likes

At the beginning of this month, I expressed confidence that the nature of software would eventually favor the defense over the offense:

[M]y instinct is that in the long run, the battle of hackers versus defenders ends up favoring the defense. The reason is that it’s probably possible to make any piece of software impregnable — if you just go over your code and very carefully remove all vulnerabilities, there’s just no way for a hacker to get in…That means that as AI gets more powerful at reading, evaluating, and rewriting code, at some point the defense just wins. How long that takes, or how much money it takes, is another question, which is why I do think AI-driven cyberattacks are an issue — especially as AI-written code proliferates like wild, and AI capabilities temporarily overwhelm the security of human-written legacy code.

So far, things are basically playing out as I expected. Pretty much all of the vulnerabilities AI agents are now finding in the foundations of the internet are flaws in old legacy human-written code. As AI patches — or simply rewrites — more and more of the world’s code, that overhang of human-generated vulnerabilities will dwindle and disappear.

This appears to be the expectation inside the big labs as well. Here’s Jeremie Harris:

In case anyone's wondering, the expectation at the frontier labs is basically…We grit our teeth as the world slogs its way through the cyber apocalypse…Hope that AI eventually gets good enough at cyber defense that it can make software essentially unhackable…Out of all this, a new internet emerges - hardened, but possibly also less connected.

That sounds pretty much like my baseline prediction — perhaps 18 months of chaos, followed by the slow, grinding reassertion of order and security by the big labs and their dominant AI models.

But going forward, how expensive will continued cybersecurity be? The demons that now haunt the internet realm are never going away. Up until now, cybersecurity costs were a manageable expense. How manageable will that expense be in the future, with hyper-capable AI agents constantly running around the internet, working at their own purposes or doing the bidding of human masters?

Some prominent AI figures are pessimistic that the internet will ever again be as secure as it appeared just a few months ago:

NIK
@ns123abc
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman: "I don't even know a dramatic enough word to use… models can find bugs that are outside of the normal threat model of what we think a hacker can do… hardware-level, insane stuff… I no longer think we're gonna be able to just patch all the bugs." It's
5:05 PM · Oct 22, 2026 · 1.56M Views
367 Replies · 454 Reposts · 5.12K Likes

If Altman is right, the vast sums of money that companies are now spending trying to harden their software systems won’t be a fixed cost — they’ll be a variable cost. The only way to operate safely on the internet will be to pay Anthropic or OpenAI (or some Chinese company) to constantly monitor your online presence for attacks and vulnerabilities. Every company in the world will have to choose between A) forsaking the internet, and B) paying a gigantic permanent tithe to the people who own the most capable frontier models.

That would mean the end of the internet as a public good. Essentially, this is a world in which the government loses its monopoly on the use of force. In the physical world, governments can use overwhelming force to suppress piracy, arrest criminals, and secure public spaces. This is why shipping companies don’t have to hire their own private navies, and this is why every bank isn’t defended by armed guards.

But the government can’t police the cyber realm — it doesn’t have the technical capabilities. Only Anthropic, OpenAI, and maybe some Chinese companies have those capabilities. It’s like a few private companies owning all the guns or all the missiles. It’s a return to the world of security as a private good.²

That could severely attenuate the economic benefits of the internet itself. An ocean filled with pirates is of dubious economic value, even if private navies exist.

No one is going to stop AI from being able to do this

My second worry about Black October — as the cybersecurity people are calling it — is that it spells the end of any attempt to “pace the frontier”. A growing chorus of voices in the U.S. has been calling for a coordinated slowdown in AI progress, in order to give alignment/safety research time to catch up and make sure that AI doesn’t go rogue and kill us all.

My suspicion is that Black October will spell the end of such efforts. The reason is just boring old game theory — the U.S. is now trapped in an arms race against China.

Many (most?) of the recent wave of cyberattacks have involved abliterated open-weight Chinese models:

Andrew Curran
@AndrewCurran_
Many recent lone-actor incidents used ARTEX with DeepSeek 4.1 Flash as the primary model (including the South Korean bank attacks documented by CrowdStrike). This is an abliterated version of that model with the guardrails removed. Great for defense too, but as always, dual-use.
Abliteration @abliteration_ai
Now live: abliterated-model-large-flash (our version of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017). It is a cheaper alternative to our GLM-5.3-based model for product owners and defenders who need access to the most cyber-capable models. - 1M context - Vision - Zero input/output retention or
4:18 PM · Oct 23, 2026 · 46.8K Views
38 Replies · 67 Reposts · 832 Likes

In fact, one popular theory is that the recent release of a new DeepSeek model precipitated Black October. Nor are Chinese models slowing down. The new Kimi release is one of the most impressive publicly available models:

Before Black October, the AI arms race between the U.S. and China was a hypothetical thing, motivated by the idea of national competition — “We can’t let China get better AI than America”, and so on. As of now, it’s a very real thing — Chinese AI models and American AI models are slugging it out in open combat all over the internet.

And airy, high-minded nationalism is no longer the main motivator of that arms race — the main motivator is pure economic survival. If your business is going to survive on the internet, you now need to have access to the best models. (For now, American companies have access to Chinese models, but they won’t in the near future.) Any government that tries to “pace the frontier” by restricting its own AI models is simply exposing its own companies to hacking by another country’s models.

Thus, either the U.S. and China cooperate to pace the frontier, or the frontier will not be paced. And I’m not optimistic about that sort of sincere, good-faith cooperation happening — not when AI is such a potent weapon, and development of better models can continue in relative secrecy.

That means we can expect AI to continue to get more capable at something like its recent, rapid pace (or even faster if recursive self-improvement gets going). Whatever scary things AI might be capable of, we will be facing those capabilities very soon.

Software can be patched, but our bodies can’t

And of course the scariest capability of all is bio — AI’s ability to design viruses or other pathogens that wipe out much of humanity. When I wrote a post two months ago warning of an AI bio catastrophe driven by lone bioterrorists with no scientific skills or equipment, a lot of biologists minimized the risk, intoning about how hard it is to design effective viruses without real-world feedback. But after watching the speed at which AI agents performed feats of hacking that no human could ever do, people are starting to wake up and get scared.

There are two fundamental reasons why bio risk is much, much scarier than cybersecurity risk. The first is that the stakes are much higher — if the internet goes dark for 18 months, it won’t be the end of the world. Even if the internet becomes permanently more expensive to use, human life will still go on. But 18 months of every dumb angry teenager developing and releasing deadly viruses with abliterated Chinese models would be devastating to our entire species.

Death is scarier than hacking.

The second reason bio is much scarier than cyber is that the flaws in the human body are very, very hard to patch. Cyber probably favors the defense in the long term, but as many people are now pointing out, that’s not true in bio. The human body doesn’t have a clearly well-defined and observable set of vulnerabilities. And even when we find vulnerabilities, we can’t always figure out how to patch them; we don’t have the luxury of simply rewriting our source code in a tighter, more secure way.

AI safety people, fortunately, are generally smart people. Instead of raising a hue and cry over the cyberattacks — other people are already doing plenty of that! — they’re skating to where the puck is going, and using Black October to warn people about how much worse things would get if a similar thing happens in bio. Here’s Jeremie Harris again:

While this is going on, we probably get the bioweapon version of Black October. A new dangerous pathogen pops, and then possibly another a few weeks later, and so on…The bio moment could happen accidentally or on purpose…On purpose: some psycho uses a fine-tuned open-source model, or jailbreaks a frontier model… A smart enough agent will find a way…The cyber stuff is baked in at this point. A lot of damage will be done. But it's not too late to stop the bio[.]

AI capabilities in real-world biology are advancing very quickly. A startup just injected a man with an AI-designed virus for the first time. Anthropic is making its own wet labs, in order to teach AI models how to operate them.

Black October is a dark portent for our biological security. But if there’s one silver lining to the internet apocalypse, it’s that it might serve as a relatively inexpensive warning to the complacent people in the U.S. government, the national press, and the scientific establishment. We (mostly) sat there and watched complacently as the AI cybersecurity meteor streaked down toward our world. That’s over and done, and we’ll just have to deal with the consequences. But we have a chance to do better with bio, and hopefully now we’ll take it more seriously.

Share

1

“Gladstone” is almost certainly a reference to the Hyperion novels. Kudos to the founders for a good company name.

2

Technically, governments never really policed the internet against cybercrime. But cybercrime was so hard, when it was just humans doing it, that private security came cheap. That’s done.

The Crisis Next Time

Three paths to a bad economy

Paul Krugman
Oct 25
∙
Preview
 
READ IN APP
 

At some point in the not-too-distant future, the U.S. economy will experience a slump that is severe, protracted, or both.

How do we know this? Because as the bumper stickers don’t quite say, stuff happens. Twice in my lifetime — during the long boom of the 1960s and again during the so-called Great Moderation from the mid-1980s through the 1990s — some economists have dared to proclaim that major recessions were a thing of the past. Each time events made such proclamations look foolish.

Thus it’s safe to assume that sooner or later the economy will deteriorate and perform badly. And despite wild assertions by Donald Trump and his minions that we’re in an economic Golden Age, there are troubling aspects of the current economy that could potentially be harbingers of the crisis to come. Here is my list:

· Inflation has been persistently elevated and the Fed could be forced to significantly raise short-term interest rates.

· The immense AI boom could easily turn out be a bubble.

· Long-term government bond yields have been rising, and there are rumbles about the possibility of a debt crisis.

Each of these three aspects could lead to big trouble in the economy. But today’s primer isn’t about providing a forecast. What I offer, instead, is an explanation of this menu of possible disasters. Ominously, none of them can be ruled out. As I will explain in this primer, there are at least hints of the potential for each type of disaster in current data. I’m especially concerned about the risks of a liquidity trap if the AI investment boom collapses. But again, this is a menu of possibilities rather than a forecast.

Beyond the paywall, I will address the following:

1. Why recessions are often, but not always, easy to cure

2. Risk #1: Stagflation

3. Risk #2: The liquidity trap

4. Risk #3: Debt crisis

5. Unknown unknowns...
