Scammy fundraising is a big problem

It’s tough to say anything meaningful about the midterms at this point, but Democrats should think harder about their fundraising.

Matthew Yglesias
Oct 26
 
READ IN APP
 

As we get closer to Election Day, it feels a bit like entering the event horizon of a black hole, at least from an analytical point of view.

Back in June of 2025, I think I was able to offer important and useful observations about the upcoming midterms. My key theme was that given the intensification of Donald Trump’s assaults on the pillars of the American republic, a 2018-style rebuke in which he actually gained Senate seats would not be sufficient to give us even momentary relief from the crisis.

The stakes were elevated by the fact that while it’s easy to look at the 2026 Senate map and simply proclaim it unfavorable for Democrats, the 2028 and 2030 maps aren’t any better. Given the American political alignment that emerged in the 2016 / 2020 / 2024 cycles, there simply are no favorable maps — even Joe Biden’s very strong popular vote performance in 2020 only carried 25 states.

There is no way to rescue the country without Democrats becoming meaningfully competitive in multiple states that Trump won three times in a row.

I argued that summer that to achieve that, Democrats would need both to be smart about candidate recruitment (which they basically have) and to reposition the national party’s image (which they really haven’t). I did not specifically discuss the possibility that Trump would fall into the surprisingly common G.O.P. trap of initiating an economically destructive war in the Middle East, though I did tell everyone in November of 2024 that Trump’s team seemed like people who would start a war with Iran.

From the standpoint of today, though, all I can really do is look at the polls, and all anyone really wants to know is whether the polls are correct.

And I just don’t know.

What I do know is that they’re annoyingly close. Marist’s latest Texas poll has James Talarico up by two. If he instead loses by one, they’ll say that they were pretty close. But if the current narrow Democratic leads in Texas and Alaska and Iowa and Kansas and Maine and Michigan all turn into narrow Republican wins, that’s a wildly different outcome for the country.

So which will happen? I don’t know. Do prediction markets give us strong evidence independent of the polling? Not really — the markets just tell us that assuming the polls are approximately right works pretty well on average. There’s just no further insight to be gleaned about the thing everyone wants to know.

What I do know, though, is that like many of you during these final weeks, Slow Boring HQ is being inundated with last-minute requests for money, including this rather absurd request from Massachusetts Governor Maura Healey:

There’s a broad spectrum of sketchy fundraising behavior, from outright scams to bad ideas, and I think this is something that Democrats should think hard about, structurally, over the next several cycles.

While the strong alignment of America’s billionaire donors behind the MAGA movement is a potentially enormous problem for Democrats, the saving grace is that Democrats do a lot better in small-dollar fundraising and, for various legal reasons, a contribution of $5 to Josh Turek accomplishes more than the $5 Elon Musk spends on behalf of Ashley Hinson. But to maintain this advantage, Democrats need to avoid exploiting or misleading their own small donors. People who make these kinds of contributions are not getting kickbacks via government contracts and need confidence that fundraising appeals are being made in good faith.

Do not give $5 to Maura Healey

I want to say first that I really like Governor Healey. Kate and I both went to college in Massachusetts and have affection for the state. I met Healey once and found her smart and charming and funny, and I think it’s too bad that she’s never “in the conversation” as an example of an interesting Democrat. She’s also quietly doing abundance (or at least as close as one can in New England), not just on housing but on natural gas, and she’s talking sense on rent control.

I’m a fan. I’m a booster. If she were actually facing a meaningful electoral challenge, I’d be all-in on helping her win.

But guys. MAGA Mike Minogue is not going to become governor of Massachusetts. If you’re doing small-dollar online donations, this is not the race you should be worrying about.

Subscribed

Again, I like Maura Healey. I’m not here to hate. But she is someone who should be supported by good old-fashioned transactional donors. Are you a Massachusetts labor union? Be a good soldier and chip in. Do you work in government affairs for a company that has business interests in Massachusetts? Could be smart to make a donation. You’re an actual friend or acquaintance of the governor or a senior member of her team? Sure.

But there are tons of people in the United States who are — rightly — acutely frightened about the state of our country. Recall that in the winter of 2020-21, Donald Trump made a somewhat half-assed but fundamentally genuine effort to overturn the results of a legitimate presidential election. People committed crimes in pursuit of this cause! Trump is utterly unapologetic about the attempted putsch, pardoned the criminals who tried to carry it out, and has self-consciously staffed his second administration with people he believes are more personally loyal to him.

Democratic Party senators routinely embarrass appointees to executive and judicial branch jobs by asking them who won the 2020 election, and the appointees always dissemble about it. Trump has been doing political purges of the military officer corps and overtly abusing the prosecutorial functions of the federal government. And a large fraction of the wealthiest and most powerful figures in corporate America have chosen to bandwagon behind him.

The good news is that the public seems sick of Trump. The bad news is that the sickness really does seem to be largely contingent on things like gasoline and diesel prices, not revulsion at Trump’s hostility to democracy and the rule of law. Those of us who are revulsed by this incredibly alarming situation need to be smart with our resources, not throwing them at dumb stuff like defeating MAGA Mike in Massachusetts.

Waste, wishful thinking, scams and cons

Obviously I think this is the optimal list of people to give money to. But there’s a broad “reasonable people can disagree” range here. I want to see more candidates like Josh Turek in the future rather than more candidates like Abdul El-Sayed, so Turek is on my list and El-Sayed is not. If you have the reverse preference about future candidates, it would make sense to reverse those choices. If you’re indifferent, then both races are important and both could use money.

I’m also recommending campaigns that I think are underfunded at the margin. James Talarico is a monster fundraiser, so I didn’t put him on my list, but it’s not like giving him money is a mistake — I just feel confident that lots of other people are doing it.

Outside of the core battleground races, a lot of people have been urging some fairly undisciplined behavior.

I have no problem with Scott Colom, who’s running for Senate in Mississippi. But the idea that additional fundraising is going to help Democrats flip this Senate seat doesn’t seem remotely credible to me — this experiment was tried with Jaime Harrison in South Carolina and Amy McGrath in Kentucky in 2020. I’ve had to not recommend gubernatorial candidates I like, including Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins in Alaska and Aaron Ford in Nevada, just because I don’t think the races have large strategic implications for people who don’t live in those states. But that’s a judgment call. If you have some connection to those states or candidates or think there’s some angle I’m missing about the larger significance of the races, then fair enough.

The gubernatorial races in Texas and Florida, by contrast, have big strategic implications in terms of redistricting and just the large size of the states, but putting money into them seems like wishful thinking to me. Still, while I don’t think any of these races are a particularly good use of money, these are things people of good faith can disagree about.

A lot of this is just misdirected enthusiasm. But there’s also the reality that people make money off of political campaigns. There are vendors and consultants who have contracts with David Jolly or Gina Hinojosa, and they benefit specifically from donations to those candidates rather than other candidates, even if other candidates would be a better use of your money. And most people — even highly trained professional political pundits like me — don’t have visibility into the web of financial relationships connecting different people and institutions.

And that’s to say nothing of outright scams, like PACs that say they’re supporting candidates but mostly just fund themselves. Take a look at Politico’s description of End Citizens United:

The group has continued to promise in fundraising appeals aimed at small-dollar donors that their money will go toward boosting Democratic candidates and fighting to overturn the Citizens United decision. But its primary PAC spent four times as much on operating expenses as it did on donations to candidates and independent expenditures during the 2024 cycle, according to a Politico analysis of data from the F.E.C. As of the end of March, it has spent more on fundraising costs than at this point in any previous cycle.

I think Adam Bonica’s pieces about “spam PACs” paint with way too broad a brush in collapsing the distinction between actual scams and just the basic architecture of online fundraising. But beyond the fact that some of these PACs are genuine scams, the broader point I would make is that I can’t think of any good reason why it would be better for a small-dollar online donor to funnel their political giving through a PAC.

Subscribed

It’s not that all PACs are scams, but if you want to raise small-dollar donations for a finite universe of candidates, you just don’t need a PAC to do that. The Slow Boring slate (which I really do recommend you give to — yes, late money is still helpful!) is just a page with donation buttons for the candidates. All the money goes to the candidates we’re supporting; there’s no legal or financial entity between you and the candidates. There are plenty of valid reasons that people launch and give money to PACs, but these reasons involve large donors and lobbying machinations.

If you have modest sums of money to give and just want to help good candidates win, then give directly to those candidates.

I don’t know exactly what the party can do to crack down on bad PACs or fundraising solicitations from candidates like Healey who are way outside the “reasonable people can disagree” standard for optimal donations. But they’d better start thinking harder about it. Keeping the small-donor engine running is vital to keeping Democrats in the game electorally, and that means giving donors some assurances that their money is being well spent.

The Oligarchs Lose a Big One

Brazil refuses to be bullied

Paul Krugman
Oct 26
 
READ IN APP
 

How many people in the United States realize how big Brazil is? South America’s most populous nation has more than 200 million people, making its presidential election yesterday a momentous event. But beyond Brazil’s sheer size, yesterday’s election was also momentous because it was a harbinger for the rest of the world.

For it was a contest between the progressive left of Ignacio Lula da Silva, the incumbent president, and the revanchist right of Flavio Bolsonaro — the son of Jair Bolsonaro, the former president, who is in prison for his attempt to overturn Brazil’s last presidential election. The global right thought it had the election in the bag, and even the prediction markets indicated that Bolsonaro would win. Thus it came as a shock when Lula came out on top.

Having been gaslighted by the right, some of the global media appeared to have difficulty wrapping their minds around the outcome. Here was the headline in the Financial Times as I write this:

“Knife-edge vote”? Lula won by 3 percentage points, twice Donald Trump’s margin in 2024.

And he did so despite efforts by the right, in Brazil and elsewhere, to rig the election against him.

Voting was extended by two hours because widespread disruptions to public transportation had made it difficult for working-class voters to get to the polls. Lula’s campaign alleged that these disruptions were engineered by pro-Bolsonaro mayors, a claim that was clearly supported by the evidence in some cities, and was generally plausible given recent political history — specifically, Bolsonaro senior’s attempt to overturn the last presidential election.

And Brazil’s own right wasn’t alone in seemingly trying to rig the election for Bolsonaro. U.S.-based social media companies, Meta in particular, appeared to put their thumbs on the scale. After the first round of voting, Reuters reported that

Meta employees acknowledged in internal communications that the Instagram accounts of Brazilian ​President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva were hindered by ‌restrictions during the country’s election, newspaper Folha de S.Paulo reported on Friday, citing messages it reviewed.

The messages also acknowledged the platform recommended the profile ​of challenger Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, as well as his ​WhatsApp channel, according to the report.

And in an article titled “Meta Unseats Musk as Tech Villain for Lula in Brazil’s Election,” Bloomberg reported that

Lula — who has attracted more than 10 million supporters to a WhatsApp channel dubbed “Lula’s Army” in recent days — has alleged interruptions to his account, restrictions on Instagram posts and unequal audience engagement. His campaign also said Meta AI, the company’s generative artificial intelligence tool, is refusing requests to create images related to Lula while generating campaign material favorable to his opponent.

Meta said that these incidents reflected “unrelated technical problems,” a claim that would be more credible if all of these supposed technical problems hadn’t tilted the playing field in the same direction.

Is it a mere coincidence that in the United States, Meta suspended the No Kings Day Instagram account right in the middle of the day’s protests? It later claimed that this action had nothing to do with politics, that it was an error because its automated security systems detected a possible rise in bot traffic.

Again, it’s funny how Meta’s technical problems always seem to tilt the political field in the same direction.

Can we prove that Meta deliberately tried to put the Bolsonaros back in power? No, at least not yet. But we aren’t in a court of law: We’re simply trying to figure out what happened. And the people in this photo are not entitled to a presumption of innocence and good intentions:

Although Meta’s denials lack plausibility, we can’t prove that Mark Zuckerberg deliberately tried to deliver Brazil into the hands of a right-wing authoritarian. However, there is no question that Elon Musk intentionally and strongly intervened on the side of Vladimir Putin in his efforts to conquer Ukraine. Musk keeps changing his story about what happened — first denying any involvement, saying that the order came from the White House, and now claiming that Ukraine violated its terms of service. But this charade is completely implausible because Musk has long made it clear that his sympathies in this war lie with Russia.

So let’s celebrate the Brazilian people, who have refused to be bullied by Bolsonaro, by the American oligarchs, and by Trump — who imposed high tariffs on Brazil in 2025 because it put a traitor and insurrectionist (Bolsonaro Sr) on trial. Let’s hope that in a little over one week’s time Americans will be equally clear-sighted and vote for democracy.

Roundup #90: In which Noah joins a Japanese VC firm

The humanities; Data center crowd-out; Chinese local governments; AI and capitalism; How Japan builds; Phones bad; Chinese manufacturing; Rent control

Noah Smith
Oct 27
 
READ IN APP
 

I have a fun announcement today, which is that I have a new side gig. I’ll be joining the Japanese VC firm Coral Capital as a Venture Partner! That’s less prestigious than it sounds — basically I’ll just be doing a few blog posts and helping to introduce them to folks in the U.S. But it’s still cool, and the Coral team is really great. The reason I’m doing this, of course, is to encourage more American investment into Japan, in order to revitalize that country’s economy. That was the subject of my book, The Weeb Economy (alternate title: Weebs Will Save Japan), which Coral helped to promote. I also want to contribute to Japan’s ability to defend themselves from an increasingly threatening regional environment; Coral is involved with defense tech as well.

Anyway, here are some excerpts from Coral’s announcement:

Today we’re thrilled to announce that Noah Smith is joining Coral Capital as a Venture Partner…Noah is one of Japan’s greatest champions on the world stage…He lived in Japan for years, speaks the language, and has spent two decades studying its economy. Last year he published Weebs Will Save Japan (Nikkei BP), a book on how Japan’s cultural gravity and industrial strengths can power its next era of growth. His next book, now in progress, covers Japan’s defense tech sector and national security. He has argued forcefully that Japan should attract more foreign capital and talent, that Japan can be America’s arsenal, and that Japan’s manufacturing prowess is one of the most underpriced assets in the global economy.

Long before we started working together, Noah was already making the case we’ve built our firm around…

The world’s focus is shifting from bits back to atoms. Reindustrialization, defense, energy, robotics, and physical AI are the defining investment themes of the next decade, and they play directly to Japan’s strengths. In these industries, language and culture barriers matter far less than monozukuri, the process power and manufacturing know-how Japan has compounded over decades. And as the world de-risks from Chinese supply chains, Japan has a once-in-a-generation opportunity to deepen its ties with the United States and fill the manufacturing voids being left behind…

Japan is America’s most important ally. It is the largest foreign direct investor in the United States, and Japanese companies support more American manufacturing jobs than any other foreign investor. Japan hosts more US service members than any other country in the world. The US-Japan corridor is the most consequential economic relationship in the world right now, and we intend to be the firm that bridges it.

This is the thesis we laid out in JAPAN IS BACK, and it’s why we’ve partnered with companies leveraging Japan’s strengths to compete globally. Anduril is not just selling to Japan but building in Japan, with plans to invest billions in manufacturing capacity here. Kyoto Fusioneering, TeraWatt Technology, Ookuma Diamond Device, GITAI, and many more are taking Japanese hard tech to the world…

The lost decades are over. It’s time the whole world knew.

So anyway, you’ll be hearing a little more about that in the coming weeks and months!

OK, on to the roundup. First we have a very fun podcast appearance, in which I discuss a wide variety of topics with former streamers Lukas and Saila on their podcast, Plausibly Deniable:

And here’s a Spotify link if you prefer.

OK, on to this week’s interesting stories!

1. The humanities are dying

Back in 2022 I wrote a post arguing that the boom in humanities and social science education had created “elite overproduction” — too many educated people expecting high-status jobs, and not enough academic, journalistic, legal, political, and nonprofit jobs to satisfy their dreams. I argued that this was one reason for the social unrest of the 2010s, as legions of frustrated smart people spent their energy and extra time attacking the American system they felt had jilted them — and applying ideas they had learned in academia to modern American politics via social media.

But whether or not that argument was right, I don’t think overproduction of humanities scholars is going to be a big problem going forward. From a new study called “The Humanities in Crisis” by Ober et al., here’s a chart of the number of humanities dissertations in the U.S.:

Interestingly, the humanities decline has been going on for over a decade, while the decline in the social sciences is post-pandemic.

Why this is happening is not clear yet. Most people talk about the humanities being colonized by wokeness and driving reasonable people away from the field (Ober et al. discuss this theory at length). I personally suspect that the difficulty of getting a job as a humanities PhD is probably a bigger factor. Fewer undergrads are majoring in the humanities because they think it isn’t a good route to getting a job; this means less demand for humanities profs, and thus for humanities grad students.

But whatever it is, the humanities are clearly dying in American academia.

2. Krugman’s data center crowd-out story is fishy

I love Paul Krugman, and he’s usually right about things, but I do think he’s had a bit of a blind spot when it comes to AI. In a recent post, he argued that the data center boom is crowding out other types of investment:

Massive spending on data centers is crowding out investment in everything else in the economy…Surges in private spending, like the current immense AI boom…drive up interest rates. And that is where we are now: the surge in AI spending is driving up interest rates and crowding out all other investment. Indeed, in my October 4 primer I argued that the AI boom is the main cause of soaring long-term interest rates…

In other words, all that money going into construction of datacenters and purchasing foreign produced semiconductors comes at the expense of investment in everything else…[C]onstruction of datacenters appears to be diverting funds and resources from the construction of housing, office buildings, and factories — more or less everything that isn’t AI-related.

But as Alex Tabarrok notes, the first chart Krugman uses to tell his story — courtesy of Steve Rattner — actually tells the opposite tale:

First of all, how is $51 billion of data center spending supposed to crowd out $120 billion of other spending? If supply curves slope up and demand curves slope down like they’re supposed to, a positive shock to the demand for data centers should only partially crowd out other spending.

Of course it’s possible that non-data-center investment is being crowded out not just by current data center spending, but by forward-looking expectations of even more data center spending in the future. That’s perfectly reasonable — interest rates might have risen in response to those forward-looking expectations, choking off non-data-center investment immediately.

But as Tabarrok also points out, the timing for that story is very odd. Rattner’s chart shows non-data-center construction falling off a cliff sometime in mid-2025. But the big rise in real interest rates happened three years earlier in 2022-23:

Why would it take three years for rising rates to start crowding out non-data-center construction? It’s not clear.

So for Krugman to be right, the sequence of events has to have gone like this:

  1. Real rates rise in anticipation of AI boom (1/2022 - 10/2023)

  2. GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 make everyone realize AI is a big deal (12/2022-3/2023)

  3. Non-data-center construction falls years later (8/2025)

That could be true, I suppose — any macroeconomic story will generally hold up if you throw in enough assumptions about long and variable lags — but it seems pretty fishy! In any case, just posting charts of “data center go up, other stuff go down” is not sufficient to prove that significant crowd-out is occurring.

3. China’s local governments are in big trouble

Because of the history of how Europe developed strong governments, we tend to associate state capacity with high taxes. But that’s not always the case. Despite its fearsome state capacity, the People’s Republic of China has always been a low-tax country. A lot of the responsibility for paying for public goods — and, until recently, for industrial policy — was farmed out to local governments. But instead of collecting taxes — much of which they would have to remit to the central government — those local governments often chose to sell real estate to pay for their operations.

That strategy is now hitting a wall. The country’s property sales are crashing:

So China’s local governments are no longer taking in nearly as much money as they used to. As a result, they’re going deeply into debt. Shih and Elkobi have a new paper showing the extent of the problem. They write:

[W]e show that fiscal autonomy has been heavily eroded in the vast majority of localities in China since 2018. The bond data show that by the end of 2025, average monthly debt servicing had surpassed 50 per cent of monthly budgetary and extrabudgetary income for all but seven Chinese provincial units.

The problem is the collapse in property sales (“EBF”):

The central government will pick up the bill, but it’s heavily indebted as well, so it will pay the local governments’ bills only reluctantly.

The upshot here is twofold. First, the relative provincial autonomy that drove China’s dynamism during the 1990s, 2000s, and early 2010s may now be over; everything looks likely to be increasingly centralized. And second, China’s local governments are going to be too burdened by debt to do much of anything for a few years. China’s local governments were one of its strongest engines of growth during the long boom, but that era looks like it’s over now.

4. Is AI the vindication of financial capitalism?

The speed of AI progress has been truly dizzying. A lot of this has come in the form of cost declines — each AI task keeps getting much much cheaper every year. Epoch AI has a good chart showing this:

But Karthik Tadepalli estimates that if we look at AI’s cost decrease as a function of how much we’ve spent on AI research, it doesn’t stand out as much:

In other words, a big reason AI is getting so cheap, so fast, is that we’ve been pouring unprecedented amounts of cash into making it better. In fact, we’ve been basically spending all the cash that we saved over the previous decade and a half of hoarding cash.

James Gilliland wonders if this was the plan all along:

It pains me to say this, but if we actually “get AGI,” the resulting boom in industrial capacity from robotics and massive society-wide wealth creation will look like a total vindication of neoliberalism…The discourse about financialization and offshoring being a generational mistake may be replaced by a very different historical interpretation: that the late 20th and early 21st centuries were an enormous capital-accumulation phase, freeing up civilization-scale pools of liquid capital that could ultimately be deployed to accelerate and bring about the most consequential technological phase-change in human history…In that telling, what looked like deindustrialization and betrayal from inside the period (I grew up in the Rust Belt, I know) becomes the prelude to reindustrialization on an almost unimaginable scale.

For decades, it looked like financial capitalism was broken — no one was thinking for the long term, everyone just cared about quarterly numbers and shareholder buybacks, equity couldn’t fund massive investments, everyone just wanted to maximize short-term profits and outsource anything capital-intensive to China, and so on.

Then AI came along, and suddenly it looks like we were actually saving up for something useful. We weren’t, of course — no one knew AI was as big of an opportunity as it’s proving to be. But maybe financial capitalism worked. Maybe companies like Google just looked at the available investment opportunities before AI and said “Nah” — just like Corporate Finance 101 says they were supposed to do.

And then finally a good investment opportunity came along, and they poured in every dollar they had — and it worked.

5. A cool Japanese trick for building more housing and infrastructure

Going to Japan can be a radicalizing experience for Westerners. The cleanliness, the lack of crime, the artistry, the attention to detail, and plenty of other things make Japan feel almost magical. But one of the most magical things is the housing. Japanese cities build enormous amounts of housing — far more than their counterparts in the U.S. Housing in Tokyo or Osaka isn’t exactly affordable — Japanese salaries are far lower than American salaries — but regular people can afford to live fairly near the city center, and Japanese rents haven’t risen for a long time.

How do they do it? A lot of analyses focus on Japan’s streamlined, efficient zoning laws. The fact that they use bureaucrats instead of courts to do environmental review speeds things up a lot as well. But an often-overlooked factor is how Japan gets local political buy-in for new housing development projects. Instead of either trying to steamroll NIMBYs or kowtowing to them — the two approaches used in the United States — Japan manages them as stakeholders in the process of local development.

Cremieux had a good blog post about this about a year ago:

Cremieux Recueil
"Yes, and..." Urbanism
Alternative subtitle: “What can we learn about zoning from how other places manage it…
Read more
a year ago · 81 likes · 27 comments · Cremieux

One of his sources is this World Bank case study by Matsui Minoru, which explains Japan’s approach of “land readjustment”.

In the U.S., when we think of “redevelopment”, we think of a developer basically kicking existing tenants out of their homes and building something else where their homes used to be. But in Japan, it often involves building the existing tenants a new home on the same spot, which they are then entitled to rent for the same price they were paying before. Here’s an illustration:

Japan actually has incredibly strong tenant protections. You’d think this would make it harder to tear down old buildings to build new housing, but thanks to land readjustment, it’s easier than in America.

Cremieux then goes on to explain how Japan uses land readjustment in lieu of America’s more forceful eminent domain laws to build high-quality infrastructure:

With land readjustment, no one is expropriated. Everyone maintains a plot and infrastructure gets built. People only compromise on size, proximity, to other plots, and so on. As a means of provisioning urban infrastructure, this is obviously going to be more acceptable to large numbers of people than is the use of eminent domain. But is it better than simply not building at all?

People who already own land might wish to keep it a certain way. Land readjustment might not be for them, and it’s likely to make them very upset because the people around them might vote to change their claims around. But enough people will agree to land readjustments in enough places that it can have radical impacts on economic geography, rewarding those who accept it with access to new infrastructure and higher densities. There will even be some people who elect to have the government or firms build infrastructure on their jointly-held parcels, letting them bid to build on their land. When the building is through, it’ll be returned to its owners in their newly-arranged plots.

People who stubbornly insist on thinking of Japan as a hierarchical, conformist, collectivist society will surely find ways to convince themselves that this is the kind of thing American individualism would never allow. But in fact, Japan’s system has far stronger protections for individual renters, while America’s system often only gets things done using the heavy hand of government.

What Japan’s land-use system really shows is the value of negotiation, compromise, and respect for individual dignity. Those are all lessons we could stand to learn.

6. Phones bad

As someone who has been shouting about the ills of smartphone-enabled social media for years now, it gratifies me to see that more people around the world — and especially in developed countries — are coming to see social media as something that’s bad for democracy:

That’s in addition, of course, to other negative effects — cognitive difficulties, reduced emotional well-being, and ultra-low fertility.

What can we do about the problem? One thing we can do is to make sure people grow up without overdosing on phone-enabled social media, so that they can learn to use it when they’re older without it shaping their personalities and minds as much. Greece is leading the charge — its legislature recently passed a ban on social media for children under the age of 15.

7. China is losing market share in low-end manufacturing

Most countries’ industrial development follows a familiar pattern. They start out making simple stuff like clothes, furniture, and toys, and doing simple electronics assembly. They then shed those labor-intensive starter industries as they move up into more capital-intensive, high-tech, higher-value sectors like machine tools, autos, electronics components, and so on.

A lot of people are saying that China is going to buck this trend. The leadership has declared that even as the country moves up the value chain in traditional fashion, it wants to keep the cheap labor-intensive stuff from migrating overseas as it usually does. This is being called the “China Squeeze”, and people are writing that it threatens other countries’ path to development. If China keeps outcompeting Bangladesh, Vietnam, Mexico, etc. in the low-end industries, how are those countries supposed to industrialize?

Except the China Squeeze doesn’t seem to be succeeding. Despite the leadership’s wishes, China is losing market share in lots of labor-intensive industries:

And which countries are gaining in these industries at China’s expense? Bangladesh, Vietnam, and Mexico (and some European countries):

Modern pundits often just assume that the Chinese state is industrially omnipotent — that if Xi Jinping declares “This industry shall remain in China”, then indeed it shall. But the outmigration of low-value labor-intensive manufacturing industries looks like a law of nature that even the mighty CCP can slow, but not halt.

Good.

8. Rent control bad

John Burn-Murdoch did the Lord’s work when he synthesized the results of 112 studies on rent control into a single chart:

Basically, rent control helps one narrow group of people (existing tenants in the area covered by the policy) in one very specific way (restraining their rents). But it removes the incentive for developers to build new housing, which raises rents in other nearby areas and drives some people to homelessness. It also removes the incentive for landlords to upkeep their properties, resulting in decay. (And that’s not even getting into the ways that rent control policies can be gamed.)

I know lots of people love rent control, but it’s really a loser of a policy. Just build a lot more housing and hand out housing vouchers to the poor.

Trump Doesn’t Give a Damn About Your Problems

As the midterms loom, he’s finally admitting the obvious

Paul Krugman
Oct 27
 
READ IN APP
 

ExxonMobil stock price: Source: CNBC

If Republicans do implode as badly next Tuesday as the current polls suggest, there will be two main reasons. One is Trump’s epic corruption, which finally seems to be getting traction as a campaign issue, second only to the cost of living. The other is soaring energy prices, which are both a major cause of overall inflation and especially visible since they’re posted on big signs in front of every gas station across the country.

It’s a highly ironic situation because Trump’s promises to slash those prices were a key theme of his 2024 campaign. These promises were explicit: he cited numbers, asserting that he would cut energy prices in half within 12 months.

Disastrously for Trump and the Republicans, the opposite has happened, with gasoline and especially diesel prices way up, mainly because of Trump’s catastrophic war with Iran.

One measure of energy prices I find useful is the average price of the products refined from a barrel of oil — typically 2/3 of a barrel of gasoline and 1/3 of a barrel of diesel. I focus on refined products because those, not crude oil, are what people actually burn. And refined products are up in price both because crude prices are up and because the “crack spread” between crude and refined products has soared.

Here’s what has happened to the price of refined products:

Those prices are roughly back to their Biden-era peak, and far above the prices Trump inherited when he took office. Furthermore, Biden wasn’t responsible for that temporary surge in prices, which was mainly caused by post-Covid supply-chain disruptions. Trump, on the other hand, bears almost all the responsibility for current high prices: his war of choice has disrupted the flow of oil, both crude and especially refined products, out of the Persian Gulf. (Ukraine’s strikes on Russian refineries are also contributing, but the Ukrainians are only doing what they must — and Trump, who is effectively backing Russia, has no standing to complain.)

The cost to American consumers of the Trump spike in energy costs is remarkably high. The U.S. consumes about 7.5 billion barrels of petroleum products annually. As you can see from the chart above, Trump’s war has raised the price of these products by about $75 a barrel. So this war is costing U.S. consumers around $560 billion a year at an annual rate, which is a lot even in a $30 trillion economy.

But Trump claims not to care:

The United States oil and gas business is making hundreds of billions of dollars. I don’t give a damn, I’m going to say it — we’re making a freaking fortune.

The obvious response is, what do you mean “we,” white man?

It’s true that oil and gas companies are making a lot of money thanks to the fallout from the Iran debacle, and oil-company stock prices have soared. But this does nothing for ordinary Americans who aren’t big investors in oil-company stocks, such as workers paying more for their daily commute and farmers who need diesel for their tractors.

So when Trump says “We’re making a freaking fortune,” what he really means is that his policies are taking more than half a trillion dollars at an annual rate out of the pockets of ordinary Americans, and giving that money to the oil industry (which gave 88 percent of its 2024 campaign contributions to Republicans.) Some people might consider this a bad thing, but by his own account he “doesn’t give a damn.”

Remind me again why people call Trump a “populist”?

Why I don’t write about A.I. all the time

It might be the most important issue right now, but I’m not history’s main character.

Matthew Yglesias
Oct 27
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

Every so often I mention that I agree with many of the founders and technical employees at the major artificial-intelligence companies that their work stands a non-trivial chance of killing everyone.

When I do, I’m typically asked why, then, most of my posts are about other stuff — things like the upcoming midterm elections or the permitting reform bill that’s hopefully going to pass during the lame-duck session of Congress.

My answer is that while I completely respect people who feel like making a wild career pivot, most of us are going to keep working in our same basic professions. And I think that the best way that I can contribute to the world is to continue doing my job — the noble work of the generalist politics columnist — as best as I can. That means clearly stating things that I believe to be true (such as that existential risk from A.I. is real) but mostly trying to deliver a varied mix of content that is accurate and interesting and informative and induces people to continue subscribing to and sharing my work.

Intellectual influence isn’t achieved by just stacking up more words on a subject.

To influence important debates, the newsletter has to be successful. So whatever my views about what is and isn’t important, I still have to factor in considerations about running a successful newsletter.

But beyond the question of influence, there’s just something a little bit odd about believing that something is objectively very important and inferring that you must therefore try to situate yourself at the center of it.

I think sometimes about my two grandfathers who were both involved in World War II, one fighting in the Mediterranean theater and the other administering the footwear rationing system. As it happens, these turn out to have been pretty peripheral fields of endeavor in the grand scheme of the war. It would be “better” from the standpoint of being at the center of the drama to have participated in the Normandy landing rather than the invasion of Sicily.

But everybody can’t be doing the thing that is most important. The United States Navy did, in fact, need different people all around the world doing different things, not just doing the one specific thing that was most likely to get written up in the history books.

Similarly, all those troops who landed in Normandy needed boots. A whole elaborate system of shoe rationing was in place to make sure that there was plenty of rubber and leather available for military use. It sounds pretty comical to be waging war on Hitler from an office where your job is to tell civilian women how many pairs of shoes they can buy — they are definitely not making movies about those guys — but if everyone refused to do the random jobs, things would have been much worse.

It is good and correct to want to have a positive impact on the world, but an impulse to be at the center of attention or try to get your name into the histories isn’t really the same thing.

Situational awareness

To people who work on A.I. safety and just earnestly want to see it written about more because they care about it, I want to call attention to something that happened recently.

OpenAI employees used their voice and their implicit power to get Greg Brockman to stop funding the Leading the Future super PAC, which was spending against politicians who favor A.I. safety legislation and (more to the point) paralyzing a lot of legislators into not wanting to touch the subject.

Since that happened, we’ve seen OpenAI’s policy guy, Chris Lehane, making remarks on safety legislation that are really helpful and constructive. So it seems that a debate that happened inside the company about OpenAI’s political engagement has been quite fruitful and unlocked some bigger possibilities. Garrison Lovely reported that my writing played a small but real role in these debates:

On September 14, one employee revived the thread with a quote from journalist Matt Yglesias to suggest the storm wasn’t abating: “Nobody working professionally in American politics believes” that OpenAI wasn’t supporting Leading the Future.

That wasn’t just a random comment of mine.

I was saying at the time — in this newsletter, on my Twitter feed, on “Politix,” and on “The Argument” — that safety-minded OpenAI employees should try to act collectively to get Leading the Future defunded. I wrote and spoke about this specific point pretty frequently for a concentrated period of time because I felt like this was a situation in which I actually had some real expertise and the potential for influence. I am not a technical expert on A.I. But I am someone who knows what pragmatic, winning-oriented Democrats are saying to each other.

And the chilling effect of Leading the Future spending was very real in those circles. More to the point, OpenAI executives were telling OpenAI employees that the super PAC was not speaking for the company, but nobody in Washington politics believed that or saw it that way.

All this information I had was relevant to A.I. safety debates, but I had access to it precisely because I spend a lot of time on general politics news.

And I think it illustrates the point that it’s better for the cause of A.I. safety to have a bunch of broadly “safety-pilled” people doing lots of different kinds of jobs. The world is a large and complicated place that is fairly unpredictable, and unexpected things can end up being relevant.

By the same token, I don’t know for sure what the next Congress will hold, but I hope we’ll see action on some kind of A.I. safety legislation. The world is going to need those debates to be covered not just by A.I. specialists but by people with (ideally large and influential) general politics audiences, which again means I’m mostly just doing the day-to-day work of generalist politics writing. Obviously the world needs specialists in all kinds of things, but I think the most useful thing for me to do on basically all issues is try to do a good job of being a generalist politics writer who has a broad and influential audience and can intervene strategically on particular topics when it’s actually useful.

The center of the action

Beyond that general defense of posting as a vocation, though, a lot of the activity I see in this space strikes me as suspiciously self-dramatizing.

Or to put it another way, while people come to this topic from a lot of different directions and it’s a long-running literary preoccupation going back to before the invention of digital computers, I personally was introduced to it through effective altruism circles.

One of the major tenets of E.A. is that people have a tendency to be a bit egotistical in their efforts to help others. There are social and psychological rewards to working on stuff that lots of other people — especially your own peers — are already working on. That’s not the worst thing in the world. Participating in something good or helpful in part because you know other people who are doing the good or helpful thing is a lot better than being purely selfish all the time or just being at home alone on your phone.

But if you think about it, it’s pretty easy to see that oftentimes, the way to be most helpful isn’t to copy other well-intentioned people. It’s to try to address something that’s neglected.

If you were to go back even three years ago and say you’re throwing yourself into A.I., that would be a deeply contrarian choice. But now everyone knows that A.I. is a hot topic. Every start-up is A.I. Every investment thesis is about A.I. — even if you’re not excited about A.I. as an investment, the thesis is now about a bursting bubble. Every policy dinner in D.C. eventually turns to A.I.

Which is not to say it’s wrong for A.I. to loom so large. I remember observing a year ago that well-qualified economists seemed to disagree as to whether A.I. progress would push interest rates up or down, but it was an important question. As of today, the answer looks to be “up,” and this has wide-ranging implications for all kinds of policy conversations. But it does also mean that plunging headlong into A.I. work no longer involves being a weirdo talking about something everyone is ignoring — you’re moving toward the spotlight. That’s not bad, per se, especially if you’re just starting out in life or you have other reasons for wanting to make a change. But it’s a different kind of impulse and worth scrutinizing.

I don’t know what the future will hold, exactly. Maybe the world will end and maybe it won’t. Maybe the singularity will arrive and maybe it won’t. Maybe space will be colonized by nice liberal robots with good values and maybe it won’t.

What matters about all of this is what actually happens, not whether you or I or anyone else manage to insert ourselves into the historical record.

Hack Apocalypse Now

The dark side of AI is already here

Paul Krugman
Oct 28
 
READ IN APP
 

Like everyone who has been paying attention, I have worries about the possible negative effects from AI. And it’s a long laundry list of worries. One, there is the technology’s anti-labor bias, which may accelerate our downward spiral into oligarchy. Next, there is the fact that the data center boom is crowding out investment in almost everything else, yet data centers employ hardly any workers. Third, I’m worried about the high probability that AI looks like a bubble, particularly given the sheer size of the AI boom. If it is indeed a bubble, it will inevitably burst and will probably plunge the U.S. economy back into a liquidity trap due to its size.

Oh, and Anthropic tells me that AI may well wipe out the human race, which is why I should invest in the company’s IPO.

But I guess I haven’t been talking enough to the technologists, because I wasn’t aware until last week of the strong possibility that AI will render the internet as we know it unusable — not at some point in the distant future, but in a matter of months.

It has already started. Reuters reports:

Government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline on Wednesday after the disclosure of ​critical vulnerabilities in a widely used programming language sent website operators around the world scrambling to protect their systems.

Developers of the PHP programming language on Wednesday released urgent new fixes to vulnerabilities that had been lurking ‌in their software for years until they were uncovered using AI, saying all users were “encouraged to update immediately.”

With tech firms warning that some hackers were already exploiting the flaws, government agencies across Europe were among those that took sites offline as a precaution.

Because a fix is now public and artificial intelligence tools are able to reverse engineer the bug with little effort, experts said they were bracing for a wave of intrusions as hackers jumped to get ahead of the updates.

AI was powering a “race to exploit,” said Costin Raiu, co-founder of cybersecurity research and incident response firm TLP:Black. He ​said the next step was the “mass compromise of every vulnerable web server on the internet.

And this is just the beginning of what Zvi Mowshowitz calls The Hackening. Two days later, Reuters reported that:

Advances in artificial intelligence have uncovered a stream of new software vulnerabilities that are almost ​certain to trigger more disruption along the lines of the outages that percolated across global government websites this week, according to seven cybersecurity professionals who spoke to ‌Reuters.

It quoted one expert as saying “I think we’re going to have a couple years where every single week it’s going to feel like the sky is falling.”

Azeem Ashar, whose Substack Exponential View has been one of my main guides to what is happening with AI, calls what happened last week “The internet’s Wuhan moment” — as in the emergence of the coronavirus that caused the Covid pandemic, which killed millions and also temporarily plunged the whole world economy into a deep slump.

I’m not a technologist, but here’s how I understand the problem: Websites run on complex, multi-layered software that, because of its sheer complexity, inevitably contains security flaws that bad actors could potentially exploit. Worse, much of the software is old — PHP dates from the early 1990s — and was hence designed in an era in which modern hacking techniques didn’t exist.

And AI models, it turns out, are incredibly powerful hacking tools. Merely human evildoers may lack the time, patience and attention to detail to go over old code line by line, finding security flaws that may have gone unnoticed for decades. AI models suffer from no such limitations. Institutions that learn about security threats may be able to install patches that block them — but the very act of disseminating a patch gives hackers the information they need to go after institutions that didn’t apply those patches immediately.

And Azhar tells us that regulating AI by requiring “safety training” — instructions to the models that deter destructive actions — will be far less effective than one might hope. Why? Because such training is relatively easy to “abliterate,” which means reversing a few key prompts in a way that undoes most of the safety training.

So what are we going to do? I don’t think we’ll be going back to carbon paper and filing cabinets. For the most part we probably won’t even have to rely on air-gapped local networks that are fully cut off from the internet. Azhar thinks that we’ll move instead to a system of partially closed domains, like AOL in its early years or the SABRE system used by travel agents, which are difficult but not impossible for people and institutions outside those domains to access.

Such closed domains are often called “walled gardens,” but I’d suggest that a better analogy is “gated communities,” like the one my late parents lived in toward the end of their lives. People who didn’t live in their community could visit them, but only if my parents had provided their names to the staff manning the gate. It worked — they could invite friends from outside over — but it was annoying and time-consuming compared with life outside the gates, where everyone could come and go freely.

Similarly, a digital society that imposes annoying security restrictions and checks but is much less vulnerable to AI-powered hacking should be workable. But security will come at a cost. How much of a cost?

Some back-of-the-envelope calculations, which I won’t share here, suggest that the advent of the open internet raised GDP by around 10 percent. A more secure system of gated digital communities will mean giving up only part of that gain — in the long run.

But I’m much more worried about the short run, because our whole economy is currently designed to work with an open web. Suppose, for example, that we’re forced to revert to the old system in which you had to physically visit a travel agent with a secure SABRE link to buy plane tickets. I remember that world, and it wasn’t horrible. But most of the travel agents and offices that used to perform that function are gone and can’t be instantly conjured back into existence. And you have to imagine that problem occurring all across the economy.

Again, this isn’t a hypothetical future risk. It’s happening as you read this.

Just the other day AI enthusiasts were talking about how their miraculous technology would soon generate 10 or 15 percent a year economic growth. That was always silly. But now there’s a very real prospect that for the next few years AI, by empowering bad guys and forcing us to suddenly adapt to new threats, will make us poorer.

Those who work and those who post

Mamdani seems surprisingly moderate because mayors need to govern.

Matthew Yglesias
Oct 28
 
READ IN APP
 

Last week in The Atlantic, Jonathan Chait hailed New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani as a pragmatic moderate in his approach to governance.

I’ve toyed with this theme and basically agree with Chait’s points. But for the sake of offering a different perspective, I don’t think Mamdani’s pragmatic and moderate approach to doing the job of mayor means he’s not really a leftist.

The clearest precedent I can think of for the way he’s governing is Bernie Sanders as mayor of Burlington. Sanders won narrowly in a three-way race, thanks in part to support from the police union, and by all accounts gained support during his time in office.

As mayor, Sanders did not do socialism in one small New England city. He did really normal good mayor stuff, like deliver cost-effective city services, keep the streets clean and safe, and promote economic development. Being somewhat familiar with Sanders’s record as mayor, I found what I’d heard about Sanders offering advice and mentorship to Mayor-elect Mamdani reassuring.

Notably, though, Bernie spending eight years as a pragmatic mayor of Burlington didn’t mean he stopped being a leftist. He ran for the House as a leftist, moved up to the Senate as a leftist, and is obviously an extremely eager left-wing factional politician.

The reason a hardcore leftist can spend eight years being a pragmatic mayor is that leftists care a lot about building political power. Once they’ve won a mayoral election as a leftist, the best way to build leftist political power is to do a good job as mayor. The alternative, on display in Brandon Johnson’s Chicago, is to flounder and discredit the left.

Governing like a pragmatic moderate for the sake of leftist power-building is different than actually being a pragmatic moderate. In a lot of ways, the former probably works better in municipal governance because it means left-wing members of the media will criticize the leftist cranks who protest you when they might side with protestors against a more moderate mayor.

Which is all just to say that in a lot of ways, I think the fact that the center-left finds itself surprisingly pleased with Mamdani shows that while the divide between moderates and progressives gets a lot of coverage, there’s an under-discussed divide between politicians who have (mostly executive) jobs featuring real accountability for outcomes and the bulk of backbench legislators, who are basically just posting.

As a professional poster myself, I know full well that factionalism between posters gets intense. Actual governing, though, tends to produce consensus instead.

The reverse-Mamdanis of the U.S. Congress

You can really see this in action with politicians who’ve moved from executive office to Congress.

I believe Maggie Hassan, Jeanne Shaheen, and John Hickenlooper, all former governors, think of themselves as pragmatic moderates. And if you look at their records as governors, they clearly were pragmatic moderates. They won what were, at the time, tough races in swing states.

And while they were, of course, more progressive than their Republican opponents, they did not take huge progressive policy swings. New Hampshire, notably, continued to be a state with no tax on earned income under the leadership of Hassan and Shaheen. Hickenlooper refused to take a position on a 2011 ballot initiative to raise income and sales taxes to increase school funding. He fought with teachers’ unions about pensions, and he declined to push for a law that would grant collective bargaining rights to Colorado state and local public employees.

And when they became senators, it’s not as if they became wild-eyed leftists.

But as legislators, they don’t tangle with any progressive interest groups. They all (at least officially) endorsed the more expansive multi-trillion version of Build Back Better that was cut down by Joe Manchin into the Inflation Reduction Act. As governors, none of them were proponents of dramatic expansions of the social safety net, but as senators, they were.

Or look at someone like Abigail Spanberger, who as a House member was known as a “moderate” in the sense that she sometimes fought with the Squad, but she wasn’t a thorn in the side of party leadership or someone who refused to endorse major interest-group priorities. But when she ran for governor, she said she wouldn’t repeal Virginia’s right-to-work status because she believed it was good for the business climate of the state. As governor, she’s been fighting with the legislature about a proposal to do public sector bargaining because she thinks the way it’s been drafted is going to be bad for local government finances.

The basic difference is that if you’re a governor or a mayor, you need to brag primarily about things that are happening in your state. Kathy Hochul and Maura Healey, neither of whom are particularly moderate as a question of factional identification, are both trying to get new natural-gas pipelines built because they are worried about state energy prices. If you’re a legislator, you can brag just about positions you’ve taken.

A Democratic House member can talk all they like about taxing the rich and being pro-labor. But a governor or a mayor needs to sit down and really think through whether the outcomes of a particular policy choice are actually going to be good for the state or city. And while of course people disagree to an extent about values on the basis of overall political ideology, in practice I think they don’t actually disagree all that much. Mamdani doesn’t want Wall Street firms to close their New York City offices and send those jobs to New Jersey or Texas. Everybody brags when crime goes down and not when it goes up.

Reasonable people can and do disagree to an extent about which policies will generate good outcomes. But I think the existence of these reverse-Mamdani figures underscores that disagreement about the facts isn’t actually the main difference.

The difference is that the natural state of the safe-seat Democratic Party legislator is to say “yes” to a lot of different interest-group asks without thinking too hard about them or whether they’re contradictory. You figure that someone else is going to pick and choose what actually happens and that your job is mostly just to be a people-pleaser and coalition-manager.

President Senator vs. the strong mayor

For an executive, pure people-pleasing doesn’t work nearly as well.

That’s why, unless they only care about Israel, there’s a lot for moderates to like about non-moderate Mamdani and a lot to dislike about self-identified moderate Joe Biden.

A friend who spent years working in the Senate joked to me that Biden conducted himself as President Senator, very much declining to set priorities and say, “We’re going to do this and not that.” Nobody finds it particularly remarkable that Chris Coons and Lisa Blunt Rochester are just baseline Democrats who sign on to all the normal bills and don’t think very clearly about tradeoffs. That’s just life as a safe-seat senator. But from a president, it was actually quite odd. His team was aware that affordability was a pressing crisis, but nobody on the team was empowered to make any pro-affordability decisions that would get them crosswise with labor unions or environmental groups. They could care about the economic impact of international oil sanctions because green groups didn’t lobby on that, but they didn’t apply the same logic to the Interior Department’s setting of drilling fees since that was something those groups did lobby on.

Mamdani is more left-wing than Biden. He’s also a much stronger leader.

The City Council tried to bully him into giving public-school paraprofessionals a bonus, and he wouldn’t do it. Mamdani also fought, successfully, to delay implementation of a state-mandated reduction in class sizes that he’d voted in favor of as a state legislator. He ran on making the bus free and then appeased more technical transit advocates by revising it to “fast and free.” But actually doing free buses would cost a ton of money and not be very beneficial, so now he’s just focused on speeding up the buses, which is a better idea because it doesn’t impair his ability to spend money on other things.

He hasn’t reinvented himself as an anti-spending libertarian. New York City is still a very high-tax, high-spend jurisdiction, and he’s working to make spending higher.

But he does face fiscal constraints, and he wants to focus on a specific goal — expanding child care offerings — so he’s trying to not get sucked into other commitments. Activists want him to pick a fight with the police commissioner because that would build their political power, but it builds his political power to have a good working relationship with the governor (who likes the police commissioner), and there’s no actual problem with the N.Y.P.D. status quo, so he’s not doing it.

The ideological content of Mamdani’s administration is genuinely not that different from Bill de Blasio, who was mayor quite recently. But de Blasio, despite a number of admirable qualities, was a pretty weak Biden-like figure who was seen as delivered into office by an interest-group coalition and who in return governed largely by parceling out doses of interest-group slop. The equivalent 2025 figure would have been Brad Lander.

Mamdani emerged somewhat independently of the interest-group ecosystem and has more leverage to stand outside the system and insist on his priorities rather than accept slop. This is not exactly moderation — it’s all in pursuit of the larger goal of democratic socialism — but it’s not not moderation.

Posting versus governing

For 2028, I really want moderate Democrats — by which I mean people who admire the Blue Dog Coalition and think that Biden, Chuck Schumer, and Hakeem Jeffries are too left-wing — to let go of their terror of a leftist winning the primary.

A big part of this is just that, to a large extent, I really do think fear is the mind-killer. My ideal 2028 outcome is that someone runs a smart moderate campaign based on a smart moderate critique of the Democratic Party establishment and wins. That would be great and, in my opinion, better than nominating Ro Khanna or Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

But I don’t want to panic and bandwagon behind some tired establishment figure like Gavin Newsom or Kamala Harris just to box out someone from the left. If someone from the left wins, they’ll just end up stuck dealing with the same problems of practical governance.

Because the fact is, moderates are right about what the practical problems of governance look like. If President Ocasio-Cortez is sitting in the Oval Office in 2029, she’s not going to want to burn a bunch of political capital on a totally undefined ICE abolition agenda. She’ll achieve whatever is easy to achieve through new leadership and new orders and move on to trying to get Congress to act on her top priorities. She’s also not going to overhaul the entire $5 trillion-a-year health-care system in one fell swoop any more than President Newsom would. But she’ll get something done on health care, and hopefully progressives will be happy with it because they’ll believe she tried in good faith, just like they believe in Mamdani even though he’s delivering only a fraction of what he promised.

A lot of what passes for factional disputes between the establishment and the left right now is really just left-wing backbenchers doing posts.

“We should abolish ICE” or “the government should give everyone free health care” aren’t really plans for governing. It’s just posting takes. If you don’t actually need to set priorities or deal with recalcitrant legislators or stay within a fixed budget, you can fire off whatever takes you want. And I’m not per se opposed to people posting takes. I’m a takesmith myself. But I have all kinds of takes, such as “We should do a revenue-neutral carbon tax with the price set at the globally optimal social cost of carbon and the revenue used to offset regressive payroll taxes.”

Well, so what? I do think that we should do that. If you ask me in a mailbag or during the Q&A session at the end of a panel, I will offer that take. If it comes up in a referendum, I will vote for it. I also think we should “abolish ICE” and have a consolidated federal police agency.

But these things are not going to happen. They’re just opinions. As an opinion columnist, I think it’s important that I try to have correct opinions, and I like other columnists to also have correct opinions. But I find the impulse to assess politicians as if they’re columnists to be a bit perverse.

Legislators, after all, can accept the responsibility to govern. I don’t really agree with Senator Sheldon Whitehouse’s takes qua takes, but he sat down and did the work of negotiating a really good bipartisan energy permitting bill.

The truth, though, is that members of Congress have the option of having successful careers as politicians basically just by posting and never buckling down to the work of writing bills, aligning stakeholders, and setting priorities. Executives also can duck the work of governance, but when they try — like Biden in the White House or Johnson in Chicago — they tend to fail in obvious ways. There’s a kind of objective incentive for a mayor or a governor or a president to try to be responsible, while many legislators can get away with just posting.

Still, even backbench legislators can attempt to seize the wheel and participate in the governance of the country if they want to. Sometimes when they do that, they cook up ideas that are dumb. But just as the responsibility that’s inherent in executive leadership tends to push people to exercise better judgment, the practical need to count votes and make deals tends to force legislators to think harder about what they’re actually saying. Otherwise, they’re basically just out here doing my job — a job that I think should be left to me.

A golden age of science is coming

AI can do things humans researchers can’t, even in groups.

Noah Smith
Oct 29
 
READ IN APP
 

It’s almost hard to remember, but just a few years ago, a lot of very smart people thought that science was in terminal decline. Respected researchers were writing papers with titles like “Are Ideas Getting Harder to Find?”, “Papers and patents are becoming less disruptive over time”, and “Slowed canonical progress in large fields of science”. In 1996, science writer John Horgan even published a book called The End Of Science: Facing The Limits Of Knowledge In The Twilight Of The Scientific Age.

The fundamental idea was that the Universe only has so many insights to discover, and that we’ve picked the low-hanging fruit. It was the idea that Joseph-Louis Lagrange expressed when he said that “we cannot find more than once a system of the world to establish.” As the big ideas and the simple ideas get mined out, we’re forced to throw ever more brains at the mysteries of nature just to keep scientific progress going at a fraction of its old pace:

It looked like science was hitting a wall. Then along came AI.

It’s far too early to tell how much AI will eventually speed up the growth of total factor productivity. But already we can see signs of a speedup in science. Anthropic Founder Jack Clark assembled some of the hopeful data points in a recent lecture:

Dror Poleg
@drorpoleg
"If you pick different parts of science, you see the same pattern show up: Progress is accelerating, and it has started to accelerate in the last two years."
Jack Clark @jackclarkSF
I’m speaking at the IMF in an hour about the singularity and why I believe it has begun and the choices we'll need to make. Watch live here: https://t.co/Hj9HzcXx5h

2 Replies · 10 Reposts · 123 Likes

Claude also appears to be enabling rapid progress toward a treatment for food allergies. OpenAI, meanwhile, announced a possible breakthrough treatment for neurodegenerative disease.

Meanwhile, Google Cloud Chief Scientist Pushmeet Kohli has a list of recent scientific advances that have been enabled by its new Gemini model, including breakthroughs in nuclear fusion reactor design, rare disease research, and quantum computing:

Pushmeet Kohli
@pushmeet
Gemini 4 Argon is a step change in model performance. In recent weeks, it has had a transformative impact on the Science projects in our team at @GoogleDeepMind and our external collaborators, and helped make a number of remarkable advances across scientific disciplines. 🧵👇
4:47 PM · Oct 13, 2026 · 36.5K Views
8 Replies · 41 Reposts · 497 Likes

But as cool as these stories sound, they’re just very minor, preliminary efforts. There are a number of reasons to think that AI is going to propel us into a golden age of scientific discovery. That age might not last forever — AI might still run into diminishing returns eventually. But the next few decades are probably going to be an absolutely amazing time for human science.

The number of “effective researchers” is no longer limited

The most important input into science is scientists themselves. Until this year, that meant human brains — talented, highly trained human brains. The number of trained human brains could be increased by sending more people to grad school, but only to a point — the smartest people tend to be sent into the hardest research fields first, and if you 10x the number of researchers, the average quality will go down. This constraint was already starting to bite, as Ekerdt and Wu argued in 2024:

We argue that a substantial portion of the downward historical trend in U.S. research productivity is a composition effect resulting from self-selection in researcher ability and the dramatic expansion of the research sector…[W]e find that this composition effect has lowered average researcher ability by between 37% and 53%[.]

And of course, low fertility was making the problem worse, because fewer children meant fewer people who were able to become future scientists.

AI just blows up this constraint completely. If an AI agent can function as an autonomous researcher, there’s no constraint on the number of researchers in the world — you can just build more of them, by building more computer chips and data centers that enable the running of more AI agents. Whether or not massive hordes of agents can collaborate to solve individual problems much faster, increasing the number of agents allows them to tackle many different research questions in parallel.

What’s more, these AI “researchers” can be trained incredibly quickly compared to human beings. A human scientist takes decades to train, and more years to reach the frontier of their research field by diligent reading and conversation. This is the “burden of knowledge”, and it’s commonly believed to be one reason ideas have been getting harder to find — by the time human scientists can get up to speed, they’re often so old that their ideas are no longer novel.

AI just annihilates this constraint — it can assimilate the entire literature and reach the frontier of research extremely quickly, and it can also tell human scientists where the frontier lies without forcing them to discover that for themselves. It can also pivot to new research directions more easily than humans can.

And there’s also a self-reinforcing economic cycle here. Because scientific advances enable higher GDP, they enable more resources to be invested into the creation of yet more electronic “scientists”.

Now that doesn’t mean the amount of scientific research goes to infinity — there may still be some essential bottleneck task that human researchers are still needed to perform. There are some indications that AI’s progress on open-ended conceptual research tasks is slower than in other dimensions, and it may be that humans are still needed to provide some of this long-term conceptual thinking. I’d bet against this being true for much longer, but it might be true for a long time.

Even in this most “pessimistic” case, though, the amount of effective capital that scientists can use to leverage their work just went up by a lot.

AI eliminates the theory bottleneck

Science proceeds by an iterative process of theory and experiment. The theory part of that cycle is typically short, but non-trivial — it took a couple of years after the blackbody radiation spectrum was observed for Max Planck to come up with the quantum hypothesis to explain it, and decades longer before quantum theory as we now know it was created. It took about a year for Watson and Crick to figure out the shape of DNA after the requisite data was gathered.

AI will basically eliminate the theory bottleneck entirely — or at least shorten the turnaround time between experiment and theory by an order of magnitude. AI is an absolute beast at math. Recently, an OpenAI model solved some of the most important open problems in computer science, math, and theoretical physics, and no one even batted an eyebrow because that sort of triumph is becoming increasingly commonplace. One of those solutions was a proof that the Standard Model of Particle Physics could be mathematically well-defined — a problem that human theorists had so far been unable to tackle.

Not all research relies equally on theory, but understanding novel experimental results almost always involves some important component of either mathematical or spatial reasoning. That part of the task has now been made much, much faster. And on top of that, science is now open to a greater number of humans who aren’t naturally good at theorizing.

AI can read the whole literature

Much of the work of human scientists involves reading and understanding endless amounts of papers and going to endless conferences and seminars. The purpose of that work is to understand the existing scientific literature. Understanding the literature allows scientists to do the following things:

  1. Come up with new ideas for hypotheses to test

  2. Avoid doing research that someone else has already done

  3. Synthesize approaches from different areas or fields

AI can reduce this effort to almost zero. Consider this excerpt from OpenAI’s blog post about their new research into neurodegenerative disease:

The team divided the analysis among thousands of AI agents powered by GPT‑Rosalind, an approach we call distributed biological reasoning. The agents examined a whole-brain CRISPR atlas…a dataset showing how gene disruptions affect different types of cells across the mouse brain. Each agent investigated a gene disruption, analyzed cellular responses, searched scientific literature, and proposed explanations for the results. Their reports were combined into a reasoning atlas linking genes, cellular effects, relevant publications, and possible biological mechanisms.

The research team estimated that comparable human analysis and literature review, conducted one perturbation at a time, would take months to a year. The agents reproduced findings from human analyses while uncovering additional leads. Their assessments of novelty and scientific value also aligned with judgments from blinded human experts. These findings help prioritize further experiments needed to test the proposed biological mechanisms.

Some of these insights point to new leads for understanding brain disease. [emphasis mine]

This is one case in which parallel work by a large number of agents really does make a huge difference:
