@haider1
this is actually insane openai deployed thousands of GPT-Rosalind agents to analyze millions of mouse brain cells in 32 minutes, work that could take human researchers months to a year also the agents uncovered new leads for brain diseases like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's
OpenAI @OpenAI
GPT-Rosalind surfaced a new lead for drug discovery: could restoring cholesterol transport protect neurons from degeneration? DCTN1 is a gene linked to Perry syndrome, a rare neurodegenerative disorder. In mouse-brain data, disrupting it increased expression of genes involved in
2:41 PM · Oct 21, 2026 · 51.5K Views
26 Replies · 95 Reposts · 1.26K Likes

Not only does instantaneous literature review vastly speed up the research process, but it allows AI to make novel conceptual leaps from combining approaches from wildly different fields of research. AI regularly does this in math research, combining results, approaches, and theorems from far-flung places that no human mathematician would have thought to combine.

It can do it in science, too. Much of scientific innovation, historically, has been “recombinant” innovation — scientists applying insights from one field to another. With AI, essentially all research is now cross-disciplinary — AI can read not just the literature on a particular subject, but the literature on a million other subjects that might have produced useful techniques or insights for the problem at hand.

Superscience

So far, all of the factors I’ve listed are ways that AI can speed up science as it’s already done. I’ve basically described how AI can send gigantic hordes of superhumanly fast, superhumanly well-read, superhumanly mathematically gifted researchers to re-accelerate scientific discovery.

But it’s also possible that AI will enable types of discovery — and ways of understanding the natural world — that no network of humans, no matter how large or how brilliant it was or how long it had to work, would ever be able to discover. In a post back in July, I wrote about how that might work:

What if there are lots of…aspects of the Universe that [are] too complex to understand in terms of simple laws, but not so complex that they just dissolve into unknowable chaos? It’s possible that we can reliably control these complex phenomena with AI, even if we never reduce them to the kind of principles that we can teach a grad student in a textbook…

Another way of saying this is that there may be laws of the universe that humans can’t understand but AI can. I call these “cloud laws” — causal regularities that can be exploited by technology, but which are too diffuse and complex for an individual human being to either intuit or communicate…

Perhaps social sciences like economics, sociology, and political science obey similarly complex regularities, and AI can help us find them. Perhaps there are physical processes — plasma, or topological materials, or aerial turbulence, etc. — that obey cloud laws instead of chaos?…

[H]uman collaboration is bottlenecked — it’s limited by our ability to intuit patterns at an individual level, and to communicate these patterns from one individual to another. AI, being a computer, just doesn’t have this sort of limitation; it can work with vast, diffuse patterns without having to break them into pieces or simplify them in order to compress them into the tiny pipelines of person-to-person explanation…

If much of the Universe turns out to be ruled by cloud laws, we could be on the precipice of a scientific renaissance.

In order to discover cloud laws, AI will need huge amounts of data about the natural world. AI figured out human speech by assimilating essentially all of the text humans have ever written. If it’s going to figure out hidden patterns in biology, neuroscience, materials science, etc., it’s going to need similarly massive amounts of data from physical instruments.

That data will be far, far more than humans — individually or collectively — would be able to parse, label, characterize, or model. But AI was built to do this. If scientists simply build huge arrays of sensors to measure complex phenomena like the brain, the cell, the economy, etc., they may be able to feed this flood of data to AI directly and bypass human cognitive intermediation entirely. AI would then learn about the world directly, and it might learn things that humans never could.

This “superscience”, if you want to call it that, would actually go beyond the kind of science humans have done heretofore. Many of the technologies it yielded would be beyond human comprehension — indistinguishable from magic. But to the AIs, they would make perfect scientific sense.

In any case, it seems clear that the scientific slowdown that threatened human progress will now be delayed — at least for a while. Unless humans have somehow found most of the actual exploitable regularities in our Universe, we’re about to enter a new golden age of science.

How I would fix all of America’s major problems

Let’s stop being practical for once.

Matthew Yglesias
Oct 29
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

When you’ve finished reading today’s post, I hope you’ll check out the latest episode of “The Argument” podcast, where Jerusalem and I explore Hannah Arendt’s “The Human Condition” and what artificial intelligence could mean for everything from the future of work to the purpose of human life. Paid subscribers can watch or listen ad free and read the transcript and show notes here. If you’re a free subscriber, you can catch the episode on YouTube here or listen wherever you get your podcasts.

Subscribe: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts

Arguing about electoral politics is annoying at times, so I thought today it might be more fun to go back into “One Billion Americans” mode and uncork some policy takes about how I think everything ought to work.

Before we begin, I want to acknowledge that one way in which I’ve become more politics-brained over the years is in recognizing that at a certain level of detail, it doesn’t make sense to hold too strongly to your policy opinions.

I believe my April take that dogs aren’t people has largely stood the test of time. But in the course of expressing the view that dogs and humans are different in politically and morally relevant ways, I got a little cranky about dog parks. And I don’t think what I said about that in particular really holds up. I don’t own a dog, so I don’t care about dog parks, and if it were totally up to me, I probably wouldn’t build any. But I don’t play pickleball either and yet we have pickleball courts. It’s fine if I’m outnumbered and people want to build recreational facilities I don’t personally use. Tastes differ and that’s okay.

So, some of the ideas below are going to be — deliberately — a little vague because I think a certain amount of vagueness is appropriate. We have a pluralistic democratic society, and there’s never going to be one totally definitive way to do things.

Still, I think we can say a few things about the United States pretty clearly:

The U.S. is a rich country with relatively poor public-health outcomes given our prosperity. The material living standards of the poorest Americans are shockingly bad given the overall high living standards. Health care has a lot of problems, but trying to fix them requires that we pay attention to a lot of fussy technical details. Housing, on the other hand, presents a lot of problems that are quite straightforward and relatively simple. Our long-term budget problems, which everyone’s grown bored of hearing about over the years, are in fact not so “long-term” anymore and need to be dealt with. We need to make policy in the national interest, but that interest is best advanced through openness to the world and especially through collaboration with other open societies.

Now, on to the takes.

Helping those in need

While the U.S. is a lot richer on average than, say, Germany, it’s still the case that poor Americans are worse off by many measures.

The simplest fix is to give unconditional cash benefits to kids (in effect, to their parents). The most politically expedient way to do this is to make the program relatively cheap by having an income phaseout. But I think the best way to do it is not to characterize this as a targeted anti-poverty program but as a universal transfer from non-parents to parents, just like public schools.

This should probably feature a big one-off payment when a kid is born (a “baby bonus”), followed by generous monthly payments for the first year (“paid leave”), then somewhat less generous payments for the next few years (a “child care subsidy” or a “home care allowance,” depending on what you do), then further reduced payments when the kid reaches school age. Finally, it should phase down for older teenagers on the expectation that they can get part-time jobs (with some provision made for disability and other relevant considerations).

To do this at reasonable payment levels would be incredibly expensive, but I think it makes a lot more sense on the merits than the current smorgasbord of family policy ideas that Democrats are proposing. And it scales up or down smoothly — you could do it just for kids under three and still accomplish a lot and then work for expansion to older kids over time.

The other big thing in this bucket is medical care.

Medicare for All has become this endless factional discourse object that only serves to make people angry at each other, but there ought to be a system whereby everyone can get free or nearly free health care at government expense.

This should be financed with a value-added tax, which would be progressive relative to the existing structure of health insurance premiums but also relatively efficient. The idea is that consumption of “stuff that is not health care services” would pay to subsidize a free tier of health care services. How high should the VAT be? How generous should the free tier be? I don’t think these questions have definitive answers; experts and voters will argue and go back and forth. Since this is a wealthy country, we should expect that most people will supplement with out-of-pocket purchases or private supplemental insurance. And we should also acknowledge that health outcomes are only very partially about health care services. But there is some sense of “necessary and useful medical care” that everyone should be able to get and that is provided by the public, just like roads and parks.

A healthier country

A lot of what makes life in America tough for the poor compared with life in other developed countries is that Americans — and especially low-income Americans — are exposed to a lot of violence. Beyond the lives and money directly lost to murder, robbery, and reckless driving, a tremendous amount of time and resources is wasted on avoiding these problems. Big strides have been made against crime over the past 30 years, but it’s still the case that the most dangerous city in France has a lower murder rate than low-crime rural states like Montana or Nebraska.

Law-abiding people should be allowed to own handguns for personal defense or amusement, but there should be a national registration system and real penalties for people who don’t report the loss or theft of a handgun in a timely manner. There should be a major federal enforcement effort around the networks selling and transporting black- and gray-market weapons to criminals. People convicted of crimes should lose their right to carry a gun for a period of time, and there should be vigorous enforcement not only of the rules against carrying a gun illegally but against helping anyone without a license get a gun.

We should invest in the policing pipeline, perhaps through something like a national service academy for police officers or a program modeled on Teach for America, with the mission of getting idealistic young people to serve as officers in high-crime cities. There should be a consolidated federal policing agency — i.e., we should “abolish ICE” — so federal enforcement resources could be used more flexibly in the most high-impact ways.

We should invest in technology and surveillance (yes, including Flock cameras) and emphasize supervising parolees better, especially because if we could make parole work better (frequent drug and alcohol tests, GPS surveillance), then we could let people out of prison sooner. And we should treat unsafe driving seriously as a form of crime that harms people.

Murder and traffic accidents aren’t the only source of bad public-health outcomes, of course. The inflation-adjusted tax on alcohol should be much higher than it was in 1991, not much lower. Legal marijuana is fine, but the taxes on it should be high, which means we need vigorous enforcement against gray-market pot. We should tax sweeteners and stop subsidizing commodity grain production.

The Robert F. Kennedy Jr. concept that we all need to eat based on regenerative agriculture is unworkable, and we’re not going to get everyone to forget about grocery costs and just eat liver. But we should acknowledge that many more people are overeating nutrient-poor food than are going hungry in this country and do whatever is feasible to discourage mindless consumption of garbage food. SNAP should probably just be cash, but we could also implement programs where poor people get an in-kind allotment of free frozen vegetables if they want them.

Housing first

I’m always a little peeved that while everyone readily acknowledges that housing is a huge share of the economy, it’s also considered a boring, technical issue that doesn’t count as a “big idea.” This doesn’t make sense.

Housing scarcity is the number one economic problem facing young Americans. Everything in life involves tradeoffs, but housing reform is not a zero-sum transfer from old to young or from homeowners to renters — it’ll make the overall pie larger and deliver broad second-order economic benefits in terms of higher G.D.P. and better-paying jobs. Housing abundance will also contribute, in small ways, to things like making it more feasible for people to get married and have kids and thus at least partially address some widespread anxieties about the state of American society.

YIMBYs already have a bold vision for solving the housing crisis

Matthew Yglesias
·
Aug 26
Read full story

ROAD to Housing was a nice start, but everyone knows it’s just nipping at the heels of the problem.

The federal government doesn’t write local zoning codes, but the overarching theme of its efforts ought to be something like taking ROAD’s tweak of the relatively minor Community Development Block Grant program, which provides federal funding for local housing and infrastructure projects, and applying it much more broadly.

Large federal investments in things like surface transportation and even schools ought to be allocated with a formula that penalizes jurisdictions where housing supply is not allowed to meet housing demand. We don’t even need to call it a penalty. Federal money is an investment in the future of the country, and if a county has low objective demand for housing, that’s fine — maybe they really need federal help. And if a county has objectively high demand for housing but residents don’t want to allow the built environment to change, that’s also fine in some sense — but they’re not going to get any federal help. And when some places lose their federal dollars, that money should go instead to places that are facilitating growth.

Subscribed

At the same time, the federal government should address things that are clearly within the scope of federal competency.

  • We don’t need to go all the way back to the 2006 vintage of mortgage regulation, but we’ve made it too hard to get a home loan.

  • The federal government should be willing to sell off non-park land in the West for housing development.

  • We should push states to adopt modern building codes that allow for cheaper materials and more efficient floor plans.

This is a pretty radical agenda, and I think it would have large benefits for the country.

An open society

We should answer “The Indian Question” with an enthusiastic yes.

If people of above-average intelligence and drive want to come to the U.S., we ought to give them the opportunity to do so. People with job offers that pay above-average salaries should be allowed to move here. So should students with high SAT scores. Even low-wage workers can be fiscally beneficial, but they should probably come in on temporary work visas, pay taxes (and their employers should pay a special employer-side payroll tax), and then go home with some savings in their pocket.

It seems like a good idea to have some kind of values-based screening to try to weed out people who hate America or are fundamentally hostile to democracy or the Constitution. But instead of endlessly debating the fiscal impact of immigrants (the restrictionists are mostly wrong about this), we ought to be letting in immigrants on terms where the fiscal impact is positive.

In the real world, there are limits to what people will put up with in terms of even an orderly immigration system. I grew up in New York City, surrounded by a very multi-ethnic, multi-lingual community, so I don’t personally have the nostalgia for a whiter 1980s America that some people seem to. My personal preference is for a very high level of local diversity, probably higher than is politically viable in a national context. But all signs are that the voters are enthusiastic about skilled legal immigrants, so we should be able to go pretty far with immigration in the national interest.

We should be mindful of the strategic concerns involved in trade with potentially hostile countries. We do not want our entire economy to rely on Chinese-made batteries or to sell them the finest microchips and lithography machines.

But broadly speaking, the current “affordability crisis” should teach us not to sneer at the very real upside to being able to buy cheap socks from foreign factories. We should be doing everything possible to promote the free flow of goods and services across the U.S., Europe, the big Anglophone countries, Japan, and South Korea and trying for even deeper economic integration with Latin America and the Caribbean.

It was easy during the long period from 1984 to 2019, when inflation was basically always low, to develop a condescending attitude toward cheap consumer goods as a policy goal.

But it turns out that people care a lot about cheap consumer goods.

This column will reach infinite length if I get into artificial intelligence here, but I think a current problem for the A.I. industry is that while large language models do a lot of stuff that is demonstrably impressive, I’m not seeing anything I buy getting cheaper as a result of this powerful new tech. Some of that is a lack of imagination from the companies themselves, and some of it is the policy environment. But we should be rolling out robot taxis, cheap 24/7 medical consultations, and other tangible new products as fast as possible while trying to slow (and ideally halt) the race toward superintelligence that could disempower all of humanity.

A serious fiscal policy

The cost of money — most of all mortgages and auto loans — is part of the cost of living. And these interest rates are in part a function of the broader macroeconomic environment. I spent the Obama years cursing that with interest rates and inflation low, we should run a more stimulative fiscal policy. Now we have the opposite problem and need deficit reduction to address inflation and interest rates.

A lot of this should be on the tax side. But I think it’s been a mistake to spend so much time contemplating exotic, hard-to-implement, and potentially unconstitutional new tax concepts.

The main solutions that we need are enforcing the existing tax code much more vigorously, ending the “stepped-up basis” rule, closing a few well-known strategies to avoid estate taxes, capping the value of all tax deductions, and then just increasing the rates somewhat in a normal way. This has somehow come to feel like a harder political lift than designing an entirely novel tax system from scratch. But in the real world, raising the tax rate on corporate income is clearly the most feasible way of addressing the concern that a handful of business owners are piling up too much wealth.

Subscribed

This ought to be paired with action on the spending side. I do think the evidence supports the view that genuine fraud is not a large share of overall American federal spending, but there’s not zero fraud, and voters are bothered by it, so we ought to address it. DOGE was weirdly uninterested in longstanding Government Accountability Office program-integrity recommendations and decided to target medical care for African kids instead. But it’s worth going back and doing that stuff right and making a big show out of it.

There’s also a lot on the spending side that’s not “fraud” but is either known not to work (many job training programs) or else deliberately inflates costs (lots of procurement rules).

Of course, to really get serious about spending, you need to look at spending for the elderly. This is, famously, a political hot potato. On the merits, though, would it really be so bad if senior citizens in the top third of the income distribution received the same Social Security benefits as seniors in the middle third? Would that actually violate our sense of what we owe our elders? Medicare Advantage is a disaster zone of overspending and cons. We of course “can” just raise taxes and use the proceeds to cover these costs. But it would be good to reduce the deficit, which requires raising taxes, and there are things we should spend more on. So it really makes sense to spend less on things that aren’t needed.

To wrap this up, a point I would make from trade to immigration to housing to technology is that if you want things to be different, something has to change.

A lot of recent American politics feels to me like political entrepreneurs complaining about the status quo but then also promising to stop all change or maybe make things like they were in the past, except you don’t need to give up anything you like about the present. This might just be what happens in aging societies: The electorate gets brain-poisoned by nostalgia, and nobody wants to run on themes of hope and change anymore.

But I hope that’s wrong and we’re just trapped in a bad equilibrium a bit arbitrarily.

Will the AI Investment Splurge Last?

The boom is hitting two walls at once: Financing and public hatred

Paul Krugman
Oct 29
 
READ IN APP
 

The boom in AI-related spending is already enormous relative to the size of the U.S. economy and is widely expected to grow even bigger. Indeed, a widely cited projection by Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh of the Columbia Business School concludes, based on announced plans by major players in the industry, that this will be the biggest investment boom in U.S. history, measured as a percentage of GDP:

Source: Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh

Well, I’m going to make a prediction: This will not happen. Instead, the splurge on AI will run into two walls that will force either postponement or cancellation of many of those announced projects.

First, the money to fund all this AI investment spending simply won’t be there. Much of the spending so far has come from established industry giants like Google and Microsoft, who in the early phases of the boom could rely on retained earnings from their existing businesses. But the size of the buildout is now so big that it is increasingly dependent upon massive levels of borrowing.

And lenders are getting cold feet. Many observers have long argued that AI is an impressive technology, but profits will be elusive. And it’s now apparent that companies that are spending hundreds of billions on frontier technology are unlikely to generate enough profits to justify their huge outlays. There are a variety of reasons why, with the most obvious being competition from much cheaper and less powerful, yet commercially adequate, models from China.

After all, we’ve seen this movie before. The IT boom of the late 1990s changed the world, but it also ended with many tech leaders going bankrupt because they couldn’t monetize their achievements. During the last few weeks, lenders to AI companies seem to be having a collective Wile E. Coyote moment — the point at which the animated character, having run off a cliff, looks down and only then, obeying the laws of cartoon physics, plunges to the ground.

The financial data now clearly show that fear is spreading in the loan markets. Starting in the summer, CDS spreads — the price of insurance against default — have soared for a number of AI companies:

Coreweave, which basically sells compute, is in a league of its own in terms of high default risk. But other companies are also starting to show strain, especially Oracle. As yesterday’s Bloomberg headline put it,

With lenders running scared, and either demanding much higher interest rates or refusing to lend altogether, it’s increasingly difficult to see how the hyperscalers can realize their gargantuan investment plans unless someone is willing to take massive losses.

Furthermore, the AI investment boom is facing another huge obstacle: Most Americans really, really hate data centers and AI in general.

The polling on data centers is astonishingly negative. Not only do most Americans oppose construction of data centers near where they live, an almost equally large majority oppose building them anywhere in the U.S. And the opposition is much more intense than the support:

This hostility no doubt has multiple sources. Data centers impose real costs on communities through their consumption of water and electricity, as well as pollution if they build their own power supplies. At the same time, data centers, once up and running, provide almost no local jobs.

At a more cosmic level, there are widespread fears that AI will lead to mass unemployment and possibly even human extinction — fears that have been spread by the industry itself, in the belief that fear of apocalypse is good for their IPOs.

More generally, the race to build data centers, often accomplished through back-room deals with corrupt local politicians, feeds into the public sense that big-money elites are rigging the system against ordinary Americans.

But the American public is now fighting back, pitchforks in hand. Grassroots opposition is having a big effect because permits are needed to build giants data centers — permits that more and more local governments are refusing to grant in the face of local opposition. One important contributor to Oracle’s problems is the repeated rejection of permits for a natural gas pipeline to provide power to Project Jupiter, Oracle’s massive data center project in New Mexico.

Elsewhere, New York State has introduced a one-year moratorium on all construction of large new data centers, while a number of other states and local governments are considering major restrictions. Furthermore, the political environment is unlikely to become more favorable after the midterms given how well Democrats are polling across state and local races.

Granted, neither financing problems nor political opposition are likely, by themselves, to completely stop AI investment. But I predict they will greatly slow it down. And this would be a very good outcome, perhaps even allowing the AI bubble to deflate rather than bursting and thereby delivering a body-blow to the overall economy.

Yes, some companies – such as Coreweave – may very well go bust and many investors will be hurt. However, under current investment plans, there’s a high probability that a lot of that investment money would have been wasted and total losses would be many times larger. Thus, in the end, angry locals and panicky lenders may well end up saving investors from themselves. And, more importantly, slowing this juggernaut down may save the American economy from the devastation of the bursting of a gigantic AI bubble.

The underrated — but hated — insights of Econ 101

Plus remote work, ethnostates, and my interview with Mehdi Hasan

Matthew Yglesias
Oct 30
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

There is a midterm election coming up soon, as you have probably heard, and I am hoping that Democrats will do very well in it.

One reason for this is that due to the way our political system is constructed, the Democrats I have the biggest doubts about are definitely going to win no matter what. Melat Kiros and Darializa Avila Chevalier are coming to Congress even if Democrats underperform the current polling by 11 points or whatever. But there are a whole bunch of people who I really like — Josh Turek, Mary Peltola, Adam Hamilton, Bobby Pulido, Johnny Garcia, Jamie Ager, just to name a few — who will win their seats if and only if Democrats win by margins about as big as what Nate Silver is forecasting. Indeed, the slightly stupid way the House speaker election works means that if Democrats have a huge majority, then Hakeem Jeffries will be installed with no problem, but if it’s a very narrow majority, then the hard left can block him and hold the caucus hostage to their nutty ideas. If Democrats flip the Senate, then the big story will be the senators who flipped Senate seats — Turek, Peltola, Hamilton, Roy Cooper, Sherrod Brown, and James Talarico — but if they don’t, then it’s the Abdul El-Sayed Show.

But the other reason is that I really would like to see the spell of Trump mania come to an end. I don’t hold to Obama-in-2012 delusions that “the fever will break.” But there are just tons of conservative ideological causes and policy positions that keep getting dragged down by Trump’s bluster, corruption, and incompetence. Yet the leaders of those causes have spent the past few years taking the bet that working with Trump to try to consolidate authoritarian power is their best chance forward. I think a good midterm drubbing is the best opportunity to talk them out of that and into the idea that they should try to advance a 2028 candidate who’ll stand for right-of-center policy ideas but not stand for slavish devotion to personality cult politics and endless assaults on the rule of law.

Anyway, on to your questions.

Trisha Jha: Is the idea that prices communicate useful information and we mess with them at our peril the most hated insight of Econ 101?

This goes back to something I’ve noted before, which is that it would be useful in many cases to have a clearer index of exactly what the conventional wisdom is. My sense, personally, is that the fact that we mostly don’t see a lot of price control policies being implemented is evidence that the basic point about the value of prices is pretty well-understood.

My personal vote for a widely underrated Econ 101 insight is the explanation of why a certain class of policy ideas doesn’t scale up.

I write a Substack. If you created a cumbersome licensing system before other people were allowed to launch their own Substack, that would be narrowly good for me. Similarly, if it was illegal for Americans to read takes written by foreigners, that might also be good for me. Anything you can do with regulation, trade policy, immigration, or whatever else to block the supply of new takes helps the existing stock of takesmiths. This is pretty widely understood, and you see lots of examples of different groups of people clamoring for various sorts of protections and often getting them — or at least getting a serious hearing.

What Econ 101 tells you is that each of these moves imposes very small costs on a very large number of people, such that the aggregate costs exceed the benefits.

This means that while you can boost the fortunes of any given occupation by creating barriers to entry, doing so across a large fraction of occupations will end up making everyone worse off than if you hadn’t done it. You can help auto workers by imposing tariffs on foreign-made cars, but if you put tariffs on everything, then everyone is worse off. If you block new housing on Long Island, you can inflate home values and increase the wealth of incumbent homeowners, but if you block new housing in every desirable suburb of every city, the whole country will be much poorer on average.

What makes this insight powerful is that the people pushing for specific protections aren’t “wrong.”

When the Air Line Pilots Association pushes to maintain the unreasonable 1,500-hour rule for new pilots, they’re correct that this benefits their members. Keeping Waymo out of a city benefits Uber and Lyft. Blocking the importation of Canadian softwood lumber helps American loggers. But politicians who are sympathetic to these kinds of claims, normally because they are made by specific interest groups they like, are actually harming more people than they are helping.

A lot of progressive-minded people who in general put a great deal of stock in credentials and formal signifiers of expertise take a very dim view of the idea that economists have relevant expertise on economic policy questions or that mainstream consensus in the profession should generally be given more weight than the views of outliers. What tends to happen here is a kind of faux sophistication where people learn that according to Econ 101, all that Econ 101 stuff about market prices being optimal really only applies if you can assume a perfectly competitive market. Then you look around and it turns out that very few markets meet that standard. So you convince yourself that you can reject the Econ 101 points. The more prudent take is that since real-world markets are only approximately competitive, the Econ 101 models are only approximately true. But they are still offering a lot of insight relative to just guessing or making stuff up.

TW: It would be interesting to hear your detailed views in response to Martin Gurri’s book, “The Revolt of the Public and the Crisis of Authority in the New Millennium”? Much of the political instability in the U.S., and the see-sawing of voter preference between parties, is showing the same pattern in most of the major Western democracies, which means the forces driving this aren’t uniquely American. I thought Gurri’s analysis was prescient and illuminating. Do you agree?

Gurri is an interesting figure because he voted for Trump in 2024 but his whole analysis and register of speaking are closer to the dopey idealism of an academic leftist than the normal cruelty and cynicism of the MAGA right.

I put this answer under the Econ 101 one because I think it’s an illustration of the fact that in the real world you actually do need responsible elites to make technocratically sound policies. Otherwise, you get huge fuckups and people are angrier than ever. I don’t per se disagree with his structural analysis of how elite control over the discourse has weakened or that some aspects of this more democratized public square are normatively desirable. But if you look at problems like the weak American labor market from 2009-14 or the failures of European energy policy that were exposed when Russia invaded Ukraine, these are actually just failures of technocratic elites to do the technically correct thing. There are a lot of emotional aspects to the immigration policy debate in Germany, but the fact that the country never built the state capacity to remove people whose asylum claims are rejected is a really boring kind of failure. Voters understandably get angry at would-be technocrats who don’t govern effectively, but now in America we have Trump who is also not governing effectively, and people are angry about that.

Max Haas: You argue that the popularity of do-nothing governors is evidence against campaigning on bold change. While it’s true that voters don’t like “we’re gonna end police” levels of boldness in campaigns, I think you’re confusing what voters like their politicians to do (nothing) with what they *think* they want their politicians to do (something). Can you imagine, say, David Jolly actually saying in his ads “I will be doing nothing?” I don’t think you’d advise that.

So what are the things people like David Jolly and Ken Casner should run on? Or should they simply argue “I’ll make the legislature pump the brakes?”

It’s not that you want to say you’re not going to do anything. It’s that you want to take a relatively small number of relatively modest changes and make a big deal out of them. Gretchen Whitmer vowing to “fix the damn roads” or Trump characterizing some relatively mild changes to NAFTA as scrapping the whole thing strike me as two different kinds of examples of playing voters’ mixed feelings about this well.

Siddhartha Roychowdhury: You keep rejecting debates with FdB because you don’t like the format. Technically you had an interview with Mehedi, but why did you agree to that when you know that he’s a jackass and wouldn’t have a friendly conversation with you? You are argumentative in the written formats like X but you’re very polite in person and rarely become very confrontational in these scenarios. Do you regret doing that interview?

I’ve done a lot of podcasts with a lot of different hosts who I have a lot of different disagreements with, and honestly, I was taken aback by how hostile that interview was. I did not really think of my disagreements with Hasan as shouting across a huge political void. We both support the same candidate in the Michigan Senate race, for example, and while he was sharply critical of Kamala Harris’s approach to Gaza in 2024, he also argued that supporters of Palestine should vote for her and that Trump would be worse.

I am interested in trying to reach different audiences with my ideas, and I was not expecting to be treated as “the enemy” in that kind of way — very few podcasts operate on that format. I should have researched the show more thoroughly before agreeing to go on, and my advice to people in the future would be not to do it.

Share

Sasha Gusev: Some popular 80% policies end up failing (assault weapons ban) and some unpopular 20% policies end up being durable (bush tax cuts). What are some 80% policies Democrats should avoid and 20% policies they should take a hail mary on?

Just to set the table, I think 80-20 is an exaggeration here. I see a Gallup poll showing support for an assault weapons ban at 52-47 and the general idea of stricter gun laws at 56 percent.

But I think the Republican approach to taxes is instructive here. Conservative policy elites believe, very sincerely, that low taxes on the rich are very good for long-term economic growth even though taxing the rich is popular. They see the natural tendency of majoritarian institutions to promote redistribution as a major bug in democracy and see participation in a political movement that musters majoritarian sentiment on other issues in order to block majoritarian sentiment on redistribution as really good and morally praiseworthy. And they are really very focused on this point in two different ways:

  1. They pair tax cuts that they strongly believe in with other tax measures that they don’t think have a strong basis on the merits (think “no tax on tips”) in order to try to broaden the overall political appeal of their tax message.

  2. They are quite flexible on cultural issues, deploying opposition to same-sex marriage to great effect in 2004 but entirely dropping it by 2016 in order to prioritize their tax ideas.

Notably, “prioritize” in this sense is pretty literal. Republicans never vote to raise taxes on the rich, and every Republican Party trifecta votes to reduce taxes on the rich. On other topics, the policy agenda swings around quite a lot based on Republicans’ read of the policy environment. Prioritize does not mean “talking a lot about the issue.” It means that there is a rank ordering of policy priorities and low taxes on rich people is always near the top of that stack.

Democrats seem to me to really struggle with this prioritization concept. The tendency is to take whatever happens to be spiking in the news on any given week and treat it as a transcendent moral cause but then drop it three weeks later. I think it’s honestly pretty immature. But, just as an example of an unpopular stance I am glad Democrats are pretty stubborn about, voters love the idea of “work requirements” on social safety net programs, but these requirements generate a lot of hassle on vulnerable people and have very little upside in terms of getting more people working. Precisely because this stand is not popular, I don’t think it’s helpful to run around shouting from the rooftops about it, but it’s good that Democrats fight in the legislative trenches to try to stop it.

Daniel: It seems to me that two of your takes are in tension: on the one hand, that young workers should be ready to grind out the extra hours, and on the other hand, that Americans need to get out of the house more. The tension I see is that, back in your (and my) day, grinding out the hours was also a social activity. (Fun anecdote: I remember Deborah Liu telling FB moms and assorted future parents “we shouldn’t strive for work-life balance, but work-life integration”, causing her audience to freak out a bit. Fidji Simo followed that up by talking about how she flies her entire family with her whenever she travels for work to achieve this integration, which didn’t help to say the least.) While work-life integration was a viable approach in the 2000s and 2010s, today it means isolating yourself in front of your laptop talking to Zoom or to OpenRouter for 12 hours a day. What advice do you give to young people trying to navigate the noxiously antisocial workplace of 2026?

I am kind of skeptical about remote work in general, but it’s worth being clear that the vast majority of jobs are not done remotely because most people work providing in-person services. Even in the white collar zone, it’s not like every single workplace is 100 percent remote now. Most people who I know seem to work in “hybrid” workplaces with an expectation of two or three days in the office and where, to the best of my knowledge, you are allowed to come in on the other two or three days. Slow Boring operates on a “flexible” principle where the expectation is that you’ll come in, but it’s always okay to not come in if something is happening.

My advice to young people, in particular, would be to try to find a job that has people in the office. It is true that commuting is a hassle, but the solution to this is to prioritize finding an easy commute when looking for a place to live. Accept a smaller apartment or a worse neighborhood. Middle-aged parents face much more acute tradeoffs around home size, price, and school quality and also benefit more from extra time at home. But if you’re 24, prioritize finding a commute you can live with and show up and meet people.

Pat T: What do you envision being the near-to-mid term future of EVs in the US? Biden admin went big in on EVs, and with the incentives scrapped by Trump, sales have fallen. It doesn’t seem like something that Dems are willing to invest political capital in again when it isn’t popular with the general public, and especially because of Elon’s heavy involvement in the industry/propensity to benefit. But charging infrastructure is legitimately getting better, and the cars are generally pleasant to drive.

Could EVs turn the corner and become increasingly normalized, or will they continue being an unusual choice to make for most Americans?

You almost never hear about an electric vehicle owner switching back to internal combustion. E.V.s have a lot of desirable performance characteristics, and while Democrats (I hope) will not return to centering E.V.s in their policymaking, I assume they will adopt stricter fleetwide tailpipe emission rules that incentivize automakers to sell more E.V.s or plug-in hybrids.

The fundamental issue for E.V. adoption in the United States, though, remains the fact that gasoline is very cheap here. If the gas tax had been indexed to inflation in 1993 rather than raised in nominal terms and allowed to decline ever since, gasoline would be a lot more expensive. You would have marginally fewer people buying the kind of large trucks for which the electric options currently available aren’t very good and more people eager to save money by going electric even if it’s a hassle on road trips. Then greater E.V. adoption would naturally lead to more provision of charging and the balance of considerations would tilt more and more to the electric cars. As long as gas is structurally cheap, the fact that you can pour liquid into a tank faster than you can charge a battery remains a pretty solid feature for gas.

Share

Still, the balance tips one way or another. I think about the family across the alley that had a Tesla and installed one of those fast chargers in their parking area. They sold the house and moved out. The new people who moved in don’t have an electric car, but they didn’t un-install the fast charger (why would you), so whenever they buy their next car, the home charging infrastructure is already there for them, which is a little thumb on the scale of electrifying. You’ll see the incentive structure keep shifting in dribs and drabs toward electric. It seems like a good bet that batteries will improve faster than internal combustion engines, and as E.V. adoption rises, the political consensus in favor of defending cheap gas above all other considerations will start to wane.

Something I want environmentalists to consider about the bipartisan permitting-reform bill pending in Congress is that making electricity cheaper tilts the balance of considerations toward E.V.s and that even if the extra electricity is 100 percent generated by burning natural gas (which in practice it won’t be), burning methane in efficient combined-cycle turbines is much cleaner than burning gasoline in car engines.

Tom Hitchner: What would a consistent opposition to the idea of an “ethnostate” look like? Do you think opposition to ethnostates is a reasonable principle to uphold? You’ve defended Austria-Hungary as being arguably preferable to what followed; is that still relevant to world politics today? Or will “ethnostate” just be an ad hoc way of attacking Israel?

Like a lot of center-left diaspora Jews, I am of two minds about this. On the one hand, I think the general milieu of 19th-century European ethnic nationalism from which modern Zionism emerged was basically a bad idea that had a lot of bad consequences for a lot of people around the world. I am proud to be an American, and part of that pride is pride in our decidedly non-ethnic conception of citizenship.

That being said, if Israel decided to drop the Law of Return in favor of a new immigration concept centered on a points-based system emphasizing labor-market prospects, family ties to Israel, and Hebrew language ability, I don’t think that would transform international perceptions of Israel. Nor does anyone seem particularly upset by Japan having a special ethnic preference in immigration policy or the fact that both Egypt (the Arab Republic of Egypt) and Syria (the Syrian Arab Republic) have officially ethnic conceptions of national identity.

The difficulty for Jews like me is that Israel is frequently accused of things that it is, in fact, guilty of and that we don’t approve of but that lots of other countries are guilty of too and yet don’t seem to be treated nearly the same way. The “ethnostate” thing just seems like one on a long list of examples.

Farewell, my Captain

A TV character gave us a glimpse of what humanity might become.

Noah Smith
Oct 30
 
READ IN APP
 

“That is the exploration that awaits you. Not mapping stars and studying nebulae, but charting the unknowable possibilities of existence.” — Q

There’s something about the mindset of really hardcore Star Trek fans that’s very difficult to describe to people who don’t share that fandom. I can’t speak for all of us, of course, but for many of us, there is a sense in which the world portrayed in Star Trek is not quite fictional. No one regards it as an exact description of the future, of course, but there is a sense in which it represents one possible future that we must achieve — a “Star Trek timeline” that either we’re on or that we need to return to. The United Federation of Planets isn’t some fantastical interstellar alliance, but an organization that we must create, and whose ideals we must instantiate as the governing ethos of humankind.

Our quasi-religious commitment to this utopian future came from watching the Star Trek TV shows, but the different series inspired us in different ways. The original “Kirk and Spock” series, which aired in the 1960s, was more of a technological vision — the idea that one day we would zip around the cosmos getting into adventures, as easily as we’d zip around the world in a boat today. But Star Trek: The Next Generation, which aired in the late 1980s and early 1990s, gave us a different kind of vision. It was a moral future for the human race — a depiction of a better way that we could face the unknown and master our own personal challenges.

There has never been another television show like Star Trek: The Next Generation, and there might never be one again. It is the greatest TV show ever made, not by dint of a difference in degree, but because of a difference in kind. It is a drama of pure optimism. Every other show tries to thrill us by showing us how bad or how ridiculous or how exciting someone else’s world could be; Star Trek: TNG thrills us by showing us how beautiful our own world could become.

For such a show to be put on the air required an incredible confluence of coincidences. For one thing, it was syndicated in its first run, meaning that it was free from constant interference by network executives. The showrunner,¹ Michael Piller, also did something highly unusual when he opened the show up to outside script submissions; this allowed in a whole lot of highly innovative episode ideas.

But the real secret sauce of Star Trek: TNG was the creative vision of Star Trek’s original creator, Gene Roddenberry. A lot of people — and even a lot of science fiction writers — assume that even as technology makes us more powerful, human nature will remain basically the same, with all its old petty short-sighted hatreds and jealousies and selfishness and so on. Roddenberry believed otherwise. He famously declared that the people of the future would actually be better people, free from the flaws of his day. And so he mandated that Star Trek: TNG have no internal conflict in its plotlines.

Some of the writers chafed at that constraint. Interpersonal conflict is the bread and butter of drama — and always an easy plot device to fall back on when you need something to go wrong. But because Roddenberry decreed it, the writers of TNG were forced to envision how the ideal human being would deal with various personal and external obstacles. And so every episode gave us a thoughtful, probing exploration of what the ideal human beings — or at least, people much more morally and emotionally advanced than us — would look like.

No character embodied that ideal more than Captain Jean-Luc Picard. It’s not his personal life that’s ideal — he famously puts career over family, leading to a life full of self-doubt and regret — but his approach to the world. Picard is the ultimate Reasonable Man. He will always try to understand the alien before he opens fire. He is a legendary battle commander but would always rather negotiate than fight. He’s not necessarily the kind of man you’d want for a father, but he felt like one anyway. He values all life, and all uniqueness, intrinsically; he is zipping around the galaxy in a starship in order to discover the Universe, and occasionally to save it, but most of all to understand and respect it.

Understanding and respect, in fact, are Picard’s greatest weapons. He is a brilliant man, with many brilliant people under him, and occasionally he uses his intelligence to defeat an external threat. But he’s no swashbuckling space cowboy — more often than not, he succeeds in understanding the threat, and figures out how to help it achieve its goals without sacrificing his own. Picard realizes that the highest application of intelligence is not to thwart your enemies, but to design a world in which you and they can live in mutually beneficial coexistence. 1990s America was a uniquely hopeful and liberal time in the world, and Star Trek’s greatest captain embodied the spirit of that too-brief moment.

The character of Captain Picard was brought to life by the peerless acting skills of Patrick Stewart, who died two days ago at the age of 86. Stewart’s acting career went far beyond Star Trek — he’s widely considered one of the greatest Shakespearean stage actors of his generation, if not of all time, and he played in dozens of films. But the tributes that are flying thick and fast around the world today almost all focus on his role as Captain Picard.

I’m of two minds about this. As a very slightly famous person, I can tell you that public and private personas are very different things — if you meet me in real life, I won’t quite be the character you’ve imagined from my writings. That goes triple for actors, whose job is literally to pretend to be someone else. Patrick Stewart was not Captain Picard, but a man with a life and a personality all his own. He was, by all reports, a good man, well-loved by those who knew him and worked with him, but his strengths and his flaws were very different from those of the man he played on television. To mourn his passing as the passing of Captain Picard is to engage in a parasocial relationship.

And yet, I do. I can’t help it. I never knew Patrick Stewart, but I did know Captain Picard, and the death of the real man who brought that fictional man to life makes me remember what I loved so much about the latter, and there is value in that.

Nor am I alone. Today the internet is flooded with tributes to Picard, praising Stewart’s portrayal as an embodiment of an ideal liberal politics, an exemplary moral figure, and even as a model of masculinity:

The remembrance of Captain Picard comes at a pivotal moment for our species. The advent of artificial intelligence — machines that can out-think us — will naturally cause a shift in what it means to be human. As with the Industrial Revolution and the advent of agriculture, we will have to figure out a new way to live — new lifestyles, new forms of government, new systems of economic production and distribution, new reasons to value ourselves and each other.

There are many reasons that the particular future portrayed in Star Trek — one in which human beings, as they exist today, take the lead in physically exploring the galaxy — will never happen. AI is one more reason. This is in spite of the fact that Star Trek: The Next Generation is probably the single best prediction of modern AI ever to appear on the screen. The “engineers” on the Enterprise are clearly vibe-coding and prompting the ship’s computer,² which is so powerful that it sometimes accidentally creates human-level intelligence as part of a holographic entertainment program.

But in real life, the physical requirements of deep space exploration are such that it will never make sense for human beings to be at the forefront, except potentially as digital uploads. And even if we did go, AI’s superhuman intelligence, data assimilation capacity, and speed would remove most or all of the need for human judgement in the loop. If the Romulans attack us, it will be Claude or GPT who handles them.

But outer space is not our true final frontier. The true space that we, as humans, are exploring is our own set of possibilities. In fact, Q, a whimsical omnipotent trickster-god-being that serves as Picard’s foil throughout the series, says this to Picard in the final episode of the show — see the quote at the top of this post. It is our quest to chart the unknowable possibilities of our own existence.

The ultimate destiny of humankind is a consistent theme of Star Trek: TNG, and the show strongly implies that we’re ultimately destined to ascend to some sort of godlike posthumanity. There are multiple instances of humans or human-like beings turning into some sort of higher cosmic being, and Q himself implies that he’s testing humanity for admission into the realm of the space gods. This is probably where we’re headed in reality — our new AI scientists will help us figure out how to expand our consciousness and merge it with the digital realm, until we become something greater than we can currently imagine.

But before that happens — and perhaps even after it happens — it’s possible to envision a better version of Humanity Classic. It’s possible to imagine that through the right combination of technology, governance, and culture, we can put the lie to the old saw that “human nature never changes”, and become more like the characters in Gene Roddenberry’s universe.

In fact, though the overall picture is murky and the road has been stochastic, there is some evidence that we’ve already been moving in a more humane, rational direction — that Captain Picard is less alien to the human race of 2026 than he would have been to the human race of 1626. We once embraced slavery as a way of life; today we regard it as anathema. We once tortured cats to death in public for entertainment; today that would land you in prison. We are far less murderous than we once were.

It is not clear exactly what led to these improvements. Perhaps with scarcity alleviated — with our bellies full, and tractors instead of slaves — we are naturally gentler and more magnanimous. Perhaps more information has given us more empathy toward people far away. Perhaps the social adaptations needed to handle modern economies — markets, property rights, police, democracy — have tamed and civilized us.

Whatever it was, it offers the hope that we can do more of it — that whatever cosmic ascension we might eventually undertake, human beings as they exist in 2026 are not the best we can do in the current form factor.

I won’t lie. The last quarter century has been brutal to the hopes of those raised on Star Trek: The Next Generation. The promise of a liberal society has not been eliminated, but it has been tarnished by over a decade of social media hatred and rising authoritarianism. Neither greater prosperity nor more information nor giving voice to the voiceless has made our societies more like the United Federation of Planets. Sci-fi marvels are coming to life around us, but every day the people who lead our species seem less like the crew of the Enterprise.

But as the 1990s were not the end of history, neither are the 2020s. Moral progress is not a smooth upward line; there have been reversals before (and there certainly are plenty in the Star Trek timeline). It’s about time to pick ourselves back up and start the journey again. We should all go back and watch Star Trek: The Next Generation, with its silly haircuts and its dated special effects, and remember who we thought we could become.

Farewell to the great Patrick Stewart. And farewell also, Captain Picard. In the greatest trek of all — our search for the possibilities of our better selves — you will always be our Captain.
