The seven most important midterms of all time

A subjective — but objectively correct — list

Matthew Yglesias
Nov 2
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

Wanted to draw everyone’s attention to the Substack Midterms Hub which is going to have content from Slow Boring and many of this platform’s other fine outlets today, tomorrow, and beyond — a great place to go for updates, results, commentary, analysis and more.

One week before Election Day, Nate Silver’s model said that Democrats had a 76 percent chance of taking the Senate tomorrow, while Lakshya Jain’s model said they had a 65 percent chance.

I know the people who do this kind of work mostly focus on questions like “does this model give good gambling advice” and ignore metaphysical issues. But I’m always interested in what these claims really mean. Statistically speaking, to get enough power to reliably distinguish between these forecasts, you’d need to test them across 100 elections, which you obviously can’t do because this is a real-world event and not an experiment.

In other words, while we’ll soon know which party controls the Senate, we will never know which model was correct.

And the models themselves don’t clearly distinguish between claims about epistemic uncertainty (things we do not know about the underlying state of the electorate) and a more metaphysical uncertainty (the ability of events-to-come to shape the future). Almost nobody actually cares about this, but even as a devotee of quantitative models who consumes them heavily, I find something unsatisfactory about this.

So, with nothing more meaningful or satisfying to say about the events that will unfold this week, I thought it could be interesting to take a tour of some of the most significant midterm elections of American history.

Midterms lack the personalistic drama of American presidential elections, but outside of foreign policy, Congress really is the main driving force of the American constitutional system, and midterm votes often bring big changes. The phenomenon of “midterm backlash” is something we’re accustomed to, but while it now operates more or less as a law of the political system, it’s not an actual law of physics — whether any given backlash emerges is somewhat contingent and actually drives much of the drama of American politics.

So, with that in mind, here are my picks (in chronological order) for the seven most consequential midterm elections.

1826 — the first midterm brushback

The 1824 presidential election featured the breakdown of the Virginia dynasty dynamic that dominated the early American republic and a passing of the torch from the founding generation to a newer one. Part of that breakdown was that for the first time, there was a strong multi-candidate field, a basically non-party election, and an Electoral College deadlock that was resolved by the House of Representatives.

This is arguably how the Constitution was “supposed to” function in the minds of its authors.

John Quincy Adams got Henry Clay’s supporters to back him in the congressional vote, and then Clay became secretary of state in the Adams administration. This kind of thing happens in all kinds of democracies and is a very normal part of representative government.

But supporters of the defeated Andrew Jackson castigated it as a “corrupt bargain” and began the work of organizing the country’s first modern political party — the Democrats — to elect supporters of Jackson all across the country.

Heading into 1826, pro-Jackson forces already held a majority of Senate seats, and they gained another. They also picked up nine House seats (there were only 213 members at the time) and flipped control of the majority there. What’s especially noteworthy is that though Jacksonian political power was anchored in the South, the party organization was genuinely national — Martin Van Buren of New York was a key organizer, most of the Jacksonian midterm House gains came in upstate New York, and the 1826 Senate pickup was in Maine — and created a quasi-stable political order that lasted until the Civil War.

The actual policy stakes of these 1820s controversies are a little low by contemporary standards, but I think the 1826 midterms really set the pattern of how American institutions actually work in practice.

1862 — the Union prevails

If you’re familiar with the broad patterns of American politics, it’s not a big surprise that Abraham Lincoln’s Republican Party lost ground in the 1862 House elections.

Notably, though, they retained their majority and actually gained ground in the Senate. As a result, Lincoln and the Republicans were brushed back but fundamentally able to continue governing. Appropriations, appointments, and so forth could continue on a party-line basis, and Republicans were granted two more years to prosecute the war and make the case for Lincoln’s re-election.

This is sort of the inverse of 1826.

The election results themselves were not particularly dramatic, but the lack of massive backlash was very consequential. Indeed, the Lincoln administration’s policies end up becoming more radical: The Emancipation Proclamation came in January 1863 and General Order 143 organizing the United States Colored Troops came in May of that year.

1874 — the end of Reconstruction

As an alternate history fan, I get a lot of questions about the disputed presidential election of 1876, which was resolved on terms that put a stop to Union military involvement in the South and basically ended Reconstruction.

I think the smart take on this, though, is that Reconstruction was basically cooked by the huge rebuke dealt to the Grant administration in the 1874 midterms.

The sweeping Democratic gains — nine Senate seats and 92 House seats — were not necessarily because of opposition to Reconstruction. A lot was in the mix in this race, notably the financial Panic of 1873 and corruption. But the baseline question was whether a Democratic Party that had fully incorporated barely reformed traitors and rebels in its Southern wing could be acceptable to Northern public opinion.

You could easily imagine a world where the answer is not yes and the cross-sectional Democratic Party basically doesn’t get rebuilt.

But what we saw in the 1870s was that Northern white views on Reconstruction were mixed at best and that lots of Northern whites agreed with the basic idea that re-incorporating white Southern elites into the American political system was more important than securing the rights of loyal African American Southerners. The 1874 outcome not only made the logistics of Reconstruction hard to maintain but also fundamentally convinced Republican leaders that this was a loser of an issue for them.

1918 — Wilson repudiated

Woodrow Wilson’s second term was an odd duck. He was narrowly re-elected in 1916 on a pledge to keep the United States out of the Great War, but his Democrats lost seats in Congress and actually fell short of a majority in the House of Representatives. Despite Republicans winning more seats, though, Democrats retained control of the chamber via a coalition agreement with Progressive Party and socialist members.

By Election Day 1918, America had entered the war and the public was sick of the Democrats.

They lost 22 House seats, the Progressive Party was wiped out, and Republicans picked up six Senate seats and four governorships while a bunch of state-level prohibition initiatives passed. These results doomed Wilson’s hopes for the United States to enter the League of Nations and set the stage for Republican domination of the 1920s.

In some ways this is a typical “six-year itch” midterm — we normally see the president’s party do especially badly in the midterm elections of his second term. But I think it’s noteworthy because the dynamic whereby Wilson led America into the war, America won the war, and then America walked away from the victorious wartime leader’s preferred resolution was pretty odd.

It’s also hard not to note that the fighting ended basically a week after the election and to wonder if the results would have been different had Germany signed the armistice sooner.

I’m not sure that world history would, in fact, have turned out radically better had Democrats done better in 1918 and America joined the League of Nations. But F.D.R. and his Secretary of State Cordell Hull and many other New Deal figures definitely believed that, and it played an important role in their thinking about the United Nations.

1938 — the failed purge

This was in some respects another typical “six-year itch” midterm where Republicans gained eight Senate seats, 81 House seats, and a staggering 12 governorships amidst a fairly broad-based backlash to the Roosevelt administration.

On the other hand, this still left Democrats with large majorities in both houses of Congress. Just on the numbers, it superficially looks like a replay of 1862, where what’s really significant isn’t the losses but Democrats’ ability to retain control.

The real story of this midterm, though, and what makes it unique, isn’t in the general elections but the primaries.

F.D.R. was frustrated by the number of conservative Democrats, especially from the South, who were blocking some of his New Deal program ideas despite his willingness to go along with Jim Crow — a willingness that extended to being unwilling to even verbally endorse an anti-lynching bill.

Roosevelt decided to dedicate a fireside chat to the need to defeat obstructionist Democrats in primaries, and he actively campaigned against several incumbent Democratic Party senators.

This attempted purge basically backfired. Almost everyone he targeted won re-election, and having been targeted only made them angrier at the White House. The fact that the purge was tried and failed emboldened other Southern Democrats who had some misgivings about the administration to defy it. In effect, a bipartisan “conservative coalition” took control of Congress in these midterms and mostly held on until Lyndon Johnson’s presidency.

But this midterm became mega-consequential beyond even those particulars simply because it established a strong bit of conventional wisdom that it was unproductive for a sitting president to publicly pressure same-party members of Congress in this way. Donald Trump successfully taking out John Cornyn and Bill Cassidy in primaries is so striking in part because it repudiates the lessons of 1938.

1994 — the birth of the modern House

Republicans gained a lot of seats in 1994 in a way that basically sealed the fate of the more progressive strands of Bill Clinton’s thinking.

What’s more important here, though, is that Republicans disrupted 40 straight years of Democratic House control.

For most of the post-New Deal period, the real question in the House was whether you’d have the aforementioned bipartisan conservative majority. The Reagan Revolution of 1981-82, for example, happened during a period of Democratic control of the House. But conservative “Boll Weevil” Democrats demanded that Tip O’Neill allow votes on Reaganite measures that split the caucus and often joined with Republicans to pass them. At other times, like during the Great Society or the late Nixon/Ford years, progressive majorities in Congress passed liberal bills. Republicans actually winning the majority fundamentally shifted how Congress operates toward a more parliamentary dynamic. The minority party now works relentlessly to try to win the majority, and the majority party exerts ruthless control over the floor.

Everything modern observers know about “how Congress works” is downstream of tactics Newt Gingrich used to win control in 1994, of the fact that they worked, and of how he chose to wield power after winning it.

Subscribed

2014 — the one I’m personally mad about

This election still upsets me whenever I think about it. Democrats lost nine Senate seats, some of them extremely closely, and hanging over the whole thing was an insane media panic about Ebola that vanished immediately after the story had done its necessary work for the G.O.P.

I think conservatives have lodged some valid complaints against liberal media bias over the years, but the way this midterm was handled, the coverage of Hillary Clinton’s emails, and the monstering of Joe Biden over ending the war in Afghanistan are the three huge counterexamples.

And precisely because the mainstream press does tend to have a liberal ideological inflection, negative coverage hurts Democrats way more than it hurts Republicans because soft Democratic voters care a lot about mainstream press coverage.

There was all this mockery of Mark Udall for constantly warning people that control of the Supreme Court and the future of Roe v. Wade could be at stake in the election, and he was 100 percent right. When I asked Claude if this one belonged on my list of the seven most important midterm elections, it told me no, that the only real stakes were the judiciary and that 1986 was very similar in that regard. Just so you all know that this is a human-written column, I rejected that bit of feedback. That year was a blip that turned out to be consequential for the Robert Bork nomination; 2014 eliminated the moderate wing of the Democratic Party.

We’re now having a refounding moment for Common Sense Democrats, but today’s reborn moderates are clearly in the tradition of Barack Obama rather than that of the old-time “to the right of Obama” moderates who had their last stand in 2014.

Honorable mentions

A lot of people talk about the 1974 Watergate midterm, which was certainly important in the sense that a lot of prominent 1980s and 1990s Democrats got their start in 1974. But I don’t actually think that crop of late-1970s Democratic majorities accomplished much that was interesting or noteworthy.

The 1810 midterms saw Henry Clay win his first congressional race and then get elected speaker as a freshman (a weird occurrence), and he was then an influential spokesperson on behalf of going to war with Britain. But I don’t really think the War of 1812 was consequential in the long term, and while Clay was a very important historical figure, I don’t really think that initial two years in the House was the important part of his legacy.

The 2006 midterms will always have a special place in my heart because I was there for them, but I think in the grand scheme of things, they’re a pretty standard-issue “six-year itch” story.

The 1866 midterms that delivered a decisive anti-Johnson majority in Congress and led to his impeachment are a cool story, but since he ultimately wasn’t removed from office, I think the significance is somewhat limited.

The 1998 and 2002 midterms that broke the pattern of the president’s party losing ground are both interesting, especially since they happened so close together. But I don’t think anything particularly huge happened as a result of them, and it really is just a coincidence that they occurred one after the other — it didn’t actually represent a departure from the historic pattern.

It’s also interesting to go way back to 1798, when John Adams’s Federalists gained seats in the midterms. But of course that was not exactly the wave of the future — the party lost the presidency in 1800 and eventually disappeared.

So, conceding that 2014 is a bit of an idiosyncratic choice, that’s where I stand. And we’ll see what happens tomorrow.

Moment of Truth

Can we still save America’s soul?

Paul Krugman
Nov 3
 
READ IN APP
 

If the stakes were lower, tonight wouldn’t be too stressful. The polls, expert analyses, and the prediction markets all say that Dems have a lock on the House and around an 80 percent chance of taking the Senate.

But since the very idea of America is on the line, I’m as nervous as everyone else. Talking about what the election means and what Democrats should do feels like jinxing at this point.

I’m finding this stripped-down version of the Battle Hymn of the Republic, recalling another time the nation’s soul was on the line, somehow appropriate.

What not to watch tonight

Avoid the most common election night fallacies with these simple strategies

Matthew Yglesias
Nov 3
 
READ IN APP
 

A quick reminder that the Substack Midterms Hub is up and running and full of content from Slow Boring and many of this platform’s other fine outlets today — it’s a great place to go for updates, results, commentary, analysis and more.

The fact that the outcomes of the midterm elections are not knowable in advance is a real challenge for editorial planning.

I’ve been asking if they’ll just tell me who wins under embargo so that I can plan things out, but everyone I ask insists that they can’t actually forecast the future. At best, well-informed people give me sophisticated takes about which early outcomes they’ll be looking at as indicators of the national mood.

For example, a strong performance for Democratic House candidates in the Miami area is probably good news for the Democratic House candidates in South Texas, according to one friend who believes that Latino subgroups differ more in their baseline partisan preferences than in how their voting patterns shift from election to election.

Other qualified professionals, however, say that’s wrong and heterogeneity is understated — so even here we’ll need to count the actual votes. Disappointing!

That being said, I’ve been doing this long enough that I’ve seen pundits make certain kinds of predictable election night errors cycle after cycle. These analytic errors are largely inherent to the geography of the United States of America and the state-by-state variation in voting patterns, both of which change at a slow enough pace that we can be pretty confident that we’ll see these mistakes in 2026, just as we did in 2022 and 2018.

So here’s my exclusive Slow Boring guide to what not to watch for in tonight’s results.

Subscribed

Demographic analysis based on exit polls

This one is huge. A fundamental challenge of polling is that survey response rates vary by demographic subgroup, so if you just naively put a survey out in the field, you’ll get a skewed sample.

If you’re trying to get a poll that tells you something about all American adults or all registered voters, you can fix this with demographic weights (the Census Bureau will just tell you what share of the population is white or over 65 or another variable of interest).

You still need to be a little bit careful. There are lots of questions about exactly which demographics matter and how to weight them. You can pretty easily make sure you have enough Latinos in your sample, but are you only getting English-dominant Latinos when you need Spanish-dominant ones? Do you have the right balance of Cubans vs. Puerto Ricans vs. South Americans in your Florida poll? It’s a hard business. But it is possible.

Polling likely voters is harder, though, because you don’t actually know who will vote. But you can at least develop an explicit model explaining how you’re defining the likely electorate.

The exit poll is a real problem, however, because you do know the election result but you do not know who voted.

It’s the opposite of an all-adults poll where you know what the demographic composition of the population is but are trying to find out who they voted for. Since the exit poll is just kind of guessing what the electorate looked like, it is spectacularly unsuited for the problem of figuring out the behavior of different demographic subgroups. Suppose Black turnout unexpectedly craters in Georgia and causes Jon Ossoff to lose his re-election bid. The exit pollsters will know that Ossoff lost but won’t know about the turnout crash. They’ll weight their survey to the outcome they know and to the electorate they were expecting and end up giving Ossoff too little support among both Black and white voters because they don’t realize that what actually happened is few Black voters showed up.

Months later, Census and voter file information will come out about who actually voted, but by then the narratives are baked.

In the immediate aftermath of an election, the best way to obtain demographic information is (unfortunately) to commit the ecological fallacy. If Democrats really overperform in the most heavily Asian precincts in America, that is decent evidence of a Democratic surge in Asian support perhaps driven by backlash to “The Indian Question” right. Stat-heads will point out that this is not a fully valid inference. Most Asian Americans do not live in heavily Asian precincts, and lots of non-Asian people do live in heavily Asian precincts. But it really is the best we can do since the exit polls are a mess.

Who wins the first races

The polls close really early in Kentucky.

Kentucky is obviously not a swing state. But there is one House district in Kentucky that is kinda sorta maybe, if you squint at it, competitive, largely due to the fact that Democrats have a seemingly good recruit in Zach Dembo. Dembo is on the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee’s official “red to blue” list, and he’s also a Blue Dog PAC endorsee.

That being said, when you look at the demographics and partisan composition of this district, I don’t totally understand how it got to be red to blue.

Or, rather, I think you have to understand this as in part about the fact that there’s an incentive to not permanently write off whole states. Kentucky has a Democratic governor and a lot of people like Andy Beshear. You want guys like Dembo who have strong bios to feel they’ll be supported if they take a crack at longshot races. I think when it comes to long-term party building, investing in races like this is the correct call. But I also think the conjunction of the investments with the polls closing at 6:00 p.m. Eastern generates a maybe higher level of awareness of this one district than it actually merits. Even in a D+9 national environment, it’s a real stretch. Dembo will probably lose, and there’s no real significance in that.

The national popular vote

Speaking of the D+9 national environment, any analysis of an individual race needs to be contextualized in terms of the overall national vote.

If a guy like Dembo loses a district like that by one point in a D+9 environment, that’s a good race. If he loses by one in what’s actually a D+11 environment, that’s less impressive for him but better for Democrats overall. If he loses by one in what’s actually a D+7 national environment, that’s very impressive for him but means that Democrats are underperforming their polling.

Unfortunately, though, we’re not really going to know anything about the national popular vote tonight. It’s not just that we’re not going to know when the polls close in Kentucky at 6:00 p.m. We’re still not going to know tomorrow morning.

The problem here is California.

California accepts mail ballots that are sent by Election Day, which means that many ballots will not arrive until days after post-election takes have been written. This mail situation reflects an understandable impulse to make it easy for people to vote, but California compounds the delay by counting the actual votes slowly. They keep getting away with this because California is not a swing state and everyone knows Democrats are going to win the big races there. But something like 12 percent of Americans — and a much larger share of Democrats — live in California, so the slow counting of California votes meaningfully distorts our understanding of the national political climate.

We’re going to know how Sherrod Brown and Abdul El-Sayed and Josh Turek and Roy Cooper and James Talarico did before we know what the national popular vote was.

What we do know is that the popular vote in California will be way bluer than the national average, so whatever the national climate looks like tonight, the reality will be bluer than that. This then means that in the short term, every individual Democratic candidate in the South, Midwest, and Northeast will look more impressive relative to the national climate than they actually were.

The races that happen to be called first

Florida is on the East Coast, its polls close early, and it counts votes fast. Also, back in 2018, Florida moved considerably to the right relative to the national average, meaning that Republicans did well in Florida’s elections that year. This led to an early evening narrative about Democrats’ disappointing performance and the forecasted “blue wave” failing to materialize.

In fact, the 2018 polls were extremely accurate, and the overall national wave was exactly what had been forecasted.

Subscribed

Polling is never perfectly accurate, but on the whole, 2018 was probably the single most accurately polled election year of my career. It just happened to be the case that Republicans did well in one state where the votes were counted early in primetime.

In retrospect, I built a lot of my worldview around the opinion that the 2018 midterm result was sneakily bad for Democrats. After all, they lost Senate seats. These losses happened in deep red states, so at the time a disappointing performance was chalked up to a “bad map.” But the 2026 map is also bad and the 2028 map will also be bad. Basically all the Senate maps are bad, so you can’t grade Democratic electoral performance in any given cycle on a curve. They either win (as I hope they will tonight) or they lose (as they did in 2018).

The practical upshot of the 2018 election was that Trump was able to keep governing the country, and I’m very concerned that a “good night” for Democrats in 2026 isn’t good enough — they need the Senate. But to that point, we won’t really know whether Democrats have a good enough night until we know what happened in Alaska, which happens to be in an inconvenient time zone for those of us on the East Coast.

What you should watch instead

Instead of falling prey to nonsense and fallacies, what you really ought to do is join the election night watch party that Slow Boring, The Argument, Silver Bulletin, and GD Politics are collaborating on. We’ll be liveblogging plus live on video for many, many hours, and we’ll have guests and accurate quantitative insights and good takes!

Normal Americans punished MAGA

Normies exist, and there’s only so far you can push them before they get mad.

Noah Smith
Nov 4
 
READ IN APP
 

The MAGA people appear to have been laboring under a number of delusions.

First, they seem to be genuinely surprised by the fact that they suffered a crushing defeat in the midterm elections. In fact, polls, forecasts, and prediction markets had all been calling a Democratic victory for months now. But a lot of MAGA types appear to have believed that America always has some big hidden reservoir of shy Trump supporters out there that everyone always misses, and that this silent majority would ride to the GOP’s rescue and prove all the pollsters and forecasters wrong, as they did in 2016.

To put it mildly, that did not happen. The election night surprise actually favored the Democrats, who won a far more extensive and decisive victory than almost any of the pollsters and forecasters had anticipated.

@RonDeSantis
Dems will get 55 Senate seats and 250+ House seats. Looking at the Senate map and considering such a massive House margin, it is very unlikely Republicans will recapture the Congress in 2028. Might not have a shot at Senate control until 2032.

The 2010 margin was 6.8 points, an election remembered as a generational wipeout. Tonight is expected to almost double that. 2008 was 10.5 and 2006 was 8.0. A thirteen point win would be the biggest congressional margin in fifty years.

Even Trump’s traditional demographic support base — white voters without a college degree — abandoned the GOP in droves this time:

Hunter📈🌈📊
@StatisticUrban
Non-college white voters, theoretically THE bread and butter, the special sauce, of MAGA, shifted sharply towards Democrats in virtually every state tonight.

Trump could try to challenge this electoral verdict — to cry that the vote was rigged, to declare a state of emergency and suspend the Constitution, to abuse the powers of the presidency to nullify the popular will. But my gut says that he won’t, and here’s an important reason why:

Peter Hamby
@PeterHamby
Democrats won young white men tonight by 17 points, per CNN exits Trump won them *28 points* in 2024
5:24 AM · Nov 4, 2026 · 490K Views
113 Replies · 598 Reposts · 5.66K Likes

As long as the MAGA people could tell themselves that Trump’s opponents were a bunch of old people and women, they could fantasize about prevailing in the street confrontation that would erupt in the wake of an autogolpe. But if young men — and especially young white men — aren’t on Trump’s side, then starting some sort of civil war would likely not go well for MAGA.

Anyway, as of this writing, here’s what the Senate election map looks like:

Kansas is colored blue. So is South Carolina. So is Iowa. Mississippi will probably end up blue as well.

And most of all, Texas is blue. Not just the Senate race, either — the GOP governor, Greg Abbott, has been unseated by Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa. Bo French, who tweeted alarm at seeing Indian American football fans at a University of Texas game two months ago, lost his bid for Texas Railroad Commissioner to Democrat Jon Rosenthal.

The fall of Red Texas is an epochal, era-defining event. Growing up in Texas, I saw Dems win statewide office occasionally, but these were always old-school conservative Southern Democrat types. Yesterday’s election saw Gina Hinojosa and James Talarico, both staunch progressives, win the governorship and one of the Senate seats. In fact, the only Republican now holding a statewide office is…Ted Cruz.

How did that happen? Part of it was bad candidate selection — MAGA primary voters tossed out the popular mainstream Republican Senator John Cornyn for not being slavishly loyal enough to Trump, and replaced him with Ken Paxton, a man who has been repeatedly indicted and investigated for financial crimes and corruption. But Abbott was a popular, mainstream Republican incumbent governor with a strong economic track record, and he still lost to a progressive upstart challenger.

Rightists were simply unprepared for a world in which this was possible. Here was Jonathan Keeperman, whom I recently debated about Indian immigration, just yesterday:¹

Jonathan Keeperman
@L0m3z
What model of the American electorate has Texas voting for a guy who says God is trans? Someone steelman this for me. I’m having trouble getting there.
1:38 AM · Nov 3, 2026 · 331K Views

The only possible interpretation of this huge wave election is that it was a referendum on Donald Trump. Trump is now among the least popular presidents in living memory, rivaled only by George W. Bush at the end of his presidency. I wrote about why most Americans despise Trump, and my analysis hasn’t really changed:

The second Trump presidency is a world-historic failure

Noah Smith
·
Oct 3
Read full story

Trump was elected to tame inflation, but he raised taxes on almost everything Americans buy from overseas, and raised gas prices by attacking Iran. When people complained about the cost of living, he told them to buy their daughters fewer dolls. Trump was elected to stay out of Middle Eastern wars, but he plunged us into an expensive quagmire. He has relentlessly promoted the interests of Vladimir Putin, whom normal Americans hate with a passion. His antics — threatening to invade Greenland, trying to bully people into renaming the Gulf of Mexico, Lake Ontario, and artificial intelligence, and so on — seem dangerously unhinged.

Then there’s the corruption. Trump has relentlessly looted the country to fatten the pockets of himself, his family, and his close political allies:

The American people noticed. This is from last week:

Voters are now more concerned about government corruption than any other issue, including high grocery and gas prices, according to the final CNBC All-America Economic Survey before the Nov. 3 midterm election…[T]he results nevertheless align with other recent polls showing corruption has shot to the top of voters’ list of pressing worries…A Fox News poll published last week found 60% of registered voters are extremely concerned about government corruption, surpassing concerns about inflation and high prices. A Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll released Sunday found some two-thirds of respondents think Trump is using the presidency to enrich himself, up 10 percentage points since September 2025. Gallup recently found perceptions of government corruption in the U.S. have hit multi-decade highs. And an August poll from Reuters/Ipsos found nearly 7 in 10 Americans believe Trump’s businesses influence his presidential decisions.

And here’s their chart:

Republicans seemed to somehow labor under the delusion that regular Americans were going to just ignore all this. Perhaps they thought that Trump’s charisma, which allowed him to bounce back from the January 6th coup attempt, made him invincible. It’s possible they reasoned that Americans had simply become so jaded about corruption that they would ignore dozens of scandals that each would have ended any other presidency. Perhaps they believed that no matter how bad Trump got, Americans’ dislike of woke culture and progressive governance would always make the Republicans the lesser of two evils.

Maybe they believed that Americans never really cared about inflation in 2024, and that worries about the cost of living were just people’s way of expressing their worries about immigration and wokeness. Or maybe they believed America would blame Dems for the assassination of Charlie Kirk, and reject them at the ballot box accordingly. Perhaps they thought they could scare Americans away from the Democrats by calling them “communists” and screaming about “Western civilization”:

Matt Walsh
@MattWalshBlog
I am not here to tell you that Republicans have done a wonderful job. I am here to tell you that the Democrat Party has been fully captured by communists who want you dead and seek to destroy western civilization itself. Go vote against them. It’s the only choice.
6:31 PM · Nov 3, 2026 · 2.53M Views
7.4K Replies · 7.47K Reposts · 61.7K Likes

This was MAGA’s greatest delusion — the idea that the average American sees things similarly to the rightists on X. The truth is that the average American does not see “Western civilization” as a fortress under siege. The average American does not spend all day in a state of panic that brown immigrants and their children are invaders bent on subjugating the white race.

One gets the sense that the MAGA people believed that the average American doesn’t even exist. For decades, ideologues and extremists in both parties have shouted — often in direct contradiction of the evidence — that swing voters don’t exist, that polarization rules everything, that moderation and appealing to the center are useless, and that electoral victory goes to whichever party mobilizes their base to come out and vote.

That was always probably wrong, but MAGA seems to have taken this flawed logic one step further, convincing themselves that the country consists only of “the left” and “the right” — that every voter is either a blue-haired trans communist or a chisel-jawed defender of Western Civilization who spends all day posting memes on X about gender-swapped Draco Malfoy. If you have no idea what the heck gender-swapped Draco Malfoy is, or why on Earth anyone would think it’s politically important, rest assured that you’re not alone.

Texas and Kansas and South Carolina have been turned blue by a coalition of voters who aggressively, emphatically neither know nor care about gender-swapped Draco Malfoy, or Anakin Skywalker memes, or any of the other nonsense that bounces around the rightist echo chambers on X and 4chan. It was a coalition that never read Elon’s never-ending stream of tweets about James Talarico wanting to “trans your kids and destroy the border”. It was a coalition that does not know or care whether it’s white French people or brown French people burning down Paris this week.

It turns out that normal Americans do exist — in great numbers, in fact. It’s possible to keep them divided with relentless partisanship. It’s possible to drive them to jaded apathy with relentless he-said-she-said accusations and manufactured scandals. It’s possible to get many of them to stay home on election nights, simply by ignoring their wishes for long enough. But if you push them hard enough — if you step on their face again and again, with corruption and mismanagement and disdain for their daily struggles — they will eventually bestir themselves and rise up and smack you down. They will remind you of who won the Second World War, and why.

So the Democrats, ideologically divided as they are, took a well-deserved victory. The risk now is that they don’t learn their lesson from watching Trump’s implosion. Just as MAGA convinced themselves that the average American was a meme-spouting rightist, Democrats might marinate in their own echo chambers, egged on by leftist activists and progressive pressure groups and Bluesky cancel-culture warriors.

Democrats might convince themselves that what Americans really care about is Palestine rather than the cost of living. They might embark on a borrowing binge in order to throw more money at health care, resulting in rising interest rates and rising prices. They might try to halt inflation with price controls, with predictably terrible results. They might spend their political capital on billionaire taxes of the type that California’s electorate just rejected. They might forget the lessons of 2024 and try to admit as many illegal asylum-seekers as possible.

And if so, I’ll be writing another version of this post in 2030 or 2034, explaining why a Democratic president got hit with a red wave in the midterms.

It Wasn’t (Just) the Economy, Stupid

2024 was a blip. This was America.

Paul Krugman
Nov 4
 
READ IN APP
 

What happened last night was no ordinary election. It was a mass affirmation that most Americans still believe in our nation’s basic values, and a mass rejection of a movement that wants to destroy everything our nation stands for. And no, it wasn’t just economic dissatisfaction.

Yes, Trumpflation created by tariffs and the Iran debacle helped. But an election swung by public anger over high prices looks like 2024, when Trump won the popular vote by 1.5 percentage points. Last night Democrats appear to have won the popular vote by 13 -14 percentage points.

What drove this amazing victory? Hispanic voters, who swung to Trump in 2024 in the naïve belief that he would bring prices down, turned massively against a regime that is arresting, imprisoning and deporting their friends and families. Blacks turned out in droves against a transparently racist party that is trying to take away their voting rights. Americans of every kind were repelled by the administration’s cruelty and its rampant, brazen corruption.

After 2024, large swathes of the elite rushed to prostrate themselves before Trump, somehow convincing themselves that the narrow defeat of Democrats in a year when incumbent parties were defeated almost everywhere heralded a permanent transformation of U.S. politics, that corrupt authoritarians peddling hate would rule forever. There’s a lot to be written about why oligarchs in particular were so willing to believe that small-d democratic values were a thing of the past — and one of the main things big-D Democrats need to do now is hold not just Trump’s officials, but also his enablers, accountable. But that’s a topic for another day.

The main point for now is that MAGA took 2024 as proof that Americans want fascism, and acted on that premise. But tens of millions of Americans in effect said, no, that is not what we want. That is not who we are.

The damage done over the last two years is incredible, and I don’t know how much of it can ever be repaired. But there is, at last, hope. For last night America showed that it is still America.

Seventeen thoughts on an epic repudiation of Donald Trump

We did it!

Matthew Yglesias
Nov 4
 
READ IN APP
 

  1. I’ve been saying for two years that the most important thing in American politics by far is Democrats finding a way to win a Senate majority, and Democrats found a way to win a Senate majority. That’s the most important thing here.

  2. A huge House majority is also nice! The hard left was semi-openly hoping for a narrow majority that would allow a dozen or so members to hold Hakeem Jeffries’ speakership hostage to various demands. It now seems like there will be a very comfortable majority that will avoid that.

  3. Beyond Congress, Democrats sweeping statewide elections in Texas seems huge. I assume Gina Hinojosa is going to become a huge star. Business people seem semi-panicked that she’s going to bring Texas’ data center boom to a halt, though it’s not clear to me how true that actually is.

  4. A number of people told me that they thought a huge Democratic landslide would kill the caucus’ appetite for doing a bipartisan permitting deal. I hope Democrats think harder about that. You can’t win a huge landslide on the back of an affordability message and then immediately abandon a bipartisan affordability bill.

  5. Our Slow Boring slate did great! Bobby Pulido and Johnny Garcia are part of the Texas sweep. Don Davis, Manny Rutinel, and Lindsay James won. Keisha Lance Bottoms and Anita Earls won. And, of course, Josh Turek won. Bale Dalton, sadly, fell short but came very, very close. Thank you to everyone who helped.

  6. Candidate quality matters! Obviously the gaps you see between good candidates and bad ones are modest in scale compared to the huge swing in the national political environment between 2024 and 2026. But if you look at how Peggy Flanagan performed in Minnesota, it’s clear she would have lost in Iowa or Kansas.

  7. Conversely, despite intensive coverage of Haley Stevens endorsing Mike Rogers, there is zero evidence that this mattered — Abdul El-Sayed won very comfortably in a Democratic landslide year. Nobody particularly cares about Stevens, and there are very few single-issue pro-Israel voters in America — especially at a time when Israel played a key role in getting America embroiled in a toxically unpopular war.

  8. At the same time, Josh Shapiro thrashing his opponent so badly that the whole Pennsylvania governor race wasn’t even covered at all calls into question how many people really care about this issue from the other side either.

  9. The real ideological fuckup was in ME-2, the only House seat that flipped from blue to red, where Democrats replaced Jared Golden with Bernie-endorsed Matt Dunlap, who lost despite a huge blue wave.

  10. The only three Republicans I’m aware of who put up impressive electoral performances were Susan Collins (who lost anyway) and the Republican governors of New Hampshire and Vermont. These two aren’t charismatic dynamos and voters aren’t rewarding them for delivering sweeping change — people just kinda like do-nothing governors.

  11. In that vein, I expect Bottoms and Hinojosa to end up being pretty popular once in office because they’ll be checked by Republican state legislatures, and I think one or both of them may end up becoming major national political stars.

  12. A friend texted me at 11:23PM: “New concern is we won by too much.” And I do see where that’s coming from. How much of Democrats’ margin was provided purely by Donald Trump blundering into a war with Iran that spiked gas prices? You don’t want to get complacent given that Democrats can’t just count on that happening again in 2028.

  13. I want to push back, though, against the view that Democrats didn’t actually change anything and only got lucky. The things some of the key candidates said about fossil fuel production, girls’ sports teams, and even immigration — notably including some strong remarks from El-Sayed — would have been unthinkable in the 2024 or 2022 cycles. It’s important to keep these changes in mind, because Democrats are going to need to stick with their new, better messages if they want to win in the future.

    Subscribed

  14. The most interesting failure of the cycle is Dan Osborne in Nebraska. He overperformed by a large amount in the bleak national political climate of 2024 and in principle should have won given the scale of the national swing. It seems to me that in the intervening two years, he lost a lot of his independent brand and also stopped emphasizing his conservative views on immigration.

  15. In Montana, an effort to replicate the success of Osborne 2024 ended up backfiring and making the race unwinnable for Democrats by splitting the vote. In Alaska, the “find another guy named Dan Sullivan” tactic also seems to have backfired. By contrast, having moderates win the primaries in Kansas and Iowa was hard work, but it turned out to be totally doable. I think Democrats should focus less on gimmicks and more on simply doing the work of trying to have good candidates win primaries.

  16. Is this going to be, in some sense, the end of the Trump Era? I hope so! There’s also something sort of bleak about the fact that if the Trump Era ends, it will have ended because of moderately high gasoline prices rather than January 6. But you’ve got to take the opportunities that life hands you.

  17. It’s a great day for America.

The way forward

How to build on commonsense gains and drive a stake through the heart of MAGA

Matthew Yglesias
Nov 4
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

If you’re looking for my initial takeaways from last night’s unprecedented midterms, check out my post from this morning — it’s free for all to read. This longer, more detailed analysis is for Slow Boring’s paid subscribers. Paid subscribers also have a few more hours to submit questions for Friday’s midterms Mailbag. Get them in by 3 p.m. Eastern!

Subscribed

In some ways, pessimism is a frequent rhetorical register of Slow Boring and has been since its inception. I’m the one warning people that the Senate map doesn’t get any kinder after 2026, that the median voter in Iowa doesn’t share the concerns of the median Bluesky poster, and that state elections are a constant reminder that public appetite for sweeping change is actually quite limited.

But what I want the dominant register to be is actually something different: agency.

I want everyone reading to see that the choices made by politicians, staffers, aligned nonprofits, and even highly engaged citizens who pay for subscription newsletters or post about politics online make a difference. That politics isn’t just about “vibes” or vertical video skills or superficial rhetorical choices.

And I think this is truly what we’ve seen over the past two years.

The exact same country that delivered a real mandate to Donald Trump in 2024 — a mandate to secure the border and bring down inflation — turned sharply against him because he utterly failed to bring down inflation and embarked on an alarming orgy of corruption. Those choices set the table for a plausible Democratic Senate majority despite the map, and then Democrats ran very good candidates in a lot of key races.

In Texas and Kansas, strong Democratic candidates ran against bad Republican candidates and crazy things happened. Florida is not, in principle, less winnable than Texas, but the Florida G.O.P. put up reasonable candidates and Democrats did not have a Josh Turek or an Annie Andrews in the Florida Senate race. It turns out that in the right circumstances, even South Carolina can be on the map.

But note that part of winning in South Carolina was that Andrews had to align with public opinion on women’s sports teams. Progressives seem to have been happy with James Talarico, and I am happy for them, but he pulled off a win by campaigning for the kind of all-of-the-above energy strategy that post-Obama Democrats abandoned and Slow Boring has argued they should bring back.

The key to carrying all this momentum forward is to remember — and to remind people — that good things don’t just happen because of small-dollar fundraising or campaign gimmicks.

What candidates say they’ll do in office matters, and what they actually do matters even more.

In the context of 2026, that meant Trump’s broken promises were the most important factors in this election. In the context of 2028, his choices will continue to matter but so will the choices of the newly empowered Democratic majority. If they make smart choices, they can spend the next two years putting the boot on the neck of MAGA and the four after that restoring the country’s confidence in Democrats.

If they get sloppy, lazy, or undisciplined, we’ve seen over and over again that large electoral swings are very real and they happen in both directions.

But if the kinds of people who won these tough races dig in and make sure the right lessons are learned and the right momentum is carried forward, we can transform the party, and the country, for the better.

Winning the narrative and the transition

Back in 2018, moderate Democrats flipped critical House seats and gave Democrats a majority. But a handful of left-wing primary winners in deep-blue districts — the Squad — managed to make themselves the story of the midterm.

Common Sense Democrats as a community need to do a better job this time around of focusing on the people who won the tough races and put up the most impressive performances.

A Common Sense Democrat manifesto

Matthew Yglesias
·
November 12, 2024

Years ago, I coined a phrase — the pundit’s fallacy — to describe the belief that to win elections, a political party needs to cater to the exact views of the pundit writing the column.

Read full story

Roy Cooper and Josh Shapiro attracted very little media attention over the course of 2026 because their races were blowouts and their prior electoral performance suggested the outcomes were never really in doubt. I get why “dog bites man” stories get ignored, but looking back over the results, winning by such crushing margins is actually really interesting and we should learn from those candidates — just as we should learn from the top Republican performers like Kelly Ayotte and Phil Scott. If even voters in Vermont prefer a moderate Republican check on a progressive legislature, what does that say about the national public’s appetite for sweeping left-wing policy?

Ballot initiatives also give us a sense of the public’s moderate preferences on policy. A women’s sports referendum that was written in a sloppy and draconian way (I wouldn’t have voted for it) looks set to pass in Washington state, and a wealth tax initiative failed in California. These are very blue states — and even many of those voters have significant doubts about major aspects of the progressive policy agenda on both economic and cultural issues. Abdul El-Sayed’s story is inspiring to a lot of people, and his win represents a triumph of good sense in the face of Islamophobia and the ongoing financial might of AIPAC, but it’s also true that an A.E.S.-like performance would not have delivered the win in Iowa or Alaska or Kansas or South Carolina.

On our election night livestream, Nate Silver told me that nobody will care about these small distinctions in candidate quality in the face of a massive Democratic sweep.

But I think a lot of people care what Nate Silver thinks (we certainly had a lot of viewers) and that if he just says the straightforward true thing, it will make a difference to the public’s understanding. A lot of new analytically minded, highly quantitative donors are coming onto the board thanks to the Anthropic and OpenAI I.P.O.s, and they could become a financial base for building momentum behind good candidates and smart politics.

Beyond the narrative, I also wonder about the transition. Joe Biden won the 2020 primary and then spent the next 18 months acting like his job was to win over the Democratic Party staffer class rather than for staffers to learn from his victory.

It’s going to be a real battle over the next several months getting all these newly elected moderates staffed by teams who want to work for commonsense politicians and will spend their time building horizontal networks on the Hill and throughout D.C. to support smart politics. There’s a risk that they instead end up hiring Progressive Establishment types who dedicate themselves to bullying their bosses into orthodoxy.

I don’t totally know how to solve for this, but I think Majority Democrats and The Bench did a great job delivering campaign support to smart candidates, and I know Third Way has been working on these staffing issues. I’d really encourage anyone who reads Slow Boring and wants to help staff aligned candidates in a way that helps them stay aligned to reach out. I’ll do what I can to help make that happen.

Delivering accountability, not infighting

What’s going to be hard once the new Congress is seated is that while I don’t think the Democratic base demands ultra-left policy, they are definitely going to demand a hard line against Trump.

That is good and correct, and I want to push frontline members to run some political risks for this specific cause. It’s true that your voters, at the margin, probably sent you to Washington more to worry about the price of groceries than to worry about the stability of American democracy. But the stability of American democracy actually matters more, and in your heart, you probably know that’s why you ran. If you’re going to run risks, run risks for that.

But I also urge partisan Democrats not to be dupes for leftists who want to weaponize accountability.

The most obvious opportunity is holding hearings to fish around for Trump scandals that embarrass Republicans; that’s a win for everyone in the party. But if every revelation turns into a push for an impeachment vote, you’re taking the spotlight off Trump and onto Democratic infighting.

Similarly, there’s a difference between investigating corporate collusion with Trump in a manner that’s designed to punish the worst actors and reveal the worst behavior by the White House and trying to discredit all of capitalism. The goal of looking at corporate America should be to encourage segments of the business community to flip and rat out the worst actors, not to make them feel like there’s no way to get to yes with Democrats. It’s fine to be angry at some of the behavior we saw from business leaders bandwagoning with Trump over the past two years, and it’s appropriate to demand some measure of penance. But we also need to exert emotional self-control and be willing to forgive people who come clean and tattle on bad acts by others.

Subscribed

The other thing is that Democrats have to be able to walk and chew gum at the same time. I saw polling just before the election showing that voters overwhelmingly prefer bipartisan collaboration on affordability to a relentless focus on fighting Trump.

It would be absurd to take that entirely at face value and naively duck partisan combat.

But Democrats should take it seriously and try to deliver at least a few tokens of earnest policymaking. The low-hanging fruit is to say yes to the permitting deal during the lame duck so everyone will be able to tout a big energy affordability measure.

Candidates — and ideas — matter

Looking ahead to the 2028 Senate map, Democrats have decent pickup opportunities in Wisconsin and North Carolina and then a stretch chance in Iowa. And after last night I suppose we need to consider Kansas and South Carolina as potentially on the map as well.

But I can’t emphasize enough that another D+12 national environment is pretty unlikely and also that there is a type of candidate who can win these states and a type of candidate who cannot.

Democrats’ strong 2026 performance should leave the party with a credible bench of candidates who could run those races.

That said, I think this is undercut by the tendency of moderate politicians to cast their successes as purely personal triumph.

Leftists try to find charismatic candidates and run good campaigns. But they also always explicitly affirm the connective tissue between, for example, Melat Kiros and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. They emphasize that these politicians are not just beautiful unique snowflakes but people with shared ideas and common ground. There are, of course, big differences between Cooper and Shapiro and Talarico and Turek and Andrews, and the best campaign for Pennsylvania is not the best campaign for Texas. But doing well in 2028 is going to require a strong national campaign from a strong presidential candidate, and that’s going to require someone who can articulate on an ideas level what compelling politics looks like.

And compelling politics is not just “give in to demands from progressive advocacy groups but then also be nice to crypto lobbyists and try to raise pro-Israel money.”

I think across candidates who did well in tough races — notably including El-Sayed, at times — you see a willingness to emphasize concrete economic issues over post-material identity politics or environmentalism and a commitment to be tough on crime and deliver a secure border.

The path forward for Common Sense Democrats

Matthew Yglesias
·
February 20, 2025

I published “A Common Sense Democrat Manifesto” on November 12, full of pep and vim in the wake of the election, and started fleshing out the nine points with individual pieces during the transition.

Read full story

This is why, beyond saying that we don’t need Gavin Newsom or Kamala Harris, I keep resisting the impulse to get too sucked into the debate about specific personalities for 2028. What we need is for the nominee, whoever they are, to be willing to run a disciplined and focused campaign rather than whatever this “D.E.I. is back” slop from Ro Khanna is supposed to be.

Ro Khanna
@RoKhanna
DEI is back!
5:24 AM · Nov 4, 2026 · 111K Views
444 Replies · 363 Reposts · 3.08K Likes

No politician and no campaign is as good as they look in a favorable national political environment or as bad as they look in a bad one. And most likely, 2028 will not be as good a year for Dems as 2026.

But one key lesson here is that parties and candidates, to an extent, can create their own climates. There’s always the risk of complacency and backsliding after a good result, but there’s also a tremendous opportunity to present an exciting slate of fresh faces to the world and have them actually govern differently from Biden-era Democrats. Democrats in 2027 have an opportunity to move forward in a way that puts this whole horrible episode of American politics in the rearview mirror.

What Democrats Can Do

Yes, Trump has veto power. Force him to use it.

Paul Krugman
Nov 5
 
READ IN APP
 

Marketing note: I have a new ebook, Navigating the Chaos: Chronicles of Economic and Political Madness, which uses material from this Substack to construct a thematic narrative of the past two years and the issues that Democrats must now address to build an enduring progressive movement. Available from Amazon, Kobo, Bookshop, and Nook.

The American people have just delivered a stunning rebuke to Donald Trump. If we had a parliamentary system, the moving trucks would already be at the White House. As it is, however, an increasingly deranged and debilitated Trump will remain in control of foreign policy, national security, and many of the federal government’s domestic operations for two more years. He will also, as he made a point of emphasizing on Truth Social as the returns came in, retain the ability to veto legislation. And Democrats, despite their huge margins in both houses of Congress, won’t have enough votes to override his vetoes.

So what can Democrats do with their new majorities?

One important answer is that they will now hold committee gavels, hence the ability to conduct investigations and hearings backed by subpoena power. This matters more for the Trump gang than it would for a normal administration. Everyone paying attention knows that Trump and his cronies have been stealing billions, but many Americans probably don’t grasp the full extent of the corruption. Gaining the ability to bring this corruption into the sunlight is critical to rebuild Americans’ faith in the integrity of government, as well as to hold Trump and his vandals accountable. Moreover, knowing that his days are numbered, the Trump gang have every incentive to engage in a wholesale smash-and-grab spree.

And Democrats know it. On Tuesday night Rep. Robert Garcia — the probable chair of the House Oversight Committee — had a blunt message for everyone associated with Trump: “Lawyer up.”

On the eve of the midterms, when election modelers anticipated a blue wave but not this awesome tsunami, I thought that control of those gavels would be the main payoffs. However, the gargantuan size of the win showed that Americans want fundamental change, a decisive break with Trumpism. Yet, with Trump still wielding the veto pen, what should they do in the remaining two years of his term?

I think I know the answer to that question: Pass highly popular legislation that would clearly benefit ordinary Americans and not the oligarchs, knowing full well that Trump will veto the legislation. Emphatically, the Democratsshould not try to make deals with Trump, a man who never agreed to a deal that he didn’t subsequently try to break.

Democrats should craft an expansive menu of legislation to address the issues plaguing ordinary Americans. When Trump vetoes a bill, they should attempt to override that veto, forcing each and every Republican to either to uphold Trump’s obstruction — making it clear that they are as culpable as he is — or to develop a spine and supply the additional votes required for such overrides.

And given how toxic Trump has become with the American public, it’s even possible that some Republicans will break with him to pass a few good laws.

What kind of laws do I have in mind? They shouldn’t shy away from really ambitious plans, like Medicare-for-All, even though they have no chance of becoming law for now: Democrats need to be clear that they stand for real change. But they should also offer more modest initiatives, like a buy-in to Medicare for Americans under 65. And they should offer legislation immediately restoring the Affordable Care Act subsidies that Trump and his allies killed, leading to soaring premiums for health insurance and plunging enrollment.

On foreign policy, they should pass legislation strengthening sanctions on Russia and restoring aid to Ukraine. A significant number of Republicans might even join them in overriding Trump’s veto. Bear in mind that only 3 percent of the U.S. public sympathizes with Russia more than with Ukraine; only 4 percent of Republicans sympathize with Russia. And I believe that many Republicans in Congress are privately ashamed to see Trump so obviously siding with Vladimir Putin.

Other obvious examples are:

· Refusal to spend more billions of dollars on a failed war with Iran

· Ending the Trump tariffs

· Policies to safeguard Americans against the dangers of AI and data center hegemony

· Reforming tax policy so that it no longer benefits the wealthy and enables corporate tax evasion

· Ending ICE abuses

· Ending self-harming immigration policies

· Reconstituting the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and giving it enforcement powers

· Levying a windfall profits tax on oil companies

· Policies that benefit cost-effective green energy, like solar and wind farms

· Legislation that eliminates the ability of politicians and their family members to benefit financially from their offices

On all these issues and more, the Democrats should force Trump to use his veto power, making it clear to the country that he is the reason Americans are suffering under destructive policies that benefit the oligarchs, Trump and his cronies.

All of this Democratic legislation should be well crafted and objectively good. Furthermore, it can serve as the basis of the arsenal of policies upon which Democrats fight the 2028 election for both president and congress.

Yes, Democrats today are overjoyed about Tuesday’s results. But we should also be clear that they will still have to fight Republican obstruction over the next two years, as well as a hostile Supreme Court majority. So let’s have our celebration, but also be clear that this is, to quote Churchill, not the end, not even the beginning of the end, but perhaps the end of the beginning of the fight to reclaim this country.

And now for something completely different: The stock market is not the economy, and historically tells us almost nothing about where the economy is going. Still, given how often Trump has warned that Democrats would destroy the economy if in power, it’s at least interesting that the day after their smashing midterm victory oil prices plunged — probably because investors believe that the scale of Trump’s defeat made renewed war with Iran less likely — and the Dow rose 1500 points.

The rapid demise of the bipartisan pro-Israel consensus

It’s so over for AIPAC

The rapid demise of the bipartisan pro-Israel consensus

Matthew Yglesias
Nov 5
 
READ IN APP
 

After you read today’s post, I hope you’ll take a break from midterms coverage to listen to the latest episode of “The Argument” podcast, where Jerusalem and I discuss the new Elizabeth Holmes documentary, the difference between fact and fiction, and what makes a “true story” trustworthy. Paid subscribers can watch or listen ad free and read the transcript and show notes here. Free subscribers can catch the episode on YouTube here or listen wherever you get your podcasts.

Subscribe: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts

I used to have a bit where I would tell people that the real secret to AIPAC’s power wasn’t their famous (or infamous) financial clout — it was that voters basically agreed with them on the issue.

Not that voters deep in their hearts agreed with every detail of U.S. policy toward Israel or truly felt that the United States should be sending aid money with no strings attached. But that in a big-picture sense, Americans had a clear view that Israel was “the good guys” in an entrenched conflict.

This meant that there was a simple playbook for taking out basically any member of Congress who drew the organization’s ire: AIPAC would put the word out that money was available to anyone who wanted to challenge said member, and politicians would leap at the opportunity because it was basically free money.

Sure, the person you’re challenging could complain that they were being targeted by the nefarious Israel Lobby. But most Americans didn’t actually think the Israel Lobby was nefarious, because they didn’t think Israel was nefarious.

The challenger wouldn’t even talk much about Israel during the campaign — very few people cared that much about it. They’d just use the money to run good ads on whatever subject their voters did really care about.

What we saw in the 2026 cycle was the degenerative version of this strategy, what happens when AIPAC tries to win purely on financial clout without having the sympathies of the public on their side.

And what happens is that it doesn’t work very well.

In 2026, a candidate really could say, “hey, I’m getting hit with tons of AIPAC money and that’s bad,” and large swaths of the electorate would agree that it was bad. Rather than wanting their financial clout to be known for the sake of the intimidation factor (like how the crypto people bragged about their spending in the 2024 cycle), AIPAC started disguising their spending because association with them was harmful to the candidates they supported. And it became relatively easy to countermobilize support and money based on being the candidate who stands up to AIPAC.

These dynamics were most present on the Democratic Party side this year and are driving the formerly bipartisan pro-Israel consensus to become sharply polarized.

Except it’s worse than that for AIPAC, since Donald Trump on Election Day just randomly announced that he wants to end aid to Israel and then Vice President JD Vance put out an election response essay on Twitter basically blaming the U.S.-Israel relationship for the G.O.P. wipeout.

It’s so over for AIPAC.

The V.P.’s aggressive election analysis

I honestly don’t think much more needs to be said about the Democratic side of this. AIPAC put everything they had into beating Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, but “everything they had” was just money, and El-Sayed could also raise money. There just was not any amount of cash that was going to turn Mike Rogers into a winner in Michigan in the political climate of 2026. Beyond that, while you can find me any day of the week waging Twitter war on behalf of the claim that El-Sayed was an electoral underperformer, there’s no reason to think his much-litigated stances on Israel were a major source of underperformance.

Subscribed

We don’t have an example at hand of a politician saying “no aid to Israel” while also having moderate views on internal-combustion-engine cars or sex-segregated school sports teams. Haley Stevens was, in fact, quite left-wing on those issues, so we didn’t even get variation on those fronts in the primary.

If you look at Michigan politicians, El-Sayed ran weaker than most of the Democratic House candidates, but one of the exceptions is Will Lawrence, a fellow leftist who is more associated with the Green New Deal than with being anti-Israel.

Instead, what I find really shocking is the shift on the right over the past week. Here’s what Vance said about the election:

But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone.

Another pollster—one of the smartest people I know in politics, told me yesterday we’d lose the generic ballot by 13 points. I felt negative going into Tuesday, but even I was shocked by this. In his polling, he saw that a lot of Trump 2024 voters were angry and planning to vote for Democrats. He asked those voters who had abandoned us what would cause them to come back on our team. The top four answers, accounting for nearly all of the responses were:

1) End the war
2) Focus on cost of living/inflation
3) Put America First
4) Change our relationship to Israel

Our voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats. This is according to a pollster who nailed the results.

Between 2.5 and 3.5 of the four factors are just Israel.

And this puts pro-Israel Republicans in the pain cave because while Vance is massively over-blaming Israel (what about tariffs, corruption, health care cuts, immigration agents murdering two American citizens, or the bizarre decision to embrace A.I. accelerationism?), you can’t reasonably deny that the war was very politically costly for Republicans. The absolute worst time to be turned into a scapegoat is when you are, in fact, guilty. And make no mistake, that’s what’s happening here — one genuinely disastrous bit of decision-making is being made to carry all the weight for the Trump administration’s many, many errors of judgment.

But if Trump does pivot in this direction and Vance becomes his successor, where is pro-Israel support supposed to flow?

This cycle showed that AIPAC’s presence in Democratic primaries has become toxic, and pro-Israel institutions just spent the past three months whining that it’s not good enough to disagree with El-Sayed about Israel — you need to embrace wildly over-the-top criticisms of him and become a Republican to stay kosher in their eyes.

So what’s left here?

The perils of overreach

I think the extent to which AIPAC and other pro-Israel institutions basically brought this fiasco upon themselves is really striking.

If you go back to Barack Obama’s term in office, there was a solid bipartisan pro-Israel consensus. The thing that shattered that consensus was not anything Palestinian activists did; it was the nuclear deal with Iran.

Obama upheld all the main elements of traditional pro-Israel American foreign policy — aid, recognition, diplomatic support, arms sales — but also pursued diplomacy with Iran focused on America’s non-proliferation interests. Benjamin Netanyahu did not think this deal was good for Israel, which is certainly his right. But then pro-Israel groups went to war with Obama over this, massively resetting the bar for what constituted pro-Israel policy and rightly annoying lots of Democratic Party partisans and foreign policy hands.

Then Trump became president and tore up the deal in a way that created an unworkable situation for the Biden administration. Joe Biden very loyally stood by Israel after 10/7, making this the one issue on which he really meaningfully held firm against criticism from the left.

But what Biden wouldn’t do was get America into a war with Iran, so even as the Biden/Harris administration took on water from the left, they got little reward from pro-Israel groups, many of whom just basically preferred Trump.

Under Trump, they finally got the war they wanted.

And while Vance is wrong to solely attribute the Trump administration’s political problems to Iran, it is unquestionably true that the war supercharged anti-Israel sentiment in the United States by imposing massive costs not just on Palestinians but on everyday Americans — and for that matter, on literally billions of people around the world.

Subscribed

It’s of course wrong to cast this as all Israel’s fault. It’s Trump, not Netanyahu, who bears responsibility for Trump’s bad decision-making. Neither Obama nor Biden did this, and Trump could (and should) have simply told Netanyahu no. But while Trump is responsible for Trump being terrible at his job, it is factually true that this is the outcome Israel wanted and worked toward for years across multiple presidents, and voters are right to be angry about it.

I honestly have no idea what happens next. But I am quite worried that while American Jewish institutions were going all-in feuding with Democrats over foreign policy, they’ve been ignoring the rise of totally unambiguous Jew-hatred on the American right.

🇻🇦Bombardment
@AestheticBmbder
"Anakin. They are saying you dont think it was 6 million"
7:37 PM · Oct 31, 2026 · 149K Views
44 Replies · 844 Reposts · 16.1K Likes
Rogue Scholar Press
@RogueScholarPr
“Anakin, JEDI stands for Jews, Equity, Diversity and Inclusion. You need to check your privilege”
7:28 AM · Oct 31, 2026 · 93.9K Views
47 Replies · 468 Reposts · 7.52K Likes

The specific ideological valence of Jewish American identity politics is different from other strands of ethnic-minority identity politics. And the factional alignment of pro-Israel institutions is different from the way most of “the groups” are positioned.

But in terms of overreach, backlash, counterproductive behavior, and a preference for expressive rather than instrumentally useful conduct, the structural pathologies are pretty similar. I hope the collapse of pro-Israel politics simply lands the U.S.-Israel relationship in a healthier position. But pushing so long and so hard for unreasonable levels of American support could lead to some really bad failure modes unless the leaders of and donors to these organizations are prepared to admit — fast — that they need to dramatically change course.
