For the Democrats, now comes the hard part

The Dems have to figure out what they stand for, and what they want to do.

Noah Smith
Nov 5
 
READ IN APP
 

Democrats won a historic victory in Tuesday’s election. It was the best possible outcome — Donald Trump has made so many mistakes, engaged in such flagrant corruption, and committed such egregious acts that for his party not to have been punished at the polls would have boded poorly for America’s future. But as it is, I’m cautiously encouraged — normal Americans reasserted control, delivering a rebuke to the extremists who had used a moment of division and chaos to seize the commanding heights of power in our country.

It was the biggest midterm wave in half a century. Obama’s midterm loss in 2010 and Trump’s in 2018 don’t even come close. You have to go all the way back to 1974 and 1976 to find wipeouts like this:

Wait…1974 and 1976? 1974 was the year Nixon resigned due to Watergate, and 1976 was the year Jimmy Carter was elected president. Did either of those election victories herald an era of Democratic dominance in America? No, they did not. In fact, the GOP bounced back shortly afterwards, dominated American politics in the 1980s, and pulled the country to the right for decades.

So before they go patting themselves on the back for winning everything, forever, Democrats should think about that history of brief success followed by long-term failure, and ponder how to avoid a similar outcome this time. After Hannibal won a great victory, one of his generals is said to have told him: “You know how to win a victory, Hannibal; you do not know how to use it.” The Democrats must figure out how to use their victory.

That’s a tricky question. Democrats now control Congress, but that doesn’t mean they’re in power; Trump can and will veto most legislation they pass. With their limited capabilities, the Dems have to do the following, all at once:

  1. Block as many of Trump’s bad policies as possible

  2. Keep the spotlight on Trump even though he’s now a lame duck

  3. Demonstrate a clear ideology and a clear plan to the American people despite not being able to pass much legislation

That’s possible to do, especially if — as seems very likely — Trump keeps being corrupt and making mistakes and alienating the country. The Dems won the 2006 midterms, and went on to put Obama in the White House two years later. Trump seems like he’s on a similar track:

Nate Silver
@NateSilver538
I know the "smart" conventional wisdom is that midterms don't predict future election results. But then I look at this. And 2006 is the only modern lame-duck term with a wave like this.
11:57 PM · Nov 4, 2026 · 165K Views
49 Replies · 124 Reposts · 1.82K Likes

But it doesn’t always happen — the GOP lost to Obama in 2012 after their big midterm wave in 2010, and the Dems barely eked out a victory over Trump in 2020 (with a lot of help from Covid) after winning the midterms in 2018.

If Democrats are going to translate midterm success into presidential victory — to say nothing of long-term partisan dominance — they’re going to have to work hard at rebuilding their brand, their sales pitch, and their policy platform after the disastrous years of 2016-2024.

This was a center-left victory

One important point, which a lot of other people have already made, is that the big Democratic wave was mostly won by moderate Democrats. Here’s the NYT:

For much of the midterm campaign, progressive Democratic insurgents commanded the spotlight…But the path to Democrats’ sweeping victory this week, when they seized control of both chambers of Congress, was paved overwhelmingly by moderates who had spent months persuading voters in Republican-leaning states and competitive congressional districts…

The scale of moderate gains was reflected in the growing ranks of the centrist groups on Capitol Hill. The Blue Dog Coalition, a caucus of moderate and conservative Democrats in the House, announced on Wednesday that it had added at least 14 to its ranks, nearly doubling in size, and other centrist groups including the New Democrats and Problem Solvers strengthened their numbers substantially.

Some of this is purely mechanical. Far-left types tend to win by unseating moderate Dems in primaries in deep-blue districts and states, while moderates tend to win in swing districts and states; thus, when a wave is bigger and the Dems win more swing districts and states, moderates tend to do proportionally better than leftists.

However, there are signs that this election cycle actually represented a broad endorsement of moderate center-leftism. Ballot initiatives have rejected various leftist policies all over the country, and leftist candidates have been losing to center-left ones in deep blue strongholds:

Nor have many prominent Dems done the kind of “woke” cultural signaling that they regularly did in 2020 and 2022.

There are two parts of the basic story here. First, the “woke” cultural wave of the 2010s, which peaked in 2020-21, continues to slowly recede. You can see this in continued voter support for conservative positions on cultural issues like trans sports:

Second, voters have not yet embraced the socialist movement, as demonstrated by the relatively weak performances of Bernie Sanders-endorsed candidates and the failure of the billionaire tax in California.

That means that Democrats understand that this 2026 midterm victory is a contingent and fragile one. Normal Americans have risen from their apathetic torpor and their jaded hyperpartisan paralysis, and are prepared to punish extremists of either party:

The normie uprising has brought center-left Dems to the fore, and it has also forced more progressive Dems to tone down or strategically compromise their more extreme positions.

But moderation itself is neither an ideology nor a policy program, and herein lies the big challenge for the Dems over the next year and a half or so.

The headless Dems

Right now, my assessment is that most Democratic voters — including Independents and swing voters who lean toward the Dems — aren’t thinking very hard about how the country ought to be governed or what the future of America should look like. They’re simply thinking short-term thoughts about the immediate threat. They hate Trump and MAGA, and they want them gone, and it’s really as simple as that.

Nate Silver calls this “Heather Cox Richardsonism”, after the extremely popular Substack politics-and-history blogger Heather Cox Richardson:

Silver Bulletin
What is Heather Cox Richardsonism?
First, it was Blueskyism. Now, it’s “Heather Cox Richardsonism”? Given the changes to the algorithm, tweets don’t really …
Read more
a year ago · 1248 likes · 228 comments · Nate Silver

Silver wrote:

The third faction [of the Dems is] Richardsonism or a term I’ll treat as synonymous with it: #Resistance Libs. They’re older, with extremely high educational attainment, predominantly female, and very highly politically engaged. This is the audience for a cluster of political activism encompassing things such as the No Kings protests and some highly popular anti-Trump Substacks along with certain prominent podcasts and much of Bluesky.

Nate has a bunch of criticisms of “Heather Cox Richardsonism”, most of which I disagree with. I like Heather Cox Richardson. I like suburban moms who listen to NPR all day and who feel physically ill when they see Donald Trump on a screen. Their instincts are good. Trump is an extremely bad president — and not just bad, but uniquely bad, in ways that are degrading the long-term stability and effectiveness of the United States itself. It’s eminently reasonable and understandable to be mad about this, even to the exclusion of all other political viewpoints and causes. As for the No Kings protests, they seem to line up perfectly with — and probably contributed to — this week’s midterm results.

And for most regular people, being mad about Trump is enough. Most citizens are not political philosophers or movement leaders or intellectuals. It’s not reasonable to ask them to think about where the country should go after Trump, or what ideologies and ideas should guide us in the absence of such imminent threats.

But someone has to think about those things. Otherwise Democrats will prove just as unable to govern as Trump was — well, maybe 70% as unable to govern, which will be bad enough. And our politics will continue to be an endless series of backlash-to-the-backlash-to-the-backlash, as each party focuses all its energy on getting to the day of the revolution and none of its energy on what happens the next morning.

Right now, the problem with Resistance Liberalism is that it’s headless. In Trump’s first term, the Resistance was animated by various identity movements, unified by the idea of a struggle against structural racism, misogyny, and so on. Hillary Clinton made a conscious choice to frame her 2016 campaign as a battle of antiracism versus Trumpian racism, Kamala Harris did something similar in 2020, and Joe Biden quietly let his administration push what would have previously been considered extreme versions of various identitarian social causes.

In fact, the American public still thought those versions were extreme, and punished Democrats in the polls accordingly. The end of the woke revolution lopped the head off of the Resistance — it left them with all of the same rage, but without a vision of a future America.

As I see it, there are basically three factions vying to replace identity politics as the guiding ethos of the Resistance. These are:

  1. The leftists — Abdul El-Sayed, Zohran Mamdani, Bernie Sanders, and so on

  2. The Warrenite progressive intellectuals

  3. The Abundance movement

Each of these has deep flaws that I think will end up basically disqualifying it.

The leftists are organized, purposeful, disciplined, and driven, and they probably want the job of leadership more than the other factions. But their movement has some fatal weaknesses that make it a bad choice to lead the Dems. First of all, the leftists are intensely factional, focusing relentlessly on knifing the Democratic establishment rather than building a big tent.

Second, their policies tend to be so extreme that they overreach and backfire. The failure of the California billionaire tax is a case in point. Americans want to tax the rich more, but the billionaire tax was so extreme and poorly designed that voters didn’t just reject it — they approved a competing ballot proposition forbidding such taxes in the future.

Third, leftists instinctively ally themselves with bad people and bad causes. Leftist streamer Hasan Piker has praised terrorists and supported Vladimir Putin’s seizure of Crimea, incoming leftist congresswoman Darializa Avila Chevalier founded a group claiming to be dedicated to “the total eradication of Western Civilization”, and so on.

And fourth, although leftism is sometimes viewed as an alternative to wokeness, leftists themselves tend to be very woke. Just for fun, check out the famous footage from the 2019 DSA convention, or watch this widely mocked display from Representative Ro Khanna:

Ro Khanna
@RoKhanna
DEI is back!
5:24 AM · Nov 4, 2026 · 2.19M Views
4.38K Replies · 878 Reposts · 6.65K Likes

These shortcomings ought to prove fatal to the leftists’ chances of taking over the American left — and they probably will.

The second faction vying to take over the Resistance are the Warrenite intellectuals, who are laser-focused on attacking the rich — specifically, the rich people in the tech industry. Although Warren failed to catch fire in 2019, her faction had great success putting its people into positions of power during the Biden years.

But it kind of backfired. The New Antitrust movement got little done in a practical sense, and more fundamentally it failed to advance any kind of rewrite for our antitrust law. Years of frothing with rage against Mark Zuckerberg and the old FAANG companies just ended up looking silly when AI came along and disrupted their business models. The intellectual movement to “steer” the development of AI toward more pro-worker technologies (whatever that would even look like) is going nowhere.

In addition to being composed primarily of a bunch of egghead intellectuals who routinely fail to catch fire with voters, the Warrenites have a fatal flaw — they’ve chosen the wrong target. Democrats are entirely focused on hating Trump, while the Warrenites are focused on hating Mark Zuckerberg and Jeff Bezos. Americans just fundamentally aren’t that mad at the fact that Zuckerberg and Bezos are rich. They generally despise Elon Musk, but only for his right-wing activities and his online attitude — when he was just a businessman selling electric cars and reusable rockets, they didn’t mind his billions.

The Warrenites are simply never going to convince the nation that the billionaire techbros, rather than the rightists of MAGA, are the biggest threat to our way of life.

Anyway, the third faction is Abundance. Of the three, this would definitely be my choice if I had to pick, since I really like what the Abundance movement stands for. Abundance policies, like the bipartisan permitting reform bill now making its way through Congress, are both smarter and more politically feasible than almost all of what the leftists and Warrenites want to do.

The problem with Abundance is that it’s primarily an intellectual movement, not a political one. It’s all about policy — about whispering in the ears of princes, rather than marching in the streets. Abundance’s leaders are nice guys like Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson who just want to see everybody be happy and get a puppy.

And all of the Abundance ideas, to a rounding error, are good ones. Many of them are going to get implemented, especially concerning housing and energy. But they will do so because elites — including some leftists and some Republicans — will be intellectually convinced that they are good things to do, not because they have the ability to harness and direct years of pent-up anti-Trump anger. Abundance will win, but it will not win all the things the Democrats would need it to win.

The Democrats need something more than any of these movements has to offer. They need an ethos that both inspires popular passion and has a chance of pragmatically working. They need something that will give regular, normie Americans — the voters who just rose up to throw out the GOP — a reason to believe in the future, and a reason to believe that the Democrats can take them to that future.

That ideology exists. It was harnessed by FDR and his successors a century ago, first to fight the Depression, then to win World War 2, and finally to build the modern society that came after the war. I’m talking about liberal nationalism:

America needs liberal nationalism back

Noah Smith
·
May 29
Read full story

Here’s what I wrote in that post half a year ago:

In the 20th century, America had an ideology that was committed to forging a single national identity from a dizzying array of backgrounds. That ideology was liberal nationalism…

FDR ended forced assimilation policies for Native Americans, and gave them greater autonomy on tribal lands. He maintained a group of Black advisors, created plenty of programs to help Black people economically, created cultural programs to publicize Black achievement, and preserved the testimonials of former slaves. He created campaigns promoting interfaith understanding and cooperation, helping to reduce America’s traditional anti-Catholic prejudice as well as antisemitism. His Federal Writers Project employed writers to document America’s cultural diversity…FDR also strongly promoted the notion of America as a nation of immigrants — an idea that still deeply holds sway over the American psyche, despite rightists’ attempts to get rid of it…

FDR and the liberal nationalists were not modern multicultural progressives. They strongly believed in national unity. This obviously meant patriotism, respect for American institutions, and a shared sense of national purpose during World War 2, but it also meant a lot more. FDR and the New Dealers — and especially the Office of War Information — advanced the notion that America had a unifying culture, set of democratic ideals, sense of history, and way of life that transcended Americans’ different backgrounds. The history of the New Deal is littered with examples of attempts to forge American-ness into a sort of shared civic religion.

The Democrats can have liberal nationalism back if they want. Moderate figures like Jon Ossoff and James Talarico can use Rooseveltian pluralistic patriotism just like Barack Obama did, in order to go beyond good-governance centrism and opposition to Donald Trump. The intellectuals of the Abundance movement can use liberal nationalism to add passion to their policies — after all, isn’t it precisely because we’re Americans that we deserve material abundance?

Right now, Americans hold a bunch of basically Rooseveltian beliefs, and many Democrats still have the Rooseveltian instincts they’ve inherited from their party’s past. But we’re still not to the point where liberal nationalism has filled the vacuum of passion and inspiration left by the demise of “Woke 1.0”. The Democrats have a year and a half to resuscitate that vision.

Doing so will require some clashes — with leftists who believe that America is an evil empire, with Warrenites who want to destroy big tech companies instead of harnessing them to the national purpose, and with identitarian activists who believe that promoting a unified national culture is a form of racist oppression. But if this is not undertaken, the Democrats will either continue to drift aimlessly from backlash to backlash, or fall under the sway of highly suboptimal captains.

Building the future in opposition

There’s also the more pragmatic question of what Dems should actually do over the next two years, while they hold Congress but not the presidency. This is an inherently difficult problem, because Trump can just veto almost any legislation the Dems pass. The usual tactic here is to just obstruct anything the president wants to do, hoping that making the president’s term in office look like a failure will help the opposition in the next election.

But I believe Democrats can do better than this. First of all they can, and should, investigate Trump and his family and friends for corruption. Corruption turned out to be a huge issue in these midterms — even more important than I realized it would be.

Tim Alberta
@TimAlberta

65 Replies · 704 Reposts · 2.17K Likes

Even in opposition, Democrats can shine some sunlight on the Trump administration’s seemingly endless parade of dirty deeds. And in fact, it looks as if this is going to happen:

Corruption topped the list of concerns for voters who ousted Republicans…Now, the newly empowered Democratic Party is putting the issue front and center…Senior Democrats in both chambers of Congress have vowed to marshal the subpoena powers and larger investigative staffs that come with their soon-to-be majorities to probe what they say is the self-enrichment that President Donald Trump and people in his orbit have done at the public’s expense…

House Democrats are preparing a vast oversight agenda to look at how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office…Garcia, the top Democrat on the Oversight and Government Reform Committee, has outlined five priorities, including Trump family business dealings, the administration's handling of the Jeffrey Epstein investigation and Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations. Rep. Jared Huffman of California, the ranking Democrat on the Natural Resources Committee, said he wants to dig into Trump's White House ballroom and other construction projects, as well as the Trump family's role in mineral deals…In the Senate, Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., who is expected to become the chairman of the Homeland Security Committee's Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, said his panel will want to look into Trump's real estate projects around the nation's capital and his crypto dealings with special envoy Steve Witkoff.

This is great. But other than this, and perhaps some bipartisan deals and some obstruction and oversight of Trump’s worst abuses, what can the Dems in Congress do?

What they can also do is to workshop their economic policy program under low-stakes conditions. America has two big economic challenges looming — the out-of-control national debt, and AI. Dems can start demonstrating — and at the same time, start figuring out — how they’d address both of these challenges if they had the presidency.

The debt is actually the much harder piece of this in political terms. Deficit reduction is inherently painful, as it involves some combination of spending cuts and tax increases — both of which tend to be unpopular with the electorate. If Dems submit budgets that go all-out with spending cuts and tax hikes, Trump will just veto those budgets, and Americans — who have not yet been forced to reckon with the need for debt reduction — will praise Trump for it.

Instead, Dems will need to introduce only parts of their ultimate deficit reduction plans. Sunsetting the Trump tax cuts on pass-through businesses is one good idea — there’s basically no reason for people like me to pay lower taxes than Americans with W-2s, just because we’re self-employed.

AI is ultimately the thornier policy challenge, because we really don’t know how AI is going to affect the economy. But putting in place measures to protect human labor from the inevitable disruptions — flexible welfare programs, employment incentives, social wealth funds, and the like — has little downside, and it offers Democrats a way to sell a vision of harnessing the benefits of technology for the public good. The Dems can observe how these ideas go over with the public, and make the popular ones part of their candidate’s platform in 2028.

This midterm blowout was the first step toward building a better country and putting the chaotic, shameful Trump Era behind us. But there’s a lot of work to be done, both on the ideological side and in terms of crafting a policy program. The morning after the revolution is always when the hard work begins.

America’s Backlash Against Oligarchy

Why the megabillionaires lost big Tuesday

Paul Krugman
Nov 6
 
READ IN APP
 

Marketing note 1: I have a new ebook, Navigating the Chaos: Chronicles of Economic and Political Madness, which uses material from this Substack to construct a thematic narrative of the past two years and the issues that Democrats must now address to build an enduring progressive movement. Available from Amazon, Kobo, Bookshop, and Nook.

Marketing note 2: I’m doing a live, in-person event with the inimitable Heather Cox Richardson Wednesday Nov. 11 at 6:30 PM. Seating is fully booked, but it will be livestreamed: details and registration here. We’re trying to find a way to livestream it on our Substacks too, and I’ll let you know if we can.

Now, today’s post:

The midterm result was a tale of many backlashes. There was the backlash of erstwhile Trump voters, particularly young white males, against high gasoline prices and the Iran War. There was the backlash of Hispanic voters against ICE and Trump’s horrific deportation policy. There was the backlash of Black voters against Republicans’ gerrymandering to negate their votes and Trump’s open racism. There was the backlash of women against the destruction of abortion rights and suppression of the Epstein files. There was a backlash of ordinary families against the loss of healthcare coverage. There was a general backlash against Trump’s bottomless corruption and lies. And there was a backlash of patriotic Americans against Trump’s bromance with Putin.

Yet one of the most stunning blows was against the class of oligarchs, whom voters reasonably believe have been major enablers Trump and the Republicans, allowing them to inflict significant economic, social and strategic harm the country.

Since the 1980s, America’s society and economy have become increasingly oligarchic. The share of wealth held by the top 0.0001% — roughly 200 people — is now more than 7 times what it was in 1980.

That tiny billionaire elite spent massively in this year’s midterm elections, with the spending overwhelmingly in support of Republicans:

Note: Andreesen and the Brockmans are very right wing, but their bars aren’t red because they give a lot of money to tech groups that aren’t explicitly pro-GOP.

But to the credit of American voters, the oligarchs’ party and their preferred candidates lost, bigly.

Elon Musk, in particular, was nearly the sole funder of Ken Paxton’s senatorial campaign in Texas. Overall, he spent more than $200 million in the state — only to see James Talarico beat Paxton by 12 points, and Gina Hinojosa become the next Texas governor. Musk has been the leader of the tech bro faction trying to promote a move to Texas away from liberal California. Now, suddenly, the broligarchs’ promised land has turned blue.

You should not conclude from Tuesday’s humiliation that concerns about the threat to democracy from extreme wealth concentration are unfounded. Wealth still buys power; oligarchs played an enormous role in supporting Donald Trump’s return to the White House, throwing billions behind Trump, Republicans, and their aligned PACs. And they will surely keep trying to buy elections until and unless steps are taken to limit their excessive wealth.

Yet the results of the midterms do suggest that there are some inherent factors that limit the ability of malefactors of great wealth to sway elections. Indeed, their support can backfire, inflicting serious damage to the political prospects of whomever they support. I would identify four factors in particular:

· Big money can be self-defeating in American politics

· Big money feeds big corruption

· Billionaires live in bubbles of self-delusion

· Parties supported by billionaires also end up trapped in bubbles

Big money can be self-defeating: Money obviously matters a lot in political campaigns. A well-financed candidate can afford to run ads, hold rallies, hire staffers to get his or her message out. But getting the message out is self-defeating when the candidate doesn’t have a message that resonates with voters. In fact, the messages that Republicans delivered in the midterms alienated voters.

The October AP-NORC poll asked voters whether a number of issues were “One of the most important.” Leading the list were “the economy” and “the cost of living,” followed by healthcare and the war with Iran. What could Republicans say about these issues, when the Trump era has been marked by surging inflation, government cuts that have led millions to lose health insurance, and a military debacle in the Persian Gulf? They could echo Trump’s “who you gonna believe, me or your lying eyes” proclamations that everything is great and we’re living in a Golden Age, but that would do them more harm than good. Instead, the Republicans offered personal attacks, cries of “communism”, AI-generated misrepresentations, and tired culture-war broadsides.

Not only that, the massive flood of big money has sensitized American voters to the fact that the oligarchs are, in effect, trying to buy their vote. And we should commend the many principled Democratic politicians who trusted the instincts of voters and foreswore accepting superPAC funding, like the newly elected senator from Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed.

Big money feeds big corruption: Suppose you’re a billionaire who wants some changes in government policy, almost always involving decisions that directly affect your personal wealth. One way to get those changes is to finance campaigns by politicians you believe will act in your favor. But there’s also a more direct route: Just give money directly to officials who deliver what you want.

So when a party of, by, and for oligarchs took power, it was inevitable that we would see raw corruption on an unprecedented scale — although Trump’s personal greed and lack of self-restraint made that corruption especially lurid.

True, much of Trump’s personal profiteering involved crypto bros rather than the mega-donors listed in the chart above, and Jared Kushner has been raking it in largely from Middle East potentates. But corporate America rushed to fund Trump’s pet projects, like his grotesque ballroom, and the support of big money fed a general attitude within the administration that anything goes.

And voters noticed. Both pre-election polling and the exit polls show perceptions of corruption as a major factor in the election — possibly, depending on the phrasing of the question, comparable in importance to the cost of living. As a result, the cozy relationship between oligarchs and the G.O.P., which enabled this unprecedented corruption, may well have hurt Republicans far more than lavish campaign funding helped them.

Billionaires live in bubbles of self-delusion: The obscenely rich are different from you and me. They live in a bubble, populated by yes-men and yes-women, who never dare to tell them that they are dangerously deluded. They have no conception of ordinary Americans’ concerns or their struggles. So when Elon Musk rants that all Democrats are communists, uses his megaphone X to promote the Great Replacement conspiracy theory that Democrats are deliberately trying to replace whites with immigrants, or uses his control of Starlink to aid Putin’s war against Ukraine, there is no one willing or able to inform him that these are self-defeating acts.

Furthermore, because oligarchs like Musk have effectively bought the G.O.P., they are able to impose the delusions and obsessions that festered inside their bubbles on the Republican Party as a whole. Notably, Musk also was a leading forcebehind the remarkably large amount of Republican anti-transgender messaging during the midterms, with more than $280 million spent on anti-trans broadcast and connected TV ads. Not only were these ads full of lies, but nobody cared about the issue. It always ranks dead last when voters are asked about which issues they consider important.

Finally, by providing Trump and the Republican party virtually unlimited financial support, making them feel impervious to the concerns of ordinary Americans, the billionaires have dragged Republican politicians and influencers into their bubbles

Parties supported by billionaires also end up trapped in bubbles of self-delusion: While the scale of the Democratic midterm victory surprised almost everyone, the victory itself came as no surprise. Generic ballot polls had shown a 9-point Democratic advantage (it actually came in at 13.) This predicted advantage, according to modelers like G. Elliott Morris and Nate Silver, translated into a near-certain Democratic takeover of the House and approximately 80 percent odds of taking the Senate.

Yet like Trump, many Republican activists and politicians appear to have been completely shocked by their defeat. Why? Because they were living in a self-referential bubble, getting their information from right-wing influencers and Fox News, who led them to believe that the polls were either outright fakes or massively understating Donald Trump’s popularity.

Indeed, at this point I’m starting to believe that Musk’s purchase of Twitter, and his conversion of the app into a safe space for fascism, has actually been harmful to the right wing, because it means that the Republican elite is marinated in misinformation, including misinformation about the U.S. political scene.

Now, while Democrats have every right to savor their historic midterm victory, I will paraphrase what I wrote in yesterday’s post: to quote Churchill, this is not the end, not even the beginning of the end, but perhaps the end of the beginning of the fight to reclaim this country from the oligarchs. A lasting victory will require greatly reducing megabillionaires’ power, which means reducing their share of national wealth.

Tuesday was, however, a good start.

The enigma of Trump

A midterm Mailbag

Matthew Yglesias
Nov 6
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

Well! Election season is a very busy time at our small shop, but reflecting back on the epic seven-hour livestream we did with GD Politics, Silver Bulletin, and The Argument, what really strikes me is the extent to which the wild inferences we drew right at the beginning of the evening from the early ballot drops in Indiana proved accurate.

We were all on there covering our asses and saying you can’t just assume that things that happen in Hamilton County will reflect national trends, but in this case, it turns out they did! It was a ton of fun, and I’m very grateful to everyone for letting me participate. Personally, though, I prefer writing to speaking live on camera, so I’m glad to be back doing election takes here in writing.

David W Lavoie: What is Trump’s play here? Is he really so shallow to say that as long as the border stays secure and the ballroom gets completed, Dems can do what they want?

My dominant answer here is that I have no idea. Donald Trump is such an incredibly overexposed figure that it’s easy to overlook how mysterious he is.

It’s relatively simple to understand, broadly speaking, what Paul Ryan thought was interesting and important about American politics. You could see which things he really emphasized and where he was more flexible. Trump sometimes seems like he doesn’t care about anything and is only interested in money and weird construction projects. But he sometimes seems borderline fanatical about tariffs and immigration. On the other hand, he rarely actually discusses his administration’s immigration policy in any detail. He gambled his presidency on a war with Iran but seems largely disengaged from it. And it’s not like there’s no reporting on this stuff; it’s just that the piling-on of information doesn’t really clarify the picture.

There were various points during Trump’s first term when it seemed like his indolence would lead him to be willing to do bipartisan deals with Democrats on reasonably favorable terms for the center-left. But as time went on, those deals always seemed to collapse and it seemed like he was a faker. But then the CARES Act did come together. And then he did a half-assed coup after he lost the election. But even there: Why? Was there really a lot of tangible upside to that? It was one of the most insane events of American political history, and the motivation behind it — especially given the shambolic nature of the plot — remains fairly obscure.

I did not spend the weeks leading up to the midterms doing dire warnings of Trumpian election theft. But it certainly occurred to me as something that might happen. When the results were in, though, he seemed almost indifferent.

So fair enough, what does Congress have to do with him? But he personally set in motion an incredible amount of redistricting drama in the House. He hand-picked disastrous Senate candidates in Texas and South Carolina. Why do this stuff if he doesn’t care?

I don’t know, and I don’t think we ever will know.

Spencer Roach: Early 2028 speculation: are Vance and Rubio still the most likely Republican POTUS nominees? On the one hand, the midterm results seem to discredit the Trump admin, making an outsider nominee more likely. On the other hand, most Republican primary voters will probably still be loyal to Trump, though it’s possible that the midterm result gives Trump loyalists permission to stop drinking the Kool-Aid.

I’ve said this before and I’ll say it again: My best guess is that a viable outsider candidacy won’t come from an “anti-Trump” figure but from someone I’d call a post-Trump figure.

This is someone who is basically aligned with the administration on domestic issues but says the war in Iran was a mistake, wasn’t personally involved with the administration, and makes some hand-waving claim like Republican turnout was bad because the party establishment abandoned the anti-abortion cause.

I’m not saying that outgoing Tennessee Governor Bill Lee would be the candidate to run that campaign, but it would be someone like Bill Lee — just some normal Republican Party politician who has been in no way “anti-Trump” but isn’t identified with Trump or especially well-known. Someone who will start popping up in New Hampshire diners and on podcasts talking about having implemented a broadly Trumpy (but more aggressive on abortion) agenda in a red state. Someone who doesn’t have a foreign policy record and who has a broadly more professional demeanor.

Weary Land: You mentioned examples of moderate preferences on policy proven at the ballot box. I’ll add that Question 3 in Wisconsin, which would ban anything remotely like affirmative action, passed by nearly 13 pp. That’s a notably higher margin than any statewide Democrat in Wisconsin (who seem to have mostly run behind the national environment). Do you think that elected Democrats “get it”? Do you think they’ll actually stay focused on affordability --- or is the siren’s call of unpopular left wing priorities too strong? Maybe an influx of candidates from swing districts will help?

One of the very first Slow Boring articles was about the failure of an affirmative action referendum in California in November of 2020.

This is one of those issues where I am genuinely uncertain what it is that Democrats think the political situation is. The information is plainly available for people who want to see it. Affirmative action performs terribly when it is placed on the ballot. It polls terribly in surveys. It appears to be the case that Democrats not only have access to this knowledge but that they are tacitly aware of it. I think this post from Bernie Sanders aide Warren Gunnels explaining that the whole progressive platform is supermajority popular is pretty dishonest, but obviously Gunnels is not so dishonest as to claim that affirmative action belongs on the list.

Warren Gunnels
@GunnelsWarren

So why, according to Gunnels, does this super-popular progressive agenda not just carry the day at every election? Progressives tend to anchor on baroque conspiracy theories about “the establishment,” but the obvious explanation is that while voters like some progressive ideas, they hate other ones — notably including ones that progressive and mainstream Democrats agree on.

But at least Gunnels is aware that he shouldn’t put affirmative action on his list, right? So that’s good news about messaging. But then, as I mentioned yesterday, there’s this bizarre “D.E.I. is back!” take from Ro Khanna.

Ro Khanna
@RoKhanna
DEI is back!
5:24 AM · Nov 4, 2026 · 1.73M Views
3.39K Replies · 803 Reposts · 6.18K Likes

You could run this same play on the moderate side. Shake a moderate Democrat and he’ll tell you the party needs to focus like a laser on kitchen table issues and affordability and eschew politically toxic left-wing ideas like abolishing ICE. That’s fine as far as it goes, but few if any of them are daring enough to take this one on.

In research from David Broockman and Josh Kalla, moving to the center on race-based college admissions has a larger impact on electability than moving to the center on asylum claims or on trans girls playing on school sports teams. But none of the electability-minded moderates who’ve moved to the center on those issues want to move to the center on this other one that’s a bigger deal in electoral terms. And even stranger, none of the activists who are mad about Democrats moving to the center on the sports issue are advising them to pick something else — like affirmative action — that’s more potent instead. It’s basically the Moderation That Dare Not Speak Its Name. I once met a charismatic oyster farmer who was thinking about entering politics as a populist outsider, and I floated to him that this would be a great heterodox-but-populist stance that would be very popular with working-class voters in the whitest state in America, but he did not take me up on that idea and turned out to have some other flaws as a candidate.

Share

Eric: Does this mean the AI build out is dead?

I doubt it. If you ignore all the A.I. aspects of A.I. policy and just focus on the literal aspects of data center construction, here’s my basic model of what’s going on:

You start out at Time One and there is in fact relatively little interest in building data centers. The vast majority of people aren’t thinking about data centers at all, but if you show them a picture of one, they don’t want it near their house. Most politicians are also not thinking about data centers, because nobody is talking about this. The people who are thinking about data centers are a handful of construction contracting companies and building-trades labor unions who like the idea of having jobs. They shop legislation around to give tax breaks for data center construction, arguing plausibly that even net of the tax breaks, these things are strongly positive in fiscal terms. Some states or counties pass laws like that, others don’t, and data centers get built in places where they are politically welcome.

But as demand to build data centers starts ramping up, the political dynamics suddenly change.

It was previously the case that most places didn’t want data centers but also that not that many data centers were getting built. The minority of places that did want them were bidding against each other for the privilege of hosting them. As demand suddenly and unexpectedly soared, the competition dynamic ought to have flipped. Instead of local jurisdictions bidding against each other to offer the best possible tax deal to data center developers, developers ought to have been bidding against each other to offer the best fiscal deal to local jurisdictions. If the ramp up had occurred gradually over a 20-year time span, that could have been a gentle recalibration of the dynamic. Instead, you’re seeing very sudden, earthquake-like shocks that cause some weird political disruptions.

At the end of the day, though, it’s just still the case that data centers — similar to warehouses or shopping malls or any other large non-residential structure — are potentially useful fiscal assets that have something concrete to offer their host jurisdiction. The reason they are getting built, meanwhile, is that there is a lot of money in A.I. It just stands to reason that there is some appropriate flow of that money to local governments and to utility ratepayers that is win-win for everyone and that it will get worked out one way or another.

JM: Do you have thoughts on Mike Johnson’s time as speaker of the house? My impression of the narrative when he became speaker was that he is in over his head and is going to be dog-walked by bomb-throwers in his caucus. But over the last 2 years I feel like we haven’t heard much about him despite the very thin majority which seems like a point in his favor.

My most niche conspiracy theory is that I don’t believe that Mike Johnson exists at all.

You may remember that the whole Republican caucus was in total disarray over leadership selection when suddenly out of nowhere this “Mike Johnson” character emerged as a dark-horse compromise candidate. I had never heard of him until the very moment that happened, and I think the reason is that he’s not a real person. In their moment of despair, Republicans just decided they needed some fake guy to serve as figurehead leader, so they came up with the most generic name imaginable — it’s not even a Louisiana-sounding name, just kind of off-the-shelf white guy. Then they used A.I. to gin up some photos of a generic-looking politician guy, and they’ve been snowing us ever since.

After all, I’ve never met Mike Johnson — have you? As you say, you basically never hear anything about him. There’s no juicy reporting on his inner circle, no fun anecdotes, no sense of how he feels about JD Vance versus Marco Rubio. He’s a total enigma, as if he doesn’t exist at all — because he doesn’t!

Share

Paul G: This question may seem a little tone deaf given that it’s not election-related. But then again, maybe we all need some non-election content right now. One enduring beef I have with pundits is that many of them feel the need (whether personally or commercially) to opine on things they don’t really understand, resulting in weak, uninsightful, or just plain wrong analysis. Are there subjects you avoid writing about because they’re out of your depth, or areas you would like to write about but don’t because you don’t feel qualified to write about them?

Most foreign policy issues fall in this bucket.

I would love to do a piece about how the United States can constructively intervene in the conflict happening in the Tigray region of Ethiopia, but I have no idea. I’ve written a little bit about the civil war in Sudan, but I think my understanding of the U.A.E.’s interest in this is pretty superficial. I’ve read several articles about it, but I didn’t find the articles themselves to be very deep or probing, and I’ve never had the chance to really badger an expert about it and answer my questions to my own satisfaction.

But there’s not a ton of this stuff, because normally when I develop a strong desire to write about something, I set about to try to learn enough about it to write something.

When I first started writing about housing, for example, I had lived my whole life on the East Coast and had no idea about Western water issues. But these issues are very salient in Western housing policy, so I started to get questions about them. I tended to defer on the grounds that I didn’t really have a handle on that whole policy area, but it came up enough over time that I was motivated to learn about it and developed some conclusions.

Now I know that the real water-heads feel that my take on this is too simplistic. But I have the considered view that my take is actually good and correct and what’s happened here is that a community of expertise has grown up around a dumb system and has developed a kind of insular tunnel vision about how dumb it is.

Chris Granner: Matt—have you done an alt-history on “Bernie wins the nomination in 2016?”

I really want a Bernie fan to write one since I genuinely don’t understand what it is that they think would have happened. Like, say Bernie won the nomination and then beat Trump. And let’s be really generous and say this also flips the Senate elections in Wisconsin and Pennsylvania, so Bernie gets a Senate majority. This narrow majority confirms a Supreme Court justice to replace Antonin Scalia, which is a big deal. But what does the rest of the “political revolution” look like in a world where your Senate majority includes not just Joe Manchin but Joe Donnelly, Claire McCaskill, Heidi Heitkamp, and Jon Tester? Is Medicare for All happening?

Bernie’s 2016 campaign platform featured a carbon tax. Would that have happened?

I originally became a Twitter enemy of the Bernie faction mostly just because I spent the 2016 primary pointing out that obviously none of this was on the table and the whole perceived stakes of the primary were fake. It rubbed me the wrong way that the Bernie influencer community wouldn’t admit this even though it was obviously true, just like it rubs me the wrong way now that they won’t admit leftists underperform in electoral terms. In both cases, I don’t think the object-level factual dispute is the most important thing in the world. But these just are not difficult factual questions to judge — there was no path from “people vote differently in the 2016 Democratic Party primary” to “a single-payer health-care system in the style of Canada except with dental and vision benefits.” Beyond my annoyance, though, I would love for someone to spell out how the story of the Political Revolution doesn’t just end in a frustrating congressional term, a wipeout in 2018, and some very painful negotiations with Senate Republicans during Covid in 2020.

A Lesson for Republicans: Mean, Implausible Lies Do Not Win Elections

Without a positive message to run on, Republicans leaned into gratuitous personal insults of their opponents, thinking that’s worked for Trump before. But it didn’t, and doesn't.

Josh Barro
Nov 6
 
READ IN APP
 

Dear readers,

During the closing weeks of this campaign season, I was repeatedly dumbfounded by the way Republicans talked to voters about Democrats. Filled with contempt for their opponents, they spoke to voters as if they could not imagine anyone who did not share that contempt. They told nasty, mean, personal lies that they clearly expected their audiences to eat up. But the lies Republicans told weren’t plausible, they weren’t relevant to the issues voters cared about, and the gratuitousness of the lies just made Republicans even less likable than they already were.

The obvious example here is Vivek Ramaswamy’s disgusting attack ad against Ohio Governor-elect Amy Acton. But I actually want to start by talking about the bizarre tenor of the campaign against James Talarico, because I think it is the most vivid example of how Republicans lost the plot this cycle by failing to imagine a voter who wasn’t similarly consumed by hatred for Democrats.

The anti-Talarico messaging started with the obvious material: Texas Republicans seized on weird and unpopular statements and positions from his past, including comments that there are six biological sexes and that we would need to reduce meat consumption for carbon-footprint reasons. But Talarico, wisely, distanced himself from his old comments. He declared that there are only two sexes, admitted he had been “annoying” when he argued that the non-binary nature of God told us something important about public policy, and ate as much barbecue as he could on the campaign trail.

Nonetheless, Republicans persisted in falsely claiming Talarico was a vegan. They slapped him with the nicknames “low-T Talarico” and “Talafreako.” And when that didn’t work, they got weirder. A spokesperson for the Republican National Committee alleged that he had a “serious pedophile problem,” with the evidence for this incendiary claim being that he had offered to respond to text messages from his middle school students about their homework. Another RNC staffer cited an old Talarico post expressing excitement about a field trip he would lead with sixth grade boys to again imply he was a pedophile.

At a rally in October, Vice President JD Vance insinuated Talarico was gay, responding to a supporter who had shouted “I love you” with “I love you too, sir. In a totally platonic way, to be clear. I’m the vice president, not James Talarico.” (Talarico in fact has a girlfriend of four years.) Vance also engaged in the pedophile innuendo. He alleged that Talarico had “said something to the effect of ‘an 11-year-old in drag was a very beautiful thing,’” — this is an apparent reference to a Pride event Talarico once spoke at that also featured a child drag performer, though contrary to Vance’s claim, there’s no record that Talarico said anything about the drag performance or even saw it — and added that “people who say stuff like that tend to have some pretty unusual search histories.” (Vance then admitted that he was “just guessing.”)

Republicans also claimed Talarico — who is not trans — was trans. Top White House aide Stephen Miller called Talarico the “first transgender Senate candidate,” while Kari Lake, appointed by Trump to run Voice of America, suggested that Talarico had disappeared from the campaign trail in September to have a vaginoplasty. Other Republicans obsessed over a different theory of Talarico’s absence: That he had a mental breakdown and had checked into an institution in Ohio. (Talarico, a type-1 diabetic, had a rough case of the flu, and showed The New York Times video footage proving that he was at home in Austin during his time off the trail.)

Obviously, none of this worked. Talarico just won statewide in Texas by double digits, the first time any Democrat has won a statewide race there since 1994. But why did Republicans think a campaign of gratuitous, implausible and juvenile lies would work? And why did they keep trying it around the country?

Similarly to the Texas Senate race, Republican messaging against Amy Acton dripped with contempt. Vance attacked her as “a crazy person,” “an unstable maniac,” and a drunk. Her opponent Vivek Ramaswamy groused that she complained too much about having been abused as a child, saying Ohio deserved a governor with a positive vision instead of focusing so much on “what someone did to her.” And when Ramaswamy plucked Acton’s estranged mother out of the car where she was living with her cats to cut an ad calling Acton a liar,¹ Vance defended the ad, saying politics was “a tough business” and that he was “disgusted” by fellow Republicans who objected to the ad, declaring that they should “stop whining.” Ramaswamy was so convinced of the effectiveness of this nasty, unconvincing ad that he spent $4 million airing it across Ohio, before he went on to lose by a margin three points wider than GOP Senator Jon Husted. In South Carolina, Trump called Senator-elect Annie Andrews “Tranny Annie,” a nickname NRSC head Tim Scott also used for her. Needless to say, name calling didn’t work in that state either.

Obviously, Republicans are, at least in part, trying to repeat the success they had in 2024 attacking Democrats as extreme and out of touch on trans issues. But the reason the “Kamala is for they/them” ad was so devastating was that it was a clean hit: Harris really had argued that the government should pay for sex changes for prisoners (and immigration detainees), and in 2024, she was unwilling to either defend or repudiate that position. The ad stood up on that truth; it sent a credible message that she was reckless with taxpayer money, obsessed with niche identity issues, and overly attentive to the concerns of criminals. This cycle, candidates like Andrews and Talarico responded more effectively by renouncing unpopular positions; indeed, Andrews faced criticism from some trans activists for an ad in which she rejected “biological men” playing women’s sports.

Upgrade to paid

But the main thing to note here is that the “they/them” ad did not allege that Kamala Harris was herself transgender. Neither did it accuse her of having a penis or being a lesbian or a vegan or having checked into a mental institution — none of that would have made any sense, but it would have been in line with the bizarre and ineffective lying Republicans have been doing this cycle.

What I see happening in the Republican Party resembles a cargo cult. The original cargo cults, which emerged in Melanesia in the wake of World War II, involved native populations acting out the behaviors of Western military personnel in an effort to manifest the delivery of food and other supplies that had once been dropped by military forces. Similarly here, Republicans saw Trump tell mean lies and win elections; therefore, they believed that if they told mean lies, they would also win elections. But mean lies are not actually at the core of Trump’s appeal², and Trump also has better judgment than some of his imitators about when it is useful to lie — or, at least he sometimes does. He did, after all, defend Ramaswamy’s gross ad, too.

Everyone is wondering what exactly the Republican Party is going to look like after Trump is gone. Perhaps one thing they could do is stop being so dishonest, unpleasant, and mean? John Cornyn suggested as much in his I-told-you-so op-ed about the Republican wipeout in Texas, in which he complained that Republican primary voters have been actively seeking out candidates with repellent personalities:

A strange reverse personality test has taken root. If a candidate talks like an affable, reasonable person, he must be a sellout. If he makes bizarre comments or has past scandals, that’s considered authenticity… This is a losing mindset that Republicans must outgrow. It selects for nominees who can’t win general elections.

I hope that Tuesday’s repudiation of nasty liars at the ballot box will lead to a return of civil and polite candidacies in Republican politics.³ After all, treating others with courtesy and respect isn’t just the right thing to do — it’s also a more effective way to campaign than whatever all this was.

Very seriously,

Josh

Share

1

Remember, Acton and her mother agree that the two have not seen each other since Acton was 12, when Acton was removed from her mother’s care due to accusations of sexual abuse against her step-father, accusations for which he was arrested and charged prior to fleeing justice with Acton’s mother. Acton’s mother has faced legal problems and charges over the years, for fraud, animal neglect and other offenses. This is who Vivek Ramaswamy chose to make the face of his campaign!

2

Republicans and Democrats alike tend to overlook how Trump moved his party toward the center on Social Security, Medicare, gay rights and abortion while tapping into voter discontent over border chaos that establishment politicians disregarded. And then Trump himself overlooked how his political appeal had been built on promises of lower prices and no new Mideast wars. Trump has a very mixed record of political success, and his inattention to the promises that had produced those intermittent successes was the key reason Republicans were in no position to compete in these midterm elections.

3

Perhaps Utah Gov. Spencer Cox would like to run for president? The Republican Party could use some forthright Mormon virtue right about now.

content:
Bo French was just one among the many losers in last Tuesday’s statewide Democratic sweep in Texas.
 ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­  
 
Compact

Against Bo French-ism

By Charles Fain Lehman • 6 Nov 2026 View in browser
View in browser
Scott Menchin
 
 

Bo French was just one among the many losers in last Tuesday’s statewide Democratic sweep in Texas. French, who was running for a seat on the powerful Texas Railroad Commission (which regulates the state’s oil and gas industry), had attracted public outrage for an X post of a photo of Indian students at a UT Austin football game. “I heard UT graduation this year looked like this,” French wrote. “I didn’t believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.” 

It’s unclear whether French’s remarks were what cost him his election. Gov. Greg Abbott lost by roughly the same margin, and Senate nominee Ken Paxton by nearly twice as much. But all three performed worse than other statewide Republicans. And French measurably underperformed in South Asian areas, specifically.

For some, though, the obvious cause of Republicans’ comprehensive defeat was the demographic change that had alarmed French in the first place. “Demographics is destiny,” wrote commentator Benny Johnson, noting that Texas is fifty percentage points less white than it was in 1970. Greg Bovino, the former Border Patrol commander who led the crackdown in Minneapolis, blamed Abbott’s loss on votes from H-1B immigrants from India, of whom “70 to 80 percent vote democrat.” Other pundits piled on with the same message: Democrats won, in Texas and elsewhere, because non-white immigrants voted for them overwhelmingly.

The trouble with this argument is not just that it is wrong on the facts, although it is. Nor is the problem that these influencers are speaking some forbidden truth. The trouble, rather, is that their theory absolves Republicans of responsibility for their historic loss. When you blame an election on the inexorable march of demographic change, you erase the poor policy choices that caused the electorate to swing wildly against the GOP in just two years.

“Their theory absolves Republicans of responsibility for their historic loss.”

In a much-discussed 2019 essay, Sohrab Ahmari (who would go on to co-found Compact) diagnosed a pathology of the “Never Trump” right that he labeled “David French-ism,” after now-New York Times columnist David French. David French-ism, in Ahmari’s telling, is the compulsive love of principled losing, a tendency to be a stickler for rules and norms even if and when following those rules and norms allows the left to run roughshod over America. The Trump-inspired right, if it stood for anything, was then understood to be against David French-ism. What mattered was winning.

Today, parts of the post-Trump right have developed their own pathological love of losing. Call it Bo French-ism. This French-ism has found particular purchase on the online right, but also influence offline, especially on the mind of Elon Musk. While Bo French-ism did not cause Republicans’ historic loss, it threatens to cement it, by abandoning the nascent Trump coalition—a sustainable path forward for the GOP—in favor of the pleasures of pessimism.

Bo French-ism starts with the belief that, as Johnson put it (echoing many others before him) “demographics is destiny.” Devotees divide American electoral politics into whites (especially white men) who vote for the GOP; and everyone else, who votes for the Democrats. Thus the inference that, for example, Republicans’ historic loss in Mississippi’s and Kansas’s senate races are attributable to demographic change in those states. 

Implicit in this view is the idea that turnout, not persuasion, is what drives elections. To win, Bo French-ists tend to argue, conservatives should play to (what they believe to be) the base, rather than trying to pull the median voter into the coalition. Non-white voters’ are taken to be not only Democrats, but inalterably so—they can’t have their minds changed. Therefore, the most important factor is the ratio of white turnout to non-white turnout.

This theory of turnout affects how the new Frenchists think about political rhetoric. When French himself tweeted his alarm at seeing Indians having fun at a college football game, he was presumably trying to mobilize a base of voters who share that sentiment, even at the cost of upsetting Indians. These are the same people, presumably, that the Department of Homeland Security is trying to talk to when it promises 100 million deportations, or that Bovino was trying to impress with his fancy get-up in Minneapolis. In all of these cases, the goal is either to mobilize the base or—as often, if not more so—simply signal your commitment to principle, even at the expense of electoral success.

In all of this, the Bo French-ists demonstrate an interesting parallel with the DSA wing of the Democratic Party. Bernie Sanders Progressives, too, tend to emphasize turnout over persuasion, arguing that their policy priorities will mobilize the base even if they alienate the center. As my Manhattan Institute colleague Jesse Arm has noted, the GOP’s activist class is for the first time to the right of its voters, much as the Democrats’ activists have long been to their voters’ left. It’s thus no coincidence that the same attitude prevails among influential parts of both parties: the way to win is to go whole hog on what they believe.

What’s wrong with this theory? Whites do tend to vote for Republicans, while non-whites do tend to vote for Democrats. But these tendencies are not, contrary to the French-ists, immutable. That’s clear even in the most recent election. Exit polling finds, for example, that Latino men swung by 25 points, from voting majority Republican to voting majority Democrat, in just two years. Nor, for that matter, are whites an immoveable bloc for the GOP. Democrats won this cycle with the support of young whites generally and young white men specifically. That’s part of the steady loss of the GOP’s support among college-educated whites. 

Indeed, such shifting electoral preferences were central to Donald Trump’s victory in 2024. Trump gained enormous ground among non-white voters of all stripes, especially non-white men—a gain in turn that’s part of the GOP’s longer-term erosion of Democrats’ control of non-white voters. He accomplished this, moreover, not through racial and ethnic pandering, but through focusing on economic and culture-war issues where the median voter was aligned with him—rather than trying to focus on only his base. Ads talking about gender ideology, public safety, and inflation resonated with median Americans, not just the base, and helped propel Trump to victory.

Some will object that by criticizing this tendency, I am trying to censor discussion of the electoral effects of immigration. While I personally dislike French and others’ rhetoric, I also think reasonable people can have concerns with, and vote to address, the pace of immigration. Failure to recognize the electorate’s legitimate unhappiness with 11 million illegal border crossings in four years is part of how Kamala Harris lost to Donald Trump in 2024. 

Nor is it the case that Bo French-ism itself cost Republicans the 2026 midterms. That was plainly the combination of an unpopular war in Iran and ever-shifting tariffs contributing to the nation’s affordability crisis, compounded by the administration’s botched efforts at implementing its deportation agenda and the president’s shady dealings while in an office of public trust.

However, Bo French-ism is sufficiently influential in certain corners that it could cause the broader movement to fail to internalize the election’s lessons. It offers a ready-made, ideologically acceptable explanation not only for what happened, but for why all future elections will probably cash out the same way. It offers the tempting idea that the GOP doesn’t need to learn from its loss, or try to actually persuade Americans it’s worth letting the party govern again.  

There is a narcotic comfort in such complacency. But politics is about winning. That means assembling a durable majority coalition, including through persuasion. If Kansas and Mississippi can turn blue in just two years, then surely anybody’s votes are up for grabs. Conservatives should act like it.

The problem with the “zombie Reaganite” right, the Trump right used to say, is that they prefer losing on principle to winning. The trouble with the Bo French-ists is that they, too, would prefer to be beautiful losers.

Why Voters Turned Against MAGA

By Darel E. Paul • 5 Nov 2026 View in browser
View in browser
AP
 
 

It has been nearly twenty years since the United States last experienced a wave election. Contemporary hyperpartisanship suggested that big shifts in the House and Senate were a thing of the past, the detritus of a bygone era of median voters, candidate-centered campaigns, and competitive electoral districts.

Tuesday’s elections proved that big waves are still possible. NBC News projects that Democrats will take 258 seats in the House and perhaps fifty-six seats in the Senate. This would be the biggest partisan shift in the Senate since 2014 and the biggest in the House since 2010. The headlines write themselves. Democrats won every statewide election in Texas, their first US Senate election in South Carolina since 1998, their first trifecta (governor, state house, and state senate) in Pennsylvania since 1993, and their first Senate seat in Kansas since the Great Depression. The best social media summary came from an anonymous X account: “Pete Hegseth wanted people to watch a public execution, well they’re seeing it tonight.”

The most significant conclusion to draw from this election is that national populism, which promised prosperity through industrial policy, tariffs, and immigration restriction, is down and probably out. American voters have shown in two consecutive elections that they will not tolerate inflation, even the rather moderate 4 percent consumer inflation they have experienced over the last year. Obviously, the war in Iran is a source of the widespread voter discontent over prices. But so, too, are Trump’s aggressive tariffs and immigration policy. 

Before 2025, it was possible for national populists to project imaginary economic outcomes of its policies (as it does across Europe) without having to prove itself in power. After two years of Really Existing National Populism, voters can no longer do that. Keeping out Canadian lumber and Mexican construction workers drives up home-building prices, and voters seem to prefer cheap houses over Trump’s vision of national identity. Today, only 20 percent of Americans support the tariff status quo, while 60 percent are open to a partial or complete removal of Trump’s tariffs. Voters only marginally back Trump on immigration overall, and are strongly against his deportation policy. If they are smart and disciplined, Democrats will resume working toward more regular and controlled immigration with more naturalization of those immigrants, without replaying Biden’s disastrous open borders policy. They won’t have to work hard to sell this to moderate and independent voters skeptical of free trade and free flows of labor with the promise of affordability. The American swing voter dislikes globalization by name, but likes it in its effects.

“Winning a wave election doesn’t necessarily mean voters like your party.”

While basking in the glow of victory today, Democrats should curb their enthusiasm over the next two years. In a two-party system, winning a wave election doesn’t necessarily mean voters like your party or its platform. They may simply hate the other party and use yours as the only viable outlet for their anger. The wave against Trump and his loyalists drowned many state and local Republican candidates through no fault of their own, but typical conservative policy positions won multiple referenda across the country. Voters in California rejected a state wealth tax. Voters in North Carolina passed mandatory voter ID and a cap on property taxes. Voters in Iowa passed requirements for a legislative supermajority to increase income taxes. Voters in Arizona, Washington, and Colorado are likely to require student-athletes in their states to compete on teams that accord with biological sex. All this suggests that many Democrats probably won on Tuesday despite themselves. They would do well to admit this if only to themselves.

Democrats’ prospects in 2028 obviously depend in part on their behavior over the next two years, but the implications of mischief in the legislative branch pale in comparison to the implications of mischief in the executive. The second Trump administration is proof positive of that. If Republicans nominate Vice President JD Vance or a member of the Trump cabinet in 2028, the next presidential election will be fought on the same grounds as the midterm elections. It will be a second referendum on the Trump years, and will produce an outcome similar to what we’ve just witnessed.

The near future for social conservatives looks grim. Many immediately noticed that they are probably staring down the barrel of two conservative Supreme Court justice retirements within the next six years. The chance of Republicans having a Senate majority before 2031 is zero and before 2033 is low. Appointing someone as conservative as Clarence Thomas or Samuel Alito will therefore be a complete nonstarter. The 2026 midterms showed that, when put to a popular vote, social libertarianism usually wins. An attempt to repeal the constitutional right to abortion in Missouri failed by ten points. Both Virginia and Nevada voters constitutionalized the right to abortion by very comfortable margins, although a similar measure failed in Idaho. The attempt to ban the sale of recreational marijuana in Massachusetts flopped 39-61. Nebraskans’ refusal to legalize sports gambling was a notable exception to the trend.

The Iran war is not the only reason national populism has failed to deliver. Perhaps two years in the headwinds of a foreign policy fiasco is an unfair test, but that is the test our constitution requires any policy agenda to pass. January 3, 2027 is the beginning of the end of the Trump era. Democrats and Republicans alike have spent a decade alternately lamenting and celebrating the indelible imprint he has made on the country. But national populism has now had its day in court, and the jury has found its arguments wanting. One day, perhaps in the early 2030s, long after the plans for a triumphal arch have been mothballed, the War Department has returned to the job of defense, immigration levels started increasing again, and Liberation Day tariffs have been eliminated on all but China and Russia, the only sign that Donald Trump was ever president of the United States may be the size of the national debt.
