Is the Democratic Majority Finally Emerging?

By John B. Judis • 5 Nov 2026 View in browser
View in browser
Scott Menchin
 
 

In our 2002 book The Emerging Democratic Majority, Ruy Teixeira and I argued that if Democrats continued to gain middle-class professionals and the growing minority vote, while maintaining sufficient support—we estimated 40 percent—among the white working class, they could rebuild the enduring majority they enjoyed between 1932 to 1968. Since the collapse of that majority, American politics has been on a teeter-totter where it has not had a dominant party. One party has held control of the presidency and both houses of Congress for only fourteen of the last forty-six years. Since the 2008 election, power has changed hands in one of these three centers of power in every biennial election. Power has been elusive. The electorate has been volatile. In that sense, the 2026 midterms were not unusual.

“Power has been elusive.”

But in another respect, they were unusual—and we should therefore ask again whether a new Democratic majority is on the horizon. Since 1954, both chambers have changed hands in an election only three times: in 1994, 2006, and 2026. The 1994 election completed the realignment of the South to the Republicans, which had been delayed by Watergate. That realignment had a lasting impact on the electoral map: The automatic Democratic hold on seats in Southern states was gone. In 2006, the backlash to George W. Bush’s disastrous foreign policy adventures set up Democrats to further press their advantage in 2008, but most of those gains were wiped out in the 2010 midterms. It was back to the teeter-totter. 

Does this week’s midterm result more closely resemble 1994 or 2006? I think the answer is obvious. The Democrats would have probably picked up seats if a different Republican had been president, but it was Donald Trump’s performance in office that triggered the tsunami that has engulfed his party. In 2016 and 2024, Trump ran and won on a program that included securing America’s border while deporting those who had committed crimes; using tariffs and tax expenditures to revive American manufacturing; “draining the swamp”; eliminating the excesses of what Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez recently called “Woke 1.0”; ending (not starting) “forever wars”; and “drill baby drill” to push down oil prices. But the law-and-order appeal of Trump’s immigration approach has been clouded by ICE’s killing of Americans. Instead of a coherent plan to revive manufacturing, we have an arbitrary and erratic tariff regime. Instead of draining the swamp, Trump has overseen the spread of corruption. The list goes on.

Trump’s behavior during the recent campaign was purely self-destructive when it came to his party’s own interests. He forced out senators in North Carolina, Iowa, and Texas who might have won re-election, and championed others in South Carolina, Texas, and Georgia who were destined to lose. And he forced Vivek Ramaswamy down the throats of Ohio's Republicans. In late October, he told voters to “pretend I am on the ballot.” But after the rout became clear, he assured voters that “I wasn’t on the ballot, and if I was, we could have won IN A LANDSLIDE.”

Although the scale of their victory owes so much to Trump’s missteps, the Democrats have a chance, as they did after the 2006 and 2008 elections, to create an advantage for themselves that could outlast the current gains—to get America off the teeter-totter. The election showed that it was possible for Democrats to win a majority even in the new America created by southward shifts in population and industry. Barack Obama and his administration failed to do it because they were unprepared to do what Franklin Roosevelt managed beginning in 1933: to stem a steep economic downturn and financial crisis and forge a winning coalition in the process. Today, America once again finds itself in a quagmire, although of a different variety. Will the Democrats, in the coming years, find a way out that builds a lasting majority? 

 

The political history of California may soon play out elsewhere on the national stage. For most of the last century, the state’s two parties traded off control of its major offices. Think of the governors: Pat Brown (D) was followed by Ronald Reagan (R), Jerry Brown (D), George Deukmejian (R), Pete Wilson (R), and then Gray Davis (D). Many of the Republicans enjoyed Hispanic support. In 1986, 46 percent of Hispanics voted for George Deukmejian; in 1990, 47 percent for Wilson. But in 1994, Wilson, behind in the polls, enthusiastically backed a Republican measure, Proposition 187, that would have denied public services to illegal immigrants. The campaign was waged with xenophobic language and imagery. About 75 percent of Hispanics opposed it, but it passed narrowly. California Hispanics abandoned the GOP in droves and have never come back. In 1996, the Republicans lost the state assembly and have never won either house of the state legislature since then.  

Add one other factor in California becoming solidly Democratic. California Republicans always had a powerful moderate segment, even when Reagan was governor. Wilson was thought to be a moderate and in 2010, he was the campaign co-chair of another Republican moderate, Meg Whitman, when she ran unsuccessfully for governor against Jerry Brown. Moderate Republicans dominated much of the suburban vote in the state. But they began to disappear and are now extinct, and the great metro areas of the state around Los Angeles, San Francisco, Sacramento, San Jose, and San Diego have become Democratic. Add that to the Hispanic defection, and you have a solid Democratic majority.

“If you look at Texas today, there are hints of the same trends.”

If you look at Texas today, there are hints of the same trends. Republican governors in the state, beginning with George W. Bush in 1991, did reasonably well with Hispanic voters. In Governor Greg Abbott’s first gubernatorial race in 2014 against Democrat Wendy Davis, he won 44 percent of the vote and actually won Latino men, 49 to 48 percent. In 2024, Donald Trump famously won several predominantly Hispanic counties in the Rio Grande Valley, and Republican legislators redistricted Republican Congressional seats on the assumption that they could win the Hispanic vote. But this year, in the face of Hispanic fury at ICE’s conduct and Trump’s failure to fix the economy, they completely abandoned the Republicans. In the Senate race, James Talarico won the Hispanic vote by 70-29, a forty-two-percentage point swing from 2024. The counties that went Republican in 2024 went back to the Democrats. Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa enjoyed similar success.

The other factor in Talarico’s and Hinojosa’s victories was their success in Texas’s huge metroplexes. As the political analyst Sean Trende has pointed out, Texas may have large stretches of sparsely populated land, but about half the population now lives in eight metro big counties that combine city and suburb. These counties have been moving from the Republican to the Democratic column in the last fifteen years, and Talarico routed Paxton there. For instance, he won Dallas by 72 to 26 percent; Harris (Houston) by 66 to 33 percent; he won a Dallas suburb, Collin, which Trump won in 2020 and 2024, by 55-43 percent. Hinojosa also won these counties, but by slightly smaller margins. If Democrats can hold these metroplexes and the Hispanic vote in Texas, they have a good chance of turning Texas from a dependably Republican state to a swing state, if not a reliably blue one. 

There are other states where a version of the same story is being told. In Georgia, North Carolina, and Virginia, Democrats have benefited from the growth of Democratic-leaning metroplexes. The suburbs around Atlanta were once dependably Republican. Newt Gingrich once represented Cobb County, north of Atlanta; Democrat Jon Ossoff won it by 67 to 33 percent in the Senate race. There are even hints of change in states like Mississippi, where Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom is leading incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith. Colom benefited by heavy black turnout partly in reaction to Trump's redistricting efforts, sanctioned by a Republican-dominated Supreme Court, which eliminated in black majority districts across the state. He won majority-black Jackson easily, but he also edged out Hyde-Smith in Jackson's majority-white suburban Madison County, which Trump won easily in 2024.

A durable Democratic majority didn’t emerge after 2008 because the party lost too much of the white working class—or as I would now put it, of voters outside the metroplexes. In 2026, they again have the makings of that majority. The New York Times data on voter trends finds that Democrats got 40 percent nationally of the white working-class vote. That could be the beginning of a beautiful marriage—or it could lead, as it did previously, to another messy divorce.

How Lindsey Graham Lost the Midterms

By Daniel McCarthy • 4 Nov 2026 View in browser
View in browser
AP
 
 

The biggest political loser of the 2026 midterms wasn’t even on the ballot—because he’d died nearly four months earlier. This election was not so much a referendum on Donald Trump as it was a referendum on Sen. Lindsey Graham. The Republican Party that faced voters on Nov. 3 was not the party Trump led on election night 2024. It was instead a GOP defined by the late Senator Graham’s vision of the party, which the Trump administration had unwisely, indeed unfathomably, chosen to adopt as its own.

Trump had a successful formula. Why did he change it? 

His critics will insist he didn’t: He was judged on his record of immigration enforcement, tariffs, and zero tolerance of Iran’s nuclear ambitions. These were themes he campaigned on two years ago, and in the time since then his administration has delivered dramatically hardline policies on all three of those fronts. Voters in 2024 just didn’t know what they were getting into, and this year, after they’d seen the results, they turned against the party of the man they had restored to the White House at the last election.

Trump won every battleground state in 2024. This year, Republicans lost even in many of the reddest states, including Texas, Kansas, and Ohio. It’s a complete reversal, and people who never supported any of Trump’s policies in the first place naturally want to see this election as a repudiation of the last one. This time the verdict is final—though last time, when it went against the anti-populists’ interests, it was not. The game stops when the right team is ahead. 

But a midterm election is less than a presidential election, no matter how striking its results may be. Bill Clinton’s party lost the House and Senate in 1994, yet he easily won re-election in 1996. He was more than just a political winner: Clintonism, a blend of statist liberalism, market liberalism, the use of military force in support of the “liberal international order,” and acceptance of homosexuality and recreational drug use, prevailed for the next twenty years despite Republican congresses and a two-term Republican president sandwiched between the Clinton and Obama administrations. Clintonism didn’t vanish even after Trump’s election in 2016, and its influence lingers today.

“Clintonism didn’t vanish.”

Trumpism will face many more tests after this week, and not even the 2028 presidential election will be the last of them. Nor was 2016 the beginning of Trumpism—before Trump, it was the right-of-center anti-globalism common to Pat Buchanan and Ross Perot in the 1990s. Restricting immigration, advantaging America’s industrial workforce and production over foreign rivals, and a foreign policy that does not involve unending large-scale interventions in the Middle East is a program that would not soon disappear from American politics even if this year’s midterms had been a retrial of the 2024 election.

What was actually placed before voters this year was, however, something quite different from the Trump program or 2016 or 2024. That program had been “America First” in the sense of putting domestic priorities first. This year, the Trump administration went to war, and the war has had drastic consequences for the economy, fueling inflation and making voters feel as if they were re-living the Joe Biden years. Donald Trump knows better than anyone just what Americans think about Biden. He also knows how they feel about wars in the Middle East. 

But this year it was the Republicans who were the party of the “Biden economy,” as well as the party of a foreign policy voters repudiated as long ago as 2006, when Democrats did to George W. Bush’s party what they have now done to Trump’s GOP. What made Trump turn away from his own successes, as recently as two years back, to give voters a Republican party of the mid-2000s instead?

 

The answer lies with the late senator from South Carolina. Lindsey Graham imagined a winning coalition yet bigger than Trump’s. It would be a coalition consisting of Trump voters and Bush voters, or perhaps, more aptly, John McCain voters. It would be the Republican party times two, the old and the new together. Graham, himself a representative of the old guard—not only in his foreign policy but also in his history as an immigration dove in the Senate’s “Gang of Eight,” which also included McCain and Rubio—would assemble the grand coalition by becoming one of Trump’s most enthusiastic allies, while in return he would ask Trump to grant the fondest wish of the old-guard hawks and deliver the war with Iran they had long sought.

Trump didn’t have to concede anything: He was already an Iran hawk. The Graham design would just make him more of one. The Israelis would approve, and so would the whole world once the tyrannical regime in Tehran was defanged or destroyed. Trump would have the glory of beating the old Bush and McCain Republicans at their own game, doing what they never could or would, just as he had easily moved the US Embassy in Israel from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem. Graham made it all sound so simple, so plausible. 

The point here is not to single out the late senator for his role in persuading Trump to launch a major campaign against Iran. The personal aspect is one thing—what’s more significant is the ideological vision. Most neoconservatives and Republican internationalists were allergic to Trump from the start, and many have deported themselves out of the Republican coalition and the conservative movement in reaction against Trump. Hardly anyone else dared dream of what Graham imagined, a Trump GOP that could also be John McCain’s. Graham believed in that combination passionately, and he evangelized for it relentlessly. He won converts, including the one that mattered most.

“Beating the establishment was easy.”

Beating the establishment was easy, and Trump was enticed by the possibility of more. The old guard would come to love him the way Lindsey did. And if they didn’t, it was only because they prioritized their hatred of him over dedication to the success of their very own principles. Yet that did not have to be the case; they could be like Lindsey Graham. Even in his first term Trump seemed to take pride in gaining the loyalty of the defeated GOP establishment. His first impulse in this year’s primary season wasn’t to support Ken Paxton for Senate in Texas, but to back the incumbent, Sen. John Cornyn. After Lindsey Graham died, Trump sought to replace him in the Senate with the closest approximation possible, his sister Darline. 

The story here is more interesting than the hackneyed narrative promoted by Democratic partisans and pundits. It’s not the case that Paxton beat Cornyn in the primary because of Trump, and Cornyn would have beaten Talarico in the general election. That storyline is convenient if everything has to be Trump’s fault. But Trump only backed Paxton once Texas Republican voters had already made it clear they were prepared to dump Cornyn. And Cornyn, who couldn’t survive a primary within his own party, would not likely have been spared the fate of the rest of the ticket if he had somehow made it to the general election. Tuesday’s results nationwide ended the careers of many a moderate, old-guard Republican, as well as those of figures like Paxton.

Darline Graham showed her complete inexperience in debates and on the campaign trail, but the story isn’t just that she was rejected by South Carolina’s voters as a whole, she was opposed by the more conservative Republican she had defeated in the party primary, Ralph Norman. Would someone like Cornyn have been well-positioned to win the general election if Paxton had dropped out of the primary but the party’s right-wing continued to oppose him? Would Paxton have been able to pull through in the general election if Cornyn had supported him? Looking at the midterms as a whole, the answers are pretty plain. Fratricidal tendencies hurt the GOP across the map, but even party unity could not overcome the party’s overwhelming unpopularity in the face of high prices at the gas station and in the supermarket. And voters understood those prices were among the costs of Lindsey Graham’s war.

His sister lost, and Graham did not live to see the judgment rendered upon his projects: the war itself, and the political coalition he imagined would be stronger for waging it. Trump was charmed by the mirage. The reality is very cold—and very different from the success Trump enjoyed when he followed his own formula and not the South Carolina senator’s.

Compact

MAHA’s Identity Crisis

By David Moulton • 3 Nov 2026 View in browser
View in browser
AP
 
 

In late October, Calley Means resigned from his position as senior advisor to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. One of the architects of the Make America Healthy Again movement, Means has continued to praise both Kennedy and President Trump since his departure, but according to Politico and The New York Times, he stepped down out of frustration that the White House was siding with pesticide manufacturers, at odds with the movement’s priorities. It was just one sign that, two years into its alliance with Trump’s GOP, MAHA is going through an identity crisis. As The Wall Street Journal recently reported, MAHA-aligned donors and PACS have largely steered clear of the midterm elections. 

By some criteria, MAHA has been a success. In just a few years, it went from being a minor dissident movement to having key allies in the White House and Congress. However, many now seem to feel disillusioned by the compromises that go along with being part of the establishment. A MAHA summit held in Washington in September provoked a backlash from grassroots activists appalled by the sponsorship of corporate giants like WalMart and UnitedHealth. None of this should surprise us. MAHA was destined to disappoint because of the political and philosophical contradictions at its core. 

“The movement’s politics never fit neatly into America’s partisan landscape.”

The movement’s politics never fit neatly into America’s partisan landscape. Kennedy was a lifelong Democrat before he campaigned for president as an independent, and was then successfully wooed by the Trump campaign after his withdrawal from the race. Kennedy’s central message is that corporate America has been putting toxins in our food, medicine, and environment for decades, and that as a result of this process, Americans have developed all kinds of chronic illnesses. On the face of it, this sounds like a left-wing message. Democrats traditionally have been the party of protecting the environment as well as regulating the food and drug industry. 

It was the politics of Covid that changed that. RFK gained prominence in the early 2020s from his opposition to the Covid vaccines. At the height of the pandemic, he published The Real Anthony Fauci, which became a bestseller. At the time, Americans were bitterly divided over their trust in scientific consensus and medical institutions. Many Democrats, including the president of the United States, had suggested that Americans should have to be vaccinated to keep their jobs and participate in public life. Kennedy spoke against such medical coercion, setting him at odds with the party with which his family’s name was so closely associated. 

Although I never voted for RFK or contributed to his campaign, in a sense I’ve been a “fellow traveler” of MAHA. Over the course of 2020, I concluded that we had let the institutions of medicine and public health reorganize all of society for the sake of suppressing a single virus. In practice, this meant closing schools and businesses, silencing dissent, and requiring people to wear masks, and refusing to consider any of the trade-offs involved. When the vaccines appeared in 2021, they were touted as miracle drugs, but they turned out not to be as effective as advertised at halting the spread of the virus, and much of society continued to be shut down. I can vividly recall the despair of wondering if and when normal life would ever return. As a lifelong leftist, I felt especially isolated knowing so much of the support for lockdowns came from my own political faction. RFK’s ascent indicated that I wasn’t alone. 

However, the book’s flaws may offer some insight into the impasse of the movement it helped inspire. Kennedy tries to give the reader a genealogy of the Covid crisis, but his analysis often does not stand up to scrutiny. His outrage at the establishment is so intense that it often leads him to advance mutually incompatible lines of argument. For instance, one of the book’s most controversial parts is Kennedy’s attempt to rehabilitate the Berkeley biochemist Peter Duesberg. Once a highly respected figure in his field, in the late ’80s Duesberg became notorious for disputing the idea that the retrovirus HIV was the cause of AIDS. In his view, AIDS was not a communicable disease at all, but rather the result of a lifestyle of heavy drug use. Duesberg was roundly denounced as a “denialist” and murderer by Anthony Fauci and others.

Kennedy sees Fauci’s suppression of Duesberg as a precedent for the censorship of opposing views during Covid. I think there is something to this argument, but there are problems with the way Kennedy goes about making it. The mainstream history of AIDS would have us believe that Fauci and the establishment acted far too slowly in recognizing the cause of AIDS and approving drugs to fight it. Duesberg and other dissidents argued the opposite: that the establishment had settled too quickly on a single cause of the disease. Setting aside the question of who is right, both the mainstream and dissident version of AIDS history are internally coherent. Kennedy, in contrast, wants them both to be right simultaneously because they both make Fauci look bad. 

Kennedy writes that because the scientific establishment delayed the announcement that HIV was the cause of AIDS until 1984, “thousands of hospital patients and hemophiliacs received tainted blood from blood banks, and many of the already infected unwittingly spread the virus.” Never mind that in the very same chapter, he also says Duesberg was right to question whether HIV was the cause of AIDS in 1987 and for years afterwards. Moreover, Kennedy argues that the first antibody tests for HIV were useless. It’s unclear, therefore, why he would be upset that these tests weren’t used sooner. AIDS is a mind-bendingly complicated medical controversy, and I don’t begrudge anyone for not being sure what to think. The problem is that instead of expressing doubt or nuance, Kennedy appears to be absolutely convinced of contradictory things. 

This ambivalence points to a fundamental incoherence at the heart of his critique of the medical establishment. As much as Kennedy rails against that establishment, he shares a number of its assumptions. For instance, in his book’s first chapter, Kennedy claims that the early use of Ivermectin and Hydroxychloroquine could have prevented hundreds of thousands of deaths in America. Not only is this empirically false, it is the mirror image of the establishment’s similarly false claim that Covid could have been eradicated if only everyone wore masks and got vaccinated. Kennedy can never decide if the problem is too much medicine or not enough. 

A more serious critique would have questioned whether preventing all death from Covid was even the right goal. Coronavirus was a pathogen that overwhelmingly targeted the elderly. A large number of those who died were nursing home residents already at the end of life. These people deserved to be able to die with peace and dignity. The vain attempt to keep them alive at all costs led to grotesque scenarios in which they were forced to die in isolation without seeing their loved ones. We need to be able to acknowledge our mortality; the failure to do so only leads to more suffering in the end. 

Kennedy’s other key concern, central to the MAHA agenda, is the explosion of chronic conditions among Americans since the eighties. Even though I think he is right to call attention to this alarming trend, here again his analysis has major problems. Kennedy generally avoids the complex social, cultural, and environmental factors that have led to more and more Americans becoming sick and disabled. Instead, he is always searching for the single external factor that causes disorder. The most famous example of this is his fixation on the idea that autism is caused by mercury poisoning in vaccines. 

Kennedy is aware of the concept of iatrogenesis, or medicine-created illness. He uses the adjective iatrogenic when describing the ghastly side effects of early AIDS medication. However, he misses the point that iatrogenesis isn’t always just a chemical process; it can also be social and cultural. More and more people learn to see their problems in life as illnesses, which leads to increasing dependence on the medical system and the creeping medicalization of everyday life. In my view, social iatrogenesis is the most plausible explanation for the growth in disability and mental illness. But in Kennedy’s worldview, the individual toxin becomes a scapegoat for all kinds of problems in life. This leads him to foster false hope—in the same way the pharmaceutical industry pushes new drugs with the promise that they will restore health. Kennedy would have us believe that America will be healthy again if we’re just able to eliminate all the bad agents making us sick. 

 

The confusion of RFK’s thought has been matched by the incoherence of MAHA as a political movement. In 2024, it attached itself to MAGA, despite the fact Donald Trump had never given any prior indication of caring about nutrition or the environment. The Republican Party has always been in favor of deregulation, and in this respect Trump acted as a typical Republican during his first term. Despite his lip service to RFK’s concerns, Trump again appointed industry insiders and former lobbyists to key positions. Soon after he took office in 2025, his EPA lowered protections on mercury in the environment. Previously this had been Kennedy’s signature issue, but now that he himself was part of the administration he did not object.

It’s tempting to say that MAHA were played for dupes by the GOP, but this is only half the story. The other half is that during the Covid years, the Democrats became the enforcers of scientific orthodoxy and defenders of the pharmaceutical industry. Mainstream liberal opinion became almost cartoonishly hateful towards anyone wary of these views, with one Los Angeles Times op-ed even suggesting it was good to mock the deaths of the unvaccinated. The left tried to paint all Covid dissent as rightwing. While this wasn’t accurate initially, the left made it true by driving everyone with a different view into the arms of the right. I can personally attest to this. I voted Republican for the first time in my life during the 2022 midterms as a way to punish the Democrats for having become the party of maximalist Covid madness. 

“I’ve maintained my independence, and so, it seems, have many MAHA fans.”

A one-time protest vote didn’t turn me into a loyal Republican. I’ve maintained my independence, and so, it seems, have many MAHA fans. As the MAHA-MAGA alliance unravels, their votes may be up for grabs. Progressive Democrats like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Abdul El-Sayed have tried to incorporate aspects of MAHA into their own platforms. Yet bitterness over Democrats’ draconian Covid policies and attitudes still lingers. As a former Kennedy speechwriter remarked, “The only thing that is holding MAHA in the Republican camp is, perversely, the Democrats’ reflexive hostility toward it.”

Far too often, the content of American politics is arbitrary and purely relational. Democrats believe things because they’re the opposite of what Republicans believe and vice versa. During the pandemic, someone close to me said he liked to wear a mask as a way to piss off people who don’t like masks. I suspect this attitude was common. Even as our principles keep changing, however, the form of our politics stays the same. The bipartisan system remains robust. Dissident energy easily gets channeled into get-out-the-vote campaigns. Then, when the opposition party comes to power again, dissent is easily co-opted and incorporated into the establishment. 

This is a bitter pill to swallow. Today I generally try to avoid politics, but I still feel strongly that the Covid era exposed the emptiness of scientific consensus and the harms perpetrated by the medical establishment. For all his flaws, Kennedy did give voice to the dread so many of us shared at a crucial moment. I hope that in the future, someone will be able to channel these concerns into a more coherent political project.

Vivek and the End of Meritocracy

By Travis Alexander • 2 Nov 2026 View in browser
View in browser
Gage Skidmore / CC BY-SA 2.0
 
 

For decades, the achievements of South Asian immigrants were celebrated across the political spectrum as proof that the combination of liberalized immigration policies and meritocracy could bolster the American imperium. No one embodied this ideal better than Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee for Ohio governor. The son of Indian immigrants—an engineer and a psychiatrist—he earned degrees from Harvard and Yale before co-founding a biotech startup. Ramaswamy was well-positioned to demonstrate that America’s greatness lay in its recruitment of global talent. His 2024 presidential campaign attempted to leverage that proposition into politics.

His timing was bad. By the time he came on the scene, much of the GOP was souring on the globalist consensus that previously had made the immigrant entrepreneur one of its favorite advertisements. The more stridently Ramaswamy defended the old paradigm, the more the immune system of the movement he had embraced treated him like a foreign body.

“His timing was bad.”

Ramaswamy saw the shift coming and tried to get ahead of it. During his presidential run, he called the H-1B system “a form of indentured servitude” and promised to “gut” it, though his own company, Roivant, had used the program twenty-nine times. His proposed replacement, however, was revealing: “The lottery system needs to be replaced by actual meritocratic admission.” He wanted fewer H-1Bs, but more merit. 

The right’s working consensus on high-skill immigration fractured irreparably around December 2024, when Trump named the Chennai-born venture capitalist Sriram Krishnan as his senior adviser on AI. Laura Loomer called the pick “deeply disturbing,” and the right’s restrictionist wing followed her lead. Elon Musk and Ramaswamy, jointly tapped to lead the newly formed Department of Government Efficiency, rushed to the defense of the H-1B program. Musk wanted the world’s best engineering talent—tech’s “Jokićs and Wembys.” 

Ramaswamy went further. American culture, he declared in an X post that became infamous, “has venerated mediocrity over excellence for way too long.” It had celebrated “the prom queen over the math olympiad champ” to its disadvantage. 

The backlash against Ramaswamy and Musk revealed just how large a swath of the right preferred the prom queen. Even former South Carolina Governor and 2024 presidential candidate Nikki Haley, herself the daughter of Indian immigrants, sided with the restrictionists, holding that “we should be investing and prioritizing in Americans, not foreign workers.” By Inauguration Day, Ramaswamy had left DOGE to run for the governorship of his home state. And by September 2025, the administration had imposed a $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions—a measure that subsequently became mired in litigation. First as online farce, then—at least from Ramaswamy’s perspective—as policy tragedy. 

Ramaswamy, it seemed, had bet on the premise—not so strange, really, until recently—that America’s national interest could be advanced by the productivity of anyone willing to contribute to it. The restrictionist wing of the America First movement, conversely, held that nations owe their first and final obligations to their “legacy” citizens, regardless of the value loss their promotion represents.

These debates came out into the open after Bo French, the Republican nominee for Texas railroad commissioner, complained on X about the number of South Asian students attending a University of Texas football game. In a podcast with Christopher Rufo, the right-wing publisher Jonathan Keeperman explained the controversy by saying that because Indians have become the “symbolic node” of twentieth- and twenty-first-century mass immigration, they are “bearing the brunt” of the right’s displeasure with the Hart-Celler regime. 

This observation helps clarify a changing dynamic on the American right that can otherwise be encrypted in meme warfare and buried under avalanches of irony. It is a turn away from the utilitarian notion that attracting top talent is a boon to American power and toward more categorical thinking about duty and first principles. It might be necessary, said Keeperman, “to incur some costs for keeping some amount of immigrants out who are high-skilled and might be a benefit to the economy.” He went on to say: “I like having a high-trust society.” It’s not that merit, in other words, has been wrongly calculated. It’s that merit is a second-order good.

The restrictionists face an awkward problem: What is to be done with America First’s own Indian Americans? Keeperman’s answer is to claim the exceptions. “You’re going to go after Usha Vance? … Harmeet Dhillon? Give me a break, man. These people are incredible patriots.” But their welcome is conditional. What would help, he says, is “prominent Indian-Americans, people in Vivek’s situation… making public statements” that “indicate to Americans: no, like, we’re on your side here.” 

Ramaswamy has spent years making precisely such declarations of allegiance. His presidential campaign was an extended performance of something approaching patriotic camp, his political identity inseparable from his unencumbered readiness to eulogize America’s civilizational exceptionalism. But that dog won’t hunt so long as the new demand isn’t simply that he profess his loyalty but that he disavow the vision of American greatness that made his own biography possible. The immigrant success story is welcome, apparently, provided it no longer serves as an argument for the system that produced it.

A year after the “prom queen” debacle, Ramaswamy answered his critics. “Americanness isn’t a scalar quality that varies based on your ancestry,” he wrote in The New York Times. Two days later, at Turning Point’s AmericaFest, he went further: “The idea that a ‘heritage American’ is more American than another American is un-American at its core.” It was a declaration of loyalty, but for the restrictionists, it expressed the wrong sort of allegiance—to the creedal America they repudiate. 

Indian Americans aren’t the first group that has come to embody the contradictions of a changing socioeconomic order. In his classic account of modern antisemitism, Moishe Postone argued that the figure of the Jew, in the antisemitic imagination, personified capitalism’s abstract dimension: money, circulation, mobility, the apparently placeless power of value itself. The historical experiences of European Jews and Indian Americans, it goes without saying, are hardly comparable; but the mechanism of personification is. There is a symbolic operation taking place in the American right whereby the successful Indian-American becomes globalization made flesh: the mobile talent whose arrival signifies the displacement of the rooted American. 

Nor is the right alone in revising its relationship to the Indian-American success story. The inversion has taken an almost opposite form on the left. If the Indian American has become an emblem of meritocracy’s dysfunction for the restrictionist right, he can serve for segments of the socialist left as an especially satisfying agent of meritocratic renunciation. 

Consider Vivek’s doppelgänger: the progressive political strategist Saikat Chakrabarti. Another son of immigrants, Chakrabarti was an early engineer at Stripe, where he accumulated a fortune before leaving Silicon Valley to work on the Bernie Sanders campaign. He then co-founded Justice Democrats and served as AOC’s chief of staff after helping propel her campaign to victory. 

Chakrabarti calls himself a “class traitor.” Here, globalization’s exemplary subject is deriving a political identity from an act of public repudiation of the ideal of upward mobility inertially attached to him. The satisfaction this character arc makes available to the left is, in miniature, the pleasure of finally seeing capital buckle under the weight of its own accelerated antagonisms.

Needless to say, neither Chakrabarti nor other leading South Asian progressives—from Jacobin founder Bhaskar Sunkara to Rep. Pramila Jayapal or New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani—need to present themselves explicitly in these terms. The point, rather, is that their prominence can function as a kind of symbolic exorcism of the older meritocratic immigrant ideal, while modeling a different position, at odds with the waning neoliberal order.

 

Ramaswamy’s predicament is that he has pledged loyalty to MAGA without renouncing the meritocratic worldview, which much of the movement now views as a toxic residuum. The contradiction registers the difficulty of reconciling two distinct paradigms of national greatness: one in which America triumphs by drawing the world’s talent into its productive machinery, and another in which the pursuit of such efficiencies balkanizes and enervates the nation.

This contradiction is evident in his campaign for governor of Ohio. Ramaswamy carries Trump’s endorsement as the GOP nominee in a state that has trended firmly Republican since Obama left office. He won the primary with 82 percent of the vote, even as his obscure opponent, Casey Putsch, drew nearly a fifth of the vote while calling Ramaswamy an “anchor baby” and joking about a “cowboys vs. Indians” fight, clarifying his meaning: “feather, not dot.” Ramaswamy’s general election contest with Democrat Amy Acton has proved unexpectedly difficult. As of mid-October, several major polls had Acton ahead by four to five points. 

“A structural verdict has already been rendered.”

None of this proves that it’s Vivek’s defense of meritocracy that Ohio Republicans have rejected. His campaign has generated controversies having nothing to do with immigration. But it’s hard not to read the race diagnostically. Whatever Ohioans decide on November 3, a structural verdict has already been rendered. Trump’s acceptance of the entrepreneur-cum-loyalist shouldn’t be confused with the restrictionist right’s acceptance of the meritocrat manqué. 

Nor is it clear that the left’s incipient inversion will prove any more functional. Ro Khanna, the California congressman who has become perhaps the most prominent Indian-American in Democratic politics, proposes in the name of “economic patriotism” to redistribute the tech economy’s rewards to American citizens. However, unlike the post-neoliberal restrictionist right, he won’t disavow the global talent recruitment of which the Indian-American engineer is such a potent symbol. Redistributive, then, but not penitential: Khanna does not engage in the ritual of renunciation. 

The old meritocratic dream is dying. What succeeds it—and which of its old apostles will be allowed to adapt to the new dispensation—is an open question.

Compact

The Atheist Case for Christ

By Justin Germain • 30 Oct 2026 View in browser
View in browser
Scott Menchin
 
 

The look on Josh’s face made clear he had never heard anything like what I had said. We had met at a dinner party, where I had learned that Josh was a student at a very liberal seminary. He loved Jesus, but hated evangelical Christianity and mistrusted most modern manifestations of the church. What was the earth-shattering opinion I laid on him? I explained that although I was an atheist, I thought everyone who could be a believing Christian should, and that those who can’t, like me, should still practice Christianity. When Josh asked me why an atheist would believe such a thing, I answered: “Even though I don’t believe in God, I do believe in his people.” This didn’t make sense to Josh, and perhaps it doesn’t make sense to you either. Allow me to explain.

I grew up Christian, attending a dying Baptist church in an almost completely Catholic Latino neighborhood. There were maybe fifteen people in the pews every Sunday morning. All over sixty save for my mother and me. But they loved me. Invested in me. By the time my peers in other congregations were old enough to go to Bible summer camp, I was reading the book of Daniel in my one-person Sunday school. And not the easy parts of Daniel, about lions or furnaces, the heavy prophecy. By the time I was in high school, I spent my lunch periods leading Bible studies and sharing the gospel. During college and young adulthood, I drank yet deeper of the waters Jesus said would forever satiate their drinker’s thirst. 

So I lived as a Christian. But did I really have a relationship with Jesus Christ? I no longer believe that I, or anyone, has ever had a relationship with Jesus, except for perhaps the handful of people who walked with the historical Jesus. But I did love the Lord with all my heart, and with all my soul, and with all my mind, and all my strength: the greatest commandment. 

That was part of the problem. Christ was the adored, and I was the adorer. As anyone who has been in that relationship dynamic knows, the romance can get a bit one sided. I pursued my adored all the way into graduate school where I learned Greek to read the New Testament in the original. Big mistake. It may be odd to say that a desire to know God better was what led to my eventual apostasy, but that’s exactly what happened. The more I read the text in Greek and the more I learned about the textual tradition, the less I believed that the Bible was the word of God.

Then New Atheism hit. I read Sam Harris while living abroad. I listened to Christopher Hitchens on weekends pulling reserve duty for the Air Force. Once I began to see the world without the presupposition of God, I couldn’t unsee how much it seemed to make sense. At first, I was angry. I felt I had been lied to by the culture in which I had been immersed, and by the God I was becoming increasingly skeptical of. Jesus had promised that whoever drinks of the water he offered would never thirst again. I drank. Deeply. I was still thirsty. I knew there was more out there. I read Plato and Marcus Aurelius, but it was Ricky Gervais who landed the killing blow. He pointed out that even though we can’t absolutely disprove the existence of Vampires, no one is agnostic about them. Why would God be any different? I took on the title of “atheist.” God didn’t strike me down for my apostasy. 

“A lot of deconverts like myself were angry.”

I didn’t stop questioning. I noticed that a lot of deconverts like myself were angry. And those silly, superstitious Christians, were as joyful as ever. Even when I told them their religion was a bad joke, they mostly just looked at me with pity-filled eyes and said they would pray for me. Conversely, the deconverts might no longer have believed in a god, but they still believed in devils—lots of them. By trading my Christian world view for a secular humanist one, I had traded a world view with one devil for a world view with many. But I was done accepting propositions on faith. When I told my atheist brethren that I didn’t believe their devils existed— that I didn’t believe Christians were so bad after all—they responded with shaming and rage. 

A more unexpected realization was that as Christianity’s truth decreased, its beauty and value increased. Consider the Bible. If it is the Word of God, then God’s got some explaining to do, given the contradictions, lacunae, and moral conundrums theologians have spent millennia trying to justify or cover up. The atheists aren’t wrong about any of that. On the other hand, if the Bible is the work of man, those less flattering parts are understandable, even forgivable. The system of slavery described in Exodus 21 isn’t great. But compared to slavery in the Greco-Roman world, it’s a moral improvement. What about the parts of the Bible that were ahead of their time? Those whispers across millennia of men who chased a golden ideal? 

And what of the Church? If it really is a divine institution, then it leaves much to be desired. But if it is simply a body of flawed human beings trying to bring about what they perceive as the resplendent kingdom of God among men, then what institution can boast of enabling such human flourishing over such a long period of time? And Jesus? Well, if he’s not the Son of God, he should be. A God that washes feet and hangs on a cross to wash away sins is a God worth worshiping. 

Put differently, if Christianity isn’t true, then everything it has accomplished, all of the world it has baptized in its cult of mercy and grace, it did so without any divine aid. If Christianity is true, then its great success can easily be attributed to God. If it is not true, then it must be attributed to God’s people, and would have to be considered the greatest social technology of all time. 

Before Jesus said “love your enemies,” the Greeks said, “do good for your friends and harm your enemies.” In the pagan world, Achilles was the moral exemplar. Plato challenged this ideal, and in some ways, Socrates was a type of proto-Jesus. But it wasn’t Platonism that ended infanticide and gladiatorial combat in the ancient world. And there was a reason those practices were so common in the first place. The values of Achilles were strength, power, resilience, and dominance. Yes, Achilles could be merciful too. But that’s not how we remember him. His mercy came only when his power was ascendant, once he had taken his vengeance and Hector lay dead before him. As Friedrich Nietzsche lamented, it was Christianity that made mercy, humility, forgiveness, justice for the weak, the ascendant virtues. Christianity unionized the minnows against the pike. Who would you rather have as a neighbor, a disciple of Achilles, or a disciple of Christ? 

What of prayer? No God is necessary for prayer to change you. The Lord’s prayer teaches gratitude, dependence, a willingness to forgive others and to acknowledge one’s own flaws. It asks for moral courage and discipline. Consider what kind of individual you get if someone prays for those things, meditates on them, seeks avenues in their life to practice them. What kind of civilization do you get when people, corporately, recite that prayer generation after generation for two thousand years? A civilization that even atheists would want to live in. 

 

Whatever broke in me in respect to belief when I left my faith behind has yet to be repaired. Perhaps one day it will be. But none of us choose what we believe. Yet I am also not one of these “cultural Christians” we keep hearing about. Truth be told, I have serious doubts that civilized Christianity can survive without at least a few barbaric pagans to defend it. I’m not saying let’s make America Christian again to win elections. Nor am I arguing that only by embracing Christianity can the West defend its legacy. My point is broader. I believe that Christianity makes bad men good and good men better. 

That is why I take my family to church, and why I am raising my daughter as a Christian. It’s simply a better life. I am no longer certain of anything the way Josh still is. I’m not sure if I am correct and there is no God and nothing happens when we die. I’m not sure if I’m doing the right thing trying to practice a faith whose supernatural claims I do not accept. But when I remarried, I took vows before God. Those were real. My wife is real. If there is a God, may he give me the humility and strength to honor those vows every day of my life. If there is no God, then it’s up to me to keep them, and if praying for my wife and marriage makes me a better husband, and I believe it does, I don’t have the liberty not to do it. The stakes are too high. 

Perhaps it’s a placebo. But the placebo effect works even if you know it’s a placebo. I don’t know if the Bible got God right. But I believe it got humans right. And I’ll take all the help I can get. That is why a man who once said, “my child will never see me bow a knee before any god or man,” is again kneeling in church every Sunday. 

That’s the atheist case for Christ.

Compact

The Last Election, Forever

By Ashley Frawley • 29 Oct 2026 View in browser
View in browser
AP
 
 

In 1992, a young man named Doug Lain decided to run a goldfish for president. Dr. Philip B. Carp, a rubber fish, was the candidate of the Random Surrealist Party, which Lain had also invented. Just old enough to vote in his first presidential election, Lain was outraged by the Gulf War and a political system that seemed to offer up candidates with few discernible differences. The answer to such absurdity was, to him, to become more absurd still. And so he not only wrote the name of his toy goldfish on the ballot line, but also campaigned for it, printing pamphlets at Kinko’s and urging people to vote “surrealist.”

Lain, now in his fifties, reflects on his youthful stunt in the opening of The Last Election, a new documentary from Sublation Media. The idea, he explains, “was to produce a joke so shocking, funny, or strange that it might somehow change everyone’s minds and start a revolution.” Needless to say, the revolution never came, and sifting through newspaper archives of the time it seems not to have made a blip on the historical radar. But it was a sign of things to come. Absurd, jokey rejection of existing institutions has become a familiar mode of political engagement, as has Lain’s youthful disregard for what happens if the rejection succeeds.

The Last Election, centering on the 2024 presidential contest, is equal parts Louis Theroux, Adam Curtis, and ’80s vaporwave. An open-ended exploration of a particular moment in American political culture, it reveals the way political rebellion has become the pervasive style of politics, even as the causes it advances are often unclear. We watch as bored-looking attendees of the Democratic National Convention say things like, “This is Obama-era um, politics now. Well, first African American President, male, now we’re fixing to have the first African American female. So… I’m excited” in unintentionally comedic monotone. Meanwhile, outside the convention, probably the most articulate interviewee delivers a rousing monologue about the uselessness of the Democrats in whiteface, while holding a bloodied baby doll she plans to hang from her genitals. The absurdity that Lain once sought to highlight with surrealist provocation now seems to need no embellishment.

The documentary approaches the predicament through four generations of political rebellion. David Shields, a Baby Boomer and author of more than twenty books, stands in for a generation that approached political contestation through cultural experimentation and an attempt to unsettle the relationship between truth and knowledge. Shields even bears a certain resemblance to Foucault. Lain himself belongs to Gen X, typically associated with ironic detachment and bored irreverence. Benjamin Studebaker, a millennial political theorist, embodies a more earnest effort to recover substantive political alternatives after the disappointments of Bernie Sanders and Occupy. Finally, Wyatt Verlen, a former socialist turned Trump supporter, shows us the transgressive, ironic, overly online political rebellion of Gen Z.

What connects their sensibilities is not simply that they failed to change the world, but that their subversion of it has become more and more difficult to distinguish from the political order against which they rebelled. Shields’ postmodern skepticism toward truth, for instance, is oddly mirrored by established authority, and especially by Trump. The film invokes Walter Benjamin’s figure of the flaneur, the detached and distant urban wanderer, to describe a predicament that had already emerged with the rise of Ronald Reagan. A former actor turned politician, Reagan seemed to enact the same distancing from reality that writers like Shields had cultivated as a form of opposition. “How could Shields wander through and observe the world critically, after a flaneur just like him had been elected president?” Lain wonders. The Trump era made the shrinking distance between the critic and the object of his criticism even more striking. As Shields observes, it is as if Trump has absorbed the entire history of postmodern literature without ever having read Picasso or Breton. 

Studebaker’s version of millennial rebellion is more political than aesthetic, but even here we see the difficulty of converting rejection into something less ephemeral. The Sanders campaign seemed to offer a genuine alternative, and Studebaker and many of his contemporaries had approached it with an earnestness that Lain’s generation had abandoned. But Studebaker, in Lain’s telling, mistook a campaign intended to influence the establishment for a genuine rebellion against it. 

For Verlen, meanwhile, Trump’s transgressive style was attractive specifically for the things that most repulsed the old order; he was a hilarious joke played on the smug educated classes who thought they could govern an insane world. But the thrill of provocation dissolved when the provocateur took office and had to govern. Now, Verlen says, politics doesn’t interest him so much. He’s more interested in the great outdoors and figuring out how to impress women.

“The politics of rejection have triumphed in the figure of Trump.”

In all of these generational portraits, we see the gestures of political rebellion reflected back at the would-be rebels by the establishment itself. In some ways, the politics of rejection have triumphed in the figure of Trump, but this only leaves the film’s subjects more disoriented and unsure of what their rebellion was trying to achieve. Their experiences are different, but they reveal a political culture that is adept at expressing dissatisfaction without being able to overcome what caused it.

Both the Republican and Democratic conventions come across in the film as strange and lifeless affairs. The personalities that linger are not the weirdos screaming about God outside the RNC nor the oddly robotic DNC attendees feigning excitement about a Kamala Harris win, but the people Lain meets on his way home.

Lain finds himself seated on a flight next to two men whose political commitments would seem irreconcilable. A hippie, a Republican, and a communist (Lain himself), they turn what sounds like the beginning of a bad joke into a whiskey-soaked conversation about the failures of the Democrats, the attempt on Trump’s life, and eventually, the pain of divorce. They continue their conversations into a barbecue a few days later hosted by the Republican, an ex-marine who jokes—or is it a joke?—that he is also FBI. There, somehow, everything we hear about American society becoming more polarized falls away, as they talk about their inability to change a political system that has served none of them. At the barbecue, a young man is asked whether he plans to vote. He responds: “I don’t like playing a game where I’m not able to win.” And so perhaps begins another round of rejection.

In this sense, Lain’s youthful experiment was more prophetic than he could have imagined. Americans really did, in a manner of speaking, elect a goldfish. Trump became the embodiment of decades of political rejection, the absurdist gesture elevated to the presidency. After watching the film, I asked Lain what would have happened had his goldfish really won. He seemed surprised by the question, like it was the first time he had thought about it. “I guess I would have helped him select a cabinet,” Lain mused. “I would have turned to my friends for advice. The inaugural would have been very quiet, just a gurgling sound.”

The title of the film recalls how Americans were warned not just that the 2024 election would be the most “consequential of their lives,” (Americans had heard that before) but that it could be the last election. Now, coming toward the midterms, Trump has warned of another ending. As he posted recently on Truth Social, “The Dumocrat Agenda is a plan to extinguish Western Civilization.” Without the ability to think through what a beginning might look like, we seem condemned to live the last election, forever.

It is now conventional wisdom that the United States is lurching from one blunder to the next.

Multipolarity Has Failed

By Thomas Fazi • 28 Oct 2026 View in browser
View in browser
Scott Menchin
 
 

It is now conventional wisdom that the United States is lurching from one blunder to the next. By antagonizing Russia and China simultaneously, it pushed them into each other’s arms; by weaponizing the dollar and slapping tariffs on friend and foe alike, it has accelerated de-dollarization. In Iran, meanwhile, the US has failed to achieve regime change while sustaining massive damage to its bases in the Middle East. Finally, there is broad agreement that Ukraine—and by extension NATO—is losing its war with Russia, dealing yet another devastating blow to American power. America’s terminal decline, it is widely assumed, will force Washington to accept a diminished role and accommodate a new, multipolar world order. 

I have made this argument myself more than once. But lately, I have started to wonder whether those of us who welcome the rise of a new multipolar order have allowed our wishes to get ahead of reality. The evidence of the past year points in a different direction, nowhere more clearly than in the growing paralysis of BRICS, the organization of emerging economies that has positioned itself as a counterweight to US dominance. 

It is necessary to distinguish here between relative weight and relative power. In terms of weight—especially economic weight—multipolarity is already a reality. The US economy accounts for a much smaller share of the global economy than it did a decade ago, thanks above all to China’s rise. But has this decline in relative weight been matched by a comparable decline in power? Not really. 

Power can be exercised by structural or openly coercive means. A state exercises power over its citizens in structural terms, in that obedience rests not only on the threat of punishment but on the sense that following the rules is normal and correct. By contrast, a crime syndicate exercises power mainly through naked coercion. Since 1945 the United States has enjoyed enormous structural power, rooted in its control of the world’s financial, logistical, and military infrastructure, and legitimized by the idea of the “rules-based order.” 

That structural power has undoubtedly diminished. China has not only become an economic, technological and military superpower; it has also quietly built an alternative financial infrastructure that allows countries to operate outside the dollar system—a project that gathered pace in response to Washington’s weaponization of that system. That is why the most extensive sanctions regime in history failed to cripple Russia. 

 “The second Trump administration has exposed the limits of this process.”

But the second Trump administration has exposed the limits of this process. US structural power, though waning, remains formidable—and in some areas, it is growing. Further, Washington has increasingly supplemented this structural power with open coercion. And BRICS has proven incapable of mounting an adequate response. 

Over its own bloc, Washington arguably exercises more control today than at any time since 1945. Europe is cut off from Russian energy and dependent on American supplies, and locked into a NATO command structure that the current rearmament drive is entrenching. A similar dynamic can be observed among the members of the “global NATO.” Australia, Japan, and South Korea have all adopted a more hawkish stance towards China. Like European countries, and indeed most countries around the world, they largely acquiesced to Trump’s across-the-board tariffs in 2025. Only China pushed back in any meaningful way. 

Washington is also regaining ground in what it has long regarded as its backyard: Latin America. The victories of US-friendly candidates in Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, and Honduras has given substance to the “Trump Corollary” to the Monroe Doctrine set out in last December’s National Security Strategy. The US-led “Shield of the Americas,” a NATO-inspired, US-led security alliance launched in March with twelve Latin American governments, now counts nineteen members. Lula’s narrow victory in Brazil is a reminder that this reassertion of US hemispheric dominance has limits, but it is very real nonetheless. 

These countries are responding to the reality of continuing American power. Washington can still inflict severe economic pain by cutting countries off from the dollar system. As Russia’s resilience has made clear, large, resource-rich economies can withstand US economic coercion, especially with help from China. But smaller ones cannot. Years of sanctions had already devastated Iran’s economy before this year’s war, and only Russia, China and a handful of others defied them. When Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned governments to stop working with Iranian airlines or be “knocked out of the dollar system,” every country in the region promptly suspended Iranian flights. For all the efforts to loosen its financial stranglehold, Washington retains significant structural power with which to shape policies around the world. 

 

Under Trump, the US has combined its structural power with more open coercion. In less than a year, Washington has invaded Venezuela and abducted its president; repeatedly bombed Iran and blockaded its oil exports, a significant share of which went to China; imposed a total blockade on Cuba; attacked commercial vessels on the high seas; continued to back both Israel’s multi-front war and Ukraine’s escalating drone campaign against Russian infrastructure. 

Russia and China have responded with little more than diplomatic platitudes, while continuing to court Trump in search of favorable deals. Beijing is capable of retaliation: When its own core interests were at stake in the 2025 trade war, its rare-earth export controls forced Washington into a truce. What Xi Jinping has shown no willingness to do is extend that protection to Iran, Venezuela, and Cuba. Meanwhile, Russia hasn’t responded in kind to de facto NATO attacks on its territory. 

The response of BRICS as a whole has been feebler still, as last month’s summit in New Delhi made clear. The declaration issued at the summit did not condemn the US-Israeli strikes on a member state, Iran. It instead made a generic call for restraint—a step back from last year’s Rio declaration, which condemned the summer 2025 strikes. The Ukraine war, meanwhile, does not appear anywhere in the 140-paragraph text. Unilateral sanctions are denounced, but the country imposing them goes unnamed. 

In part, this reflects the very nature of BRICS. It is not an alliance, much less a “bloc,” and it has no supranational structures comparable to those of the EU or NATO. The loose structure of BRICS enabled cooperation between countries that would have resisted more binding arrangements, not least because of long-standing rivalries (think of China and India), while avoiding the kind of panicked reaction in Western capitals that a harder formation would almost certainly have provoked. But the slow construction of this alternative order rested on a fundamental precondition: a degree of accommodation from the West. 

“American assertiveness has fundamentally altered the playing field.”

That precondition no longer holds. American assertiveness has fundamentally altered the playing field. It is one thing to coordinate among countries whose governments diverge in terms of their degree of their integration with the West and the pace of their delinking from the existing order. It is quite another to coordinate among countries some of which are at war with the West while others are its allies, in a context in which shunning the dollar or trading with sanctioned states can entail heavy costs. 

This has opened up deep fractures within BRICS, as its members find themselves in wildly different strategic situations. Russia is fighting a proxy war with NATO; Iran has been bombed in an attempted regime change operation. China, on the other hand, faces no immediate military threat and is playing a long game aimed at outlasting the US while avoiding a head-on collision. India and Brazil, like China itself, are deeply integrated into Western markets and anxious to avoid ruptures with Washington. The UAE, meanwhile, sits on the other side of the Iran war. Its Al Dhafra air base served as a key hub for the US campaign, and Iran has fired some 2,500 missiles and drones at Emirati territory. Considering that two BRICS members have effectively been at war with each other for months, it is hardly surprising that BRICS has proven unable to organize any coordinated response to the war with Iran. 

All this raises serious questions about the future of BRICS and similar non-Western institutions—and about the transition to a multipolar order itself. To say that non-Western countries are currently woefully ill-equipped to deal with the Western-led assault is not a criticism but a statement of fact. Can a world in which the US remains free to launch military and economic strikes, unchecked by any other power, really be called multipolar in any meaningful sense? 

 

One might object that Washington’s aggression has undermined its soft power and cost it more than it gained, vindicating China’s strategy of patience. Perhaps. But the US has already imposed enormous costs on Russia through a protracted proxy war, could inflict heavy damage on China by threatening chokepoints such as the Strait of Malacca, and has shown that it can seriously damage China’s partners. Given that Beijing has staked so much on global connectivity, that is no minor threat. 

Advocates of multipolarity urge a rejection of “bloc mentality.” But whether non-Western countries like it or not, the West is a bloc, and a highly cohesive one at that. It is fanciful to imagine that it could be challenged by anything but a similarly cohesive grouping. But that prospect is hard to contemplate. A NATO-style non-Western bloc, even if it were politically feasible, would likely trigger a devastating global confrontation. American power may erode in the coming years, opening opportunities for challengers. Countries under attack will go on resisting, as Iran has shown. For now, however, we continue to live in a unipolar world. When the US seeks to bend others to its will, especially the weaker links in the multipolar system, no force is capable of stopping it.

title: The Left’s War on Men
content:
The explosive rape accusations leveled against seven Cornell students have revived the gender wars of the #MeToo era, offering a reminder of the dramatic transformation undergone by the feminist movement—and the left more broadly—in recent decades.

Compact

The Left’s War on Men

By Chris Wright • 27 Oct 2026 View in browser
View in browser
AP
 
 

The explosive rape accusations leveled against seven Cornell students have revived the gender wars of the #MeToo era, offering a reminder of the dramatic transformation undergone by the feminist movement—and the left more broadly—in recent decades. In the 1960s, feminists demanded legal equality and the end of patriarchal paternalism, arguing that women should be free to make their own choices with regard to sex, family, education, and career. Today, feminists demand that women be protected against men, and that, in many contexts, they be treated as not responsible for their own decisions. In effect, this is a demand for the resurrection of paternalism under feminist auspices.

The assumption guiding the left-wing reaction to the Cornell case seems to be that because the accused are men, they are guilty, for men are by definition guilty. Is it any wonder that millions of men in recent years have turned away from a left that seems to hate them?

Consider what has transpired. No less than Governor Kathy Hochul and Attorney General Letitia James, as well as leading leftists including Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Zohran Mamdani, have talked as though the Cornell case has already been decided. Not only is the presumption of innocence thrown out the window; it is obvious that even if the accused end up being found innocent, most liberals and leftists will remain certain of the guilt of the “Cornell 7.” They’re men, after all.  

“Online mobs are out for blood.”

Online mobs are out for blood. Demands to kill the accused have gone viral on social media. Friends and family of the accused men have been harassed by thousands. So was the family of an innocent man who happens to have the same name as one of the accused. Of course, people have also attacked Jane Doe in similar terms. But these parallels only show that elements of the left have adopted a misandry as raw as the misogyny found on parts of the right. Left-wing outrage is allegedly motivated by concern for the safety of women, but these episodes illustrate the extent to which the atomized, polarized culture of social media has created a left that reflexively assumes the worst of men, exploits controversies for social media clout, and contributes to social breakdown. 

Leftists seem blind to the irony of a feminism that infantilizes women. Given the texts Jane Doe sent after the infamous party, it’s perfectly plausible that this was an episode of consensual, intoxicated group sex, which the accuser later regretted. But the prevailing left perspective, embraced by Governor Hochul and others, is that if a woman is intoxicated and gives consent throughout the night, the intoxicated man should know what is in her interest better than she does and act as the mature, sober adult. He should refrain from sex because she, supposedly, has lost all self-control and—unlike him—is not able to make good decisions. This is a “feminism” that views women as weak, passive victims, and men as the only ones capable of agency. 

Identitarian feminism is an excellent recruiting tool for the right, as Steve Bannon observed years ago. It tends to dismiss men’s concerns and problems—their loneliness, their declining wages, their rising rates of unemployment and high suicide rates—because it sees men themselves as the problem. Is it at all surprising that a manosphere has emerged to shore up men’s sense of self-worth, albeit in unhealthy ways? By abandoning universalist policies of class uplift in favor of parceling out benefits by race and gender, the left has helped birth its nemesis, a masculinist and racist far right. The conviction that white men are the enemy has, in fact, turned many white—as well as non-white—men into the left’s enemy.

A rational left would, instead, condemn mob hysteria as contrary to civilized values and the rule of law. It would avoid leaping to conclusions in any given case of alleged sexual assault, while repudiating misandrist strains of feminism and taking seriously the crisis men face today. It would broadcast the message that men are no less valuable and valid than women, and that the left will address their problems. This would entail promoting a different kind of feminism, not only a labor feminism but also what one might call a feminism of dignity and accountability—one that teaches women to take themselves seriously as moral agents. It isn’t only men who should act responsibly; women should too. The way forward for the left is not sexist paternalism, but belief in human dignity and equality.

Lula Won—‘Lulismo’ Didn’t

By Alex Hochuli • 26 Oct 2026 View in browser
View in browser
AP
 
 

On October 25, Brazil’s President Lula da Silva bucked the global anti-incumbency trend to win the most hard-fought election since Brazil returned to democracy in 1985. The election’s first round occurred amid widespread apathy. Lula came in second. But then his campaign went into overdrive, bringing millions onto the streets and ending the right’s decade-long advantage online. 

A decisive moment came in the final debate on Friday night. Debates count for little nowadays as televised events, but clippable and shareable moments are worth quite a lot. Lula’s opponent, Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, made mocking reference to the incumbent’s nine fingers. In response, Lula underlined his connection to working people. “If there’s someone who knows about work it’s me,” he said. “If there’s someone who lost a finger at seventeen it was me. … He never worked in his life.” Another factor was the Workers Party’s (PT) ability to bring people onto the streets in the lead-up to the vote. The largest left-wing demonstration in São Paulo’s history took place on October 11, only to be exceeded when up to half a million people occupied Avenida Paulista on election eve, in perhaps the largest demonstration ever held in Brazil. 

This mobilization was matched online, thanks largely to André Janones, a federal deputy from Minas Gerais who gained fame as one of the leaders of a huge truckers strike in 2018. Janones’s “Lula’s Army” WhatsApp channel had 3 million members at the start of the election but now totals over 10 million members—a staggering 7 percent of the electorate.

Sunday’s vote was marked by voter suppression in some municipalities as anti-PT mayors ran reduced bus services. This plus heavy rains in some Bolsonaro-supporting areas led both camps to petition the electoral court to delay the shutting of polling stations. A justice nominated by former President Jair Bolsonaro refused to act, but then a Lula-appointed Justice of the Supreme Court mandated a two-hour extension, fifteen minutes after polls had closed. This created electoral chaos and generated the basis for litigation. Still, Lula’s margin of 4.3 million votes will make it difficult to mount a viable challenge to the result. 

“Lula’s biggest strength is also his biggest weakness.”

Lula’s biggest strength is also his biggest weakness. He has an incredible record of winning the presidency. He won two terms in the 2000s, then managed to get his little-known handpicked successor Dilma Rousseff elected twice, and now has won two more consecutive mandates. But these victories have been achieved through alliances with centrist establishment figures that have often hurt down-ballot candidates and demobilized Lula’s own base. The result is that the PT is hollowed out and dependent on its charismatic leader, who due to age and a limit on consecutive terms will enter office as a lame duck. Lulismo has cannibalized Petismo (PT-ism), leaving the party’s post-Lula future uncertain. 

The president will face a hostile congress. The Bolsonaro-dominated Liberal Party (PL) has ballast in the Chamber of Deputies and control of the Senate, and holds governorships up and down the country. This reverses the pattern that held for decades, where the PT was one of the largest parties and one of the few with a recognizable ideological identity. Bolsonarismo has become comparably large and cohesive, even if not altogether ideologically coherent. If Flávio had won, he could have remade—or unmade—the republic. Now, Brazil’s progressive constitution has a stay of execution. 

When Lula won in 2022 on a “save democracy” ticket, I argued that instead of positioning itself as a defender of the status quo, the left needed to wage its own holy war to compete with the apocalyptic fervor of evangelical-tinged Bolsonarismo. At minimum, a viable left needs a national project, something to tie together collective destiny with individual advancement. On this front, Lula didn’t deliver. His third government rested on democratic restoration, rebuilding institutions, and a set of piecemeal reforms. 

Some of these were valuable. For instance, he granted those earning under $1,000 a month (84 percent of the population) exemption from income tax. Other moves followed as the election neared: the reduction of the working week from six to five days, a ban on betting—which had rapidly become a social plague—debt relief for microenterprises, an increase in Bolsa Família welfare payments. But for many Brazilians, life remained difficult. Although inflation had abated, prices remained high, and debt had increased. This is why the polls remained tight.

Despite eking out another win, Lulismo today is a pale version of what it was—because of the PT’s complacency and its many compromises, because of difficult Congress, and above all because there was no growth to redistribute. Its national project was always more centered on individual social mobility than class uplift or social transformation. In his third term, Lula became what the center-right used to be: an appeal to individuals and families on pocketbook issues twinned with the promise of stability, over and against the chaos of Bolsonarismo. 

This time, that message proved adequate. Flávio, Jair Bolsonaro’s first-born, presented himself as a moderate version of his father, but that would mistake style for substance. Bolsonaro senior is from a humble background and was formed by the military. He has charisma of a sort, and rode a wave of raucous anti-politics to the presidency in 2018. In contrast, Flávio was raised in gated condominia as the son of a federal representative; his first employment was a phantom job in Congress—a fact the former shoeshine boy and metalworker Lula mocked extensively. 

Many progressives voted for Lula as a means to avoid thinking about politics for another four years. But the next four years will not be smooth sailing. The PT has lost direction, relying now on a broad front with the anti-Bolsonarista center, and Lula still has no successor in sight. But for now, that is just about enough. In the words of Lula’s 1989 campaign song, sung loudly across Brazil on Sunday night, Lula lá (“Lula is there”). A star confirmed itself in the firmament, and good-vibes progressivism will hold out for a little longer.

There are few projects that better capture Mohammed bin Salman’s ambitions for Saudi Arabia than NEOM.
