The Foucault Century

By Michael C. Behrent • 15 Oct 2026 View in browser
View in browser
 
 

Michel Foucault, by some counts the world’s most cited author, was born a hundred years ago today. Though he died forty-two years ago, the controversial philosopher’s image remains remarkably cutting-edge. Foucault’s signature concepts—power/knowledge, panopticism, biopower—still sound deliciously subversive. Though he died too soon to be drawn into our never-ending culture wars, he continues to be associated—negatively or positively—with queer theory, the critique of the gender binary, prison abolition, and postcolonialism. 

Yet if one visits Foucault’s granite tombstone in a gray, drab cemetery along a country road in the Poitou region of France, it is hard not to see him from a different perspective. He seems old. As he turns one hundred, could it be that Foucault stands out less for his ongoing relevance than as a throwback to a world we have lost? 

Ever since he burst onto the intellectual scene in France in the 1960s, then crossed the Atlantic to become a leading figure of “French Theory” or “postmodernism” in the United States in the 1970s and ’80s, Foucault challenged conventional wisdom and proposed giddily new ways of thinking. His work on the historical conditions of knowledge, the dissemination of “micropowers,” and the social function of “normality” seemed to overtake and then lap the twentieth century’s most radical forms of thought. Foucault appeared to out-Marx Marx, psychoanalyze Freud, and achieve a deeper level of authenticity than existentialism. He was fond of slogans that showcased his readiness to dispense with the past. He predicted the “death of the author,” described “man” as a recent “invention” that was “nearing its end,” and dismissed the state as a concept that was useless to political analysis. He described a book by Jean-Paul Sartre—the defining French intellectual of the postwar era—as a failed “attempt by a nineteenth-century man to understand the twentieth century.” 

The sense of Foucault’s prescience continues to shape how he is seen today. In July, a New York Times essay declared: “From AI to the Deep State, Michel Foucault Foresaw It All.” Many conservatives find fault precisely with Foucault’s radical modernity, as do some left-of-center critics of wokeness, such as Susan Nieman and Yascha Mounk. 

“Consider the world in which he lived.”

Foucault’s birth centenary may be the moment to ask whether his avant-garde reputation is exaggerated. Consider the world in which he lived. Foucault was born to a bourgeois family in the regional capital of Poitiers, where his father and grandfather were both prominent doctors. He remained in this milieu until, at the age of eighteen, he moved to Paris to study in 1945. Foucault’s concerns were decisively shaped by the provincial world in which he was raised. 

In his published work, Foucault constantly interrogated the nature of medicine and its social function. He published a study called The Birth of the Clinic, devoted much of The Order of Things to examining life sciences, and theorized that modern forms of power drew on medicine and the promotion of public health. It is thus not surprising that Foucault was born into a medical dynasty, with several generations of physicians on both sides of his family. His father lectured at the local medical school and worked at the town hospital in addition to having a private surgical practice—the family’s main income source. Though a respected figure in the community, his father also embodied some of the medical profession’s idiosyncratic perversities. He spoke approvingly of Serge Voronoff’s theories (now regarded as quackery) that transplants of chimpanzee testicles could re-masculinize patients and even cure homosexuality. He also delivered an eerily jocular paper about a peasant woman he had treated who had slipped a glass into her vagina for an “unmentionable purpose.” Foucault’s later view that medical knowledge had acquired real power in modern society and his suspicion of its claim to be guided purely by disinterested truth are rooted in these early experiences. As he once put it, in the “provincial medical milieu” in which he was raised, “rationality assumed an almost magical prestige.”

Foucault was also fascinated by fascism, although he never devoted a full-length study to it and most of his reflections on power focused on the early modern period and the nineteenth century. In Foucault’s conception, fascism serves as something like an asymptote—a line towards which power tends but rarely attains. That said, Foucault’s conception of it was not fanciful. From the ages of thirteen to seventeen, he lived in German-occupied Poitiers. German soldiers patrolled the streets, local hotels and public buildings were taken over by Nazi authorities, and an internment camp was set up nearby. He also witnessed the eagerness with which many French people cooperated with the Vichy regime (whose policies and moral authority extended into the occupied zone). Vichy doctors warned of the dangers of medical and psychological “abnormality,” and called for a concerted “social defense” against deviant behavior and the promotion of health, vigor, and normality. Such rhetoric was in many ways the template for the discourses that Foucault would critique in his work. 

What troubled Foucault about Vichy was less its authoritarianism than its moralism. Years later, Foucault criticized the socialists who came to power with François Mitterrand’s election in 1981 in similar terms. Commenting on a socialist who had denounced bourgeois selfishness, Foucault remarked in a 1983 interview: “I was not very old when Pétain came to power in France, but this year I recognized in the words of this socialist the very tones which lulled my childhood.”

Foucault’s childhood was also deeply shaped by Catholicism. He served as an altar boy at Saint Porchaire church, down the street from the family’s townhouse, and his brother later recalled that they regularly attended Mass with their maternal grandmother. The family doesn’t seem to have been particularly devout—indeed, there were republican and freethinking tendencies among some of his forebears—but they belonged to a milieu in which Catholicism remained central to social life. Foucault’s high school years were spent at a Catholic school run by the La Salle brothers. The canon Georges Duret, a much-admired local theologian, would have been Foucault’s philosophy teacher had he not been arrested by the Gestapo for his involvement in the Resistance. His replacement was a Benedictine monk at the nearby Saint Martin Abbey, the oldest continually operating monastery in Christendom. Foucault befriended him and rode his bicycle to the monastery from time to time to visit him. 

There is no evidence to suggest that Foucault was ever a believing Catholic. Yet it is equally clear that he considered Catholicism profoundly important. The narratives of many of his early books, such as Madness and Civilization and The Order of Things, begin with powerful evocations of late medieval Christendom and its theological worldview. Foucault was intrigued by asceticism, perhaps inspired by the priests and monks he knew as a young man. The final volume of his History of Sexuality is devoted to early Christianity’s role in shaping Western idea of sex. At his 1984 funeral, a Dominican monk read passages from The Order of Things. In 1978, Foucault confessed: “The church thrills me,” because it “is a superb institution of power … completely woven with imaginary, erotic, affective, bodily, sensual elements.” He regretted that it had become “extraordinarily weak,” given that it had been “the West’s great knowledge apparatus for centuries.”  

None of this is to suggest that Foucault’s thought was simply a redescription of prewar provincial France in philosophical terms. Whatever one thinks of his positions, he was a thinker of unusual insight, with a gift for articulating new problems and reformulating old ones in strikingly original ways. But considering his early years does call attention to just how much he was shaped by the France of the early twentieth century—which itself was in many ways a continuation of the nineteenth. When describing the medical milieu to which his father belonged, Foucault remarked that it “still belonged to the nineteenth century.” Before we rush to tout Foucault’s modernity, it is worth considering the extent to which his idea of modernity was shaped by the world of yesteryear.

 

Understanding what Foucault understood by modernity is also crucial to assessing his politics and positions on cultural issues, as well as to grasping the significance of what has come to be known as “postmodernism” and “French Theory,” categories into which Foucault is lumped but with which he never identified. Put crassly, Foucault was not “woke.” He was not woke because the politics he embraced—both because of and in reaction to the world he had grown up in—had little to do with the aims and values of contemporary progressivism.

It is too often overlooked that Foucault, like many of the so-called postmodernists, was unapologetically Eurocentric in his intellectual interests and operated comfortably within the framework of “Western civilization.” His books dealt exclusively with Europe, and primarily with France. With the exception of a few European stints early in his career, most of his research was done at the old site of the French National Library in Paris—a short drive or bicycle ride from his home in the city’s fifteenth arrondissement. The philosophers he most liked to think with were solidly anchored in the canon of Western philosophy: Kant, Hegel, Husserl, and Heidegger, as well as Descartes, Malebranche, Rousseau, and Bentham. Foucault liked avant-garde art and literature—the Surrealists, Bataille, Blanchot, Char—but his books are also full of references to Shakespeare, Cervantes, Diderot, Velázquez, and Manet. Not only did he deal exclusively with Western literature, but he regularly referred to Western Civilization as a concept, even emphasizing its distinctness from the East. In his book on madness, he spoke of the difference between Western rationality and “the Orient,” while in his work on sexuality, he distinguished the West’s science of sexuality from the East’s erotic arts. The abundant commentary on Foucault’s brief stint in Tunisia in the 1960s and his trips to Iran in the late 1970s only confirm the broader pattern. Viewed from today’s standpoint, Foucault’s oeuvre seems like an advertisement for the merits of Western Civ courses. 

“Foucault’s point was not to defend Western civilization.”

To be sure, Foucault’s point was not to defend Western civilization, though his work reminds us that earlier forms of radicalism were compatible with an exclusive focus on its classical texts. But even Foucault’s radicalism seems out of sync with contemporary progressivism. Consider Foucault’s famously complex views on sexuality, many of which he proposed in the 1970s. Foucault argued, first, that rather than being something concrete, “sex” was in fact an abstraction that various attempts to understand sexuality had invented by lumping together a wide range of very different phenomena. Foucault did not mean that humans do not engage in reproduction through genital penetration. What he meant is that far more gets roped into what we call sex than mere reproduction: desire as well as gender, and private activities as well as a ritualized social institution. It can be legally regulated, endowed with spiritual meaning, and targeted as a political concern. Foucault’s claim is that the many traits associated with sex cannot be derived from its simple biological definition. Furthermore, Foucault maintains that in the West, sex is particularly valued as an object of knowledge and, consequently, something that must be talked about. For Foucault, the most striking thing about the Western experience of sex is not that it is repressed, but that it is relentlessly discussed, as both Catholic confession and Freudian psychoanalysis make clear. Saying this amid the emancipatory ferment of the 1970s was shocking. There is a real sense in which Foucault sought to be the sexual revolution’s party pooper.

Foucault’s insights, to be sure, cut different ways. In his reflection on hermaphrodites, he questioned why nineteenth-century scientists, when confronted with people who had sexual traits of different sexes, were committed to determining their “true” sex. “Do we truly need [the idea of a] true sex,” he asked. His point was not to affirm the existence of multiple sexes, but to question why ambiguities that humans had been content to live with for centuries had to be settled with the decisive criterion of truth.  

Other positions Foucault took on sexuality were considered disturbing even in the 1970s. The same views that made him sympathetic to nonconforming sexual identities also made him skeptical of the category of sex crimes. In a 1977 discussion, he wondered whether in punishing rape, “one should be punishing physical violence and nothing but that.” Is there really a difference, he mused, “between sticking one’s fist in someone’s face or one’s penis into their sex”? If one did accept that rape was different, it meant viewing sex as something more than the clumsy catch-all Foucault’s work had shown it to be. It meant saying that “sexuality as such, in the body, has a preponderant place” and that “the sexual organ isn’t like a hand, hair, or a nose,” and that it must be “protected, surrounded, invested” with legislation. Foucault never claimed rape should be abolished as a crime, but his deep suspicion of modern conceptions of sexuality and punishment made him openly skeptical of the category. 

The Trump administration has recently given us another unexpected Foucault moment. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth’s proposal to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan was met with widespread indignation among progressives, as well as from some on the right. Hillary Clinton denounced the decision as “barbaric” and “beneath the dignity of our country,” while Senator Chris Murphy called it “medieval.” Yet what exactly are the principles upon which such criticisms are based? Opposition to the death penalty is a coherent position; but when it exists, why should the same ideal of transparency that is upheld as a virtue in other realms of public life not apply to the highest punishment? What makes Foucault interesting is his willingness to ask these very kinds of questions and to needle the inconsistencies of progressivism’s good conscience. 

Foucault famously began Discipline and Punish with an account of the brutal public execution of the regicide Damiens in 1757, before reflecting on the fact executions would soon cease to be public spectacles. Henceforth, punishment became “the most hidden part of the penal process.” Consequently, “justice no longer takes public responsibility for the violence that is bound up with its practice.” In modern times, trials have become the key moment in the judicial process. The “execution itself is like an additional shame that justice is ashamed to impose on the condemned man,” so “it keeps its distance from the act.” As Foucault’s analysis of Damiens’s demise showed, public executions were complex events, in which bloodthirsty crowds served as a check on the executioners’ power—protesting botched executions, cheering on criminals who showed dignity in the face of death. There is perhaps more honesty and less constraint in so-called barbarism, Foucault suggested, than in demands for “humane” punishment.

Foucault was a radical, but his radicalism belonged to his age, not ours—an age shaped by the shadow that nineteenth-century culture cast over the twentieth century, the experience of the Second World War, and the mixture of rising prosperity and changing mores that characterized postwar society. Despite his popularity among college-educated progressives, he must also be treated like that uncle whose outrageous Thanksgiving outbursts have to be politely ignored and occasionally airbrushed away. A prominent Foucault scholar, when discussing one of the philosopher’s lecture series, is shocked that all the women he mentions are “prostitutes or hysterical” and that the “children are idiots and always masturbating,” while tut-tutting him from his “unpleasant dismissal of how the victims may have felt.” 

 

Foucault’s hundredth anniversary coincides with a rediscovery of a new attention to his work from the late 1940s and 50s, when he was in his twenties and thirties. In recent years, manuscripts that were long unavailable have been published. Just as the discovery of previously unknown writings made it possible to speak of a “young Marx,” it is now possible to speak of a “young Foucault.” 

Foucault was particularly concerned with the meaning of the human: not abstract reflections about human nature, but the place of the human in the story of knowledge. Specifically, he was interested in “anthropology,” which is the philosophical field concerned with understanding man. Foucault’s most important statement from his early period is a set of lecture notes from the early 1950s called “Knowledge of Man and Transcendental Reflection,” which was published in France in 2022. What Foucault shows, by way of a history of philosophy, is that so long as knowledge was primarily oriented to understanding God, a genuine philosophy of man was impossible. The existence of human beings was never in doubt; but at least as objects of understanding, Foucault suggests, they had no unique status in creation. During the Scientific Revolution, nature is reconceived as subject to laws of nature whose scope is infinite, and God becomes understood as the guarantor of this legal order. Yet this system, too, is unable to grant man a unique status within the realm of knowledge. 

Everything changes, Foucault maintains, with the onset of modern times in the eighteenth century. What changes is a radical break in knowledge’s theological grounding. Man becomes conceived as a creature who is radically finite. This finitude has two dimensions. Man is a finite object, in the sense that he is a physical being that is also mortal. But most importantly, man is a finite subject, with a limited capacity for knowledge. The key figure in this new outlook is the German philosopher Immanuel Kant, who had a decisive impact on Foucault’s thought. Kant proposes a critique of pure reason precisely because he recognizes that there are certain things humans are incapable of knowing simply by virtue of being human. Kant can also be read as demonstrating that only finite beings can have knowledge—that the task of knowing is an idiosyncrasy of imperfect creatures. God doesn’t “know,” at least in any way that is remotely related to human knowledge. Only at this juncture does knowledge of human beings become not only possible, but necessary. 

“This complex philosophical plot has a twist.”

Yet this complex philosophical plot has a twist. Kant’s goal had been to define the conditions necessary for knowledge in general. He was not actually trying to propose a theory of nature. But over the course of the nineteenth century, thinkers such as Hegel, Feuerbach, and Dilthey would interpret this new understanding of knowledge as a human trait. Because knowledge is a human activity par excellence, “anthropology”—knowledge of humanity as such—would be the field through which all other forms of knowledge had to be sifted. Furthermore, finitude becomes associated with unprecedented expansion of man’s will to know. Never more than when man professes the limited character of his understanding has knowledge spread so exponentially.

In his earliest work, Foucault thus critiqued the humanist or “anthropological” moment in knowledge, not because it was a “social construct,” but because it was wrong—an inadequate basis for founding knowledge. In ways that are often unacknowledged, these concerns shaped the work for which he later became famous. It is true that in Madness and Civilization (1961), Foucault considered the way that the mad had been historically excluded from society. But his point was also that the most extreme form of exclusion occurred paradoxically when they were conceived as mentally ill and confined to asylums—in other words, when madness was seen as an entirely human phenomenon, as something that happens to human minds rather than as possession by diabolical forces. 

In The Order of Things (1966), Foucault showed how the knowledge of any given time period was shaped by an underlying framework or “episteme.” But he did this in many ways to pinpoint the historical peculiarity and intellectual incoherence of an age in which knowledge was conceived as purely human phenomenon, as he expressed through his prophetic intimations of man’s imminent “demise.” The young Foucault allows us to consider the paragon of “French Theory” and the patron saint of postmodernism in a startlingly new light. Many of the ideas he is most associated with derived from a quite different set of philosophical concerns. Before he became the theorist of power, knowledge, and sexuality, he was a philosopher deeply concerned with—and deeply ambivalent about—the place of the human in philosophy. 

 

Foucault’s earliest—and oldest—thought could perhaps also be the most relevant to our own moment—even more so than the ideas he hatched in the 1970s and ’80s, now that the cultural salience of these decades is waning. First, Foucault’s reflection on the human and its place in knowledge is significant at a time when the transcendence of the human has become a concrete possibility, as tech lords devote vast resources to pursuing transhumanist fantasies of digital immortality. The young Foucault’s insight was that a decisive turning point in the history of knowledge was reached when humans acknowledged their finitude: He believed that this made possible both the experimental method, which defined a program of knowledge for beings with limited faculties, as well as forms of philosophy that ceased to rely on the hypothesis of an infinite being. How should we conceive what AI knows? Do LLM simply push to the limit what finite knowledge can know? Or is humanity now encountering a new form of infinity, in a way that once again renders uncertain man’s status in the domain of knowledge? The concerns of the young Foucault resonate with these contemporary dilemmas.

Second, though the young Foucault had little to say about politics, his thought could prove fruitful for pondering the political transformations we are living through, particularly the decline of liberalism. In a surprisingly Foucauldian register, Patrick Deneen’s Why Liberalism Failed examines liberalism’s ill-conceived “anthropology.” He emphasizes notably its commitment to voluntarism and the idea that man is separate from nature. Could these claims be seen as ultimately deriving from finitude? Are an atomistic conception of the individual and the belief that man is something distinct from his natural surroundings conceivable without the premise that humans are finite creatures? While not specifically prefigured by Foucault, these, too, are concerns that follow from his work. 

Third, the young Foucault offers insights into the state of sexuality that are at times more interesting than those theorized by his older self. In an essay from 1963—the year in which, according to Philip Larkin, sexual intercourse was invented—Foucault argues that the modern fascination with sexuality is tied to the death of God. Once we have lost the “limit of the Unlimited,” the only limits that remain are those of our finitude. Just as, for Kant, knowledge is always perversely drawn to what it cannot know, so sexuality, too, in modern times, becomes obsessed with transgression—with going beyond the very limits that define it. Foucault also notes that, in modern times, sexuality is not a return to nature but a flight from it, as evidenced by how contemporary sexuality is essentially cultural—a matter of words, images, and memes. Foucault’s point is not that sexuality has become a new God or that we have regressed to pagan amorality, but that sexuality is the means by which we explore boundaries after these have become entirely human. 

For better or for worse, Foucault’s thought has long been assessed from the standpoint of its novelty. As a thinker of the radical social change the Western world underwent in the late twentieth century, he has had a very good run. But his centenary should be an invitation to look back to an older, stuffier, less hip, and more intellectually dated Foucault—and one that our bewildering times might find newly meaningful.

title: The Marxist Who Foresaw the AI Bubble

The Marxist Who Foresaw the AI Bubble

By Ted Reese • 14 Oct 2026 View in browser
View in browser
Scott Menchin
 
 

Like the 2020s, the “Roaring Twenties” of a century ago witnessed a technological revolution: The rise of the automobile, widespread electrification, and mass production had all transformed everyday life. In his speech accepting the Republican presidential nomination in 1928, Herbert Hoover declared that America was closer than any society in history to the “final triumph over poverty.” But trouble was brewing. 

Beginning in 1926, a little-known Polish political economist named Henryk Grossman gave a series of lectures at the University of Frankfurt in which he argued that the era’s great productive forces had been built on a fatally unstable foundation. While America’s material prosperity was real, much of its enviable monetary fortune was in fact fictitious. Profits were not growing fast enough to keep pace with the ever-greater amount of capital seeking a return. Following the figures closely, he noticed that in 1927, “industry and commerce have watched their production fall, their sales decline, and their profits contract,” even as bank deposits swelled. Capital was instead flowing into speculation in stocks and real estate. The United States felt as if it were whizzing toward the peak of the mountain, when it was actually about to slam into it at full speed.

In his well-timed The Law of Accumulation and Breakdown of the Capitalist System, which appeared just months before the Wall Street crash of 1929, Grossman argued that the reason for the problem he had identified was simple. Each wave of mechanization allows firms to produce more with fewer workers, cheapening goods and allowing the most efficient to win out against competitors. But this also ties up more and more capital in machinery. Output soars while average returns sink lower and lower. Eventually, there is more capital seeking profitable outlets than production can absorb, and the excess spills into speculation. This is why the money wealth of the 1920s was perilously fictitious. It consisted of claims on future profits that the real economy would never generate. 

“Grossman wasn’t alone in worrying.”

Grossman wasn’t alone in worrying, but he saw a mechanism underneath it that others didn’t. The governors of many Federal Reserve Banks and a majority of the Federal Reserve Board had begun to suspect that stock market “investment” was largely amounting to speculation that merely inflated corporate valuations and diverted resources from actual productive growth in agriculture, industry, and commerce. The Fed could see that an unusually large bubble was forming, but its explanations focused on speculative behavior and the misuse of credit. Its warnings to the public went unheeded. A new industry of brokerage houses, investment trusts, and margin accounts sprang up, enabling an increasingly large proportion of the public to borrow funds with which to purchase corporate equities. Buyers could put down a fraction of the price and borrow the rest using the securities themselves as collateral. The rising demand catapulted stock prices to previously unthinkable highs. 

The Fed’s skeptics never successfully wrestled with or understood the real underlying issue. Grossman did, warning that America was suffering not from an epidemic of bad behavior, but “an excess of capital” and crucially, too few investment opportunities to absorb it. As he worked on the book, his foreboding grew: There were “growing signs of an impending crisis in the United States,” he warned in May 1928. By December, as the Wall Street selloff was underway, he became even more explicit: “The great crash that is coming already casts its shadow.” Less than a year later, the stock market collapsed.

 

A century on, we find ourselves living through another technological “New Era.” Artificial intelligence promises arguably the greatest ever leap in productivity, the automation of vast quantities of human labor and, in its most utopian versions, a future of almost unlimited abundance. In March 2025, Elon Musk told an all-hands Tesla meeting: “A future of abundance for all, where really anyone can have anything. It sounds impossible… But what I’m here to tell you is that that will indeed be the case.” He later posted on X that “The future is going to be AMAZING with AI and robots enabling sustainable ABUNDANCE for all!” In July of this year, he told The Economist that he expected money to be obsolete by 2036. To get to the promised land, mega-corporations are committing sums of capital on a scale scarcely imaginable even a few years ago. The combined capital expenditure of the “hyperscalers” Microsoft, Google, Meta, and Amazon has risen to over $700 billion this year, up from roughly $140 billion in 2023, as AI enthusiasm helped drive American equities to record highs. 

Does this extraordinary technological dynamism demonstrate that capitalism has once again reinvented itself? Grossman suggests another possibility: that the very forces we take as evidence of the system’s ascent may again expose its limits. What is happening now should generate the same alarm felt by Grossman nearly a century ago. 

The concentration of investment in a single new technology is reproducing familiar pre-bust patterns at extraordinary speed. AI-related capital formation, including spending on data centers, IT equipment, and software, is now around five percent of US GDP, rivaling the dot-com buildout of the nineties, but taking just three to four years instead of the latter’s eight or nine. In just eighteen months, the top ten AI stocks’ share of the total value of the S&P 500 roughly doubled to 28 percent from 14 percent between early 2023 and mid-2024, surpassing the 2000 dot-com peak of 27 percent of the equivalent tech stocks. By 2026, just forty-four AI-linked companies accounted for a record 45 percent of the index and 71 percent of its earnings growth. Goldman Sachs warned in May that tech stocks accounted for 85 percent of the S&P 500’s gains so far this year; without them, the index had risen just three percent. Beyond tech, the rest of the economy looks comparatively starved.

As in the Roaring Twenties, speculation is justified on the growth of future returns, with one recent study reporting that about 95 percent of corporate earnings-call discussion of AI-related productivity refers not to present but expected future gains. AI infrastructure is capital-intensive and AI generates its products so quickly and abundantly as to almost instantly devalue them. A $200 dollar per month ChatGPT plan can burn through thousands of dollars worth of compute at OpenAI’s standard rates. OpenAI posted an operating loss of $21 billion in 2025 on $34 billion of spending, yet OpenAI and Anthropic represent 89 percent of the annualized revenue of thirty-four leading AI startups. The other thirty-two share only about $9 billion in revenue between them, and yet hundreds of billions are earmarked for the data center buildout. The free cash flow of the hyperscalers has fallen sharply since its 2024 peak, meaning they have less and less internally generated cash with which to fund the AI buildout they are driving. At the same time, the strategic reserves that have helped hold down oil prices during the war on Iran are starting to run low, threatening to raise the cost of sustaining that buildout just as its financing has become even more strained.

Leading-edge chips, meanwhile, are superseded roughly every twelve to eighteen months, rapidly reducing the value of existing hardware and requiring expensive regular upgrades. The share of national output needed just to replace worn-out or obsolete private equipment and buildings has risen to around 14 percent today, up from about eight percent in the early 1950s, while net private investment has fallen to around four percent of GDP, down from roughly nine percent in 1950.

Just as in the late 1920s, rising indebtedness can eventually manifest in rising interest rates, since lending to the increasingly indebted is a riskier and riskier business. As rates go up, refinancing debt―paying off old debt by taking out new debt―becomes prohibitively expensive for many borrowers, while lenders grow wary of the risk. After years of near-zero rates following 2008 and again during the pandemic, long-term interest rates have trended upward and are now at their highest levels in nearly two decades. The government is attempting to force rates down by buying back the long-term government debt that financial institutions and foreign central banks are less willing to hold, and with borrowing costs rising, the deficit and national debt are snowballing. Servicing old debt is taking up a greater and greater chunk of the government’s budget. Because the buybacks are financed by issuing short-term debt to buy long-term debt, the government will have to refinance its debt more and more frequently, leaving it more exposed to rising rates and making lending to the government more and more risky.

“Investment in people is increasingly unprofitable.”

Following government bailouts and expanding support and subsidies to private industry since 2000, the US debt-to-GDP ratio has risen to nearly 124 percent, higher than at the end of the last world war, after which a boom followed as soldiers returned to productive work and had children. Now we have falling rates of workplace participation and falling birth rates as investment is increasingly dependent on capital-intensive infrastructure. Investment in people is increasingly unprofitable.

When Musk, like a revenant Hoover, proclaims that a moneyless utopia of abundance is around the corner, he raises the expectation that we are on an inexorable path of progress. Grossman would once again be sounding the alarm and warning of the opposite: a frighteningly deep investment slump, severely curtailing not only the possibility of leading-edge innovation but general production and maintenance. From Grossman’s point of view, the question is when the house of cards crashes down, not if.

Grossman calculated that such great crises would not only recur, but that they would tend to erupt with ever-greater force. Crises, he wrote, “are simply a healing process of the system,” wherein profitability is re-established “even if forcibly and with huge losses.” Companies fail, assets are devalued, and what remains can begin earning a profit again. Today’s economists might see this as “creative destruction,” but Grossman called it “a safety valve for the capitalist class as a whole” whose outcome was not necessarily a benefit to society. Willing workers are thrown out of employment and useful goods and services are destroyed even as “social needs remain massively unsatisfied.” The 1930s, for instance, saw the US government slaughter more than six million pigs to raise the price of pork even as a third of households had someone out of work and many went hungry. 

And yet such actions provide only a temporary reprieve. The crash clears away the excess, but survivors will yet again find themselves mechanizing production to stay alive. The result might be an overall more efficient society, but capital only piles up again chasing ever sparser returns, and the potential for crisis and destruction grows. For Grossman, the most drastic form of reset is war. By destroying factories, infrastructure, and wealth at an enormous scale, war leaves far less capital competing for profits, and rebuilding gives surviving capital somewhere profitable to go. This destruction and devaluation is, for Grossman, “a means of warding off the imminent collapse,” creating “breathing space” for the accumulation of capital. He cites one contemporary estimate that the First World War destroyed around 35 percent of the world’s wealth in just four years. “If the early crises of capitalism could already lead to wild outbreaks,” Grossman warned, “we can imagine what crises will be like under the growing weight of accumulation.”

There are signs that a new pileup is already underway. Even in a time of phenomenal innovation, US money market funds held a record $8.4 trillion by mid-2026, which, in Grossman’s terms, suggests that excess capital is once again struggling to find profitable outlets. It is worth noting that these holdings also climbed sharply in the run-up to the crashes of 2001 and 2008. 

 

Grossman was ignored in his time, and is neglected now; if he were alive today, he would be dismissed as a “doomer.” But if he is right and prosperity itself, at least upon the basis of which it is presently produced, continually generates surplus capital, speculation, and pressure for new outlets, then neither laissez-faire nostalgia nor state-directed spending or redistribution will solve the underlying contradictions of a system that technology is making increasingly outdated.

Musk is surely right to say that technology is making money redundant. In this, Karl Marx would be in full agreement with the billionaire capitalist: As machinery and automation increasingly displace human labor from production, he predicted, labor time will cease to be an adequate measure of wealth. The productive forces created by capitalism itself will eventually blow its own foundation “sky-high.” 

Grossman likewise saw dramatically increased productivity creating the material foundations for a system of distribution that moves beyond our current mode of managing scarcity. Figures like Musk dimly see the future our system is trending toward. The paradox that Grossman identified, however, is that while capitalism creates the productive powers capable of overcoming scarcity, it can sustain them only so long as money invested returns as more money. It can bring us to the threshold of abundance, but can only ever slam the door shut just as we are about to cross it.

How the Movies Learned to Love Christians

By Germán S. Díaz del Castillo • 13 Oct 2026 View in browser
View in browser
IMDB
 
 

When the film God’s Not Dead was released in 2014, it was panned by critics. The film follows a Christian college student who is told to renounce his faith or fail a class. In addition to mocking the film’s performances, script, and production value, critics aimed fire at its plot, which they dismissed as an unrealistic portrayal of the predicament of Christians in the West. The following year, the Norwegian authorities forcibly removed the five children of the Bodnariu family from their parents in what many have called a case of anti-Christian persecution. The family’s story serves as a basis for Cristian Mungiu’s new drama, Fjord. And while God’s Not Dead received no mainstream awards, Fjord won the Palme d’Or at Cannes, arguably the most prestigious award in cinema.

The plot follows Romanian Mihai Gheorghiu, his wife Lisbet, and their children, who relocate to Norway, Lisbet’s birthplace, to be closer to her family. The devoutly evangelical family (the film’s stand-in for the Bodnariu family) initially receives a warm welcome, but is soon thrust into a legal and bureaucratic nightmare when Norway’s version of Child Protective Services, suspecting the parents of physical abuse, removes the five Gheorghiu children, including their still-breastfeeding baby.

Part of what leads to the confrontation is the Gheorgius’ open attempt to evangelize their neighbors. Lisbet is told at the retirement home where she works that religion is never to be brought up with the patients, and Mihai is admonished for briefly playing “Amazing Grace” on a keyboard in the school cafeteria. In spite of this, the Gheorghius continue to proclaim their faith. Lisbet also cares for Åke, the disabled and neglected senior patriarch of their neighbors, the Halbergs, who is coping with aphasia and whose condition improves—as his faith is restored—under Lisbet’s care.

We might expect a mainstream secular film to hedge its sympathies toward its Christian protagonists, but Fjord is straightforward in its depiction of the Gheorghius’ predicament. What initially seems to be genuine concern on the part of the authorities is gradually revealed to be a cut-and-dried case of religious intolerance. And while Mungiu doesn’t romanticize the Gheorghius and leaves certain ambiguities around the family’s inner life, the authorities’ abuse of power is never in doubt. The film’s court scenes in particular make it plain that an injustice has been done.

“Fjord is an indictment of Nordic secular humanism.”

Fjord is an indictment of Nordic secular humanism. The film opens with a stunning shot of Norway’s inlet landscape, and the recurrent displays of its overwhelming and barely habitable coastline link the harshness of the land with the harshness of the people who inhabit it. Mungiu sets the Gheorghius against the liberal and progressive Halbergs, who, while never engaging in the “physical abuse” of which the Gheorghius are accused, live in an emotionally fraught environment that causes their daughter Noora to cut herself and act rebelliously.

What is to be done about these cultural differences? Fjord’s answer is a bleak one. Although the Gheorghius are given a brief reprieve from their troubles, authorities make it clear that it is only a temporary one. Accepting the incompatibility of their worldview with the secular humanism of Lisbet’s country, they decide to abandon Norway. In the end, there is no possibility of assimilation or coexistence.

The film’s existence suggests the situation may be less bleak. Fjord is distributed by Neon, one of America’s most respected independent film distribution companies; it stars Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve, two of the world’s most sought-after stars; and has been acclaimed by critics. That a film placing Christians in a believable framing of victimhood can be made as a prestige independent product, and not just a niche, jeered-at film, points to a shift in the artistic class’s perception of Christianity. Although it is arguably easier to be a public-facing Christian in 2026 than it was in 2015, it is difficult to imagine a film with this plot structure—the often award-winning victim narrative—being made about Christians a decade ago.

Recent data show the decline of Christian affiliation halting in the United States and slowing in Europe, which may reflect a reduced antagonism toward Christianity. A decade ago, films in which Christianity was portrayed as an obstacle to tolerance—such as the 2017 Oscar winner The Shape of Water—were met with acclaim. But as the artistic class comes to understand Christians as a cultural minority, perhaps it will ascribe to them the narrative framing that it once reserved only for other groups, for there is nothing they love more than a good story of group victimization. That doesn’t mean that God’s Not Dead was a good film, but suggests it was ahead of its time.

How the Omni-Cause Swallowed Amnesty International

By Julie Bindel • 9 Oct 2026 View in browser
View in browser
Scott Menchin
 
 

In July, Amnesty International UK published a report called “A Growing Threat: The Anti-Rights Movement in the UK.” Written by Chiara Capraro, Amnesty’s gender justice director, the document prompted complaints from the organizations it had labelled “anti-rights,” among them feminist, lesbian, and gay groups (including the Lesbian Project, which I co-founded with Kathleen Stock) as well as a number of other bona fide human rights organizations. The report’s principal charge was “transphobia.” 

This was not the first time Amnesty had defamed organizations standing up for the rights of women and girls. It had already published “Like a Snowball: The Growth and Impact of the Gender-Critical Movement in the UK” in May, though that report had gone largely unnoticed. One organization named as “anti-rights” in both reports was Beira's Place, which was founded (and is solely funded) by author and philanthropist JK Rowling. 

“Longstanding supporters of Amnesty were dismayed.”

As the reports circulated, longstanding supporters of Amnesty were dismayed and outraged to see the organization turn on individuals, groups and services that were, in the main, set up to counter human rights abuses against women. Initially, Amnesty claimed that the report’s “use of language does not reflect the position of Amnesty International UK,” and a spokesman said—implausibly—that it had been “uploaded without going through the established internal review processes that are in place to ensure consistency, accuracy and alignment with Amnesty International UK’s positions,” adding that it remains “committed to defending human rights, including both the rights of women and the rights of trans people.” Before long, the heat was turned up significantly, especially when Rowling offered to fund any women’s organization wishing to take legal action against Amnesty. But the icing on the cake was a strongly worded letter from lawyers for Beira’s Place in mid-July, demanding that the report be withdrawn, that a public apology be issued, and that an external review examine how it had come to be published. On July 28, after new information had come to light, the Beira’s Place lawyers sent a second letter, this time warning that the organization had been “maliciously defamed.” 

It wasn’t just those directly affected by the reports who had objections. Iseult White is the granddaughter of Seán MacBride, the Irish republican activist, politician, and diplomat who co-founded Amnesty alongside Peter Benenson. She tells me she is “appalled” at the direction the once revered human rights organization has taken. “Releasing that report,” she says, “is essentially a form of propaganda: designating groups as not worthy of speech because they’re ‘anti-rights,’ and not worthy of freedom of association.” Amnesty’s “original approach,” she adds, “was based on meticulously researching a case, establishing that this was a prisoner of conscience, and building a campaign around that: letter-writing, cards, and so on. It was based on valid, real research. There’s no research behind that report; it’s just a set of opinions.” There is little question whose opinions those are. In November 2025, when Capraro, the second report’s author, appeared on the Guilty Feminist podcast, she said of the so-called anti-rights organizations: “In the same way that we are a global feminist and human rights movement, they are like the dark side. And they’re smart, they work globally, they collaborate.”

 

Amnesty International was founded in May 1961 by British lawyer Peter Benenson, who decided to act after reading a newspaper article on two students who had been sentenced to seven years in prison for drinking a toast to liberty at a restaurant in Salazar’s Portugal. In response, Benenson wrote an article for the Observer that launched the “Appeal for Amnesty 1961” campaign, which looked at the issue of prisoners of conscience, and called for their release. A prisoner of conscience was defined as anyone imprisoned anywhere in the world for their beliefs, race, or religion, provided they had neither used nor advocated violence. What began as a discrete twelve-month campaign elicited a huge response around the world, prompting its organizers to set up a permanent human rights organization dedicated to stopping abuses worldwide.

“In its early days, Amnesty held firmly to its specific principles and aims.”

In its early days, Amnesty held firmly to its specific principles and aims. For example, in 1964, it declined to declare Nelson Mandela a “prisoner of conscience” on the grounds that he advocated armed struggle. And though Amnesty thus angered many anti-apartheid activists, the organization saw itself as maintaining its integrity in the face of competing political pressures. 

“Amnesty should be fairly neutral,” says White, “because it should operate at the higher-order level of the most fundamental rights, the fundamental UN Declaration of Human Rights, and being anti-authoritarian. These days, it seems lost in omni-cause-style politics.”

An insider who has worked at Amnesty UK for several years, whom I will refer to as Sam, told me that Amnesty is “more of a men’s rights organization than human rights. They are far more interested in men that claim to be women, than actual women.” And as Gita Sahgal, employed as inaugural head of the Gender Unit between 2002 and 2010, told me: “When I entered Amnesty, I knew Amnesty was abysmal on women’s rights. But it was worse than I had imagined.”

In 2010, Sahgal was suspended following a very public dispute with her bosses over their support for the pro-jihadi, Taliban-supporting group Cage (formerly Cageprisoners) run by Moazzam Begg. Two weeks later, she resigned, accusing Amnesty of “ideological bankruptcy” and “misogyny.” She told me that there is a requirement that everyone in the organization toe the party line, and that staff are terrified of being disciplined for wrongthink. 

At the time of the Begg scandal, Sahgal, along with other feminists and secular activists, were accused of being “Islamophobic” or “racist” for opposing partnerships with religious political figures. Sahgal, who describes herself as “pro-Palestinian” but opposed to Hamas, says: “Going from refusing to support Mandela to collaborating with a group led by a man who supported the Taliban is surely an indication of ‘mission drift.’”

“Treating Begg as a human rights defender was clearly crazy,” says White. It also meant overlooking certain attacks on human rights. “Amnesty was only talking about state abuses. Meanwhile, the fundamentalists in Algeria were killing probably more people than the state was killing. They were killing women who were not wearing hijab.” 

During the controversy, Sahgal thoroughly researched both Begg and Cage, and was able to confirm that they were clearly associated with promoting and defending figures including key al Qaeda clerics and prisoners. “This was not a human rights campaign but one dedicated to spreading their ideology,” she says.

 

When did Amnesty lose its way? A shift began around the time that Amnesty caved in to pressure from feminists to adopt a policy on abortion. In July 2007, after Amnesty reversed its previously neutral stance on abortion to what Bishop William S. Skylstad (president of the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops) described as a “pro-abortion position,” he wrote to the organization, saying that its action “undermines Amnesty’s long-standing moral credibility, diverts its mission, divides its own members (many of whom are Catholic or defend the rights of unborn children), and jeopardizes Amnesty’s support by people in many nations, cultures and religions.” Prior to that decision, announced on the eve of its International Council meeting in Mexico, the debate within Amnesty had been raging for a period of two years. 

“I believe that Amnesty’s adoption of a position on abortion was where it started to go wrong.”

This may sound odd coming from a lifelong feminist, but I believe that Amnesty’s adoption of a position on abortion was where it started to go wrong. White feels similarly, telling me: “I’m pro-choice myself, but I still don’t think it’s Amnesty’s business to be in that arena. It’s legitimate for pro-life people to express their opinions on that, and it’s fine for Christians to have organizations that represent and advocate for their rights.” 

As far back as 1974, Amnesty began debating whether to recognize people imprisoned for homosexuality as prisoners of conscience. Following lobbying by external lesbian and gay rights movements, it formalized this position at its International Council meeting in Yokohama, Japan, in 1991, adding those imprisoned for being gay or lesbian to its core mandate. It was not a decision taken lightly: There had been seventeen years of internal discussion and debate.

This was an early shift of the organization’s priorities from political rights to social rights. Some within Amnesty were concerned that this could be a slippery slope. Once they acknowledged same-sex activity as an unjust cause for imprisonment, they would be forced to do the same for, for instance, those involved in extreme BDSM (which had started to be defined as part of the “LGBTQI+” movement). And once the mandate had been broadened to include defending people imprisoned for homosexual acts, Amnesty began to campaign for so-called LGBTQI+ rights. Since then, the organization has also run separate campaigns for intersex rights as well as several targeted global and regional campaigns focusing specifically on transgender rights, which resulted in its intervention in the UK Supreme Court case brought by For Women Scotland against Scottish ministers in 2025. Amnesty’s UK Office has also put pressure on libraries to center books aimed at “queer youth,” and has run a “Trans Love Letters” campaign.

According to White, young staffers fresh out of university think Amnesty needs to adopt all of these ideological positions to stay relevant. They compare what they see as the ill treatment of trans-identified people in the UK to the plight of prisoners in other parts of the world. The hypocrisy is staggering. In 2012, Amnesty showcased the documentary Umoja: No Men Allowed at the Amnesty International Film Festival to raise awareness of women’s rights and struggles in rural Kenya. This organization is willing to champion African women’s resistance to male violence abroad, yet dismissive of feminist concerns about male violence and women’s sex-based rights at home.

The organization’s shifting stance on prostitution is another case in point. In 2014, I received a call from a whistleblower who told me that Amnesty’s International Secretariat was about to announce a new policy document on this topic. I met the whistleblower later the same day and was shown the document. I was told that the draft document had not gone out for consultation, either among Amnesty personnel or its members, but was about to become official policy. The next day, I exposed Amnesty’s plans in a national newspaper, and within hours, feminist groups from all over the world began to organize on social media against the organization rubber-stamping a policy on decriminalization of the sex trade. 

As part of the My Body My Rights campaign, launched in March 2014, Amnesty described its support for decriminalization as akin to having autonomy over “bodies, reproductive capacities, and sexual choices.” In its draft policy document, Amnesty also took the line that disabled men have a right to access sex via prostitution: “For some—in particular persons with mobility or sensory disabilities or those with psycho-social disabilities that hamper social interactions—sex workers are persons with whom they feel safe enough to have a physical relationship or to express their sexuality.”

The backlash, under the war cry “No Amnesty for Pimps,” continued. In July 2015, weeks before the vote, celebrities including Meryl Streep, Kate Winslet, Emma Thompson, and Lena Dunham signed an open letter opposing the draft policy, and the media took note. Articles were soon appearing everywhere, and even Rolling Stone published a piece condemning Amnesty.

Nevertheless, on August 11, 2015, Amnesty voted to support the decriminalization of “all operational aspects” of the sex trade. With this vote, a pimp became a manager, a sex buyer a client, and a prostituted person a “sex worker.” “Amnesty International is opposed to the criminalization or punishment of activities related to the buying or selling of consensual sex between adults,” read the first line of the document. “Amnesty International believes that seeking, buying, selling and soliciting paid sex are acts protected from state interference as long as there is no coercion, threats or violence associated with those acts.” The wording on disability survived unchanged into the adopted policy. According to Amnesty, “men and women who buy sex from consenting adults are also exercising personal autonomy.” It is notable that Amnesty has, like so many groups and individuals that hold a pro-decriminalization position, gender-neutralized both the buyer and seller of prostitution, even though the vast majority of sex buyers are male, and that most of those at the supply end are female.

After the vote, I and other opponents of prostitution received word from a number of the rank and file of Amnesty in various countries expressing anger and shame that the organization could have adopted such a policy. In the meantime, Amnesty personnel continued to argue that full decriminalization provided the best outcome for prostituted people. As the Amnesty insider, Sam, tells me: “Whatever Amnesty, at least in the UK, believes on an ideological level, that will become carved in stone, even before any on the ground research or internal polling has happened,” says Sam. “All the progressive leftist talking points, whether so-called ‘Islamophobia,’ the sex trade, Gaza, the trans stuff, they tick all the boxes.”

White is heartbroken that her grandfather’s vision in setting up Amnesty has been abandoned. “For him, freedom of speech and association were the fundamentals of human rights, and that’s what’s so astounding to me about the Amnesty report: It’s saying we shouldn’t have the freedom of speech to say that sex matters, for women and for lesbian, gay and bisexual people, in policy and in life. It’s insanity that an organization claiming to be a human rights organization isn’t respecting the most fundamental human rights, freedom of expression and freedom of association.”

On Amnesty’s website are the words: “We uncover the truth and hold the powerful to account.”  Its support for powerful and harmful ideologies and practices, including political Islam, prostitution, and gender ideology, has made it the antithesis of what it was set up to be.

title: The Great Feminization Comes to Cornell
content:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul emphasized her gender when asked on October 3 about her appointment of a special prosecutor to investigate a possible rape at a fraternity house at Cornell University in 2024. Hochul is the first woman to serve as New York’s governor.
 ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏  ͏ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­  
 
Compact

The Great Feminization Comes to Cornell

By Helen Andrews • 8 Oct 2026 View in browser
View in browser
AP
 
 

New York Governor Kathy Hochul emphasized her gender when asked on October 3 about her appointment of a special prosecutor to investigate a possible rape at a fraternity house at Cornell University in 2024. Hochul is the first woman to serve as New York’s governor. Letitia James, the woman she appointed as special prosecutor, is the state’s first female attorney general. Seeing these two women take on the Cornell case has a special symbolism, Hochul explained. “I’ve heard from a lot of people,” she said. “The image gives them comfort to know that two women perhaps are looking at this differently than men would in the same position.”

She is right. The approach to the law reflected in the New York Democratic officials’ handling of the Cornell case represents a distinctively female perspective. Unfortunately, that perspective is incompatible with the rule of law.

Hochul said she felt it necessary to appoint a special prosecutor because she had “lost faith in the Tompkins County DA’s ability” to handle the case. That district attorney is Matthew Van Houten. He is no backwoods sheriff. The motto “Inclusion Through Diversity” appears at the top of all the documents his office has published regarding this matter. The reason he did not bring charges two years ago was because, on the basis of the accuser’s sworn statement, no crime had occurred. The sexual conduct that night was, in Van Houten’s words, “voluntary, conscious, and consensual.”

More facts have come out since that determination was made. On balance, the new facts make the story less favorable to the accuser. Text messages from the days after the incident show her telling one of the men she would later accuse of rape: “At the end of the day non [sic] of the sexual stuff was illegal”;  and “everyone needs to grow up cause sexuality and sex and shit is changing and stuff like this is going to become more common.”

During the hearing held on March 2, 2025, as part of Cornell’s investigation into the incident, “Jane Doe” described the intoxicating effects of ketamine, which she ingested that night. “You look like an operating human being,” she explained. “You don’t look dead or asleep necessarily. So, lights are on but nobody’s home.” The fact that the effects of ketamine are hard for an outside observer to detect tends to exonerate Scott Kretzschmar, who was not found to have had any sexual contact with Jane Doe by Cornell’s investigation, but who finds himself included among the so-called “Cornell 7” because he entered the room where the orgy was taking place and then left without attempting to stop it. (Scott Norris, another one of the accused, likewise says he had no sexual contact with Jane Doe.)

Recordings of phone calls between Jane Doe and some of the fraternity brothers were leaked to ABC News this week. Her call with Matthew Ingalls took place on November 7, 2024, which was three weeks after the alleged assault and one week after Jane Doe received a call from the fraternity president telling her she was disinvited from their Halloween Party, a step that seems to have changed her attitude toward the frat. In the phone call, she seems to be trying to trap Ingalls into incriminating himself. She asks him to describe what occurred in detail, supposedly because “the only way for me to heal is to know what happened.” 

“If prosecutions are brought in this case, it will be a corruption of the legal system.”

If prosecutions are brought in this case, it will be a corruption of the legal system. Letitia James has already stated that it was “horrific and unacceptable” what Jane Doe was “forced to endure” and added, “We stand with you,” as if her role did not require at least an appearance of impartiality. The standards of the kangaroo courts that proliferated on college campuses after President Obama’s 2011 Title IX guidance will have invaded the grown-up court, much as I predicted in “The Great Feminization.”

 

The Cornell outcry takes place against a backdrop of increasing administrative hostility to Greek life. Many college campuses have banned fraternities or limited their activities in recent years. In 2019, Swarthmore College eliminated its fraternities entirely after “allegations of racist, homophobic, and misogynistic behavior,” according to CNN. President Valerie Smith, a scholar of black literature whose books include Not Just Race, Not Just Gender: Black Feminist Readings, stated, “Fraternities and sororities will no longer exist at the College.”

I spoke at a conference at Furman University in South Carolina in 2024, and at the dinner afterward, I listened to Furman’s president boast about how she had faced down angry alumni in order to abolish fraternity houses. Under her new rules, which came into effect in 2020, all undergraduates are required to live on campus and off-campus events at fraternity houses are banned. The purpose was to keep students safe and reduce risk, she said.

Harvard attempted to ban fraternities and sororities in one fell swoop in 2016 under President Drew Gilpin Faust, making members of single-sex organizations ineligible for student leadership positions (including athletic captaincies) or referrals for scholarships and fellowships such as the Rhodes or Marshall. This policy was rescinded in 2020 after a federal lawsuit. Other universities, such as Stanford and Columbia, took a lesson from Harvard’s failure and instead attempted to chip away at their fraternities more gradually by depriving some individual frats of their housing, among other pinpricks.

Martha Pollack, president of Cornell from 2017 to 2024, was an enthusiastic proponent of the anti-frat trend. “Those of you who are at least seniors know that I’ve been sort of fighting this fraternity battle since I got here,” she told a meeting of the University Assembly in November 2022. “My first year here, I put in place a bunch of regulations that were supposed to make a difference. Then we put in place more regulations.”

Writer Ani Wilcenski offered a different perspective in a 2024 essay for Tablet. The Cornell administration “has been waging a determined war on frats for years, wielding an arsenal of nitpicky, draconian, and sometimes openly unfair policies to keep many fraternities in a near-perpetual state of punishment,” she wrote. In addition to President Pollack’s strict new rules for frats in 2019, Cornell implemented a ban on all fraternity social events in November 2022 that lasted for the remainder of the fall semester after some students alleged that they had been dosed with Rohypnol. This ban was announced before these allegations were investigated.

Notice what Valerie Smith, the president of Furman, Drew Gilpin Faust, and Martha Pollack have in common: All are women. Pollack asked a fraternity member at that assembly meeting in 2022, “Do you think the benefits any longer outweigh the downsides of the fraternity system?” It was clear that her own answer was no. It is not surprising that women in positions of authority fail to see the point of fraternities. Fraternities are for men. But that is no reason to abolish them.

“All were presidents of their fraternities.”

Why not get rid of fraternities altogether? It has always struck me that all four leaders of the passenger revolt on Flight 93—Todd Beamer, Mark Bingham, Tom Burnett, and Jeremy Glick—were stereotypical all-American guys: a varsity baseball captain, a football quarterback, a rugby player, a judo champion. All were presidents of their fraternities, except Beamer, who went to Wheaton, where there is no Greek life. The heroism they showed on September 11 was partly a result of the training they received in those institutions. 

Just five months ago, the public awareness campaign “Fraternities Know Men” was launched in order to highlight the growing body of evidence that young men are lonely and atomized and fraternities have a proven record of building social bonds, self-possession, and community-mindedness. The campaign is sponsored by the Fraternities Forward Coalition, a national body formed in 2020 as an alternative to the century-old North American Interfraternity Conference, which the breakaways believed was too passive in the face of college administrators’s growing intolerance of Greek life. The FFC's launch announcement promised “an unapologetic and swift defense for individual and organizational rights including, but not limited to, the right to be single-sex organizations, freedom of association, and fundamental fairness in conduct processes.”

Ironically, single-sex comradeship stood a better chance of helping Jane Doe than anything else in her undergraduate world. She had a designated “big sister” in her sorority, who received a text message soon after the fraternity incident: “Have you heard the rumor about your little?” The big sister confronted Jane Doe, who said of the rumors with a laugh, “unfortunately they are true.” The big sister later told investigators, “I could tell that—just from personal experiences—that what she was going through is that she had not yet processed what had happened.”

At a time when all the other voices around Jane Doe, including the Cornell administration, were encouraging her to explore her kink and embrace every kind of pleasure, no matter how depraved, her big sister took seriously her responsibility to tell Jane Doe that having ketamine-fueled group sex at a fraternity house was a bad idea. Jane Doe experienced this as shaming and wrote to one of the frat boys via text that “everyone knows” and this is “RUINING my life temporarily.” The key word is “temporarily.” The purpose of this kind of moral policing among sorority sisters is not to humiliate girls who make bad decisions. It is to teach them to make better decisions in the future.

When Furman announced its anti-frat reforms in 2019, the president of the Interfraternity Council told the student paper that fraternity houses “serve as way more than just venues for parties.” He continued, “We joined our Greek organizations to find values that are not shoved onto us every second by Furman.” The values of Greek organizations are indeed very different from the therapeutic values of the modern university. It will be a pity if the latter succeeds in eliminating the former.

Nordic cultural capital is at an all-time high. But the “Nordic” export is more of a vibe than a specific flavor profile or iconography.

Compact

There Is No ‘Nordic Model’

By Felice Basbøll • 7 Oct 2026 View in browser
View in browser
Christophe Thibault / CC BY 3.0
 
 

Nordic cultural capital is at an all-time high. But the “Nordic” export is more of a vibe than a specific flavor profile or iconography. Most trendy shopping districts will have a Nordic concept café or a fashion house; department stores will carry a “Scandi” line, often with little relationship to anything Scandinavians would tend to have in their homes. The concept of hygge as a way of life is Denmark’s most recognizable export. But its meaning—rougly “making ordinary, everyday things more meaningful, beautiful, or special”—is equivalent to “in my culture, we value food and family.”  

Nordic coffee bars are less likely to be run by Scandinavians than by people who believe their home countries could benefit from some Nordic “slow living.” Drip coffee has become a symbol of appreciation for noticing your surroundings and everyday processes, all the things the screens have taken away. Scandinavians like errands, value their time off, and take pride in filling it with the mundane. Their mix of modern interior design and progressive politics usefully permits things like home making, country living, knitting, and sourdough to be decoupled from the trad wife aesthetic.

The appeal of Nordic aesthetics was always bound up with the political ideal represented by the region’s generous welfare systems and egalitarian ethic. Men push baby carriages and the state provides generous maternity and paternity leave. Always leading in foreign aid contributions, Nordics consider themselves humanitarian frontrunners. On climate, too, Denmark is a key exporter of windmills, and Sweden gave the world Greta Thunberg. The education system has little stratification, and most institutions aim at making young Scandinavians “good enough.” No one should get too big for our shared boots. We are far more comfortable being dependent on the state than on each other. The Nordics have grown in appeal as “well-being” has replaced liberty as a primary target for measuring human flourishing. 

However, it is becoming harder and harder to see the Nordic countries as representative of a single “model.” Denmark’s big companies like Novo Nordisk and Mærsk are a source of national pride, but new start-ups quickly move their operations elsewhere. Sweden and Iceland, by contrast, have the highest numbers of tech “unicorns” outside the United States and Israel. On immigration policy, meanwhile, the Nordics are far from a unified bloc. Sweden welcomed Syrian refugees while Denmark pulled up the draw bridges. Only now are the other Nordic countries following suit. 

People do not open up a Nordic-style café because they admire Mette Frederiksen’s record on immigration policy, but in recent years, Denmark has gained some cachet on the right. This is no small feat; as much as the Nordic model was admired and invoked by Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the “socialist” states of Northern Europe have been longstanding bogeymen for the American right. Many decades back, President Eisenhower took a swipe at Sweden for being overrun with paternalism and drunkenness: “Lack of ambition is discernible on all sides,” he said. But today, the Nordics have started to look more promising to a new postliberal right that hymns community, trust, and strong culture. 

“We’re happy to forgo such comforts.”

There are natural barriers to immigration in Denmark that are hard to reproduce in the Anglosphere. Danes speak English, today’s lingua franca, but speaking Danish is necessary in order to settle and thrive long-term. The egalitarian ethic is enticing at a distance, when it is constrained to your local café, but somewhat less so when it comes with the heavy tax burden and few paths to excellence. As a result, there are high levels of short-term high-skilled immigration; people leave when they can no longer stand it. We have fewer Deliveroo drivers and cleaners, because we like housekeeping and running errands, and because these services are more expensive on Scandinavian wages. We’re happy to forgo such comforts.

Denmark’s hard line on immigration is a question of pragmatism more than principle. A favorite refrain in Danish politics is that a policy must not lead to “absurd” outcomes. Policies are directed at fixing specific problems; anti-ghetto laws, which allow the government to carry out evictions and demolitions in areas that are more than 50 percent “non-Western,” are no exception. These policies were designed expressly to avoid “Swedish conditions”—the pockets of violence that our neighbor nation has allowed to fester. 

For similar reasons, the Nordic economic model has come a long way since its socialist beginnings. Scandinavian countries have a generous benefit system, but very few worker protections. The Danes pay far more in taxes, but Britain’s tax system is far more progressive. Even the children of the wealthiest Danes receive a generous government grant as students. A third of apartments in Copenhagen are so-called andelsboliger, which are part-owned through an association. These used to provide housing for the working class, but in practice, because they are passed on by knowing someone who knows someone, they have become hotbeds of nepotism and corruption. Just before the 2026 election, the government announced a fødevarechek, or food allowance, in order to combat rising cost of living prices, which was paid out to a third of the Danish population. Political opponents criticized the payout as tantamount to bribery. 

Beneath the surface, Scandinavia is very far from the dreams of the left and the right. The Nordic tradeoff in the twentieth century was to retain old-fashioned institutions, but without their spiritual heft. Generous welfare provisions ensure that Scandinavians are never interpersonally financially dependent on each other, and even married couples file their taxes as individuals. The fødevarechek was given to some Danish millionaire households for this reason: Distribution was based on individual rather than household income. We may on paper be more religious—70 percent of Danes are members of the Danish national church—and collectivist, but in practice we have religion without God and marriage without dependency. We have little responsibility for each other beyond our tax payments.

In a 1955 article in Time, a Swedish man was quoted as saying: “The only difference between our behavior here and behavior in other countries is that we face the facts.” He was referring to acceptance of sex before marriage, but Scandinavians pride themselves on their pragmatism on a wide range of issues. Denmark is a country run on egalitarianism, soft nepotism, and “reasonableness,” and it wouldn’t work otherwise. Sweden embraces its own contradictions by preserving socialist vibes in an increasingly libertarian business environment. Finland famously earns its title as the happiest country in the world by having low expectations. Perhaps there is something to admire in this flexibility, but it is no “model.”
