How ‘Woke 1’ Radicalized the GOP

By Gregory Conti & Aaron Sibarium • 6 Oct 2026 View in browser
View in browser
AP
 
 

On May 30, 2020, five days after the death of George Floyd, the head of a prominent DC-area think tank issued a stentorian condemnation of the killing and the bigotry she said had enabled it. Echoing The New York Times’s 1619 Project, which sought to “reframe the country’s history by placing the consequences of slavery…at the very center of our national narrative,” Kay C. James described racism as a “fatal wound” that had permanently bloodied the American project. “How many more black people must die,” she asked, “until America admits that racism is still a problem in this country?”

Such statements were to be expected from a progressive nonprofit or a virtue-signaling corporation. James, though, was the president of the Heritage Foundation—the conservative think-tank that would go on to develop Project 2025 in the lead-up to the 2024 election. Just five years after James made her statement on Floyd, her successor, Kevin Roberts, would plunge the institution into turmoil by defending Tucker Calson’s interview with a Holocaust denier, Nick Fuentes, who has stated that “white people are every single bit justified in being racist.” (Roberts subsequently apologized.)

The contrast is a synecdoche for the arc of the contemporary right. Haunted by the legacy of “Peak Woke,” conservatives are now rejecting the terms of a cultural settlement that prevailed, with bipartisan support, through Donald Trump’s first term. Behind all the culture-war bluster stood a GOP establishment that was positively tame by today’s standards, less extreme than liberals portrayed it at the time, and more accommodating of progressivism than many Republicans recall. 

The first Trump administration celebrated the “contributions of our great minority-owned businesses” and maintained the racial set-asides that gave them preference. The second barred affirmative action in federal contracting.

In 2017, a year after Trump said Caitlyn Jenner could use the women’s restroom in Trump Tower, Texas Republicans killed a bill that would have limited transgender access to public toilets. As of 2026, almost half of US states have passed such measures.

The stated objective of Trump’s first term was border security, a goal that mainstream Democrats professed to share. The stated objective of his second—mass deportations—is anathema to the center-left.

On nearly every culture-war flashpoint, from affirmative action to immigration to transgender issues, the Republican Party has moved to the right of its Trump I baseline, embracing policies and rhetoric that were outside the Overton Window as recently as 2020. The shift cannot be explained by Trump himself, who is if anything a moderate within his own coalition. (Consider his defense of the H-1B program to an exasperated Laura Ingraham.) Nor can it be explained by the regular pendulum swing of partisan politics, given that in his second term Trump has undone not just the policies of his predecessor but those of his first administration.

“The radicalization of the right is best understood as a reaction to the left.”

Instead, the radicalization of the right is best understood as a reaction to the left, which underwent its own transformation over the course of Trump’s first term and, with even greater force, in the aftermath of Floyd’s death. From the race-based allocation of Covid drugs to the proliferation of woke vocabulary in government documents, policies that seemed unthinkable under Barack Obama became the norm under Joe Biden as wokeness hardened into a governing program, conquering institutions and impinging on ordinary life in a way that old-school political correctness never had.

Now, nearly two years into Trump’s second term, the backlash to that program has transformed the conservative movement. “Woke 1” may have peaked, but the backlash to it has been institutionalized, creating a GOP that is more militant—and arguably more effective—than it would have been if Democrats had policed their left flank during the “Great Awokening.”

The New Deal and Great Society are often seen as inflection points in the history of American conservatism, left-wing projects that durably reshaped the right. The woke era, which lasted roughly from 2014 to 2024, may be remembered in a similar light. Wokeness did not just change the character of liberal institutions or disrupt the pre-woke status quo; it kickstarted a conservative revolution that made a return to that status quo impossible, redrawing the lines of the culture war in ways that leave less room for ceasefire and détente.

That revolution ended more than a half-century of Republican support for affirmative action, which was institutionalized in federal contracting by none other than Richard Nixon. It created a conservatism that is at once race-conscious in its approach to immigration and radically colorblind in its approach to civil rights. It eroded the live-and-let-live attitude of groups like the Log Cabin Republicans, which in August rebranded itself as an “LGB” organization amid rising hostility to the “T.”

Above all, it has killed off the air of invincibility that left-liberal cultural politics had acquired by the end of Obama’s presidency and which, to a surprising degree when we look back now, endured during the first Trump presidency.

 

Start with racial preferences. For years, the right’s stance on affirmative action could be summed up by two Clinton-era slogans: “safe, legal, and rare” and “don’t ask, don’t tell.” Conservatives grumbled about reverse racism, sure, and often raised the specter of unqualified diversity hires in fields like medicine and transportation. But outside of college admissions, the GOP tolerated racial preferences provided they weren’t too overt, turning a blind eye to the sort of thumb-on-the-scale discrimination that characterized corporate hiring in the pre-DEI era. Nixon, Reagan, and both Bushes pursued affirmative action in federal contracting, at times against the wishes of their own cabinets, and the issue was not a high-profile litmus test for judges the way abortion or gun rights were.

Republicans also enforced disparate impact law, a legal doctrine that prohibits race-neutral policies, including standardized tests, if they disproportionately exclude minorities. And they left untouched a Nixon-era rule that required federal contractors to set diversity “goals” (supposedly distinct from quotas) if their percentage of minority employees was lower than that of the relevant labor pool. During Trump’s first term, that rule was enforced by Craig Lean, the director of the Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs and a former member of the Florida Bar’s Diversity and Inclusion Committee. He would go on, in a 2023 podcast with the Federalist Society, to praise the Biden administration’s focus on “intersectionality.” 

For several decades, there was a sort of gentleman’s agreement that affirmative action could continue so long as it remained subtle and illegible, with enough obfuscation and doublespeak that employers could claim plausible deniability in the event of a lawsuit. The premise of this tacit accord was that affirmative action would prove unacceptable if the practice became too open and unabashed. Euphemisms were essential, because most elites regarded racial preferences as a necessary evil rather than a positive good, something to be tolerated rather than celebrated.

But by 2020, that modus operandi had collapsed. If the old approach to affirmative action was “don’t ask, don’t tell,” the new approach was more like “shout your abortion.” Companies advertised fellowships that explicitly excluded whites and Asians, banks lowered interest rates for companies that hit their diversity targets, and both state and private health systems allocated life-saving medical care based on the color of their patients’ skin. (During the pandemic, one hospital gave “Non-White” patients seven points in its allocation scheme for monoclonal antibodies—more than the six points it would have given an obese patient who had hypertension, diabetes, and asthma; the hospital eventually scrapped the scheme amid legal threats.)

It was in this climate that Trump’s anti-DEI agenda was hatched. Conservatives began to suggest that the new affirmative action regime had roots in the old one, citing policies like the Nixon rule to argue that wokeness, far from a postmodern import or irrational “mind virus,” was in fact derivative of federal policy.

One of the most influential articulations of that thesis came from Richard Hanania. His 2023 book The Origins of Woke argued that Republicans should target DEI at private businesses, stop enforcing disparate impact law, and revoke a 1965 executive order that required affirmative action in contracting. Trump did all that and more, going so far as to eliminate the Minority Business Development Agency—created by the Nixon administration to provide capital to black businesses—as part of his sweeping purge of the bureaucracy. The Trump Justice Department also released a legal opinion arguing that disparate-impact liability is unconstitutional because it forces employers to adopt racial quotas. And it has investigated a raft of law firms, universities, and corporations over their alleged use of racial preferences, extracting multi-million dollar settlements from Deloitte and IBM this year.

“The GOP is more hostile to racial preferences now than at any point since 1968.”

The result has been an unprecedented polarization of the affirmative action debate. As a matter of policy, the GOP is more hostile to racial preferences now than at any point since 1968. Democrats, meanwhile, are still pursuing the sort of race-based policies that radicalized the right against affirmative action, such as a scoring system in Portland, Ore., that prioritizes “BIPOC households” for homeless services.

In other words, the two parties are no longer debating exactly how much affirmative action is permissible so long as it is handled with a relatively light touch. Peak Woke transformed the debate into an all-or-nothing proposition, pitting radical racialism against maximal colorblindness. Insofar as conservatives are winning that debate—65 percent of Americans, including 48 percent of Democrats, opposed race-based college admissions in a poll taken shortly after the Supreme Court outlawed the practice—it is unlikely that the most overt forms of racial preferences (as opposed to more covert ones) will return anytime soon.

 

Wokeness also polarized the transgender debate, an area where the right was surprisingly conciliatory throughout Trump’s first term. During his 2016 campaign, Trump spoke warmly of the greatest symbol of transition in the country, Caitlyn Jenner. He later declined to criticize the Bostock decision, written by Trump appointee Neil Gorsuch, which enshrined transgender identity as a protected category in employment settings. (Contrast this muted response with the anger Trump has expressed about the recent tariff judgments.)

Meanwhile, red states that sought to restrict transgender people’s access to public restrooms largely abandoned those efforts in the wake of widespread backlash. Republicans were even afraid to touch the sports issue that became such a lightning rod during Peak Woke: As late as 2021, future DHS secretary Kristi Noem, then the governor of one of the reddest states in the country, vetoed a bill banning biological males from participating in women’s sports. (Noem later reversed course amid a primary challenge.) 

In short, a decade ago Republicans seemed poised to reach a begrudging truce with the transgender movement, which had begun winning over centrists and moderate conservatives in the same way that the gay rights movement had. A useful bellwether was former Fox News firebrand Megyn Kelly, by that point a news anchor at NBC, who in 2018 hosted five transgender youths for a segment on the “GenderCool Project,” an online campaign promoting “positive stories about transgender and nonbinary kiddos.” Kelly sympathetically explored her guests’ struggle for “acceptance,” warned about the “rollback of transgender equality rights,” and used the preferred names and pronouns of everyone on stage. “I had no wish to cause offense,” Kelly later recalled. “Trans people were tortured enough, it seemed to me, by nature of their dysphoria and society’s disdain for them in general. So I complied. I went along with it.”

In the intervening years, however, transgender activism did not diminish. Rather than declare victory with the Bostock decision, which outlawed the most significant forms of discrimination against transgender people, the LGBTQIA2S+ movement (to use one of the acronyms from this period) began to manufacture new identities and demand new modes of redress. Activists argued that natal males should be able to participate in women’s sports, that schools should socially transition kids without parental consent, and that “gender-affirming care” was “life-saving” for minors. Preferred pronouns became mandatory, kindergarteners learned about gender identity, and the Biden administration replaced the term “mothers” with “birthing people” in government documents.

It became common for left-leaning pundits and politicians to claim that unless one accepted the full slate of demands from the transgender lobby, including the metaphysical claim that transwomen really were women, one was radically limiting the freedom of one’s fellow citizens and causing trans kids to commit suicide. These ideas were given the imprimatur of the medical establishment, which insisted the science was settled (it was not) and espoused patent falsehoods that lit its credibility on fire. In a since deleted video, for example, Boston Children’s Hospital claimed some babies know they were transgender “from the womb.”

Such excesses prompted Kelly to disavow her past support for preferred pronouns (they’re a “gateway drug,” she said in a 2023 monologue) and to campaign with her erstwhile nemesis, Donald Trump. The latter’s viral 2024 ad, “Kamala is for they/them, President Trump is for you,” suggested that Kelly was far from alone. Many Americans had soured on transgender activism, and what seemed like unnecessary cruelty in the 2010s now seemed like a needed dose of common sense.

Trump’s second inaugural announced that it was “the official policy of the United States government that there are only two genders: male and female,” and a day one executive order focused on “defending women from gender ideology extremism and restoring biological truth.” Bathroom bills that failed in Trump’s first term were signed into law, and the White House forced the University of Pennsylvania to expunge from its records the transgender swimmer Lia Thomas, whose victory in the women’s NCAA championships became a cause célèbre in 2022.

There have also been more draconian measures that go beyond anything attempted between 2016 and 2020. While the first Trump administration imposed some restrictions on transgender military service, for example, the second has tried to ban all “individuals with gender dysphoria.” (The Secretary of War recently celebrated a military that had “no trannies,” as well as no “fatties, beardos, weirdos, wimps, or radicals.”) This year Kansas became the first state in the nation to retroactively invalidate the driver’s licenses of transgender people, and Oklahoma passed a law that bars taxpayer-funded gender care for adults.

Such policies were well outside the Overton Window before Peak Woke, which led Republicans to conclude (rationally) that appeasement was a failed strategy. With Democrats largely refusing to moderate on transgender issues—one Democrat who tried, Seth Moulton, was forced to issue a groveling apology for his comments about women’s sports—it is hard to imagine an armistice anytime soon.

“An ersatz traditionalism is gaining ground.”

This dynamic has reversed what many saw as a positive trend from Trump’s first term: a growing tolerance for gays and lesbians on the American right. Unlike Obama, who publicly opposed gay marriage in 2008, Trump never campaigned against the practice, and he was clearly comfortable with minority sexual identities, an unsurprising fact given his past life as a New York libertine enmeshed in the entertainment industry. One reading of Trump’s 2016 victory was that LGBT issues had been somewhat depoliticized, and that Republican support for gay marriage, and gay people, would continue to increase. Instead, the opposite has transpired, with the unpopularity of the “T” apparently spilling over into other parts of the acronym. Republican support for same-sex marriages and relationships has fallen substantially, and right-wing culture has grown more heteronormative (if not more chaste) in response to the Great Awokening. If a “live and let live” ethos led conservatism in 2016, an ersatz traditionalism is gaining ground in 2026.

 

The most consequential legacy of wokeness may be the right’s restrictionist turn on immigration, which began in 2016 but accelerated dramatically after 2020. Trump violated many rules of decorum when discussing this subject in his first presidential campaign, but for all his polarizing rhetoric, his stated goal in 2016 was ostensibly a bipartisan one. Obama oversaw 3 million deportations during his tenure, leading some left-wing critics to refer to him as the “deporter in chief,” and even as Hillary Clinton dismissed a border wall as wasteful and unrealistic, she endorsed the basic principle of border security, noting that she had voted as a senator “to build a barrier to try to prevent illegal immigrants from coming in.” Her primary opponent Bernie Sanders was, if anything, more hawkish on immigration, deriding open borders in a 2015 interview with Ezra Klein as a “Koch brothers proposal” that would “make everybody in America poorer.” 

“You’re doing away with the concept of a nation state,” Sanders told Klein. “I don’t think there’s any country in the world that believes in that.” Evidently, the Democratic Party had not yet gotten the message that no human is illegal. 

And it was illegal immigration with which the first Trump administration was principally concerned. Citing the need to reduce unauthorized inflows, Trump spent much of his political capital on the border wall, which he said would have a “big, fat beautiful door” so that people could “come in legally.” Though his administration did cut refugee admissions and the number of green cards issued, these moves were not emphasized rhetorically, and Trump himself seemed more worried about the rule of law than about the ethnic composition of new arrivals. As he had put the point on Cinco De Mayo in 2016 amidst his first campaign: “The best taco bowls are made in Trump Tower Grill. I love Hispanics!”

On immigration, in other words, both sides were still largely operating within a shared normative frame: Legal immigration was good, illegal immigration was not, and border enforcement was legitimate so long as it was “smart” and “effective,” as Chuck Schumer put it in a 2018 speech opposing Trump’s wall. The debate was over the meaning of those terms.

Then came the Biden border crisis and the racial politics that fueled it. Progressive leaders associated immigration enforcement with white supremacy and condemned traditional limitations on entry and residence as racist and immoral. During the first Trump term, slogans like “Abolish ICE” migrated from the activist left to the liberal mainstream, marking a complete break with Democratic rhetoric under Obama and Clinton. Meanwhile, the foreign-born share of the population reached its highest level since the Ellis Island era. The surge was driven largely by the Biden administration’s abuse of the humanitarian parole system, meaning that most of the new arrivals were technically legal immigrants—the category long seen as unproblematic by Democrats and Republicans alike.

All the while, progressives salivated over reports that the white share of the population was in decline. “This is fabulous news,” former Washington Post columnist Jennifer Rubin said of one such report in 2021. “Now we need to prevent white minority rule.”

“The right’s approach to immigration in Trump’s second term has changed.”

As a result, the right’s approach to immigration in Trump’s second term has changed qualitatively. If the first Trump administration focused on keeping illegal immigrants out, the second is focused on deporting those already here. Trump II has also cracked down on legal immigration—including skilled immigration—with unprecedented measures such as a $100,000 fee on H1-B visa petitions. And his executive order revoking birthright citizenship (struck down by the Supreme Court in June) was meant to change a fundamental aspect of America’s self-understanding, and of its constitutional order, so as to deter future entrants to the country.

Conservatives have also grown more willing to connect critiques of legal immigration to concerns about race and ethnicity. Some influencers contend that closing the border is necessary to preserve America’s white majority before it disappears forever, and note that progressives who cheer white demographic decline seem to be rooting for the “Great Replacement,” a phrase that was beyond the pale before Peak Woke. The term “Heritage American” is now mainstream on the right, and the perception among Republicans today that immigration per se is a threat to the American way of life has effaced Bush-era conservatism more completely than anything in Trump’s first term. With the conspicuous exception of white South Africans, whom Trump has alleged are the target of a “genocide,” the State Department has effectively barred all refugee admissions, ending fifty years of refugee policy.

 

All this suggests that the radicalism of Trump II is better understood as a response to Peak Woke than as a continuation of a coherent ideology already in place during Trump’s rise. Despite his unorthodox and boundary-pushing rhetoric, in his first term Trump largely respected the cultural consensus of the Obama years, poking at its edges but leaving the most important assumptions intact. It was wokeness, not Trump, that dissolved that consensus. If liberals had clamped down on their woke flank, many of their preferred policies would likely still be in place, and Trump’s second term (on the assumption that there was one) would have been more moderate in many respects. Instead, the GOP has moved so far right that there may be more daylight between Trump I and Trump II than there was between Obama and Trump I. When historians look back on the cultural politics of the first quarter of the twenty-first century, the killer blow to left-liberalism will likely be seen not to be the 2016 election, but the apotheosis of wokeness in the years that followed.

“There may be more daylight between Trump I and Trump II than there was between Obama and Trump I.”

For Republicans, there is an equally unpleasant truth to be faced: Namely, that much of what they now decry as “cultural Marxism” or “gay race communism” was perfectly acceptable to them in practice until only very recently. Wokeness didn’t slip in behind their backs, imposed by devotees of postmodernism or a globalist cabal; it grew out of policies and practices with which the Republican Party, including Donald Trump, had largely made peace. If conservatives are now opposed to the “woke mind virus,” it’s because their own views changed in response to a pathogen they helped create.

In any event, the pre-woke consensus is not coming back, and there’s a good chance that the next Republican administration will make this one look downright docile on race, gender, and immigration. Many centrists hoped the election of Joe Biden would put the excesses of wokeness to bed, since wokeness, they believed, was principally a reaction against Trump. But this did not come to pass, and the Democratic Party continued to sprint left.

Likewise, the GOP may continue to move right even if there is no second Great Awokening. For better or worse, the memory of the original episode of wokeness is seared in the conservative mind. How long it will take to forget it is anyone’s guess.

The Bleak Truth Behind France’s Riots

By Michael C. Behrent • 5 Oct 2026 View in browser
View in browser
AP
 
 

Hegel said that a tragic situation is one in which both sides are right. The violence that has recently broken out at French high schools comfortably fits this definition. On the one hand, a movement supported by leftists—notably Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s party, La France insoumise (Unbowed France) or LFI—is protesting against inadequate resources and the dire state of many lycées (high schools). On the other side are the French state and its security forces, which are responding forcefully to the protesters’ brazen rejection of elementary standards of civic behavior. The violence in which the movement has engaged is indeed deplorable, resulting in the destruction of several schools and the beating of police officers. At the same time, the French government’s police state reflexes are also on full display. Yet this exclusive focus on violence overlooks the fact that, despite all that sets them against each other, the grievances expressed by parties in the conflict are surprisingly similar. 

“France manages to combine the worst elements of neoliberalism with the worst elements of social democracy.”

Even as they fight one another, the students and the police have both experienced the profound degradation of French public services in recent years. Both represent institutions that feel they no longer have the means to carry out the tasks they are expected to fulfill. Both, moreover, have suffered from the policies France has pursued for decades, and which have been heightened during President Emmanuel Macron’s decade in power. The French state has increasingly adopted neoliberal approaches to public management, even as it borrowed money at astronomical rates. France manages to combine the worst elements of neoliberalism with the worst elements of social democracy. Financial incoherence is matched by political dysfunction. For all intents and purposes, France lacks and seems incapable of finding a governing majority. Many fear that the chaos afflicting many high schools is merely a foretaste of the civil discord that could erupt during next year’s presidential election. 

The student uprising began in the Paris region in mid-September, a little more than two weeks after most schools returned from summer vacation. According to the government, between 400 and 500 schools have currently suspended classes. Over 400 people have been arrested, and both sides claim to have been the victims of violence resulting in bodily harm. 

The student movement primarily denounces the inadequate staffing and poor physical conditions found in many schools. Students complain about large class sizes, crumbling infrastructure, buildings that are boiling in the summer and freezing in the winter, and a lack of school doctors. They express concerns about tracking. They object to Parcoursup, a web portal established by the French government to manage university applications that students find cumbersome, stressful, and untransparent. Even if they use the language of mental health that is the norm for their generation, most of the students’ concerns are about academics. One of their most serious complaints is that some of the classes they are required to take have no teachers assigned to them. French high schools don’t offer students a stand-alone diploma, like in the US, but prepare students for an end-of-studies exam known as the “bac” (or bacalauréat), consisting of exams in a range of subjects. If a class has no teacher, the students can’t just be arbitrarily assigned credit for it. It means they are not getting adequate preparation for the exam. According to Ryad Rani, the nineteen-year-old president of the main high school union, “the problem now at lycées is not having a teacher the year you take the French bac, not having a French teacher for several months.”

France’s educational system has long been a source of national pride and a vital element of its democratic system. The lycées were founded by Napoleon to introduce meritocracy into education. The public school system was established in the late nineteenth century to bring republican ideals to all French people and wean them from the education provided by Catholic priests. Unlike in America, the education minister plays a prominent role in French politics. Yet because education is so central to French identity, it also becomes the focal point at which many social tensions converge. The National Education Ministry, which employs 1.2 million civil servants—every public-school teacher in France—is a vast bureaucracy that cannot be easily reformed. Despite a formal commitment to equality, there are considerable discrepancies between public schools based on where they are located. Schools in suburbs with large numbers of racial minorities are particularly deprived, in part because while teachers are mostly paid by the French state, school facilities are financed by local government. 

French presidents regularly attempt to reform the education system. Macron is no exception. While he considers himself a booster of the school system—he married his teacher, after all—his conception of education was in keeping with his entrepreneurial ethos. He wanted an education system that was leaner, adaptable, efficient, and, in certain instances, selective. But his reforms have met with criticism and have yet to reap clear rewards. He reformed the bac exam so that it was based on a common set of courses rather than early specialization. But some claim this has created a system in which poor schools offer the basics while rich schools can supplement them with fancy electives. The bac aimed at vocational education was reformed by significantly reducing the amount of time students spend in class and replacing it with internships and work experience. 

Most of all, Macron has, in successive budgets, eliminated teaching positions. Some unions claim he has cut more than ten thousand positions since becoming president, and the current budget, announced in the midst of the school riots, seeks to cut over 1,500 positions for 2027. While it can be necessary, misguided reform can also produce disturbing results. The city of Paris is currently dealing with a crisis resulting from a 2013 reform that sought to improve student wellbeing by shortening the school day and introducing more extracurricular activities. The latter made it necessary to hire a large number of non-teaching staff. Not all of them were ideal candidates, and sexual abuse was reported at 184 Parisian schools.

 

Much of the coverage of the school riots has focused on violent confrontations between students and the police. Yet the French police have complaints not all that different from those of the students. The police, too, claim that an institution central to the functioning of the nation is inadequately funded, and that politicians care little about whether it achieves its mission. A demonstration organized by the main police union was held last January. In a Facebook post, the union declared “our colleagues ensure the security of French people with professionalism and courage, but without the human, material, logistical, and juridical resources required.” It adds: “The National Police is doing very poorly, [and] police officers … are at the end of their rope.”

“The French police had to exfiltrate the mayor of Alès from his own town.”

These grievances are not confined to the police. There exists widespread public concern with high levels of brutal crime, as evidenced in several cases that have received extensive coverage. Last May, an eleven-year-old girl named Lyhanna went missing before it was discovered that she had been raped and murdered by a man who had already been charged nine times for pedophilic crimes. The Lyhanna Affair called attention to a range of shortcomings in the judicial system: understaffed prosecutors’ officers, overwhelmed magistrates, outdated case-tracking software. Meanwhile, a Mexican-style drug cartel named DZ Mafia has been formed in Marseilles and extended its operations throughout southern France. Last July, the French police had to exfiltrate the mayor of Alès from his own town because the cartel had made a credible threat to kill him. The incident suggested that French security forces were incapable of holding their own against organized crime. At a more prosaic level, France witnessed a 9 percent increase in 2025 of refus d’obtempérer, that is, refusals on the part of drivers to pull over. 

It is difficult to know the extent to which these problems are due to insufficient resources or disrespect for authority. As with the school system, France continues to devote extensive resources to the police and the judicial system. Yet it seems clear that many police officers, like students, feel they are forced to work in decrepit circumstances with inadequate support. And police and students either bemoan or testify to the French state’s dwindling authority. Few use the term, but the sense that France could become a failed state pervades its political culture. The background to this situation goes back many decades. Since the 1980s, France has, despite its longstanding statist reflexes and its population’s attachment to the welfare state, undergone steady neoliberalization. It has privatized public services, cut taxes on high incomes, and deregulated its labor market. 

Some of these trends have continued under Macron—who, unusually for a French president, openly embraces business culture. He eliminated the wealth tax and managed to reform the pension system by raising the retirement age to sixty-four (until politics required him to postpone its implementation). Yet at the same time, France has significantly raised social spending. The political scientist Kevin Brookes observes that between 1974 and 2008, France saw “a greater overall rise in the generosity of its social system than other [European] countries and by 2008 was the third most generous welfare state in Western Europe.” These measures are far from systematically egalitarian. But the biggest problem with this zombie neoliberalism is that it depends on colossal amounts of borrowing. The national debt currently exceeds $4 trillion, which comes to about 119 percent of GDP. In 2026, the cost of the interest on this debt will exceed $80 billion—making it the most expensive item in the budget, above education and defense. 

The problem, as some French politicians are trying to point out, is not simply that France is financially irresponsible, but these interest payments are wasted money. Every euro the French spends on paying down the debt is a euro that France won’t spend on building a school or improving its judicial system. France finds itself in the curious situation of being a country with a robust welfare state that nonetheless lacks the funds to make meaningful investments in public services. Whether you blame the current riots on the students or the cops, the underlying problem is an enormous failure in leadership on the part of France’s political class. 

 

Financial mismanagement is exacerbated by political failure. Part of the point of a representative democracy is to mitigate social tensions by channeling them through democratic institutions and deliberations by elected representatives. Yet this system depends on the existence of a majority party or coalition—one that, at the end of the day, has decision-making authority—which France no longer has. Currently, the parliament is split into three roughly equal groups: the far left (LFI), the Macronist center, and the far right. The reasons for this system are complex, including factors such as the weakness of French political parties. Yet the proximate cause of this situation was Macron’s irresponsible decision to call snap parliamentary elections in the summer of 2024. As a result, he lost his (already wobbly) quasi-majority and condemned the remainder of his presidency to inaction. 

Not only do the actions of the French government lack political direction, but the stalemate has led most political actors to ignore the slow boring of hard boards in favor of electoral one-upmanship in view of next year’s presidential election. The fact that two of France’s largest parties (LFI on the left and the National Rally on the right) have never been elected to government and embrace what are widely regarded as extremist views adds further fuel to this fire. Even if the roots of their concerns are similar, the police and the students have starkly different political allegiances: the young (particularly those of immigrant background) are LFI’s target audience, and the police are championed by the far right. It is not unreasonable to see the current riots as an expression of the pent-up tensions that could find no outlet in the country’s sagging democratic institutions. 

Public coverage is understandably focused on videos of burning high schools or police officers being kicked in the head by teenagers. In France, such images seem to confirm the fears of civil war that has haunted writers such as Michel Houellebecq and Laurent Obertone. It is also surprising to observe the degree to which LFI seems to be doubling down on its support for the student movement, even as that movement has taken a grisly turn: Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s party seems confident that this stance, far from being a liability, will earn it votes in 2017. Many French people no doubt fear that this will not be the last instance of political violence in the upcoming election cycle. 

“Democracy is ceasing to be the framework in which the French can solve their problems.”

The high school riots are an extraordinary disruption of civic life in what is supposed to be a functioning Western democracy. Protest is, of course, essential to democracy; yet the wave of contestation underway in France is something different—meaner, more desperate, more hostile than healthy dissent. Democracy is ceasing to be the framework in which the French can solve their problems and settle their differences. Some two hundred and thirty years ago, France, at the dawn of the democratic age, taught the world the many and often frightening ways democracy could be born. Now that we find ourselves at what may be at the end of the democratic era, France may have much to tell us about the many and often frightening ways democracy could die.

How Anti-Corruption Politics Destroyed Brazil

By Alex Hochuli • 2 Oct 2026 View in browser
View in browser
AP
 
 

Brazil’s upcoming election pits President Lula da Silva, eighty, against Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, forty-five. If he wins, Lula will serve a record fourth (non-consecutive) term. His opponent is the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. To much of the unenthusiastic electorate, it feels like an election about nothing. Both candidates have rejection rates between 45 and 55 percent. Lula’s slogan is “Brazil, ready for more” (of what?); Flavio mainly wants to get his dad out of jail. It is the old versus the not-quite-new. 

“No one really rules Brazil.”

That isn’t to say that matters of great importance won’t be decided. The issues at stake include the growing national debt, who has access to rare earth minerals, and a slew of soon-vacant seats on the Supreme Court. The problem, however, is that no one really rules Brazil. After a decade defined by an unending string of scandals, the country suffers a crisis of legitimacy and a void of political authority. 

Lula’s Workers Party (PT) has held the presidency for seventeen of the past twenty-four years. But with a small minority of seats in Congress, the party has proven unable to impose a governing program in the way holding office would suggest. The Bolsonaro clan still has leadership of the conservative camp, having supplanted the moderate center-right eight years ago in a radicalization similar to that which took place across Western Europe or North America. But Jair Bolsonaro is imprisoned and unhealthy, and his sons inspire little loyalty beyond the base. Their response to the impasse has been to look up for salvation—to North America and Donald Trump.

On the issues that pollsters say most concern Brazilians—security, above all, but also the cost of living, health and education—there is little concrete debate, let alone vision. Instead, Brazil is riven by scandal and institutions at each other’s throats. Most notable is the Supreme Court. Justices launch accusations at colleagues in public sessions while Congress threatens to impeach them. It is comeuppance for an institution that has become far too powerful, and in particular for one justice who made himself sovereign.

At the center of the latest scandal is Daniel Vorcaro, a disgraced banker responsible for the country’s largest ever banking fraud and a much less-discussed scheme for legally ripping off public workers through a payroll-deduction credit card. In only a few years, Vorcaro became incredibly well-connected, benefiting from the benign neglect of the Central Bank president and paying off other directors at the institution. He hosted bunga-bunga parties in New York for Brazil’s financial and political elite and traveled on one of his multiple private jets to Courchevel with his “friend for life,” an influential senator to whom he was paying monthly stipends of between $60,000 and $95,000. The scandal around Vorcaro’s defunct Banco Master revealed a compromised regulator, a drained state bank, bought-off politicians, a prison suicide, plunder of public funds, and a very bad bit of cinema.

Of greatest consequence are Vorcaro’s links to Supreme Court justices. He hosted them at lavish dinners, went into business with one, hired the spouses of others as lawyers for exorbitant fees, and in general held contacts that a sober judge should judge untoward. We know all of this because institutional politics in Brazil is now conducted through that most contemporary and mercurial of means: leaks, especially of private communications. And in Brazil that means WhatsApp. 

To take one example: Two days before Vorcaro was sensationally arrested at the airport as he tried to flee to Dubai, he messaged Moraes, “does [Central Bank President] Galípolo know? By Monday do I need to be gone?” Other messages retrieved from Vorcaro’s phone signal his life-long gratitude to Moraes. The messages were written in the iPhone Notes app, screenshotted, and sent as one-time view messages, a mode of communication Moraes himself had classified as an obstruction of justice in another case. Moraes’s phone was not seized, meaning his replies are unknown and the justice’s complicity is unproven. But the stain of scandal remains.

It is less clear who benefits electorally from Vorcaro’s fall. In 2025, Moraes sentenced Jair Bolsonaro to twenty-seven years imprisonment for an incompetently attempted coup in early 2023; the judge had also been running an almost autonomous, wide-ranging inquiry into “fake news” that saw him summarily take social media accounts off air, leading to a spectacular clash with Elon Musk. All of this allowed him to cast himself as the guarantor of Brazilian democracy (of a bulletproofed, not-very-representative sort). As such, he has become associated with the institutional left, with the PT, and with Lula. 

The scandal around him should therefore help Flávio: Who wouldn’t desire the destruction of his father’s jailer? But dig deeper and there are always further complications. Another justice, Dias Toffoli, is even more implicated with Vorcaro and Banco Master, but he was not investigated and his communications not leaked, because the justice who holds rapporteurship, André Mendonça, is a Bolsonaro appointee. Two weeks ago it came to a head in a degrading spectacle, with justices calling each other liars. Brazilians now once again know the names and faces of those they maybe shouldn’t—those who should be quiet and demure upholders of the Constitution. 

 

Does anyone care? According to pollster Datafolha, nearly half the population feel the Supreme Court and Master scandal will influence their vote, with over a third saying it will have a big influence. Flávio voters care more than Lula voters (by 45 to 26 percent), and greater numbers think the left is more implicated than the right.

If the scandal helps to put an end to Lula’s political career, it would be the most ironic, and bathetic, of denouements. Since 2014, Brazil has undergone a series of rolling crises, centered around corruption revelations. These crises intersect with—they are both cause and consequence of—economic downturns and strangling institutional dysfunction. 

In 2014, the Lava Jato corruption probe revealed an arachnoid scheme of overbilling and kickbacks between the state-controlled oil giant Petrobras, huge construction companies, and multiple political parties. Running until 2021, it led to the arrest of business leaders and sitting politicians including Lula himself, who spent 580 days in jail. The revelations served as political fuel, but not legal justification, for impeaching Lula’s successor, Dilma Rousseff, in 2016. The first irony is that it was the PT who had first empowered the judiciary and the public prosecutor to carry out the relevant investigations. Then a radical section of the judiciary, wedded to highly legalistic conception of society, pursued Lula for years.

The second ironic reversal was the revelation in 2019 that the anti-corruption campaign was itself corrupted. A series of leaks revealed the judge and the prosecutor were in cahoots, with the lead judge back-seat driving investigations and orchestrating leaks to the media, whose reporting was sometimes even used as corroborating evidence. Lula was released, and his and many others’ convictions were annulled. 

When former army captain Jair Bolsonaro was elected on a wave of anti-political sentiment, he hired Lula’s jailer as his justice minister. The latter quit after a year under a cloud of disgrace and his own discomfort at being used. Bolsonaro’s disgovernment was characterized by institutional chaos amidst the pandemic, as he set out to deliberately impede governmental capacities. Pursuing re-election, he turned on the fiscal firehose—a “secret budget” of congressional amendments that would ultimately total some $10 billion by the end of 2022, equivalent to a quarter of discretionary fiscal spending. It became part of a process by which the legislature would become ever more powerful, hoovering up pork for itself. 

Lula returned, promising to save democracy. As if to prove the point, Bolsonaristas caused chaos in order to prompt the military to intervene. They also cooked up a scheme to assassinate Lula along with Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who would take on the rapporteurship of the coup-attempt case. 

Moraes—known as Xandão (in English it would be “Big Lex”)—had always been associated with the center-right. But in another one of these strange reversals of political polarity that mark our age, Moraes became a hero to the left: scourge of coup mongers, jailer of Bolsonaro, and in the clash with Elon Musk over social media takedown orders, defender of national sovereignty against the Trump-aligned magnate. Moraes was even placed under sanctions by the Trump administration.

For the left, the myth of the impartial judge had been buried in the febrile atmosphere of the right-wing anti-corruption crusade of the mid-2010s. Moraes’s pursuit of Bolsonaristas did the same for the far right, which in turn re-enchanted the left with the counter-majoritarian power of the togas and the courts. It would be yet another irony if Xandão’s implication in the Master scandal gives Flávio Bolsonaro the narrow edge to put an end to Lula’s political career. 

“Now it is the Supreme Court in the crosshairs.”

Forty-five percent of Brazilians now distrust the Supreme Court, the highest on record. It is about the same level as for Congress, political parties, and the presidency. These latter numbers are actually down on the historic levels of distrust—indeed, disgust—that they hit last decade, when they reached the high sixties. But it is not so much that these institutions have recuperated any of their legitimacy as that the spectacle of scandal has moved on. Now it is the Supreme Court in the crosshairs.

This is the institutional razed earth of the anti-corruption crusade, its long hangover. If we understand politics as the union of ideals and interests, concretized in a program, and advanced by representatives of the people, then this whole practice has come to be undermined, degraded. Lava Jato presented itself as a noble attempt to put an end to corruption once and for all but, behind this moralistic ideal, there was a great deal of cynicism about any national project for Brazil and the grubby compromises that always accompany capitalist politics. The radical judiciary believed that no progress could be made until Brazil was set on its proper legal footing. That puts the cart before the horse. The history of development around the world shows that there is no order before progress. 

Instead of enabling progress, moralistic fervor and resigned disappointment have lowered expectations. Scandal-mongering has become the central tool of politics, wielded first by the right, then by the left, and now by the right again. Indeed, the left now keeps trying to pin Vorcaro on the right. It has some basis for doing so: Vorcaro made hundred-million dollar payments to fund a (still-unmade) hagiographic film about Jair Bolsonaro; the suspicion is that this was to cover living costs for Flávio’s brother Eduardo Bolsonaro, self-exiled in the United States after being sentenced for lobbying against his own country.   

At every turn, politics becomes further demoralized. Congress has become fat on pork but has no desire to lead. Having suffered the scare of Lava Jato, during which one-sixth of legislators were under investigation, congressmen aspire to little more than remaining in office. Meanwhile, over 90 percent of the federal budget goes on mandatory spending and the share remaining to the president is shrinking fast. The executive cannot really lead, and government can only be accomplished by diving into the swamp. 

The upper ranks of the judiciary sought to fill this vacuum of authority, but every activist step it took in attempting to right the republic undermined its role as guarantor of the constitution. Who elected them anyway? So it is perhaps fitting that Brazil’s latest leak-lubricated scandal has come for the judiciary. 

Whoever wins October’s election will not really rule Brazil. Lula’s workout videos do not disguise a loss of political vigor. He does not feel like a man in tune with his times, and he has no credible successor. But if Lula can’t lead, Flávio doesn’t want to. His clan’s imbrication with organized crime and subservience to Washington tells you all you need to know about their ultimate ambitions. Finance, agribusiness, and the extractive industries will win again.

title: We Must Become Gods

We Must Become Gods

By Ashley Frawley • 1 Oct 2026 View in browser
View in browser
Scott Menchin
 
 

When I was a kid, there were long periods when we didn’t have television. Bored senseless, I read all the books on my shelf. When I was finished with those, all that was left was the Bible. So, naturally, I picked it up and began my quest to read it cover to cover. I think I only made it to Leviticus, but the exercise did leave me with one lasting impression, or rather question: Why was the God of the Old Testament so different from the God of the New? Why was I finding here this God of wrath and domination, where in school I’d been taught to pray to Abba, Father, with an affectionate familiarity? In my ten-year-old mind, I smoothed out the contradiction: We all must have a little bit of God in us, and when we die, we join God, and He grows according to how much humanity has grown.

In the Enlightenment and the century that followed, it was common for thinkers to imagine that a child’s development retraced the history of humanity in miniature. They would not be so surprised, then, to see that my childish questions and answers belonged to much older debates about the relationship between God and man. But as faith in progress, once associated with the left, has migrated uneasily to the right, these questions have acquired strange new political significance. When I read God saying, in Genesis, “Behold, the man is become as one of us, to know good and evil,” was this a transgression or a responsibility? Was I—are we—to wait to become divine in heaven, or make it real on earth? Should humanity continue to expand its powers, or learn to fear them?

“In humanity and our history, Spirit comes to know itself.”

Years later, when I encountered Hegel for the first time, and then Marx, the answer seemed obvious. Hegel appeared to echo my childhood resolution: In humanity and our history, Spirit comes to know itself; we are moments in the unfolding of Spirit in the world. But Carl Sagan’s sci-fi tinged secular-cosmic register spoke more to me: “We are a way for the Cosmos to know itself.” Matter comes to know itself, to think itself, through the human being. Marx’s inversion seemed to offer an exciting double meaning that hinted at where we were headed: “In direct contrast to German philosophy which descends from heaven to earth,” he wrote, “here we ascend from earth to heaven.”

It was through Marxism that I encountered Prometheanism, and with it the exhilarating realization that both man and the world are unfinished projects. We could master nature and democratize abundance and freedom through technological innovation. And anyway, I thought, we were already doing it, even as the walls of our economic system pressed up against our ambitions. But I found that I was oddly alone in my excitement. At every rally and protest, allegedly among comrades, I found people recoiling at this decidedly Western and “anthropocentric” view of the world. No, instead we needed to de-grow, to pull back, to recognize limits, and accept once and for all that the human hand on history was a destructive one, at least in the West, and that we needed to look elsewhere for inspiration on how to do politics and how to live.

And so today, we are witnessing a strange political realignment. The backward pull, the ideal of limits, has found a home on the left, while modernism and the hubristic impulse to push forward have turned up in unlikely pockets of the right. It is often there, in rhetoric oddly tinged with religiosity, that we must rummage if we want to find that old Promethean confidence once attributed to Marx, that we can build, discover, master necessity, enlarge freedom, and become something that we are not yet. It is figures like billionaire tech entrepreneur Peter Thiel who hopefully declare “the forces of chaos and nature can and will be mastered,” so that “the tyranny of chance will give way to the Providence of God.” Meanwhile, Vice President JD Vance is telling summits that “we should embrace the future head-on.” 

Perhaps Thiel is right that the “movement from chaos to order begins in Genesis,” and that Christianity preserves a confidence in humanity that the secular world has lost. But if Christianity has found itself keeping alive the Promethean flame, it doesn’t follow that it knows what to do with it nor that it fully realizes where it leads. If becoming more like God is to be less a burden and punishment than a responsibility, we must have the courage to follow wherever that “becoming” takes us.

 

In some ways, the affinity should never have seemed odd at all. For two thousand years, Christianity has promised that human beings might become “partakers of the divine nature,” while the Jewish tradition can be read as carrying a radical current toward emancipation from divine authority. Both carrying the serpent’s foretelling that “you shall be as gods,” they have anxiously guarded the flicker of a revolutionary anthropology all their own.

In his appropriately titled, You Shall Be as Gods, Erich Fromm explores the Fall not as man’s original sin and shame, but his first act of freedom. He traces how man does not simply obey but gradually argues with God, demands that even God answer to principles of justice, and moves toward a mature freedom of human responsibility and autonomous judgment. 

Fromm’s reading of the Talmudic story of the Oven of Akhnai is a powerful case in point. In trying to resolve a dispute, Rabbi Eliezer calls upon successive miracles to vindicate his judgment. Each time, the miracles appear until the very heavens themselves cry, “Why do you dispute with R. Eliezer, seeing that in all matters the halakhah agrees with him!” But rather than bow down, the rabbis still refuse to yield. “It is not in heaven!” Rabbi Joshua cries. The Torah has long since been given to man and it is man’s to adjudicate. Later, Rabbi Nathan asks the prophet Elijah how God reacted to this affront, and Elijah responds, “He laughed [with joy],” and said, “My sons have defeated me, my sons have defeated me.”

That man no longer needs God, Fromm concludes, is precisely what pleases Him most. In the Hebrew tradition, one can see man becoming “God’s partner and almost his equal.” Eventually he must become independent, even from God. This is, of course, Fromm’s radical humanist reading, not doctrine, but he finds it significant that a tradition founded on divine law and obedience could nevertheless produce an anthropology that reaches beyond both.

However, the trajectory that began with the Fall was not simply that man would be freer, but that “you shall be as gods.” What that means depends on what God is. When Moses asks God for a name, He responds: “I am who I am” (Ehyeh asher ehyeh). For Fromm, it is significant that the Hebrew verb ehyeh is the imperfect form of to be: “It says God is, but his being is not completed like that of a thing, but is a living process, a becoming.” God refuses a proper name because he is not an object. He is not finished or fixed; He is the living God.

This is why Fromm sees the injunction against idolatry as the essence of the Hebrew tradition, so that “the acknowledgment of God is, fundamentally, the negation of idols.” Idols, once forged, are fixed and frozen. But God is alive. He quotes Isaiah asking, “Shall I bow before a block of wood?” Should I cook my dinner with a tree that I’ve cut down and prostrate myself before the stump left in the ashes? For Fromm, the contradiction between idolatry and embrace of the living God is “that between the love of death and the love of life.” The Hebrew tradition resonates for him less as a warning that man might reach too far, but that he might recoil from life and dig his hands and head in the dirt; that he might bow before what he has already made, before what is dead. Being made in the image of God, he must not succumb to the temptation of idolatry and instead recognize himself too as becoming, as a creature “with a capacity for an evolution of which the limits are not set.”

Fromm is not alone in such readings, nor is the idea of becoming like God distinct to Judaism. In the seventh century a debate erupted within the Byzantine Church concerning the number of wills of Christ. Did he possess only a divine will or also a human one? Maximus the Confessor, a Christian monk and theologian argued that the latter was obviously true: When Christ said, in the Garden of Gethsemane, “Father, if possible, let the cup pass from me,” he showed the “weakness of his very own flesh,” that he was both “properly human” and divine, and accordingly in possession of two wills, one human and one divine. In other words, Christ’s humanity was not negated by his divinity.

What appears at first as an obscure theological dispute leads Maximus to a more radical destination—though it was for defending the former, the doctrine of two wills, that he lost his right hand and tongue. God’s becoming in the flesh, his becoming fully human as Christ without ceasing to be God, worked both ways. “Man will remain whole man in soul and body, owing to his nature, but will become whole God in soul and body owing to the grace and splendor of the blessed glory of God.” This doctrine, known as deification, remains central to the Orthodox Church and is affirmed by the Catholic Church. It is Athanasius’ more startling fourth century wording that still echoes in the latter’s catechism: “He was made man that we might be made God.”

“For Maximus, deification does not entail the destruction of human nature.”

Crucially, for Maximus, deification does not entail the destruction of human nature. Christ, he writes, “completely divinized us, without in any way violating or essentially altering our nature.” Christianity then, contains within it a transformation in which man can become something radically more than what he is now without abolishing himself, without becoming something other than human. Our task is not a divine but very human one: To become as gods, while remaining fully human.

 

It is not difficult, then, to see why hope in the future is often expressed today by the religious. But if theology guards the radical notion that we can become as gods, the twentieth century has given us reason to question whether we really should. The modern acquisition of powers once imagined as the sole province of gods did not lead us to the heavens but rather more deeply in the opposite direction: world wars, the atomic bomb, failed revolutions. History until now reads as a never-ending replay of humanity reaching and failing to grasp.

In the memorable opening lines of Dialectic of Enlightenment, Adorno and Horkheimer remark that Enlightenment “has always aimed at liberating human beings from fear and installing them as masters. Yet the wholly enlightened earth is radiant with triumphant calamity.” Whatever the complexities of their argument, the suspicion of the ideal of human mastery would reverberate across the modern left. Who could blame them, writing as they were in the shadow of fascism and in exile? Their time had shown the terrifying results of mankind’s hubristic impulse. The ability to create and destroy with a seeming wave of a hand (or the touch of a button) had produced enough on the destructive side to know in which direction things were likely to continue. Slowly, the old confidence gave way to a rather different rallying cry: Enough!

And yet not everyone writing in the shadow of fascism and war gave up on the serpent’s promise. The German Marxist philosopher Ernst Bloch wrote that humanity had learned fear “in a terrible fashion” and that now it was a matter of “learning hope.” This didn’t mean blind confidence that everything would turn out well, but only that history had to be actively made. The future, he continued, does not “come over man as fate, but man overcomes the future and enters it with what is his.” Elsewhere he went further, stating that the “only true original sin” is “not wanting to be like God.”

This “sin,” this refusal of responsibility to which Bloch alluded, can take many forms. In Fromm’s telling, man’s expulsion from Eden begins to unfold his freedom in the world, but it also opens a wound. Separated from Eden’s original wholeness, he bitterly regrets his newfound freedom. Man’s history from that point on is tinged by a longing to heal the fracture, to go back to a world where he did not yet bear the burden of knowing and choosing. The idol, Fromm says, “represents the object of man’s central passion: the desire to return to the soil.” 

This is why the Israelites, almost comically, have to be warned away from idols nearly every time Moses turns his back. Freedom has delivered them into such uncertainty that they pine for the security of slavery, where at least they ate “bread to the full.” The idol gives their longing a fixed object, takes a familiar shape from their past (a calf recalls bovine imagery common in Egypt), and in submitting to it they are, however temporarily, able to surrender the independence that tore them from those things in the first place.

“Whether or not one believes the biblical narratives, they record a human intuition.”

Whether or not one believes the biblical narratives, they record a human intuition. At some point we became aware of ourselves as having been thrown out of nature, as beings in possession of free will but set upon a world we don’t fully control. Not quite animals, not quite gods. Something in between. We have been trying to get back ever since. 

Retreat is essentially the attempt to hand off the responsibility for the answer to the question “what should we make of the world?” to some fixed authority beyond ourselves. While Fromm is reading the Hebrew tradition with fascism clearly in mind (the surrender to “blood and soil” in the idol reappears frequently), this impulse isn’t always backward-looking. We can easily see techno-optimism as representing the opposite pole, where transcendence and becoming are achieved by leaving the human behind altogether. The winner of the 2024 Turing Award, Richard Sutton, has remarked that we should not fear human succession by AI, but rather embrace and prepare for it. “Why,” he asks, “would we want greater beings, greater AIs, more intelligent beings, kept subservient to us?” While Sutton thinks of this as a hopeful development, indeed the only hope for humanity’s long-term future, it’s like saying the world’s problems are so far beyond us that we are better off leaving them to other beings. Unfinished humanity in its embodiment and frailty is seen as simply the latest condition to be superseded. But the Christian tradition that we saw in Maximus holds the crucial reminder that transformation need not, must not, mean self-abolition. Man can become something radically different from what he is now while still remaining man. To become as gods, we do not need to cease being human.

However, the more familiar renunciation runs in the opposite direction, where the Edenic desire is represented by a retreat from modernity. Perhaps more than any other, indigenous people have been made to carry this fantasy for everyone else. Again and again, I have seen problems indigenous people like myself face attributed to a kind of “Fall,” where colonization is our own Eden story, and restoring what is lost acts as a magical solution to social problems. In its most radical expression, proponents of “land back” wish to “reclaim our right to restore, uphold, and protect our symbiotic and just relationships with Mother Earth,” by “returning stolen lands” and “reclaiming everything that has been taken by colonization.” In its more reserved form, we can find it in Canadian politicians like Justin Trudeau gushing that indigenous peoples are stewards of the land “since time immemorial” whose “relationships with the environment will continue to guide Canada—and the world—to protect our planet for future generations.”

These statements shouldn’t grate on me as much as they do. Aren’t they flattering my own culture? Aren’t they apologizing for very real past wrongs and promising, however half-heartedly, to restore something that is at least partially my birthright? As it happens, I engaged in my own “return” to the land recently, though without the political significance, and found myself at a ceremony with family, sitting around a sacred fire. I was trying not to let my ambivalence about the situation affect my guilty nostalgia for it all, when my dad stood up and started talking about the guidance of the Seven Grandfathers and finished with a thought about the spirit that moves through all things. “The spirit of God is within us,” he said. “Didn’t the Church use to say that?”

I laughed. I pictured the holidayers coming through, hoping to peep the authentic world of what was lost, and confronting even here the same questions. God and man again; what are we? What are we becoming? I’m sure history could have gone in many different ways, but it went in this one and we’re all on this course now, whether we like it or not.

It’s worth mentioning that there is an entire indigenous sci-fi tradition through which indigenous peoples themselves refuse to be relics of the past, and there is even a Marxist version of indigenous futurism. The Red Nation declares that “by carrying this history forward, we actively create the world in which we want to live,” reveling not in a lost past but rather imagining a “coming indigenous future.” And yet even here the backward pull proves impossible to resist. The Red Nation calls socialism “the natural state of humanity” and speaks of restoring “correct relations with Mother Earth.” While denying that they are trying to “recreate the past,” they state that their purpose is to “steer Indigenous nations back” onto a communal development path uninterrupted by capitalism. It’s turtles all the way down.

 

And so we find ourselves back at those strange corners of the quasi-religious right to which progress has retreated. Here we can still glimpse a politics that believes humans can build, invent, explore, raise families, and act boldly in the world. But it too makes a final renunciation. It has reclaimed human power, while relinquishing any control over the conditions within which that power is exercised and so implicitly acquiesces to limits. When its hopes collide with economic conditions, it resolves the contradiction in exhortations and in the imagination, in heaven. 

In JD Vance’s Communion, we find a particularly illustrative example of this. As he surveys the wreckage of American capitalism, one almost expects him to realize that something quite serious—and material—is amiss. Instead, he proposes that we ought to think about things differently: “If the goal is to promote economic activity, the interests of families will often take a back seat to the demands of businesses. A Christian approach to economics would demand something different: concern for GDP, yes, but only insofar as it promotes human flourishing.” People like Vance are standing in front of the market and begging it to protect families and everything that humans hold dear. All well and good, but we should ask, people have been making this same demand to simply refocus on something other than GDP for decades or more. Why doesn’t the market respond?

When Abraham is told by God that he will destroy the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah, Abraham is horrified. “Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?” He challenges God, tries to subdue God to a living sense of justice. “Peradventure there be fifty righteous within the city,” Abraham offers tentatively, “wilt thou also destroy and not spare the place for the fifty righteous that are therein?” And God responds: “If I find in Sodom fifty righteous within the city, then I will spare all the place for their sakes.” Abraham eventually bargains God down to ten: “I will not destroy it for ten’s sake.”

For us, economic necessity is even more powerful than God and can be bargained with even less. The markets are more providential than the word of God. When confronted with the terrifying question, “What should we make of the world?” the right is prepared to surrender to an external, unchanging, answer. Nature says. Tradition says. The market says. Even, “God says…” But the answer is not in heaven!

Preserving the human cannot survive market fatalism. The market is not first and foremost for people, and it can’t be made so by asking. It’s for profit, and it has to be. Companies locked in fierce and global competition can’t and won’t sacrifice themselves on mere moral exhortation. They can’t simply refocus on “what really matters in life” over what really matters if they are to survive the next cycle. God is not there. The trouble is that no one quite knows how to move beyond it.

“We are now like the Israelites wandering in the desert.”

In many ways, we are now like the Israelites wandering in the desert. We know that there is some freedom and possibility just beyond the horizon, but we cannot seem to get there, and we may never. For years, impatient with the slow and seemingly slowing pace of progress, I lashed out at the failure of the left to embrace its Promethean history to pull us out once more from this void. Humanity was frightened of itself and abandoned progress, I thought. The New Jerusalem is up one more hill, but we have lost our nerve. I want more!

But I realize now that reluctance is not necessarily pure reaction. The biblical tradition is full of reluctant prophets. Moses begs God to send someone else, Jonah boards a boat in the opposite direction, even Christ himself prays, “Let this cup pass from me.” For Fromm, the core of prophethood is rejecting it: “Anyone who wants to be a prophet is not one.” The first poisoned fruits of our ambitions should have destroyed naïve Prometheanism. Becoming frightened of our own powers may be a sign of our maturation. But in what direction does that fear take us? The biblical figure of the prophet gives us an image of human greatness that is compatible with a deep sense of dread and responsibility but not renunciation.

Theology doesn’t give us a blueprint for what we should do with this or that policy tomorrow. It does however leave us with the conviction that history remains open because man remains capable of becoming something which he is not yet. Human beings must remain the subjects of progress. The biblical tradition still contains both halves of what is required to embrace this: We shall be as gods. But we shall also remain human.
