The Jury Trial Is Under Attack

By Erin Hagood • 30 Sept 2026 View in browser
View in browser
AP
 
 

After a Massachusetts judge announced a mistrial in the Lindsay Clancy case on September 4, it didn’t take long for the media to turn its focus from the trial to the jurors. We learned that the jury was hung by a single holdout juror who wanted to convict Clancy. We also soon discovered that the jury deliberations had been heated. According to the majority of the jury, the holdout juror stated during deliberations that he did hold reasonable doubt as to Clancy’s mental state at the time of the murders, yet he refused to apply the legal standard for non-responsibility. For his part, the holdout juror claims that he was essentially bullied by the other jurors, who repeatedly cut him off, and that he never had any doubt as to Clancy’s guilt.

The veracity of these claims may determine Clancy’s fate. Clancy’s lawyer has asked the judge for permission to probe the holdout juror for possible misconduct, and on Tuesday, the court heard arguments concerning a motion to dismiss all charges. If there is a retrial, the media interviews with the jurors will serve as market research for the prosecution and defense to tinker with their theories and modify their jury selection strategies. And given the attention the case has received, assembling an impartial retrial jury will be a serious challenge. In the meantime, the holdout juror has reportedly received death threats and has been hiding out in an undisclosed location. 

“It is a good moment to ask ourselves: What are juries for?”

The Clancy jury is hardly the first panel to face public criticism in recent years. The juries that acquitted Kyle Rittenhouse, convicted Derek Chauvin, and freed Casey Anthony, to name a few, were also subjected to public scrutiny. It is a good moment to ask ourselves: What are juries for? Why do we trust twelve regular people with decisions of freedom, justice, life and death?

After the mistrial was announced, the prosecutors vowed they would obtain “justice” for Clancy’s three children. But trials exist not for the victim, but for the accused. If we did not have a justice system, anyone suspected of a crime might be killed by a mob. (Just read the comment section of a true crime video if you need convincing.) This is, in fact, how justice was often carried out in the ancient world. There can be no justice for the victims. The murdered children certainly won’t come back to life. So the only question is what society is to do with the criminal. 

Criminal trials occur not to obtain justice for what can never be righted, but to decide the dispute between “the People” and the accused concerning the facts of the case and the spirit of the law. The accused has a right to a jury of his peers because his freedom is at stake. He has the right to be judged by those who might also find themselves in his position. He has the right for his fate to be determined not by the arbitrary power of the state nor even the passions of public opinion, but by members of society ready to defend the spirit of social freedom.

There is a long history of juries passing judgment not just on the facts of the case, but on the law itself. In 1670, the soon-to-be founder of Pennsylvania, William Penn, and his associate William Mead were arrested in England for preaching Quakerism in violation of the Conventicle Act, which outlawed religious assemblies of more than five people outside the official Church of England. The jurors refused to return a guilty verdict, repeatedly offering partial findings that omitted the charge of unlawful assembly. The infuriated judge locked the panel up for two days without food or water to coerce a conviction. When the jury held firm and acquitted the defendants, the judge fined the jurors and committed them to prison until paid.

Foreman Edward Bushell challenged his detention through a writ of habeas corpus. Chief Justice John Vaughan ruled that a jury could not be punished simply on account of its verdict. Bushell’s Case established the inviolability of the jury in the modern era. It has been invoked at various times throughout history to defend unpopular or contentious jury verdicts. It is the ability to protect the citizen from an arbitrary state that led Sir William Blackstone to call the right to a trial by jury “the glory of English law.” 

In the early days of the American Republic, it was assumed that the jury was to judge both the facts of the case and the justness of the law. This latter power is known as “jury nullification.” Jury nullification is not legally recognized as a valid power of the jury today, although most admit it is impossible to stop a jury from returning a not guilty verdict if its members don’t believe in the justness of a law. A recent example of this is the “DC Sandwich Guy” case where a grand jury in Washington, DC, refused to indict a man who threw a sandwich at an ICE officer. 

Jury nullification was first called into question amid conflicts over slavery and Reconstruction. Juries in the antebellum North refused to convict those guilty of abetting runaway slaves in violation of the Fugitive Slave Act (escaped slaves were denied the right to trial by jury at all). After the Civil War, Southern juries nullified civil rights and enforcement laws to protect Ku Klux Klan members and government agencies from prosecution for everything from violence to property violations. In response, lawmakers and judges sought to curtail the jury’s right to nullify laws they found unjust. 

The crisis of the social revolution of free labor in the industrial revolution corresponded to a crisis of the general social will, leading to the suspicion that juries could not be trusted to reason about the appropriate application of laws. The attempt to change social practices through the enforcement of laws upon a hostile public pitted juries against Congress. The Fourteenth Amendment reopened the question of how jury trial was understood in American law by giving Congress the right “to enforce” its provisions, and the 1895 Supreme Court decision in Sparf v. United States ended the practice of legally recognized jury nullification, subordinating the spirit to the letter of the law given by the state. The generation of the Civil War sought to give this social crisis a political meaning in terms of freedom. 

 

The Clancy case has given rise to the rather paradoxical notion of “reverse jury nullification.” During the jury deliberations, the jury asked the judge to instruct the holdout juror as to the definition of reasonable doubt. Members of the jury say that they did this because the holdout juror was refusing to follow the law and the judge’s instructions. He allegedly admitted in deliberation that he had reasonable doubts as to Clancy’s mental capacity, but refused to find her “not guilty due to lack of criminal responsibility” as a result. The majority jurors argued that this was an attempt to judge the law rather than simply judging the facts. 

This characterization is not unproblematic. The holdout juror’s dissent in this case would not be in favor of nullifying a law, but of enforcing it. It would therefore be subject to appeal, since a guilty verdict can be disputed. What we’re really saying is that the holdout juror may disagree with the Model Penal Code guidelines for an insanity defense, written in the 1960s and used in states like Massachusetts, which open the door for psychosis to be considered a valid defense in a murder case. 

If this is the case, none of the jurors were actually following Massachusetts common law in their deliberations. Massachusetts law involves a two prong test for insanity defenses. If a defendant lacked either the cognitive ability to understand the crime or the volition to stop himself from committing what he knew to be a criminal act, he can be found not guilty. In post-trial interviews, the jurors seem unaware of these categories. Instead, they focus solely on whether Clancy was able to judge right and wrong in the moment of the crime, which is an old legal standard from the nineteenth century no longer used in most states. The claim that Clancy was compelled by voices alongside the post-partum psychosis diagnosis would suggest the defense is saying she lacked volition, but the majority jurors report being swayed by the idea of “altruistic feticide,” which defends Clancy on the grounds that she believed by killing her children she was doing what was best for them. Some jurors even appeared more moved by the hospitals’ negligence towards Clancy than by any evidence of her mental state. 

“The people want to know: Who is to blame?”

A hung jury encourages the state to come to an agreement with the defense rather than using its resources to mount another trial. If the prosecution does not pursue a retrial, Lindsay Clancy will likely be declared not guilty due to lack of criminal responsibility and confined to a mental institution, potentially for the rest of her life but perhaps just until the psychologists decide that she is ready to leave. This result seems designed to simply enrage all involved. The people want to know: Who is to blame? Who can we punish? The drive to punish someone, anyone, plays out in viral social media posts, whether they demand that Clancy be jailed or put to death, spin delusional theories that her husband Patrick Clancy must be responsible for her crime, or fault the health care system for its negligence in treating Clancy. 

What nobody can seem to reckon with is the fact that we live in a world where a woman can murder her own children. It feels like this either means she is filled with some terrible evil, or that the world compelled her to do the unthinkable. We imagine that the psychologists and psychiatric expert witnesses are capable of resolving this problem for us and telling us what is happening in the human mind, but as it turns out, even they can’t agree on a formula for what makes a murderer. Moral philosophy and psychiatry are mute in the face of the deeper social question. 

The holdout juror has denied that he had reasonable doubt. But even if the story of the majority jurors were true, the right of a juror, correct or not, to dissent from the majority opinion should be protected. What made the jury the glory of the English legal system, a bedrock of the early American Republic, and the foundation of modern freedom was the idea that a group of ordinary people exercising their reason—through agreement and disagreement, however bitter—are the best judges of how to protect the rights and freedoms of both society and individuals. The jury of the Lindsay Clancy trial has said that guilt cannot be determined in this case as tried. If the jury is unreasonable, it reflects the irrationality of society. In our thirst for retribution, will we punish them instead?

content:
The surprising electoral success of avowedly socialist candidates in big-city mayoral campaigns and some congressional races has raised the profile of the Democratic Socialists of America, forcing people to ponder what the term “democratic socialism” actually means.

What Democratic Socialists Want

By Fred Block • 29 Sept 2026 View in browser
View in browser
Scott Menchin
 
 

The Blueprint: How Socialism Can Work in the Real World
By Mike Beggs, Ben Burgis, and Bhaskar Sunkara 
Verso, 432 pages, $29.95

The surprising electoral success of avowedly socialist candidates in big-city mayoral campaigns and some congressional races has raised the profile of the Democratic Socialists of America, forcing people to ponder what the term “democratic socialism” actually means. By some accounts, it means a system along the lines of Scandinavian social democracy: guaranteeing all citizens access to health care, child care, affordable housing, and support in old age, while leaving capitalists in charge of their firms. For President Trump and his allies, conversely, democratic socialism is a euphemism, and its advocates are communists and jihadists who hate capitalism and want to destroy economic and political freedom.

Neither answer is accurate. Most leading democratic socialists envision an eventual transition away from an economy dominated by profit-maximizing firms. They recognize that in the decades after World War II, the United States and other nations created a regulated capitalism that limited inequalities of income and wealth and assured a certain level of prosperity for working-class people. But the last five decades saw the dismantling of many of these regulations, allowing the return of vast inequalities of wealth, more economic insecurity for working people, and the accumulation of ever greater political power by billionaires. 

Democratic socialists believe that radical changes are necessary to undo this economic and political damage. However, they invoke the aphorism that the definition of insanity is to repeat the same thing and expect different results. They insist that another experiment with regulated capitalism will end with capitalists again using their power to liberate themselves from higher taxes and new regulations. They believe that the only reliable path to a more egalitarian society is a series of reforms that eventually eliminate the control of capitalists over the economy’s productive resources. In short, they favor creating a socialist economy.

 “The Soviet model of state socialism failed economically.”

But how would a socialist economy be organized? For all of its defects, capitalism has dramatically raised the standard of living in Europe, North America, and other places. Would a socialist economy be similarly dynamic, or would it bring about a significant decline in living standards? The Soviet model of state socialism failed economically. The revolt against Soviet communism began in East Germany, where it was obvious that living standards were far below those of its West German neighbor. But similar discontent ultimately doomed the Soviet model across Eastern Europe and Russia. Meanwhile, China and Vietnam responded to this failure by opening their economies to private profit-oriented firms. 

A new book, The Blueprint: How Socialism Can Work in the Real World, argues that an economically productive socialism is possible. The book is written by Mike Beggs, a political economist, Ben Burgis, a philosopher, and Bhaskar Sunkara, the founding editor of Jacobin—the leading socialist publication in the United States. The authors believe that the path to that productive socialist economy requires understanding why the Soviet planned economy proved a failure.

Beggs, Burgis, and Sunkara are refreshingly dismissive of some of the cherished ideas of earlier generations of socialist thinkers. Even the title is a dig at Marx and Engels, who repeatedly insisted that their job was not to provide a blueprint of what a future socialist society would look like. The founders of Marxism claimed that once the capitalists were overthrown, the emancipated working class would figure out how to reorganize society. The authors of The Blueprint disagree, arguing for the need to articulate a compelling vision of a socialist economy. 

Their second heresy is to argue that classical Marxism’s hostility to markets was deeply mistaken. They see the idea of organizing an economy entirely around central planning as the fundamental defect of Soviet socialism. They accept the arguments made by Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek in the aftermath of the Bolshevik Revolution that central planners could not possibly have the information required to balance the supply and demand for thousands of different products. Moreover, they also reject the idea that banks of supercomputers solving simultaneous equations could ultimately make central planning work.

Beggs, Burgis, and Sunkara also break with the Marxist belief that the end of class domination will result in an end to alienation and a withering away of the state. In their vision of socialism, there will continue to be conflicts and disagreements and people will have to use democratic means to reform institutions that are not working effectively. Their blueprint is not of a utopia, but of a society that is significantly more egalitarian and more democratic than what we have now. 

Their version of market socialism combines employee-owned firms with a large public sector that provides health, education, many care services, public banks, and regulatory agencies. The employee-owned firms would compete on the market to provide consumers with products and many of those would be sold in stores that would also be collectively owned by their employees. Wage rates for different industries would be set by a national wage board, and wages could be supplemented with dividends as firms distribute profits to their members. In larger firms, employees would elect representatives to manage the firm while smaller firms could engage in collective democratic decision-making.

The authors go into considerable detail about the organization of these employee-owned firms to avoid some of the historic difficulties that employee cooperatives have encountered. Most new investments that firms undertake would be financed by loans from a large network of public banks. Interest rates would be more favorable when projects were good for the environment or could lift up a less prosperous region. A central bank would continue to manage interest rates to avoid the economy overheating or sliding into recession. 

The authors draw on the economic successes of cooperatives such as Mondragon in the Basque region of Spain to make the case that these employee-owned firms could be as productive and as innovative as capitalist firms. But they also recognize that some employee-owned firms will seek to enrich their members by imposing costs on consumers or the environment, and that regulatory agencies will have to step in to curb such behavior. Their point, however, is that regulators are more likely to be successful when they do not have to fight privately owned firms with deep pockets and friendly politicians and jurists.

 

The authors of The Blueprint build on market socialist ideas elaborated by Oscar Lange, Alex Nove, John Roemer, David Schweickart, and others. They also contend with the critiques of socialism developed by neoclassical economists. While their mastery of the vast literature debating the feasibility of a socialist economy is admirable, it comes at a cost. They don’t contend adequately with the ways in which capitalist economies today differ from the industrial economies of the mid-twentieth century. 

“Some of these changes make socialism appear even more practical.”

Some of these changes make socialism appear even more practical. In the 1950s, more than a third of the work force worked in factories or in farms; today, 80 percent of people work in services. And the simple reality is that for-profit firms are pretty ineffective at delivering high quality services. This is most obvious with care services, but it is also true of many other parts of the service economy. Many of us would prefer a bakery or a house-cleaning service or a real estate office organized as an employee cooperative over a similar firm committed to returning profits to shareholders.

A second relevant change is that today, most key innovations no longer originate in corporate laboratories. Instead, they emerge out of collaborations between private firms and researchers at government laboratories or government-funded scientists on university campuses. And in many cases, much of the initial development funding to turn these innovations into products is provided by public agencies. 

For example, Tesla’s success in producing electric cars was not a product of Elon Musk’s genius. Rather, Tesla hired engineers who had been working with government funding for twenty years to develop electric vehicles. Moreover, it was a large government loan that gave Tesla the resources to start production. Hence, it is entirely plausible that employee-owned firms working with government assistance would be able to match or even exceed the rate of technological innovation achieved by capitalism.

Finally, the regulatory authorities in a socialist economy would be far more likely to stop any firm from unleashing an artificial intelligence program or a genetically engineered virus that could have devastating social, economic, and human consequences. Nothing makes a stronger case for socialism than the out-of-control race for corporate dominance in artificial intelligence.

Beggs, Burgis, and Sunkara acknowledge that there will be inequalities of income as people will still need incentives to take on more demanding jobs or those that require highly specialized skills. However, they argue, the differentials would be much smaller than under capitalism because the people working at firms would have a vote on the compensation for managers and people with rare skills. 

Here, the authors would have done well to incorporate the idea of complex equality developed by the political theorist Michael Walzer. Walzer’s point is that income is only one dimension of inequality. People are also differentiated by the amount of political power they have, by their access to quality medical care, by their ability to afford higher education, by the esteem they are granted by others, and their standing with the system of justice. The great defect of capitalism is the ease with which money can buy privileged access to all of those other goods. Walzer argues that in a regime of complex equality, incomes would vary, but the capacity to use money to jump the queue for all of those other goods would be drastically limited. 

 

Focused as they are on demonstrating how a democratic socialist economy could work, the authors of The Blueprint avoid the pressing question of what strategy might make possible a transition into this new form of society. This omission is related to a larger problem in their institutional design. They slip into a centralizing bias that has been a weakness of the left for decades. Their blueprint focuses on only three sets of actors: employee-owned firms, a network of public banks, and then a central government that includes regulatory agencies, a wage board, and a central bank. Missing from this picture are lower levels of government for towns, cities, counties, and states. They offer no delineated tasks or responsibilities for these more localized governmental entities.

This is a problem when it comes to assuring the democratic nature of the envisioned society. Part of the theory of representative democracy is that people learn political skills by participating in local government and that increases their knowledge and effectiveness in assuring the accountability of the people they elect to higher offices. But in most capitalist democracies, power and economic resources have been monopolized by central governments. The result is that lower levels of government are strapped for resources and citizens have less incentive to participate.

Beggs, Burgis, and Sunkara perhaps imagine that participating in the management of their firms might teach employees the political skills needed to hold their elected representatives accountable. But the reality is that people live their lives in local communities and the quality of those lives depend on the housing supply, services including education and health care, the availability of amenities such as parks, playing fields, and libraries, the transportation system, access to the arts, and so on. 

It follows that a democratic socialist society has to give people much greater opportunities to shape their towns, cities, counties, and states. This requires redistributing resources and power back down to lower levels of government. Some version of participatory democracy is necessary both to create vibrant and sustainable communities and to ensure that locally empowered citizens can effectively control the formidable powers concentrated in the central government.

content:
We live in an age of inversions. With class inversion, college-educated professionals have moved inexorably leftwards, while once left-leaning blue-collar workers have veered to the right.

Compact

The Man Reviving Left Antisemitism in France

By Michael C. Behrent • 28 Sept 2026 View in browser
View in browser
AP
 
 

LFI: Anatomie d’une perversion 
Edited by Pierre-André Taguieff
David Reinharc, 424 pages, $26

We live in an age of inversions. With class inversion, college-educated professionals have moved inexorably leftwards, while once left-leaning blue-collar workers have veered to the right. A few years ago, there was also talk of a demographic inversion, as affluent populations that used to be drawn to the suburbs moved back to cities. However, few inversions have been as striking as the shifting political valences of antisemitism. In her contribution to Pierre-André Taguieff’s new edited volume on left antisemitism in France, sociologist Eva Illouz describes it this way: “Today, the heirs of Pétain defend the Jews while the [radical] left has become antisemitic.” The National Rally, the party whose founder Jean-Marie Le Pen was repeatedly convicted for making antisemitic remarks, positions itself as a defender of Israel and French Jews, while La France Insoumise (LFI, or Unbowed France), the largest left-wing party, has moved in the other direction.

LFI’s leader, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, has achieved the rare feat of becoming France’s most controversial politician, a title long held first by Le Pen, then by his daughter Marine, whom Mélenchon could well face in the runoff of next year’s presidential election. He has done this in part through his propensity to make comments that test the boundary between criticism of Israel and outright antisemitism. In the pages of Taguieff’s book, the Jewish essayist Alain Finkiekraut says of LFI: “For the first time in my life, I am afraid, physically afraid of a political party.”

Taguieff’s new volume mobilizes the energies of nearly sixty intellectuals to expose Mélenchon’s party as a political “perversion.” Though it considers LFI from multiple angles—extremism, the politics of victimhood, a predilection for “deconstruction”—many of the essays zero in on LFI’s attitude to Jews. Taguieff, a philosopher who studies racism and anti-Semitism, is known for documenting the rise of a “new Judeophobia” in France, associated not with the far right but with French Muslims and hostility to Israel. Taguieff’s work is controversial. Some accuse him of conflating antisemitism and anti-Zionism, and even of exemplifying the racism he criticizes. 

Taguieff’s book stands in the tradition of what the French call livres noirs—“black books” that present the dark side of a political phenomenon. Yet while it documents many of LFI’s most troubling features, it also explores the reasons for left-wing antisemitism’s emergence. It raises the question: Why, in 2026, has the Jewish question become central to the left’s current identity? 

 

Antisemitism and philosemitism have long histories on the French left. The emancipation of Jews during the French Revolution is considered a foundational moment in the development of republican secularism. By the same token, left opponents of republican democracy have, at certain historical junctures, laced their critiques with antisemitism. Supporters of the military strongman Georges Boulanger in the 1880s, for instance, blended attacks on Jews with denunciation of political corruption.  During the Dreyfus Affair, socialists were initially reluctant to criticize the Jewish captain’s mistreatment, on the ground that he was, after all, bourgeois. More recently, in the 1970s, left-wing writers associated with the journal La Guerre Sociale flirted with Holocaust denial. 

Thanks to LFI, these tendencies have returned, especially in the wake of Hamas’s attack on Israel on October 7, 2023. After the attack, the LFI parliamentary group released a statement that described the action as an “armed offensive by Palestinian forces led by Hamas.” It noted that the action occurred in a “context in which Israeli occupation policy in Gaza, the West Bank, and East Jerusalem had intensified,” and deplored “Israeli and Palestinian deaths.” The statement was widely perceived as minimizing the massacre’s significance by failing to call it an act of terrorism and suggesting that Hamas’ actions were no worse than Israel’s. Mélenchon was subsequently questioned by the police on suspicion of justifying terrorism.

LFI members have also been accused of questioning the loyalty of French Jews. After Prime Minister Élisabeth Borne, whose father was an Auschwitz survivor, accused LFI of conflating a “terrorist organization” with a “democratic state,” Mélenchon accused her of “rallying a foreign point of view.” When the president of the National Assembly Yaël Braun-Pivet visited Israel several weeks after the massacre, Mélenchon said she was “setting up camp in Tel Aviv to encourage massacres.” 

A lightning rod in these debates is Rima Hassan, a member of the European parliament who was born as a stateless Palestinian in a refugee camp in Syria and migrated to France as a child. Now thirty-four, Hassan is one of LFI’s leading voices on Palestine. In May 2024, following Israeli airstrikes on Rafah, she declared: “Israel is a monstrosity for which there is no name.” On March 26 of this year, she shared a post on X attributed to Kozo Okamoto, the former leader of a Japanese terrorist group that killed 26 people at Lod Airport in 1972. The quote read: “As long as there is oppression, resistance will not only be a right, but a duty.” Hassan was arrested and forced to stand trial for “apology of terrorism.”

Hassan is not the only member of Mélenchon’s party with strong views on the Israel-Palestine conflict. In October 2023, Danièle Obono, a Gabonese-born LFI member of parliament, described Hamas as a “resistance movement.” In 2024, Aymeric Caron, another LFI member of parliament, suggested that because Israel killed children, it could not “belong to the same humanity as me.” In 2025, Julien Théry, a historian of the Middle Ages with close ties to LFI, criticized an open letter signed by twenty public figures, most of whom were Jewish, calling on President Emmanuel Macron to refrain from recognizing the Palestinian state until Hamas had released every Israeli hostage. Théry described the authors as “twenty genocide perpetrators who must be boycotted under all circumstances.” 

LFI has also worked with figures who are even less guarded in their rhetoric. Mélenchon marched in a demonstration against Islamophobia sponsored by the Algerian-born political activist Houria Bouteldja and her organization Indigènes de la République—the “indigenous people of the republic”—which links systemic racism to the country’s colonial past. Bouteldja is particularly interested in the connection between racism, colonialism, and Jewish-Muslim relations. In 2016, she published an essay later translated into English under the title Whites, Jews, and Us: Toward a Politics of Revolutionary Love. The book’s claim that just as “no one can be white innocently,” “no one can be Israeli innocently” provoked considerable debate. 

LFI has also been accused of employing classic antisemitic dog whistles. In March 2025, LFI published a poster advertising a protest against the extreme right. It featured an image of Cyril Hanouna, the controversial host of a popular talk show on a television station run by the businessmen Vincent Bolloré, who is seen as promoting far-right ideas through his media empire. Hanouna is a Tunisian-born Jew. The picture showed Hanouna’s scowling face against a dark background. The poster was immediately denounced for invoking anti-Jewish stereotypes of the sort found in the Nazi propaganda film Jud Süß. LFI claimed the poster was a mistake and quickly withdrew it. 

“Then there are the many controversial statements made by Mélenchon himself.”

Then there are the many controversial statements made by Mélenchon himself. A politician reputed for his oratory, he speaks in the stirring cadences of socialists of yesteryear. So popular are his speeches that during his 2017 campaign, he used holograms to address multiple audiences at once. It seems unlikely that a figure who cares so much about words would use them lightly. In a 2020 interview, Mélenchon remarked: “I don’t know if Jesus was on the cross—he was put there, apparently, by his compatriots.” The remark has been interpreted as invoking the old antisemitic trope that the Jews were responsible for Christ’s death. During a rally earlier this year, Mélenchon pronounced Jeffrey Epstein’s name with an exaggerated Yiddish accent. As audience members booed, Mélenchon, clearly enjoying himself, responded: “oh, sorry, I meant to say Epstein, but [the other way] sounds more Russian!” At an earlier rally in Perpignan, Mélenchon mispronounced the last name of the center-left politician Raphaël Glucksmann in a way that appeared to call attention to its Jewishness. Glucksmann tweeted: “OK Jean-Marie Le Pen”—an allusion to the late National Front leader known for his tasteless antisemitic jokes.

Seeking to explain LFI’s gravitation towards antisemitism, contributors to Taguieff’s volume offer several overlapping if not entirely consistent explanations. One is Islamic entryism. Florence Bergeaud-Blackler notes that some members of the Muslim Brotherhood, notably Yusuf al-Qaradawi, argued that Western societies should be changed not through force, but by exploiting civil liberties to join and influence organizations like political parties and unions. In 2025, the French parliament produced a lengthy report on Islamic movements’ entryism in political parties. An alternative theory holds that the far left has cultivated the support of Islamist movements to tap into their revolutionary potential. In 1994, the British Trotskyist Chris Harman argued that because white workers were abandoning socialist parties, the left should align itself with the main oppressed group in contemporary society: Muslims. In her contribution, Martine Gozlan cites the belief that Islam could “revive revolutionary élan.” In France, this position was initially embraced by Trotskyist parties like the New Anticapitalist Party, then co-opted by LFI. 

Another explanation is that the LFI’s antisemitism is simply an election strategy. Populations of immigrant origin—many of whom are Muslim—are a demographic mostly ignored by other parties and are thus ripe for the picking. Recognizing the potential of this voting bloc, LFI has actively sought to recruit “les jeunes des cités”—the “housing project youth.” Marc Knobel observes in his essay that winning this electorate was a priority of Mélenchon’s 2022 presidential campaign. Polls indicate that in that election, he won nearly 70 percent of the Muslim vote. 

Other explanations emphasize that targeting Muslim votes is only one element of LFI’s “deconstructionist agenda.” At times, Taguieff’s volume is not really about antisemitism, but rather LFI’s thoroughgoing reversal of all values. Contributors describe LFI as embracing a new “grand narrative” based on victimhood and diversity, promoting “decivilization,” “subversion,” and “sedition,” and engaging in “political gaslighting” (a term has been imported into French, with nary a concern about American “cultural imperialism”). LFI is denounced for being the main political vehicle of le wokisme. According to Taguieff, the “ideological synthesis” that now defines the LFI consists of “radical anti-Zionism, wokeness, and decolonialism.” 

Yet the latter argument sits uneasily with one of the book’s central claims: that antisemitism is a historically unique form of discrimination. If antisemitism is just a drop in the bucket of progressive madness, is it really LFI’s main problem? This question relates to the main theoretical problem the book grapples with: Are anti-Zionism and antisemitism the same thing? This is a tricky question, and some of the book’s outspokenly anti-woke contributors don’t help matters when they borrow the woke tactic of cherry-picking objectionable phrases without regard for context. 

 

The story of French left-wing antisemitism recounted in Taguieff’s book is full of accusations, counteraccusations, and ideological murkiness, but there is one throughline: the leading role of Jean-Luc Mélenchon. Love him or hate him, Mélenchon has managed to revive a hard left politics that is confident and sure of itself at a time when so many leftist parties in the Western world seem disoriented and lifeless. The allegations of antisemitism that surround LFI are the dark side of Mélenchon’s singular success in keeping a certain idea of the left alive.

Mélenchon’s idiosyncratic political career has been defined by two seemingly contradictory imperatives: Whenever possible, seek the most radical ground; and always focus on achieving power. Born in French Morocco in 1951, Mélenchon returned to France and later participated in the May 1968 protests. After becoming a high school teacher, he joined, in the early 1970s, a small Trotskyist organization known as the Organisation Communiste Internationaliste. The OCI was led by Pierre Boussel—that rare instance of a genuine professional revolutionary, best known by his nom de guerre, Pierre Lambert. The influence of the Lambertistes (as his followers are known) is the subject of never-ending fascination in France. The Lambertistes are the perfect conspiracy theory, since their story is largely true and their goals were partially achieved. 

The OCI’s members saw themselves as Marxist-Leninist purists, committed to building a socialist society through a revolutionary vanguard. They formed a secret society of sorts, and are said to have required members to donate 10 percent of their annual salary to the party. What distinguished them was their strategy. Lambert advocated entryism—the same tactic that Islamist groups are now accused of practicing to control the LFI. OCI sought to punch above the weight of its several thousand members by joining and influencing the orientation of parties, trade unions, civil society organizations, and even masonic lodges. A former friend of Mélenchon’s says that, when pressing the flesh in public, he knows how to recognize a mason’s handshake. 

The Lambertistes’ primary target, however, was the Socialist Party—the spruced up version of the old Second International party, taken over by François Mitterrand in 1971. The Lambertistes who join the Socialists are described as “moles” or “submarines.” Several played key roles in the socialist era that began after Mitterrand won the presidency in 1981. The most prominent OCI mole was Lionel Jospin, who became the head of the Socialist Party. Another was Mélenchon, who became France’s youngest senator in 1986. Julien Dray, a left-leaning socialist who was friends with Mélenchon in the 1980s, now thinks that Mélenchon may have been actively reporting to the OCI on the ins-and-outs of the Socialist Party during this period. Both Jospin and Mélenchon strongly supported Mitterrand during the first two years of his presidency, when he nationalized banks and businesses, lowered the retirement age, and shortened the work week. 

In 1983, the Mitterrand presidency entered a new, more uncertain phase. Faced with capital flight and a fragile economy, the socialist government adopted austerity measures. The 1983 turn is now seen as Mitterrand’s quiet endorsement of a form of neoliberalism, resulting in free-trade policies and numerous factory closings. In this context, Mélenchon carved out a place for himself in a left-wing caucus known as the Socialist Left. In 2000, he was appointed to his first—and only—cabinet position by fellow Lambertiste Jospin, who had become prime minister after winning parliamentary elections. By all accounts, Mélenchon was an effective minister (his portfolio was professional development). He also seems to have relished the taste of power. 

The making of Mélenchon’s distinctive political brand occurred in the wake of the 2002 presidential election. In the first round, Jospin trailed behind Jean-Marie Le Pen, the leader of the National Front, resulting in a face-off between the latter and incumbent Jacques Chirac. While Chirac was easily reelected, the 2002 election was a turning point. Though it would take another three presidential elections before the far right began regularly making it to the runoff, it was clear that the National Front’s anti-immigrant, national-populist agenda was transforming French politics. 

As the left clung to the center and radicalism drifted rightward, Mélenchon began to experiment with the ingredients that could give the left a bigger kick. In 2004, he broke ranks with the Socialists and campaigned against the European Constitutional Treaty, which he denounced as a stalking horse for free-market capitalism. His identification with the “antiliberal left” (in the sense that it was opposed to economic liberalism) led him to leave the Socialist Party in 2008. He founded the Left Party, blending hostility to capitalism with an overt admiration for the authoritarian populism of Hugo Chávez. In the 2012 election, he ran to the left of François Hollande, the embodiment of the Socialists’ rightward drift and Mélenchon’s bitter enemy. 

Mélenchon then began building a new organization, La France Insoumise. It was conceived less as a party than a movement, and not so much on the left as a new form of populism. At the time, he was influenced by the political theorists Chantal Mouffe and Ernesto Laclau, who maintained that, at a time when all major parties had become neoliberal, the divide between elites and the people had become the most explosive political cleavage. In the 2017 election, Mélenchon appeared to have found the right formula at the right time. While much attention was focused on the rising political star of a previously unknown economics minister and his likely showdown with the National Front’s new face, Mélenchon benefited from the implosion of the center left in the wake of Hollande’s disastrous presidency. Though Emmanuel Macron and Marine Le Pen came out ahead, Mélenchon won 19 percent of the vote. On the left, he had cleared the field.  

“Mélenchon decided that only one move could make him a serious contender.”

Vindicated in his attack on the center left, convinced that he was the only alternative to the far right, yet eager to achieve power on his own terms, Mélenchon decided that only one move could make him a serious contender for supreme power: appealing to voters of immigrant background, specifically Muslims. Dray notes that of France’s estimated ten million Muslims, about six million are registered to vote, only 30 percent of whom vote in presidential elections. In 2022, about 70 percent of the latter voted for Mélenchon. By tapping into this reservoir of votes, Mélenchon could make it to the presidential runoff. Dray observes that it is the “hope tied to this calculation” that explains “LFI’s position after October 7, 2023.”

This electoral gambit required Mélenchon to renounce some of his long-held positions. Despite their radicalism, the Lambertistes were staunchly secular, in a way that overlapped seamlessly with French republicanism. Mélenchon 1.0 firmly embraced this outlook, asserting that the public sphere must remain religiously neutral and denouncing “communitarianism,” the French term for identities that claim priority over national allegiance. In 2010, he described the burqa as “degrading,” calling it a “clear provocation on the part of various fundamentalist circles against the Republic.” In 2015, Mélenchon delivered a passionate eulogy of Charb, one of the cartoonists killed in the Charlie Hebdo massacre, bemoaning that he had been murdered by “our oldest, cruelest … and most narrow-minded enemies: religious fanatics, bloodthirsty cretins.” Yet by 2019, Mélenchon, sensing political opportunity, not only was denouncing Islamophobia, but also began speaking of a “New France.” Mélenchon argued that as a territory that had experienced repeated migratory waves over thousands of years of history, France is simply the sum of its “great replacements” (a term that he coyly borrowed from Renaud Camus). In a country formed by “creolization,” the “idea that migrants from Europe have greater legitimacy is absurd.” 

 

For the most part, Mélenchon and his LFI colleagues don’t refer—overtly, at least—to Jewish racial stereotypes or suggest a Jewish cabal is running the world, and none of their policies targets French Jews. Mélenchon is Trumpian in his fondness for provocative remarks, betraying a mischievous pleasure in shattering politically correct norms while preserving plausible deniability. Yet LFI members do betray exasperation and impatience when they are accused of demeaning Jews, even as they regularly denounce the stigmatization of other minorities. They play fast and loose with the distinction between Israel and Jews, even as they claim that the charge of antisemitism is just a ploy to declare criticizing Israel out of bounds. 

“This is not your father’s antisemitism.”

Moreover, there is little question that Mélenchon and LFI have contributed to making virulence in denouncing Israel the new benchmark of leftist radicalism. Taguieff’s point is that this is not your father’s antisemitism: The new iteration has its own buzzwords, rules, and logic. The question, of course, is whether an ideology that completely revamps its buzzwords, rules, and logic is still the same ideology. Many French Jews are not particularly concerned with this ambiguity. In 2025, 6,000 of them migrated to Israel, nearly a twofold increase since 2023.

What seems undeniable is that LFI’s complex and troubling attitude towards the Jews is the terminal point of the French left’s prolonged crisis, of which Mélenchon is the most striking symptom. In some ways, Mélenchon’s dilemma is similar to the one Lenin faced a century earlier. Historically, socialists have been the party of revolutionary change. But what if you happen to live in a time when the prospect of change seems faint, when even socialists have rallied the status quo, when economic precarity and social discontent seem incapable of finding an effective political vehicle? Is being a socialist—like the Legal Marxists in imperial Russia or François Hollande in contemporary France—just a commitment to manage the capitalist economy efficiently? And what if you are also tired of fringe parties that revel in their marginality? These questions haunt many twenty-first century leftists. Perhaps Mélenchon’s flirtation with antisemitism is his paradoxical answer to them.

Does Mélenchon really believe his innuendos and insinuations? Or is he just a cynic, riding an antisemitic wave he hopes will benefit him politically? When what is at stake is political power, this distinction becomes nebulous. Did Lenin really believe in a workers’ state? Maybe, maybe not. But he was convinced that championing the working class was a path to power. Paradoxically, cynicism reflects sincere beliefs about the nature of reality. Mélenchon believes that the “New France” is firmly on the side of the Palestinians. While Jews were a minority that in many ways found a home in the secular republic, the latter has been less kind to immigrants and more recent minority communities. A new rhetoric of emancipation must have new priorities. So much the worse for the Jews.

Why I Call It ‘Assisted Suicide’

By Kevin Yuill • 25 Sept 2026 View in browser
View in browser
Scott Menchin
 
 

One sunny day in June, I opened up my university email, which I only do occasionally now that I am retired, to see an email marked “confidential” in my inbox. In it, the deputy vice-chancellor at my former employer, the University of Sunderland, informed me of an external complaint concerning my recent public social media activity. When I eventually managed to see the much-redacted complaint, it found fault with the “tone and nature” of my online engagement on the topic of assisted suicide. I was accused of “Public Misrepresentation and Lack of Empathy.” The letter writer also objected to my use of the word “Orwellian,” which I had used to characterize campaigners’ refusal to call “suicide” the act of deliberately ingesting poison with the intent to die, even as they advocate a change to the Suicide Act 1961. I had also said their object was “to make killing acceptable in law.”

This spurious complaint gives insight into how political aims are furthered by capturing and policing our language. Assisted suicide is a case in point of a much broader trend. Rather than engage in difficult discussions, campaigners change the terms of the debate, ostensibly to avoid offending others. So campaigners in favor of assisted suicide redefine words like “suicide” or “killing.” When questioned, they declare that using the proscribed terms is offensive.

The campaign to legalize assisted suicide has sought to inject new terminology into the discussion. Its propaganda is peppered with phrases which, upon examination, fade into meaninglessness. The most egregious is the use of the phrase “assisted dying” to obscure the reality that euthanasia and assisted suicide involve either homicide or suicide. Phrases like “dying people” and “choice at the end of life” do similar work. One of the justifications for distinguishing between “assisted suicide” and “assisted dying” is that when terminally ill people kill themselves, they are choosing between two ways of dying rather than, as with suicide, simply choosing to end their life. The organization Dignity in Dying points to the “clear difference between helping someone to die who is terminally ill and helping someone to die who is not.”

None of this stands up to scrutiny. If someone hangs himself after being given the news that his cancer is inoperable and likely to kill him in the coming weeks, is that suicide? If it is not, how can we say that someone who is terminally ill but with a longer prognosis who jumps in front of a train is a suicide? Is the definition of suicide dependent on the method of killing oneself? If ropes and guns are suicides and pills are not suicide, is such a distinction useful for homicide cases too? Does murdering someone with poison amount to a “dignified and peaceful” death?

The clear purpose of this rebranding is to remove the moral stigma from the act of ending a life, and thereby to make killing more palatable. It began with a movement to remove the phrase “commit suicide.” As an article in the Australian Psychological Society website states bluntly: “Suicide is not a sin and is no longer a crime, so we should stop saying that people ‘commit’ suicide.” But if suicide is no longer a sin or morally wrong, why would we prevent it? The therapeutic reasoning behind this move prompted many to adopt more sensitive language, forgetting, perhaps, that maintaining the idea that suicide is a bad act at least gives some reason to prevent it.

The US-based organization Death With Dignity noted these changes, adopting the rebranding as a way to make assisted suicide more palatable. They note on their website that the change occurred in the 1990s when “advocates were facing an uphill battle for support.” Eli Stutsman, lawyer and main author of the Death with Dignity Act in Oregon, which passed in 1994, said: “At the time, the issue very badly needed to be rebranded and repositioned. And that’s what we did.”Barbara Coombs Lee, an author of Oregon’s model law and president at the time of another pro-assisted suicide group, Compassion & Choices, remembers a meeting in 2004 where her group discussed which terminology to use going forward. The impetus “was probably another frustrated conversation about another interminable interview with a reporter who insisted on calling it suicide,” she said. A phrase like “medical aid in dying,” Compassion & Choices concluded, would reassure patients that they were taking part in a process that was regulated and medically sanctioned.

Those who favor legalizing assisted dying are offended by the use of the word suicide. As one supporter, the anthropologist Anita Hannig, puts it in her book The Day I Die, “many still find it hard to shake the stigma and sense of transgression that cling to the idea of ending one’s own life. … Calling an assisted death a ‘suicide’ has been harmful to patients and families.” Cat Eccles, when her fellow MP Danny Kruger used the term “suicide,” interrupted him: “The honorable gentleman is using incorrect language. It is not suicide. That is offensive. I ask him please to correct his language.” The term “suicide” when referring to “death with dignity,” is “offensive and inaccurate,” declares Death With Dignity.

“Many admit that their purpose in twisting language is political.”

Many admit that their purpose in twisting language is political. The philosopher Gerald Dworkin, an advocate of legalization, stated that “the use of the term ‘physician-assisted suicide’ is now politically incorrect, for tactical reasons. I understand that the popular prejudice against suicide makes it more difficult to rally support for the bills I favor.”

One of the ways that pro-assisted suicide organizations manipulate our language is by “capturing” ostensibly neutral bodies and forcing them to accept the new vocabulary. The American Association of Suicidology board passed a statement in August 2017 titled “Suicide” is not the same as “Physician aid in dying.” In August 2023, the organization “retired” the statement, but was later successfully lobbied to reinstate it. As the website for Dying with Dignity puts it, the change occurred after “months of relationship-building, education, and thoughtful engagement with AAS leadership.”

In Britain, campaigners against legislative change have insisted on the term assisted suicide. In recent debates in parliament, many simply refused to bow down to the language police. On September 11th, in the debate concerning Lauren Edwards’ terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill, MPs Shivani Raja, Rosie Duffield, Jim Shannon, Ashley Dalton and many other lawmakers referred exclusively to assisted suicide, refusing to be cowed. As Carla Lock, Democratic Unionist MP for Upper Bann, said: “Yesterday was World Suicide Prevention Day; the irony should not be lost on any Member of this House.” Ben Spencer, a member of parliament and former psychiatrist who opposed the bill, noted that the bill “frames the debate—the intervention—as shortening the death process or some form of assisted dying rather than what it is, which is physician-assisted suicide.”

That the bill was defeated indicates that we have been successful in pushing back against those who would police our language. When we wrest back control of our terms, it removes one of their most powerful weapons in their fight to make a form of suicide palatable. It is not surprising that frustrated campaigners are complaining about language used by me and others concerned about the implications of legalized assisted suicide.

Compact

Don’t Miss the Grand New Films About Charles de Gaulle

By Peter Hitchens • 24 Sept 2026 View in browser
View in browser
Pathé Films
 
 

The future world statesman, in full military uniform, leaps athletically on to the table. Then he reaches up into the ceiling lamp of his hotel room and pulls out a concealed microphone. It has been placed there by his American allies, or perhaps by the perfidious British. Or possibly by both at once. There are a lot of wires. If there is one brief scene which encapsulates the two vast new films about Charles de Gaulle, I think this is it. They recount the astonishing melodrama of the rebirth of France after humiliation and defeat. And they do so through a patriotic epic about the Second World War in which Hitler makes no appearance, FDR is the villain, and Churchill often an American patsy. The hero is the metaphorical and literal (6’5”) giant, General de Gaulle, a man so tall that furniture always seemed too small to him, and so did most other people.

We owe these films to Julian Jackson’s peerless biography of de Gaulle, a book that tears through the mind like a storm. This book (for me at least) revived the forgotten belief that individual human greatness can force open the grimmest, most unassailable fortresses. Read it. See the movies. You will not be sorry. 

“De Gaulle revived his country with no weapon apart from his personal force and belief.”

De Gaulle revived his country with no weapon apart from his personal force and belief. He was driven by one of the most significant intellects of our age, by an austere, patriotic, Christian upbringing, and by war itself. Most men remotely like him died and were eaten by rats at Verdun or the Somme, between 1914 and 1918. He lived on, thanks to two battlefield miracles which saved his life. But he did not fit in the post-1918 world, and knew he was disliked for surviving into a drabber, less honorable world. After Philippe Pétain had formed his collaborationist government in Vichy and fraternized with Hitler, de Gaulle responded to those who criticized his stiffness by saying “If I were easy to work with, I would be on Marshal Pétain’s staff.”

The two films, which are really one, make his defiant awkwardness very plain. The first, De Gaulle: Liberté, and the second, De Gaulle: Résistance, both show us the General outplaying Churchill and Roosevelt in the three-dimensional chess of wartime diplomacy. He is also seen neatly derailing his American-backed rival, Henri Giraud, who never realizes what has hit him. In a few brief moments we notice that he is secretly amused by the game he is playing, in which he well knows, as he once said, “There is no action in which the devil has no part.” The future French president’s personal life is almost entirely excluded.  Once, for a moment, we glimpse through a windowpane his beloved daughter Anne, born with Down’s syndrome and probably the deepest passion of his life. His acerbic, courageous wife Yvonne, possibly the only adult person not overborne by him, is also briefly seen. Winston Churchill is for once depicted as a whole man, dangerous and sometimes wrong, rather than as the storybook hero he was not. He is also revealed, and this is true, as understanding just as much as de Gaulle did, that Britain was in danger of becoming an American vassal at the end of the war. Worse, he is shown as reluctantly preferring this fate to the sort of sovereignty de Gaulle, all too briefly, obtained.

FDR appears as a frosty, manipulative, tricky cynic, rather like the nameless and ruthless president so well-portrayed in Allen Drury’s novel Advise and Consent. He does not see any point in reviving an independent France, and wants an American-dominated Europe instead. He dismisses de Gaulle as the head of some committee or other. De Gaulle informs him, in the White House, that he does not represent any such committee. He represents France. FDR tells de Gaulle that the United States has rescued France, as any good person would rescue a child in peril. De Gaulle retorts that France is not a child. I could scarce forbear to cheer at this, despite being in a modish movie theatre in North Oxford, that citadel of liberalism.

De Gaulle would not be patronized, especially by people who purported to be friends. He was furious that his eternal France had been overpowered and muzzled in 1940 before she had properly drawn her sword. He believed that those who had surrendered and collaborated had simply failed in their duty to fight on, and for the rest of his life he treated the Vichy interlude as an event that had not in fact happened. France, as far as he was concerned, had remained in existence as a nation for as long as one man continued to fight. This can of course be written off as colossal arrogance. But view it through a different, older lens, and it is like the tales I used to read in my childhood encyclopedias and storybooks, of undefeated, unbowed men who fought on to the end. These stories, I would be told when I was older, were romances. The world was not really like that any more, if it ever had been. The true battlefield was the peace conference. Most of me still believes this, but after reading Jackson’s book and seeing these movies, I am tempted to resume my seven-year-old worldview, littered as it is with dying heroes, whispering moving last words, from Nelson at Trafalgar to Wolfe at Quebec—both, of course, killed in combat with That Sweet Enemy, France. Charles de Gaulle is the closest our era has to such people, and what do I care if he is French rather than British? He was fighting a battle with which I wholly sympathize, the struggle for sovereign countries to remain fully in control of their destinies.

This is the thing which makes these two great screen dramas sing (and they do literally sing fierce patriotic songs, more than once).  It is not about politics as we know them, nor about the dismal compromises we nowadays accept as diplomacy. It openly challenges this sapless, lifeless version of man’s destiny. It is about actual patriotism, a burning love of country which will never buckle to a foreign conqueror or lower its flag, which fights on even when it is quite mad to do so. This gives purpose to two extraordinary battle scenes, among the best I have seen in any cinema, at Bir Hakeim and on the Mareth Line, both in North Africa and widely unknown. Let us hope they will now be better remembered. The semi-mythical figure of General Leclerc, a nom de guerre any traveller in France has seen on a score of boulevards and squares, appears here as what he was, a taciturn nobleman from generations of warriors, with the rare gift of command and a desire to fight as furious as de Gaulle’s. I will not forget a brilliant shot straight down a German tank’s gun barrel, as viewed by the French soldier at which it is pointed, and the sinister glow which presages that soldier’s death, or the scene in which Leclerc growls into the ear of a journalist, amid the thunder of artillery, that he must leave so that he can tell the story of the Mareth battle, even if nobody else survives it.

Throughout the story, reason jostles and wrestles with emotion. We glimpse the great Resistance leader Jean Moulin undergoing Gestapo torture, but, thank Heaven, we do not see the full horror of what happens when such demons are let loose upon a civilized country. If you can bear to look up Moulin’s detailed fate, do so. If man is indeed made in the image of God, this was a true blasphemy. Aware of such things, we can only know that we must, ever afterwards, ensure that such creatures never come into our countries or are allowed to flourish in them. But there they were, and we see, in a final exposition of the whole purpose of these histories, the liberation of Paris and the expulsion of the monsters who had befouled it for four interminable years.

I watched this passage through a mist of tears, taking place on streets which I have many times walked along, wondering at the terse plaques commemorating the deaths of Resistance fighters in the last hours of occupation. I shall never see them in quite the same way now that I have viewed this particular realization of those hours. And now I should mention that the French version of the second film bears what to me was the mysterious subtitle of “J’écris ton nom” (“I write your name”). This is the first line of a poem by Paul Eluard, who began, in the midst of German occupation, intending to write of his love for his wife. But he found himself instead writing of his love for liberty. As he put it, “the woman I loved embodied a desire greater than her.” And in the portrayal of the actual minutes when liberty returned, some of it archival film, a 1944 recording of Eluard reading the poem is played. We see once again, as the sky clears and the torturers surrender or flee, that, as Adam Mickiewicz warned us long ago, “my country, you are like my health. Only he who has lost you can know how much you should be prized.”
