How ‘Boys Love’ Conquered Asia

By R. Taggart Murphy • 23 Sept 2026 View in browser
View in browser
Scott Menchin
 
 

In the last week of July, two incidents involving disruptive Chinese fans of a genre of Asian media triggered something close to a crisis in international relations.  Security personnel had forcibly removed a Chinese woman from an event in Bangkok. Patrons of this type of event, known as a “fan meet,” pay considerable sums to see their favorite entertainers in person, hear them being interviewed, and watch them perform song-and-dance routines. Tens of thousands of Chinese went online to accuse the Thais of mistreatment of and discrimination against Chinese fans. 

Four days later, a group of what appeared to be largely Chinese fans mobbed two Chinese actors at Bangkok’s Suvarnabhumi Airport. Thailand’s foreign minister was forced to step in, while embassies in both Bangkok and Beijing attempted to calm outraged feelings. Although the controversy was extensively covered by media in Thailand, China, Taiwan, and Hong Kong, nothing about either incident appeared in mainstream Western outlets. 

This lack of attention is especially noteworthy considering that one of the viral media sensations of the past year in Western countries has been the Canadian show Heated Rivalry, a drama about gay hockey players. The show attracted millions of viewers and the online equivalent of a spring snowmelt of posts, reactions, and comments. But in Asia, filmed depictions of erotic attraction and love between two males had in fact been drawing in tens of millions of viewers and making lots of money since well before Heated Rivalry came along; it was shows in this genre that provoked the incidents in Bangkok in July. But few in the Western critical establishment have paid attention to this phenomenon.

The genre in question is known as “Boys Love” or “BL.” It was invented in Japan in the early 1970s by a group of women artists writing manga directed at girls. These artists penned fantasies of impossibly beautiful boys with the hots for each other, and in the process revolutionized shojo manga (comics for girls). The new millennium saw the advent of filmed depictions of BL using live actors. Largely set in offices rather than high schools, colleges, or historical or mythical places, most of these shows starred established actors (none of them openly gay), and did not feature boys even in minor roles. 

So why are these shows called Boys Love dramas? Wouldn’t they better be termed “gay” or “LGBTQ” or “queer” programs? The answer lies with the creators and the intended audience. Like the manga and anime in the tradition from which they emerged, the majority of these dramas continued to be conceived by (straight) women for women and girls.

In 2014, the first live BL drama appeared in Thailand. The show in question, Lovesick the Series, exploited the runaway popularity of Japanese BL manga and anime among girls and young women and aimed, in the words of the scholar Thomas Baudinette, to make “the Japanese BL elements legible to a Thai consumer.” Its creators followed the conventions of Thai media, including background songs sung by the actors, extensive use of product placement in lieu of disruptive commercials, and serialization. But for the first time ever on Thai television, it featured a romantic relationship between two males as the central plot pillar.  

Lovesick’s success demonstrated to Thai media companies the potential appeal and commercial possibilities of the genre, and over the next five years, nearly a hundred BL dramas appeared on Thai television, a plurality of them produced by GMMTV, a division of Thailand’s largest media empire, with many more financed by investors from China, where streaming of Thai BL dramas became immensely popular.

“GMMTV and its competitors constructed a new business model.”

GMMTV and its competitors constructed a new business model. Live-action Japanese BL dramas had been typically filmed on very tight budgets as a means to boost the sales of the manga on which most of them were based. The shows tended to air on late night television; if the producers and distributors even bothered with overseas audiences, the shows were licensed to streaming platforms such as GagaOOLa or Viki that in turn required viewers to pay for subscriptions.

The Thais, instead, monetized the actors themselves, a practice they adapted from South Korea. Building on the country’s prior success in exporting manufactured goods from automobiles to consumer electronics, Korean entrepreneurs in the 1990s turned their attention to popular culture—in particular, a form in which the Japanese had conspicuously failed to penetrate Western markets: singing and dancing boy bands. They honed in on the talent agency that had dominated Japanese pop music for two generations: Johnny and Associates, whose founder “Johnny” Kitagawa had built an industrial machine for the spotting of attractive boys and their fashioning into “idols” who could and would electrify millions of besotted pubescent girls. Of course this was not the first time in history that handsome young male musicians had filled concert halls, theaters, and stadiums with screaming females, but no one had ever done it on Kitagawa’s scale. Through open auditions and informal scouting, he recruited thousands of pre-teen and teenaged boys into his workshop where they were drilled in singing, dancing, and stagecraft. Those whom Kitagawa deemed most likely to succeed would debut in splashy events backed by the full weight of his publicity machine which already, by the 1970s, was far and above the most formidable in Japan.   

Kitagawa was dogged by allegations that he had sexually abused boys under his management. A documentary released after his death brought these claims before a wider audience, raising the uncomfortable possibility that Kitagawa’s nose for star potential was totally wrapped up in his sexuality.  

Johnny’s stars never found a fan base in the United States and Europe, despite periodic attempts, but beginning in the 1990s, their Korean counterparts managed to do so. The greater attention to the spit and polish of what was on offer was one reason for the Koreans’ success. But the deliberate and systematic cultivation of global audiences was at least as important. The Japanese had treated the outside world as an afterthought when it came to cultural (as opposed to manufactured) products. Not so the Koreans. One key factor lay in their early grasp of the internet’s potential, something Kitagawa had completely missed. With a mindset locked into the age of television and print media and obsessed with maintaining control of his stars, Kitagawa had deliberately suppressed online distribution of their songs and performances. But in 2007, the Korean boyband Big Bang embraced Youtube; the even more famous BTS would go on to use free online content as a means to build a global fan base.

Perhaps the most fruitful—and certainly the most profitable—result of Thailand’s infatuation with both Japanese and Korean influences lay in the adoption of methods the Koreans had used to globalize K-pop, but applying those methods to actors in BL dramas rather than members of boybands. Between 2015 and 2020, GMMTV perfected the formula for a hit show: two handsome leads falling in love with each other, an open declaration of love by one or both at some point later in the series, a breakup near the end triggered either by external events or internalized self-doubts, followed by a reconciliation and a happy ending. While many of these recurring plot elements had their origins in the Japanese genre, GMMTV modified things in a number of significant ways. The more aggressive macho “top” (seme in Japanese) vs. the more submissive, boyish “bottom” (uke) tended to dissolve into a more egalitarian relationship (egalitarian at least in an erotic sense; class tensions did surface in many shows). Attraction was a matter of romance rather than overt lust. Perhaps most importantly, external homophobia was no longer an issue. Parents, friends, and colleagues were increasingly shown to be supportive and if any stigma was felt, it was an internal feeling that had to be overcome.

In 2020, helped by the arrival of the pandemic that forced people indoors, the Thai Boys Love model reached full fruition with the runaway hit 2gether: The Series. The plot borders on the preposterous, but the show was a massive success thanks largely to the looks and charisma of the two leads. Its reach extended far beyond Thailand: At one point, it generated more posts on Twitter than any other television show anywhere and racked up total viewership in the range of one billion (that’s not a typo).  

In the process, GMMTV had hit upon a formula for monetizing the success of these shows: distributing BL dramas on easy-to-access free platforms such as Line TV and YouTube while relying on product placement, celebrity endorsements,  and fan meets to generate revenue. That was the Korean boy band model, but with a twist. GMMTV sought to monetize not simply the charisma of the actors, but the idea of what Baudinette calls “homoerotic imagined couples” who, following a successful debut, go on to appear together in live concerts and “fan meets” while continuing to be cast as lovers in new shows with no plot connection to the original drama. 

After the success of  2gether: The Series, Thai studios issued dozens of BL shows every year. No matter the theme or plot conceit—or how well or badly made or how much or how little was spent on production—the love interest in every one of these dramas centered on the relationship between two young males. Programs such as Bad Buddy, Gelboys, and ThamePo garnered tens of millions of viewers, with a fan base extending far beyond Thailand’s borders to the whole of southeast Asia, China, and the subcontinent. Most recently, Thai BL dramas have begun to reach Latin America, particularly Brazil and Bolivia where, if GMMTV is to be believed, some of its programs have claimed the number one spot on streaming sites.  

Even Japan succumbed. Fans coined the term tai-numa (literally, “Thai swamp”) referring to addictive infatuation with Thai BL dramas and their stars. Annual visits by leading Thai BL stars pack concert halls and stadiums while enterprising travel agencies organize tours by Japanese visitors to sites in Thailand where some of the more popular dramas were filmed. Thailand has thus joined Japan and South Korea in staking out a major claim on the landscape of global popular culture.  Hollywood doesn’t yet realize it, or want to realize it, but in the process cultural hegemony continues to leak from Los Angeles and New York to Tokyo, Osaka, Seoul, and now Bangkok.

 

Why does the largely female fan base of Boys Love want to read about or watch boys and young men (or even older men) in lust or in love with each other? That many women enjoy gazing at attractive males is not news. Nor is it a surprise that many women are aroused by depictions of handsome virile males in the grip of uncontrollable passions awakening feelings of love and lust in the object of said passions.   

But why in East and Southeast Asia, and now South Asia and Latin America, did male-on-male tales displace stories of male-on-female romance—or if not displace them, come to compete with them on practically equal terms? One common notion among observers attempting to explain the enormous popularity of Asian BL among Asian women is that tales of male-on-male romance and lust feel less threatening. As this account has it, patriarchal culture tells Asian women they aren’t supposed to have strong sexual feelings, but they do anyway; watching an older and a younger guy go at it allows them to explore otherwise taboo thoughts.

But there may be something more subtle at work that helps in understanding the recent global reach of these dramas. Even a well-acted, well-written depiction of heterosexual romance carries implicit expectations of who leads, who yields, how desire is expressed. By contrast, many BLs allow viewers to witness intimacy and vulnerability stripped of expectations of how people are “supposed” to behave.

The open, unembarrassed, sentimentality of Thai BL is another key factor. At the dramatic peaks of many shows, the action ceases while the soundtrack features the lead actor singing of the emotions he is experiencing, often accompanied on screen by a series of flashbacks. (An accomplished singing voice forms a great boon to aspiring BL actors.) Thai BL inherited this dramatic convention from lakhorn (the traditional melodramatic soap operas) but it is hardly unique to Thailand. Opera during the Baroque period functioned in much the same way – action stopped while singers gave voice to their emotions. Kabuki employs something similar—at peak dramatic moments, the stage freezes, the actors strike extravagant poses, and off-stage musicians articulate the emotions being felt. 

“This sort of thing also used to happen in Western popular culture.”

This sort of thing also used to happen in Western popular culture. Hollywood musicals once showed actors stopping to sing about what they were feeling. We don’t see that any more but it isn’t because films such as the 1961 West Side Story or the 1965 Sound of Music were box office bombs. Rather, the Anglophone arts establishment seems to have been overtaken by a paralyzing fear of sentiment without a protective wrapping of snark. Well, if Hollywood can’t figure out a way to allow viewers to revel in unabashed displays of sentimentality, Bangkok will step in. Perhaps the pure sweetness goes down more easily because it is being administered by two young men in love with each other; one can watch, cry, thrill, and shake with ecstasy all the while retaining hip “progressive” credentials.

That brings us to the most important matter that the global success of Thai BL raises—and perhaps helps us grasp why the Western critical establishment shies away from confronting what has been happening. The young male Thai stars who pack stadiums from Mexico City to Yokohama to Manila, whose faces seem plastered over all the Skytrain and subway cars in Bangkok and to pop up in every second TV commercial on Thai television, got to where they are not simply because of their looks and their talent, but because they made their reputations on the pretense that they had been romantically and sexually involved with other men and boys. One would have to reach back to Renaissance Florence or Edo-period Japan and the cultural supremacy of the wakashu (alluring youth) or, even farther, to ancient Athens and the worship of the beautiful boy to find something comparable. 

A number of scholars have begun to ponder the meaning and significance of seemingly “queer” media attracting large audiences across national and cultural borders, not to mention those of gender and sexual orientation. These scholars argue that Thai BL represents an important new means of “queering” heretofore heteronormative societies. 

These theorists can certainly marshal plenty of evidence to support their views, beginning with Thailand’s approval of same-sex marriage in 2025, in which the enormous popularity of BL almost surely played a role. Beyond Thailand, any perusal of social media is enough to demonstrate that legions of “queer” youngsters throughout Southeast Asia to Brazil and India find in these shows affirmation for their feelings. 

Yet the majority of BL fans still appear to be straight women and girls. While the genre has moved beyond its women-writing-for-women roots and large numbers of men (many of them openly gay) are involved in the production of the shows in Thailand and elsewhere, there remains a strong female presence among the writers and directors.

 

Are BL dramas “queer”? Thomas Baudinette explains that he is “inspired by the seminal definition of queer from theorist David Halperin as ‘whatever is at odds with the normal, the legitimate, the dominant.’” Does BL constitute a threat to the “hierarchical” and the “normative”? In China, the authorities certainly think so: They have censored BL shows and blackballed the actors while fining and imprisoning writers. What seems to bother a Chinese regime reflexively suspicious of any mass movement that it does not control is not so much the content of BL but the way the genre came out of nowhere and proceeded to spawn millions of fans while no one in authority was paying attention. 

“Are BL dramas ‘queer’?”

Another factor may be the CCP’s worries about the plummeting Chinese birth rate. A study of Chinese fans of Thai BL by a Taiwanese academic notes that many report that their parasocial relationships with Thai BL actors provide them with whatever intimacy they feel they need, and quotes a Chinese woman saying  “I have three husbands and two boyfriends—all in Thailand—I wish I could tell my parents don’t ﬁx me up with anyone.” Meanwhile, a group of conservative men in South Korea have called for the banning of BL because it promotes unrealistic standards among Korean women for male beauty. Yet birthrates had begun to fall in both South Korea and China well before the surging popularity of BL in those two countries, and they have also fallen to comparably low levels in countries such as Italy which have yet to join the global BL boom. As for the idea that growing numbers of gay male fans of these dramas will rush out, marry women, and father children if they are suddenly deprived of the opportunity to watch ripped hunks and fetching youths professing love for each other—well, it is palpably absurd.

More widely, any notion that declining birthrates can be blamed on these dramas runs into the unavoidable reality that a large majority of at least the live-action BL dramas depict loving romance in which genuine affection and concern for the other trumps lust. Long-term commitment is seen as the goal, not short-term sexual release. Cheating and dishonesty are the great no-nos, and family and friends are usually depicted as loving and supportive. Indeed, if it weren’t for the sex of the principals, most live-action Asian BL dramas would seem to champion precisely those values needed to reverse the decline in birth rates. The values in question even include the promotion of family formation with the curtain falling on pairs of lovers whose first act as they build lives together is to adopt children.

That points to the discomfort many progressives feel over the genre: that it caters to “regressive” female hunger for domesticity. Meanwhile, many gay male activists contend that BL is little more than female wish fulfillment. In the typical BL show, a teenaged boy or young man is awakened not to his sexuality but to his love for another young male with whom, after the overcoming of obstacles that make for necessary dramatic tension, he settles down for a life of marital bliss. The notion that this fantasy has anything to do with the actual lives of gay males is clearly a stretch.  

But the core of progressive discomfort with the BL genre may lie less with the fantasies on display than the challenge it poses to the notion of immutable sexual identity or orientation. The idea that one is born “straight” or “gay” did not exist in East and Southeast Asia until introduced by Westerners in the nineteenth century. Gregory Pflugfelder began his magisterial book, Cartographies of Desire: Male-Male Sexuality in Japanese Discourse, 1600-1950, by noting that there was no single word for “homosexuality” in the Japanese language during the era of the Tokugawa shoguns. The general assumption was a kind of universal bisexuality, to use a term that likewise would not have been easily understood. Men who did not like women or did not like boys were considered somewhat odd. 

So the women who invented BL as a genre in the pages of manga for girls in the early 1970s were harking back to an understanding of sexuality that had only recently been superseded by the introduction into Japan of Western notions of homosexuality as a species of either sin or deviance, and the “homosexual” as somehow standing apart from the rest of humanity. The underlying conceit of most Thai, Chinese, and Japanese BL dramas is that lovers do not exist in a separate category of human being. The Asian BL presentation of human sexuality therefore complicates identity-based conceptual frameworks.

What messages does the BL genre tell its audiences that resonate so deeply?   Among them is that “affection between men is normal” to quote one of the more perceptive commentaries. Another: people need close friends. Many Thai BLs elevate the friend group to a status equivalent to family, and the working out of the dynamics of the friend group, as opposed to those of the erotic partnership, are at the core of many BL dramas. A third: the essential role of male bonding in a healthy society.  That Thai BL openly acknowledges and celebrates the power of male bonding surely accounts for some of its global reach. 

Where the power and allure of BL can be seen most clearly lies in the way in which BL places the forging of relationships firmly at the center of its stories.  Everything else—especially notions of identity and categorization that have so obsessed the West in recent centuries—is relegated to side issues, given a role to play only when they strengthen (or threaten) love, friendship, and affection between human beings. People are not labels; over and over again, in both subtle and blatant ways, BL dramas preach this message.

The recent series Ticket to Heaven uses the prism of the formative institution of Western civilization, the Catholic Church, to underscore the primacy of relationship formation—that without love, all else is “nothing” to quote Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, referred to several times in the drama. Set in a strict Catholic boys school, the story is predictable enough: a straight laced, faithful honor student being groomed for.the priesthood has his whole persona shaken by the arrival of a defiant “bad boy” transfer student who intuits the “good boy’s” repressed feelings and sets out to tear down his walls. A crisis of faith ensues. The show does not shy away from noting Catholic condemnations of lust, and of homosexual lust in particular. But it juxtaposes these with what is palpably love—devotion to the other, and the drama revolves around the clash between these two seemingly irreconcilable commandments: to eschew all forms of overt homosexual eros and to place love above all else.

To be sure, much of the drama could be construed as LGBT propaganda—among other things, a hateful, homophobic religious fanatic of a father is juxtaposed with an older saintly trans woman—and, in an unusual departure from typical Thai BLs, one of the principals declares his orientation. But the series avoids condemning the Church—just the reverse, in fact.  The final scene brings together most of the key characters at an ordination celebrated in an atmosphere of faith, hope, and love, to choose words deliberately. The director, colloquially known as Aof, is by his own account, a practicing Catholic, albeit also married under Thai law to another man. 

 

Perhaps the greatest significance of BL, particularly its Thai variant, lies in its potential to undermine the categorization of human beings by erotic urges. This category-undermining is clearly visible in the recent Thai show Class Crush Crisis (available on Netflix); indeed, it forms its underlying theme. A mother distressed at her son’s lack of devotion to his studies forces him to transfer to an elite girls school that for the first time is accepting a group of boys. Excitement runs high: the girls finally have cute boys right at their proverbial fingertips; the boys, for their part, rejoice that landing a girlfriend will just be a matter of identifying a girl who fits one’s “type” and then going after her. The school is a gossipy place with everyone glued to their screens; rumors fly over who is with whom.  

But all the rumors turn out to be false, and in the process, people are hurt. Two of the girls are already in a relationship with each other. Other girls, “educated” by a decade of BLs, start “shipping” two of the boys; while they are right that homoerotic feelings exist among some of the boys, they get the “ships” wrong. The central character, who starts a club for the boys both as a form of self-protection and as a means for the boys to help each other find girlfriends, is blinded by categories and rules—who is whose “type,” people shouldn’t date those close to them—only to find it all blown up by his own feelings and those of his friends not to mention the boy he finally has to admit to himself he loves. He comes to understand that erotic feeling and attraction to another is ultimately a mystery and that efforts to pin it down with labels and categories risk turning people into things to be classified rather than their own human selves.

Class Crush Crisis is a feel-good romance featuring a gaggle of cute teens (the actors are actually teenagers, not people in their twenties pretending to be adolescents.) But the underlying message encapsulates the central values of the BL genre—that people are not labels—and demonstrates its potential as an art form that lies between the “queer” and the heteronormative.

The Truth About Indian Americans

By Razib Khan • 22 Sept 2026 View in browser
View in browser
Scott Menchin
 
 

On September 13, Bo French, the Republican nominee for Texas Railroad Commissioner, wrote on X, “I heard UT graduation this year looked like this. I didn’t believe it,” referring to a photograph that showed a few dozen Indian American students celebrating the University of Texas’s football win over Ohio State. This resulted in a massive online debate, pitting Indian Americans and their defenders against the group’s critics. If it was happening in a vacuum, you might wonder if too much attention has gone to an obscure politician attempting to farm engagement. But the context for French’s post was a national debate about the nature of immigration to the United States, demographic change, and the role of Indians in America dating back to Vivek Ramaswamy’s 2024 day-after-Christmas tweet declaring that “American culture has venerated mediocrity over excellence for way too long.” A few days after French’s post, Dallas-based commentator Kaylee Campbell shared a photograph of the National Merit Scholars at Heritage High School. The finalists were all ethnically Indian. Campbell went on to assert that Frisco, a suburb of Dallas, “is overwhelmingly Indian.” 

“The rate of change has been noticeable, alarming even, in affluent Texas cities.”

Words have a meaning, and it is hard to support the proposition that Indians are overwhelming Frisco, the state of Texas, or the United States as a whole. But the rate of change has been noticeable, alarming even, in affluent Texas cities where tech workers congregate. Frisco and the Austin suburb of Cedar Park have seen Indian Americans grow from 1 percent of the population to as much as 30 percent and over 15 percent, respectively, in the twenty-six years since the 2000 census. This rapid growth from a low baseline is reflected nationally. Pew Research estimates there are about 5 million Indian Americans in 2026; that’s thirteen times the 387,223 counted in the 1980 US Census. In 1980, Indian Americans were 0.17 percent of the population. Today they are over 1.5 percent. Two-thirds of Indian Americans are born abroad, and more than half entered the country after 2010. If there is one thing we know about American history, the arrival of a new and foreign population will trigger a backlash. In the 1820s, about fifty thousand immigrants arrived from Ireland to the US. That increased to nearly 800,000 in the 1840s. This influx powered the rise of the anti-immigrant Know Nothing Party, which won 22 percent of the vote share in the 1856 presidential election. It also led to urban conflicts of the sort fictionalized in The Gangs of New York. 

But Indians differ from immigrants of the Ellis Island era, or the Irish and Germans who arrived before the Civil War, because of their comparative prosperity. Indian Americans have an average household income of $151,200, compared to $83,700 for the population at large. Seventy-seven percent of Indian Americans have a college degree compared to 35 percent of Americans more generally. The Indian subcontinent did not send its “huddled masses yearning to breathe free.” The Indians who began arriving after the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 tended to be professionals in medicine or science. More recently, the stream of migrants from India has skewed toward software engineers (the “H1-B wave”). Indian immigrants reflect India’s diversity, which encompasses dozens of languages and several world religions. But they tend to be drawn from the elite. Around 70 percent of Indians in India fall into marginalized castes that can get affirmative action in that country. Less than 15 percent of Indian Americans would qualify for such consideration. It is no surprise that economists see few downsides in Indian immigration. John J.S. Soriano of the University of Dallas contends that a “skilled immigrant pays hundreds of thousands of dollars more into the system over a lifetime than they ever draw out,” while their “innovation spills over onto the Americans working beside them.”

Because of their affluence and professional background, Indian Americans have often been analogized to Jews. At the height of the financial crisis in 2008, Jewish-American opinion journalist Matthew Yglesias opined that the appointment of Neel Kashkari to oversee the Troubled Asset Relief Program (TARP) signaled a changing of the guard, heralding the rise of Indian Americans and the decline of America’s Ashkenazi ascendancy. But Kashkari’s own life offers up a window into how the Indian American trajectory differs from that of Ashkenazi Jews. In 2008, Kashkari was married to a fellow Indian American he met in college, but they divorced in 2011. In 2015 he was remarried, to a Chinese American woman, with whom he has two children. His ex-wife also remarried, to a German American. The best estimate is that about 30 percent of Indian Americans born or raised in the United States marry people of non-Indian ethnicity. In the 1960s, three generations after the massive wave of Eastern European Jewish migration, exogamy rates among Jews were only 5 percent. One reason for this difference is changing social attitudes. American society is much more open to a “mixed” marriage, like JD Vance and Usha Vance’s, than it was sixty years ago. But Ashkenazi Jewish identity was also relatively unified, formed in the Pale of Settlement and bound together by a common religious tradition and Yiddish language. 

Indian Americans lack that level of social cohesion, because they speak disparate languages, worship in varied ways (even if Hindu) and consume different cuisines. Vivek Ramaswamy and Apoorva Tewari, despite both being Brahmins, would be seen as having a mixed marriage in the Indian subcontinent. His family is from the South, and speaks Tamil, while her family is from the North, and speaks Hindi—an Indo-European language closer to English than it is to Tamil. In the Indian subcontinent, communal affinity revolves around an ethnographic unit termed jati, roughly, sub-caste, of which there are three thousand. Traditionally most people marry within their jati, and it is within the jati that customs, traditions, and folkways are passed down. In other words, to paraphrase Harvard geneticist David Reich, there are three thousand types of Indians. A quick scan of the New York Times wedding pages indicates that well over half of Indian Americans who are marrying other people of Indian origin are engaging in an inter-jati relationship (often it is inter-regional and inter-linguistic, like Ramaswamy and his wife). The third and fourth generation of Indians in America will probably be analogous to the Catholic “white ethnics” of the 20th-century of mixed backgrounds, with Irish, German, Italian and Polish forebears blended together in a new quasi-ethnos. But without any shared religion, food, or language (besides English), over time they are likely to intermarry with other secular liberal professionals.

 

Of course, the issue with Indian Americans isn’t just about their ethnic peculiarity. Their religious distinctiveness is critical in understanding the often negative reaction to their arrival en masse to American shores. About 80 percent of India’s population is Hindu, so it may surprise people that only 48 percent of Indian Americans identify as Hindu, according to a 2022 Pew survey. About 15 percent are Christian, 8 percent Muslim, 8 percent Sikh, and 3 percent are other religions. Though India’s religious minorities are overrepresented in the American diaspora (Sikhs and Christians are about 2 percent of India’s population each), it seems likely that the 18 percent of Indian Americans who are “religiously unaffiliated” are from Hindu backgrounds. Only 24 percent of Hindus say religion is “very important,” less than the 38 percent of the general American population. For many Indians, religion is less about fervent belief and more about maintenance of cultural traditions. 

Controversy around the growing public presence of Hinduism has erupted around the 90-foot-tall Hanuman at Sri Ashtalakshmi Temple in the Sugar Land area, southwest of Houston. At nine-stories, it is North America’s tallest Hanuman statue. The erection of such an exotic religious monument in a region with a large number of Evangelical Protestants has resulted in outrage, recalling the words of Exodus: “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth.” The US has changed a great deal since 1844, when Protestant mobs burned down two Catholic churches after a dispute about Bible reading in public schools; for all the tough talk online, it seems unlikely that angry mobs will tear down Hindu statues to appease their jealous God. But, these statues, and the often ornate and baroque temples that accompany them, do pose questions both of religious pluralism as well as questions of shared taste and mores. America is now only 62 percent Christian. Can such a country really resist the public expression of other faiths?

“Historically, the US has been a culturally Protestant nation.”

Historically, the US has been a culturally Protestant nation. True, religious pluralism has been a notable foundation of the American republic since the Founding, from George Washington’s 1790 welcoming letter to the Hebrew Congregation in Newport, Rhode Island, and Thomas Jefferson’s assertion in 1821 that his authoring of a religious liberty law “meant to comprehend, within the mantle of its protection, the Jew and the Gentile, the Christian and Mahometan, the Hindoo and infidel of every denomination.” But this pluralism emerged out of the context of debates in eighteenth-century England and its colonies between factions within Anglo-Protestantism. In The Cousins’ Wars: Religion, Politics and the Triumph of Anglo-America, Kevin Phillips argues that the Whiggish Low Church Dissenter variant of Protestantism came to be dominant in the American colonies, while Tory High Church Anglicanism was established in the United Kingdom. The spare and modest Congregationalist meeting house and the strip mall church both reflect an American faith that is more focused on earnest belief in private and rambunctious public confession than architectural majesty. Though Will Herberg’s Protestant–Catholic–Jew, published in 1955, argues for the emergence of a pan-religious ecumenical American identity, it can be argued that American Catholics and Jews were forced to fit themselves into a Low Church Protestant cultural order.

No religion is as opposed to the understated Protestant aesthetic as the dominant form of Hinduism, Sanata Dharma, which celebrates the divine with pageantry, public procession, and spectacle. Most fellow citizens of new Hindu Americans have reservations, to put it mildly, about the public displays of a religion so at variance with national mores. Unsurprisingly, this view is found among some Indian Americans raised in the US, who have assimilated into the dominant culture to such an extent that arguably their understanding of their religion has been “Protestantized.” One of the most prominent expositors of this view is California lawyer Vishal Ganeson, who has argued for a “Hindu Case Against Hinduism.” If American history is a guide, the “Hindu problem” will likely solve itself through time. 

 

Getting there, however, won’t be easy. For much of this century India has been dominated by a Hindu nationalist social, cultural, and political project that has revived national pride and assertiveness. This helps explain some of the recent tensions around Indian migration. A doctor fleeing Nehruvian socialism fifty years ago was bound to have a different mindset from that software engineer recently transferred from Google’s India location to one in California. The arrival of large numbers from foreign nations has caused conflict and tension in the past, and it continues to do so today. Not only do Indians today arrive with very different values and mores, something observed even by Indian Americans who were born in the US, but they come to a nation arguably less assertive and self-confident than in earlier generations. As I look ahead, I am filled with foreboding. There may not be rivers foaming with blood, but the American political landscape could benefit from more peace and less discord. Assimilation is inevitable, and occurring even today, but the firehouse of migration may serve as a check on its progress in a more self-consciously multicultural America.

Numbers are of the essence in these discussions. In a nation of 340 million, and a Texas that is already 55 percent non-white, one needs to keep the scope of the “Indian question” reasonable. There are a wide range of policy fixes on offer for our immigration crisis, from a sharp reduction analogous to what occurred after 1924, to a more self-interested system that focused on skills and needs rather than family reunification. A national conversation about cultural compatibility and assimilability may also be needed, conducted  in respectful, but candid terms. We can notice differences with engaging in demonization and name-calling. Use of such tactics is likely to be self-defeating. Bo French may have a problem with the number of Indians in the US, but he has also called for expelling Native Americans and Chinese. French has called for the deportation of 100 million Americans, which seems to point a strong sympathy with a white ethnostate. 

This is a non-starter in the America of 2026, when the vice president and likely Republican nominee is married to a Hindu woman and the most likely alternative Republican candidate is a Latino man. French and his fellow travelers must remember, in a favored phrase of the new right, “what time it is.” The assimilation of Indians into the American body politic is feasible, and arguably inevitable. But the Republican Party will only be the natural ruling party in Texas so long it embraces its role as the cheerleader for Texas being America’s America, rather than a hot, dry imitation of a European ethnostate.

Compact

The Death of the Professional-Managerial Class

By John B. Judis • 18 Sept 2026 View in browser
View in browser
Scott Menchin
 
 

In the wake of Kamala Harris’s defeat in 2024, one heard often that Democrats needed to focus on class rather than identity. But what exactly does it mean to focus on class? And what class is it that Democrats need to focus on? The party’s surging left wing has a clear answer—the working class—and usually offers an expansive conception of who is included in that category. “I think if you have to work to pay your bills,” New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has said, “I think that is one definition of being a part of the working class.” 

However, some have taken exception to this characterization and questioned whether Democrats like Mamdani are really speaking to the working class. Citing the high levels of education and relative affluence of voters supporting progressive candidates, they claim that Mamdani and his allies’ true base is the “professional-managerial class,” or PMC. 

As one writer recently put it, “The ‘PMC,’ as it has become known, was beginning to dominate the political left even in 1977; today, it arguably forms the Democratic Party’s most important voter base.” In the words of another, “Fifty years ago, the professional-managerial class swung right. Today, in America's biggest cities, they’re voting for leftists like Zohran Mamdani.” 

The idea of the PMC was popularized by the left-wing social critics John and Barbara Ehrenreich in a 1976 essay in Radical America. Over the past decade, writers from various points on the political spectrum have revived versions of this concept in discussions of resurgent progressive politics, from Julius Krein and Michael Lind to Gabriel Winant and Catherine Liu, whose 2021 book was entitled Virtue Hoarders: The Case against the Professional-Managerial Class. 

Is the distinction between the working class and the professional-managerial class, common to all these accounts, useful? Returning to the origins of the PMC concept makes clear how it seemed plausible at the time, but also why it has now outlived its usefulness except as a polemical term against left-wing politicians. 

Before the Ehrenreichs wrote their Radical America essay, they had introduced the idea of the professional-managerial class in debates within the New American Movement (NAM), a socialist organization to which they and I belonged. (NAM later merged with Michael Harrington’s Democratic Socialist Organizing Committee to form the Democratic Socialists of America.) The Ehrenreichs had several targets in mind when they formulated the idea of the PMC, but the principal one was the idea of a diversified working class that several of us at the journal Socialist Revolution had developed, which had become inscribed in the New American Movement’s political platform. 

The starting point of these debates was Karl Marx’s conception of class struggle as the fulcrum of political transformation. Marx defined membership in a class by a person’s relationship to the process of production. Owners were capitalists; workers who had to sell their labor power to capitalists were members of the working class. One’s consciousness of being either a worker or owner is or can be integral to a collective politics. This common consciousness does not need to be articulated in the words “working class.” An agitator might instead use terms like “working people” or simply “the people.” But the shared position of workers was the basis for a common struggle against owners. 

Some Marxist theorists have relied on the historian E.P. Thompson’s argument that English industrial workers didn’t become a class until they were conscious of being one. Class consciousness, for Thompson, is something that is “made” in the course of a class struggle and is premised on the awareness of a common condition and common adversary. In the United States in 1976 and today, there is not a “working class” unified in its understanding of itself. The question, then, is what might prove the basis for the emergence of such an understanding. 

“Marx’s dynamic conception of class and of the class struggle has endured.”

Marx’s theory was that as capitalism suffered persistent and growing crises, workers would organize themselves into unions, form a party, become conscious of their common condition, and attempt to wrest control of the government and economy from the capitalist class. Theses suppositions proved wanting, but Marx’s dynamic conception of class and of the class struggle has endured, and is taken for granted in controversy over the professional-managerial class and the working class. For all participating in the debate, class defines a common condition that is conducive to a collective struggle.

 

Marxists have debated why Marx’s predictions hadn’t come to pass since the late nineteenth century, but the rise of the New Left in the 1960s posed a challenge to the specifics of Marx’s theory of class. The New Left began as a liberal reform movement to secure racial justice and to demand a negotiated peace in Vietnam, but by the middle of the decade, it acquired a radical edge, with many of its militants arguing that the only way to end racial injustice and imperial wars was through a revolution. New Left groups called themselves “socialist” or even “communist” even though their core constituency wasn’t industrial laborers but college students and recent graduates. (The Students for a Democratic Society, or SDS, is an obvious case, but even the Black Panther Party was founded by two students at Merritt College in Oakland.)

Some of these socialist political tendencies, typified by the group Progressive Labor, fell back on the traditional Marxist idea of class struggle. Holding fast to the orthodox Marxist view that only blue-collar workers could bring about revolutionary change, they sent their members to work in factories, as truck drivers, or in related occupations. Other groups, typified by the Black Panther Party and the radical SDS splinter group Weatherman, abandoned any notion of the working class as the revolutionary subject. They argued instead that blacks, and sometimes other minorities, were part of a global anti-imperialist movement against American power. Organizations dominated by whites could function as auxiliaries to Third World revolutionaries. By their account, blacks in the US were colonized subjects, and their struggle was an anti-colonial one.

Those of us who joined the New American Movement, founded in 1971, saw ourselves as the descendants of the original SDS, which had promoted participatory democracy and shunned Marxist-Leninist orthodoxy. But the New American Movement was also an attempt to reconcile the older Marxist theory of class with the development of service workers and professionals who now outnumbered blue-collar factory workers. The explosion of college attendance after World War II, and particularly in the ’60s, had swelled the ranks of college-graduates who worked for wages and salaries and were under the authority of managers and executives. The New American Movement saw these new workers, its Political Perspective of June 1972 declared, as part of “increasingly diversified and stratified working class created by large-scale corporate capitalism.” The document, which the late James Weinstein and I had a hand in writing, went on to state: “The task of socialists is to clarify the origins of the internal divisions in the working class and to find the basis for unity.”

“We were trying to describe an incipient majority that could win power.”

Our idea of a diversified proletariat did not describe an existing class consciousness, but the basis for developing one, whether it explicitly went by the name of “working class” or not. It was meant to describe an incipient majority that could win power. It was based structurally on opposition to a capitalist class, which even if it didn’t directly employ a nurse or a janitor, did so indirectly through the power it wielded over the state and its expenditures. There were, to be sure, differences in income and social standing between the parts of this diversified proletariat, but the key to a common understanding was that the college-educated were increasingly subject to what Marxists called proletarianization. 

Like the craft workers of the nineteenth century who found themselves robbed of their status and autonomy and deskilled by the industrialization of their professions, the college-educated white-collar workers were increasingly subject to a loss of autonomy. That was particularly significant for the so-called professionals who judged their products primarily by standards of excellence rather than profitability. Teachers were judged by whether their pupils learned; nurses and doctors by how well they treated their patients; software developers by whether they produced “cool code.” (During this period, I published an interview in Socialist Revolution with a computer programmer who in those days was still using punch cards.)

Marx had depicted the working class as a “universal class” whose interests were identical with those of the society as a whole. For Marx and for the early socialists, that meant the working class was equipped to govern society. In The Promise of American Life, which appeared in 1909, the progressive journalist Herbert Croly ridiculed that idea. “The action of a majority composed of the ordinary type of convinced socialists,” he wrote, “could and would in a few years do more to make socialism impossible than could be accomplished by the best and most prolonged efforts of a majority of malignant anti-socialists.” Croly’s quip was not entirely unwarranted. However, a decade later, Thorstein Veblen prophesied in Engineers and the Price System that the widespread employment of engineers and technicians would raise the possibility of self-government without a capitalist class. NAM’s concept of a diversified working class incorporated Veblen’s optimism about self-government. This new working class, we argued, was equipped with the skills to manage an economy and govern a country.

Inside the New American Movement, the debate with the Ehrenreichs over the nature of the working class began in the mid-1970s and came to a head with their essay in Radical America, which drew a sharp distinction between the working class and the professional-managerial class. The working class consisted of “craftsmen, operatives, laborers, sales workers, clerical workers, service workers, [and] non-college educated technical workers.” The shorthand Marxist version would be wage-laborers engaged in the production and distribution of commodities, but it might extend to include lower-level office workers in finance, whom Marx would have regarded as unproductive workers.

For its part, the professional-managerial class included not only nurses, welfare workers, teachers, entertainers, writers, engineers and other technical workers, but also “middle-level administrators and managers.” The Ehrenreichs defined the PMC as “salaried mental workers who do not own the means of production and whose major function in the social division of labor may be described broadly as the reproduction of capitalist culture and class relations.”  Schoolteachers and entertainers, for instance, are “directly concerned with social control or with the production and propagation of ideology.” 

On this basis, the Ehrenreichs stipulated that members of the PMC were “objectively antagonistic” to the working class—that is, they were a distinct class with opposing interests that couldn’t be grouped together, as the proponents of a diversified working class had suggested, in a coalition against the ruling class of business and financial magnates. This point would seem obvious in the case of middle managers and administrators, who could be expected to side with their immediate superiors. But the Ehrenreichs also held that registered nurses, schoolteachers, or actors occupied an objectively antagonistic stance toward factory workers, truck drivers, and grocery cashiers. 

Their argument derived in part from a visit to China in 1975. The Ehrenreichs, as I learned when they stayed at our house in Oakland after their return, had come to admire the Chinese Cultural Revolution. “Our exposure to the tail end of the Cultural Revolution in China and our involvement in the developing feminist critique of professionalism here fed into our thinking about the class dynamics of the American left,” they wrote in reply to critics of their thesis. They were particularly taken by the Chinese attempt to remove the “conflict between manual and mental workers” by forcing mental workers to integrate with and share the labors of manual workers. That effort, they believed, was preventing the deskilling of the working class that had taken place earlier in the United States.

A feminist critique of expertise was another key influence on the Ehrenreichs’ thinking. In the United States, beginning in the late nineteenth century, activities like medical care and education had been transferred from working class communities to experts hired by cities, states, and the federal government. The PMC, they wrote, existed “by virtue of expropriation of the skills and culture once indigenous to the working class.” They went on to state: “The professional-manager workers exist. only by virtue of the expropriation of the skills and culture once indigenous to the working class.” Feminists had made this argument about midwives and obstetricians, but the Ehrenreichs extended to the working class as a whole. 

In the mid-1970s, the Ehrenreichs had on their side the fact that many professionals, whose autonomy and income was protected by guild-like professional associations, and who often owned their own firms or worked in partnerships in small firms, did think politically like middle managers. They were likely to be free-market Republicans, and large numbers of them backed Ronald Reagan in the 1980 and 1984 elections. According to the American National Election Studies (ANES) surveys, a majority of professionals did not back a Democratic presidential candidate until 1988. But after that, the basis for grouping professionals together with managers weakened—and with it, the basis for the Ehrenreichs’ account of the PMC.

 

Since the 1980s, if not earlier, professionals and managers have diverged in their party and candidate choices; professionals have increasingly backed Democrats, while managers have stuck with the Republicans. In his 2010 book, Red State Blue State, political scientist Andrew Gelman, using American National Election Studies data, charted the different presidential choices of occupational groups:

The downward trajectory shows professionals moving away from Republicans, even as support of Republicans remained consistent among managers. 

One could argue that an occupational group’s choice of party candidate has no bearing on its class consciousness. But on at least one defining class issue, Democrats are 45 percentage points more likely to approve of labor unions than Republicans, according to Gallup. Likewise back-of-the-envelope tabulation based on the 2024 General Social Survey shows that while there is no significant difference in the responses of managers and professionals when it comes to, say, abortion, 80 percent of professionals reported having at least some confidence in labor unions, while a majority of managers reported having “hardly any.” 

Moreover, managers are not organized into unions—if anything, they are the antagonists of unions—while professionals now account for many of the members of the four largest labor unions: the National Education Association, the Service Employees International Union, the American Federation of Teachers, and the American Federation of State, County, and Municipal Employees. Among the professionals represented by SEIU are doctors, registered nurses, physician assistants, pharmacists, physical therapists, social workers, research technicians, lawyers, engineers, court employees, librarians, IT professionals, law enforcement officers, adjunct professors, university researchers, academic counselors, and K-12 early learning professionals.

I could find no comprehensive studies of the political differences between American professionals and managers, but University of Toronto sociologist D.W. Livingstone has written on how Canadian professionals differ in class outlook from managers. In Tipping Point for Advanced Capitalism, Livingstone analyzed surveys of workers in Canada, the United States, and Western Europe to see how they would respond to questions of whether owners of corporations should be able to make gains at the expense of their workers and whether corporations should be prohibited from replacing striking workers. He found a sharp difference between professional employees and managers on two of these questions: “whether owners of corporations make gains at the expense of their workers” and where “management should be prohibited by law from hiring workers to take the place of strikers.” Livingstone rated the responses as either pro-labor, pro-capital, or contradictory. Professionals’ answers, he found, were most similar to those of industrial workers and diverged from those of corporate capitalists, large employers and upper managers.

I would expect that American industrial and service workers and professionals would not display as much “oppositional class consciousness” as their Canadian counterparts, but the differences between employees, including professionals, and managers would hold. All of this suggests that after the 1970s, when the Ehrenreichs were writing, there is scant evidence for supposing managers and professionals occupy a unified class that is antagonistic to wage-laborers. 

Why have professionals and managers diverged over the last half-century? Our predictions in the early 1970s that professionals were being proletarianized seem to have been borne out. Over these decades, many professionals have experienced a loss of autonomy and of expected income. Seventy-five years ago, professionals—typified by the dentist, pharmacist, lawyer, and architect—owned their own firms, and thought politically as a small business owner does. Many were conservative Republicans. Today, many professionals work for corporations that set their income and impose conditions on how they deliver their services. One survey of doctors found that “physicians identify third-party practice acquisition (83 percent) and rapid consolidation (74 percent) as major contributors to autonomy loss, and more than seven in ten (75 percent) support stronger state oversight to safeguard physician leadership in care decisions.” 

“Salaried professionals find their freedom constricted.”

Salaried professionals find their freedom constricted. Tech, once considered a highly desirable career, is rapidly going down the path of deskilling. Jobs that involve data analysis have either been automated with artificial intelligence or shipped overseas; software engineers have become proxies for artificial intelligence. As one site for programmers declared: “You were never an engineer; you were a code monkey. AI is a better code monkey than you could ever be.” Many jobs that have not been automated through AI have been outsourced thanks to remote work. 

Overall white-collar salary growth has stagnated in the last two years. Much of the reason is a weakening market for professional labor due to outsourcing, artificial intelligence, and corporate consolidation. Between 2023 and 2025, there was declining demand for software developers, business analysts, technology analysts, market researchers, and data analysts, among others. But the pressure on incomes goes farther back. Compared to 2010 and calculated in real wages, many professionals have seen their average salaries go down. These include dentists, architects, pharmacists, economists, engineers, nurses, writers, and actors.

Proletarianization manifests itself most dramatically in the lack of opportunities for young people who go to college and even graduate school with the expectation that they will gain secure, well-paying jobs as professionals. They are the would-be professionals. According to a study by the Burning Glass Institute, five and ten years after obtaining their degrees, 45 percent of college graduates are “underemployed” in jobs that don’t require college degrees. Close to half of those who obtained degrees in biology and biological sciences remain underemployed. 

Noam Scheiber recounts in his book Mutiny: The Rise and Revolt of the College-Educated Working Class how young college graduates’ disappointments in the labor market have radicalized many of them. Scheiber cites a Gallup Poll finding that among the college-educated, support for labor unions had risen to over 70 percent by the early 2020s. Opinion analyst Nate Silver found that the “most Democratic voting group” was “voters with postgraduate degrees but lower-to-middle household incomes of $30 thousand to $60 thousand per year.” Many of these voters, one assumes, are would-be professionals subject to proletarianization, whose political consciousness and situation are dramatically different from those of managers.

In a 2016 follow-up to their original essay, the Ehrenreichs themselves acknowledged that because of the process of proletarianization, the PMC “lies in ruins.” They concluded: “The debt-ridden unemployed and underemployed college graduates, the revenue-starved teachers, the overworked and underpaid service professionals, even the occasional whistle-blowing scientist or engineer—all face the same kind of situation that confronted skilled craft-workers in the early twentieth century and all American industrial workers in the late twentieth century.” 

 

Does this mean the diversified working class that we talked about at Socialist Revolution and in the New American Movement is now a living reality? Would it be accurate to describe Mamdani as the candidate of the “working class”? That would be, to say the least, a stretch. As many professionals and would-be professionals suffer downward mobility and begin to manifest the rudiments of a working-class consciousness, many industrial and lower-level white collar workers in the United States have gone in the opposite direction. There may be some convergence in economic conditions, but not in consciousness.

That much is clear in voter preferences for the pro-union Democratic party. If you look at Andrew Gelman’s graphs, skilled and non-skilled workers became less supportive of the Democratic Party between 1976 and 2008. That trend has continued. When Gallup asked about approval of unions in 2024, respondents who had gone to college were 9 percentage points more approving of unions than those with only some college and 11 points more approving than those who had not gone to college. If you were able to translate these figures into occupational categories, and to remove managers from the college-educated, the disparities between salaried college-educated professionals and wage-laborers would be even larger. 

In other words, as far as shared class consciousness goes, a diversified working class does not exist. There are many reasons for this. Differences over cultural issues of race and sex and over socio-economic issues like immigration have divided the potential members of a diversified working class. These differences often intersect with differences in political geography, creating a gulf between the world views of small town and metropolitan America. Divisions have also arisen in between private sector industrial and white-collar workers and the unionized public sector workers whose salaries they pay in taxes. These divisions have contributed to the disapproval of unions among workers who might have been expected to support them. Ruy Teixeira and I described some of these tensions in our book, Where Have All the Democrats Gone?

“There are some grounds for optimism.”

But there are some grounds for optimism. If you want to nourish hope that the diversified working class we described in the early 1970s will become conscious of itself, consider the history of the American labor movement or of the European socialist parties. In all these cases, initial leadership did not come from the bottom rungs, but from the top of the labor force. The American Federation of Labor, which would eventually become the AFL-CIO, began among craft workers suffering from proletarianization. The German Social Democratic Party had its beginnings in the late nineteenth century among skilled artisans and craftsmen rather than among unskilled laborers. In these cases, worsening economic conditions and skilled political leadership eventually created common ground, exemplified in the political transformation of the Democratic Party during the New Deal era. 

Those conditions do not currently exist in the United States. There are still large gaps in income and status between wage-laborers and professionals, and the political leadership that would unite them is absent. The labor movement is weak and divided. No more than a few percent of Americans could even name the current head of the AFL-CIO. Many Democratic Party leaders are still in hock to culturally progressive lobbies, foundations, and think tanks. The organization to which Mamdani and his allies belong, the Democratic Socialists of America, purports to speak for the working class but enthusiastically embraces the most extreme stands on immigration (open borders), crimes (abolish the police and prisons), sex (biological men in women’s sports) and race (reparations). The PMC may be in ruins, but the diversified working remains, at best, a work in progress.

title: How Britain Defeated ‘Assisted Dying’
content:
Every developed country faces a deeply uncomfortable problem: People are getting older. This means a fiscal crisis sometime in the coming decades, because it results in more dependents on the welfare state and fewer taxpayers.

Compact

How Britain Defeated ‘Assisted Dying’

By Dan Hitchens • 17 Sept 2026 View in browser
View in browser
Henry Nicholls / Getty
 
 

Every developed country faces a deeply uncomfortable problem: People are getting older. This means a fiscal crisis sometime in the coming decades, because it results in more dependents on the welfare state and fewer taxpayers. Equally, it means a cultural crisis, because the habits of mutual dependence and reverence for age are being eaten away by the culture of Now. Simply put, we don’t know what to do with the dependent and unproductive people in our midst.

No wonder some people are mulling the obvious solution. Writing for the leading magazine of the British left, The New Statesman, the commentator Oli Dugmore recently observed: “All over the country our elders sit in cell blocks bathed in the stupefying light and sound of Bargain Hunt, Location, Location, Location, Tipping Point, unvisited by relatives who are preoccupied by the rhythm of their lives, or perhaps unable to summon the courage to witness the degeneration of the once totemic figures of their lives, their mum and dad.” His answer: “Let them die.”  

That exhortation was a reference to the assisted suicide bill, which Parliament voted on for the last time on Friday. The legislation, Dugmore said, would not only rid us of those awkward inhabitants of care homes but would drive down “the pensions bill, the NHS bill and the care bill.” Everyone wins except, perhaps, the people receiving a dose of lethal drugs. But then it was their choice. Or maybe it wasn’t exactly, but never mind. 

Dugmore was unusual in his candid advocacy of death as a policy solution. For the most part, the campaign for “assisted dying” has been insistently, self-righteously innocuous. All we are asking for, the proponents like to repeat, is dignity, choice, compassion. Most of the bill’s parliamentary supporters seemed genuinely puzzled by what one of them, on Friday, called “all these objectors.” The bill’s original proposer in 2024, the Labour MP Kim Leadbeater, often appeared to be saying that anyone not on board must be either “fundamentally opposed, which I totally respect” (translation: some kind of religious nutcase) or just a bit confused. Leadbeater and allies did not realize that, for many people, the “Dignity in Dying” campaign was at risk of giving us a “Let them die” law: a new social norm that—as the comedy duo Mitchell and Webb put it in a surprisingly savage attack on the bill—“When you’re getting in the way, call it a day.”

Misunderstanding your opponents can be fatal. In 2025, when Leadbeater put together the requisite House of Commons committee on the bill, she cynically ensured that the opposition voices would be led by Danny Kruger, a populist Evangelical who gets up the noses of the Labour majority in the Commons. But Kruger is also a formidable mind with a special interest in the mechanics of government. How, he repeatedly probed, would this state suicide service be funded, administered, regulated, and monitored? How would it relate to our existing laws on safeguarding, mental health, drug approval, and to our existing health and social care institutions? And how—getting to the heart of things—would it interact with the glaring deficiencies in how Britain looks after the elderly, the sick, and the disabled? For instance, if someone’s family was being crippled by care costs—a frequent occurrence—could they get an assisted death on that basis?

This was the kind of issue Leadbeater’s side needed to grapple with. But they refused to see its significance. Look, she replied to Kruger, there are medical criteria and safeguards. Yes, he pressed, but what if the (pretty broad) criteria are met and the (pretty formulaic) safeguards are checked off? Can the state give you a massive dose of lethal drugs because your care is too expensive?

As Leadbeater frowned and prevaricated over such questions, the case for the bill began, very slowly, to disintegrate. Watching the committee proceedings, one Labour MP, Karl Turner, found himself transfixed, “like a mad person, glued to the computer screen.” He had supported the bill, and he despised a Tory just as much as any red-blooded Labour man. “The people who were speaking were the people who I would naturally and instinctively think were talking crap…the hard right-wing Tories, who you would instinctively think were talking nonsense, if you’re a socialist like I am, were actually persuading me that there’s a question mark that needs to be addressed.” 

Turner’s experience was a microcosm. Everywhere, people—even those sympathetic to assisted suicide in theory—began to conclude that this wasn’t primarily a question about how to help a tiny number of people whose agony was beyond the reach of medical care. It was about whether to accept a new blueprint for dealing with the weakest members of society.

The pollster Luke Tryl has said that the anti-assisted suicide movement was, with along with the movement for gay marriage, the most successful British social-issue campaign of the twenty-first century. It was a generous remark, but possibly misleading, since this was not a campaign in the traditional sense. There was no particularly brilliant messaging, no capturing of the media narrative. What happened was more organic: the coming-together of a sort of coalition of trepidation. The psychiatrists looked at what the bill was asking them to do, and gulped. The disabled people’s organizations, previously neutral on the issue, asked what the bill would mean in practice, and decided it was deeply sinister. Doctors, domestic violence charities, NHS bigwigs, academics, lawyers, and investigative journalists began to sound frankly panicked. So did people who realized that the terms of the bill would apply to then. “I was given six months to live,” one member of the House of Lords remarked, “thirty-seven years ago.” Even the new prime minister, Andy Burnham, nominally supportive of assisted suicide, said that the care system needed sorting out before such legislation could be debated.

To all of this, the bill’s supporters responded with the same stories of terrible deathbed scenes, which they believed constituted an unanswerable case. People are vomiting up their own feces, they said again and again, and you don’t want to see them killed? Last Friday, this detail was once again relayed by the bill’s sponsor Lauren Edwards. Her Labour colleague Zubir Ahmed stood up and replied: “Can I reassure my honorable friend, as a practicing surgeon who deals with bile duct cancer, that there is almost never a reason why someone should be in that state, with fecal vomiting, if they were treated appropriately and all the relevant palliative care measures were in place?” 

The problem with an argument based on anecdotes is that eventually you come full circle and the anecdotes start pointing in the opposite direction. No speech on Friday was more affecting than the one from Ashley Dalton, another Labour MP, who has stage 4 cancer. Like Ahmed, she is a former health minister, and was eloquent on the practical gaps in the bill. But she also unmasked the inhumanity of the arguments for it. “Until we can say,” Dalton told the House, “that everyone who needs it has access to high-quality palliative care, we are offering nobody a choice. A terrible death or an assisted death is not a choice: It’s a threat.”

“It is a joy and a relief.”

On Friday morning the anti side estimated the likely result as 283 votes for, 283 against. In the end the difference was sixteen votes; sixteen votes for a society that cares for the vulnerable rather than saying, with Dugmore, “Let them die.” Other countries are going to face this choice too. It is a joy and a relief to see Britain take a first step onto the narrow, uphill path.
