Compact

Don’t Blame Phones for Teen Sadness

By Dario Marino • 16 Sept 2026 View in browser
View in browser
Scott Menchin
 
 

Young people are unhappy, and many observers think they know what is to blame: technology. The most influential argument in this direction comes from the psychologist Jonathan Haidt. In his 2024 book The Anxious Generation, Haidt argued that giving young people smartphones in the early 2010s “rewired” childhood, which led to large upticks in anxiety, depression, and related ailments. Haidt’s argument has begun to influence policymakers in many locales, informing efforts to limit phone use in schools and to restrict youth access to social media platforms. 

It is understandable why this story has proven attractive. The diffusion of mobile internet technology was a big change, and it’s easy to imagine that being constantly connected makes us feel anxious, self-conscious, and dissatisfied. However, there are problems with this account. For one thing, what do we make of the fact that English-speaking countries are significantly sadder than other countries where youth smartphone access is just as widespread? If it were just the phone, wouldn’t teens in other parts of the world be just as unhappy? It would be one thing if Anglophone youth reported greater use of digital technology than their counterparts elsewhere, but they don’t. 

If you rank the six regions in the 2026 World Happiness Report by how much time teenage girls spend on social media, English-speaking countries aren’t in first place. Latin America has a larger share of heavy users, five or more hours a day, than the Anglosphere does. But Latin American girls at the heaviest use levels report far less unhappiness than English-speaking girls at the same use levels, and English-speaking countries still post the steepest collapse and the highest ceiling of low life satisfaction of any region. If dosage explained the outcome, the region with the heaviest users should look the worst. Instead, the region with more heavy users looks better, and the region with lighter use looks worse by a wide margin. An almost identical social media usage pattern can be found in Western Europe, but its users are happier at any level compared to teen social media users in the English-speaking world. Likewise, in a cross-cultural study comparing Britons and Arabs who spent the same amount of time on social media, the Brits came out significantly less happy.

Some theorists have attempted to explain these discrepancies by arguing that in the English-speaking world, smartphone use has combined with a lack of strong interpersonal ties to produce the decline in happiness. But there is no obvious basis for arguing the Anglosphere is the worst off in this area. If anything, Germans and Koreans plausibly have looser social ties, but neither country exhibits the same effect. It is more likely that this phenomenon has to do with something that can be more easily transmitted to a vulnerable young population whose primary language is English.

An alternative explanation of why Anglo young people are sadder than non-English speakers, even though both groups have a similarly high share of teen phone usage, is that it isn’t just the medium, but the message: specifically, the Anglophone strand of left-wing ideology known as wokeness, which taught young people to think about the world in terms of harm, threat, and victimhood. The discourse around woke may seem stale, but with some distance from “Woke 1,” we can perhaps assess its broader cultural consequences more objectively than we could a few years ago. 

Alongside the spike of sadness that began in the early 2010s, we saw not only the widespread youth adoption of smartphones, but the surging popularity of the website Tumblr. The usual date given for Tumblr’s aggressive shift to woke discourse is 2012, the same year cited as the youth smartphone watershed. Tumblr was a predominantly English-language site, which means that unlike the smartphone, its consequences were unequally spread by language and culture. Tumblr’s growth in this period was impressive. The number of blog posts on the platform grew from around 7 million in 2010, to 17.5 million in 2011, to around 76 million by the end of 2012, to 141 million in 2013, and 207 million in 2014.

“Tumblr allowed a niche ideology to be spread to a receptive public.”

The ideas that circulated on Tumblr were not born in 2012, but the conditions for the spread became mature when three things converged. First, in the years after the 2008 financial crisis and during the Obama presidency, questions of race and social justice reached a new moral urgency. Second, the internet, and specifically sites like Tumblr, could reach young people on the older adolescent side, disproportionately students at the high school and college level that were able to introduce these concepts to a more left leaning audience that was already more ready to adopt that framework. Third, these ideas could only become a societal force once enough of that cohort was online to reach critical mass. Tumblr allowed a niche ideology to be spread to a receptive public. Newsrooms then absorbed the people and the vocabulary from the platforms teenagers were already feeding on. A content analysis of language in The New York Times found that words describing prejudice, victimization, oppression, marginalization, and related terms rose sharply starting in the early to mid 2010s. 

Tumblr wasn’t only the platform where woke started; it also favored and encouraged other forms of negative self-perception. There were entire corners of the site devoted to pro-anorexia content and many other forms of self-harm. When Tumblr tried to ban this content in late 2012, researchers who went back and counted found 559 pro eating disorder blogs in 2010 and 593 in 2012. The phone was a way in, but a phone could have shown any message at all. Instead, for a specific set of people (mostly teen girls and LGBT individuals), it showed self-harm content and politically enraged communities. The self-harm niche remained a relatively local but worrying phenomenon. However, the politically enraged niche then went mainstream once the Tumblr discourse crossed over into journalism, and polarization pushed a much larger share of teens toward sadness accordingly.

If ideological “software” rather than hardware was doing the main damage, then we would expect that to show up along ideological lines even inside the same country, using the same phones, in the same year. It does. A Columbia University study of 86,138 US twelfth-graders tracked depressive affect from 2005 to 2018 broken out by self-identified political belief. Conservative boys and girls barely move for a decade. Liberal girls flatline through the 2000s and then peel away from everyone else right around 2011 to 2012—the same years Tumblr scales up—and never come back down.

The evidence suggests that young English speakers, across otherwise different cultures and continents, caught the same sadness virus, despite not even being the heaviest users of the devices everyone wants to blame for what ails them. If Woke 1 has receded from its peak, let us hope that the consequences are kept in the English-speaking containment dome, and that they can be rolled back to improve the happiness of teens who were spared being young in the 2010s.

Germany’s China Shock Will Push Voters Right

By Peer Illner • 15 Sept 2026 View in browser
View in browser
AP
 
 

The German political establishment’s so-called firewall against the far right is crumbling. This month, the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) secured 44 percent of the vote in the state elections in Saxony-Anhalt, and the party is now polling at 37 percent in the upcoming vote in nearby Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. Those alarmed by the AfD’s rise in the former East might take comfort in the fact that the party currently polls at roughly half those levels in the country’s western states. However, there are reasons to think that situation won’t last. A second story unfolding this year is a 12 percent decline in German exports to China as a consequence of Beijing’s muscular industrial policy. Germany’s growing trade deficit with China looks set to prompt mass auto-sector layoffs, which would likely boost the AfD to similar levels in the country's former West.

American economists coined the term “China Shock” in the 2010s to make sense of the loss of US manufacturing capacity and the tendency among those left behind by deindustrialization to vote for right-wing Republican candidates. Their story went as follows: In the wake of China’s admission to the World Trade Organization in 2001, American manufacturing—specifically in the low to medium range of furniture, toys, and electronics—faced stiff import competition. In the first decade of the new millennium, the United States experienced a 33 percent drop in manufacturing employment, while its imports from China rose by a staggering 264 percent. 

Offshoring of production further accelerated manufacturing layoffs. In China, hundreds of millions of agricultural workers migrated to burgeoning manufacturing hubs like Shenzhen and Dongguan from the 1980s onwards, creating an almost limitless pool of cheap labor. As a Special Economic Zone, Shenzhen offered tax breaks and export-oriented policies, creating incentives for foreign producers to offshore their operations. American firms soon began to produce in China at a fraction of the cost. After 2000, Apple, Dell, and HP all moved their laptop and smartphone production to China, where they partnered with contract manufacturers like Foxconn and Pegatron, plugged into Chinese supply chains, and were able to ramp up production rapidly and at scale. According to the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, a total of 3.5 million American manufacturing jobs were lost between 2000 and 2010 to import competition and offshoring.

The total number of laid off workers may seem like a drop in the ocean of a 159-million-strong labor force, but concentration, not scale, is what made the shock politically explosive. As the economist David Autor has shown, the manufacturing losses eviscerated entire communities in the Southeast and the Industrial Midwest. In West Hickory, N.C., once the “furniture capital of the world,” manufacturing jobs plummeted from 34.1 percent in 1990 to just 15 percent by 2016. In Martinsville, W. Va., once the “sweatshirt capital of the world,” the manufacturing share of employment nosedived from 45.1 percent to 13.4 percent over the same period. 

“A survey of the social consequences of the China Shock makes for grim reading.”

A survey of the social consequences of the China Shock makes for grim reading. The laid-off workers mostly stayed unemployed, and in the affected counties, welfare payouts tripled, with low-skilled white males most affected by long-term unemployment. The consequences included soaring alcoholism and drug abuse, crumbling marriages, and a surge in “deaths of despair”: a combination of suicides, overdoses, and liver disease. Beyond the personal and social devastation, the trade shock’s most explosive fallout may have been political. Autor and his colleagues found that the hardest-hit districts veered sharply to the right, suggesting a stark correlation between deindustrialization and extreme political polarization. Their models suggest that the effects of the China Shock in deindustrializing parts of Michigan, Wisconsin, and Pennsylvania played a pivotal role in Donald Trump’s 2016 victory. 

Autor is careful to describe the China shock as a catalyst, rather than a cause, of Trump’s rise. Similar right-wing surges among blue-collar voters occurred in the Netherlands, Sweden, and France, none of which faced comparable import competition, as well as in Germany, where the AfD built its eastern base during the 2010s. But the China Shock did not have to be the sole cause of America’s rightward shift to be decisive. In swing states on a razor’s edge, a small shift often determines an election. 

 

Germany was mostly spared the China Shock because its industry was concentrated in the high-end manufacturing sector, where China was yet to compete. Indeed, Germany’s economic story during the first two decades of the twenty-first century was in many ways the opposite of America’s. While US exports to China drastically contracted during the 2000s, German exports to China skyrocketed by 227 percent, growing at four times the rate of its exports to the rest of the world. Between 2003 and 2019, China and Germany forged a powerhouse partnership: German automobiles, machinery, and chemicals helped industrialize China, expanding its industrial base and growing its middle class, while China’s insatiable demand became the engine of German prosperity.

Germany’s error was to mistake this temporary grace period for a permanent advantage. When Chinese exports to the United States plateaued after the Great Financial Crisis eroded American buying power, Beijing refused to remain the West’s low-cost workshop. Instead, it pursued a deliberate strategy to close the technology gap with advanced economies. By the 2010s, Chinese manufacturers had moved into high-value sectors, directly competing with Germany in the production of machinery, robots, and automobiles. Backed by a coordinated state effort at every level of government, and fueled by relentless investment in engineering talent, education, and R&D, China’s firms unleashed a second wave of export growth directed at the European market. 

The result is that today, Germany faces its own China Shock. The numbers illustrate the scale of the reversal. Since their high in 2021, German exports to China as a percentage of GDP have plummeted by over 40 percent. If the recent decline were to continue for three more years, exports would fall below what Germany exports to Austria or Switzerland. At the same time, imports from China rose 8.9 percent in 2025 alone, pushing Germany’s trade deficit with China to a record $104 billion. 

“At the heart of the collapse is the vaunted German car industry.”

At the heart of the collapse is the vaunted German car industry. By remaining wedded to the internal combustion engine as China invested in EV production, German auto makers have been left behind for the first time in history and are paying a steep price. With many Chinese motorists preferring to buy domestically produced vehicles, German car exports to China fell by 66 percent between 2022 and 2025, reaching their lowest level since 2009. Since 2022, Porsche’s share has fallen 61 percent, while Volkswagen’s China joint-venture profits have dropped 60 percent. Meanwhile, China’s car exports have surged, hitting the 10 million a year mark in 2025, which analysts hadn’t expected to see until 2030. Even in the streets of Berlin, it is increasingly common to see cars made by BYD, Polestar, or MG Motor, as Chinese EVs technologically outcompete German ones at a fraction of the price. As German automakers are simultaneously pushed out of China and squeezed at home, the panic around job losses has hit. Over the next few years, VW is set to close at least three factories and cut 30,000 jobs in Germany. 

The German automotive sector accounts for a quarter of domestic industrial revenue. Together with mechanical engineering, chemicals, and electrical technology, German industry makes up 20 percent of the country’s economic output, surpassing any other European country. In contrast to other countries, the German industrial model is disproportionately reliant on exports. Germany ranks as the world’s third-largest exporter after China and the United States, but while exports account for just 10 percent of US GDP and 20 percent of China’s, they make up a staggering 40 percent of Germany’s economy. This export prowess is now turning into a liability, with China not only reversing its trade deficit with Germany but also increasingly rivalling German manufacturers in third markets worldwide. The risk to industrial jobs is acute. According to Jürgen Matthes of the Cologne Institute of Economic Research, at the peak of Germany’s export boom in 2021, around a million German jobs, or 2.5 percent of total employment, directly depended on the Chinese market. Since then, it is estimated that about half of these jobs hang in the balance due to the collapse of Chinese exports.

Predicting how laid-off workers might vote is a speculative endeavor. However, according to the economist Lutz Schneider, who studied the political repercussions of different waves of deindustrialization in Germany, the AfD vote is strongest in places where a long industrial tradition meets a sharp employment decline. A compelling example is Pirmasens, once the center of Germany’s shoe industry in southwestern Palatinate. As foreign import competition hollowed out the sector over the last 30 years, industrial employment plummeted by 50 percent. The political fallout was stark. In the 2017 federal election, the AfD captured 16 percent of the vote, one of its strongest results in western Germany at the time. In last year’s Bundestagswahl, the party’s vote share reached 25 percent.

Like West Virginia and North Carolina, Pirmasens suggests that the rapid collapse of historic industrial sectors drives gains for right-wing populism. Germany’s China Shock neatly fits this pattern, with jobs in established strongholds like Bavaria, Baden-Württemberg, and Lower Saxony now threatened by a sudden contraction, just as they were in the United States. But instead of an import-driven shock of low-value competition, Germany now confronts an export-driven shock, in which China’s industrial ascent replaces German goods in global markets. This looks more like decimating Silicon Valley than closing the garment sector of North Carolina. 

According to analysis by EY, Germany shed 124,100 industrial jobs last year alone. In the automotive sector, one in seven jobs has disappeared over the last six years. While the AfD already polls at over 40 percent in East Germany, it stands at roughly 20 percent in Germany’s industrial heartlands. Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg were never AfD strongholds—immune, until recently, to the social decline and reunification trauma that built the party’s base in the east. If deindustrialization is now doing in the west what post-reunification grievances did in the east, the AfD’s West German results may soon mirror those of its East German peak.

 

The fact that German leaders didn’t anticipate China’s rise is a testament to their geopolitical arrogance. They assumed that integration into global trade would naturally lead to deregulation, privatization, and free trade. Instead, China opened its markets enough to attract foreign investment and technology transfers, while shielding strategic sectors from full competition. Where the German playbook envisaged the state retreating as markets grew, China’s state capacity expanded as it poured resources into infrastructure, education, and R&D. 

German economists complain that Chinese subsidies distort competition, but they have less to say about the practice of automakers funneling profits into shareholder payouts instead of reinvesting in production. In 2023, Volkswagen paid out $11 billion in dividends, while its EV transition lagged far behind Chinese rivals. With the chips and the dividends down, Germany is now scrambling to shore up its industry with protectionist measures, joining France’s call to regulate trade with China through tariffs, import reductions, and price controls. However, companies like Siemens, BASF, and Volkswagen have cautioned against imposing stricter tariffs for fear of retaliatory measures that would further reduce their share of the Chinese market.

“The AfD offers no way out of this bind.”

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz must therefore choose between protecting the profits of Germany’s national champions and admitting those champions can no longer compete without EU-wide measures that stop Chinese EVs from beating them on their home market. The effect on German jobs, meanwhile, risks being zero-sum: Maintain free trade with China, and you preserve export-dependent jobs at the cost of those that rely on protection from Chinese imports; impose trade barriers to protect domestic workers, but risk endangering export jobs through Chinese retaliation. The AfD offers no way out of this bind. In fact, its manifesto doubles down on free trade, committing to rolling back “economically damaging sanctions” on China with no plan for the unemployment this is set to create. Nonetheless, it is positioned to capitalize on voters’ disillusionment with the establishment in areas where industry is facing collapse.

Within Europe, Spain has pursued an alternative approach that German leaders could do well to learn from. The continent’s second largest car producer, with 600,000 auto jobs and a sector worth 10 percent of GDP, Spain has treated Chinese capital not as a threat to be fended off with tariffs but as a lifeline. It has marketed itself as China’s gateway to Europe, inviting SAIC, Chery, CATL, and Leapmotor to reactivate idle plants like Nissan’s former Barcelona factory in exchange for jobs, technology transfers, and local production commitments. 

Madrid’s strategy is a mirror of the one Beijing pursued in relation to Germany two decades ago: Open the market enough to capture investment, know-how, and job growth, while using the state, rather than the market, to set the terms. Germany already welcomed foreign industrial capital when it allowed Elon Musk to build a Tesla gigafactory outside Berlin. It is time to extend the same logic to China. An industrial base that absorbs Chinese direct investment and expertise on terms that benefit German workers would be a more honest reckoning with the end of the country’s industrial supremacy. Without such a change in strategy, the AfD will keep feeding off the discontent of workers abandoned by an elite too proud to accept the new reality.

Behind MAGA’s Anti-Colonial Turn

By Geoff Shullenberger • 14 Sept 2026 View in browser
View in browser
AP
 
 

Not long after he arrived in Ireland over the weekend, President Donald Trump declared that it would be “fantastic” and a “cool thing” if the island were to be politically unified, offering an unexpected boost to the Irish republican cause. This came just a few weeks after the administration announced it was “reviewing” its position on the British claim to the Falkland Islands, long claimed by Argentina. This statement galvanized the Trump-allied Argentine president, Javier Milei, to ratchet up pressure on Britain over the contested territory.  

These aren’t the only instances in which the Trump administration looked ready to dismantle the remnants of old world empires. During the crisis occasioned by the influx of migrants into the Spanish enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla, there was speculation that Trump, who is friendlier with Rabat than Madrid these days, might back the former’s claims over those territories. Then there is Trump’s desire to end Danish rule over Greenland, which stands with the Falklands among the few territories in the Western hemisphere still owing fealty to a European monarch.  

What is peculiar here is that, in other contexts, leading members of the administration have expressed wistfulness about the waning of European overseas empires. In his speech to the Munich Security Conference in February, Secretary of State Marco Rubio fondly recalled the lost era when the West was sending “its missionaries, its pilgrims, its soldiers, its explorers pouring out from its shores to cross oceans, settle new continents, build vast empires extending out across the globe.” He went on to lament the “terminal decline” of Western imperialism after World War II, which he said was “accelerated by godless communist revolutions and by anti-colonial uprisings that would transform the world and drape the red hammer and sickle across vast swaths of the map.”

What Rubio left out was that it wasn’t only Moscow that backed decolonization in the postwar era; it was also Washington, which both rhetorically and materially supported the political independence of many nations previously under European imperial rule. This history has been taken up by some New Right thinkers to claim that US foreign policy in this period was run by communist subversives. The more complicated truth is that Cold War era US leaders recognized the potency of anti-colonial movements and the weakness of Western empires in the wake of two world wars, and sought to steer the regions of the world coming out from under European rule in a direction friendly to American interests.

Something similar is happening today. The much-heralded emergence of BRICS nations and the relative weakness of countries like Britain and Spain may be a factor behind the strategic shift toward countries like Argentina and Morocco—even if this realignment seems at odds with the “civilizationalist” rhetoric of Rubio’s speech and other official statements. But there are also ideological factors at play. Although Rubio’s State Department recently issued a report denouncing the “Third Worldist,” anti-colonial current of left-wing ideology, which it portrayed as an outgrowth of the Cuban Revolution, there are a number of currents on the right that could also be aptly described as anti-colonial. 

“There are also ideological factors at play.”

The first is a strand of European New Right. The Russian nationalist philosopher Aleksandr Dugin often sounds indistinguishable from left-wing decolonial academics when he denounces the West’s “unitary episteme” and calls for the “decolonization of political consciousness.” For Dugin, the invasion of Ukraine is an effort to defend Slavic autonomy from domination by the imperialist West. In Western Europe, meanwhile, French Nouvelle Droite thinkers like Alain de Benoist have long cited the work of anti-colonial philosophers like Frantz Fanon both to denounce Anglo-American cultural imperialism and to argue that mass migration constitutes a form of colonization. 

A more mainstream version of this vision can be found in National Conservatism, the movement founded by Israeli academic Yoram Hazony during the first Trump term and closely allied with the MAGA movement. The movement’s statement of principles echoes Hazony’s 2018 manifesto The Virtue of Nationalism in calling for “a world of independent nations” and rejecting “imperialism and globalism.” Like Dugin and de Benoist, the exponents of national conservatism argue for a world of autonomous cultural spheres liberated from universalist imperial schemes; unlike them, they denounce Russia and China as imperialist actors while also assailing the liberal imperialism of the West.

The “America First” version of MAGA articulated a decade ago by Trump’s strategist Steve Bannon—a sometime interlocutor of Dugin—implied a withdrawal of American power from foreign entanglements and a retrenchment in the homeland. But the second Trump term has been defined by its unabashedly imperial ambitions, from its conversion of Venezuela into a US protectorate to its efforts to foist regime change on Tehran. Trump has sought to resolve the tension between this outward thrust and his “America First” messaging by simply renaming everything he can “America”; once the whole world is America, presumably anything and everything an American leader does can be seen as “America First.” But this is not, to say the least, the vision of the world promised by Trump’s national conservative allies.

Seen one way, the White House’s endorsements of Irish and Argentine nationalist causes are part of a long history of empires fomenting separatist movements and insurrections to weaken their rivals, from France’s support of the Continental Congress to imperial Germany’s backing of Irish republicans to America’s bankrolling of the Afghan mujahideen. Of course, others can play at that game, and no doubt will. Washington’s blatantly coercive attempts to dominate Latin America are already creating openings for Chinese influence in the region. 

Such moves also raise a larger question: What sort of world order does the current administration seek to establish as the postwar system continues to collapse? Rhetoric aside, the White House’s actions suggest a continued weakening of what remains of the Western-led global order without any coherent vision of what will emerge in its place. The resulting vacuum will likely be filled, in a chaotic and unpredictable way, by ambitious actors from the emerging BRICS block. Despite having recently declared “Third Worldism” America’s ultimate nemesis, Trump may well prove to be our most Third Worldist president to date.

Losing Kinship

Why Anthropology Went “No Contact” with Its Parents

Aaron Ansell
Nov 7
 
READ IN APP
 
Listen to post · 25:39

Why do so few anthropologists study kinship anymore? It used to be our bread and butter. If you wanted to understand an Indigenous society, you had to start with questions about kinship: When a child is born, does it belong more to its mother’s family line or its father’s? More subtly, what does that child owe to each of these groups, and what does each owe to him or her? When an elder dies, who inherits their belongings? Who should the child marry when she or he grows up, and who is off-limits? And when they marry, does the groom’s family give wealth to the bride’s or the other way around? And should the young couple move to live next to the groom’s family or the bride’s? And what do different family members call each other? Are your mother’s sisters also called “Mom,” and if so, what does that imply about their relationship to you and your biological mother? And if your community is run by a council of some kind, what kin groups are represented and by whom? And when a person of one kin group transgresses against another, what obligations do the families of these parties have to make redress, take vengeance, etc.?

The list goes on, but this is enough to show how the organization of kinship is consequential for every corner of people’s existence—especially in Indigenous societies where the functions of government, religion, kinship, and economy are rarely differentiated institutionally.

But now, hardly anyone in anthropology seems to ask these questions anymore. Kinship studies aren’t exactly gone, but the classical study of descent, marriage, alliance, and familial obligation has become something of a niche pursuit. Why? I have some ideas that cut to the heart of the major changes in anthropology, especially those related to the current discussions about our discipline’s excessive politicization.

Subscribed

The decline goes back some time, at least to the early 1990s. Look no further than the following self-diagnoses from the early 2000s: “The Fall of Kinship” (Sousa 2003), “Whatever Happened to Kinship Studies?” (Lamphere in Stone 2002); and the more optimistic “Theoretical Implications of New Directions in Anthropological Kinship” (Stone 2002). So the decline in kinship studies is not new, but I suspect it’s gotten worse.

Could kinship be for anthropologists something like what having a boyfriend has become for feminists: embarrassing? As Chanté Joseph reported last year in Vogue, women have begun concealing their boyfriends in social media posts, showing only:

“a hand on a steering wheel, clinking glasses at dinner, or the back of someone’s head... Women are obscuring their partner’s face when they post, as if they want to erase the fact they exist without actually not posting them.”

Like heterosexual desire, we’re stuck with family (unless we’re so unlucky to have little or none). When the concerns of our disciplinary forefathers oppose our youthful progressive community, do we still need to pose for photos alongside them? Again, embarrassing.

I think the classical kinship questions (some of which I listed above) have become intellectually unfashionable partly because of what they came to represent within anthropology: biology, formalism, traditional social arrangements, cross-cultural comparisons, and positivist science. Worse, the analysis of kinship was the mainstay of those early to mid-20th Century British social anthropologists whose research was enabled by, and in turn supported, colonial rule. For many, kinship was fruit of this poisonous tree.

The moral condemnation of classical kinship studies was also given an epistemological rationale: the problem was not simply that anthropologists had studied kinship in the service of colonial rule, but that colonial assumptions had shaped what they claimed to discover. The Nigerian anthropologist Peter Ekeh argued that colonial anthropology helped naturalize the idea that African politics and society were fundamentally organized through kinship and tribal affiliation, in contrast to the institutional complexity attributed to European states. This very contrast, as far as Ekeh was concerned, could only be explained by European racism. In like manner, scholars have argued that anthropology’s models of kinship have reproduced assumptions about race, heterosexuality, ability, and belonging that could only be produced by the power differentials of colonialism (Kim 2024).

There is perhaps something deeper to anthropology’s current allergy to kinship. Anthropologists had long considered kinship to stand at the intersection of the immutable biological fact and the zone of “freedom” (inter-group variation) that we call culture. Kinship, as a topic, puts us in contact with questions of mate choice, sexual fitness, and other such practices that are inevitably heteronormative—another reason for today’s progressive anthropologists to be embarrassed by kinship studies.

On the issue of immutability, it was never really the case that anthropologists saw biology as fully constraining kin relations. We had long made clear to ourselves that kin were something people creatively make, rather than simply something into which they are born. In What Kinship Is—And Is Not, the late Marshal Sahlins argued that kinship concerns people who understand themselves as participating intrinsically in one another’s existence, who share a “mutuality of being.” Biology was only one among various idioms through which people framed this intrinsic relatedness, one that often served as a metaphor for other relations, e.g., blood brothers, godparents, etc. Sahlins argued that the biological facts of sexual reproduction don’t control kinship because the answers to the kinship questions always depend upon prior cultural understandings of what reproduction entails—kinship is culture all the way down. Fair enough, but Sahlins wouldn’t even allow that biology remained important as the enduring referent that demanded sense-making by every human group, insisting that “human birth is not a pre-discursive fact.”

(I have never found this argument compelling. Of course, human birth is interpreted through culture. But so is everything else we experience. By Sahlins’s rationale, nothing is “pre-discursive,” which rather empties the term of significance. Biological reproduction and cultural understandings of kinship are not mutually exclusive explanations (Bloch 2013). Relations of procreation, descent, and parenthood provide a recurring empirical center around which diverse kinship practices develop. And this matters because kinship, however culturally constructed, confronts us as something given. We experience certain relationships as immutable, their obligations as unconditional, and their basis as a shared substance that precedes our choosing. We can make new kin and renounce old ones, of course, but we’re swimming upstream when we do so.)

Whatever the shortcomings of Sahlins’s argument, he was doing a service to the study of kinship. By insisting that the stubborn facts of sexual reproduction were secondary to kinship, he was not merely rescuing it from biological determinism. He was also rescuing it from a more radical critique that threatened to invalidate kinship as a category of cross-cultural comparison altogether. David Schneider (1984), anticipating the postmodern tendency to deconstruct scientific concepts, had argued that anthropologists mistakenly projected Western understandings of kinship onto the societies they studied. Thus, when they claimed to find patrilineal descent groups in their field sites, they were imposing a Western conceptual framework on Indigenous people who might understand these relationships quite differently. For Schneider, the problem was not simply that anthropologists had defined kinship too narrowly, but that kinship itself was a peculiarly Western conceptual construction. Sahlins, by contrast, offered a way out of this impasse: his notion of kinship as a “mutuality of being” preserved the possibility of identifying kinship across societies without presuming that it must be grounded in biological reproduction.

But even if Sahlins secured permission for anthropologists to continue studying kinship around the world, the classical questions nonetheless became passé. Why?

There is one perfectly valid reason for the topic’s declining prominence, one I alluded to above: kin relations were becoming less central to some of the institutional arrangements anthropologists studied. The twentieth century saw the integration of Indigenous peoples into modern nation-states complete with distinct institutions of governance, church, economy, formal employment, and increasingly urban and otherwise mobile populations. In this context, the anthropologist could legitimately doubt the ongoing primacy of kinship as a basis for social organization. More important (or so we thought) were issues of migration, general-use currencies, civil war, environmental destruction, labor strife, state corruption, land conflict with private capital, etc. To insist on looking at kinship in the midst of all this risked fetishizing a frozen tradition in the face of far more consequential social upheavals.

But this impression of kinship’s obsolescence is largely an illusion. Ask a scholar of immigration like Maxine Margolis (1994) about the importance of kin networks for settling newcomers. Look at Robert Lynch’s (2026) findings that “suggest that religion plays an important role in cultivating stronger relationships between relatives, something that sociologists call ‘bonding social capital’, at least for women.” When capitalism gets tough, kin not only provide fallback support; they help organize entrepreneurial motivation, capital accumulation, business expansion, and succession (Yanagisako 2002). In fact, even the tension between a society’s kin-based traditions and its modern transformations is of crucial importance to the world today. Across many populations, kinship obligations routinely compete with commitments to impartiality, meritocracy, and universalistic principles of distribution. Indeed, what appears as nepotism from the perspective of the modern bureaucracy may appear as moral responsibility from within the family. This is a central concern of what we call the “anthropology of corruption” (Muir and Gupta 2018).

I don’t think the problem is that anthropologists believe kinship-related knowledge is irrelevant to modern life. If anything, I think it’s the repressed opposite: the problem may lie with what many of us suspect to be true and important about kinship— but dare not investigate. Such suspicions include the following:

- that everywhere mothers and fathers contribute differently to the socialization of their children, i.e., that gendered parental roles and contributions are not interchangeable;

- that in Western societies children who are raised in stable, two-parent households tend, on average, to enjoy developmental advantages over children raised in less stable family circumstances, even if the causal contribution of family structure is difficult to disentangle from economic and social selection effects;

- that everywhere kinship is one of the principal mechanisms through which inequality is reproduced across generations—not merely through inherited wealth, but through the transmission of social capital, cultural competencies, aspirations, and advantageous connections;

- that kinship is not necessarily egalitarian, voluntary, or emancipatory. Its capacity to organize care, cooperation, and intergenerational continuity often depends upon durable asymmetries of authority, obligation, and responsibility that cannot simply be dissolved into freely chosen relationships among equals.

Some of these claims pose an awkward problem: what if some of the genuine benefits of kinship come from arrangements that offend our political sensibilities? What if hierarchical, enduring, and involuntary obligations often do good things for people?

I would speculate that we anthropologists fear that if we prioritize kinship too readily, we will back ourselves into a corner that we long ago refused to enter. It has a name: the culture of poverty.

In the early 1950s, the anthropologist Oscar Lewis emerged from the study of impoverished peasant communities to ply his trade on urban Mexican families. He argued that prolonged material deprivation could generate enduring habits, values, and family arrangements that were transmitted across generations, even as he understood these as adaptations to structural disadvantage (1959). These included, crucially, familial instability: unstable partnerships, frequent household changes, and particular patterns of child socialization that Lewis believed could help reproduce disadvantage. Daniel Patrick Moynihan’s controversial 1965 report, The Negro Family: The Case for National Action, carried a related argument into American social policy, identifying the instability of Black family life—particularly the prevalence of female-headed households—as both a consequence of historical oppression and a mechanism perpetuating racial inequality. Soon after came the progressive repudiation: Moynihan was “blaming the victim” (Ryan 1976), and so too, by extension, was Lewis—and potentially any social scientist following in their footsteps.

One of the relatively few later anthropologists to revisit some of the culture-of-poverty questions was Philippe Bourgois. His work on poor Puerto Rican men in Harlem brought into view patterns of behavior that Lewis might have regarded as part of a culture of poverty: drug dealing, confrontational demeanors in the workplace, and “a street culture [that] takes for granted a father’s right to abandon his children” (2002: 276). Bourgois, however, interpreted such practices within a framework of “resistance” to racial and economic subordination. As such, he remains an eminent figure in good standing. But how many other anthropologists have dared follow suit?

The impulse to avoid victim-blaming (or even its appearance) is understandable, especially at the historical moment when the culture of poverty emerged as a concept. Indeed, the history of American welfare policy offered ample reason to fear that judgments about the family lives of the poor could become instruments of punishment. It took until 1968 for the U.S. Supreme Court to invalidate an Alabama welfare regulation denying benefits to families on the basis of a mother’s relationship with a man who was not legally obligated to support her children. The ruling helped curtail such notorious “man-in-the-house” rules. In the 1980s, the poor (disproportionately Black) family came under renewed policy scrutiny when conservatives like Charles Murray argued in Losing Ground (1984) that welfare incentives discouraged marriage and helped reproduce an entrenched underclass. The sociologist William Julius Wilson, in The Truly Disadvantaged (1987), famously criticized culture of poverty explanations, but he accepted that family structure mattered. For Wilson, the decline of working-class men’s employment undermined the “marriageable male pool,” contributing to family instability and, through it, a range of social problems.

A post-Lewis generation of feminist anthropologists approached these questions differently. Most prominently, Carol Stack (1974) argued from her ethnography that family functioning should not be equated with the co-residence of a married couple, that important forms of support could emerge through exchange relations across households, and therefore that public policy misunderstood poor families when it treated the self-contained nuclear household as the natural unit of social reproduction. Others, including Collier and Yanagisako (1987), challenged the naturalization of gender and kinship arrangements, while feminist scholars in adjacent disciplines, such as Sands and Nuccio (1989), argued against the stigmatization of “matrifocal” (mother-headed) families which reflected dominant ideologies about women’s proper social roles.

These arguments were not without merit. Stack, in particular, showed how impoverished people developed elaborate and morally meaningful systems of reciprocal care in circumstances that conventional household statistics rendered nearly invisible. But a problem arose when the demonstration that alternative family arrangements could “function” (help families get by) was taken to imply that these arrangements were producing equivalent outcomes to others. There remained a lurking distinction between demonstrating that alternative kinship arrangements help people survive and demonstrating that they produce good long-term outcomes. If this ethnographic literature was to inform claims about the comparative merits of family structures, it needed to investigate the latter question. Generally, it did not. The best it could do was challenge the stigma attached to matrifocal families and the like. A worthy achievement, certainly, but hardly the end of the matter.

It is around this time that classical kinship studies began losing their central place in anthropology. Perhaps the thinking among some urban anthropologists was that if we continued to investigate the “functionality” of alternative family formations, we might find ourselves playing into the hands of the enemy (Murray and his ilk). For those anthropologists working in more traditional settings—overseas, largely rural populations in the developing world—they soon faced a version of this same question as the World Bank and other development agencies began asking them to study the role of culture in economic advancement (or lack thereof). Kinship here is central, as when, for instance, expensive funeral obligations in West Africa divert resources away from savings, investment, and long-term wealth accumulation (Oks 2026). Questions about whether cherished kinship obligations might also impose substantial costs became difficult to discuss without considerable throat-clearing and self-exorcism.

The decline of classical kinship analysis was only one part of the story. There were eddies in the river. A new, more specialized kinship literature arose, one that emphasized not descent structures and inherited obligations so much as creative energy. We went from kinship structure to kinship agency, to the practices of kinning (Howell 2003), i.e., making a person into one’s own relation. In racial justice-oriented anthropology, some speak of “kin-work” as a mode of survival amidst anti-Black governmentality (Dubuisson 2024). So too for lavender anthropology: a literature arose focused on the “queering of kinship,” on, in Kath Weston’s titular words, Families We Choose (1991). More recently, the sociologist Rin Reczek has extended this conversation through Families We Keep (2022, with Emma Bosley-Smith) and Families We Lose (2026). Reczek’s broader argument is that adults, including many LGBTQ people, go “no contact” with their families when they encounter conflicts between traditional expectations of enduring familial obligation and newer expectations of individual autonomy, mutual respect, and acceptance of individual identity. For scholars invested in these new directions, the focus on kin-making as practice opened a gateway to the old topic while correcting classical kinship theory’s tendency to neglect the perspectives of women and minorities, domestic experience, racial and gendered inequality, and power (Lamphere 2002).

Of course, there’s nothing especially new about the idea that kinship is made rather than merely inherited. As noted, classical anthropologists knew that perfectly well long before anyone spoke of “kinning.” What’s new is not the recognition that kinship is culturally constructed, but the moral significance attached to particular kinds of kinship construction.

The recent scholarship glossed above resuscitates the study of kinship by harnessing it to counter-normative projects. Most of these works emphasize the value of alternative kinship formations only (cf. Patterson 1982), particularly those that challenge inherited structures of authority and exclusion. Or perhaps more precisely, they celebrate what Reczek calls “democratized kinship” (the expectation that family relationships must meet standards of mutual respect, safety, and accountability) over “compulsory kinship” (the assumption that biological family obligations endure regardless of relationship quality). The former is a source of autonomy and liberation; the latter appears as a source of coercion.

Kinship is thus being reimagined, not so much through a denial of innate biological connections—for we learned long ago that all cultures do some of this in their classifications—but through a shift in emphasis from the relationships that bind us to a received order regardless of our wishes to those we voluntarily create in the name of personal fulfillment and social upheaval. Instead of enjoining us to sustain connections in the face of conflict and disappointment, much of the newer literature encourages us to dissolve such connections and form others that feel easier and more equal.

Of course, chosen kinship can generate obligations every bit as taxing and hierarchical as those of biological kin. And inherited kinship can be nurturing, flexible, and egalitarian. But the difference in emphasis is hard to miss. It is now often easier to celebrate kinship when people are making it anew than when they are submitting to obligations they never chose.

This newer literature has certainly kept kinship alive within anthropology, but it has seldom taken up the classical questions that were once the touchstone of ethnographic inquiry. Indeed, the older questions have sometimes become difficult to ask precisely because they direct attention toward the enduring, involuntary, and frequently unequal relationships through which human beings organize their lives.

My problem with some of these new lines of research is that they seem more interested in destigmatizing the alternative kin formations of marginalized populations than in asking whether these kin formations serve the long-term interests of those populations.

There is an irony here. Anthropologists who celebrate voluntary kinship sometimes seem to practice their own form of unconditional solidarity—or kinship—with the populations they study. But unconditional solidarity with a marginalized population should include dogged evaluation of how their practices shape their fate. For instance, if we want to help LGBTQ youth make better choices when they feel torn between birth and chosen families, we should aspire to open-ended investigations of the long-term effects of such decisions on the people in question. This means asking not only when estrangement protects people from serious harm, but also when it cuts them off from the wisdom of older relatives whose unwelcome perspectives on their choices may be precisely what they need to hear.

Anthropologists have grown gun-shy of such conversations. Not universally, of course, and not always consciously. But I suspect our moral sympathies have helped determine which questions about kinship strike us as urgent and which appear outmoded, even suspect. The result is not the total disappearance of kinship from anthropology, but a narrowing of the circumstances under which we feel comfortable affirming its value.

Let me return to the close-hitting metaphor of the embarrassing boyfriend, or the embarrassment of just having a boyfriend. I wonder if the anthropology of kinship has on its hands a version of “heterofatalism,” which Jean Garnett described as an impasse between women’s continued desire for romantic relationships with men and their growing disillusionment with heterosexual dating culture. The anthropological parallel: our discipline is stuck between its fascination with kinship as a source of bone-marrow belonging and its political commitments to defending nontraditional family ties. Thus, in a discipline accustomed to proclaiming successive intellectual (and political) revolutions, mainstream anthropologists find the kinship studies of their intellectual parents and grandparents increasingly difficult to embrace without embarrassment.

Perhaps that is the real irony. A discipline that has taught us so much about the power of enduring kinship obligations has become increasingly reluctant to acknowledge its obligations to its own intellectual ancestors.

Why I’m becoming a China bear

The country was perfectly positioned to win in a world that no longer exists.

Noah Smith
Nov 7
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

When I tell people I’m becoming a China bear, they’re often surprised. “Weren’t you already a China bear?” they ask me.

Well, no. I’ve always been a China bull — I’ve always believed that China’s economic growth would be robust, that they would master advanced technologies, and that their geopolitical influence would grow. This is exactly why I was also always a China hawk¹ — I recognized the very real possibility that China would become a global hegemon, and I didn’t especially want to live in a world ruled from Beijing. It’s why I advocated so strongly for friend-shoring, for export controls, and for military alliances to balance out China’s awesome and growing power.

This was true even as China began to show visible signs of weakness in the late 2010s and early 2020s. Xi Jinping proved himself less competent than his predecessors, and the country’s real-estate-heavy growth model hit the skids. But despite those stumbling blocks, I still predicted that this would be the Chinese Century. The country had what seemed like unassailable advantages in human capital, market size, and state capacity, even as all of its possible rivals were convulsed by internal division. And the one thing that most people cite as China’s big weakness — demographic decline — never struck me as much of a threat to the country’s power.

Now, however, for the first time I can remember, I’ve found myself becoming actually bearish on China. I still think it will be an immensely powerful country — perhaps the most powerful single country on the planet. I still think it will be at or near the forefront of technology, and that it will generally be a safe, moderately prosperous, and tolerable place for its people to live. But more and more, I’m starting to think that global hegemony of the type the U.S. enjoyed throughout most of the 20th century will be out of reach. I’m also starting to think that China’s bid for technological dominance is weaker than I had believed.

And just as my previous bullishness made me a hawk, my increasing bearishness makes me more of a China dove.² I still think friend-shoring is important, export controls are good, and we need robust military alliances to make very sure China doesn’t try to conquer Asia. But I no longer feel the same sense of desperate urgency about these prudent measures — they feel more like an insurance policy now.

There are basically three reasons I’m revising my China expectations downward. The biggest reason is AI. China’s system is incredibly optimized for an era of technology and economic production that is very quickly coming to an end. AI will change everything, and modern China is not the kind of country that adapts well when everything changes.

The other reasons are less important but still worth mentioning. China’s new economic model — the government-supported push to capture all of global high-tech manufacturing — is not likely to succeed. And third, the country’s political situation appears to be deteriorating. Just as the Deng/Jiang/Hu era illustrated the strengths of authoritarian political systems, Xi Jinping is giving us a much-needed lesson on the weaknesses of those systems. His spiraling paranoia is turning the country inward, just as his economic policies are running out of steam.

Anyway, let’s start with those economic policies. This is an economics blog, after all.

China’s manufacturing push is hitting its limits

In a nutshell, Xi Jinping’s economic strategy is to dominate manufacturing — to have China be, in the words of Damien Ma, the “make-everything country”. I’m increasingly convinced that this approach is already beginning to backfire.

Going all-in on manufacturing is a strategy you see a lot of developing countries use during their periods of rapid catch-up industrialization. And there are some good reasons for that. When you’re poor, what your people need most aren’t video games or dog-walking services, but houses and cars and refrigerators. Manufactured products are also easy to export, and poor countries don’t have big domestic markets to rely on. It might also be easier to reach the technological frontier in manufacturing, since you can reverse-engineer physical products more easily than services.³

Usually, as countries get rich and their needs evolve from the physical to the ephemeral, they move out of manufacturing and into services to some degree. But Xi Jinping decided that this was a mistake. He reasoned that if China continued to behave like a developing country forever, and promoted manufacturing at the expense of everything else, China could dominate the globe.

This was an interesting hypothesis, and it might have worked — indeed, there’s still some chance it might work. Militaries, after all, depend on manufacturing above all else, so in a big protracted WW2-style war, being the master of manufacturing might give you an automatic win.

And dominating key nodes in global supply chains lets you use export controls to bully other countries without actually bombing them. In fact, China is doing this more and more, using export controls on everything from tunnel-boring machines to rare earths to drones to medicines as bludgeons to force other nations to do its bidding.

In order to make China dominate global manufacturing, Xi unleashed a wave of industrial policy bigger than any the world had ever seen, spending about 4% of GDP per year on subsidizing manufacturing industries — usually through cheap bank loans, but sometimes just by sending cash directly.

For a while, this seemed to be working spectacularly. A 2024 paper by UNIDO got a lot of attention for predicting that China’s share of global manufacturing would be 45% by 2030 — equal to the United States right after World War 2. But cooler heads pointed out that China’s manufacturing share growth had already slowed; more reasonable predictions put its 2030 share at maybe 35-36% — still enormous, but more like America in the 1960s or the early 1920s.

And in U.S. dollar terms, China’s share peaked during the pandemic and has been drifting down since then:

In fact, despite Xi’s push, manufacturing is a shrinking share of China’s economy. China is now less industrial than South Korea, despite being less than half as rich:

The reason is simple, and it’s something I’ve written about many times before. Unlike South Korea, China is a very large country. That means most of China’s manufacturing production is going to have to go to the domestic market. Even if other countries don’t slap big tariffs on your products, export markets will simply saturate. One of the most reliable empirical laws in all of economics is the gravity model of trade, which says that trade volumes drop off rapidly with distance.

Of course, some countries will put tariffs on China. The EU recently forced China to make a deal to limit auto imports, and if that doesn’t work, stronger measures are likely. That will only accelerate the natural saturation of China’s export markets.

And despite everything you’ve read about the “Second China Shock” and the big export boom, China is still far less export-intensive than Korea, and that’s not going to change:

China simply can’t be Giant Korea; it’s so big that its manufacturers need to rely on its domestic market. But that domestic market is becoming saturated even faster than the global market. Profits in the auto sector, the steel sector, the solar sector, and many other manufacturing industries are all collapsing. Weak domestic demand from China’s real estate bust has encountered massive oversupply from government subsidies, and the result is that few companies in China are making much money. That will force lots of businesses to close and consolidate, and it will starve dynamic private-sector companies of R&D budgets, forcing them to rely more on research handed down by the distant, unresponsive, and unaccountable government.

Government subsidies can keep the party going a lot longer than it ought to, but already the limits have probably been reached. Chinese manufacturing indicators are faltering, and manufacturing investment seems to have topped out as well.

In fact, this isn’t even the only example of Xi Jinping taking a developing-country strategy and pushing it far beyond its limits. Infrastructure is another. For many years, China invested huge amounts into building more roads and bridges and high-speed trains than they knew what to do with. But there was a limit to that process, and China has now hit the limit. The Economist reports that China’s infrastructure investment has leveled off:

China’s years-long splurge on bridges, tunnels, expressways, high-speed rail and airports is beginning to tail off…In July this year a senior transport official said China’s main transport network was “91% complete”, and the country would pivot from expanding to upgrading existing infrastructure.

But it isn’t so easy weaning yourself off of infrastructure overinvestment. China built so much infrastructure that it will have to spend a lot of money just to upkeep all those roads, trains, and bridges. That’s the iron logic of depreciation. And since much of China’s infrastructure isn’t really carrying many passengers or much cargo, that means China is stuck spending a significant fraction of its GDP upkeeping stuff that people don’t really need — unless, of course, it chooses to let some of that infrastructure decay into ruin.

All of this means growth will slow. And of course, it’s all happening against the backdrop of weak demand from the continuing, protracted fallout from China’s real estate bust. There are signs that the real economic damage in that sector is only getting started:

Weak domestic demand won’t just be a drag on China’s headline growth — it will also make it harder for China’s manufacturing sector to maintain its 30% global market share, much less expand it to 35% or more. Xi seems to think that China can just sort of pull resources off of real estate development and put them into manufacturing, one for one, like a corporate manager reassigning engineers to a different project. But it doesn’t work like that; demand matters, and China’s manufacturing triumphs in past decades depended heavily on the tailwind that the long property boom had been delivering.

Chinese economists realize this, but Xi seems to have stopped listening to economists, and to have purged his government of anyone who was inclined to listen.

(And of course as the years go by, China’s accelerating population decline will reduce its domestic market size by more and more, compounding the pressure on manufacturing. I don’t expect this to be a big factor until at least 2040 or so, but it’s worth mentioning.)

In other words, Xi’s “make-everything country” strategy is likely to see only modest short-term success. It will not let China conquer the world. And the failure of this strategy will come just as a massive new technological revolution upends the global economy — a revolution that China, despite all reports, is not well-prepared to take advantage of.

China will probably flub the Age of AI

A lot of people I talk to believe that China will eventually dominate the AI industry, just as it has come to dominate the auto industry, the shipbuilding industry, and various other industries. They view it as a sort of law of nature that once China “decides” to win in an industry, it’s only a matter of time.

So far, that has not been true in the case of AI. The United States has seized a commanding lead in building compute, which is the basis for all AI. China’s share of global compute has actually shrunk in recent years:

A big reason for America’s compute advantage is our timely implementation of export controls on AI chips and chipmaking equipment. Without American, European, Japanese, Korean, and Taiwanese technology, China’s national champions have consistently failed to build anywhere near the amount of compute or memory that the country’s industry would need:

And even if it doesn’t lead to an “intelligence explosion”, the imminent advent of recursive self-improvement — AI making AI better — should expand America’s advantage over the next few years.

Another pro-China thesis has been that although America will continue to rule in the software realm, China will take the lead in hardware, as it supposedly always does. America can have the best chatbots and AI coding agents, this story goes, but China will have the best robots.

That may eventually be true, but so far it’s not happening. Chinese physical AI companies like Unitree, the famed maker of the dancing robots, have seen their stock prices collapse in recent months.

A narrower index of just AI stocks has performed even worse.

China’s stock market isn’t used for fundraising, but it’s an indicator of where Chinese people think things are headed. The basic problem with China’s physical AI companies is, again, demand — dancing robots are cool but nobody really wants them yet. Robots have yet to reach the point where they can build other robots, or any complex machinery; American robotics entrepreneur Joseph Chen recently toured Unitree’s factories, and found that the robots were still being built mostly not by machines, but by cheap human labor.

Again, this could hit a tipping point when robots get good enough. But lack of demand is only one of the fundamental problems facing China in the age of AI. Another is culture and politics. In polls, Chinese people are a lot more bullish than Americans on AI technology. But as the technology advances and fears of job loss become more widespread, that will probably change.

The U.S.’ enduring advantage over its technologically advanced rivals in Europe and Asia was always its flexible labor markets. America simply doesn’t protect people’s careers; it tries to make sure that employment levels are high, but doesn’t really worry about which jobs people are employed in.

Every country looks like it has flexible labor markets during its rapid development phase. People move from agriculture to manufacturing, and then they hop around between a bunch of low-paying factory jobs. But once countries become developed and their people get good white-collar human-capital-intensive jobs in established companies, they tend to become less flexible. People value the stability of their careers, and they often pressure the government to intervene in the economy to make sure that they don’t have to constantly retrain and hop between companies.

China’s authoritarian political system will make this pressure more intense, not less. In a country without elections, hordes of angry displaced workers have only one way to force the government to take action on their behalf, which is to riot and rebel. China’s leaders are inevitably going to have visions of displaced masses toppling the CCP, and they’re going to act preemptively to avert the danger.

We can already see the beginnings of this. Fears of AI-driven job loss are mounting, and policymakers are taking it seriously:

Kyle Chan
@kyleichan
China is taking AI-induced job displacement more seriously. “Adapting to the Development of AI and Promoting an Employment-Friendly Development Model” Some highlights: - Strengthen monitoring and early warning of employment risks from AI - Do more research on impact of AI on …
1:10 PM · Oct 27, 2026 · 12.1K Views
6 Replies · 17 Reposts · 66 Likes

My instinct is that the urge to freeze Chinese society in place will only grow stronger over time. China is not the hungry, poor country it was 20 years ago. It’s a modestly rich nation with a decent standard of living and a lot of well-established industries. AI will be disruptive to that high-level equilibrium, and China’s leaders will naturally tend to resist that disruption.

There’s one more reason I suspect China will underperform in the age of AI, which has nothing to do with government policy or culture. China’s basic advantage in high-tech manufacturing is human capital — its gigantic population and high levels of education and talent mean that it has vast armies of engineers who can optimize the layout of any factory and the design of any product. That in turn leads to distributed tacit knowledge — a vast accumulated store of little tricks and techniques — that gives Chinese manufacturers an enduring cost and quality advantage.

But in the age of AI, most of the “talent” will live inside data centers, not inside human brains. AI will be able to hoover up massive amounts of data from factory floors and products, and use these to replicate or exceed the distributed tacit knowledge that was hitherto only produced by human organizations. Here’s what I wrote back in July:

A big part of the reason China can cut off the supply of rare earths to the rest of the world any time it wants to is that other countries aren’t very good at refining rare earths. Rare earths are difficult to separate from each other in solutions; it takes a ton of little chemistry tricks to do it cheaply at scale. Chinese refiners have spent four decades building up those little tricks and techniques; American or Japanese refiners won’t simply be able to replicate their efficiency overnight, and so it’ll continue to cost much more to produce rare earths outside China.

Except in the age of AI, this might change. Suppose American rare earth refiners give their employees a bunch of equipment to record everything they do — smart glasses, gloves, and so on — in addition to sensors distributed throughout their plants. AI will be able to synthesize all that information and very rapidly suggest small ways to improve the production process. Many of those little experiments will fail; others will succeed and will quickly be adopted, allowing another round of experimentation and improvement to begin very quickly. Crucially, AI’s ability to do this doesn’t depend on its raw intelligence — only on its ability to handle huge amounts of data very quickly.

In other words, in the age of AI, distributed tacit knowledge might not be nearly as big of a barrier to technological diffusion.

There’s not really anything the Chinese government can do about this, I think. Sometimes new technology just comes along and erodes a country’s basic economic advantages.⁴ China’s basic advantage, as a country and as a civilization, is the combination of very large population with high levels of education. In the age of AI, both of those will still matter, just less than they did before.

That still leaves China with substantial advantages. Its state-directed finance system can unleash huge amounts of cheap bank loans even during recessions, while America’s market-focused investment booms tend to grind to a halt during busts. China also still has the peerless state capacity that allowed it to regiment and reorganize its entire society for Covid lockdowns. And of course domestic market size still does count for something, even if China’s current leaders don’t fully appreciate the importance of demand.

But overall, my impression is that modern China is hyper-optimized for the economic era of the 2010s — an era where human capital and incremental innovation ruled everything. The age of AI represents a decisive break with that paradigm, and while it’s possible that China will pull off another societal transformation in order to re-optimize itself to the new era, I am skeptical that it will manage this without severe disruption.

Xi Jinping continues his “Death of Stalin” arc

As a coda, it’s worth mentioning one more reason I’m becoming more bearish on China. Its absolute ruler, Xi Jinping, appears to be entering a well-known terminal phase of very strong autocrats. I’ve written a lot about this before, but it bears repeating.

A basic problem for autocracies is the succession mechanism. If a very strong autocrat becomes more powerful than any institution, he can simply declare himself dictator-for-life — as Xi basically did long ago in China. At that point, he has a choice to name a successor — in which case the heir apparent might become a threat to his power — or not to name one. If he doesn’t name one, the state can become paralyzed by preparation for the leader’s eventual death, as various factions and claimants sharpen their knives.

But that very knife-sharpening looks indistinguishable from sedition to the aging autocrat. With his mental faculties declining, he substitutes these with aggression and paranoia — the very tools that got him where he is today. What follows are endless rounds of purges, a climate of fear, and increasing policy paralysis. This was Stalin’s arc in his final years, and there are signs that Xi Jinping — whose talent for dominating a political party are historically rivaled only by Stalin — is heading down the same path.

Endless rounds of purges continue in Xi’s regime, and may even be accelerating. No one is safe:

Last week, Beijing announced that Huang Qifan, the 74-year-old former mayor of Chongqing…and a fixture in China’s economic-policy circles, was under investigation …The conviction and punishment rate in such circumstances is virtually 100%…The move stunned many political watchers. Huang had long been known as a…figure who never topples. He had navigated more than a decade of factional warfare…

Huang’s fall signals that Xi’s anticorruption campaign is accelerating ahead of the 21st Party Congress, expected for late 2027, when the party decides who joins its top leadership and how power is distributed. In the first half of this year, China’s disciplinary authorities filed roughly 538,000 cases, an average of nearly 90,000 a month, up from about 83,000 a month in 2025. At the top, 36 senior officials at the provincial or ministerial level and above were investigated or disciplined in the first half of this year alone.

Even more purges may be going on behind the scenes:

11:33 AM · Oct 29, 2026 · 44.7K Views
4 Replies · 41 Reposts · 231 Likes

The chaos at the top of China’s leadership — a chaos engineered by Xi to allow him to hang onto absolute power as long as possible — will make it harder for China to rise to the challenge of this pivotal moment in technological history. China needs the nimble technocracy of Deng Xiaoping and Zhu Rongji more than ever right now, but instead it’s going to get one old man obsessed with fending off internal challenges, and a whole bunch of people afraid to stick their necks out and make change.

The paradoxical result is that although China has one of the world’s strongest leaders, it’s likely to look increasingly rudderless for the remainder of his time in office. That convulsion couldn’t come at a worse time. It’s just one more reason I’m less worried about the Chinese bid for global dominance than I used to be.

Though some new evidence disputes this.

4

The classic example of this is when new sailing technologies allowed Europeans to bypass Middle Eastern middlemen and trade directly with Asia, thus undercutting the economies of Turkish and Arab powers in the Early Modern period. But the most important example is probably the Industrial Revolution itself, and how it enabled small, well-organized countries like the UK, Germany, and Japan to dominate larger ones for over a century before the big countries caught up.

After the Bubble Bursts

What past recessions can tell us about the AI hangover

Paul Krugman
Nov 8
∙
Preview
 
READ IN APP
 

Has AI reached its Wile E. Coyote moment? Ever since the huge boom in AI-related capital expenditures, especially data centers, began, many observers have warned that this boom looks unsustainable. AI is a remarkable technology, which may yield big economic payoffs (although these payoffs still aren’t clear in the data.) But it’s doubtful whether the companies making these huge investments will be able to capture enough of those payoffs to compensate them for the enormous sums they are spending.

If these skeptics are right, we should expect that there will be a Wile E. Coyote moment: the investors and lenders who have been backing AI companies look down, realize that they have run off the edge of a cliff, and the boom plunges to the ground. Such sudden reckonings have happened many times in the past, notably with the bursting of the dot-com bubble in 2000 and the bursting of the housing bubble a few years later.

And in the past few weeks we’ve seen growing signs of nervousness about AI’s financial prospects. Prices of hyperscaler stocks are down 27 percent since their peak; the cost of insurance against default on AI-company bonds has soared. We don’t know for sure that this is a real turning point for the industry, but the vibes have definitely shifted.

Today’s primer won’t try to settle the hotly (and endlessly) debated question of whether AI really is a bubble, let alone whether this is the moment of truth. What I will focus on, instead, is a conditional question: If AI is a bubble, and that bubble is either bursting or likely to burst soon, what are the likely economic consequences? That is, as I’ll explain, a question we can address with a lot of historical evidence. For while AI as a technology is utterly new, burst bubbles have been a recurring economic theme for well over a century, and we know a lot about the macroeconomic aftermath of bubbles.

To preview my conclusions: a burst AI bubble will almost surely cause a recession. The depth of that recession is highly uncertain, although I favor the view that it will be worse than the slump at the end of the 1990s tech boom. But even if the recession is short and shallow, history and theory suggest that recovery from that slump will be painfully slow, that unemployment will remain elevated for multiple years.

Beyond the paywall, I’ll address the following:

1. A brief history of modern recessions

2. Why recovery from burst bubbles is slow

3. Comparing a possible AI bust to the dot-com recession

4. Why the policy response to an AI bust will probably be inadequate to prevent a painful recession...
