Noah, Brad DeLong, and Dan Wang discuss the Anthropic IPO

The Hexapodia Podcast is back!

Noah Smith, Brad DeLong, and Dan Wang
Nov 8
 
READ IN APP
 

Many longtime fans of my Hexapodia podcast with Brad DeLong have been begging us to bring it back. Well, here it is! Hexapodia will now be a series of Substack Live conversations that you can tune in to, and which will be recorded as podcasts and sent out as emails.

Our first episode was a little rocky, as I got the time wrong and ended up arriving 20 minutes late. But Dan and Brad are both brilliant people, so you can watch them talk for a while before I show up! The topic of our discussion was the Anthropic IPO, inspired by my post about it last week:

Anthropic’s moat is Claude

Noah Smith
·
Nov 2
Read full story

I give the bull case for Anthropic, while Dan and Brad are both more skeptical. I think this quote sums up my side of the argument:

My bull case [for Anthropic] is not envisioning a world where Anthropic rules all businesses, rules 100% of every industry, or close to it. I’m also not envisioning a case where AI replaces human beings in their jobs.

I’m envisioning a change in the capital structure of the efficiently producing economy. I’m envisioning…a world where in order to succeed in any industry, you must create a tie-up with a frontier AI company that offers you access to an internal proprietary frontier model that will be months ahead of any model distilled from it. And…that doing this will require not purchasing services…at arm’s length from that company, but tying up your capital structure with that company so that you become in some sense a subsidiary of that company. I am envisioning that.

So I’m saying that instead of something where…AI is like oil and everyone has to buy oil or the things made downstream from oil…instead of that sort of arm of length world, I’m envisioning a world in which every company in order to succeed must become a subsidiary of Anthropic, OpenAI, [or] Google…and Anthropic is simply the biggest of those fish in a oligopolistic ecosystem of a few conglomerates competing against each other via their little subsidiaries in every single industry at the same time.

Interestingly, some economists at Google Deepmind just released a paper with a model in which this sort of thing happens. From the abstract of Imas, Koh, and Legg (2026):

When will advances in AI lead to economic transformation? We develop a model of how intelligence…matters for organizations….AI expertise is reproducible while humans’ are in fixed supply, and AIs may not face the same human limits on coordination….When AI is more capable than the average human, organizations of complementary humans can nonetheless outperform AI. Increases in AI competence can change the composition of workers within firms and decrease firm size. As AI coordination improves, however, this can break the Coasean ceiling on firm size and the market structure undergoes a phase transition toward large, concentrated AI-heavy firms. [emphasis mine]

I was envisioning a slightly more complex version, in which humans and AI are complements, where humans have private data that AI is better at using, and where one big conglomerate enters every industry but retains human workers. But I think Imas et al.’s model gets at some of the basic dynamics here.

Financial disclosure: I have no current position in Anthropic, but unless something major changes, I will probably buy Anthropic stock when it IPOs. I own stock in TypeSafe, an Anthropic competitor.

The Texas Miracle

Democracy’s biggest win in a night of big wins

Paul Krugman
Nov 9
 
READ IN APP
 

Marketing note: I have a new ebook, Navigating the Chaos: Chronicles of Economic and Political Madness, which uses material from this Substack to construct a thematic narrative of the past two years and the issues that Democrats must now address to build an enduring progressive movement. Available from Amazon, Kobo, Bookshop, and Nook.

On March 23, 2026, the Conservative Political Action Conference — which is to the global right what the Comintern once was to international communism — held its fifth annual meeting in Budapest. Viktor Orbán, Hungary’s Prime Minister, was both the host and the keynote speaker.

And why not? Orbán had long been a role model for hard-right parties like the GOP or Germany’s neo-Nazi AfD. Under his rule Hungary, while still notionally a democracy, had become a de facto one-party state in which elections were effectively rigged to give the ruling party a permanent lock on power. This freed it both to pursue harsh ethnonationalist policies and to engage in massive corruption, with no need to fear a voter backlash.

Except, it turned out, if the voter backlash was a political tsunami so large that it swamped the seawalls the regime had erected. And that’s what happened in Hungary just three weeks after that CPAC event. Orbán and his party were swept from power. The new Prime Minister, Peter Magyar, has promised to “liquidate Orban’s mafia state,” and his government — as part of a program named Project Purgatory — has launched extensive investigations into Orbán-era corruption. Some prominent figures from the former regime — including the former governor of the central bank — have already been arrested.

There are obvious parallels between what happened in Hungary last spring and what happened here last week. At the time I wrote, “Hungary has shown the way. Will America follow?” We did.

There are, however, also some obvious differences. Although the U.S. right has long wanted to Orbanize America, on the eve of the midterms the U.S. wasn’t Hungary — that is, it wasn’t a state that had lived for years under one-party rule, rule that party had used to rig the political system to make that rule permanent.

But while America as a whole wasn’t like Hungary, Texas was. Republicans have dominated the state’s politics since the 1990s, and have been ruthless about using gerrymandering, crony capitalism that rewards their allies, and other tactics to preserve that dominance. The effects of gerrymandering are still highly visible if we look at the state’s Congressional representation: Democrats swept every statewide office, yet only 14 of the 38 representatives Texas will be sending to the next House of Representatives will be Democrats. And while Republicans lost the state’s own House, they retain control of its heavily gerrymandered Senate.

Yet Democrats did sweep every statewide office. This was a truly shocking development. See the chart of Polymarket odds at the top of this post. Prediction markets are largely useless at their supposed job of, well, predicting, but they do sometimes offer a useful snapshot of conventional wisdom at any given point in time. And what we see is that until very late in the game hardly anyone gave Gina Hinojosa a significant chance of winning the governor’s race. She ended up winning by 7 percentage points.

How durable will Texas’s stunning blue shift be? It’s always dangerous to read too much into a single election. A huge number of pundits declared that Donald Trump’s 2024 victory — by 1.5 percentage points — represented a fundamental rightward realignment of U.S. politics. Such proclamations look silly now that Democrats appear to have won the popular vote in the midterms by about 13 points.

Yet there are some reasons to believe that Texas will be a blue, or at least bluer, state for a long time.

A key point is that the state’s flip was powered in part by a huge leftward shift among Latino voters. This shift was much larger than the shift among Texas voters in general, which suggests that it wasn’t simply a reaction to Trump’s total failure to deliver on his economic promises. Latinos were, almost surely, also reacting to the Trump administration’s anti-immigrant extremism and ICE’s brutal tactics. Not to put too fine a point on it, many Latinos voted Republican two years ago in the belief that Trump would lower prices, and instead found masked men arresting their friends and relatives on the street.

Could this change in political orientation be permanent? Consider the case of California, which wasn’t always a liberal bastion — remember, it elected Ronald Reagan as governor. But it became consistently Democratic after the 1994 passage of Proposition 187, a harsh anti-immigrant measure which was soon ruled unconstitutional, but nonetheless appears to have turned a large part of the state’s electorate permanently against the GOP.

It seems plausible that the Trump administration’s anti-immigrant policies will have a similar long-term effect. That effect might have faded if Trump had moderated those policies, but instead he has made Stephen Miller his new chief of staff.

And the effect will be especially large in Texas, with its large Latino population.

If Texas really has flipped persistently blue, the national impact will be immense, and not just for electoral politics. Because of its sheer size, Texas has a huge effect on many aspects of national life. For example, the Texas Board of Education is often able to determine what can and can’t be covered in high school history textbooks across the nation.

There were many startling results in the midterms, some even more amazing than what happened in Texas. Thus Mississippi appears on track to have only the second Black senator in its history; his predecessor was born a slave.

But for those of us who have been worried about the fate of U.S. democracy — which means everyone who has been paying attention — the Texas miracle is especially meaningful. Continued one-party rule in Texas was an essential assumption behind the authoritarian project. And we can all breathe easier now that the people of Texas stood up to say no.

The rise of the Hispanic moderate

New leadership can help a new majority finally emerge.

Matthew Yglesias
Nov 9
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

The biggest collective brain fart by the Democratic Party over the course of my career was almost certainly convincing itself that America’s rising Hispanic population share guaranteed a progressive hammerlock on American electoral politics.

This 2013 take from Ron Brownstein — that Barack Obama’s re-election proved culturally conservative white people had become irrelevant — had an unusually blunt headline but was typical of the spirit of the era.

This analysis never made a ton of sense, even on its own terms. In 2012, Obama won Iowa and Ohio and Michigan and Wisconsin and Pennsylvania, none of which had a particularly large Hispanic population share. This basic math was known and knowable at the time, but it was ignored amid emerging Democratic majority hype and a focus on non-pivotal states like Nevada.

But the notion that demographic changes meant Democrats didn’t have to do politics was misguided in deeper ways, and it helped set the party up for some serious tactical and strategic errors. Those mistakes led to blowing off not only the actual views of the kind of secular white working-class Midwesterners who were important to Obama’s wins but also to blowing off the actual views of most American Hispanics.

In 2020, Donald Trump shocked many liberals by making meaningful gains with Latino voters even while doing quite poorly overall. Then in 2024, with the national trends at his back, he did even better.

A huge part of the 2026 story is Hispanic voters coming back to Democrats. Trump’s own choices are the largest factor, but an important secondary one is Democrats developing a more sophisticated understanding of the Hispanic electorate. And part of that, I think, has been cultivating a larger crop of moderate Latino politicians. Slow Boring’s 2026 candidate slate featured three different Latino guys who wear cowboy hats. And if Democrats want to continue to win, politicians like that — people who actually represent their voters and know what they’re like — have to control the narrative and not let it be seized again by unaccountable NGO types spinning wildly unrealistic dreams of endless progressive dominance.

The false dawn

One serious problem with post-2012 hubris about Hispanic voters is that it kind of understandably radicalized Republican opinion against immigration.

People have a range of concerns about immigration, some more fact-based than others. But people also have lots of opinions about topics that aren’t immigration. The thrust of Brownstein’s argument was that catering to people with culturally conservative views on non-immigration topics was now unnecessary thanks to the rising Hispanic tide. This notion got rephrased by conservatives as an alarming and possibly potent narrative that immigration debates should be understood not as economic policy but as a progressive effort to perpetrate a “great replacement” of the existing electorate.

And at the same time, it generated a breakdown of ideological discipline in the Democratic Party.

With Democrats’ “old” support base, they needed to win over working-class white people who cared about tax fairness and health care and Social Security and Medicare but didn’t necessarily align with the cultural values of the kind of highly educated hyper-cosmopolitan white people I’ve been surrounded by all my life in Greenwich Village and Harvard Square and Logan Circle.

But what did we think all these second- and third-generation Hispanics were like? Did they share the cultural values of hyper-cosmopolitan educated white urbanites? Did that really make sense?

I once went to a block party in my D.C. neighborhood where they were handing out blue and pink balloons and little kids were grabbing them. Some of the adult attendees were white parents from the neighborhood and some were Latina or Afro-Caribbean nannies. A couple of adults objected to some kids having the “wrong” color balloon and started sorting the pink balloons to the girls and the blue balloons to the boys.

Do you think that the adults in question were the white Logan Circle professionals or the women of color?

Nobody has ever answered this question incorrectly. People are aware, on some level, that there is no racial magic that causes working-class Hispanic people to develop the cultural values and political opinions of Middlebury graduates. Right-wing politics, after all, exists in Latin America, and there’s no reason why people of Latin ancestry living in the United States can’t have right-wing opinions.

The momentary identity crisis among Democrats generated by Trump’s 2020 and 2024 gains with Hispanic voters has been ameliorated by evidence of a strong shift back to the party in 2026. But it’s important to understand who actually led this shift and why.

Hispanic politicians vs. Latinx staffers

An important figure here is Arizona Senator Ruben Gallego, who used to represent a safe blue House seat in Phoenix and who famously reacted to the 2020 red-shift with Hispanic voters with a social-media tirade about the term “Latinx.”

The controversy around this word was significant, I think, not because the word itself matters but because of what the word was a symptom of: the clout of people rooted in working-class Hispanic communities relative to that of people with Latin American ancestry rooted in generically progressive academic and NGO circles.

Gallego’s boldness in speaking about this mattered precisely because his House district was safe. The easiest thing in the world would have been to just continue communicating in a smart way with his constituents but go along to get along in D.C. and in national progressive circles. But Gallego wanted to run statewide and knew it would be smart to cultivate an image as someone who wasn’t a doctrinaire progressive. So he actually articulated what his constituents believed, namely that it was bizarre and insulting to revise the whole grammatical structure of the Spanish language for intersectional reasons.

Henry Cuellar and Vicente Gonzalez down in the Rio Grande Valley don’t have big social-media presences or do a lot of national press. But in the 2020 / 2022 / 2024 election cycles, they were some of the biggest electoral overperformers, and that involved things like being the only two House Democrats to vote for the Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act.

It was at an event they hosted in D.C. that I first met Johnny Garcia and Bobby Pulido, two of the aforementioned Latino guys in cowboy hats, who won last week with the support of Blue Dog PAC and Majority Democrats. Garcia is an actual cop from the Bexar County sheriff’s department. Pulido’s magic trick for winning back Trump voters is to agree with them about select energy and cultural issues:

Warming to the theme, he said: “What plays well in New York City likely won’t play well among Democratic voters in the valley. The party has become too one-size-fits-all, and that’s a big mistake.”

His main takeaway from his months running for congressional office is that Democrats “let other people define us.”

“When I first told people in this district that I was running as a Democrat, their automatic assumption was that I was going to take away their guns, that I was for trans in women’s sports, that I was going to take away their oil and gas jobs,” he said. “That’s the narrative they were fed by Republicans.”

My third cowboy hat Latino, Manny Rutinel, was a pretty conventional progressive in the Colorado legislature, but he moved decidedly toward the center — notably, again, on energy issues — en route to flipping a Trump seat.

It’s now been a thousand years since anyone has heard the term Latinx. But I think a really important question as Democrats try to hold on to the Hispanic votes they regained is whether they’re going to let this story be told by guys like Gallego and Gonzalez and Garcia who are in touch with their voters or revert to the Latinx mindset.

Who flipped Texas?

To give a pointed, Texas-specific example, Congressional Progressive Caucus leader Greg Casar is also Hispanic. When the Texas state legislature gerrymandered the map, he was stuck in a strongly red district. His response was to muscle Lloyd Doggett out of a safe seat in Austin, from which vantage point he’s been lecturing everyone on what Democrats need to do to win.

The seat he skedaddled out of is the one that Johnny Garcia just won.

Notably, while Casar held a couple of big get-out-the-vote events this fall with Bernie Sanders, these were not events that Gina Hinojosa or James Talarico attended. Talarico, of course, is not Hispanic (he’s not even Italian), but he did run in close partnership with the Hispanic mods, a partnership that included the Latino Victory Fund doing joint Spanish-language Talarico/Pulido ads full of trilled Rs.

Chuck Rocha, who worked on all these Texas races, specifically confirms in a great op-ed that while Latino voters have a diverse range of views, the key to winning Latino swing voters is specifically “running politically moderate and somewhat culturally conservative candidates in heavily Latino districts that are rural or exurban.” He said that he’s from Texas and “in many parts of my home state, border security (done the right way), oil workers, cowboy hats, and big ol’ pickup trucks dominate.”

And he’s exactly right.

I’ve been with my father-in-law to the rodeo in Junction, Texas, and the Latinos in the crowd have more in common culturally with the white people of rural Texas than they do with my neighbors in D.C.

What makes this group of culturally conservative voters much more winnable than rural whites is, of course, that the Republican Party contains a thriving wing of white racists and Hispanics don’t like that.

Whether it’s Bo French panicking about Indian American football fans or Brett Kavanaugh giving the green light to racial profiling as an immigration enforcement method, there are some big non-economic beefs between non-white Americans and the conservative movement.

But that doesn’t mean this electorate wants 100-proof intersectional progressive politics.

Hinojosa is a progressive by Texas standards, which I think mostly comes down to her being a close ally of the teachers’ unions in the state legislature. But as governor, she’s not going to ban oil and gas extraction. She did this “Pronouns” ad to distance herself from progressive cultural politics. It remains to be seen how she’ll navigate these issues in practice, but she appears to have the same tacit understanding as Rocha and Pulido and Garcia and Gonzalez and Cuellar.

A big question in my mind is whether this new crop of culturally moderate Latino elected officials will do what Gallego did after 2020 and push the message out overtly so they can influence party-wide strategy rather than allowing their victories to breed complacency.

When immigration is personal

The biggest thing here is immigration.

The idea that originally sent Democrats over the cliff was the belief that taking left-wing stands on immigration would be so overwhelmingly popular with Hispanics that it would give them latitude to go maximally left on everything else, too.

Wisdom on the topic of immigration starts with understanding what the major immigration issue was prior to 2016 and how the nature of the issue changed.

Previously, a lot of Mexican American U.S. citizens had family members, friends, or acquaintances who were illegal immigrants, most of whom arrived in the late 1980s or 1990s. Those people were interested in immigration reforms that would directly help people they knew and cared about. They also worried about being personally caught up in immigration raids or dragnets or being subject to racial profiling. There was also an anti-immigration discourse that cast the presence of Hispanic people in the United States as a threat to the country, which naturally Hispanic citizens didn’t like or agree with.

But a shift happened in Trump’s first term and in Biden’s term, when the immigration issue came to be primarily about new arrivals — many of whom were not Mexican — making asylum claims.

To both the xenophobic and the kinds of people who use terms like Latinx or BIPOC, these are continuous issues. But from the standpoint of many Latino citizens, they’re totally different.

Many Latino citizens found it jarring to see not only a chaotic situation at the border but also a Democratic Party that was pivoting away from talking about assistance for mixed-status families and toward helping new arrivals from Haiti. It also appeared that many arriving through asylum or executive parole channels were receiving better treatment than the long-resident illegal workers Obama had pledged to help.

Then after 2024 Trump came back into office with a mandate to secure the border, and he not only clamped down on asylum but also initiated draconian interior enforcement, complete with the racial profiling and other things Latinos feared from pre-2016 restrictionists.

You could say, “well you guys should have known what you were getting,” but the fact is Latinos voted for Hillary Clinton in massive numbers in 2016 precisely because they feared mass deportations and Trump won anyway and then didn’t do it. So I think it was semi-reasonable of voters to assume his 2024 pledges were also bluster. They weren’t, though, and that helped set the stage for the backlash.

But it’s critical not to overstate this: Exit polls of Hispanic voters this year showed immigration as a much lower priority than the economy and also revealed that the minority of Hispanics focused on immigration were largely Republicans.

The distinction between “Latinos were mad at Trump because of ICE” and “Latinos were mad at Trump because of the economy” is important because it has implications for other policy areas. If you’re looking at a primarily ICE-driven backlash, you can address ICE abuses and then let the Sierra Club wild out on energy policy. But what we’re actually looking at is an economy-driven backlash. You still should address ICE abuses because ICE abuses are morally wrong. But you also have to actually deliver on the economic commitment, and that means consistently addressing all kinds of energy and regulatory issues with an eye toward the cost of living.

This is an inconvenient truth for a coalition built around the idea of an immigration-focused Hispanic voter. But it’s important to know the truth.

We now have a good crop of moderate Hispanic politicians who clearly do know. But the 2028 cycle will be a nationalized presidential campaign, not a series of localized battles, and we’re going to need to raise the voices of those who know how to address these voters and get as much of the party as possible aligned with politics that works.

title: Republicans Are Losing the Populist Moment
content:
Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025 with a second chance to remake American politics.

Republicans Are Losing the Populist Moment

By Alicia Nieves • 9 Nov 2026 View in browser
View in browser
Scott Menchin
 
 

Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025 with a second chance to remake American politics. His victory was more than a repudiation of the Biden administration’s four years of economic and political dysfunction. It was a powerful vindication of a man and a populist message that much of the political establishment, including members of his own party, had spent nearly a decade trying to defeat.

For the second time, Trump achieved electoral victory by assembling an unlikely and diverse coalition of voters around a nationalist, anti-establishment agenda that challenged the prevailing political consensus on immigration, foreign policy, trade, and the progressive ideological capture of the administrative state and major institutions of American society. And this time, unlike in 2017, he entered Washington with an administration staffed by people who shared his vision and  with Republican majorities in both chambers of Congress. The opportunity was enormous. After nearly a decade of political combat, the populist electoral message finally had the opportunity to become a lasting governing framework.

In just twenty-two months, that opportunity evaporated.

The Republican Party’s sweeping defeat in the 2026 elections was not simply another instance of voters using the midterms, as they so often do, to punish the president’s party for missteps during his first two years in office. Nor is it adequate to explain the results solely through voter frustration over higher prices, the Iran war, or corruption. Those issues undoubtedly fractured Trump’s electoral coalition and damaged both his personal approval rating and the GOP’s broader standing with voters. But underlying these political liabilities was a more fundamental failure. Trump and the Republican establishment never forged the workable political relationship needed to transform the raucous populist insurgency that swept them into power into a coherent, pragmatic governing agenda.

Instead, Trump’s combative personality and the Republican establishment’s fundamental disinterest in championing populist priorities over the interests of its corporate stakeholders left the America First agenda largely confined to an increasingly isolated White House and the Republican Party without the direction and accountability of a shared national governing agenda. The result was that Trump’s most loyal and ideologically committed officials delivered on many of his promises, but frequently did so through confrontational and harsh tactics that alienated the American public.

Immigration enforcement was the prime example. Establishment Republicans stayed out of the work of building a sustainable deportation policy, stepping in only when enforcement threatened industries that depend on immigrant labor. In doing so, they ceded ground to the most hardline officials within the executive branch. Without a party willing to temper these excesses and build a durable program around mandatory E-Verify and real penalties for employers who hire illegal workers, the immigration agenda never evolved beyond Trumpism. 

“The same failure extended well beyond immigration.”

The same failure extended well beyond immigration. Turning the broader America First agenda into something more durable than a collection of executive actions required congressional Republicans to embrace the populist movement and put their own legislative stamp on its priorities. Instead, Republican leaders largely dragged their feet. Trump, for his part, often demanded loyalty and obedience rather than working with congressional Republicans to negotiate a legislative path forward. Republican leaders, meanwhile, showed little appetite for advancing his priorities, repeatedly citing Senate rules, the filibuster, and other institutional constraints as reasons for inaction. The fraught relationship between Trump and Senate Majority Leader John Thune illustrates this divide. Thune, a traditional Republican committed to preserving the Senate’s institutional authority, was frequently at odds with Trump’s populist priorities. Rather than forging a legislative partnership capable of reconciling their differences, the two operated according to competing visions of how Republicans should govern. Congressional Republicans seemed convinced that voters would not hold them responsible for the most unpopular aspects of the president’s executive actions, while still counting on the populist energy that brought him to power to carry them through the midterms. 

Democratic leaders, by contrast, embraced the populist messaging that has been emerging from their party’s activists and its socialist insurgent faction, rather than keeping it at arm’s length. Even as the press questioned the growing influence of DSA in the party, leaders like Hakeem Jeffries downplayed the party’s ideological divisions, emphasizing that Democrats across the political spectrum were united by voters’ economic frustrations and the need to address them. In the lead-up to the midterms, Democrats channeled the anger of their diverse constituencies, from suburban liberals to the socialist left, into a powerful electoral force. As Democrats mobilized their base, disillusioned voters who had supported Trump in 2024 either turned against Republicans or stayed home.

 

The political conditions that made Trump’s rise possible have not disappeared. If anything, the 2026 elections demonstrated that the populist revolt against the political establishment will likely remain an enduring feature of American politics. The question is whether the Republican Party can learn to operate in this environment during the final two years of Trump’s presidency and, more importantly, prepare to do so without him.

The answer will require more than finding a successor who can imitate Trump’s rhetoric and style. Republicans must confront their own unwillingness to embrace the populist priorities that brought their party to power and take responsibility for turning them into lasting policy. On immigration, that means putting their promises to restrict illegal immigration ahead of the interests of employers who depend on cheap foreign labor. On economic policy, it means being willing to challenge concentrated corporate power rather than simply defend the interests of the party’s business donors. And on foreign policy, it means defying the defense establishment when it seeks long, costly, and fruitless engagements. Confronting powerful constituencies within the Republican Party will be difficult, but convincing voters that Republicans are willing to deliver on their populist promises may be the party’s only viable path back to power.

For nearly a decade, Republicans could avoid making these difficult political choices. Trump’s unique political appeal repeatedly carried them back into power, allowing the party to postpone the hard work of embracing and delivering on populist promises of the election. That arrangement is coming to an end in two years. Nor can Republicans count on the Democrats’ newfound congressional power to become a political liability. Although Democrats swept both chambers of Congress, their lack of a veto-proof majority in the Senate means they will enter the next two years largely free from the expectation of delivering on their legislative promises. Instead, they will likely use their congressional power as a bully pulpit to attack Trump and sharpen the socialist-leaning populist message they hope will define the 2028 presidential election.

Congressional Republicans, meanwhile, face a far more challenging immediate predicament. The midterm results have left congressional Republican leadership in the difficult position of defending the remaining years of Trump’s presidency while preparing to make their own populist appeal to voters in 2028, without Trump. That means the congressional GOP must begin demonstrating commitment to populist issues now. It cannot continue treating Trump’s personality or institutional constraints as excuses for avoiding the difficult policy choices demanded by the movement that brought them back to power. 

“There is a silver lining for Republicans in the midterm results.”

There is a silver lining for Republicans in the midterm results. When voters were asked to decide on specific policies rather than candidates, many continued to favor traditionally conservative positions. Even as they delivered a sweeping defeat to Republican candidates, voters backed tougher criminal penalties and measures restricting noncitizen voting. Even deep-blue Colorado and Washington approved restrictions on transgender participation in female sports, while Colorado voters also backed limits on certain gender-related medical procedures for minors. And despite the blue wave, voters rejected numerous local proposals to raise taxes or issue new bonds, including in California, where a proposed tax on billionaires failed.

These results complicate the idea that the Democratic victory represented a wholesale rejection of conservative priorities. Voters may have rejected Trump’s governance, but they did not necessarily abandon their concerns about crime, cultural progressivism, and government spending. The Republican Party’s problem is not that its political priorities have necessarily become untenable. It is that Republicans have failed to convince voters they can be trusted to deliver on those priorities.

In two years, Trump’s presidency will end, but the populist era will not. And unless Republicans finally make the populist revolution their own, they may discover that the populist energy of our time has been channeled into a Democratic Party prepared to pursue changes that could permanently alter the country. The failures of governance that have defined Democratic strongholds like California and Illinois could become national policy, leaving the country poorer and more dysfunctional. Establishment Republicans may look forward to Trump’s departure, but the task before them is enormous. Their failure to meet it could prove far more consequential than another lost election.

The Cyberpunking of America (Fixed)

How the tech broligarchs tried to inflict their dystopian dreams on the rest of us

Paul Krugman
Nov 10
 
READ IN APP
 

Something went wrong with Substack, and this post seems to have gone out blank for many readers and isn’t on the app. Trying again.

Marketing note: I have a new ebook, Navigating the Chaos: Chronicles of Economic and Political Madness, which uses material from this Substack to construct a thematic narrative of the past two years and the issues that Democrats must now address to build an enduring progressive movement. Available from Amazon, Kobo, Bookshop, and Nook.

A few years ago my wife and I were driving in New Jersey, when she suddenly exclaimed, “What’s that incredibly ugly car?” It was her first sighting of a Cybertruck in the wild.

Now Tesla is finally pulling the plug on the vehicle, which one person quoted in a New York Times report describes as looking like a mechanical cockroach — an image one can’t unsee.

So what’s the big deal? Businesses make bum investments all the time. It’s true that the Cybertruck’s failure was spectacular — Dave Phillips, the author of the piece, who was clearly having fun, pointed out that it’s unfair to compare the Cybertruck to the Edsel, which had much bigger sales.

Beyond that, however, the Cybertruck was, as the article says, “a culture war on wheels.” The 7-year arc of the Cybertruck coincided with the transformation of Musk’s public image from that of a planet-friendly innovator to that of a racist, conspiracy-theorizing, African-children-killing oligarch. Once upon a time driving a Tesla was a way to signal that you were rich but environmentally conscious. But driving a Cybertruck became a signal of MAGA fealty.

Yet there is an even wider cultural context here. The Cybertruck was the physical embodiment of a dystopian ideology that has become dominant among billionaire tech bros — an ideology that draws heavily from cyberpunk novels and movies.

Wait, can fiction really have major political consequences? Of course it can. Fifteen years ago, you couldn’t really understand the behavior of many right-wing influencers until you realized how their thinking about the world was shaped by reading Ayn Rand’s Atlas Shrugged in their youth. Well, today’s tech billionaires grew up reading William Gibson and watching Blade Runner. But rather than taking cyberpunk’s visions of dystopia as cautionary tales, they saw them as manifestos. And with the great power that flows from great wealth, they have been trying to turn their adolescent dreams into reality.

For those unfamiliar with the term, cyberpunk is a subgenre of science fiction usually set in a not-too-distant future that combines advanced technology with social collapse. Predatory corporations and artificial intelligences rule the world — challenged only by morally ambiguous hackers, who live mainly in the virtual world of what Gibson called cyberspace — while homeless people sleep in piles of trash.

On immediate reflection, the cyberpunk influence on the tech broligarchs is obvious and overwhelming. For example, Elon Musk wasn’t trying to design a mechanical cockroach; he was clearly trying to build a car that looked like the vehicles in Blade Runner. Mark Zuckerberg wasted $80 billion — 40 times what Musk wasted on the Cybertruck — trying to sell the world on his Metaverse, a virtual space modeled on Gibson’s cyberspace. He even changed the name of his company to promote the doomed venture. Should we be surprised that Zuckerberg’s wild spending spree on AI is running into serious headwinds and that even the WSJ believes that Meta is doubling down on loss-making AI bets?

Furthermore, the cyberpunk influence on tech bros goes beyond bad investments. It’s also crucial for understanding the seemingly bizarre public relations strategy of the AI frontier labs: “Our technology will lead either to mass unemployment or to the extinction of the human race. Now, invest in our IPO.” To some extent this is a way of hyping the potential of what they are selling. But it also, I believe, reflects the mindset of middle-aged guys who grew up on cyberpunk and believe that it truly predicts our inevitable future.

Crucially, while you or I might read Neuromancer or watch Blade Runner and shudder at their visions of the future, billionaire tech bros surely picture themselves living in that future not as unemployed and homeless, but as edgelords ruling the world. Technological dystopia may sound like a nightmare to most of us, but for the broligarchs — despite their occasional expressions of concern and mumbling about Universal Basic Income — it’s basically a dream, which they are trying to use their financial and political power to make come true.

But the public isn’t buying it — literally in the case of Cybertrucks and the Metaverse, figuratively in the form of overwhelming voter opposition to data centers and AI in general.

So, will public opposition be enough to stop the cyberpunking of America? Stay tuned.

Bernie Sanders did not invent populist rhetoric

All Democrats can (and do) have a little class warfare as a treat.

Matthew Yglesias
Nov 10
 
READ IN APP
 

A lot of the Democratic candidates who did well last week say things about the political economy of the United States that sound like things Bernie Sanders might say.

Many on the left have pointed this out in their post-election commentary, and I agree that it’s factually accurate.

But the reason for this is that Bernie Sanders’s rhetoric about the need to unrig a rigged economic system, check the power of billionaire donors, and fight for the little guy rather than for special interests is not distinctive. It’s the kind of language Democrats have used throughout the existence of America’s oldest political party.

That’s why I find it strange that Sanders’s communications director, Jeremy Slevin, insists that pre-2016 presidential candidates did not engage in the kind of non-specific populist rhetoric that we heard from James Talarico. Slevin goes so far as to say that “anyone pretending otherwise is obviously full of shit.”

Jeremy Slevin
@jeremyslevin
Democrats did not sound like this before Bernie Sanders ran for president and anyone pretending otherwise is obviously full of shit
James Talarico @jamestalarico
A young man at our town hall asked if I was pushing class warfare. I told him: “We already have class warfare in this country — billionaires are waging war on the rest of us.”
4:09 PM · Nov 5, 2026 · 127K Views
96 Replies · 1.11K Reposts · 10.9K Likes

This is one of these things where I think a lot of people who are younger than me are genuinely confused about the history of American party politics. It is absolutely true that in the specific context of the 2016 presidential campaign, Hillary Clinton campaigned on some slightly bizarre anti-populist ideas about how breaking up banks won’t end racism, followed by putting forward an unusually character-focused general-election campaign against Donald Trump.

But that is what was unusual. Both the effort to win a primary largely by out-woking Sanders and the effort to win a general election with character attacks rather than issue appeals were idiosyncratic.

Ryan O’Donnell, who graduated from college 19 years ago, says that if I’d been working campaigns 20 years ago like him, I’d know that Bernie innovated specifically by “centering the idea that billionaires and corporations have rigged the system.”

Ryan O'Donnell
@ryanodonnellpa
some of us worked campaigns 20 years ago, and there's a real difference between promising to fight for the middle class and tax the wealthy vs candidates across the party centering the idea that billionaires + corporations have rigged the system and made your life more expensive
Matthew Yglesias @mattyglesias
I think a lot of young people are sincerely confused about this, but it's just not the case that Bernie Sanders invented the idea of campaigning on economic fairness themes — this is the common currency of ~all Democratic Party campaigns.
5:48 PM · Nov 5, 2026 · 15.4K Views
6 Replies · 30 Reposts · 232 Likes

Now, here I think the tragic reality is just that I am 45, and as a result, my political memory goes back further than 20 years.

But even within the O’Donnell window, I recall Barack Obama’s 2008 speech to the A.F.L.-C.I.O. in which he said that “for far too long, through both Democratic and Republican administrations, the system has been rigged against everyday Americans by the lobbyists that Wall Street uses to get its way.” Obama’s 2012 campaign against Mitt Romney was famously populist in its linking of Romney’s regressive tax agenda to his personal wealth and his work in private equity. I’ve often cited Obama’s second term as a break point in Democratic Party thinking, but the difference is that after Obama’s re-election (and especially after the 2014 midterms), Democrats moved left on social issues and energy.

Notably, Sanders, who used to be an immigration moderate and an opponent of gun control, also moved left on social issues.

On economics, though, while Bernie has clearly had a lot of influence within the party since his 2016 run, it’s just not true that his populist rhetorical flourishes are distinctive.

Distinctive Bernie ideas have gained ground

You can’t really talk about Bernie Sanders without talking about Medicare for All.

The concept of single-payer health care is, of course, not original to him. But it was Bernie, distinctively, who in the wake of the Affordable Care Act’s passage said “not good enough” and revived the whole idea of a push for big bang health-care reform.

What’s more, Bernie has literally redefined the meaning of Medicare for All as a slogan. When I started my career, Medicare for All was John Conyers’s H.R. 676, which was more literally modeled on how Canadian health care works — it featured a hard-capped global budget, for example — than Sanders’s version of Medicare for All. I would like to see a Medicare for All initiative that’s modeled on Australian Medicare rather than Canadian Medicare. But unlike Sanders, I do not wield a lot of influence over intra-caucus health-care politics.

Bernie also played an important secondary role to Elizabeth Warren in persuading the Biden administration to ditch a generation of consumer-focused antitrust policy in favor of a neo-Brandeisian approach that emphasizes corporate power and market concentration. While that hasn’t gotten nearly as much mass public attention as Medicare for All, it is, if anything, a clearer example of Sanders’s influence, because his people genuinely did run all the agencies.

Last but not least, Bernie has exerted a lot of influence over the specific idea of a wealth tax.

As one of the few people who actually read his book, I am aware that Thomas Piketty proposed a wealth tax in “Capital in the Twenty-First Century” as a revenue-neutral idea. When I interviewed him, he criticized property taxes as falling heavily on the middle class and for not properly distinguishing between a situation where you have $600,000 in housing wealth and a situation where you have a $600,000 home and $480,000 in mortgage debt. He wanted to replace property taxes with a progressive net-wealth tax to encourage a more equitable distribution of financial assets.

And this is what comes to mind when I think about distinctively Sandersite economic-policy ideas.

These are ideas that Democratic Party nominees have mostly not embraced, and they’re influential enough that it’s plausible the 2028 nominee will embrace one or all of them but also controversial enough that the 2028 nominee might embrace none of them.

This rhetorical stuff, on the other hand, is just how Democrats talk.

Democrats are always doing “populism”

The whole idea of the Democratic Party not only is but always has been that an electoral republic needs a mass political organization the purpose of which is to combat the concentrated power of financial capital. I am aware that the musical “Hamilton” is not a literal work of history, but part of its power is that Lin-Manuel Miranda does a good job of capturing these basic themes of American political conflict.

In the first cabinet rap battle, Thomas Jefferson calls out Alexander Hamilton’s financial schemes as dirty dealing by well-connected political insiders (“His plan would have the government assume states’ debts / Now, place your bets as to who that benefits / The very seat of government where Hamilton sits”) and celebrates productive labor over financial machinations (“In Virginia, we plant seeds in the ground / We create, you just wanna move our money around / This financial plan is an outrageous demand”).

Contemporary Democrats, of course, reject Jefferson as a slaver (Hamilton retorts, “your debts are paid ‘cause you don’t pay for labor”) and no longer hold Jefferson-Jackson Day fundraisers.

But the reason the dinners originally had that name is that Jefferson and Andrew Jackson were the founders of the party. Jackson, like Jefferson, was a slaver and extremely un-woke. But the economic-policy issue at the center of Jackson’s presidency was his effort to kill the Bank of the United States, which he and his allies characterized as a system-rigging hydra of economic and political influence that threatened the true spirit of democracy.

I don’t have time to do the entire political history of the United States, but let’s just yadda yadda yadda to the first presidential acceptance speech that I remember watching. Bill Clinton said:

I was raised to believe the American Dream was built on rewarding hard work. But we have seen the folks of Washington turn the American ethic on its head.

For too long those who play by the rules and keep the faith have gotten the shaft, and those who cut corners and cut deals have been rewarded.

People are working harder than ever, spending less time with their children, working nights and weekends at their jobs instead of going to P.T.A. and Little League or Scouts. And their incomes are still going down. Their taxes are still going up. And the costs of health care, housing, and education are going through the roof.

Meanwhile, more and more of our best people are falling into poverty even though they work 40 hours a week. Our people are pleading for change, but government is in the way. It has been hijacked by privileged private interests.

Clinton, of course, was not a distinctively populist Democrat on economics. What made him distinctive as a candidate was that he embraced the death penalty, criticized Jesse Jackson for hosting Sister Souljah, and otherwise had a moderate approach to culture. There’s a progressive critique of the substance of Clintonomics, but the way this critique worked — former Labor Secretary Robert Reich is its canonical voice — was that Clinton betrayed the promise of his populist campaign with his governance choices.

But then right after Clinton, the nominee was Al Gore, whose campaign slogan was “the people, not the powerful” and whose speeches were full of themes about a rigged system, such as “whether you’re starting out to raise your own family or getting ready to retire after a lifetime of hard work, so often powerful forces and powerful interests stand in your way and the odds seem stacked against you, even as you do what’s right for you and your family.” Next up was John Kerry, whose campaign, of course, talked a lot about national security but whose economic message was focused on the evils of Benedict Arnold C.E.O.s who were shipping your job overseas.

It’s true that Hillary Clinton largely eschewed these themes, but she’s the exception; the populist rhetorical mood is the connective tissue that holds the Democratic Party together across space and time.

Governing matters!

It’s a good idea for politicians to use good slogans and put good zingers in their speeches. But governing actually matters a lot.

I think it’s kind of weird that economic populist types who are way more left-wing than I am are excited about Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, largely on the basis of the way she blasted the data center industry even though she was explicitly disavowing any kind of income tax for Texas.

I am (famously) not that left-wing, and this is too right-wing for me. Texas is a fast-growing, high-inequality state with a high poverty rate and no Medicaid expansion. If they adopted the same 3 percent flat income tax as Louisiana (not exactly a hotbed of leftist politics), they could raise a ton of money while still having a tax competition advantage vis-a-vis Oklahoma and New Mexico, to say nothing of New York and California.

I very, very rarely write articles slamming Democrats for a lack of progressive ambition, but I think this is a real whiff on policy substance — though admittedly she’d have to run harder toward the center on culture to be able to pull it off.

Regardless, the point is that sane people don’t just care what politicians say — they care what they do.

Sanders doesn’t just criticize Obama for failing to invoke populist rhetorical tropes; he embraces a leftist conspiracy theory about Obama’s handling of the financial crisis. Progressives think it was wrong of Bill Clinton to embrace deficit reduction and at the time they were furious about free trade (today Abdul El-Sayed has emerged as a big tariff critic) and the now-forgotten 1996 Telecommunications Act. I am on the side of Obama and Clinton about that stuff, which is part of why I’m not enthusiastic about the idea of a bunch of left-factionalists running economic policy in 2029.

But this is not an argument about whether politicians should vow to fight for the little guy against the rigged system where special interests screw you over. Everyone thinks Democrats should run like that!

And beyond rhetoric, it is genuinely outrageous how Trump has prioritized the interests of his A.I. executive benefactors over the public interest in regulating this industry. That’s something every Democrat should say because the voters agree with it and because it’s true.

As a candidate for office, though, what’s distinctive about Talarico is that he took more moderate positions than establishment Democrats do on oil and gas and on transgender issues while criticizing the Biden record on immigration. He sounds like Bernie on economics in the sense that all Democrats sound broadly populist in their rhetoric and have for literally hundreds of years.

The Madness of Therapy Culture

By Ashley Frawley • 10 Nov 2026 View in browser
View in browser
Scott Menchin
 
 

All in Your Head: Illness as Identity, Trauma as Fashion, and the Desire to be Disordered
By Fredrik DeBoer
Simon & Schuster, 336 pages, $30

Traumatized: The New Politics of Public Suffering
By Catherine Liu
Verso, 192 pages, $24.95

More than a decade ago, I noticed that the walls at the university where I taught were plastered with posters designed to raise “awareness” about mental health. When students began to tell me that they were passionate about mental health, I began to suspect that the word was taking on new meanings. But it wasn’t until one passed me a leaflet in the foyer unhelpfully informing me that one in four people suffer from “mental health” that I understood what was happening. Somewhere along the way, the boundaries between mental health and mental illness had become blurred until the former meant the latter. 

Two new books, Fredrik deBoer’s All in Your Head and Catherine Liu’s Traumatized, draw attention to one of the strangest achievements of contemporary therapy culture. Even as psychological suffering has become more visible, it has become increasingly difficult to speak bluntly about its degrees, causes, and uneven spread. Everything becomes curiously melded together and flattened out. Hence, when the British royals set out some years ago to inform everyone that “we all have mental health,” no one should have mistaken what that meant. Mental health is a continuum or spectrum, we are often told, and somewhere along it sit students with exam stress and people convinced their neighbors are poisoning their water. Everyone is in some sense ill.

Well, not everyone. Even as we are all being told we belong somewhere on the “mental health” spectrum, the World Health Organization is calling for an end to “coercive practices in mental health.” The UN Disability Committee is urging states to pursue “the abolition of substitute decision-making regimes” in favor of “supported” alternatives for those we once called “mentally ill,” but who are now variously “people with mental health conditions” or “psychosocial disabilities.” These are people whose suffering often expressly means they are unable to make decisions for themselves. The rest of us are presumed fragile, but the psychotic is increasingly presumed sovereign. As deBoer writes, it has become “our transcendent obligation to pretend that a man in the grip of psychosis [is] somehow still free.”

DeBoer and Liu both show that attempts to flatten out the experience of suffering, disability, and mental illness fail to accomplish their purported aims, such as “destigmatizing” and expanding access to care. This is because reality, whether in the form of the severity of impairment or of social class, eventually asserts itself, with the consequences falling on those least able to bear them. 

For all the high-level talk of the need for mentally ill people to speak for themselves, it is rarely the severely ill or disabled doing the speaking. DeBoer describes a process whereby the relatively privileged claim conditions once associated with severe impairment, what he calls the “gentrification of disability.” The most egregious example is the expansion of the label of autism from those who will never speak or care for themselves to people who incorporate their diagnosis into a successful professional identity. But it is the latter, deBoer says, who now set the parameters of the debate. The most profoundly affected “have no ability to engage in debates that have profound consequences for them,” he writes, while those “who most actively engage in the effort to define autism and how society should accommodate it are overwhelmingly among the educated professional class and need society’s accommodation the least.” The “autism community” rejects gradations of disability on the grounds that they create a hierarchy, but the hierarchy asserts itself all the same when a mother finds that her adult son who needs round-the-clock care has nowhere to go.

In Traumatized, Liu identifies a parallel “gentrification of suffering,” in which a universalized language of trauma obscures the material and historical circumstances in which people suffer. She points to Oprah Winfrey’s The Me You Can’t See (2021), an Apple TV series that renders the pain of someone like Lady Gaga in the same language as a Syrian boy who lost his home and brother to war. What’s more, war and its causes recede into the background, treated almost like “a natural disaster the young men must endure.” Unpacking the language of trauma, Liu shows how we are invited to wallow in pain as the great equalizer, and to see emotion as the thing that matters most. The good subject must learn to “leverage her suffering for progressive politics and fame and fortune,” which becomes a new kind of bootstrapping for the professional managerial age. 

“Compared to mental health, poverty is tough to deal with.”

Compared to mental health, poverty is tough to deal with, and unpleasant to look at. If you can separate it into these isolable parts (trauma, in Liu’s focus, but elsewhere “adverse childhood experiences,” “toxic stress,” “food insecurity,” and on and on), you can attend to each, and maybe the whole injustice will become so much more tolerable, like a bad piece of furniture that’s really not so bad with just the right throw.

Perhaps the most perverse element of the gentrification of mental illness is the tendency to treat insanity as a “sane response to an insane world.” DeBoer details the onset of his own mental illness, and his experience accords him the authority to acerbically denounce anyone who suggests that madness is a form of liberation. He describes a litany of horrors, including bipolar patients who stab their spouses and coprophagics who “consume their own excrement on public transit,” and asks: “Which of the described behaviors, exactly, constitutes a ‘sane response to an insane world’?”

This romantic viewpoint might seem fringe, but deBoer argues it has seeped into our society’s common sense, tracing much of its influence to the psychiatrist Thomas Szasz, whose The Myth of Mental Illness (1961) recast mental illness as mere “problems in living.” Offering a convincing critique of Szasz’s fundamentalist libertarianism, deBoer details how Szasz’s moral philosophy could only be maintained by a studious avoidance of the truly mentally ill. Of Rebecca Smith, a schizophrenic woman who froze to death on the streets after anti-psychiatry campaigners made involuntary commitment unduly onerous, Szasz wrote, “The sad truth is that Mrs. Smith was a person who did not take care of herself.” 

Liu takes down another sacred cow of anti-psychiatry, David Rosenhan’s 1973 study “On Being Sane in Insane Places,” in which pseudo-patients ostensibly fooled clinicians into admitting them to psychiatric hospitals. If psychiatrists couldn’t tell the difference between the sane and insane, it was claimed, the distinction must be arbitrary. Pointing to evidence that Rosenhan may have suppressed and misused data, she dismisses the study as fraudulent. But the exercise leads her to a different conclusion from deBoer’s: Psychiatry’s claim to be scientific was itself a product of politics, she thinks. For psychiatrist Robert Spitzer, Rosenhan’s study was like “manna from heaven.” Trying to secure “psychiatry’s reputation as an empirical science,” he used it to push the discipline toward a checklist model of disorder much to the “detriment of personal or intrapsychic origins of mental illness.” Life, class, and context were all collapsed into a neat “chemistry of psychic disorder.”

While Liu worries about too much medicalization, deBoer worries that anti-psychiatry and destigmatization campaigns have produced too little where it really counts. He points to Joyce Brown, a schizophrenic woman who became a cause célèbre in the debate over involuntary psychiatric commitment in the ’80s, recounting how after an address at Harvard, she simply ended up back on the streets, on drugs, and exploited. In real life, deBoer concludes, “Joyce Brown acted the way a chronic schizophrenic acts.” 

Campaigners have slipped from the claim “mentally ill people are not bad” to the idea that mental illness itself isn’t bad. When a psychotic person makes antisemitic remarks, for instance, social media users are quick to retort that “mental illness doesn’t do that.” But it does, or society would not grant (in certain narrow circumstances at least) the mentally ill one of their most important protections, the exemption from criminal responsibility. That exemption, I might add, protects our legal and democratic systems too, since to say some people lack capacity implies that most of us have it.

But therapy culture has a tendency to let incapacity seep into the crevices of everyday life, and nowhere is this clearer than in Liu’s treatment of child protection. She shows how spectacular cases of abuse increasingly displaced attention from the ordinary circumstances of poverty. When Sen. Walter J. Mondale introduced the Child Abuse Prevention and Treatment Act in the mid-’70s, abuse was deliberately popularized as “a problem knowing no barriers of class, race or culture.” Child abuse became not a systemic issue, but a kind of illness. Professional class reformers could therefore carry on attending to injuries at a distance from more contentious social and economic questions. 

I would take Liu’s conclusion further. Most children in the American foster care system, for instance, are not there because of serious abuse, but rather because of “neglect,” a category that routinely conflates poverty with poor parenting. When parents see their economic circumstances improve, their involvement with child protective services in turn tends to fall. So often is poverty confused with neglect that a bill currently sits before Congress expressly aimed at amending Social Security to “ensure that child protective services systems do not permit the separation of children from parents solely on the basis of poverty.”

What is more, removing class from ideals of parenting not only obscures poverty, it also opens the door to policing families on the basis of therapeutic middle-class ideals. More than once, in debates over spanking, I have pointed out that corporal punishment remains more common in poor and working class families, only to be told that this fact itself is “offensive.” A form of discipline practiced by most of humanity is recast as a kind of brain damage, which offers moreover, a convenient explanation of poverty itself. If poverty is passed down through bad parenting, the remedy lies in simply adopting expert-approved methods, a fix now prescribed even for global underdevelopment. And so criminalization campaigns continue apace, oblivious to the disproportionate numbers of poor and working-class families who will see stressful investigations added to their plate.

 

DeBoer is most convincing on the need for modern humane institutionalization, and sometimes, involuntary commitment, practices that have been attacked in the name of liberation. But he is less so when he hopes overdiagnosis can be checked by a more assertive psychiatry, policing diagnoses as matters of “objective scientific fact.” Watching the spread of dissociative identity disorder (DID) on TikTok, he is dismissive of young women’s “fake” performances of the diagnosis and laments that clinicians who question them are shouted down. Anyone familiar with the issue will be shouting at the page at this point; this was not the first such wave.

Liu offers what deBoer omits. DID, then called multiple personality disorder, first became a fad in the ’80s and ’90s, spurred on, as Liu describes, by the talk show circuit which acted like an “infectious disease vector, where spectators and professionals could learn about the symptoms and incorporate them into their psychological and professional repertoires.” It was not just teenaged girls, but professionals themselves, who were beguiled by the diagnosis and did much to encourage others to see their pain through its prism. Rubber-stamping self-diagnoses is indeed a problem, but restoring professional authority is an incomplete remedy for fads that professionals have often helped to spread.

“Their belief in their own wellness itself a symptom.”

What neither book quite accounts for is why the current mental-health paradigm persists when it so often fails. Part of the answer lies in what Liu refers to as trauma culture’s “survivor messianism,” in which suffering confers moral authority—the counterpart to deBoer’s liberated madman. But then, what of the well? From this perspective, it is easy to see how the purported normals are complicit, their belief in their own wellness itself a symptom. As a student once summed it up to me: “It’s almost like, if there’s nothing wrong with you…what’s wrong with you?” The outsider has come to be seen as an already liberated subject, whereas the “normal” are held responsible for perpetuating society’s oppressive norms.

As material explanations fall away, ordinary behavior becomes the site of intervention, and confessing your vulnerability becomes a way of signaling that you are one of the good ones. The bad subject still labors under the illusion of autonomy, still perilously choosing to smack their kids’ bottoms while keeping their “trauma” to themselves. Those who still stubbornly believe they can manage their own lives are the last frontier. Therapy culture can accommodate almost anything as madness, except the truly mad and those who insist they are well.
